Preface

The wisdom lineage in this world

In the 25-year course for a geshe, or master of Buddhism, in the ancient Tibetan tradition, the study of emptiness according to the highest school of all comes only after twelve years of dedicated study and public debating.

The study is based of course upon the great ancient teachings on emptiness granted by Lord Buddha in such works as the Diamond Cutter Sutra, and the Heart Sutra.  The concept though is so difficult and easily misunderstood that the fledgling geshe quickly pivots to the classic shastras or medieval commentaries upon the topic.

The earliest one of these, considered the greatest of the great, is the poetic presentation of Arya Nagarjuna entitled Wisdom, in 27 succinct chapters.  This was written around 200ad; and then some four centuries later, an extraordinary explanation of the content of Wisdom was written by the brilliant Master Chandrakirti, who entitled his work Entering the Middle Way.

Over the next 800 years, dozens of Sanskrit classics were composed in Asia to clarify these two works.  Then came the present volume, entitled The Illumination of the True Thought, composed by the incomparable Tibetan savant Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419).

As you can see, the English translation of this work comprises some two thousand pages.  Je Tsongkapa leaves no philosophical stone unturned, and pushes us to confront every possible angle in his investigation.  In a way, it takes some amount of courage and intellectual endurance to glean his ideas in their entirety.

Faced—after more than a decade of labor—with the task of composing this preface to the finally finished translation, I began to collect notes for a sort of standard scholarly survey of the contents of this great classic.


A trip to the Tower

In the midst of this process, I was asked to deliver a series of lectures to an audience of about a thousand people in Xi’an, the ancient capital of the golden era of China: the Tang Dynasty.  This dynasty is dated 618-907ad, and even in its early years the population of the capital (known in those days as Chang’an) was about a hundred times larger than London of the same period.

The topic of my presentation was to be an exploration of what in the classics is known as the “path of seeing,” or a person’s first direct contact with ultimate reality: emptiness.  During these talks, I had the honor of visiting the Great Wild Goose Pagoda (seen here), where around 650ad the great master Xuanzang (602-664ad) began his massive labor of translating a great number of the 650 Buddhist classics he had collected during his 17-year journey to the many kingdoms of India and its environs.

Influenced I feel by this inspiration, I made a decision not to deliver a scholarly presentation upon emptiness, but rather to recount the details of my own direct experience of it.

This event happened on July 28, 1975, when I was 22 years old.  The direct perception of emptiness by an individual on this planet, since the time of Lord Buddha, has occurred perhaps only once in every few hundred years.  When I did see it, I instinctively felt that I should not share the experience with anyone—perhaps because the karma of not believing a person who has had the direct perception of emptiness is so extremely serious; and, after all, a person who has not had the experience themselves would find it very difficult, if not impossible, to confirm the truth of my claim.

I am now 73 years of age, and suffer from stage four kidney disease, which may well require a kidney transplant.  It is possible that I don’t have a great deal of time left in this world.  When I stood up to speak to the audience in Xi’an last week, I made a personal decision that I would try to share in careful detail my direct experience of emptiness, to inspire those who know me and would trust my description; and also to leave a record as complete as I could, of what a person can expect with this direct experience—plus my very best tips that would help a normal person reach it.

It is my personal belief that if any normal person devotes some serious time to studying the authentic classics on the topic of emptiness—such as the present translation—and also follows carefully the suggestions I make here, then they have a good chance of reaching this very rare goal within this one brief lifetime.



Organizing the experience:
the four arya truths, and the 16 aspects

The Buddha taught in this world for over four decades after his enlightenment; and the very first teaching he ever gave was in fact a description of how to see emptiness directly, by using what we call the “four arya truths” or “four higher truths.”  Someone who has been through the actual experience of seeing emptiness directly can say—from personal experience—that these four are a perfect framework for describing the experience, and helping others to reach it.

First of all we should say something about the name here: the “four arya truths.”  This is a translation of the original Sanskrit phrase, chatur arya satyani (technical spelling catur ārya satyāni).  Chatur here means four, and we see it in certain English words derived from the Sanskrit, such as quart.

Arya literally means elevated, since when we do manage to see emptiness directly we step up to a higher level of evolution—just about the mental difference between a prehistoric amoeba and Albert Einstein.  In the ancient literature, a person who has managed to reach the direct perception of emptiness is themselves referred to as an arya, or a “higher” form of life.

Satyani is the plural for the word “truth,” or “reality.”  It’s ultimately related to the English word is.

During the early years when the Buddhist classics were first being translated into English, this expression was mis-translated as “four noble truths,” and unfortunately that phrase has stuck.  Referring to the four rather as “arya” truths or “higher” truths is crucial, since it is this higher reality which frees us from all pain and death in this life.
	
It’s important to specify what makes a person “higher” once they have seen emptiness directly.  To really appreciate this, we need to recognize two facts about our life that are undeniable, but which we tend to hide from.

First of all, the fundamental nature of our normal human life is pain.  We may be born into an affluent country; we may be born into a poor country.  In the latter case, we suffer throughout our life from trouble like insufficient food and housing.  But even in the former case, we live through our short, alloted span of years and gradually—inevitably—become old and decrepit, finally dying and losing all and everyone dear to us.  It’s simply hopeless stubbornness to insist that this is not the way all normal life must go.

When we touch emptiness—when we become an arya—this process begins to reverse itself.  It’s as if a single cell of cancer has insinuated itself into the very core of our body, and now it will spread and ruin our entire life.  Except that—in the case of an arya—we can say that seeing emptiness directly inserts a single cell of eternal diamond life into the center of us: a cell that will and must spread until we finally transform into deathless creatures of eternal joy (along with all our loved ones).

And so suffering is the first undeniable truth about our life, and death is the second.  That death with the loss of everything and everyone dear to us, including our own self.  But the truth of death includes a second half to it that only a fool would deny.

When you throw a pair of dice, there are only so many numbers that can come up.  Each of the faces of the dice represents a different number, from 1 to 6.  And so there are only 11 different combinations that can ever come up from throwing two such dice down at the same time: the total numbers 2 to 12.

There is a 1 in 11 chance that any particular number will come up: if you throw the dice a hundred times, then on average for example the number 12 will come up nine times: 9% of the time.  Barring anything completely weird, there is no chance that you will never get a 12, especially if you throw the dice a billion or a trillion times.  You get the picture.

The undeniable truth then is that if we have been born into life once, we can be born into life a second time, or a billionth time.  You can say that you don’t believe this—you can say that your people or your country doesn’t believe this—but then you are just being stubborn, or prejudiced.  Just rationally—just with regard to raw truth—it’s impossible that coming into a life like this and going through it and then crashing down into hopeless pain & death can’t repeat itself.

We came here once, so we have to come here again.  Only an arya can stop this process, and re-direct it to an eternal life of total joy, along with all our loved ones.

We need to touch emptiness.


The 16 moments

Traditionally, over the last 25 centuries of the wisdom tradition in the Eastern part of our world, these four facts of life—the Four Higher Truths—have been divided into 16 different aspects: four for each truth.

These sixteen divisions of course give us a deeper understanding of the four truths that they relate to.  Over the millennia, the divisions have been referred to with different names.

One such name, in the Tibetan, is nampa (technical spelling rnam-pa).  The connotation here is of 16 “types” or “aspects.”  We also see, in this context, kechikma (spelt skad-cig-ma), which means “instant in time.”  There is, thus, one tradition that the direct perception of emptiness passes in 15 or 16 milliseconds of time, and that during each millisecond we perceive—directly—another aspect or feature of the four truths.

There is a third tradition—found for example in the sutra by Lord Buddha himself entitled Awarenesses of Pure Reality (Saddharma Smirtyupasthana) which refers to the sixteen as “examinations” of reality.

During my own direct perception of emptiness—some 50 years before this writing—I passed through a number of distinct, separate, extraordinary and direct understandings immediately after the direct contact with emptiness itself.  Each understanding had a distinct beginning and end, rising and subsiding like a separate ocean wave at the seashore.

In the hours after direct contact with emptiness, these understandings took on average a few minutes of time.  Thus I would follow the higher schools of historical Buddhism on this point, and would not describe these understandings as something that came and went in a single millisecond each.

Rather, I would refer to them as “moments of understanding” rather than “aspects” or “milliseconds”; in the sense that a “moment” of warmth with a loved one may pass in a minute or so, or continue on even to an hour, albeit unmarked.


The logic of the four

Traditionally, in Buddhist scripture, the Four Truths are listed in two different orders.  

The more common order is in fact succinctly described by the author of our Illumination of the True Thought, which you should understand is the greatest and most thorough presentation on emptiness ever written in history.  It incorporates the few mightiest descriptions of emptiness ever written on this planet to date—ranging from the Heart Sutra (Lord Buddha, 500bc); to the Wisdom of Arya Nagarjuna (c. 200ad); to Master Chandrakirti’s present Entering the Middle Way (c. 625ad); to the incomparable Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life (Master Shantideva, c. 750ad).

The incomparable Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419) then gives one version of the order of the Four Truths as follows:

Now why are the higher truths described as exactly four in number?  The components to be taken up or left off of by those of understanding always belong to one of two categories: the dark side, or the side of light.  And each of these two has two further divisions: cause, and effect.

That is, the first truth is a result from the dark side of life: the arya truth of suffering.  The second truth is its cause, also on the dark side: what we call the arya truth of the source of suffering.

The third truth then is where we want to go: the arya truth of the end of suffering.  And then the fourth arya truth is the path to that stopping of pain.

Sometimes, to get a deeper appreciation, the four truths are listed cause-effect/cause-effect.  Then we get the causes of pain; the fact of pain; the causes of freedom; and finally freedom itself.


The “truth” is the thing itself

It’s very important by the way to appreciate the four truths are not statements of fact: the first truth for example is not the concept or statement that “life is suffering.”

Rather, each of the truths is meant to be taken as the direct experience of it: when we cut our finger in the kitchen, that pain itself is the arya “truth” or reality of suffering.  When we pause in the process of getting upset at someone who has just said something unkind to us—because we understand that they are actually proceeding from seeds in our mind, planted there when we ourselves were unkind to someone else at some earlier—that pause itself is the arya truth of the end of pain.


The logic of the 16

The logic behind the order of the four moments inside of each of the four truths is not so clear.  To start with, there is even a question of whether there are four, or three, moments inside each one.

That is, the name of each one of the four higher truths is repeated inside the four moments contained by each—so that it seems that the moments or aspects of the four might even total no more than 12, and not 16.

To get an appreciation of this problem, let’s list the 16 in their traditional order.  That same sutra by Lord Buddha himself, Awarenesses of Pure Reality, is a typical source:

	A. Moments of the truth of suffering
		[1] Impermanence
		[2] Suffering*
		[3] Emptiness
		[4] No self-nature

	B. Moments of the truth of the source of suffering
		[5] Source*
		[6] Cause
		[7] Spring
		[8] Factor

	C. Moments of the truth of the end of suffering
		[9] End*
		[10] Peace
		[11] Beauty
		[12] Escape

	D. Moments of the truth of the path to the end of suffering
		[13] Path*
		[14] Logic
		[15] Means
		[16] Method

Already we can see that where the general name of the truth is repeated as one of each one’s four aspects or moments (which we’ve marked here with an asterisk), it’s not necessarily even the first of the four listed—which is really confusing if they are meant to re-indicate the name of the group.

There is one traditional source which advocates for taking them this way, and that is A Massive Commentary to the Sutra entitled “Obliterating the Galaxy,” written in medieval India by a master named Karmavajra (a back-translation of the Tibetan, Las kyi rdo-rje).  We do though see a number of older sources, including our Awarenesses of Pure Reality, which seems to treat the four moments as equally-weighted sub-categories for each of the four truths.

Here is how that sutra Awarenesses of Pure Reality describes the difference between the 16 moments:

		[1] Impermanence,
			because it involves causes and factors
			that make it happen

		[2] Suffering,
			because it it really hurts

		[3] Emptiness,
			because it is devoid of any individual

		[4] No self-nature,
			because it is devoid of any engaging
			of its own accord

		[5] Source,
			because it engages through factors

		[6] Cause,
			because it matches its result

		[7] Spring,
			because it works through all kinds
			of instigations

		[8] Factor,
			because of its absolute accordance
			with its results

		[9] End,
			because of the total elimination
			of the negative emotions			

		[10] Peace,
			because we have absolutely
			extinguished the fire of
			everything involved with 
			negative emotions

		[11] Beauty,
			because it is the single most 
			important thing in the world

		[12] Escape,
			because it is leaving the 
			cycle of pain forever

		[13] Path,
			because it is the one thing
			that allows us to achieve
			enlightenment and freedom
			
		[14] Logic,
			because it is completely
			beyond any error

		[15] Means,
			because all higher beings
			reside in it, always

		[16] Method,
			because it puts an absolute end
			to everything involved with
			negative emotions, here in the
			cycle of pain.

It’s important to note that there is no more detailed or specific description of those 16 parts of the four higher truths—in all 25 centuries of Buddhist scripture from the time of the Buddha up to the present day—than we see here.

Since the Sanskrit language is the foundation for the English language, some of our readers may benefit from the Sanskrit equivalents of the names of the 16 moments.  Here they are, along with the Tibetan counterpart—important since there are so many relevant Tibetan classics from the past 600 years or so.  The pronunciation here of both is simplified to the closest English sounds.

	A. Moments of the truth of suffering (duhkha, duk-ngel)
		[1] Impermanence (anitya, mitakpa)
		[2] Suffering (duhkha, duk-ngel)
		[3] Emptiness (shunya, tongpa)
		[4] No self-nature (anatma, dakmey)

	B. Moments of the truth of the source of suffering (samudaya, kunjung)
		[5] Source (samudaya, kunjung)
		[6] Cause (hetu, gyu)
		[7] Spring (prabhava, rab tu kyewa)
		[8] Factor (pratyaya, kyen)

	C. Moments of the truth of the end of suffering (nirodha, gokpa)
		[9] End (nirodha, gokpa)
		[10] Peace (shanta, shiwa)
		[11] Beauty (pranita, gyanompa)
		[12] Escape (nihsarana, ngepar jungwa)

	D. Moments of the truth of the path to the end of suffering (marga, lam)
		[13] Path (marga, lam)
		[14] Logic (nyaya, rikpa)
		[15] Means (pratipatti, druppa)
		[16] Method (nairyanika, ngepar jinpa)


Our relationship to the four

A famous topic from the great books is: What should our relationship to each of these four higher truths be?  The classic answer to this question is found in The Higher Line, a famed work by the future Buddha, Maitreya, dictating to the great Arya Asanga around 350ad:

An illness is something that you should come to realize that you have.  The cause of the illness is something you should rid yourself of.  Happy health then is what we need to attain; and the medicine to reach it is something we need to employ.

Just so, the truth of suffering is what we should come to realize that we have.  The truth of the cause of this suffering is what we should rid ourselves of.  The truth of the end of suffering is something we need to meet up with; and the truth of the path to this end is what we need to employ.

Seeing emptiness directly is the single method that helps us reach these proper relationships to the four truths.  And when we reach this proper relationship, then we are free of all present and future pain.  The matchless Arya Nagarjuna says it this way, in his String of Jewels, the second letter to the King:

	If we are truly able
	To acquaint ourselves
	With the sixteen aspects—

	With the impermanence
	And so forth which are
	The point of the four truths—

	Then we are able
	To eliminate all of our
	Negative emotions,

	Along with all the
	Deep seeds for these.

	Clouds in the sky disappear;
	Ice on the lake melts away;
	The candle dies out—

	And just so our mind
	Is completely freed.

Although our ideal relationship to the four truths in general is therefore quite clear, what we realize by this point in our conversation is that in the entire recorded history of Buddhism we never get a description of just what the 16 divisions of these truths would look like, in a real life.  And that means that we never really learn what’s supposed to happen during the direct perception of emptiness, which is universally described as the most important moment in the entire life of a Buddhist.

So what I propose to do here next is to draw a correlation between each of the famous 16 moments relating to the direct perception of emptiness, and my own unique experiences during that time.  In the five decades since that event, I cannot say that I have personally met another person who has seen emptiness directly—although of course they may be living somewhere in the world where I wouldn’t have had contact with them.  I can say though that if there were another such person alive today, they would be engaged in many of the same activities as I have been; for example in the diamond trade, or the preservation & translation of the classics of Buddhism.

Which is to say, it may very well be the case that in this world there is no one else alive to draw the connections I will propose in the following.  Perhaps, in time, there will come someone who could do it more accurately; but until then it is certainly crucial, I believe, that I give it my best try.  At the very least, these thoughts will help plant the necessary seeds within my readers that would help them see emptiness directly themselves.


The 16 are spread out

One idea that has become clear to me in the decades since I “touched the diamond world” is that the 16 moments in real life are not neatly organized under the four truths in the way that scripture would suggest.  We see in the surviving original teachings of Lord Buddha (where there are over 600 references to the four truths) that even the idea of four moments for each of the four truths may simply have been promoted for convenience, for symmetry: there are earlier references for example to more than four, with some of the truths.

This implies that actually drawing a correlation between the theory and the actual experience may not be as neat as we would expect; and this is indeed my personal experience.  Which is to say, in real time we may have to “jump around” to find all 16 of the actual experiences with an individual who has actually had them.

One of the first things we realize, with the actual experience, is that although many of the 16 actual experiences do indeed occur in the aftermath of the direct perception of emptiness, it is not the case that all of them do.  I personally believe that an “active” count of the 16, in my case, began some six months prior to the direct perception; with even some of those moments resulting from lifetimes of previous experience.  I can add though that all of the 16 had occurred, in some form, by the end of the day on what I call “Diamond Day”—the day of my direct perception of emptiness; that day in July 1975.


The seven groups

Looking back, I can see that my own direct experience of emptiness can be organized into seven different, specific time periods; and I think that if I make my presentation using them, it will help you plant the seeds for the same experience, and in the meantime get a more accurate understanding of the 16 special moments.  Here is a list of those seven groups of experiences:

	Group 1
	Past life influences

	Group 2
	Preparing for the diamond world

	Group 3
	The pot on the stove

	Group 4
	Touching the diamond

	Group 5
	The immediate aftermath

	Group 6
	Staying close to diamonds

	Group 7
	Passing it on, and the next 500 years
	

Group One:
Past life influences


The five baby tigers

Happily, there is an all-important precedent for the idea of seeking the roots of the direct perception of emptiness—we can call them “16 roots”—in an earlier lifetime.  The story begins in a time long past, with a prince by the name of Mahasattva: Magnificent Courage.

On a day quite typical for an ancient Indian royal, Prince Mahasattva is out with friends and family walking through the forest—oftentimes a reserve of the surrounding land set aside only for the enjoyment of the extended ruling family.

Mahasattva gets separated from the rest of the party, and his steps take him into a particularly thick and dark part of the forest.  Suddenly at his feet he sees a magnificent female tiger laying exhausted, near death from a lack of food & water.  At her teats hang five tiny tiger cubs—also on the edge of death—sucking where milk can no longer come.

The prince reflects only for a few moments before he sees what he must do: he quietly lies down next to the tigress, pushing close to her the warm scent of his own body, his meat.

But the beast is too far gone even to bite, to eat.  The Prince is perturbed, but thinks of a solution.  He rises and pulls a dead branch from a nearby tree, and gouges furrows across his chest and abdomen with it, and the blood gushes forth.

He lies down again, and happily the tigress is able to lap up the blood, and regain her strength.  Soon, she can consume the flesh as well—and then milk springs forth for her five babies.

And as he slips into death, the Prince makes one final prayer: “By eating my body, and drinking my blood, may you five children and your mother become my first disciples, when I reach my own enlightenment, as a Buddha, in future times.”

And then perhaps countless lifetimes later, it does come to be that the Prince is reborn as another prince: Siddhartha, the Buddha-to-be of our own world.  As we have heard, the Prince is carefully shielded from seeing pain or suffering, but in the end he does witness aging, illness, and death; and determines to leave the royal life in pursuit of a solution.

In the company of five forest meditators, he enters a period of extreme fasting and practice, torturing his body and mind.  Eventually he comes to the realization that these extremes are not helping him; and he undertakes a middle way of simplicity with care for his health.

Siddhartha thus in time reaches his own Buddhahood, sitting in meditation below a sacred tree in a place called Vajrasana—the “Seat of the Diamond”—and later known as Bodhgaya.  It is said that for seven weeks he stayed silent about his enlightenment, in the belief that no on would be able to understand his description of it, and how to reach it themselves.

But at the end of these weeks he finally decides to give teaching a try.  He seeks out his former group of five friends, who spot him approaching across an open field.

“Ah, here comes that slacker, Siddhartha!  The one who gave up on real spiritual practice!”

“Let’s ignore him!  Let’s pretend we don’t see him coming!  And especially let’s not show him any respect!”

They all agree, except that tradition says that one of them, their leader, by the name of Kaundinya, feels unsure about the plan.  And then suddenly the Buddha—now going by the name of Gautama, or “Head Bull of the Herd”—is standing in their midst.  And suddenly too they all feel absolutely compelled to pay him honor, preparing a cushion for him to sit on, helping to fold his outer robe.

But then again they do have a name for him, which is “Junior,” and they start using it in front of him.

“No, no,” he corrects them.  “Perhaps before I was Junior, but now I am something more.”  And he relates the story of his enlightenment, and The Five believe him.

 “Please teach us then, how we may reach the goal ourselves,” they beg.

The Buddha himself—and even this name means “The One Who Knows All Things”—must decide what is the one most powerful instruction, of all the thousands of teachings he will give over the rest of his life, to offer to his first disciples.

And that teaching was the four higher truths.  He repeated it three times through, for a total of twelve ideas (not to be confused with the 16 aspects).  The Group of Five—the first five disciples—were Kaundinya; Ashvajit; Bhadrika; Vaspa; and Mahanama.  It is said that, following the first time through the teaching of the four truths, Kaundinya (perhaps due to his reservations about “Junior”) achieves the direct perception of emptiness; and afterwards he is referred to by Lord Buddha as “Kaundinya, who understands everything.”  Then, as the truths are repeated, the other four reach emptiness directly as well.

The five first disciples were, of course, the five tiger cubs from the ancient past—who with that connection had planted the seeds to see emptiness directly.  Their mother the Tigress, by the way, was reborn as Maha Prajapati.  This is the stepmother of Prince Siddhartha, who raised him after his mother died not long after his birth—and eventually became the first Buddhist nun in this world.

We can see then the powerful effect of past-life experiences on reaching the goal of touching emptiness directly.  Let’s look at some of those that laid the groundwork for my own emptiness experience.


Dancing in the church

During the day of my direct perception of emptiness in 1975, I also had direct perceptions of my future lifetimes, which I will outline below.  At the same time, I can honestly say that I have not had any direct perceptions of my past lifetimes, at any time during this life.  I do though sometimes make a list to myself of events or impressions or urges in this life that logically must have been strongly influenced by events in my past lives.

Starting from the earliest years of my life, I was strongly attracted to being inside of churches, and one of my first and strongest memories of my life took place at a chapel called St Augustine by the Sea, which at the time (about 1957, when I was 5) looked like the photo of it you see here—this structure burned down in a fire in the 1960’s, and was replaced by a very modern style building which still stands there, quite active.

I must have been in pre-school, or just starting first grade.  I remember that the parents of the kids had a close connection to the school, and would deliver homemade lunches for everybody at least once a week.  We had a kind, wonderful priest as the head of the school, and my class had an older teacher, a woman, whose name I can’t recall.

Sometimes she would lead us all into the chapel.  She has us stand sprinkled along the aisles between the lovely wooden pews, with their lovely wooden scent, offset by the fragrance of the Pacific Ocean just outside—we are in Santa Monica, a beautiful beachside part of Los Angeles.

And then she tells us to dance: “Just dance!”  Recently online I found this photo of that original chapel; and this is exactly where we danced, little children laughing in joy and swirling and running wherever we liked in the church—among the angels and crosses, with the sunlight pouring down over the altar.

In Buddhism we are encouraged to use logic and trust in it as much as we do in our own eyes & ears.  I feel as sure that I had some previous blessing to experience these things, as those tiger cubs had to meet Siddhartha—and step onto the path to see emptiness directly.  I cannot see what happened directly, only with that undeniable sense we all have, of how things come from something else before them.

There is more, and it’s fun to relate to you.  I hope it doesn’t seem tedious, or too self-indulgent.  Thank you for wanting to learn these things.

I feel it was significant that this chapel, named after the Christian saint Augustine, was located in the area of Los Angeles named Santa Monica: the Spanish for “Saint Monica,” who was Augustine’s mother.  “Los Angeles” of course means “City of the Angels,” and I always felt it was a blessing to be born in places with such names.  Every changing thing in the universe needs a cause; and I feel that seeds from my actions I took in my past life were responsible for these names—for me—in the place where I was born.  Again, think of the five tiger cubs: everything is like that, whether we ever recognize it or not.  There are no accidents.


All Saints

When I had turned 6, my family moved to Phoenix, Arizona—which at the time was quite a small city.  My father was a builder of homes, whole neighborhoods of homes, and he correctly foresaw that Phoenix would come to grow: it is now 10 times larger than when I was a boy.

I entered first grade at a public school (which in Arizona means “not private”—a place where all the working families sent their kids) called Maryland Elementary.  Again I think it is a reflection of my past life’s good seeds that this and my high school, Washington Public High School, were filled with kids of many races, all harmonious, and extremely good teachers.

My sixth-grade teacher for example—Michael Bloom (seen here in his 80’s)—coaxed us through advanced English grammar and sentence diagraming; frequent composition of essays; algebra; astronomy; practical chemistry; and some 20 years before the first Apple computer insisted that we learn binary code, with the old punch cards: “Computers are going to be a big deal in the future!”

On top of that, he was a semi-professional baseball player and football player, which made him an automatic hero in our school.  He was also a devout Jew—very rare in our community in those days—and taught me much about the world’s religions from a stunning collection of books at his home.  Sometimes in the summer our parents would let us take special, private courses from him at the school on our own time, and these were amazing.

Again, I just mention it because I must have planted powerful good seeds in my past life to meet my many very excellent teachers in this life.  I had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Bloom some 60 years later, at dinner with myself and my wife Veronica, and he shared with me a worn paper record of an IQ test he had given me, that he had kept all that time.

These were the kind of dedicated teachers I grew up with; and it is my belief that even to be born in a country and a world which generally advocate for a good education for all the children in the country is itself evidence that we have all accumulated extraordinary karma in our past lifetimes.

But the most precious thing in those years was All Saints’ Church.

My mother—although not so much my dad—was very religious, in a very good way.  That is, not strongly attached to one religion over another, but a devoted believer of the religious teaching that we should serve everyone around us, all the days of our life.  Even as a mother of four boisterous boys, she found time to volunteer for example to drive the sick and elderly to their doctors’ appointments, and the grocery store.

And so even at the age of 6, I went to church every Sunday with my mother especially, and learned what it was to pray, and listen to the holy books and sermons.  I went through what in our church was called Confirmation, or the training for young people that would entitle them to partake of communion: the ritual bread and wine which represents the body and blood of Jesus Christ, the Great Sacrificer, a Prince Mahasattva that we spent time with weekly.

This was so much different from my school education—but it felt as though the two went together perfectly: school for learning to fill our worldly needs, church for learning to fill our eternal needs.

Unlike the horror stories we hear of some churches and priests, our church—All Saints’—was sort of a paradise sitting in the middle of the city of Phoenix.  The grounds were beautiful and well cared for, as was the cathedral itself.  The priests were extraordinary individuals.

Father Paul for example had been a wild trapper in the mountains of Alaska; one day he was caught in a small cabin in the wilderness, snowed under by a covering of many feet of heavy snow.  He had no way of digging out, and he sat down to die.  He made prayers that—if by some miracle, someone happened by and thought to dig him out, and save his life—he promised he would become a priest.  That’s exactly what happened, and us boys were so excited to have a man’s man teach us the mysteries of religion.

My Mom soon enlisted my older brother Geoff and I as acolytes; at the time these were the young men aged perhaps 10 to 16 who helped the priests during the church services on Sunday.  Our duties most importantly included assisting the priests in the preparation of the sacred bread and wine, and providing it to the members of the congregration in attendance.

There is a story here that I would like to share, again just in the interests of establishing the contours of my previous lifetimes, in preparation for seeing emptiness directly.  At my church there were probably several thousand members, and so on Sunday we had three different services.  At 7:15am we had Holy Communion—where everyone confirmed partakes of the body & blood of Christ; and this was the service for the die-hards, who enjoyed the more traditional liturgy or ritual reserved for this hour.

At 9:30am came the family people; especially those with children who would walk over to special classrooms nearby for religious instruction, so the parents could enjoy church in peace.  And then at 11am there were the sleepyheads of all types, who couldn’t get to church any earlier.

The preparation by the priests and acolytes took place in special, sacred side rooms that opened out to the great altar of the cathedral; and here we prepared the sacraments and helped each other into our religious robes.  Then when the grand organ burst out in its first notes, we would make our dramatic entrance up at the altar, in front of the hundreds of faithful.

Only on this particular day, at an early 7:15 service, we marched out in front of the altar and there was not a single person sitting in the church.

My older brother Geoff and I exchanged an excited glance.  Maybe we get to go home! it said.

Father Paul turned and faced us and the other priests.

“Remember,” he said quietly.  “Jesus said that—if one or two should ever gather in his name—he will be there with us.  We will go ahead with the service!”

And we did—we went carefully through the entire Communion, as if there were the usual hundreds of people sitting before us.  For my brother and I, this was a defining moment in our lives.  The priest was taking a very long time to go with care through the most sacred ceremony of a Christian, even if it was just for the three or four of us there in the clergy.  It truly was between us and Jesus, personally, and not for other people watching us.  Again, I sincerely hold that this event had a cause, and that the cause lay somewhere in my lifetimes before.

My father and many of the middle-aged men in the congregation had served in terrible bloody battles during the Second World War, which had ended only seven years before my birth.  They were rough & ready men, and organized a boy scout troop there at our church.

This was a group of about a hundred 11 to 17-year-old boys who were children of families at the church.  Our fathers, toughened by the war, took us out into the farflung forests and deserts of Arizona once a month, for three days of hiking, mountain climbing, and education in surviving in the wild.

Part of the training was that each one of us boys—to reach the coveted “Eagle Scout” award—had to pass 21 different courses under the supervision of a master in each subject.  These were extremely useful trainings in things like being able to fix electrical wiring; repair a car; serve as a responsible citizen in our community and nation; perform emergency first aid; and all the like.

We had a very active and successful troop, and with the help of my family I was able to make it through to Eagle Scout.  I know this sounds corny, but imagine having the karmic seeds to meet an organization and dedicated group of fine, adult male role models who taught you almost everything you need for a successful and healthy life.  Again, I count this as crops pushed up from many, many seeds planted in the lifetimes before my birth.


Singing

My mother also enrolled us in the church choir, which was very well organized and featured special robes similar to those of the priests and acolytes.  I sang in the choir for something like ten years, participating in most of the church services held during that time.

I know that to many people it may sound corny to be a young person walking up and down the church aisle in a robe and singing hymns, but in truth it is a deep religious experience in itself.  We had very dedicated and expert choir directors, and I remember one (I don’t recall her name) who was a particularly tough taskmaster.

One day we were all rehearsing a hymn in the practice room, and suddenly she broke down and started sobbing at the piano.  Some of us rushed up to see if we could help her: “No, no children.  I’m all right.  Everything is all right.  That song was just...too beautiful, and it started me to crying, for joy!”  These are the kinds of people my old lifes’ seeds were pouring out.

This interest in music expanded, and in time I joined the high school chorus.  Our director was named Mr. Shaw, and he had a decided bias towards religious music; we spent months learning the Hallelujah Chorus from Handel’s Messiah, and performed it annually for our parents and friends.  This again I count as coming from before I was born.

When I was about 12, my brother and I put together a rock & roll band that was originally named “The Gremlins” and later became “Hymn.”  My parents were already divorced (what kind of past-life seed?), and the two brothers sold a shotgun that my Dad had used for hunting and left behind in our garage; with the money we bought some guitars.

In high school we wrote and performed for an audience of several hundred students & teachers a rock opera based on the life of Jesus, just before another such opera called “Jesus Christ Superstar” became a huge hit all over the United States .  I remember that one night we snuck into the cathedral at our church and took a photo of our band members raising our guitars in offering to the Cross..  Again all this was very serious to us, and there were some deep, older forces I believe inspiring us.

The premier band in those days was the Beatles, a group of four young Englishmen who eventually sold, it is estimated, over one billion records.  This was in the time before the internet and digital music: these albums were vinyl and came in a cardboard package, so a billion is rather unbelievable!

Again I take it as the impetus from my past life that, for me, the Beatles sang extraordinarily inspiring songs about our inner life, peace, and social responsibility.  When I attended university, I took some time off to travel with a musician friend to India in search of the Beatles, who had gone there and learned to play some traditional Indian instruments.

I myself was very inspired by the classical sitar, a complex kind of guitar with about 20 strings.  Traveling on a shoestring, in the Himalayan foothills (past seeds) I learned to play the instrument from a great Muslim musician named Mubarak Masih (seen here).  This was one of the first bridges I reached to the spirituality of the East; and it came to me through the rock & roll music that all of us young people were so in love with.  The Beatles’ song “In My Life” expresses for me my deepest feelings in this life.


Books

And then there were the books: different books for school and at church, but ultimately crossing over into an enlightened whole.

Rough tough Alaska trapper Father Paul had double duty to take us through our Bible classes, later on Sundays.  The Bible—the New Testament especially, the words of divine wisdom spoken by Christ—felt extraordinary to me.  We used the old King James translation, which I can say as a life-long Buddhist translator now, has to be one of the greatest translations ever completed.

On top of this we had the Book of Common Prayer, which contained all the services and rituals for our church life.  This had been translated and composed by Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, England, in 1549—which means it partly overlapped with the life of William Shakespeare.

Many of us felt that this prayer book was so eloquent and meaningful that Shakespeare himself must have had some influence in its editing.  There was also a story that resulted from Cranmer’s deep devotion to following the advices of Christ, including the one that we should return the harm done to us by others with even greater kindness than before.  It is said thus that people would steal from Cranmer, because they knew his response would be to offer them even more money than they had stolen.  Being exposed to such books I count as well as flowing from my past lives’ seeds.

I recall clearly a day when Father Paul walked into our children’s Sunday School class and laid on the table some new books that we would be learning.  First there were works by the great Christian thinker C.S. Lewis, including his matchless Screwtape Letters.  These are notes sent from the Devil to his nephew offering advice on how to corrupt a young man; the plot fails when the fellow dies thinking of being of service to others around him.  And no one can forget the Christ-like lion, Aslan, in Lewis’ children’s stories, The Chronicles of Narnia.

But the coup de grâce was when Father showed us a little pile of books by someone named J.R.R. Tolkien—Lewis’ close friend—entitled Lord of the Rings, and told us that here we would learn even more about the supreme value of sacrificing self for others.  This was a full 40 years before the Lord of the Rings movies came out.  What kind of seeds produced all these kinds of books, and teachers who found them for us, in my world!!

At school and at home, I also discovered science fiction books; again, they didn’t just walk by by accident: they were thrust into my hands by a past-life Michael.  My Mom made the mistake of saying that I could join the Science Fiction Book Club—which sent you new titles monthly—and order as many extra volumes as I liked.  Soon our garage walls were crammed with the books I’d gobbled my way through.

I think the one sci-fi author that influenced me most was the brilliant Robert A. Heinlein, who combined prophetic scientific detail with extraordinary social commentary.  Here I recall Stranger In A Strange Land—a deep investigation of ethics and our responsibility to society; I highly recommend it as the best fiction book I’ve ever read.  I have also never forgotten the final words of a book called The Tree of Time, written over six decades ago by Damon Knight: “God is not born in a day.”

These writings inspired me to write myself, and in high school I “just happened” to be assigned to an unusual two-year accelerated course in composition taught by Mrs. Kathryn Mortensen, a graduate of Chicago University—which at the time “just happened” to put out The Chicago Manual of Style, the writing standards for the entire United States.

Mrs. Mortensen was on the verge of retirement, and was a very tough taskmaster.  Every one of her 100+ students had to write an essay every day, and late into the night she would carefully read every single one and give the writer detailed suggestions on how to improve.  She basically had two rules: For every word you misspelled in an essay, your score was dropped by a whole grade: a “B” became a “C,” which would never get you into college.  We had no choice but to learn to spell, and check our spelling exactingly.  The second rule was that you would face the same results if you “padded” an essay: if you used more words than you had to, or said too much, with too little meaning.  We were all used to getting better grades for using more words, and this second rule took a lot of learning.

As I approached graduation from high school, I applied for more than ten colleges ranging from Harvard to the Coast Guard Academy (to please my Father), and was accepted into all of them.  I chose Princeton because the word “prince” attracted me; I had never seen any of these places.  At the same moment, I received a “personal” invitation from the President of United States to visit the White House to be awarded the Presidential Scholar Medal: one girl and one boy from each state was selected.

I mention this because I really don’t believe that I was one of the two best students out of a hundred thousand kids in high school in Arizona that year.  I sincerely believe there were past-life forces working behind all these events.  One important feature of karma is that a relatively small action or thought can bloom into a life-changing event, lifetimes later.

At Princeton—even though it was the era of the Vietnam War and radical peace movements and hippies working against that war—I continued to serve in the church, as an acolyte and volunteer to help the poor and hungry in different countries.  I also continued to work as a volunteer on weekends for the United Farm Workers, dedicated to helping the conditions of immigrant farm laborers in the US.  I was assigned to help a wonderful activist priest named Father Jim; we worked very hard and had a lot of successes.


First Buddhism

I joined the Department of Religion and naturally focused on courses in Christian thought, since early on I had already been promised to Episcopal Theological Seminary in Boston, to become a priest myself.  Princeton did have a total of two courses in Buddhism, ut somehow I steered away from taking them; I think I had an intuition that if I did, I would never come back.  Finally though I attended a foundation Buddhism class, taught by Prof. William LaFleur.

Dr. LaFleur had grown up in the United States but gone to Japan as a young scholar and gotten interested in poetry by Buddhist sages such as Saigyo, from the 12th century; he produced some of the first English translations of these classics.  Dr. LaFleur was also a very hip young professor in an era of hip; us students loved the fact that he could finish a lecture on medieval Japan’s Buddhist poetry, and then walk out and jump into his flashy red Firebird sports car.

Again, it had to be past life experiences that brought me into his class, to hear his wonderful explanations of Buddhist thought and meditation; to devour his ideas.  At this point—it was about 1973—I found out that my mother was very ill with cancer.  There was a tender moment when she called us four boys into her small bedroom, and told us she had something to show us.  We were shocked when she began to unbutton her blouse, but she insisted she had something we had to see.

Bravely she pointed to a lump on her breast and told us she had cancer, and could very well die from it.  She asked us each to touch the lump so we wouldn’t be scared of it, and then calmly outlined her plans for dying and doing the best she could to make sure we were all taken care of.  Looking back, I feel astounded by her courage and calmness, and again I have to believe she was crafted by my past goodness.

Back at Princeton I was halfway through my second course in Buddhism with Prof. LaFleur; classes at Princeton were really spread out across a huge campus, and we only had a few minutes to get from one to another—I was rushing.

Approaching 1879 Hall, I saw a student from my class sitting outside under a tree.  He was a boy from India whose name I didn’t know, but in my same class.  Glancing at him, he looked exactly like Lord Buddha sitting under the Bodhi Tree, on the very verge of enlightenment.  He motions me over—I hesitate, I have never been late for a class and I will be, if I pause to talk to him—but something tells me this is important.  I sit down at his side.

“Your Mother is dying,” he says.  I don’t know how he knew.

“Yes,” I nod.

“You want to help her,” he continues.

“Yes,” I say again.

He looks me square in the eyes.  “This university, Princeton, is one of the greatest schools in the world.  But there is absolutely nothing here that will help your Mother, or help you understand why she is dying.”

I didn’t answer.  The truth of what he was saying was obvious.  There was not—and there is still not—any academic course at Princeton in learning how to die, or being of real help to another person dying.  Which is strange, since dying is something we all have to do.  I look into his eyes and see the truth there.

Nothing more was said.  We stood up and went in and made it to class on time.

Walking down through the hall I pass the Religion Department bulletin board, crowded with notices.  There off to the side is a cheap sheet of blue paper with a picture on it.  I look closer.  There are three Tibetan Buddhist monks standing, looking at the camera; one older Lama in the middle, and two younger attendants standing to each side.  They look really peaceful and happy.  They have ridiculously big smiles.

Below the photo is an announcement for an immersion course in Buddhism to be held at a tiny institute in the foothills of the Himalayan mountains.  I know immediately that I have to go; after all, the Buddha had just predicted it!

Why was I drawn to a single tiny piece of paper, in my whole world at that time?  Why was I so attracted to the robes, the very first time I saw them?  Why did I have to become a monk, and a geshe, myself, years later?  Nothing that ever occurs in this world can occur without a cause, a cause that came before it.

Princeton was happy to approve my trip, and even gave me my scholarship money for the semester in cash, to pay for the trip and fees.  This was because I had already been arrested once for helping to block—in a peaceful, non-violent way—the entrance to a research facility on campus dedicated to making a better kind of napalm, for the war going on at that moment in Vietnam.

Napalm is a kind of jelly made from pure gasoline.  You put it in a bomb and fly over a Vietnamese village and drop the bomb and the jelly sprays all over everyone—men, women, and children—and sticks to their skin and burns through their body, an agonizing death.

Princeton had warned me that if I was arrested again I would be expelled forever.  But the napalm was still being produced.  We all knew I would get arrested again if I was anywhere nearby in the coming months.  I made the flight to India, and the rest—for me—is history.

Years later I am driving in a car in Australia, where I am giving some talks on the Diamond Cutter Sutra.  My driver is a devoted Buddhist who is also a college professor and an accomplished architect.  I remark to him how wonderful his attitude and aspirations are.

“Oh Geshe La, that’s not me!” he objects.

“Well then, who is it?”

“Oh that’s Joe—all of that is Joe’s fault!”

I feel a little twinge of jealousy.  Does he have another Buddhist teacher from the West?  Who is this Joe guy, anyway?

“Who’s Joe?” I ask.

He laughs happily.  “Oh, Joe—that’s me!  That’s my past life!  I can tell he must have been an amazingly good person!  Look where he got me to!”


The Garden

There is one more, strongest, indicator for me of my previous life’s hard work; and remember, the point of all this reminiscing is to establish an experiential version of the four arya truths that—in my opinion—first began long before the lifetime in which I saw emptiness directly.

After her divorce, my determined Mom went back to college to get a teaching degree, and then as the sole source of support for us four boys went to work as an elementary school teacher.  She used to point out to us that her teacher’s salary was less than that of a city garbage truck worker.

One day she came home and informed us four boys that we would be having guests at our upcoming Thanksgiving Day dinner, which was always a major affair at our house, with a huge feast despite our finances.

We didn’t pay that much attention, and in the morning on the given day we were out in the garage working on a homemade race car that we were trying to build.  I was under the car working on something; the garage door was opened; I could see just the tires and lower body of a cute Karmann Ghia car drive up and park nearby.  The door opens and some high heeled shoes step out on the sidewalk, attached to some legs that teenage boys would be very interested in.

That’s all we can see, but it’s enough to jump up and rush in and wash the grease off our hands and change into some clean clothes.

Turns out that my Mom’s fellow teacher, Anita Hancock, had 4 amazing daughters, just our age.  I personally was immediately smitten by the youngest, whose name was Veronica.  I felt as though we had known each other for a long time even before we ever met.  Here’s the conversation between me and my Mom after the Hancock ladies left that day.

Me: “Mom!  I really like that one daughter, by the name of Veronica!  Do you think I could ask her out?”

Mom: “Well Mike, you’re in luck.  They left a saucepan here, and we have to get it back to them.  Why don’t you drive it over there tomorrow?”

Me: “What do I do?”

Mom: “Ring the doorbell, and if the mom answers, then explain that you’re bringing back the saucepan but be sure to step inside the door, so she can’t close it.  And then steer the conversation around to asking her daughter out on a date!”

Moms are Masters of the Universe, and the plan worked perfectly.  Veronica and I saw a movie together, and then we ended up taking a long walk through a beautiful garden at my church.  There in the Garden—alone together—through countless evenings, my Lady taught me.  Given what I learned, and our marriage now that stretches back those nearly 60 years, I logically believe that we must have been closely tied together, many lifetimes before.  And what she has taught me, privately, during those decades I believe prepared me to touch the Diamond World, and walk the Diamond Way.


Assigning an aspect

At this point, I propose that we pause and assign one of the 16 moments en masse to the collection of these past-life experiences, confirmed through inevitable logic: no produced thing in the universe can occur without its own causes, and each of the events I have described here for my early life—from dancing in the chapel to sacred walks in the church garden—is a produced thing.  Each one must have had its causes in a time period previous to it.  And the only time available for that would have had to be one or more past lives.

Each of the events described here helped me to see emptiness directly, and this experience itself is the most important one that any human being can ever have, in the quest to stop suffering and bring all beings to never-ending happiness.  We would thus have to assign all these events together to the fourth higher truth: the truth of the path to the end of suffering.

Inside this one truth—again—are the four “aspects” or moments that we listed for it above: path, logic, means, and method.  Which of these four we assign here is, frankly, a judgement call.  None of the moments of any of the truths seems to necessarily come in any particular sequence; nor is any of the moments ever described so specifically—ever, in the last 25 centuries—that we can with certainty assign it to any particular personal experience, although in the end it has to be such an experience.

In my opinion, after 25 years of intense study in the geshe course and an equal number of years of the same intensity since completing it, aspect [14]—the aspect of “logic” (nyaya in Sanskrit)—is the most logical aspect of the truth of the path to assign to these previous lifetimes’ events.  This is because even an arya normally requires error-free logic to perceive these past-life events, which must have triggered their realizations inside of this present lifetime.

With this, we’ve completed the first of our seven groups of experiences within the overall journey to reach emptiness directly.  Now we’re ready to move on to the second group.



Group Two:
Preparing for the diamond world


In and out of meditation

There’s an important point that it’s time to make, in our exploration of the four higher truths.  In scripture these four are traditionally divided into experiences that take place during deep meditation, and then experiences that take place outside of such meditation.  This corresponds nicely with my own personal experience.

The technical terminology here can be expressed in Tibetan as nyam-shak (technical spelling mnyam-bzhag) and jetop (spelled rjes-thob).  In this case, nyam-shak refers to the period spent inside the direct perception of emptiness, whereas je-top refers to sort of a “popcorn” period of realizations popping up very actively just after—when we are more in a discursive state of mind.

In some traditional Buddhist systems this is reflected in the wording, shepa (technical spelling shes-pa) and supa (technical spelling bzod-pa).  Shepa means “understanding,” and again refers to the period inside of a realization.  Supa normally means “patience,” but it can also connote “mastery,” meaning that we are coming out of the direct realization and entering a period of appreciating it.  The associated realization could be the direct perception of emptiness, or other topics as well.

These distinctions can help us understand the 16 moments of the four truths in more detail.  We have just reserved one of the 16 for early experiences in this present life that tie back to deduced source experiences in earlier lifetimes.  Many of these experiences would be outside of meditation.  And it is my personal experience that the same holds for most of the other of the 16, even in this present life.


Connection to the five paths

It’s a good time here to talk about the interrelation between the four truths, my own experiences, and a traditional realization flowchart known as the “five paths.”  The five paths are used to describe the period from the time that one truly becomes interested in spiritual issues, on up to the point of enlightenment itself.

The first path is called the “path of accumulation,” and it refers specifically to a period of spiritual searching in our life triggered by some kind of traumatic event, such as the death of a parent.  During this time of personal pain, we begin to “accumulate” the good karmic seeds necessary to see emptiness directly at the third path.

The second path is named the “path of preparation,” and refers to an intense period of intellectual understandings which directly pave the way for the direct perception of emptiness.  The third path then is the all-important “path of seeing,” referring to the direct perception itself.

This is followed by the “path of habituation,” a longish period during which we get used to what we saw during the direct perception, and immediately afterwards.  This accustomation then delivers us to nirvana and enlightenment itself.

“Nirvana” literally means “blowing out,” and represents the permanent destruction of all negative emotions accomplished by the realizations related to seeing emptiness directly.  And then finally countless scriptures describe how—if that nirvana is accompanied by what we call “bodhichitta,” or an intense intention to help all beings in the universe—then we come to our own total enlightenment, and become a Buddha ourselves.  The nirvana and Buddhahood here then are the fifth and final path, known as the “path of no more learning.”

Let’s look now at these five “paths” or states of spiritual growth, in my own specific case.  Again, this is not for purposes of boasting or making false claims.  I am sincerely just hoping to help you reach the direct perception of emptiness yourself.


First path: accumulation, of sadness

As I’ve alluded to above, it was the illness and death of my Mother I think that put me upon the first of the five paths to emptiness.  She loved us four brothers with a never-failing devotion: despite the abusive experiences of her marriage (which I remember included physical beatings), and the difficult financial circumstances, and the intense hard work at home and in her job, she never failed to show intense love and care for us, and for other people and the young students in her life as well.

During the troubles with my father, he had taught her to drink, at the level of a young sailor returning from war—and she had become an alcoholic.  On the day that she left to start her new life with us four boys, she stopped completely.  To see her fight her way back to a normal life in a beautiful house that she earned on her own, and then watch as the cancer took her life, represented for me the first of the five paths.

In fact I saw emptiness directly within 4 months after her very painful death; my brother found her on the floor with her entire life’s blood poured out all around her, as the cancer chewed through a major artery.  She had a Bible in her hand—and that’s who she was.

The first of the four higher truths is of course the truth of suffering, and the first [1] of the 16 aspects we listed above was impermanence, or anitya in the Sanskrit.  My mother’s sad death was, for me, this particular aspect in real life.


A different kind of emptiness

There is something confusing about several of the four aspects of the first higher truth—the truth of suffering—that we could pause and clear up here.  As we will see below, when we get to the “pot on the stove” and subsequent realizations, understandings of emptiness are not something that characterizes this first path, of accumulating sadness about the inevitable course our life here will take.

There are though two aspects here that seem to refer to these understandings, and we need to explain why they are here, out of proper order.

The first of these [3] is simply called “emptiness” (shunya, in the Sanskrit).  Given where it stands in the list, we need to take this as a continuation of the impermanence and suffering that we’ve just covered.  We need to take it as the emptiness of a life that has no meaning.

Buddhists have said for centuries that every aspect of our life is suffering, but our own experience seems to contradict this.  Here I think of the example of my Father.  He had grown up in a simple household in the midwestern United States without a lot of money, but enough to get by.  When World War II broke out, he was still in his teens, but he volunteered for military service.

He was assigned to duty on a submarine in the Pacific, which was extremely dangerous and traumatic—there were many submarines during the war that simply disappeared, never to be heard from again, presumably lying full of dead sailors on the bottom of the ocean.

When he returned a few years later—alive and much, much older—Dad recalled the weather and the economic opportunities of naval ports he had passed through during the war: places like Los Angeles or San Diego.  I think surviving a war has an effect on some soldiers where they come back really wanting to make a success of the rest of their life, and my Dad was in this category.

He attacked his life with gusto, learning the business of building whole neighborhoods of family homes.  He is responsible for entire areas of both Los Angeles and San Diego—and (in a boom or bust fashion) he made a lot of money.  During some of his best years, he bought and renovated a very expensive home nearby the ocean; met and married a very special second wife; and even bought a fairly large, retired Navy ship for overnight drinking and fishing parties at sea, with his friends.

And then—not long after my Mom passed away—he too contracted cancer, and died a long and agonizing death.  In my world, this then was the aspect or “moment” of [3] emptiness as a component of the truth of suffering: that in the end there was literally nothing that remained of my Dad’s entire life of success, possessions, and friends.  And we are all headed for that very same ending.

The next and final aspect of the truth of suffering is called [4] “no self-nature” (anatma in the Sanskrit).  Again, if taken in its usual meaning this moment belongs down in the third truth, of the cessation of suffering.  I would say here that the sufferings in our life are—in the end—what we make of them: they are not one way or another in and of themselves.

This relates to the central Buddhist practice of turning misfortunes into a path for progress.  Break-ups of friends and marriages and in our employment often end up this way: a rainbow coming out after a rainy day.  The loss of both my parents left me stranded in this life, but then I was available for the coming Fr. Tims, Prof. LaFleurs, and Khen Rinpoches.


Second path: preparing to see

Here I would like to begin to record a good number of experiences that would traditionally be included into the second path, of preparation to touch emptiness directly.  How we organize all of these events into the 16 moments, we’ll have to work on: again, we don’t have historical references clear enough to help us greatly.

First and foremost here, I did end up taking over a year off of my normal Princeton degree work to study in the foothills of the Himalayas.  These were blessed times in academia when we were encouraged to get out of the universities and actually experience other cultures first-hand.  I spent most of a semester learning with those three joyful monks in the photograph. First here was Geshe Ngawang Dhargyey, who had received received his geshe, or “Master of Buddhism” degree, after 25 years of study at Sera Monastery, which until the Cultural Revolution in China had been one of the oldest and largest monasteries in history, with thousands of monks.

Geshe Dhargyey was assisted by two young tulkus.  A “tulku” is a monk who is considered the reincarnation of a Buddhist master who has passed away, and returned as a new baby to continue helping people.  First here was Sharpa Tulku, Tenzin Trinley Rinpoche, who became a close friend and mentor during those studies.  He was accompanied by Khamlung Rinpoche, another young reincarnation and kindly friend.  As teenagers, both had lived in the Mongolian refugee community of Howell, New Jersey, which we will be meeting shortly.  They had learned English at the local high school, and were translating for Geshe Dhargyey in our classes in the Himalayas.

During these studies I received word from my Mom that she had been asked to leave her job at the elementary school, because the cancer had reached her brain and she was having epileptic seizures, sometimes in front of her fifth-grade schoolchildren.  Sharpa Rinpoche suggested that I might want to bring her there to the Himalayas to receive treatment from masters of Tibetan medicine, and also meet high lamas who could assist her through the death process, if it came to that.

This I did; Mom of course ended up organizing art classes for the local refugee kids, and within a month or two we thought it safer to bring her back to the States; she was now often having major epileptic seizures.  But she and I had the deep honor of attending daily classes taught by Geshe Dhargyey together—she propped up against a pillar and wrapped in blankets.  Together we learned The Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life, a very famous presentation of Buddhist perfections and emptiness by the 8th-century Indian emptiness master Shantideva.  In the current translation, in fact, this text plays a major role; and I ended up writing my honors thesis at Princeton on its presentation of the perfection of giving.

When it became clear that I would have to return to the States to bring my Mom home to pass away with family, I began asking around about teachers who might be in the Princeton area.  This is how I found out about Khen Rinpoche Geshe Lobsang Tharchin, and within a few weeks of my return to the US I attended lectures by him at both Columbia University and Princeton on topics such as emptiness, according to the Heart Sutra.

Upon graduation, as I will outline below, I was able to begin studies of the classics of Buddhism—especially Higher Knowledge, or Abhidharma; and Reasoning, or Pramana—directly from Khen Rinpoche for two or three hours ever day, most often in private.  It is no small factor here that—living with Khen Rinpoche—I was automatically within a two-minute walk of the only surviving copy of the Kangyur collection of Buddhist classics in the western hemisphere, not to mention Rinpoche’s own considerable collection of manuscripts.  This early work in the philosophical tradition of Buddhism was crucial for my direct perception of emptiness; foremost here was the idea of chi-jedrak, which absolutely has to be learned before we can see emptiness.  So let’s go into it some, now.


Chi-jedrak: quality & characteristic

Young monks at one of the major monastic universities typically study Buddhist logic very early on—say, around the age of 15 or even younger; this is because clear thinking is an essential for all the formal classes and work in the monastery debate ground that they will be laboring through for the next 25 years, until they take their geshe examinations.

This topic traces back to the Buddha himself—who is famous for his philosophical debates with other thinkers of his time—and is studied nowadays primarily from a medieval commentary named A Commentary on Accurate Perception, written by the Indian master Dharmakirti around 650ad.

A young geshe candidate goes through the five great topics of the geshe course on an average of five years each; the combined degree then is similar in commitment to earning five separate degrees at a typical American university.  Clear thinking though is considered so important that we devote about a quarter of the year to it, every one of the 25 years of the geshe course.

And so Khen Rinpoche was trying to get me up to speed.  Unfortunately, the ancient Asian vocabulary for formal logic especially is so difficult that it takes years to learn, even if explained in your native language.  But here we had a 22-year-old American and a 55-year-old Tibetan with almost no English trying to communicate with each other in these abstruse Asian terms.

As we will see, Rinpoche was living at a traditional Mongolian temple in the middle of New Jersey, among refugees from World War II who were very poor.  There was no housing at the temple for a starry-eyed young American, so I was bedding down in a sleeping bag on the concrete floor of a broken-down, abandoned car repair garage nearby.  I would spend the days at a small table in Rinpoche’s kitchen, and at night walk back to my dungeon to sleep.

Khen Rinpoche is trying to teach me an extremely difficult dialectics term known in Tibetan as chi-jedrak (technical spelling spyi bye-brag).  Expressed in his few English words, it is completely unintelligible.  We spent two hours on it today and basically both gave up.  I’m walking back through the pitch dark to my old garage and have almost decided just to surrender and go back to my shishi university life and try to be a professor somewhere.

I have to cross through some pretty thick woods, and I pause in a particularly dark part, under a tree naked of leaves.  This is allowing the moon to swoop down and offer me some comfort.  I look up, and the light pours in.  Slowly my mood flips, and right there right then I remember saying to myself, “Dammit, I’m going to learn this thing, no matter how long it takes!”  Instead of pursuing a career as a formal logic hater, I throw myself into mastering it.

And I did—starting with chi jedrak.

Chi usually means “general,” or “overall”; typically you would think of it as an overall group, such as all the cars in the world.  And then jedrak refers to one of the members of the group, such as the Toyota car out in your own driveway.

But then suddenly I have this unique insight into the two terms, where chi refers to a general quality of something; and jedrak refers to something being characteristic of that quality, of embodying it.  I have this breakthrough understanding of chi jedrak not as set & subset, but rather of chi as something like car-ness and jedrak as something like a particular car which has the quality of car-ness.

If we sit with this idea over the period of a fairly serious meditation, or a bunch of meditations, we can suddenly have a breakthrough where we consider the possibility that all the cars we’ve ever looked at or driven in were—somehow—opinions of car-ness.  This thought takes some time to “cook” in our mind (as Khen Rinpoche would put it), but under the right conditions it is, in my estimation, a direct ticket to the direct perception of emptiness.

That is, if the other, supporting conditions are all there; and now we’ll take a look at some of those.  But before we do, I would pause and attempt to assign a pair of the 16 aspects to these last few realizations: of undertaking a formal course of study of the mighty Buddhist classics; and enjoying that breakthrough with quality & characteristic.

Personally I would categorize an in-depth study of the Buddhist classics—and more particularly, the five geshe subjects—as [15] a “means” (pratipatti in the Sanskrit) of enabling the fourth truth, the path to the end of suffering.  My own case shows that this doesn’t necessarily involve for example decades of time spent in this current lifetime with these great books: if a person even has the karmic seeds to encounter the books or a place where they are regularly studied, or a teacher capable of imparting them correctly, this would surely indicate that the individual had massive seeds from multiple past lifetimes of contact with these readings and concepts.  In other words, people with special seeds could see emptiness directly with no more than a “brush-up” of ideas like chi-jedrak.  Similar to what happened to me.

Giving birth to an intimate realization of chi-jedrak is sufficiently crucial that I would list it as a separate aspect of the Four Truths; and I would connect it to moment [16]: “method,” or nairyanika in the Sanskrit.  This is because the structure of the Sanskrit implies that this specific concept is a sine qua non: an absolute necessity or prerequisite for touching the diamond world of emptiness.

A final note on this particular aspect.  There is, admittedly, that famous reference in the sutras which says that the Group of Five—the five tiger cubs—did receive a teaching on the four truths of an arya and did, each of them, perceive emptiness upon the completion of three rounds of hearing the four.

We also see descriptions, in sutra, of people like King Udrayana or the Lady of Pearl, who—it is said—saw emptiness directly, immediately after laying eyes on the Wheel of Life painting designed for them by Lord Buddha.

Now we noted, previously, that some of the 16 aspects here are perceived directly, in a deep state of meditation.  Others are perceived “around” such meditations, either before or after.  But I can say categorically, with no exceptions, that to see emptiness directly you must at the time be in a deep state of formal meditation, sitting in formal meditation posture.

References to people having a perception of emptiness while chopping wood or something of the like refer—without any question—to the discursive type of thinking about emptiness that we will describe below, with the “pot on the stove.”  This is not the direct perception, and does not represent “entering the stream,” or a direct pathway to nirvana and Buddhahood.

This means that what happened in these famous accounts from sutra is that people received careful and extended instruction on emptiness, and were afterwards able to go into a deep state of meditation and touch it directly.  I believe that this is reflected in the fact that the Group of Five were granted teachings on emptiness over a period of 7 years total; this period is sometimes referred to a “first turning of the Wheel of the Dharma” or “the Wheel of the Dharma on the four truths.”  Even with an exceptional previous birth, this time frame would make more sense than just a few minutes, and a quick repetition three times, standing in the heat of the West Bengal jungle.


Deep meditation:
the room at the top

Another preliminary to the direct perception of emptiness agreed upon by all authoritative sources is that we must be capable of the deep meditation—the absolute stillness of mind—necessary to catch sight of emptiness.

Textually speaking, this is the state of shamatha (technical spelling śamatha, which in classical Tibetan translates into zhi-gnas or “residing in peace”).
