During the direct perception, this is half of the ultimately powerful union of shamatha and vipashyana (technical spelling vipaśyanā; in classical Tibetan, lhag-mthong or “special sight”).  “Special sight” here refers to a deep insight into emptiness, or the fact that the object of our focus is devoid of coming from its own side.

In my own case, I had learned the traditional, accurate details of formal meditation from my teachers in the Himalayas—and again, I deduce, had come into this life with a solid habit for it from many past-life years of meditation.  And I had been training in a perfect location.

Flying back from India to finish the final semester of my degree at Princeton, I was very aware that I hadn’t arranged any place to stay once I had landed in the USA.  I had this recurring thought in my mind though that there might be an available room at the top of the priest’s residence at the Procter Foundation.  This is a beautiful classic old Princeton professor’s house in the same neighborhood where Albert Einstein once lived.

But to make those arrangements, I would have to meet and do some really persuasive talking with the current priest, Rev. Timothy Cogan—who lived there with his wife Ruth, and their two small boys John and Milo (Episcopal priests are allowed to marry and have families).

The flight though was late getting into Kennedy Airport, and it was 9 or 10pm by the time I got off the bus at campus.  The odds of arranging to “just run into” Fr. Tim were zero.  But something told me to go to the late-night student cafe, which had just opened.  There in the darkened room, alone amongst a hundred or two empty seats, was the Father, for some reason having a coffee in the middle of the night.  This is how the last days go for someone who is about to touch the diamond world.

Fr. Tim seemed to already know exactly what I would ask for, and immediately agreed that during this final semester, I would be allowed to live in the beautiful empty third floor of the priest’s residence.  I just had to babysit the kids (4 and 2 years old, respectively) two nights a week, so that the Cogans could get out for a rare date together.

The reason I mention all this is that this third-floor nook turned out to be the absolutely perfect meditation chamber.  It was elevated above the lovely medieval Princeton stone buildings, halfway it seemed into the blue sky.  On a normal day it was absolutely silent up there.

With persistent daily practice, I was able to work up to 60 minutes of truly silent meditation.  I learned that if my legs fell asleep in my half-lotus posture (full lotus I would say is not required, and even distracting), I could just wait through the pins and needles and in a few minutes I couldn’t feel them at all.  I learned to take my breathing down—very naturally, and with no pushing—to extremely slow.

The meditation subjects I focused on were very traditional, taken from the “steps of the path” (lam-rim) teachings I had received in India, with a focus on the methodology of the matchless Bhavana Krama, or “Stages of Meditation” trilogy of the medieval meditation teacher Master Kamalashila.

Somehow I had the wisdom to shave my busy Princeton undergraduate course load down, to allow me to focus on my practice.  I remember that—for the first time in my life—I had the insight that a great deal of my scholastic overworking was simple hubris, just trying to look like someone who was more than normal.

I was for example already a respectable sitar player, and had even played several concerts in India.  I had signed up for a course in classical Indian music at the very demanding Princeton Department of Music.  I suddenly realized that if I cut any unnecessary activities, my meditation could go deeper.  I went to the professor of the Indian music course and—for the first time in my life—dropped a course.

A few months later I played a concert at Princeton for a charity; I remember the quizzical look I got from the same professor when I bumped into him on the way out of the concert hall!

There was a meditation “event” here that is important I think; it gives insight into how deep we need to get, to see emptiness directly.  I was sitting in a special reading room on the northwest side of the first floor of Princeton’s exquisite Firestone Library.  The room has stacks of books all round on fragrant hardwood shelves; and several multistory walls are all glass, with soft sunlight flooding across the silent room.  I was working on some kind of homework assignment, very focused.

At some point I suddenly realized that I hadn’t taken a breath for over ten minutes.  I had been surfing since I was about 8 or 9 years old, and I knew that anybody would pass out at about 3 minutes.  It was, of course, the focus; but the event had deeper implications, the more I thought about it.  The bottom line was that my life was not being maintained by breath, or by food or water either.  I understood, in that moment, that seeds in my mind were keeping me alive: raw karma.

There is a final realization that belongs here.  As my daily meditation sessions up on the third floor were getting deeper and longer, the two toddlers started to get more and more curious about what I was doing up there, so quiet, so long.

One day they climbed up the stairs (rather noisily) and slipped into my room.  I was deep, and I decided it was more important that I stay there, than to chastise them for interrupting me.  At first they played around the room, pulling on my hair and giggling.  I determined not to move.  I stayed deep.

Suddenly, by some kind of common consent, they sat down next to me and started to meditate silently.  Strange, I thought, for a 2-year-old and a 4-year-old.  The three of us stayed in the silence for quite a long time, and from then on we often meditated together.

Soon it was the end of March, the 30th, of that year; a Sunday—Easter Sunday—and I was doing my babysitting job during the day.  My mother (staying with my brother and his wife in California) would die three days later, and on some level everyone in my family could feel it coming.  I was downstairs in Procter House, and because of the holiday they were playing the famous children’s film, Wizard of Oz, on the TV.  The boys and I were watching it together.

This movie tells a famous story about all of us having the potential to be whatever we most dream of being, if we come to recognize who we truly are, inside.  All three of us watched in silence, spellbound.  Suddenly I had the overwhelming knowledge that these two small boys were themselves already enlightened—already Buddhas—and that they were intent on guiding me there themselves.  It was a moment I have never forgotten—a synergy between the diamond world and the Diamond Way.

To summarize, the ancient classics of Buddhism over the last two thousand years or so have insisted that we need to be in that very deep state of meditation—shamatha—in order to perceive emptiness directly.  Of the hundreds of states of mind that a person can reach in deep meditation, there is a particular level—no less focused, but no less aware either—that is perfect for this direct contact with emptiness.

The level is called samten dangpoy nyerdok Michok mey (technical spelling bsam-gtan dang-po’i nyer-bsdogs Mi-lcogs med).  In my experience, you have to be able to stay perfectly unmoving in a state of deep meditation for one hour to reach it.  Frankly speaking, this means that if you cannot remain in a meditation session (and I am not including the traditional preliminary prayers and breath work and so on leading into such a session) for at least one hour, then there is no chance at all that you will ever see emptiness directly.

Remember that—according to classics of Buddhism such as the one that you hold in your hands right now—each one of us will continue to suffer through intense pain, and death, for lifetime after lifetime, unbroken, until the day that we see emptiness directly.  And so I literally beg you to get your meditation practice on track.

The only place to start is with ten minutes a day, following the instructions of a bona fide meditation master, and then build up very slowly and gradually—increasing say one minute per week—until you reach the 60 minutes deep down.  There is no other way, and you have no choice.

Reaching the ability to stay in meditation long enough to see emptiness directly is so crucial that I would assign it to one of the four aspects or moments within the higher truth of the path to the end of suffering, all on its own accord.  In my opinion, the first aspect of this truth—overall aspect [13]—corresponds to the ability to reach and remain at this level for a solid hour.  This aspect, as we have seen above, is itself referred to as “path,” or marga in the original Sanskrit.

Here within moment [13]—the aspect of the “path”—I would add another circumstance that was going on in my life at the time.  During my earlier years at Princeton I was pretty much like every other undergraduate, in my personal habits and appearance.  At my Mom’s insistence, I had appeared on campus the first day wearing a full business suit and tie.

Then though arrived the days of the hippie movement: a nationwide movement of young people away from materialism and towards inner development—which I count as another blessing sent me by my dear past-life Michael.  I had soon grown my hair out to match that of my rock & roll inspirations, and turned in my suits for worn-out jeans and tank tops.

My freshman year—following a university requirement to join a sport—I spent the whole year competing on the rowing team, and for the next two years I weightlifted, when my rowing coach said it might endanger my heart if I didn’t.

The bottom line here I think is that I took as much pride in my hippie’s physical appearance as if I had worn that suit the whole time.  Part of what I learned during my time in the Himalayas though was that I would not be able to meditate deeply if my mind was distracted, even slightly, by trying to look cool to my peers.  By the time I had returned to Princeton to finish my degree, I dressed very simply and kept my hair cut in an unremarkable way; and I believe that turning this percentage of my attention to deeper things helped me a lot to reach shamatha.

There is even a word for this sort of attitude in the ancient Buddhist books of Abhidharma, or Higher Knowledge.  It’s called du-chung chok-shey (technical spelling ‘dod-chung chog-shes).  This basically means giving up any desire to buy fancy new clothes, and making close friends with your old, comfortable clothes.

Again, this is all part of a code of simplicty in your personal life that allows you to focus all your mental space on your practice.  There’s no mental catalog of all the different pairs of shoes you own, because you only own one pair.

Remember, cooking up emptiness is no different than cooking up your mother’s favorite stew.  The recipe calls for 16 different ingredients, and you cannot leave any one of them out and expect it to taste the same as your Mom’s.  Learn the 16; learn to make this stew, and your life is saved.  Then, only then, can you save the lives of others.


My delivery to Khen Rinpoche

The first week of June that year, 1975, was a busy time for me.  After losing a year in my overseas studies, I was finally going to graduate—and I was tying things up in preparation for moving to study with Khen Rinpoche at the Mongolian temple, 45 minutes and an entire universe away.  Given that I would see emptiness directly within two more months, it’s worth it I think to go through some of the details here.

Meditation-wise, I was following not a crazy but a very regular daily morning practice.  I had cut my social calendar down to a few closest friends—guys that I played music with, or worked with at a warehouse on the edge of campus.  As part of my scholarship I was required to put in about 20 hours a week at a trucking company that handled all the university’s food and material deliveries; before leaving for India I had worked up to the student manager’s position.

I got permission to use the university trucks to drive around the dormitories and park outside the entrances, where I put up big signs to encourage especially the wealthy kids to throw their no-longer-needed winter jackets and sweaters into big cardboard boxes.  I sorted the clothes in the basement at Procter House and shipped the best and warmest items off to refugees in the Himalayan towns where I had studied.

I was also wrapping up my volunteer position with a world food relief project at the church, and I remember I was in a meeting there when Father Tim came in and led me away to his office to tell me my Mom had just died.

Over the years I had been working three jobs to make enough money to get to India, and to pay off the last of my student debt.  There was the truck driving, and in fact I missed my Princeton graduation ceremony because I had to do deliveries that day.  Secondly, I was in a “Arabic fusion” rock & roll band, and we had a weekly paying gig at a bar in town.  

During breaks at the bar, I studied for my Russian quizzes.  I had already taken three years of it and was one of the few survivors; about 90% had dropped out of the class.  I was probably the worst of the survivors, but since I was on scholarship I got first priority for student researcher jobs—and so a famous Slavic scholar named Herman Ermolaev had me writing out citations for him on piecework payment.

During that last week at Princeton, I withdrew all my savings in cash, and marched down to the registrar’s office, and paid off all my student debt, to the last dime.  It left me with just enough to survive for the next few months at my new home in the garage behind the Mongolian temple.  I think that making a clean break with my former life—especially financially—was important for clearing my mind and going deeper with my meditations, in the final months before emptiness.

Scholastically, I wrapped up as well.  I had been required to finish up a final Russian course credit, and had the good fortune to know Dr. Ellen Chances, a brilliant and caring young assistant professor.  Together we worked out a plan where I could do an independent study of work by Russian scholars on ancient Buddhist Sanskrit classics.

I chose to focus, again, on Master Shantideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life; looking back I believe this and the other Middle Way classics (such as the present translation) are crucial to helping us see emptiness.  There was an important Russian manuscript of Shantideva’s work at the Nicholas Roerich Museum in Manhattan that no one would permit out of the building.  And so once every week or two I would take the bus into New York to labor over it, and this got me to the end of my degree requirements.  

The only thing left was the final oral defense of my senior undergraduate thesis; this took place at Princeton’s Department of Religion, with a handful of my favorite professors, and again I had a very important diamond-way moment with them.  In the end I was one of the few religion majors to be awarded honors. 

A couple of times a week I would walk over to Prof. LaFleur’s home (a few doors away), and we would sit down and meditate together between huge piles of academic papers and books.  I had been told (wrongly) that Khen Rinpoche didn’t like music, so I gave my quite-expensive sitar away to the two small boys at Procter House; many years later when we had a chance to connect, they told me they never forgot it.

In the second week then of June, I was free and ready to leave the university and head off for my studies with Khen Rinpoche.  None of us had the slightest clue that I would end up spending 25 years at the Mongol temple.  Prof. LaFleur offered to drive me and my few bags, in his famous red sports car.  Father Tim and his family made one last appeal for me to spend the rest of my life at Procter House as a nanny, and I was actually tempted.  But then we were off.

Again, I tell all these things because I am trying to help you see emptiness too.  It seems it was important that I was willing to change my entire life to see it.  There was a stark difference between the wealth and ordered life at Princeton, and this tiny community of shattered and impoverished refugees in the highway strip town of Howell, where the Mongol temple was located.

Prof. LaFleur knocks on the door of the tiny house behind the Buddhist temple.  There is this most tender moment when Khen Rinpoche opens the door and takes my arm in his hand.  Prof. LaFleur lets go of my other arm: “Take good care of him.”  Khen Rinpoche: “Yes, yes.  I will make a wise man out of him.”  Prof. LaFleur turns to go back to his beautiful car, but then suddenly he presses the car key into my hand.  “You keep it.  Good luck!”  He walks out to the street and gets into the waiting car of a friend, and he’s off.  I’m standing there with my mouth wide open.  Rinpoche guides me in.


From the top of the ladder

Khen Rinpoche had survived the bombing of his monastery, and the death of thousands of his fellow monks.  He had walked over the Himalayas to survive, the last few hundred miles without shoes.  He was a tough man, and a tough taskmaster.  No Princeton undergraduate coddling at his temple!

First of all, we were both outsiders at the Temple.  This was a small town cobbled together in what had been a swamp in the middle of New Jersey, and populated almost exclusively by several thousand Mongolians.  They were a special type of Mongol, named Kalmyks.  The very name “Kalmyk” means that these were the front-line soldiers seven centuries before that had very nearly conquered all of Europe.  During that march west through Central Asia and Tibet, they had somehow become Buddhists.

Most recently, their small Eastern European country had been taken over by the Nazi army advancing towards Russia.  Most of their countrymen had been exterminated—often in concentration camps—since Asians were considered as offensive to the Master Race as the Jewish people.  What I was walking into was the few who had survived these horrors, often jumping over the barbed wire of the camps and surviving wild for years in the surrounding forests.  They were just as tough as Khen Rinpoche, and hardly understood the idea that some young American would want to come learn to see emptiness at their temple.

Khen Rinpoche though was a different sort of man; he had been sent to the West by some of the highest lamas alive, and he considered it his honor and responsibility to serve this small community of refugees.  Together we worked to make the Temple a little Buddha paradise on earth.

This included loading and driving countless truckloads of construction garbage to the local dump, then pulling out (by hand) the stumps of huge oak trees left behind.  One particularly stubborn stump took us several years of labor.  Rinpoche and I learned to mix up thousands of pounds of concrete, pouring new sidewalks and laying in beautiful flower gardens.

The Mongolian refugees had all arrived at about the same age—say, in their forties—almost 30 years before.  Now they were all equally elderly and needed our help with just about everything.  Rinpoche announced that my position at the Temple was Chipay Ta, which translates as “public horse.”

I was made available all day, every day, to take people in my snazzy red sports car to their doctor appointments; grocery shopping; and to stand in the long lines at the immigration or social security offices.  Suddenly it seemed that my impulsive decision to study Russian at Princeton had been preordained, since I could speak to all of the Mongolians, and translate for them out in the everyday world.

I became Khen Rinpoche’s personal servant and cook as well, which was actually a really good deal.  For every hour I spent under the house fixing ancient plumbing pipes, he made sure I got an hour of private classes in the greatest philosophical classics of ancient Asia.

In time, I built a large, separate structure where Khen Rinpoche could have his private quarters, along with a comfortable classroom for his public classes.  I also used the carpentry skills my Dad had taught me to build housing nearby for the 7 or 8 surviving ancient Mongolian monks at the temple.

Here’s a typical day during that labor.  I am up on the very top of a very dangerous extension ladder, finishing off painting the underside of the roof about three stories high above.  There’s no one to help me; nobody to hold the ladder steady, and if I forget say a cleaning rag I have to climb all the way down and back up on my own.

Old Man Umadikov suddenly shows up, grabbing the bottom of the ladder and threatening to pull it out and kill me in the process.  He is especially scary because he was a cavalry soldier during the Russian Revolution, for the Cossacks: the Warrior Brotherhood of Mother Russia.  The only way you get into this squad is if you fight a sword duel with another member of the Brotherhood and win.  He has a terrible long, angry scar down the side of his stone face from his duel.  I assume the other man was killed.  Now he’s like 80 years old and permanently angry.

“Hey Mike, get down here!  I gotta go to the grocery store!”

“No hey, Mr. Umadikov, just let me finish painting this soffit, and then I’ll jump down and get you there!”

“I gotta go now!  Get down here!”  He starts shaking the bottom of the ladder.  I’m going to die!

The point is though that Rinpoche demanded that we both serve all the old people with devotion, and grace.  We ended up doing so for over 25 years, and I believe that the energy from this service—even early on—was essential to my seeing emptiness directly.  

I believe that this taking care of the needy around us, with careful grace, was as much a factor in seeing emptiness as was the study and the meditation.  And that’s why I mention it here, for those of you seeking the same goal.  In my opinion, then, we can add this continual, devoted, and kindly service of the needy ones around us as a part of [15] the “means” aspect of the higher truth of the path to the end of pain—along with the general study of the classics we’ve already mentioned.

I would like to add here that specific service of individuals who are trying to spread or preserve the wisdom teachings which include instruction on how to see emptiness directly is a special cause to see it ourselves; which means I would add it, again, to [15] the aspect or “moment” of the means of stopping pain.

During my decades serving Khen Rinpoche, for example, I was almost always his driver when he needed to go somewhere; for example, to Washington DC during his English studies at Georgetown University, or monthly trips to the same city for many years to teach a group of students he eventually organized there.  When his English had reached the level that he could translate ancient classics from Tibetan, I carefully edited the books and typed them out (no computers even, in those days).

We were too poor to have the books printed, and so I studied hand bookbinding under a local master, and made all the necessary tools myself by cutting up thick sheets of brass, by hand.  Our first editions were printed on a hand press in our basement, and bound there too, one by one, painstakingly.  I add these details here because I believe that all of this kind of service of the Dharma as well contributed—in my case—to aspect [15]: the means, of the path, to see emptiness directly.



Group Three:
The pot on the stove


Momos and frozen macaroni

Khen Rinpoche and I quickly settled into a rhythm.  He stayed in the parish house, which was a tiny dwelling meant for a single monk who stepped over to the temple a few times a day to check the butter lamps were burning brightly and any elderly visitors were taken care of.  There was a super tiny bed in a little nook of a bedroom, and Rinpoche would perch up there sometimes to teach me the ancient books, while I sat on the floor.

Rinpoche was of the opinion that since I was born an American, I was automatically able to fix anything made in the United States: his watch, or the Volkswagen bug someone gave him later on.  I always gave it a go and only occasionally broke things completely trying to fix them (like that Volkswagen).  But I was handy and had soon put together a big collection of tools for all kinds of repairs around the temple grounds.

The other thing I was expected to do was to cook for him—and that was a bit of a disaster.  He quickly learned that my entire repertoire of dishes was opening cans of cheap food, or heating up frozen macaroni dinners.

On the next block though there was an ancient blind Mongolian lama who had a really good cook, a chubby smiley old Chinese monk named Gendun Jamtso.  Rinpoche enlisted him to come and give me lessons in cooking his favorite dishes—especially mo-mos, sort of a special dumpling that Rinpoche was crazy about.

Above all, I quickly learned to make Tibetan butter tea just the way that Rinpoche liked it.  This means I mixed in black Chinese tea leaves; sea salt; old butter; thick cream; tons of boiled milk and sometimes nutmeg or the like.  Then it had to be churned, sometimes in an old wooden churn: swoosh swoosh until just the right consistency, and just the right temperature.  My teacher would send back a cup of tea that wasn’t perfect five or six times, if he wasn’t happy with it.

The tea would take so long to boil to the right thickness that I learned to practice memorizing my scriptures, reciting out loud standing by myself there in the kitchen, as I watched the pot bubble.  I quickly reached the point—for example—where even before I knew what all the words meant I could recite the first three chapters of the famous Treasure House of Higher Knowledge, the Abhidharma Kosha, written almost two thousand years earlier.


Luminous images

And so on this day—July 28, 1975—four or five days after the full moon, I was standing in front of the stove, staring at a pot of water as it started to boil.  Something happened then, suddenly, but I want to make sure that you appreciate that it didn’t happen by accident, or just because of the last few hours or days before it.

That is, I hope you will think of all the pages I’ve written here so far, all the way back to things that logically must have happened long before Los Angeles, and see that these are the kinds of things you yourself will have to do, from now on, to “touch the diamond world”: to see emptiness directly.  And I repeat that—until that day—your life will be nothing but sadness, getting older, facing death, losing your friends and family and everything you have worked to own; unavoidably, inevitably.

You have a choice, and only this is it.

And so under the influence of everything that had gone before, suddenly I realized that I was not watching a pot of almost-boiling water on the stove.  I suddenly realized that our eyes cannot even see a pot of water.

Honestly I don’t know how it all works, but I do have this mental picture of my two eyeballs.  At the back of each ball, on the inside, the science teacher in my elementary school said that there are special cells—photosensitive cells.

When I look at a pot on the stove—my culture says—light reflects off the metal of the silver-colored pot and the plastic of the black plastic handle, sending pictures towards my eyes, which are detected as the cells at the back of my eyeball are struck by the light.  The cells as a group assume the outline and color of the pieces of the pot that appear to them, turning straight & black, or silver & circular.  And then, according to science, there is some back-and-forth communication with the brain:

“Hey brain, we got some shapes & colors out here!”

“Really?  Tell me what you got.”

“Two things here.  A silver circle, and then a straight black bar.”

“Ah,” says brain.  “Is Mike standing in front of the stove?  Is it Rinpoche’s tea time?”

“Exactly!”

“Well then, that’s a pot of water, just about to boil!  The silver circle is the metal pot, and the straight black line is the pot handle.”

But suddenly I saw that this isn’t quite the way it works.  Suddenly I was focusing somewhere towards the back of my head, and I saw mental pictures coming up there.  They came out of nowhere, but it felt like they were coming out of a place inside the back of my head.

The way I’ve described these images in the 50 years since is that they were luminous, meaning that they were giving off their own light, very much like the neon light on the front of a store announcing its name at nighttime.  They were perfect little luminous pots, there in the back of my head, and they were moving.

Slowly, almost gracefully, they traveled straight across my head to my forehead, to a spot between my eyebrows but further up, and then passed out of my head and down to the silver circle and black bar down on the stove.

I like to say that—in that moment—this procession of images began to settle down, one after another, on the silver and black out there on the stove.  The ancient Buddhist books say that this is happening at an incredible speed: 65 full pot images per millisecond proceeding out of the forehead and “landing” on the silver and the black.  This is, for example, just about the speed of the flow of sequential images in a decent film clip online.

When I try to describe this to my friends, I like to use the illustration of a bowl of ice cream.  Picture a bowl and inside of it say three balls of vanilla ice cream.  These balls are the individual parts of the pot on the stove: silver circles, black bar.

Complete pot images floating out from the spot at the center of our forehead then are like chocolate sauce: they continue on out and down towards the parts on the stove, and then settle atop them—unifying them into the impression of a pot on the stove.


Functionality

I can just feel you flinching a bit at that “impression of a pot” wording.  There’s a part of your mind that jumps up immediately and says “That’s not just an impression of a pot on the stove!  It’s a real pot on the stove!  The fact that you can boil water inside of it proves it’s a real pot on the stove!”

Alright alright, calm down and listen.  The way your mind, and my mind, work is that it automatically builds and maintains a cause-and-effect connection between the fire of the stove, and the boiling of the water here.  We all believe—we deeply and almost unchangeably believe—that the fire on the stove is causing the water to heat up and then boil.  And then the pot is helping to keep all this water contained in one place, and its metal is transfering the heat through to the water.

None of this functionality would be possible if the pot on the stove were just a potpourri of mental pictures.

But consider a different option here.  You don’t have to believe it yet, just consider it.  And then make a resolution to think about it in the days and months ahead.  Your life depends on it.

Suppose that it is not the fire below the pot that is heating it—and the water inside it—up to boiling.  Suppose that as minutes go by after you thought you turned on the stove, additional luminous mental images are floating across your head and out into the world before you.  Suppose that the boiling of the water is actually coming not from the fire below the pot, but actually consists of a coherent series of lightning-fast mental images proceeding from your own mind, out into the world.

Again, this is not an idea that you are required to subscribe to right away.  It’s just a proposal.  An intelligent person would listen carefully to the proposal, and then set about either proving or disproving it to themselves.  Especially if their life were at stake.

To summarize: cause & effect does indeed exist.  It just doesn’t work at all the way we always thought it did.  Any thinking person now would ask themselves, “Well, alright.  Suppose that’s all true.  Can you explain though where all these ‘pictures’ pop out of, when they show up in the back of my mind?  Is there any logic to the way it all works?”


Mental seeds

Our discussion here takes a major and life-saving turn into the question of karma.  The word is much abused in our modern world; but don’t worry much.  The poor word has been abused just about everwhere, forever.  So what does the word “karma” really mean?

A popular alternative word for “karma” in the ancient Buddhist scriptures is simply “mental seed.”  The expression “mental seed” is free of the many strange ideas that surround the word “karma”—and so that’s what we’re going to use in this essay.

And here’s exactly what we mean when we say, “mental seed.”  Suppose your neighbor is having a group of friends over, to celebrate her husband’s birthday.  She has planned a pretty fancy menu with a whole selection of different dishes.

Halfway through the cooking, she realizes that she has run out of pots to use, if she wants to make everything she was planning.
She rushes over to your house, where you too just happen to be preparing a big dinner to celebrate your parents’ wedding anniversary.  You have plans for each one of your kitchen pots today, but then here all of a sudden is your neighbor, begging to use one of them.

You really want to help her, so mentally you rearrange the meal you were planning to make, so that you can loan her the pot she needs to make her birthday celebration successful.

The strength of your willingness to help your neighbor makes an imprint on your mind, very similar to the imprint you might make with your thumb while pressing some clay into the shape of a coffee cup you are making in a pottery class.  Your willingness to help  another person crystallizes this imprint into a mental seed.

At this point, if you really want to understand what’s going on, you need to refer back through the great books of Eastern thinking to a particular teaching about the three types of changing things in the universe.

Anything in the universe that changes changes because the influences that set it into motion—the main causes (think tree seed) and the contributing factors (think soil, water, fertilizer, and sunlight)—pushed it into being with a certain amount of force, and that force as time goes on inevitably wears out.

Think now of one billiard ball struck by another: the second ball starts off across the billiard table, gradually slowing down because of the friction of the table surface and the surrounding air, finally coming to a stop.

Seeds inevitably act just the same.  Once they push out a sprout, they gradually lose their power as the sprout grows towards the sky, turning into a tall tree.  Which is to say, every tree that was ever planted on this entire planet started upwards and then eventually slowed down; stopped growing; and then in time finally fell lifeless to the earth.  The same with every baby who stood up on his or her legs, and in time laid back down dead on the surface of the planet.

Let’s get back to the seed you planted when you loaned the pot you actually needed yourself to your neighbor instead.  Your intention here was a good intention, and a good intention influences how your new mental seed eventually grows: sooner or later, it will sprout into a pot that you find very useful at the moment.

Here’s the exciting part.  It’s easy to go around saying that you get what you give, and that whatever you do—good or bad—to another person turns around and comes back to you.  If we all really believed in that enough to act upon it day to day, the world might finally become a completely sweet and peaceful place.  The reason we all don’t believe in this idea though is that no one has ever explained it to us in a way that we can really believe, and follow, in our daily life.

Well, that changes now.

When you do decide and then actually act to give something to someone else that you actually need for yourself—that last cooking pot—factors like your understanding of how the process works and the strength of your desire to help the other person help place a powerful imprint in your mind: a karmic seed.

Here in our discussion so far, we’ve actually already met the three different types of changing things in the universe.  First there is any physical object in the world that has grown through main causes and contributing factors: think of the tree, growing from the main cause of a seed and depending for its health on contributing factors like sunlight, soil, fertilizer, and the rest.

Secondly there are mental events, which grow and then fade as their inner causes wax and then wane: we read the essay, we suddenly understand how karma really works, and then unless we reinforce that understanding we get busy thinking about other things and gradually forget about the whole thing—and go back to our inexorably crumbling human existence.

Third though we have this almost unnoticed, all-powerful category of the seeds in our mind: karmic seeds, from doing something nice or not so nice to another person.  These live in our mind, but they are not made of mind.  This is because “mind” is defined by knowing, by being aware; and these seeds are not things that are aware.  They don’t think, they don’t know—even though their residence is the mind.

Karmic seeds then have no physical parameters: no color, no shape, no particular length or width.  Nor do they have mental parameters, thinking this or feeling that.  They are pure potential—pure “maybe this will happen”—and this means we will never be able to observe them through physical means.  But you don’t have to crawl under your kitchen sink to see, with absolute certainty, that a pipe there is leaking; you have a puddle that the leak created, right there in the middle of the kitchen floor, to prove the existence of the unseen leak.

Karmic seeds then are the ones invisibly spewing out those pot-on-the-stove images that pop into the back of Mike’s mind as he’s waiting for Rinpoche’s tea water to boil; the luminous images that float to the forehead and then out on the stove.  As the sutras aptly put it, “The entire world, and everything within it, is a production of karma: of how we have treated others before.”


Dependent events

According to these same holy books, the entire universe divides into two different kinds of things: emptiness, and dependence.  The fact of dependence—the fact that the entire universe rests upon our inner karmic seeds—is the one that you finally confirm, after living for countless billions of years throughout every possible corner of this universe, on the day you yourself have your own version of the “pot on the stove experience.”

Like emptiness and karma and the four “noble” truths, the grand principle of dependence has been mangled in translation.  We often hear in early Western translations of the Asian classics the term “dependent origination,” which has no real practical meaning to a normal person and just about guarantees the death of one of the only ideas that can save our life.

The common Asian translation here of “cause & effect” is somewhat better, but still wanting.  We personally prefer “dependent events.”  This is because of the deeper meaning of the original Sanskrit: pratitya samutpada (technical spelling pratītya samutpāda), or “events occurring through a dependent connection.”

That is, we have to remember that if we’re out to explain why the whole universe happens in the first place, we need to explain not only things that have happened because of causes (“grew”), but also things that have happened but which did not have causes (“happened, but not because they grew”).  Both can be referred to as events that occur; both are real; and the universe is made of both.

For an example of things that have happened because of causes, we have only to go so far as that tree we were talking about.  But there are also things that happen but which don’t have formal causes.  One of the most famous of these is anything which exists, but which exists as a simple absence.

This doesn’t have to be as complicated as it sounds.  You had a mouse in your kitchen, and your wife is one of the smart, compassionate types who realizes that a small live trap is just as good as mouse poison.  She set the (inexpensive, always-works) live trap out in the middle of the kitchen floor last night, and boom there it is this morning, with a frisky happy little mouse in it.  You even have fun taking the kids out in a meadow on the outskirts of town and dropping off the mouse—alive—to enjoy the rest of his life.  (A great life-example for the kids as well.)

In the moment that you and the kids passed through the kitchen door with the trap and its mouse in your hands, an absence came into being, there in the kitchen.  That absence (of a mouse in the kitchen) is a real thing, and it manifests as the end of mouse poop and late-night scurrying noises in your kitchen.

But that absence was not a changing entity, exhibiting the constant fluctuation say of a tree growing through its constant changes.  Mice are either there in your kitchen, or they are not: it’s an on/off sort of situation.  The lack of mice in your kitchen had a first moment of existence, and it will probably some day have a last moment of existence (when another mouse discovers your kitchen), but it didn’t gradually start up nor will it gradually wind down, the way any caused or grown sort of existence does.

The reason we mention this is so that you can appreciate that there are two kinds of events in your world: those that grow, and those that don’t, but which do really come into existence without the gradual expansion implied by the word “growing.”  And sooner or later you will have to come to the realization that both types of existing things were brought into existence by those luminous mental pictures.

Bottom line, mental pictures are responsible for everything in the universe—in your universe.  If there are two great principles behind your whole universe—dependence, and emptiness—then the early morning of the day you see emptiness directly is a time to see the first: the pot on the stove.  And then later in the same morning you will see emptiness directly, and that’s a whole different thing.


Details of the second path

We would be remiss here if we didn’t fit this pot-on-the-stove experience into the structure of the five-path flow which is so crucial to ancient Buddhist literature.  Remember, this is different from the concept of the four truths and their 16 aspects, or “moments”—which we’ll get back to after that.

We’ve seen that the second of the five paths is the “path of preparation,” during which we are preparing to see emptiness directly.  I personally would say that—for me—this path began during my formal studies, especially in the Himalayas, triggered by the first path of sadness about my mother’s illness and approaching death.

Scripturally, this second path is divided into four stages, differentiated by deepening understandings about the nature of subjects and objects of perception.  These four stages are named Warmth, Peak, Mastery, and Highest Thing Of All.  Warmth and Peak are said to represent insights into objects, and then Mastery and Highest Thing of All consist of insights into the subjects that hold such objects.

In my personal experience, I would say that Warmth and Peak occurred during my deepening understanding of that chi-jedrak: quality & characteristic.  Mastery occurred during the weeks of transition to the pot-on-the-stove experience; and it’s important to note here that, according to scripture, one can no longer be born into a lower realm (hell, craving spirits, animals) once they have reached Mastery.

From where you’re sitting right now as you read these words, it may not seem crucial or crucially interesting that you could reach a sort of spiritual “guarantee” that you would never again suffer greatly after death.  Believe me, this blasé attitude will disappear when you get close to my age!  Why not take care of this sort of thing while you are still relatively young?  Then you don’t have to worry!

The experience of the pot on the stove is, without doubt, the “Highest Thing of All” stage described in scripture for the end of the second path.  The ancient books are quick to point out that, yes, the direct experience of emptiness is itself the real highest thing of all—but the breakthrough of observing those mental images directly, for the first time, is the very “highest thing of all” in the normal world, the world of pain without hope.


A note on words
and a middle way

As you read through the ultimately detailed presentation on emptiness offered by Masters Nagarjuna, Chandrakirti, and Tsongkapa below, you will often come across wording that describes how things exist as nothing more than “labeled with names” or words.  Many of the many proofs in our opus here depend on this turn of phrase, so it’s important—I think—to identify its place here in the actual experience of emptiness.

It’s absolutely crucial here to understand that terms like “names” or “labels” or even “words” itself all refer to the luminous mental images that we just talked about.  In this context, the word “name” itself is an abbreviation for “luminous mental picture”: more of an image, then a verbalization.

From here then it’s easy to see what “merely a creation of names” is referring to in middle way philosophy: all the pots and other things we ever experience are composites of those luminous images coming out of the karmic seeds inside our own mind.  We ourselves are literally creating our world, as we behave with kindness or meanness to our fellow living beings.

From this understanding, it’s completely easy to slip into understanding the real meaning of the famous expression “middle way” itself.  From one point of view (I personally would say from the “capitals” point of view, Middle Way, or Madhyamika) this phrase refers to a highly developed philosophical school in late medieval India.  This is in fact the school that we are seeing explained here in our text, and explains even its base title: “Entering the Middle Way.”

But from a grander point of view, “middle way” is a way of looking at our world free of two extremes of opinion—which puts it in the middle.  And the pot on the stove experience gives us an unerring reference point to understand this “middle.”

The first extreme would be to believe that the pot on the stove exists the way we always assumed it did: out there, on its own, appearing to us because we took it out of the cabinet.  This “object-ive” view of reality—by the way—is the one that most of science is based upon.  And the fallacies contained in this view are the reason why science has yet to lead to human happiness.

The second extreme would be to say that—if the pot didn’t exist the way we always thought it did, in some objective way—then the pot couldn’t exist at all.  This second opinion carries all the baggage of beliefs that nothing is real; nothing really exists; it doesn’t matter how we treat other people; it doesn’t matter what we do with our life.

The middle way between these two mistaken opinions is the realization that the pot on the stove is coming from me: from the way I shared, or refused to share, my pots in the past—and planted corresponding seeds for luminous pictures, or reality itself.


Assigning moments
to the pot on the stove

And so it’s finally come time for us to assign one or more of the 16 moments of the four higher truths to our “pot on the stove” experience.  Again I believe this assignment is in some ways subjective, but again because of my unique personal experience I’m not aware of another person in this world at this moment who could make the assignment with more authority.

First I would assign [8] the moment of “factor” (pratyaya in the Sanskrit) to the luminous pictures which emerge from karmic seeds in our minds and compose every object in our world, changing or unchanging.  Again, “factors” in this sense subsume all the words in the world; and as a side note I would say that languages such as Chinese, where the pictures and words are combined, would have certain specific advantages here, for communication.

Secondly I would say that [5] the moment of the “source” of suffering consists of the fact that it is the negative mental seeds especially which produce our repeated personal existence of death and pain.  Implicit here is the fact that all the trouble that ever comes to each one of us—and repeated death itself—is all something that each one of us has created for ourselves by ourselves: it is impossible to blame another living being for anything negative that ever happens to us.

We do though have some good news happening here at the second path, and this is that we have started the process of eliminating our suffering, forever.  Because of our direct experience of the mental seeds and luminous pictures, all seeds that could create for us the image of a lower rebirth have been prevented or “spoiled”: we may still have some from before, but they are like ruined flower seeds that will never produce a plant in our garden.  As such, we have here our first steps of moment [9] the end of pain (nirodha in the Sanskrit).



Group Four:
Touching the diamond

The emptiness of things, and me

Just a side note.  The time period between seeing the pot on the stove, and the direct perception of emptiness, is a particularly intriguing subject for me.  I don’t remember a lot of details, but I know that after all those once-in-a-lifetime realizations about the luminous mental images, I did finish making that cup of tea for Rinpoche, and took it to his room for him.

Perhaps I took care of some other responsibilities after that, but the bottom line is that I ended up in the temple, on a meditation cushion on the floor, ready for my daily practice.  I believe that it is inevitable that a person who personally witnesses luminous images in action will—within a few hours—sit down in deep meditation and see emptiness directly.  

I have the strong conviction that the two events always happen, for every person in history, within a few hours of each other.  I have often reflected that those few hours are a unique period in the billions of years of a person’s life; they cannot die, I believe, during those hours, which cannot be said of any other hours among those billions of years.  And they cannot be distracted from the coming vision, by any circumstance in this entire universe.

So here is what actually happens when you see emptiness directly.

I sat down to meditate on the right side of the Mongolian temple, back towards the double doors leading to the front foyer; it is no exaggeration to say that the temple—because of what happened there that day—is a holy place, and a great place to stop by yourself someday and get some personal blessing from it.  (It’s called Rashi Gempil Ling Buddhist Temple, and is found on 5th Street in Howell, New Jersey).

I remember a distinct impression of rising up physically to a certain level of meditation, the one I mentioned earlier, almost as if I were in an elevator.  I have not typically had this sensation in my meditations either before or after that day.

And then I went into emptiness.

There’s a whole lot to say about how you can’t say anything about the actual experience.  When you go through the experience of the pot on the stove, your mind is in a discursive mode—which more or less means that you are still having your normal mental conversation with yourself, the whole time.  That also implies, naturally, that you would have quite a bit to say about what happened to you at the time.

According to the scriptures, there is a difference in the general class of object we are focusing upon during the two experiences.  During the pot on the stove, we are—naturally—focused on this object (or another one like it; but don’t forget that it’s significant that the object in this case was being used to serve a cup of tea to an extraordinary teacher who was daily explaining these things to people).  It’s important to say that by implication we are understanding, if not immersed in, at that moment a sort of emptiness as well: the emptiness of a metal pot on the stove.

When we say “emptiness” in this case, it’s crucial that you appreciate that we are not talking about some mystic space or something.  It’s a very simple and specific absence of something that we always thought was there: a pot that existed out there on the stove that was coming from its own side; a pot that was created in a factory somewhere and ended up in this particular kitchen.

In fact, ancient Buddhist scripture has a special word for people who have not seen emptiness—for the opposite of an arya, a “higher being.”  This term is tsur-tong (technical spelling tsur-mthong), which literally means “people who see things as coming this way,” towards them.  And of course when we ourselves have that “pot on the stove” experience, just before we see emptiness directly we are realizing that things come from us: that they are composites of those luminous mental images popping out of our mental seeds and flying out to create the pot in front of us.

Scripture further says that there is a crucial difference in the object of the two experiences; and we have this and other additional formal insights in that scripture simply because there have been countless individuals in this entire universe who saw emptiness directly long before I did, and who then continued on to the higher levels that we will talk about below, including total enlightenment.

And they have left us records of levels that I myself will not reach for some time; although it should be said here that the direct experience of emptiness by an arya on the first day of their aryaship is qualitatively said to be no different, in any respect, from the direct experience of emptiness on a constant basis by an enlightened being.  And so it can be difficult to find a good description of these higher levels that we will all eventually go through; the latter part of the commentary by Je Tsongkapa here is a classic source.

The bottom line is that the experience of “the pot on the stove” will typically be directed at some object in our life, such as that pot; whereas the first direct experience of emptiness in that deep state of meditation is tied up with our perception of myself—in my case, of Michael.

What’s ironic about the length of the direct perception though is that we cannot be aware of ourselves during that time.  You see, emptiness is an absence of something: it is the fact that something is not there.  It’s not easy, but conceptually—long in advance—you have to get used to the idea that you will not be seeing something: it’s not as if emptiness is like a pot or like darkness at night or unconsciousness when you get knocked out in an accident, or under anesthesia during an operation at the hospital.

Rather, emptiness is the absence of something that you thought was there; that you expected to be there.  A good friend invites you out to dinner at a nice restaurant and then when you show up on time, there is an “absence of friend” present there at the restaurant because there was a bad accident uptown, and your friend is still stuck there in a cab.

The friend, by the way, is real; and the fact of the friend not being in the restaurant at the appointed hour is just as real.

In our case here though—by the way—what we perceive during our deep meditation as something missing is something that could never have been there in the first place: Michael the Meditator who was not a composite of luminous pictures coming from the karmic seeds inside of Michael’s mind.

Experientally (and, after all, that is the priceless value of this account), we drop into the perception of an absence of a Michael who was never possible; except that in the hour that you yourself reach this perception, it will be the absence of the you who was never possible.

Again, you can have no other thoughts or perceptions for the length of this communion with ultimate reality.  You cannot be aware of yourself, because you are not emptiness: you are not ultimate reality.  You cannot be aware of how much time has passed inside of the direct perception, because time itself is not emptiness: it is not ultimate reality.

When you look back at the time you spent in this direct communion with ultimate reality, you might even feel cheated in a way.  There you were, but there was no way you could tell you were there—no way to exult inside and say, “I did it!!”  Perceiving at that time anything other than emptiness would force you out of your emptiness realization.

You did know though roughly what time you sat down to meditate, and naturally when you come out one of the first things you do is to look at the clock, to see how long you were “under.”  In my case, it was about 20 minutes, and I believe this is typical for the first direct perception of emptiness.

People have asked me if I have seen emptiness directly again during these last 50 years, and I can honestly answer “No, I haven’t!”  I admit that there have probably been months or years during this period when my meditation was not well maintained enough to reach the necessary platform to see emptiness directly.

But I do think—looking back with a half century of intense scripture study and thought under my belt—that the seeds to go into the direct perception of emptiness are simply too karmically “expensive” for a new arya to have a repeat experience of it even within decades.  We have already discussed the presumptive many past lifetimes of work I put in well before my birth into this life, and if we consider those as part of the prerequisites for the one experience in this present lifetime, we can appreciate that the direct perception may be much more rare than we ever imagined.


Assigning moments
to the direct experience

You may have noticed that the moments or aspects among the 16 that we’ve mentioned so far were heavily bunched into the first two arya truths: pain, and the cause of pain.  If you think about it, this is natural for a person who is trying to pull themselves out of the world of inevitable death.  We see what’s wrong, and then we try to find out how to stop it.

I would say that this one day on which you first spot luminous images and then go on to touch the diamond world—or emptiness—directly corresponds to aspect [9], which is itself called “the end” (nirodha in the Sanskrit).

Scripture says that we can treat “ending” here in two distinctly different ways.

The first, obviously, is the end of pain; for the day that we first see emptiness directly is the first day of what is known as “entering the stream.”  Here I always think of a Jackie Chan movie where he’s of course in a kung-fu fight with a bad guy, but the heroine is glued to a conveyor belt inexorably headed into a bunch of huge blades that are going to chop her into little pieces, if Jackie can’t get her off quick!

Except in this case, the inexorable belt is headed towards nirvana and enlightenment, and there is nothing that can prevent it.  Once we go through those 20 minutes of seeing emptiness directly, we are headed in a very short, fixed time to the end of all suffering and death.  And there is no force in the universe that can stop us: not even a fully enlightened Buddha could do so, even supposing they would ever want to.  Imagine how that feels!

There is a deeper ending here, which is the absence of all wrong ideas about where things are coming from, particularly myself.  It’s as if after seeing that the pot on the stove is made of layers of luminous images, all the other parts of the stove—the ones that are coming from their own side—suddenly just drop away.

The absence of these parts of the pot, and myself, that were never there in the first place is exactly what emptiness really is.  When our understanding reaches this point, we are finally beyond any of those strange ideas—which have covered whole countries in centuries past—which say that emptiness means sitting absolutely unmoving in front of a wall and trying to empty the mind; to think about nothing.

In a moral sense too this improved version of emptiness makes a lot more sense.  If the meaning of emptiness is that nothing really exists, or that nothing really matters or that there is no good or evil, every one of us feels deep down inside that something is missing—something must be wrong.

But if emptiness means that there is nothing that doesn’t come from luminous images flying out of karmic seeds in my mind, then that automatically implies that there is a moral basis to everything in the universe.  People who are generous with their pots always have pots, and people who steal pots from others—as these seeds ripen—never have the things they need or want.

And when people finally figure out (as they must eventually do, for after all we are all thinking creatures) that this is the way the universe works, then the world will become a place filled with moral and generous people.


Diamonds:
the perfect metaphor

Any person who goes through those 20 minutes in the direct perception of emptiness goes through another experience just after they come down out of this perception.  Sitting on our meditation cushion after that life-changing experience, we are aware for the first time that the entire universe is composed of two different “layers” of reality.

That is, we now know that there is a “higher” reality—the sheer emptiness of anything not coming from my luminous images—that is present here in every nook and corner of where we ourselves live.  And then there is the “apparent” reality that we’ve always walked through; apparent, because it seems to come from its side, and not from mine.  Sometimes this second level of reality is called “deceptive” reality, since it tends to “trick” us about where things are coming from—like kitchen pot factories or appliance stores, and not from supplying a pot to a neighbor who really needs one today.

And so now we are sure—for the first time in our life—that there really is a higher reality.  We also know, instinctively, that we won’t be able to get back to it anytime soon: the seeds that projected those 20 minutes were just too expensive, and rare—accumulated probably over many lifetimes of effort.

And so every “new” arya sitting on their meditation cushion just after the grand vision immediately begins working on this specific problem in their life: “How am I going to remember what I just saw?  Is there any object here in the normal world that I could keep close to me, to forever remind me of what I saw?  For this memory to fade would be the greatest disaster in a human life.”

Our mind searches the old familiar universe we grew up in, and for every single new arya in the history of the universe, it comes to the diamond.  And why is that?

You see, in those sort of frantic moments grasping for some way to remember, we are casting about for something which is the most of anything: the highest of anything, just like the ultimate reality of emptiness which we just came out of.  And what we realize in the opening minutes of this search is that there is nothing which is the most or the highest of anything, here in the universe.

That is, there is no longest thing in the world: you can always add another inch.  There is no shortest thing in the world: if something has any width at all, you can therefore divide it in half.  No hottest thing, no coldest thing, no farthest thing, no nearest thing.  You get the picture.  But we desperately need to find something here in the normal world which is ultimate, just the way the emptiness that we saw was.

And every human mind at this point will come up with the diamond.  I want to emphasize here that before those minutes, I had no particular interest in diamonds, and no particular knowledge of them either.  I knew that when a woman got engaged to be married in my culture, their fiancé often bought them a ring that had a diamond in it; my general impression was that this was because diamonds were really hard and didn’t break easily, and were also really beautiful, so this was a nice symbol that the coming marriage would be happy and long-lived.

I also knew that raw diamond crystals came deep out of mines somewhere—Africa was a common location, I knew—but I had never seen or touched a diamond crystal, and again had no particular interest in them.

But suddenly, having come down out of emptiness, I knew that diamond was the one object in this reality that best represented this higher reality.  Diamond is the hardest commonly available, naturally occurring substance in the universe, and under normal circumstances nothing can cut it.

I remember that in the years following my experience sitting in the Mongolian temple, I was asked by my teacher to organize educational classes for the young Mongols in the neighborhood.  After reading Buddhist stories in the temple or acting them out in little drama plays there, the kids would clamber into the tiny church kitchen for snacks.

By that time, I had a small raw diamond crystal that I would keep in a little “spring ring” that you could open or close with a press of the fingers.  I showed it to some of the kids and then got distracted getting their refreshments ready.  By the time I turned back around, they had discovered that the diamond was so hard that they could easily write their names on the temple kitchen window glass.  I remember that Khen Rinpoche gave me an earful and how the names stayed there for many years, since we were  in no mood—or finances—to replace the panes of glass.

Aside from being just about the hardest thing in the universe, diamonds are also perfectly transparent.  If you and I were sitting on chairs facing each other and there was a thick wall of pure diamond between us—and if no other source of light were reflecting on the wall—then it would be perfectly invisible to the both of us.

This also fit the ultimate reality of emptiness; every room that you and I have ever sat in has had examples of emptiness all around it: the emptiness of the chair, emptiness of the table, emptiness of the people sitting at the table.  We are—all day long—literally surrounded by examples of this highest reality, which could save our lives if we only saw it once.  And yet without special training and preparation, it is normally entirely invisible to us.

The third quality of diamond that was important to me at that moment was that every diamond in the entire universe is equally pure, with the exact same atomic structure.  This was not something I knew from study at that moment, but something I knew about diamond by instinct.  In a similar way, every object in the universe has its own emptiness, absolutely pure and absolutely equal.

And so some of my first thoughts while sitting there, fresh out of the direct perception of emptiness, were that I should try to obtain a diamond that could remind me of what I had seen; and that for the rest of my life I should try to be around diamonds as much as I could.

As for the 16 moments of the four higher truths, I would assign this experience of the diamond to [11] “beauty” (which is pranita in the Sanskrit).  This is one of the four aspects of the truth of the end of suffering; and end which is triggered by our direct perception of the emptiness which the diamond represents.  And, ultimately, the end of pain is as beautiful as a fine diamond.

There is sort of footnote here, a discrete realization towards the end.  This is where the newborn arya realizes, very clearly, that the diamond as a metaphor for emptiness is the closest thing in normal reality to emptiness, but at the same time not very close at all!  It’s like diamond is there at the top of a ladder but emptiness is a million miles further, somewhere near the next galaxy out.

Years later, in addition to the massive diamond jewelry company I will describe below, I started a smaller diamond company on my own.  When I was trying to think of a name for the firm, I came up with “Near Diamonds” to try to remember this particular realization from my “diamond day.”  But I thought the name might lead to some confusion (“What? Do they only sell fake diamonds?”) and in the end, I went with “Hancock Diamonds,” since this is my wife Veronica’s maiden name, and means a lot to me.

By the way, I firmly belief that this “close but not quite” aspect of diamonds is responsible for the name of the oldest printed book in the world, and perhaps the one book most published ever in the history of this world.  This is the famous Diamond Cutter Sutra.  

Nowhere in the entire book is diamond mentioned, not even once.  And despite the fact that the book has been mis-named “The Diamond Sutra” in different generations and countries throughout history, the original title is indisputably Vajra Chedika Sutra (technical spelling Vajracchedikā Sūtra), or The Diamond Cutter.  Now how did it get a name like that?  And what diamond is being cut?



Group Five:
The immediate aftermath

A real prostration

Eventually I stood up from my meditation cushion, and began walking towards the front of the temple.  Buddhists, from the time they are kids, are trained to walk around temples and similar holy places in a clockwise direction; and so I headed kitty-corner towards the northwestern side of the altar.

As I walked, I was looking ahead towards the massive altar that covered the whole front of the temple.  I remember the first time I laid eyes on this altar.  Remember, I had come to the temple direct from Princeton, where I had been serving as an acolyte (or altar boy) in the Princeton University Chapel, a massive gothic cathedral all carved stone and stained glass, nearly 100 feet high.  A completely silent and somber space.

Our Mongol temple was the complete opposite.  The walls were literally covered with paintings and hangings of a wild assortment of Buddhist angel and deities, with terrifying depictions of the realms of hell sprinkled almost randomly among them.  The altar was wildly populated by random statues of every Buddha you could imagine, made of every material you could imagine, dressed in every color of cloth you could imagine, with a range of artistry from classical to folk Buddhas that looked as though a child had made them at first grade in school.

I later learned that most of these images had been housed in small village temples in Kalmykia, the Mongol outpost near southern Russia.  When the Nazis came through, frightened villagers grabbed every image they could, threw it in the back of a horse wagon, and ran.  And so they had ended up here in New Jersey, along with the refugees.

It took me years to make the adjustment from the Princeton Cathedral to chaos of the Mongolian sacred space, and I had frankly been very Princetonly judgemental of the arrangements there.

But today, still under the influence of the communion with emptiness (as I was, indeed, for the entire rest of the day), I suddenly had a realization about all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas painted and sculpted here.  The very smallest, plainest, homely clay Buddha image had been fashioned by someone who had seen another image before that.  And that image, in turn, had been crafted by another person who had laid eyes on an earlier image, and so on inexorably from some very first Buddha image made by an individual who had themselves seen the Buddha in person.  

Suddenly I realized that the most simple image among this chaos of images was a direct line to an enlightened being—and a being who had once seen, for their first time, the very same emptiness I had seen for myself today, and thus entered the stream ending in Buddhahood.

And with that realization, I suddenly knew that I had to throw myself down on the floor in reverence before this evidence of enlightenment.  Us Buddhists are taught by our teachers that when we meet with an image of Lord Buddha—or any other Buddha—we should join our palms, and bow in respect.  In special circumstances, we are encouraged to do a formal prostration, most often on our hands and knees.

But today I knew that to truly pay worthy respect, I should throw myself flat on the floor, face in the floor, to everyone in this little crowd of Buddhas.  It felt very right, and I stayed there like that, silent and happy, for quite some time.  The seeds we plant with heartfelt respect of the teachings and teachings is a form of that aspect [15], the “means” to the end of pain.

Then I was drawn to sit for meditation once more—this time on the near side, the south side, of the benches used by the monks during ceremonies at the temple.


Walking the planets

Here I went into meditation; I don’t think I had a meditation cushion ready, but we had a pretty cozy carpet on the floor, that Rinpoche and I had picked out—wildly multicolored on purpose, to hide the inevitable butter lamp stains that you find all over the floor at every such temple.

I went pretty deep pretty fast, and inwardly I was “looking” straight ahead.

Suddenly a figure formed in front of me: it was my Mom, alive, looking young and pretty as I remembered her from my childhood.  She wasn’t sitting in meditation, but she was seated on the floor in front of me, slightly elevated.  She looked as though she was in some kind of cave with soft lighting.  I was looking straight into her face, and she had that look you see in a person who is troubled by something, and you can tell.

In my heart, I knew she was thinking about life: about the pain of life, both her own and that of her boys and everyone else she cared for.  And I knew that it was deeply troubling her.

Suddenly I knew that—in no small part because of my experience that day already—I could help her with her problem, help her in an ultimate way.  I could help her overcome death forever, and the death of all those dear to her.  I was on my way, I was already in the stream, it would not be long now.

And this I told her: “Mom, I know what’s worrying you; death, and pain for all whom you and I love, inevitable in this life.  But it can be stopped, it can be prevented.  And earlier today something happened to me that’s going to make it possible for me to help you, and everybody else there is.  I am coming, and it won’t be long.  I will help you, I will save you, I will stop your suffering forever.”

My Mom, as any mom would, brightened up immediately with the hope of it.  She smiled to let me know she understood, understood everything.  And then she faded, along with the light grey cave, and then another figure formed there: the image of my Father, also surrounded by soft darkness.

Dad looked the same as Mom had: he was happy to see me, but I could tell that he was very worried about something—about life itself, and his own coming death, and the death of everyone dear to him.  I spoke, in my mind, and gave him the same assurances I had given my Mother: “I am coming; I am near to enlightenment; and when I reach it I will be there to help you.  All will be well.  We will all be happy.”

Dad acknowledged my words, and believed them, and his face brightened in smile.  And then he too faded, to be replaced by my older brother, Geoff.

Geoff had the same troubled look, and I gave him the same assurances, and he left with the same comfort.  One by one, all of my close and more extended family members made their appearance, and left with the same quiet happiness.

And then came all of our neighbors back home, only a small number of them known to me by name—but receiving from me the same promise, and the same comfort.

Then came—still individually, still one by one—all the people in my city back home; and then all the people in the next city over; and all those in the next cities, until I had personally met each individual, people of all ages and backgrounds, from coast to coast in my home country.

Then came all the people in other countries, until I had met and assured every single individual living in our entire world.

And then something wonderful happened: our family dog George, who I think had passed away by that time, appeared before me, young and frisky and happy to receive my assurances.  George was followed by all the dear pets of people all over our neighborhood, and our entire city, and then gradually all of the pets in the world, friends of the world’s humans.  Each of the animals could understand what I told them, and each one left reassured.

Then began an incredible parade of every individual animal upon this entire planet, billions upon billions of them, from massive sea whales down to individual microbes.  I met each one with their own personality, and gave each one my assurances.

How much time did I spend meeting these billions upon billions of living creatures, individually, and assuring them—individually?  The subjective passage of time for me was somewhere in the vicinity of a half hour to an hour.  In the years since then, I have felt some attraction to studying the theories of the relativity (bendability) of time and space described by Albert Einstein and his fellow physicists, starting from the simple proof of these ideas they derived from observing the way in which the planet Mercury transits or passes out from behind the Sun, and the light reflected from it is bent and slowed by the Sun’s gravity on its way to us—thus effectively slowing down time itself.

We know then that time can slow or speed up; in a way we knew this from how minutes pass faster or slower as we spend time with those we love, or in the dentist’s chair.  And so even just scientifically and through personal experience, we feel that the speed of the passage of time can be manipulated.

In my case I had enough time after all that I’ve described above to undertake offering the same sorts of assurances to people and animals on other planets—in fact, upon every planet in the universe: every planet that exists.  Buddhism for example asserts that the physical universe has no outer boundary, which means that there is no end to the number of planets around us, and thus no end to the number of living beings around us.

At the same time, Buddhism asserts that a person under these special circumstances—under the influence of these unique realizations, which are considered a separate sort of consciousness altogether—can and does meet every living being in existence, to deliver them comfort.

Technically speaking, the scriptures describe the experience that I went through in those minutes as reaching a universal attitude of love known as bodhichitta, or the Wish to help all living beings become enlightened.  A person who has had this experience thereby becomes a genuine bodhisattva—and this is the true meaning of the term.

Thus we can describe a single person who has had both the direct experience of emptiness and of this universal emotion of love as a bodhisattva arya.

Personally I would categorize this last experience as aspect or moment [10]—a step in the truth of the end of suffering—which goes by the name of “peace” (shanta in the original Sanskrit).


The books are true,
and must be saved

I remember standing up then and walking past the altar down to the northeast corner of the temple: towards the side door.  Here I was close to one part of the Kangyur collection of ancient books that our temple held.
