Long before my own arrival, a very special sponsor had donated to the Temple an extremely rare, woodblock printing of the 100 volumes of this collection, which contains within it all the nearly 1,000 sutras and other teachings of the historical Buddha which survive up to the present time, in Tibetan translation.  These were unbound sheaves wrapped in individual silk covers, bright and beautiful, in individual cubbyholes reaching up to the ceiling of the Temple.

Here I paused, and here I had another wave of realization.  I was now sure—from my own personal experience—that every single sentence contained in these hundred thousand pages or so was completely true.  And in fact, these books and their commentaries (about another 3,700 ancient explanations, along with perhaps several hundred thousand more recent commentaries, in the last thousand years) contained almost everything of true value in this entire world.

Only these books were absolutely true, and absolutely capable of granting to people a life beyond death itself.  If they were ever lost in this world, then it would literally be more serious and irrevocable than if the sun above us had suddenly been snuffed out.

And so suddenly I was very, very sure that during the rest of the years left to me on this planet, I had to—every single day—do everything I could humanly accomplish to make sure that these books survived in this world, and were translated into the modern languages of this world, and spread throughout this world as widely as possible, to every human soul who might possibly be interested to learn about them.

Within the next decade then I had helped start the Asian Classics Input Project (ACIP, since renamed to ALL, or the Asian Legacy Library) with the goal of finding, digitalizing, and making free online copies of all these texts.  I see this as a project that might require the next few hundred years.  I am happy to say that we did succeed in completing—within the first 20 years or so of our work—the searchable digitalization of all the nearly 5,000 works surviving from ancient India, and they are now available without charge online, to the general public.

In the last 10 years, we have further organized the Diamond Cutter Classics non-profit organization dedicated to training young scholars to begin translating these works, and we have already completed thousands of pages of finished publications, including the present volumes.  You can find a list of all the works finished and in progress, at the end of this set of four books.  I am happy to say that in these past decades, we have attracted a wonderful group of supporters from all over the world, to help us make this dream come true.

As for the 16 moments, I would include this realization into [16] “method” (in the Sanskrit, nairyanika), which is the last of the four aspects within the arya truth of the path to the end of suffering.  This is a recognition of the fact that these records of enlightened teaching are almost literally the only thing that can help all human beings on this world to free themselves from pain.


Seven lifetimes to go

In these following minutes, there washed over me several waves of understanding about my own future years.  The most important was that I realized that I would live another seven lifetimes (including this present lifetime as the first) processing what had happened to me, and completing my own journey through the higher levels and on up to Buddhahood itself.

It was several years later that—during my continued studies of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma) with Khen Rinpoche—I came across a specific description of these same seven lifetimes.  In ancient Tibetan, the arya to live them is referred to as sipa len dunbawa (technical spelling, srid-pa lan bdun-pa-ba): “one with seven suffering lifetimes left to go.”

Now seven lifetimes of suffering, if we take each one at around 70 years, for a total of some 500 more years of pain before our own perfect enlightenment, would naturally seem quite a disaster to most of us.  But an arya, for the first time, perceives exactly how many entire lifetimes of intense pain and sadness they have gone through earlier, up to this point.

And there is no number to describe these lives of pain, for their total sum is beyond any number.  Simple logic, as we mentioned earlier with throwing the two dice, stipulates that this life must have had a life before it which helped determine its details and events: nothing happens from nothing, and no cause can ever engender a dissimilar result.  Lemon seeds don’t grow watermelons.

And so an arya looks back at infinite confirmed instances of pain, and looks ahead to those 500 more years of ever-decreasing pain, and then complete bliss for all the rest of eternity.  Not a bad deal!

I would again classify this particular realization as aspect [10]—“peace”—within the arya truth of the end of suffering.  It is a period of peace knowing that an ultimate peace is coming, soon.


We will all lay down

An arya has a related wave of realization, on that day.  Each and every one of us, at a certain point in our life—usually in childhood, with the death of a member of our extended family—becomes aware of the fact of death, and the presumption that one day we too will have to die.

We know we will have to die some time, and it is human nature at its most fundamental to believe we will not die soon.  Each and every one of us convinces ourselves that—against all history of all time to the contrary—we of all people may not have to die.  Or certainly we each act as though this is our deepest conviction.

An arya—on the day of their aryaship—has a contrary realization.  That is, I saw ahead to the day of my own death, in this present lifetime.  I saw life, for the first time, as a struggle between me and gravity.  And I saw that gravity always wins.

I have grandchildren, new grandchildren, who are just learning to walk.  They are sort of cute because for example they pull themselves up using a nearby bookcase; lean forward; and take off to walk across the floor as they’ve seen parents and grandparents do.

Inevitably they plop down on their bottoms, and in this case the layers of diapers and cloth we have to keep them in turn out to be a godsend, since there’s lots of padding and the sudden seating themselves rarely hurts.  They just crawl over to their hands and knees and try again.

They will achieve locomotion on those two unsteady sticks we call “legs,” and they will walk through life with them.  Comes a day though—inevitably—when some illness or other, or else simple old age and weakness, puts them down flat on their back and they simply cannot get up, or stay up.  A sort of permanent return to infancy.

An arya is suddenly free from that desperate hope to live forever, and sees directly ahead to the day when they too must join the rest of humanity for all of history, and lie down and let gravity cradle them again and take their last breaths.  Of all the people in the world, only an arya sees ahead to the day—seven lifetimes hence—when they will defeat death.  And of all the people in the world, only an arya is absolutely sure when and how they will lie down their last, in this life.

This awareness of their own certain impermanence—and the mission they have inherited to save other people, and save the teachings that save other people—make aryas uniquely sensitive that they only have so many minutes left in this lifetime to do what the whole world needs them to do.  If you ever meet an arya, then keep this in mind and show them some patience when they are in the middle of a life-saving operation on a dying patient—as they are at every minute.

This future-sight of the day they will lay down on the earth in this life I would place in aspect [1], “impermanence,” within the first of the four higher truths: suffering.  It sits side-by-side then—for me—with the tragic death of my Mother.

On a grander level, I would include here in summary 	the realization of an arya that nothing comes from nothing, or leads to nothing: we see that we have lived countles previous lifetimes in pain, before we came here—striving and dying again and again—and unless we do something about it, this will continue.  This we can categorize as aspect [7], “spring” (prabhava in the Sanskrit), within the arya truth of the source of suffering.


I will make progress,
I will be taken care of

During the period that I saw my death, I also saw that I would be reborn, and how that would feel.  This was an experience distinct from the awareness of seven lifetimes to go.

And so I can say that although I have not directly perceived events of my past lives, I have perceived a specific event of my upcoming lifetimes.  I had a very distinct and unexpected perception that in those lifetimes to come, I would take birth in comfortable financial and social circumstances; and that immediately upon my birth, there would be very capable teachers taking care of me, and seeing that I received a training similar to the one I have received in this current lifetime.

All of this relates to a concept called deng (technical spelling gdeng) in the ancient scriptures: a point in our life where we have accumulated such a quantity of positive karmic seeds that it is guaranteed we will be born into happy circumstances in our future lifetimes, and continue to progress upon our spiritual path.  When I really think about it, I realize that I may be the only person alive on this earth who knows exactly where they are going after they die, and what will happen there.  Ever since that hour, I have never again been subject to the constant uncertainty and fear of death that every living creature in the world faces.

Many individuals I know claim that they are free of this fear, but as an arya I know that they are not being honest, nor honest with themselves.  We all fear death, because subconsciously we remember having gone through it before, countless times, and places of long & terrible pain afterwards.  Just for this, I believe, it would be worth it to learn to see emptiness directly, and then see where we are going and who will care for us.

I would put this experience of seeing our immediately future lifetimes and circumstances again into aspect [15], “means,” within the arya truth of the path to the end of suffering, as it relates so closely to the spiritual education we see there already.


We have never done a single act
that was without self-interest

I had another realization in with this group there in front of the holy books on the altar, and I remember somehow that I was focused again on the benches at the center of the temple where I and the other monks sat every week or so to perform our Buddhist ceremonies for the congregation, whose numbers had steadily shrunk from old age until almost any random young American could come and use the empty temple to have a complete emptiness experience for a few hours!

Those benches were where I sat to offer my time and my devotions to the temple members; and us monks often took the opportunity to press the gift of a candy bar or a new rosary into the hands of young and old alike.

But suddenly I had a sad realization that I had never done a truly selfless act in my entire life; and frankly I would include here much of the teaching I have ever done over my entire life, and books I have written or translated (like the one you are reading now!).  Which is to say, normally when any one of us takes it upon themselves to teach another person, even something very holy, there is some percentage of pride involved.

An extreme super-honesty with oneself covering every action we ever undertake on behalf of others is, I think, unique to an arya.  Every single time I had ever stretched out my hand to share something with a fellow suffering human being, I had done so with at least some small percentage of self-interest: hope that they would like me, hope that people would see how good I was.

I suddenly appreciated the advice of Jesus that we should keep our good deeds hidden from others.  And I promised myself I would try to do one good thing that day that was truly anonymous, and free of self-interest.  We’re about to enjoy that one, and I will tell you about it!

I would place this awareness of our inevitable self-interest into aspect [6] within the higher truth of the source of pain; this is called “cause” (hetu in the Sanskrit).



Group Six:
Staying close to diamonds


Suffering worse than physical

I’m sure there were other realizations that went through my head on that day, but these are all that I remember now, fifty years later.  But I do certainly recall what happened next.  I felt very certain that I should get a diamond, somehow, and offer it to the Buddha.

At that point in my life I had almost no money at all.  I was standing still in that northeast part of the Temple, in front of the thousands of pages of ancient scriptures, and I looked out across the lawn towards where drove in and parked their cars.  Standing there was Prof. LaFleur’s fancy red sports car.  I had an idea!

I would go and sell the car, and then take the money to a jewelry store and buy a loose diamond.  I left quietly, and in a few minutes I was driving down to the small nearby town of Lakewood, where there was a car dealer.

As I drove up, the salesman came out of the office and stood with me next to the car.  And then something really strange happened.  So far since “touching the diamond world” I had not been around another person.  Suddenly—still under the influence of my experience—I realized that I could hear his thoughts.

There are some ancient books that describe this kind of phenomenon in terms of prana, or the “inner wind” that the Chinese call chi, and the Japanese call ki.  It is said that we have thousands of inner channels of prana running through our body, three of which are primary.

Running down the front of our backbone is the “main” or “central” channel.  When prana or inner energy flows freely through this channel, our minds are open and free.  When we have the experience of seeing emptiness directly, the prana is flowing full force.

There are two side channels that wrap around the central one.  When we are in an angry or upset mood, one of these channels fills up with prana, choking the flow of “good” prana in the central channel.  When we have thoughts like feeling very possessive—not in the mood to share with others—then the other side channel fills up and again chokes the good prana in the middle.

In terms of this prana, it is said that the full-force prana present when we experience emptiness directly returns back to normal only slowly, say by the end of that day.  This was indeed my own experience, since even a gradually dropping full-force prana is enough to inspire the deep, subsequent realizations we have described above; including now at the car dealer, the ability to hear the salesman’s thoughts.

I should mention that—like all of us—there have been countless occasions in my life when I felt that I knew what another person standing in front of me was thinking.  But this was not at all the same thing, and I can honestly say that I haven’t ever had this ability, before or after my “diamond day.”  Here’s how the inner and outer conversation proceeded.

Car salesman:
Well, this young man certainly seems naive.  I wonder if he really owns the car.
“Well hi there!  What’s your name?”

Mike:
“My name’s Mike, and I need to sell this sports car, today—now.”

Salesman:
“You got the registration?  Is it in your name?”

Mike:
“Sure,” and I hand him the paperwork.

Salesman:
Well, surprise, he really does own the car!
“Well, sure we can help you.  What kind of work do you do, anyway?”

Mike:
“I’m a cook.”

Salesman:
“Where at?”

Mike:
“I cook at a church.”

Salesman:
Inwardly rolling his eyes.  Man!  This kid is a real dummie!  Cook in a church!  I can make some real money off of him!
“No problem!  How would a hundred bucks sound for your car?”

Mike:
Prof. LaFleur’s little beauty is worth maybe three thousand dollars.  But this diamond is going to be a heartfelt offering to the Buddha.  I don’t think I should fight about it.
“Oh, that would be fine!  Thanks a lot!  But say, after that I won’t have a car.  Do you think you could give me a ride to the jewelry store in town?”

Salesman:
“Sure!  Sure!  Happy to do!”

And he hands me a hundred bucks in cash, and I sign the paperwork, and he drives me to the jewelry store.  It’s a tiny store with an elderly owner; I tell him I need to buy the best biggest loose diamond I can get for a hundred dollars.

He sells me a nice full-cut stone of ten points (one tenth of a full carat); 50 years later, I still have the receipt, which eventually I had imbedded in plastic.  Even though the paper has faded pretty badly, I also have a photocopy I made earlier on, which clearly shows the date and the details of the stone.

It’s funny that now I didn’t have a car, and neither did Rinpoche!  I had just sold it!  And so I didn’t have any way to get back to the Mongolian temple!

I walked through town to the public bus station and figured out a way to get close to the Temple on a commuter bus to New York City, and jump off when I needed to.  And then I walked the rest of the way to the Temple, and entered back through the side door.  Rinpoche as usual up to afternoon was locked up in his room reading holy books.

I went to the altar and took the diamond out of its wrapper, and then carefully placed it way back behind all the little Buddha statues, where no one would ever see it.  I felt then that I had made a very pure offering with everything I had, to honor the direct perception of emptiness.

That evening, Khen Rinpoche and I are having dinner together in the tiny temple kitchen.

“Uh Mike, where’s the car?” Rinpoche asks.

“It’s gone,” I reply, a little scared.

“You sold it.  You sold our only car,” says Rinpoche.  I nod silently, more scared.

“You sold it and you took the money and you bought a diamond,” he says matter-of-factly.  “And then you offered the diamond; you hid the diamond way back behind the altar.”

I look at him with my eyes opened wide.  He can’t possibly know all this stuff about a tiny stone much smaller than the fingernail of your little finger.

“That was a good thing,” he says.  “That was a very good thing.  I am going to take the diamond and offer it to my teacher, Trijang Rinpoche.”  And, in time, that’s exactly what he did.  And we survived without a car for quite a while and then someone gave us the ancient red Volkswagen bug that blew up on the highway; but that’s another story of its own.

Trijang Rinpoche was one of the greatest teachers of modern times; if you’ve ever read the book called Liberation in Our Hands, he was the one who wrote it out from lectures by his own teacher, Pabongka Rinpoche, and edited it into one of the greatest examples of Tibetan writing and thought in history.

Which aspect of the four higher truths do we connect here?  I’ve thought about it for years, and I have a suggestion that I think makes the most sense.  I have a theory that the universe has ordained that we are incapable of hearing the true thoughts going on in each other’s heads, simply because we would go mad from the noise and the naked self-interest there.  It has occurred to me that this sad constant conversation deserves the title of aspect [2], pure “suffering” itself (duhkha in the Sanskrit).


Get a job!

I spent the rest of Diamond Day quietly, and when I went to bed that night the “popcorn” string of realizations quieted down; starting from the next morning I no longer had these waves of understanding hitting me every few minutes, and I could no longer read anyone’s mind.  I settled down into a daily schedule of seven years of constant classes with Khen Rinpoche and another monk, an Inner Mongolian whom the locals called Gevshe Nawan Gelden; in Tibetan, Geshe Ngawang Kelden—another refugee who was from the great Drepung Monastery and who acquainted me with the classics from that institution’s 600-year history.

Not long after Diamond Day, my Mother’s estate was settled.  We had lived poor, but her own mother had been quite wealthy, and had died coincidentally not long before my Mom.  This means that one day a large amount of stocks and cash showed up in my bank account.  I was able to live and study night & day for the next eight years; I could have remained like that for the rest of my life, but suddenly we found out that our home monastery, Sera Mey, was in desperate trouble financially and might even be forced to vacate all their buildings.

And so Rinpoche and I sent them everything we had, which saved the monastery but left me with almost nothing.  My teacher sat me down and gave me a talk that changed the direction of my life forever.

“Look, Mike.  You can see by now how monastery life is; you’ve spent eight years here, and you’ve only gone home once to see your family, when your brother died, committed suicide.  You could easily spend the rest of your life here, studying and serving.

“But I want you to get a job.  I want you to work for your living.  I want you to see the troubles and challenges that normal family people face, every single day.  Some day you will be a teacher; some day you will be sharing your Buddhism with all these people.  I don’t see how you can really do a good job, if you have no personal experience at all of what they go through, day in and day out.”

Deep down I was sure I would never follow this advice; but out of politeness for my Teacher I listened and thought about it.  One day I was in a deep meditation and suddenly I saw that I should go to work, and I should work with diamonds: I should get a job where day in and day out I was touching diamonds, and remembering the emptiness I had seen.

Up until then I had figured out a funny way to be around diamonds, to remember.  Walking through the local grocery store one day with Rinpoche, I saw some rock candy for sale: you know, the big sugar crystals that they grow on little sticks that people use to stir a drink and give it a sweet taste.  These crystals were quite close, visually, to diamonds; and I used to buy them weekly and offer them on my altar, to serve as my Diamond Reminder.

I have to say that Rinpoche’s advice, and following it, was one of the most important events in my entire life.  I personally then would count having an authentic, well-trained and compassionate Teacher—and learning to live in the normal world with normal people—is itself one of the 16 aspects.  I would add it to [15] “means,” or the resources to get out of suffering.


Meeting Ofer

And so by late 1980, I was looking for a job near the Temple where I would be able to touch diamonds with my own hands, on a daily basis.  I remember going to over ten different jewelry stores all over my county, asking for work.  The conversation went almost exactly the same, in each case:

	“I need a job where I can touch diamonds every day.”

	The store owner is already suspicious!

	“Well, do you have any experience in the jewelry business?”

	“No, nothing at all.”

“Hmm.  Well, leave your application here with me, and we’ll give you a call 	if any openings come up.”

Which of course they never did.  I remember one interview at a jewelry store where halfway through a mom dragged in her daughter and forced her to have her ears pierced with a special gun that the owner had.  I was out of the door even before the little girl stopped screaming.  Not for me!

Two things then led to a breakthrough.  I started buying a lot of gemology books and studying them; and this way I learned that the Russians had discovered large new diamond mines, and were also doing very innovative research work on diamonds.

All of this was happening because diamonds at the time were essential for important industrial processes like cutting engine components and drilling oil wells.  The United States had done its best to block the Russians from world diamond supplies, and so the Russians were working hard to find diamond deposits in their own country.

Suddenly the Soviet Union was awash in diamonds.  Either they had discovered a real treasure trove, or they had finally figured out how to make genuine diamonds in the laboratory.  Since I had suffered through Russian language at Princeton, I could (with a few dictionaries) work my way through the necessary research papers and news reports.  I became something of an expert in the field, and even published articles for the global diamond syndicate, DeBeers.  I was hoping that this would provide me with an “in” to work with diamonds directly, somewhere!

About the same time, I met a young man who was a diamond sorter at a company called Lazare Kaplan, which was the largest loose diamond supplier in the US at the time.  I tried to get a job at the company through him, but he told me that I would have to do some gemology education even to get an interview.  He advised me to take a gemology degree at the Gemological Institute of America offices in New York, where I could also keep my eye out for someone who might hire me in diamonds.

And so this is what I did.  Simultaneously, I earned gemology degrees from the GIA and from the much more demanding Gemmological Association of Great Britain.  One day at a GIA diamond certifying class in New York, the teacher held up a diamond polished in a special design known as a “old mine cut.”  This particular style of cutting had pretty much died out before 1900.

Our teacher asked us: “If a customer brings a ring with this diamond in it into your store, what can you tell them about it?”  We all agreed that we could say it was quite old, and had probably been in the family for generations.

There was a quiet man in the back of the class who generally said very little, but now he raised his hand.  “Well, not really,” he noted.  “Diamond is the hardest thing we know of in the universe, and there’s no normal thing that can scratch it.  Therefore it is impossible to look at a diamond cut in the old mine style and say, from abrasion or any other sign, whether it was cut 100 years ago, or this morning!”

The whole class, including the teacher, was stunned.  Quite so!

But I was thinking different things.  I thought I would get to know this man—whose name was Ofer Azrielant—and see if maybe he could hire me, assuming he owned a diamond company.  I made an excuse to see him in his office in Manhattan, and by great good luck (past seeds) he was at that moment starting up a new diamond jewelry company—having already built one in his home country, Israel.


Andin International Diamond Jewelry

We started working together, and shortly afterwards Ofer’s wife Aya traveled from Tel Aviv to join us.  We borrowed $50,000 from a dealer in London named Shemtov; rented a larger space near the Empire State Building; and started building our line.  We called the company Andin International Diamond Jewelry.

We worked hard and grew and grew, and eventually Andin became the largest among the many thousands of jewelry makers in the world, with annual sales of about $250 million dollars per year.  I served as vice-president in charge of the worldwide diamond buying operation.

As long as we are all living in bodies that will crumble into dust within a short time—and we don’t know how very short that time might be—it doesn’t seem to make any sense for us to devote our priceless hours to collecting more money and things that we will very shortly be leaving behind.  But the fact that out of those many thousands of companies, the company that was built partly because of a deep spiritual experience became the largest of its kind in the world says something, I think, about where all money and success really comes from.

What I mean to point out is that—by dedicating ourselves to deeper spiritual goals, in a way informed by the ancient classics—the worldly goals (I mean, it’s not so bad to have a good car that works well, or a house with enough room to do all the projects you’d like to do) come automatically; our company proves it.  You can relax and be successful both in this life and afterwards too.

During my first week at Andin, I handled I think 3 diamonds.  By the time our company was bought by super-investor Warren Buffett, my department was evaluating about 300,000 diamonds per week.  I remember one day, quite some years after we started together, Ofer asked me: “One thing I always wondered.  Here you are with an honors degree from Princeton in religion; and you are one of the only westerners in history to earn a geshe degree, from one of the largest Buddhist monasteries in the world.  What the heck are you doing in the diamond business?”

I tell you this whole story because I want you to know how important the diamond is to a person who has seen emptiness directly—you would be willing to commute to New York for 3 or 4 hours a day, for 20 years, just to touch some diamonds that day.

Again, I would place these decades with the diamonds in New York in with aspect [11], “beauty”—the same as the first diamond on that first day.  If I were you and I was still trying to make up my mind whether Michael Roach really did ever see emptiness directly, I would take into account this weird fact that he spent so many years with the diamonds.

And as mentioned, we have in historical Buddhism the unexplained title “Diamond Cutter Sutra”; along with the primary enlightened beings named Vajradhara (“Holder of the Diamond”) and Vajrapani (“Keeper of the Diamond”); and the entire half of the teachings known as the Vajrayana, or the Diamond Way—where every disciple is required to have and use a vajra ritual instrument with the precise shape of a twinned octagonal crystal, relatively common with diamonds.  Surely there is something going on here.



Group Seven:
Passing it on, and the next 500 years

Real diamond cutting

People ask me if my company was ever involved in blood diamonds—the sleazy side of the diamond business—and I can honestly say that we never purchased a single stone from the entire continent of Africa.  We were jewelry makers, and as such we only bought open-market diamonds that had already been cut, from cutting centers like Mumbai, Tel Aviv, or Antwerp.

I felt an intense desire though—you can guess why—to learn the arcane art of cutting diamonds by hand.  Master diamond cutters in New York were a rare breed, handling only the largest and finest stones in the world, due to the very high cost of labor and office rents in Manhattan.  Very few masters would agree to waste their time for years training a curious jewelry company executive.

There is also a (foolish) saying among diamond cutters that it is foolish to train the person who might take away your next cutting job.  Even if a master agrees to teach you, there are secret methods that they will rarely share with anyone, even a prized apprentice.

But here, as often happened in my diamond exploits, I got lucky.  Years before I had hired a secretary from a rabbi’s office named Rachel Shmuelof.  Rachel and I pretty much built the stone buying operation at Andin together, and at some point I found out that her husband, Sam Shmuelof, was a master diamond cutter, right in the middle of the Diamond District in Manhattan!

We made a deal, and late at night for many months I trudged up to Shmuel’s cutting shop to learn the trade.  One day I reached a point where I uncovered the secret to making a perfect stone (which I won’t share with you), and then I knew I could let my literal diamond cutting career go.  I actually bought an old cutting setup from Sam and installed it quietly in the dreary unfinished basement of the little temple house back home; but I kept losing stones that fell off in the dirt, and I finally gave it up.

This literal cutting of diamonds—and the urge to do so, really—I count as one more facet of aspect [11], “beauty.”


The Diamond Cutter:
The Buddha on Managing
Your Business and Your Life

At a point in the mid 1990’s, I was trying to come up with ways to organize our growing database of digitalized ancient books—which had reached over 1,000 manuscripts.  I wrote an essay online about a fantasy project (impossible with the computing resources at the time) where the user of the database assumed an avatar—for example, an eagle—and then flew through a city where each building represented different classics.  You just soar up to the window of the book you want to study, fly inside, talk (or squawk) at the wall, and the text you want comes up.

The cutest part of this plan was that each of the five boroughs of The City represented one of the six great topics of Buddhism.  Here we could split Manhattan—the island in the middle of New York—into the two branches of Middle Way (Madhyamika); which allows for the unexpected idiosyncracies of the Bronx to cover the secret teachings (Diamond Way). 

Turns out that the religion editor at Doubleday Publishing Corporation—the largest book company in the United States at the time—came across my little essay online and was immediately intrigued.  One very busy day at my office, he called me up.  I’m sitting inbetween two tables covered with loose diamonds, trying not to sweep a pile of them onto the floor with the phone cord.

“Hi Michael, this is Trace Murphy, calling from uptown—I wondered it we could have a talk!”

Ah!  Finally, a headhunter is going to offer me double the salary to jump to another jewelry company!  I’m happy here, but let’s see what he has to say.

“Yes, how can I help you?”

“Well, I came across that essay you wrote online about a new concept for cataloging all the Buddhist books in history.  I was really impressed!”

I just about fall off the chair.  I was sure no one had read it, or even cared about cataloging all the Buddhist books in history.

“And well,” continues Trace, “we’d like you to write a book for us.”

“What kind of book?”

“Any book you want!” laughs Trace (I’m beginning to like this guy).  “And we’ll pay you $50,000 up front!”

Now I really do fall off the chair.  As of the year of this writing, that was over $100,000, even before the book was written.  I later learned that Trace received about 1,500 manuscripts per week in the mail, unsolicited, from wanna-be famous authors; and here he was calling an unknown writer.

Still, it’s all a little hard to believe.

“Well, what kind of books have you published lately?” I ask.

“I just finished up editing a book by Mother Theresa, and before that I put out the biography of the Pope,” says Trace.  These are like the two most important religious figures in the world at the time!

“Well, okay!  But I don’t need the money.  I don’t like to take money for something I haven’t done yet.”

“But you have to take it,” he laughs again.  “An advance is part of the process.”

I agreed, and went to work at home, in my spare time—in fact, sitting in the Mongolian temple at the same spot where I touched emptiness directly.

The book I had in mind was an account of the spiritual awakening I had gone through with my angel, Veronica, in the garden of our church, as teenagers—which I felt was very much like the story of Dante and Beatrice in the famous Divine Comedy, written about seven centuries earlier.

Except that in addition to meeting a Buddha, my protagonist on different nights would bump into different Buddhist thinkers from the last few thousand years, and learn a different lesson from each one.  I had a lot of fun giving each Master their own personality, each based on one of the teachers in my 25-year studies to complete the geshe degree, at both the Temple and overseas at Sera Mey Monastery.

When I was just finishing up this book—which I entitled The Garden—I was also completing a series of 18 courses in English, with the the idea of passing on the essence of the geshe course to foreigners, within a 6-year period instead of 25 years.  I taught these courses for free five nights a week in Manhattan; the study group rapidly grew from 5 people to almost 100, and we kept renting bigger and bigger spaces—ending up at the Fifteenth Street Friends Meeting House, a beautiful Quaker church in New York’s East Village.

One of these courses was based on the Diamond Cutter Sutra; I remember finishing a big part of it in hospital waiting rooms while Khen Rinpoche went through some procedures.  I suddenly saw a way to combine the sutra with a book of business and personal advice based on its principles.  I called Trace and begged him for a second book contract, before I had even finished the first.

He told me to go for it, and I literally finished the manuscript on the last day before I went into a deep 3-year silent retreat in the Arizona desert, in 2000.  I remember turning it over to my assistant just before I went through the front gate, for the last time in a thousand days.

The Diamond Cutter since has become an international bestseller, spawning a 10th anniversary edition and a 20th one too; with the black-market versions, nobody has an exact count, but it has apparently sold several million copies, in more than 30 languages.

I believe that—in the end—the image of cutting the diamond has a deep spiritual resonance in every human being: on some level, we are all aware of emptiness and its power to take us to a higher level of evolution, immortal and infinitely wise.  We may not have seen the luminous images creating every detail of our world from seeds planted in our mind by how kindly we treat other living beings; but on some level we all know: on some level we all know we should be kind to each other.

Again I would place this literary diamond-cutting in with aspect [11], “beauty,” within the arya truth of the end of suffering.


Sea change

During the 20 years or so since I completed that 3-year retreat, the publication of The Diamond Cutter book has spawned a large number of organizations dedicated to using the wisdom of the diamond in a whole variety of human endeavors.  The Asian Legacy Library (ALL) continues the work of the Asian Classics Input Project (ACIP) in locating, imaging, and creating searchable input for their free online database, which now contains tens of thousands of titles.  We hope in the coming decades to complete the 300,000 or so great books of Asia.  Much of the first decades of the project were paid for from my diamond jewelry company.

The Diamond Cutter Classics (DCC) translation team, over the last 10 years, has translated many thousands of pages of these ancient classics of Asia into modern languages, and has offered thousands of hours of free online classes in translating the languages of these texts.  Diamond Cutter Press (DCP) has published many of these books, along with secondary translations into many languages through its affiliates worldwide.  Diamond Cutter Jewels (DCJ) has produced and sold diamond jewelry designs for fundraising to support all these efforts.

The courses I wrote in New York have expanded, first through the Asian Classics Institute (ACI) and then through the 5 Houses organization.  Many thousands of people worldwide have taken their thousands of pages of courses.  The Diamond Cutter Institute Global (DCIG) for 17 years has taught tens of thousands of clients throughout the world non-religious, business-oriented classes based on the ancient classics.  The Sedona College of International Management (SCIM), for twelve years, has trained hundreds of business coaches for this effort.

Diamond Mountain Retreat Center—recently designated by Forbes business magazine as the second best star-gazing getaway location in the United States—has for over 20 years provided a perfectly silent retreat opportunity for many thousands of people from all over the globe.

Students and friends of the next generation have founded successful projects throughout the world; for example, Diamond Silk Entrepreneur University (DSEU) features the classic literature of the ancient Silk Road in a study program currently being evaluated for official accreditation.  And the Innovation Retreats organization (IR) provides business retreats for entrepreneurs worldwide who seek new sources of innovation.

The reason I mention all these projects born after my diamond world experience is that I hope to convey to you the feeling of a huge wave of cause-and-effect, across many lifetimes and worlds.  Again, I cannot see my past lives directly, but I can see them with the unerring eyes of simple logic.

Nothing comes from nothing.  There is a prior cause of every single event and detail of our thought, just as a tall tree in the front yard of our home stands witness to the principle of tree seeds that we have never seen.

And remember that these mental seeds are literally creating you, and your world, and everything that ever happens in that world.  The process of seeing emptiness directly—which is the only thing that can save human kind from endless cycles of death and suffering—is like a huge ocean wave that is born deep in the depths of many past lifetimes, and then rolls on growing more and more large and powerful, until the day that the wave breaks and we touch that diamond world.

And then on the beach where that wave lays down its water, life grows and spreads, for centuries.  The moment of touching emptiness directly is not a moment, it is an eon of change among all the history of life itself.

I would place this last section—the inevitable social consequences of a human being touching the diamond world—in aspect [12], “escape” (nihsarana in the Sanskrit), within the higher truth of the end of suffering.


Continuing education

I wanted to add one more short piece of advice here for everyone.  It takes a great amount of formal study of the classics of Buddhism to touch the diamond world; that’s why we have this huge 4-volume emptiness treatise by Je Tsongkapa here, in the first place.

But it’s important to say that—even after seeing emptiness directly—our study and practice has only just begun.  After seeing emptiness, I personally went through the entire traditional 25-year course of the geshe, or Master of Buddhism, to give long-term structure and support to my experience.  I sincerely believe that even after having this once-on-a-planet experience, we still need constant study and meditation upon the classics that have gone before.

This also applies to ordination, and taking on other vows of moral behavior such as the bodhisattva and diamond-way commitments.  I had lived the monk’s way of life at the Mongol temple—together with some 15 senior monks—for eight years, before Khen Rinpoche allowed me to take ordination.  That is, eight years after I had already reached the highest goal of studying and practice.

Here too we have the example of Lord Buddha’s first five students—the tiger cubs.  We’ve mentioned how they each saw emptiness; but what we should also say is that each one of them also became a monk: the first five monks of our Buddha’s sangha, or community.  They were so ready to take on ordination that their hair was shaved off, and the golden robes formed around their bodies, automatically—just by Lord Buddha saying “Come to me.”

It’s crucial that we appreciate this connection between vowed morality and the direct experience of emptiness.  We’ve learned how—during the “pot on the stove” experience—we see directly, for the first time, the way in which our world really is a construct of luminous images coming out of karmic seeds in our mind.  Sticking to a regimen of moral guidelines then is the only way to live our lives, since every detail of those lives is flowing out of seeds planted by this way of life.  And seeing emptiness directly is the only way that a human being can cement this understanding inside of them, permanently.

My close friends know that my daily schedule usually includes 5 hours of study and contemplation, including translating the classics into modern languages, and another solid hour of deep meditation.  The rest of my life then takes care of itself automatically, after noon, and I’m talking about the serious work of managing over 40 successful companies and organizations, now at the age of 73.  After nearly 50 years of this sort of schedule, I believe that this kind of discipline makes for a very happy and successful life.

In the modern world, this includes what my friends and I call the “Good Night Book Club.”  This is a common commitment we all keep to put away our electronics—cellphone, computer, television—by 10pm.  This is followed by a few minutes of reading the great wisdom classics in translation (such as the one you have here); and then getting a solid, full night’s sleep and rising at 6am.

The early American philosopher Benjamin Franklin noted that “Early to bed and early to rise makes a person healthy, wealthy, and wise.”  The very early morning time, before the entire rest of the world has started off on its daily race, is the prime time for a practicioner.

Again, I would categorize the different components of “continuing education” that we’ve described in this section as aspect [15]: a “means” (pratipatti in the Sanskrit) of enabling the fourth truth, the path to the end of suffering.


Living with the world

There’s sort of a final question here that we should address.  How did I describe my experience to my teacher, on that fateful day, and how did I speak of it with the other monks I was living with, and with teachers and friends for the rest of my life?

On the day that I saw emptiness, I had a strong, additional realization that I should not speak about what had happened to me.  At the time, I didn’t know exactly why; but I did know that it wouldn’t be good.

I got a hint of an answer afterwards.  Khen Rinpoche had allowed a doctoral student at a university to visit us for a few weeks at a time, to take special classes about the subject of his dissertation.  I remember that the two of us were standing on the highway near the temple, waiting to flag down a bus.

The student suddenly remarked to me that I had done a really foolish thing to sell my fancy red sports car for almost nothing, just to make an offering in the temple.  I looked sideways at his face and just for a second I thought maybe there was a demon inside of him—just for the length of those few sentences.

I am not a superstitious person and it’s not that I think about devils or demons, almost ever.  But I do believe that on that day, I saw one take over a person, if only for a few sentences.  Shortly afterwards, this individual had some terrible and sad circumstances in their life, and I always felt that their attitude had somehow contributed strongly to that.

I thought for many years that at best, people would simply not believe me if I described my emptiness experience; and that at worst they might criticize it out of their ignorance, and then make terrible trouble for themselves.  As for my teachers, it felt improper to talk about things that might seem as though I thought I was above them; which, even though it didn’t seem that they had undergone the same experience, I never did think.

And so I have spoken about the things you read here only very gradually, and partially, to close friends and students.  Now, with my health at risk and with my advanced age, I feel as though I should leave as detailed a record as I can.

Over the length of my life I have run into cynical people, particularly in the media but also otherwise well-meaning spiritual seekers, for example, who have mocked or attacked my viewpoints and way of life.  I say to them here that there is no point in expending your irreplaceable time and breath on me, if I am not what I say I am.  Go and live your life and use the few precious hours of this life to pursue something good and valuable to you.  The words here are not meant for you now; but I promise I will save them for you to enjoy one day, when you are ready!  Just relax.

This “reticence of an arya” is a common theme in scriptural treatments of emptiness which say that a person who has seen emptiness may not be able to describe it fully to others.  This is more a comment upon the “others” in question, than to imply that emptiness cannot be described in a way which helps others to see it.  Otherwise there would be no point for example to the tens of thousands of pages in Lord Buddha’s sutras on the “perfection of wisdom”—the prajna paramita (technical spelling prajñā pāramitā).  And after all, even The Buddha himself hesitated for those famous seven weeks after total enlightenment, to speak to his five tiger cubs of what he had seen.

Not teaching emptiness when the time is not yet ready can again be included, I would say, in an arya’s apect of [15] “means,” in the form of spiritual education.


Babysitting a planet

There is one final image from the day that I touched emptiness.  It occurs almost exactly 500 years from now.  On that day, I reach enlightenment, and become a Buddha myself.  I know that the Buddhist classics describe this as becoming a force on every planet in the universe; but I also know that I will have a special relationship with a single particular world.

There is a persistent image of looking down on this world from above; and beside me is the enlightened being in my own life, my wife Veronica.  I see that each one of us will live this way, as the wisdom of the diamond spreads in this world.


A summary of the 16 aspects, or moments

As we wrap up here, let’s present a summary of how—from my own experience of touching emptiness directly—I would describe the famous 16 aspects, or “moments,” of the four higher truths.  I will be putting here sometimes experiences which are personal to my own life, but they are meant to help you assign your own experiences in a similar manner.  That is, each one of us has to go through the 16 moments in our own way; and what I offer here is just meant to help you fill in the blanks on your own list.

Master Vasubandhu (c. 350ad) offers some similar advice on the four truths in his Detailed Commentary on the Sutra Taught by the Higher Being named “Never-Ending Wisdom”:

Here’s how you should proceed if you meet up with a person who can grasp things with no more than a summary presentation.  These types of people you can engage simply by mentioning no more than the names of the four higher truths.

If though you meet up with someone who understands things better with a little detail, then teach them a version of the four higher truths where you break the same four truths out into 16 aspects, or “moments.”

There are two further points we can usefully make here, about these 16.  First of all, it does seem that these may originally have been more or less than 16; it often feels that the set of four fours may be primarily for symmetry.  The great Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen has some valuable comments on this in his dialectic analysis of the great Jewel of Realizations of the next Buddha—Maitreya.

Secondly, it is recognized that some aspects might overlap one another, so that an individual experience may correlate to more than one aspect; certainly we have felt this in our study here.  As an example here, Je Tsongkapa himself describes a crossover of something that falls under both the truth of the path to the end of suffering, and the truth of suffering itself.  This for example would apply, he says, in cases of meditation by someone who is in the period subsequent to seeing emptiness directly for the first time.

In the meantime though, here is one arya’s attempt to help you discover the real meaning of the 16 aspects in your own life, which is inevitably what each of us needs to do—


The 16 Aspects,
or Moments, Summarized

	A. Moments of the truth of suffering (duhkha, duk-ngel)

		[1] Impermanence (anitya, mitakpa)

—The long illness and death of my mother, especially as witnessed in a heightened state during our studies of Buddhism together in the Himalayas.  The direct perception of an arya—immediately after seeing emptiness—of how they themselves will lie down flat on the earth, dead, at the end of this life

		[2] Suffering (duhkha, duk-ngel)

—The ability of an arya, later in the day on which they saw emptiness directly, to hear directly the inner conversation of other people, and how intensely self-interested this conversation is

		[3] Emptiness (shunya, tongpa)

—Emptiness (here as a subcategory of the first higher truth) not in the sense of the lack of an object coming from its own side, but rather in the sense of the meaninglessness of a life focused solely on the accumulation of money and material goods

		[4] No self-nature (anatma, dakmey)

—The truth of no self-nature, again, as a subcategory of the first higher truth: the fact that no undesirable experience has to lack any value for us personally; nothing is “useless” from its own side; learning from the pain of a breakup, for example


	B. Moments of the truth of the source of suffering (samudaya, kunjung)

		[5] Source (samudaya, kunjung)

—It is the negative seeds in my mind, especially, which produce my constantly repeated personal existence of death and pain

		[6] Cause (hetu, gyu)

—The realization of an arya that every act they have ever undertaken in their life so far—even good deeds—was deeply motivated by self-interest

		[7] Spring (prabhava, rab tu kyewa)

—The realization of an arya that nothing comes from nothing, or leads to nothing: we have lived countless previous lifetimes in pain, before we came here—striving and dying again and again—and unless we do something about it, this will continue 

		[8] Factor (pratyaya, kyen)

—The way in which luminous images emerging from seeds planted by our past deeds—good or bad—exit our minds in a millisecond-by-millisecond flow, and combine to create the people and the world around us


	C. Moments of the truth of the end of suffering (nirodha, gokpa)

		[9] End (nirodha, gokpa)

—Because of our direct experience of the mental seeds and luminous pictures during the “pot on the stove” or similar event, all the seeds that could create for us the image of a lower rebirth have been prevented or “spoiled”: we may still have some from before, but they are like ruined flower seeds that will never produce another full plant in our garden.  Later on the same day, we see emptiness directly, and “enter the stream” that leads directly to Buddhahood, stopping all suffering rebirths at all; knowing all things; and helping all living beings.  We see finally too that neither things nor living beings—including myself—ever come from anywhere except the mental seeds I have planted by helping or hurting others in the past
				
		[10] Peace (shanta, shiwa)

—Immediately subsequent to seeing emptiness directly, the direct experience of bodhichitta: meeting directly every single living being in the universe, and making a personal commitment to them that I will reach full enlightenment myself, and then  come to save them too.  The direct perception by an arya that they have 7 lifetimes left to go, before they become an enlightened being
		
		[11] Beauty (pranita, gyanompa)

—Every arya, every person who sees emptiness directly, casts about just after that perception for something in this normal reality that can forever remind them of the higher reality they have just seen directly, but may not be able to see whenever they want to, until they reach a higher level.  Every arya arrives at the diamond, which is the closest normal thing (although not really close) to emptiness—this is because diamonds represent a physical “ultimate” (hardest thing in the universe); because they are “invisible” (perfectly transparent); and all completely equal internally (pure carbon), wherever they exist.  This is the reason why the name “diamond” keeps reappearing in the ancient books of wisdom; for example, in the “Diamond Cutter Sutra,” and enlightened beings with “diamond” in their name; and expessions like “the diamond way.”  Here also we include the undeniable desire to work closely with physical diamonds, or their representation, for the rest of an arya’s lifetime, after touching the diamond world.  This may include especially literally learning to cut diamonds; but certainly includes as well as passing on the teachings of emptiness in books and teachings

		[12] Escape (nihsarana, ngepar jungwa)

—The inevitable consequences on the society around them during the extended period after a person touches emptiness directly; the work of the new arya for the rest of their life and lifetimes


	D. Moments of the truth of the path to the end of suffering (marga, lam)

		[13] Path (marga, lam)

—Learning the principles behind deep meditation, and then engaging in a regular practice which very gradually but surely allows us to build up to shamatha, where we are able to remain in one-pointed, focused meditation for one hour or more.  Simplifying many small and large details of our daily life in order to achieve this focus.  Staying mindful of our egoness.  Cleaning up our finances, to help free up our mind

		[14] Logic (nyaya, rikpa)

—Past life events (especially that contribute to our seeing emptiness directly in this lifetime) that we “perceive” logically, by working backwards from strong events or tendencies we exhibit in this present life; particularly in our childhood
		
		[15] Means (pratipatti, druppa)

—An in-depth and long-term study of the Buddhist classics, particularly the five geshe subjects, under a qualified master.  The devoted and intense service of the Dharma and teachers of the Dharma.  Honoring all representations of enlightened beings as if they were those beings themselves.  Having an authentic, well-trained and compassionate Teacher—and learning to live in the normal world with normal people, to help them.  Continuing, even after we see emptiness directly, in a deep and constant study of the Buddhist classics.  Seeing our immediately future lifetimes and circumstances directly; knowing we will be well taken care of and further trained.  Committing to a moral code—such as ordination, or the bodhisattva vows, or the secret commitments—in recognition of how this constantly plants the reality around me.  Committing to a daily spiritual practice, including specified periods of meditation and study of the classics, without my electronics—and including a regular schedule of 8 hours of sleep at night, and early rising to accomplish this practice.  Not speaking of having touched emptiness, or similar topics, until the listener is really ready

		[16] Method (nairyanika, ngepar jinpa)

—Study and meditation upon the ancient principle of chi-jedrak: quality & characteristic; where we learn subtleties of the relationship between the quality of “carness” in general and a particular real car in our life which is characteristic of that carness.  The personal recognition that the written records of enlightened teaching are almost literally the only thing that can help all human beings on this world to free themselves from pain






A course of study & practice

I apologize if I have gone on too long in this preface to the great Je Tsongkapa’s classic on emptiness; but I strongly feel that his highly technical (and supremely accurate) presentation goes well in tandem with an account of the same material from the point of view of purely personal experience.

I personally believe that deciding to yourself that you will commit some major time and effort to work through the teachings on emptiness from these two directions—technical presentation, and personal experience—is the very best use you can make of the months and years left to you in this life.  Later in your life, you will realize that this is the very best thing you could have done with that priceless lifetime of yours.

It is my intention to continue this work by designing practical courses, for people of different personalities, to develop within them the realizations we have outlined here.  I encourage you to go online and watch for these courses as they are released by organizations—each with their own particular emphasis and policies—such as the 5 Houses; Diamond Cutter Institute Global (DCIG); Sedona College of International Management (SCIM); Classics Soft Power (CSP); Innovation Retreats (IR); Diamond Silk Entrepreneur University (DSEU); and the Yoga Studies Institute (YSI).  Relevant translations of original and ancient classics that relate to this material will continue to be published through the efforts of the Diamond Cutter Classics (DCC) translators of ancient Asian literature; the Diamond Cutter Press (DCP); and the Asian Legacy Library (ALL).  I hope to see you there, where we can work together.

Geshe Michael Roach
Rainbow House
Rimrock, Arizona
USA

June 25, 2026

[3]
RJE BTZUN BLA MA ‘JAM PA’I DBYANGS DANG, ‘PHAGS PA YAB SRAS RNAMS KYI ZHABS LA GUS PA CHEN POS PHYAG ‘TSAL ZHING SKYABS SU MCHI’O,

In deep respect I bow at the feet of my Holy Lama, Gentle Voice, and at the feet of those realized beings, the Father & Son.  Please be my shelter.


[4]
,ZAB CING RGYA CHE’I LEGS BSHAD KUN GYI GTER,
,’JIG RTEN KUN GYI MA ‘DRIS MDZA’ BSHES TE,
,SA GSUM ‘GRO LA LAM BZANG MTSON PA’I MIG
,THUB DBANG SMRA BA’I NYI MAS RTAG TU SKYONGS,

You are a goldmine
Of every fine explanation:
The profound & the wide.
You are the best friend
Of every living being,
Unbeknownst to them.

You are the eyes 
Of all those who dwell
In all three of the lands;
O Sun of Speakers,
Lord of the Able,
Protect us always.


[5]
,RAB ‘BYAMS RGYAL BA’I ‘KHOR DU ZAB MO’I GNAS,
,YANG DAG PHUL GYI GTAM GYI SENG GE’I SGRA,
,KUN NAS SGROG LA MTSUNGS PA MA MCHIS PA’I,
,’JAM DBYANGS BLA MAS RTAG TU BYIN GYIS RLOBS,

You are beyond compare—
Among all who attend
To the billions of victorious
Buddhas there are—
In the way you proclaim,
With your lion’s roar,

That highest of all the words
Which can ever be spoken:
That deepest thought.

I pray I may always be blessed
By my Lama,
By Gentle Voice himself.


[6]
,DUS GSUM BDE BAR GSHEGS PA’I [f. 2a] THUGS KYI BCUD,
,MTHA’ BRAL DBU MA RTEN CING ‘BREL ‘BYUNG LAM,
,JI BZHIN ‘GREL PAR LUNG BSTAN KLU SGRUB LA,
,SNYING NAS ‘DUD DO BRTZE BA’I LCAGS KYUS ZUNGS,

The very cream
Within the holy minds
Of all who have Gone To Bliss,
Past & present & future,
Is the Middle Way,
Free of extremes:
The path of dependence.

From the depths of my heart
I bow myself
To Master Nagarjuna,
The one who it was foretold would come
And unfold this way.
Set, I pray, the iron hook
Of your love within my breast.


[7]
,MGON DE’I GDAMS PAS GO ‘PHANG MTHOR GSHEGS NAS,
,NYID KYIS GZIGS GANG ‘GRO LA GSAL MDZAD PA’I,
,LEGS LAM STON PA’I GTAM LA DBANG ‘BYOR PA,
,DPAL LDAN ‘PHAGS PA LHA YI ZHABS LA ‘DUD,

There was one who received
The advices of this protector
And reached the heights of realization;
Who went on to describe
The things he had seen himself
Clearly to the rest of us:

I bow thus at the feet
Of the Glorious One,
To Master Aryadeva,
Rich in the words
Which instruct us
In that excellent path.


[8]
,RJE BTZUN ‘JAM PA’I DBYANGS KYI BKA’ GRUB CING,
,’PHAGS PA’I DGONGS PA MTHAR THUG GSAL BAR MDZAD,
,GRUB PA’I RIG ‘DZIN GNAS SU GSHEGS GYUR PA,
,SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS KYI ZHABS LA MGOS PHYAG ‘TSAL,

I bow and touch
My head as well
To the feet of Buddha Palita,
Who carried out
The command of the holy
Gentle Voice;

Who clarified
The ultimate intent
Of the Realized One,
And who reached the state
Of an accomplished one,
A keeper of the knowledge.


[9]
,PHRA LA RTOGS DKA’ DRANG SRONG CHEN PO’I LAM,
,KLU SGRUB LUGS KYI THUN MONG MIN PA’I GNAD,
,YONGS SU RDZOGS PAR STON MDZAD ZLA BA’I ZHABS,
,ZHI BA LHA DANG BCAS PA’I ZHABS LA ‘DUD,

I bow as well
At the feet of the holy
Chandrakirti,
Who along with Master Shantideva
Has instructed us
In every single one

Of the unique & crucial points
Found in the system
Of Master Nagarjuna:
In the path of this great saint,
A way which is subtle
And difficult to grasp.


[10]
,KLU SGRUB ‘PHAGS PA LHA YI GRUB PA’I MTHA’,
,SHING RTA CHEN PO GSUM GYIS [f. 2b] BKRAL BA NYID,
,THUN MONG MA YIN GNAD DON KUN RDZOGS PAR,
,DRI MED BLO GROS MIG GIS LEGS MTHONG ZHING,

I have seen, perfectly,
With the eyes of 
Immaculate wisdom,
Each & every one
Of the unique
And crucial points

In the philosophical system
Of Nagarjuna and Aryadeva,
Just as this was commented upon
By every one of the three
Magnificent innovators.


[11]
,PHYOGS ‘DIR LUGS DE ‘CHAD ‘DOD PHAL MO CHES,
,BSHAD PA’I DRI MAS SBAGS PA BSAL PHYIR DANG,
,GZHAN GYIS BSKUL PHYIR YONGS DAG BSHAD PA YIS,
,DBU MA ‘JUG PA’I RGYA CHER BSHAD PA BYA,,

For this reason,
I shall now undertake
A highly accurate
And detailed explanation 
Of Entering the Middle Way;

I do so also because
I hope to clear away
The stench of the corruptions
Found in the great majority
Of the explanations of this system
Attempted thus far in our land;

And as well because I have been begged
By others to compose this work.



The meaning of the title of the book:
“Entering the Middle Way”

[12]
‘DIR ZAB PA DANG RGYA CHE BA’I DON GNYIS, PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA’I BSTAN BCOS CHEN PO DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA RANG GI ‘GREL PA DANG MTHUN PAR ‘CHAD PA LA BZHI, MTSAN GYI DON, ‘GYUR GYI PHYAG ,GZHUNG GI DON, MJUG GI DON NO,,

The great classical commentary entitled Entering the Middle Way sets forth, in an unmistaken way, the meaning of both the profound side of the teachings, and their widespread side.  Here I undertake to explain this work, following the intent of its autocommentary.  My explanation covers four broad sections: the meaning of the title of the work; the translators’ obeisance; the meaning of the body of the text; and finally the meaning of its conclusion.


	[13]
	[title]
	[f. 201b]
*,,RGYA GAR SKAD DU,
MA DHY’A MA KA AA BA T’A RA N’A MA,
BOD SKAD DU,
DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA ZHES BYA BA,

In the language of India, this book is called Madhyamaka
Avatara Nama.
In the language of Tibet, it is called Uma La Jukpa Shejawa.
In the English language, these translate as
“The Book known as Entering the Middle Way”


[14]
DANG PO NI, RGYA GAR NA SKAD RIGS BZHI YOD PA’I LEGS PAR SBYAR BA’I SKAD DU NA, BSTAN BCOS ‘DI’I MTSAN MA DHY’A MA KA AA BA T’A RA N’A MA’O, ,DE BOD KYI SKAD DU BSGYUR NA, DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA ZHES BYA BA’O,,

Here is the first.  In India, there were four major language groups; of these, the title of this classic is given in Sanskrit: Madhyamaka Avatara Nama.  Translated into Tibetan, this would be Uma La Jukpa [or, in English, Entering the Middle Way].


[15]
‘DIR GANG LA ‘JUG PA’I DBU MA NI, DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS LA ‘JUG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, ZHES GSUNGS PAS DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS YIN LA, DE YANG ‘DI’I ‘GREL PAR RTZA SHE KHUNGS SU MDZAD PA NA DBU MA LAS, ZHES MANG DU GSUNGS PA LTAR RTZA SHE LA BYA’I, DBU MA’I GZHUNG GZHAN DANG, DBU MA’I DON GZHAN LA MI BYA’O,,

Now just what is the “middle way” that the commentary is “entering” into?  It is the Classical Commentary on the Middle Way; after all, he says “because it enters into the Classical Commentary on the Middle Way.”  And in his commentary as well Master Chandrakirti often says “from The Middle Way” when he is using The Foundational Verses entitled “Wisdom” as a source.  As such, “middle way” in this case refers to The Foundational Verses entitled “Wisdom,” and not to some other major work on the middle way, nor to some other connotation of “middle way.”


[16]
MA DHY’A MA KA’I SKAD KYI BYINGS LA BRTZAMS NAS, DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS SAM DBU MA’I GRUB MTHA’ LA DBU MAR BYAS PAR SHES RAB SGRON MAR YANG BSHAD PAS, DBU MA ZHES PA TZAM LAS MA BYUNG YANG, ‘DIR DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS LA GO BAR BYA’O,,

The Lamp on Wisdom, which of course is working from the original Sanskrit term madhyamaka, also refers both to the Classical Commentary on the Middle Way and to the philosophical system of the Middle Way as “middle way.”  Thus we can say that here in the title of Master Chandrakirti’s work we are meant to understand that he is referring to the Classical Commentary on the Middle Way even when he directly mentions no more than “the middle way.”


[17]
‘O NA [f. 3a] RTZA BA SHES RAB LA BSTAN BCOS ‘DIS ‘JUG TSUL DE JI ‘DRA ZHIG CE NA, ‘DI LA KHA CIG BSTAN BCOS DER KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA’I RANG BZHIN RGYAS PAR MA BRJOD LA, ‘DIR DE GNYIS RGYAS PAR BSTAN PAS DE LA ‘JUG GO ,ZHES ZER RO,,

“Well then,” you may ask.  “Just how is it that Master Chandrakirti’s classical commentary ‘enters’ the Foundational Verses called ‘Wisdom’?”  Some have made the claim that “In that other classical commentary the deceptive and ultimate natures of things are not described in detail; whereas here they are.”


[18]
DE KHO NA NYID GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA’I RIGS PA’I RNAM GRANGS NI, ‘JUG PA LAS RTZA BA SHES RAB SHIN TU RGYAS PAS, BSHAD PA DE LEGS PAR MA MTHONG NGO,,

The fact though is that the Foundational Verses called “Wisdom” uses a much wider variety of reasoning to set forth suchness than does Entering the Middle Way.  As such, this last explanation doesn’t seem so fine to me.


[19]
RANG GI LUGS NI RTZA BA SHES RAB LA ‘JUG PA’I TSUL GNYIS YOD DE, ZAB PA DANG RGYA CHE BA’I SGO NAS SO, ,DE’I DANG PO NI RANG ‘GREL LAS, ,LUGS ‘DI NI THUN MONG MA YIN PA’O, ,ZHES MKHAS PA RNAMS KYIS NGES PAR BYA’O, ,ZHES PA DANG,

Our own position is that there are two ways in which Master Chandrakirti’s text enters into the Foundational Verses called “Wisdom.”  One is through the profound side of the teachings, and the other is through the widespread side of the teachings.  As for the first, the Autocommentary says that “Sages should understand one thing: that this is a truly unique system.”


[20]
DE NYID MA RTOGS PAS CHOS ZAB MO ‘DI SPANGS PAS, DE’I PHYIR BSTAN BCOS KYIS DE KHO NA NYID PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR BSTAN PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS LA ‘JUG PA ‘DI SBYAR BA YIN NO,

It states as well,

They fail to understand suchness, and so they have rejected this profound teaching; as such, I have composed this work, which enters into the classical commentary on the middle way, so that this classical commentary might present suchness in an unerring way.


[21]
ZHES RANG GIS DBU MA’I DON GTAN LA PHAB PA DE, DBU MA PA GZHAN DANG THUN MONG MA YIN PAR BSTAN PA DANG, BSTAN BCOS KYI DON RNAM PAR RIG PA TZAM DANG MTHUN PAR BSHAD DU MI RUNG BA LA NGES PA BSTAN PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA BRTZAMS PAR GSUNGS TE,

What Master Chandrakirti is saying here then is that “I have composed Entering the Middle Way to demonstrate, first of all, why the way that I set forth the meaning of emptiness is truly unique in comparison to the way it is set forth by other proponents of the Middle Way school.  Secondly, I wish to demonstrate how one should come to an understanding that it is mistaken to explain emptiness in the same way as those who belong to the Mentalist School do.”


[22]
TSIG GSAL LAS BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA’I TSUL DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA LAS SHES PAR BYA BAR GSUNGS SHING, RNAM RIG PA’I LUGS DGAG PA RTZA SHE DANG, TSIG GSAL DU MI RGYAS PA [f. 3b] ‘DIR RGYAS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

After all, A Clarification of the Verses advises us to consult Entering the Middle Way for an explanation of the manner in which things are projected based on a relationship of dependence; and whereas the refutation of the Mentalist School is presented in a detailed way neither in the Foundational Verses called “Wisdom” nor in A Clarification of the Verses, the details of this refutation are to be found here in Entering the Middle Way.


[23]
DE’I PHYIR GZHUNG ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS DGOS PA DE GNYIS KYI SGO NAS RTZA SHE’I DON LEGS PAR NGES PA NI, GZHUNG ‘DIS DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA’I TSUL GCIG GO ,

Thus we can say that one way in which this work “enters” the “middle way” is that a person can use it to gain a good understanding of the meaning of the Foundational Verses called “Wisdom” through these first two goals of the text.


[24]
RGYA CHE BA’I SGO NAS DBU MA LA ‘JUG TSUL NI, ‘PHAGS PA’I LUGS ‘DIR THEG PA GNYIS LA GNAS PA LA, SHIN TU ZAB PA’I DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PA’I SHES RAB YOD MED KYIS MI ‘BYED CING, RTZA SHE LAS ZAB MO’I PHYOGS MA GTOGS PA RGYA CHE BA’I THEG CHEN GYI KHYAD CHOS MA BSTAN KYANG, GZHUNG DE NI THEG PA CHE CHUNG GNYIS KYI NANG NAS, THEG CHEN PA’I DBANG DU MDZAD PA YIN TE,

Here next is how Master Chandrakirti’s text enters the middle way through the widespread side of the teachings.  Here in the system of the Realized One, the distinction of which one of the two ways a person belongs to is not drawn on the basis of whether or not they possess that wisdom which realizes the most profound form of suchness.  Furthermore—although it is true that Wisdom focuses on the profound side of the greater way teachings, and not on the details of the widespread side of these teachings—nonetheless, in examining whether it is a scripture of the greater or lesser way, we must say that it presents the greater way.


[25]
RIGS PA’I RNAM GRANGS MTHA’ YAS PAS CHOS KYI BDAG MED RGYAS PAR BSTAN PA NI, THEG CHEN PA’I GDUL BYA KHO NA’I DBANG DU MDZAD PA’I PHYIR DANG, RTZA SHER YANG DE BZHIN DU BSTAN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This is because presenting the lack of a self-nature to things in a detailed way, by using infinite forms of reasoning, is something that is done only with regard to disciples who themselves belong the greater way; and this happens to be exactly how the presentation is done in Wisdom.


[26]
‘DI YANG RANG ‘GREL LAS, CHOS KYI BDAG MED PA GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR THEG PA CHEN PO BSTAN PA YANG RIGS PA NYID DE, RGYAS PAR BSTAN PA BRJOD PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR RO, ,NYAN THOS KYI THEG PA LAS NI CHOS KYI BDAG MED PA MDOR MTSON PA TZAM ZHIG TU ZAD DO, ,ZHES SHIN TU GSAL BAR GSUNGS TE ‘OG TU ‘CHAD DO,,

This point is also made very clearly in the Autocommentary:

If one wishes to clarify the idea that there is no self-nature to things, then it is uniquely appropriate to present the greater way, since one will want to express the presentation in a very detailed manner.  In the teachings of the way of the listeners, it is sufficient to cover the lack of a self-nature to things in but an abbreviated way.

We will discuss this subject further as we continue through the current text.


[27]
DE LTAR NA GZHUNG DER BSTAN PA’I LAM LA THEG PA CHEN PO’I RGYA CHE BA’I LAM GZHAN ‘PHAGS PA’I MAN NGAG GIS KHA BKANG NA SHIN TU LEGS PAS, DE SKONG BA LA SO SKYE’I SA’I CHOS GSUM DANG, ‘PHAGS PA SLOB PA’I SA BCU DANG, [f. 4a] ‘BRAS BU’I SA DANG, SA LNGA PA DANG DRUG PA’I GO RIM GYIS BSAM GTAN GYI NGO BO ZHI GNAS LA BRTEN NAS, BDAG MED PA GNYIS KYI DE KHO NA NYID LA SO SOR RTOG PA’I SHES RAB KYIS DPYOD PA’I LHAG MTHONG SGOM PA RNAMS GSUNGS SO,,

As such, it is perfect if one supplements the path presented in that scripture with other advices from the Realized One on the widespread path in the teachings of the greater way.  We thus find in the current work descriptions of the three qualities of the levels of common beings; the ten levels of realized beings who are still learning; the level of the goal; and the way in which—at the fifth and sixth bodhisattva levels, respectively—one masters quietude, which is the very essence of deep meditation, and then uses this as a platform from which to meditate upon high insight, wherein one explores suchness in the form of the two different types of the lack of a self-nature, utilizing the wisdom of individual analysis.


[28]
DE’I PHYIR RTZA SHE’I DON YID LA BYED PA’I TSE, ‘JUG PA LAS GSUNGS PA ‘DI RNAMS DRAN NAS ZAB PA DANG RGYA CHE BA GNYIS KA TSOGS PA’I LAM GYI RIM PA YID LA BYED PA MA BYUNG NA, GANG ZAG DE LA DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA BRTZAMS PA’I DGOS PA GNYIS STOR BA YIN NO,,

Suppose then that a person is contemplating the meaning of Arya Nagarjuna’s Wisdom, but fails to bring to mind the steps of the path which combines both the profound & the widespread sides of the teaching, by reflecting upon the points just mentioned as they are presented in Master Chandrakirti’s Entering the Middle Way.  Such a person would then be obviating the entire purpose for which the latter text was composed.


[29]
DE’I PHYIR GZHUNG ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS RTZA SHE’I LAM LA RGYA CHE BA’I SGO NAS ‘JUG PA NI, DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA’I TSUL GNYIS PA’O,,

Thus we can say that the second way in which Master Chandrakirti’s work enters the middle way is the way in which we can use this text to engage in the path presented in Arya Nagarjuna’s Wisdom through the widespread side of the teachings.



The translators bow down


	[30]
	[translators’ obeisance]
‘JAM DPAL GZHON NUR GYUR PA LA PHYAG ‘TSAL LO,

I bow down to glorious Gentle Voice, become young.


[31]
GNYIS PA NI, TSIG GI DON GO BAR SLA LA, ‘JAM DPAL LA PHYAG ‘TSAL BA NI, GZHUNG ‘DI DON DAM	PA’I CHOS MNGON PA RNAM PAR BZHAG PA YIN PAS, SHES RAB KYI BSLAB PA GTZO BOR GYUR PA’I PHYIR, SNGON GYI BKAS BCAD PA DANG MTHUN PAR MDZAD PA’O,,

This brings us to the second section from above: the translator’s obeisance.  The wording of this obeisance is easily understood.  As for bowing down to Gentle Voice, remember that Master Chandrakirti’s work is a presentation of the ultimate form of higher knowledge; and as such it deals primarily with the training of wisdom.  The object of the translator’s obeisance then is selected in keeping with the decree.



Singing the praises of great compassion

[32]
GSUM PA LA BZHI, BSTAN BCOS RTZOM PA LA ‘JUG PA’I THABS MCHOD PAR BRJOD PA, BRTZAMS PA’I BSTAN BCOS KYI LUS DNGOS, BSTAN BCOS JI LTAR BRTZAMS PA’I TSUL, BSTAN BCOS BRTZAMS PA’I DGE BA BSNGO BA’O,,

This brings us to the third section from above—the meaning of the body of the text.  This section itself covers four different topics: the offering of praise, which functions as a means of initiating the composition of this classical commentary; the actual body of the commentary which is then composed; a description of how it was that the commentary was first composed; and a dedication of the virtue of having completed the composition.


[33]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, SNYING RJE CHEN PO LA SO SOR MA PHYE BAR BSTOD PA DANG, SNYING RJE CHEN PO LA SO SOR PHYE STE PHYAG ‘TSAL BA’O,,

The first of these—the offering of praise—has two parts: singing the praises of great compassion without dividing out the components; and bowing down to great compassion while making this division.


[34]
DANG PO NI, DGOS PA [f. 4b] DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS LA ‘JUG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU, GANG ZAG DBU MA LA ‘JUG PA RTZOM PAR BZHED PA ZLA BA’I ZHABS KYIS, GZHUNG GZHAN LAS MCHOD BRJOD KYI YUL DU MDZAD PA’I NYAN RANG GNYIS, MCHOD BRJOD KYI YUL DU MA BKOD PAR MA ZAD, 

Here is the first.  Let’s consider the venered Chandrakirti: the person who has agreed to compose the text of Entering the Middle Way, so that we may enter into the Classical Commentary on the Middle Way.  When he writes the traditional offering of praise at the beginning of his work, he decides not to take—as the objects of this praise—the listeners & self-made buddhas which other such classics do make the objects of this offering.


[35]
SANGS RGYAS DANG BYANG SEMS RNAMS LAS KYANG THOG MAR SANGS RGYAS KYI RGYU PHUN SUM TSOGS PA DANG PO, SEMS CAN ‘KHOR BA’I BTZON RAR BSDAMS PA SKYABS MED PA MA LUS PA YONGS SU SKYOB PA’I MTSAN NYID CAN, RGYU’I GTZO BO LA ‘BRAS BU’I MING GIS BTAGS PA’I BCOM LDAN ‘DAS MA, SNYING RJE CHEN PO LA BSTOD BAR ‘OS PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR, NYAN THOS ZHES SOGS TSIGS SU BCAD PA GNYIS SMOS SO,,

And he even goes further: rather than bowing to both the Buddhas & the bodhisattvas, he instead composes the four verses which start with “The listeners…”  The reason that he does so is to indicate that great compassion is a worthy object for us to sing the praises of; for this compassion is the “Lady of Conquest”—this expression itself being a case where we use the name of a result in reference to its principal cause.
