These last further indicate the place; the time; and the school of philosophy in which things fail to grow.  The term “things” is to indicate what it is that doesn’t grow in these three contexts—what it is that is located in the locus.  What the term refers to is “all outer and inner entities.”


[1166]
DES NA BDAG LAS ZHES SOGS KYI GZHUNG GI DON NI, PHYI NANG GI DNGOS PO RNAMS NI YUL DUS GRUB PA’I MTHA’ ‘GAR YANG BDAG LAS SKYE BA SRID PA MA YIN NO, ZHES ‘DI LTAR SBYAR TE BSHAD PAR BYA’O,,

Here then is what the entire first line—ending with “from themselves”—is saying: It is completely impossible for any outer or inner entity to grow from itself, regardless of the place, time, or school of philosophy that we are talking about.  I will present my explanation then based on this reading.


[1167]
DE BZHIN DU DNGOS PO RNAMS NI NAM YANG GZHAN LAS DANG, GNYIS KA LAS DANG RGYU MED LAS SKYE BA SRID PA MA YIN NO, ZHES DAM BCA’ GZHAN GSUM LA YANG SBYAR RO,,

And then we have to read the rest of the lines as expressing three further positions: that—in a similar way—it is impossible for things ever to grow from something else; or from both themselves & something else; or without any cause at all.


[1168]
TSIG GSAL LAS, BDAG LAS DNGOS PO GANG DAG CES BSGYUR YANG ‘GYUR ‘DI LEGS SO,,

In the Clarification of the Verses, the translation of the one section reads “Nothing grows from itself”; but the version we’ve given here is preferable.  


[1169]
YUL GYI DBANG GIS YUL ‘GA’ ZHIG TU GUR KUM MI SKYE BA DANG, DUS KYI DBANG GIS DUS ‘GA’ ZHIG GI TSE LO TOG MI SKYE BA LTA BU YIN NAM SNYAM PA, YUL DUS GANG NA YANG ZHES PAS ‘GOG PAS NAM YANG ZHES SMOS PA DON MED PA MIN NO,,

Now some might think that the not growing here refers to certain places—saying for example that saffron never grows in certain lands; or that it refers to certain times—saying that crops won’t grow in certain seasons.  As such, it is not without meaning that the verse mentions the word “ever,” in order to eliminate every possible place or time.


[1170]
DBU MA PA’I GRUB MTHA’I DBANG GIS MI SKYE YANG, DNGOS POR SMRA BA’I GRUB MTHA’I DBANG GIS SKYE’O SNYAM PA, GRUB MTHA’ GANG NA YANG ZHES PAS ‘GOG PAS, DNGOS POR SMRA BA’I LUGS LA MI SKYE ZHES STON PA MIN NO,,

Others might think that when the verse says that things “don’t grow,” it is only relative to the Middle Way school of philosophy; and that they do grow when we are speaking from the point of view of the Functionalist schools.  This idea is eliminated when the verse indicates “no matter what the school of philosophy”—although this is not meant to say that according to the Functionalist schools nothing grows.


[1171]
RANG ‘GREL LAS ‘DIR MA YIN ZHES BYA BA ‘DI YOD PA NYID KYI SGRUB BYED RANG LAS SKYE BA DANG ‘BREL GYI, YOD PA DANG NI MA YIN TE, DE DGAG PA DON GYIS ‘GRUB PA’I PHYIR RO,

At this point, the autocommentary says:

The words “there is nothing” should be combined with the proof concerning the possibility that there is something; that is, that things could grow from themselves.  And this possibility is in truth not one; which is to say, the denial of this possibility is established, by implication.


[1172]
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON NI RKANG PA PHYI MA GNYIS KYIS DAM BCA’ DANG, SNGA MA [f. 91b] GNYIS KYIS RTAGS BSTAN PAR ‘CHAD PA LTAR SO SOR MI GCOD PAR, BDAG LAS SKYE BA YOD PA MA YIN, ZHES SBREL BAR BYA ZHES PA STE GZHAN GSUM LA’ANG DE LTAR SBREL LO,,

What this is saying is that the second half of the verse is presenting the assertion, whereas the first half is presenting the reason to prove this assertion.  And as we’ve explained here, we should not divorce these two from each other, but rather combine them: “There is nothing that grows from itself.”  We are to combine the other three possibilities in the same manner.


[1173]
RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA YOD NA DE’I SGRUB BYED DU MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA GANG RUNG KHAS BLANG DGOS PAS YOD PA’I SGRUB BYED CES SMOS SO,,

If there were such a thing as something growing through some nature of its own, then one would have to agree that—as a proof of this fact—the thing would have to grow through one of the four possibilities.  This is why the autocommentary mentions a “proof concerning the possibility that there is something.”


[1174]
MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA KHEGS NA RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DGAG PA YANG SHUGS KYIS ‘GRUB PAS, DE LTAR SBYAR BA LA RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE MED MI ‘GRUB PA’I SKYON MED PA NI TSIG THA MA’I DON NO,,

Once we disprove that anything could grow in any of the four possible ways, then by implication we have disproven, as well, that anything could grow through some nature of its own.  Once we have made this connection, there is no possible problem that we have failed to prove that nothing can grow through a nature of its own—and this is the point of the closing words of this citation from the autocommentary.


[1175]
DES NA DBU MA SNANG BAR BSHAD PA LTAR MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA BKAG PA RTAGS SU BYAS NAS, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE MED SGRUB PA MI RUNG ZHES PA MIN GYI, SNGAR LTAR SO SOR GCOD PA GZHUNG DE’I DON MIN ZHES PA’O,,

Thus the corresponding reference in Light on the Middle Way is not saying that it would be incorrect to prove that things could never grow through any nature of their own by using, as our reason for this assertion, a denial that things could grow in any of the four possible ways; rather, it is saying—as we’ve mentioned above—that the point of the original scripture is not that we should divorce the two ideas.


[1176]
DNGOS PO RNAMS YUL DUS GRUB PA’I MTHA’ ‘GAR YANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA SRID PA MA YIN, ZHES SBYAR BA DANG,

And then we are to combine the statements so that they come out saying, “No matter what place or time or school you are talking about, it is impossible for things to grow from something other than themselves.”


[1177]
TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG, RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM GYIS KUN RDZOB GRUB PAR KHAS LEN GYI, PHYOGS BZHI KHAS BLANGS PA’I SGO NAS NI MA YIN TE, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR PA’I PHYIR DANG,

Now the Clarification of the Verses goes on to state—

It is only the fact of conditioned existence that we accept as being deceptive reality; it is not that we believe that it is described by these four possibilities.  Because if that were the case, then we would have to be saying that things did have a nature of their own; and moreover…


[1178]
ZHES GSUNGS PAS GZHAN SKYE NI GSUNG RAB KYI THA SNYAD MIN GYI GRUB MTHA’ SMRA BA’I THA SNYAD YIN LA, DE YANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN LA BSAMS NAS BYAS PAS, DE KHAS BLANGS NA RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR,

As such, we can say that “things growing from something other than themselves” is not a term found in the word of the Buddha, but rather one which is used by followers of particular philosophical schools.  In these people’s minds, the term connotes “things other than themselves which exist by definition.”  As such, anyone who accepts this kind of growing would then be someone who asserted that things had a nature of their own.


[1179]
LUGS ‘DI LA NI GZHAN SKYE THA SNYAD DU YANG MED DO, ,RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS NGO BO THA DAD PAR THA SNYAD DU ‘DOD MOD [f. 92a] KYANG DE TZAM GZHAN SKYE’I DON MIN TE, THA SNYAD DU CHOS RE RES KYANG NGO BO GNYIS GNYIS ‘DZIN PAR GSUNGS PA LTAR NGO BO GRUB PA YOD KYANG, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA’I NGO BOR MI ‘DOD PA BZHIN NO,,

Here in this system, the possibility that things could grow from something other than themselves cannot even in a nominal way be correct.  We do admittedly accept that, in a nominal sense, a cause is not such that to be it would be to be its result.  But this alone is not what is meant by the expression “growing from something other than itself.”  It is said that every existing thing has two types of essential natures; which is to say, even though they do possess a kind of essential nature, we do not accept that this constitutes an essential nature where they would grow through some nature of their own.


[1180]
TSIG GSAL LAS DNGOS PO BDAG LAS SKYE BA MED PA’I DAM BCA’ MED DGAG TU BSHAD PA NI, DAM BCA’ GZHAN GSUM LA YANG ‘DRA BAS, RANG BZHIN MED PAR GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA’I SKABS SU BSGRUB BYA NI DGAG BYA BCAD TZAM GYI MED PAR DGAG PA YIN TE,

The Clarification of the Verses explains that the assertion that things never grow from themselves refers to a negative in the sense of an absence; and this applies as well to the other three assertions here.  As such, the idea we are trying to prove in this context of establishing that things have no nature of their own is a negative in the sense of an absence which consists of the simple exclusion of the thing that emptiness denies. 


[1181]
TSIG GSAL LAS, ,’JIG RTEN DE NA JI SNYED SGRA YOD PA, ,THAMS CAD DNGOS MED CI YANG MED PA ZHES, ,BYA BA LA SOGS PA ‘BYUNG BAS NA, ,MED PAR DGAG PA BRJOD PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR, DNGOS PO MED PA’I DON NI RANG BZHIN MED PA’I DON YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR RO,,

It’s just as the Clarification states in these lines—

We see statements such as:

	All of the sounds
	That ever occur in this world

	Are each of them telling us
	That nothing is real,

	That nothing is there
	At all.

We view these as expressing a negation in the sense of an absence; and so the meaning of saying that “nothing is real” is to say that nothing has any nature of its own.


[1182]
RANG ‘GREL LAS DAM BCA’ BA BZHI PO DE RJES SU BRJED {%BRJOD} NAS RIGS PAS BSGRUB PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA, ZHES GSUNGS SHING, ‘OG NAS MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA BKAG PA RTAGS SU BYAS NAS, DNGOS PO RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG BRAL BAR GSUNGS PA DANG,

The autocommentary states that “The statement of these four assertions is meant to establish the point through reasoning.”  And further on it gives the denial that things could grow in the four different ways as a reason for saying that every thing that exists is devoid of growing through any nature of its own.


[1183]
TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA BKAG PA’I MTHAR, DE’I PHYIR SKYE BA YOD PA MA YIN NO ZHES BYA BA ‘DI BSGRUB PA YIN LA, ZHES GSUNGS PAS DNGOS PO RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PA SGRUB PAR MI ‘DOD PA MIN NO,,

And A Clarification of the Verses, after it disproves that things could things could grow in any of the four different ways, says that “Thus we establish the idea that ‘There is no starting at all’.”  Thus it is not the case that we believe that the fact that nothing in the universe grows through any nature of its own is left unproven.


[1184]
TSIG GSAL LAS, RJES SU DPAG PA DAG NI GZHAN GYI DAM BCA’ BA ‘GOG PA TZAM GYI ‘BRAS BU CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES GSUNGS PA NI SBYOR BA RNAMS [f. 92b] KYIS PHA ROL POS RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR DAM BCAS PA ‘GOG PA TZAM DU ZAD KYI, DE LAS GZHAN MI SGRUB PA’I DON YIN GYI BKAG PA TZAM SGRUB PA ‘GOG PA MIN NO,,

The Clarification also says, “This is so because these cases of inference have the result of presenting a position which is a simple denial.”  Which is to say, these syllogisms serve only to disprove the assertion of the other side that things could exist through any nature of their own—they don’t go on to prove anything in addition to that.  Which is not to deny that they do prove a simple absence.


[1185]
DE BZHIN DU, KHO BO CAG ‘DI MED PA DANG YOD PAR MI SGRUB KYI, GZHAN GYIS YOD PAR BTAGS PA DANG MED PAR BTAGS PA ‘GOG STE, MTHA’ GNYIS BSAL NAS DBU MA’I LAM SGRUB PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES GSUNGS PA YANG PHA ROL POS KHAS BLANGS PA’I YOD MTHA’ DANG, MED MTHA’ GNYIS RNAM PAR GCOD PA TZAM YIN GYI, DE MA GTOGS PA GZHAN MI SGRUB CES PA’I DON NO,,

Likewise these lines are saying: “We for our part are not trying to prove that this doesn’t exist, or that that does exist.  Rather, we are denying what others imagine to exist; and what they imagine does not exist.  What we want to do is eliminate the two extremes, and arrive at the path of the middle way.”  That is, all we are doing is cutting off the two extremes accepted by the other party—that things could exist, or not exist.  We are not trying to go on to make some positive assertion after that.


[1186]
MTHA’ GNYIS BKAG PA TZAM MA BSGRUBS PA YANG MA YIN TE, MTHA’ GNYIS BSAL NAS DBU MA’I LAM SGRUB PAR GSUNGS PAS SO,,

Nor is it the case that not even the simple denial of the two extremes is accomplished here; for the Realized One does in fact eliminate the two extremes, and proceeds to establish the path of the middle way.


[1187]
RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PA YANG MIN NA NI PHUNG GSUM MED PAS RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA YIN TE, RTZOD ZLOG LAS,

Now if were not the case that things could not exist through any nature of their own, there is no third option: they would have then to exist through such a nature.  Stopping All Argument states the case quite clearly:


	[1188]
,GAL TE RANG BZHIN MED NYID KYIS,
,CI STE RANG BZHIN MED LA BZLOG
,RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID LOG NA,
,RANG BZHIN NYID DU RAB GRUB ‘GYUR,
ZHES GSAL BAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Suppose that the lack
Of any self-nature to things

Were to cancel the lack
Of a self-nature to things,

And this lack of self-nature
Ceased to exist.

In that case then things
Would automatically come
To possess this nature of their own.


[1189]
DE ‘DRA BA’I BSGRUB BYA DANG SGRUB BYED KHAS LEN KYANG RANG RGYUD PAR MI ‘GYUR BA’I RGYU MTSAN NI, RGYAS PAR GZHAN DU YANG YANG BSHAD ZIN PAS MA SPROS SO,,

Even if we were to accept here something which was proven and something that proved it, these would not work in a way that was inherently effective.  The reason for this I have covered in detail over & over in other works—and so I will not expand on it here.


[1190]
‘O NA DGAG PA GNYIS KYI MTSAN NYID JI LTA BU ZHE NA,

One may ask: “How then do you define these two kinds of negation?”


[1191]
SPYIR DGAG PA NI BLOS DGAG BYA DNGOS SU BCAD NAS RTOGS PAR BYA BA YIN PAS, ,RANG MA YIN BCAD PA LTA BU DNGOS PO LA DGAG BYA BCAD PA TZAM DGAG PA MIN LA, CHOS NYID DANG DON DAM BDEN PA LTA BU SGRAS DGAG BYA [f. 93a] DNGOS SU MA BCAD KYANG DE’I DON BLO LA ‘CHAR BA NA, SPROS PA BCAD PA’I RNAM PA CAN DU ‘CHAR BA RNAMS DGAG PA YIN NO,,

Generally speaking, we define a negation as something which is perceived by the mind through the process of excluding, directly, whatever it denies.  Thus it is not a negation when all we do is exclude what’s denied in the sense of excluding everything that a particular thing is not.  In the case though of something like the true nature of things, or ultimate reality, the term itself does not directly exclude what is denied; nonetheless, when the meaning of the term makes itself known to the mind, the mind thinks of things in a way which excludes elaboration—and this process is then a negation.


[1192]
DE LA GNYIS LAS MED DGAG NI BLOS DGAG BYA DNGOS SU BCAD NAS CHOS GZHAN MI ‘PHEN PA’AM MI SGRUB PA YIN TE, DPER NA BRAM ZES CHANG ‘THUNG DU RUNG MI RUNG DRIS PA NA, CHANG MI BTUNG NGO ZHES PA NI CHANG ‘THUNG PA RNAM PAR BCAD PA TZAM ZHIG YIN GYI, DE LAS GZHAN PA’I BTUNG BA BTUNG NGO ZHE ‘AM MI BTUNG NGO ZHES MI SGRUB PA BZHIN NO,,

This process of negation comes in two versions.  In the case of a simple absence, no additional phenomenon is implied, or established, when the mind directly excludes what the negation denies.  Think of the parallel example of when a Brahmin asks whether or not it is alright to drink alcohol; the reply “don’t drink it” is only an exclusion that alcohol should be drunk—it is not at the same time a positive assertion that one should or should not drink something else.


[1193]
MA YIN DGAG NI BLOS DGAG BYA BCAD NAS CHOS GZHAN ‘PHEN PA’AM SGRUB PA YIN TE, DPER NA SKYES BU GCIG DMANGS RIGS SU STON ‘DOD PA NA ‘DI BRAM ZE MA YIN ZHES PA NI, BRAM ZE BKAG PA TZAM MIN GYI BRAM ZE LAS GZHAN PA, DE LAS THOS PA LA SOGS PAS DMAN PA’I DMANGS RIGS YIN PAR SGRUB PA LTA BU’O,,

The other kind of negation is where we deny identity.  In this case, an additional phenomenon is implied, or established, when the mind excludes what the negation denies.  Suppose for example that we want to indicate that a particular person belongs to the class of commoners, and so we say of them, “He or she is not a Brahmin.”  This is not a simple denial that the person is of the Brahmin class; rather, it is also a positive assertion that the person belongs to the commoner class—that he or she is something other than the Brahmin class, and is somehow inferior to them in education or the like.


[1194]
CHOS GZHAN ‘PHEN PA LA DNGOS DANG SHUGS DANG SKABS KYIS ‘PHANGS PA GSUM STE, DANG PO NI, BDAG MED PA YOD CES PA LTA BU STE DGAG BYA GCOD PA DANG, CHOS GZHAN ‘PHEN PA GNYIS KA TSIG GCIG GIS SGRUB PA’O,,

When we say that “some other phenomenon is implied,” there are three different ways in which this implication can occur: directly, by intimation, or from context.  An example of the first would be something like the statement that “There does exist a lack of a self-nature to things.”  In this case, a single phrase serves both to exclude what it denies, and to imply another phenomenon.


[1195]
GNYIS PA NI, MCHOD SBYIN TSON PO NYIN PAR MI ZA BA ZHES PA LTA BU STE DON GYIS BSTAN PA’O,,

The second type can be illustrated by a statement such as, “That chubby fellow, John, never eats during the day”—intimating that something else is the case.


[1196]
DE GNYIS NI DNGOS SHUGS LA ‘PHANGS PA RE RE BA YIN LA, GNYIS KA LDAN PA NI MCHOD SBYIN TSON PO NYIN PAR MI ZA BA RID PA MIN PA YOD CES PA LTA BU’O,,

These two are, respectively, examples of direct implication and implication by intimation.  A case which is both of these at the same time would be a statement such as, “That chubby fellow, John, never eats during the day—and he is certainly not skinny!”


[1197]
GSUM PA NI, SKYES BU ZHIG RGYAL RIGS DANG BRAM ZE GANG RUNG GCIG TU NGES SHING KHYAD PAR MA [f. 93b] NGES PA’I SKABS SU, ‘DI BRAM ZE MA YIN ZHES PA LTA BU RANG GI TSIG GIS MI STON PA STE, SHES RAB SGRON MA’I ‘GREL BSHAD DU DRANGS PA LAS,

An example of the third would be a case where we knew that a person had to belong either to the class of royalty or to the Brahmin class, but we weren’t sure which of the two they were.  In this instance, someone else telling us that “He or she is not a Brahmin” would not indicate, in the wording taken by itself, which one they were.  We see for example the following lines quoted in the explication of the Lamp on Wisdom:


	[1198]
,DGAG PA DON GYIS BSTAN PA DANG,
,TSIG GCIG SGRUB PAR BYED PA DANG,
,DE LDAN RANG TSIG MI STON PA,
,MA YIN GZHAN PA GZHAN YIN NO,
ZHES SO,,

A negation can imply
Something else by intimation;

A single phrase can also
Function to assert;
Both; or be insufficient,
In the wording alone,
To do the indicating.

This then is the other kind,
Where we deny
Some other identity.


[1199]
KHA CIG GZHI SGRUB PA DANG TSOGS NA MED DGAG MIN PAR SMRA BA MI ‘THAD DE, BRAM ZE SGRUB PA YIN PAS BRAM ZES CHANG MI ‘THUNG BA DGAG BYA BCAD TZAM YIN PA MI ‘GOG PA’I PHYIR TE, DPER NA SGRA MNGON GYUR YIN PAS SGRA MI RTAG PA LKOG GYUR YIN PA MI ‘GOG PA BZHIN NO,,

Some say that it is incorrect to mention a negation which is not the absence of something in the same phrase with something that does in fact exist.  A Brahmin for example is a positive entity, and so when you say “Brahmins don’t drink alcohol,” you are not denying something in the sense of simply excluding what you mean to deny.  Saying that sound exists at the manifest level of reality doesn’t deny, for example, that the fact that sound is a changing thing exists at the recondite level of existence.


[1200]
GZHAN DAG GZHI DANG TSOGS NA CHOS GZHAN ‘PHANGS SO ZHES PA YANG MI ‘THAD DE, BRAM ZE LTA BU NI CHOS GZHAN ‘PHEN MI ‘PHEN RTZI BA’I GZHI YIN GYI, ‘PHANGS PA’I CHOS GZHAN MIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Still others say that a negation in conjunction with what it applies to is the other phenomenon implied—but this is also incorrect.  Someone like the Brahmin here is what we are checking to see if some other phenomenon is implied, or not; but they do not themselves constitute the other phenomenon which is implied.



Four denials of the Realized One

	[1201]
	[VI.8]
Tebhyas ta eva na bhavanti kutaḥ parebhyo
dvābhyāṃ na cāpi kuta eva vinaiva hetum,
Tasmād dhi tasya bhavane na guṇo’sti kaścij
jātasya janma punar eva ca naiva yuktam.


	[VI.8a]
,DE NYID DE LAS ‘BYUNG MIN GZHAN DAG LAS
LTA GA LA ZHIG ,
,GNYI GA LAS KYANG MA YIN RGYU MED PAR
NI GA LA YOD,

This cannot occur through that—
And how could it occur
Through something other?

Nor could it through both.
How as well could it occur
Without a cause at all?


[1202]
DE LTAR ‘PHAGS PA’I DAM BCA’ GZHI ‘DIR BKOD PA NI, ‘BRAS BU DE NYID DE’I NGO BO NYID LAS ‘BYUNG BA MIN PA DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I RGYU GZHAN DAG LAS LTA ‘BYUNG BA GA LA ZHIG STE DE MED PA DANG, RANG GZHAN GNYIS KA LAS KYANG ‘BYUNG BA MA YIN PA DANG, RGYU MED PAR NI ‘BYUNG BA GA LA YOD DE MED DO,,

And so the assertion that the Realized One is setting forth at this point is that this result cannot occur through “that”—through some essential nature of its own.  And how could it occur (meaning, it could never occur) through something other than itself which also existed by definition?  Nor could the result occur through both itself and something other than it.  How as well could it occur (meaning, it could never occur) without a cause at all?


[1203]
DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YOD NA MTHA’ BZHI’I SKYE BA GANG RUNG GIS KHYAB STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA LA RGYU YOD MED GNYIS SU KHA TSON CHOD CING, RGYU YOD PA LA RANG GZHAN RE RE BA DANG GNYIS KA TSOGS PA LAS SKYE BA GSUM DU KHA TSON CHOD PAS DAM BCA’ BZHIS CHOG GO ,,

And if there were such a thing as something existing through some nature of its own, then it would necessarily have to grow in one of these four ways.  This is because for a thing to grow through some nature of its own, it would either have to have a cause, or have no cause: there are only two choices.  And if it did have a cause, then that cause would have either to be the thing itself, or something other than the thing itself; or else both of these two options together—there are only these three choices.  As such, a total of four assertions is sufficient to make the point.



Nothing grows in either reality

[1204]
GNYIS PA LA BZHI, BDAG SKYE DGAG PA, GZHAN [f. 94a] SKYE DGAG PA, GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BA DGAG PA, RGYU MED PAR SKYE BA DGAG PA’O,,

This brings us to the second step in denying—with regard to both realities—that things could start in any of the four possible ways.  This is presenting the proofs which establish, through the use of logic, the assertion that there is no such thing as something starting through some nature of its own.  We proceed in four steps: denying that things could grow from themselves; that they could grow from something other than themselves; that they could grow through both; and that they could grow without any cause at all.



Nothing grows from itself

[1205]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, ‘GREL PA MDZAD PA’I RIGS PAS DGAG PA, RTZA BA SHES RAB KYI RIGS PAS DGAG PA’O,,

We will discuss the first of these in two parts of its own: accomplishing the denial by using the logic employed by the author of the autocommentary; and then by using the logic employed in Wisdom.



Chandrakirti’s logic against
things growing from themselves

[1206]
DANG PO LA GSUM, DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAR ‘DOD PA’I GRUB MTHA’ MKHAN GYI LUGS DGAG PA, GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA’I THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PAR BSTAN PA, DE LTAR BKAG PA RNAMS KYI DON BSDU BA’O,,

The first of these, in turn, comes in three sections: denying the system of those who believe they have perceived some actual nature; demonstrating that things could not be said to grow from themselves even in the parlance of those who have not been influenced by any particular school of philosophy; and finally a summary of these denials.



Denying ideas of those who think
they perceive some actual nature

[1207]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, RANG DANG NGO BO GCIG PA’I RGYU LAS SKYE BA DGAG PA, RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GNYIS NGO BO GCIG PA DGAG PA’O,,

Again, the first of these three comes in two further steps: a denial that something could grow from a cause which was such that to be that cause was to be what had grown from it; and a denial that a cause could at any rate be such that to be it were to be its result.



Denying causes that are their results

[1208]
DANG PO LA GSUM, NGO BO GCIG PA’I RGYU LAS SKYE NA DON MED DU THAL BA DANG, NGO BO GCIG PA LAS SKYE NA RIGS PA DANG ‘GAL BA DANG, DE DAG GI NYES SPONG GI LAN DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Once more, the first of these will be covered in three sections of its own: a demonstration that it would be meaningless for a result to grow from a cause that was such that to be the cause were to be the result; explaining that it would contradict logic if a result were to grow from a cause that were such that to be the cause were to be the result; and then refuting replies which attempt to deny these problems.  Here is the first of these.


[1209]
DNGOS PO RNAMS BDAG LAS MI SKYE BA ‘DI RGYU MTSAN GANG LAS NGES SHE NA,

One may ask: “What reason for it can help us grasp the idea that things cannot grow from themselves?”



The pointlessness of self-existence

	[1210]
[VI.8b]
,DE NI DE LAS ‘BYUNG NA YON TAN ‘GA’ YANG
YOD MA YIN,

There would be no additional
Point at all served to this,
If it were to occur through that.


[1211]
SKYE BZHIN PA SKYE BA’I BYA BA’I BYED PA PO MYU GU DE NI, DE’I RANG GI NGO BO LAS BYUNG NA DE LTAR ‘BYUNG BA LA ‘BYUNG DGOS PA’I YON TAN LHAG PO ‘GA’ YANG YOD PA MA YIN TE, MYU GU’I RANG GI NGO BO YOD PA NYID SNGAR RGYU’I DUS NAS THOB ZIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Let’s look at this sprout, as it grows: the sprout which is the agent of the action of growing.  If it were to occur through some essential nature of its own, then there would be no additional point at all served—there would be no need satisfied—by its occurring in this particular way.  This is because the sprout’s having its own nature would have come about already, earlier—at the time of its cause.


[1212]
‘DI LA GRANGS CAN PA RNAMS RGYU RKYEN PHAN TSUN SO SO THA DAD PA RNAMS LA ‘BRAS BU THUN MONG BA GCIG NI YOD LA, DE YANG RGYU RKYEN RNAMS LA RANG BZHIN GCIG PA’I GTZO BO GCIG RJES SU ‘GRO BA MED NA MI RUNG BAS, RGYU NAS KYI RANG BZHIN GANG YIN PA YANG, RKYEN CHU LUD SOGS KYI RANG BZHIN YIN LA,

Now the followers of the Numerist School say that a single, shared result comes from causes & conditions which are distinct from one another.  They assert that it would be wrong to say that these causes & conditions did not follow upon a single primal cause; thus the nature of the cause—say, a grain of barley—must be the nature of the conditions, things like the water and the fertilizer.


[1213]
DE BZHIN DU MYU GU’I RANG BZHIN DANG DE’I RGYU RKYEN GYI RANG BZHIN RNAMS PHAR YIN TSUR YIN DU [f. 94b] ‘DOD DE, RNAM ‘GYUR THAMS CAD KYI RANG BZHIN RNAMS DE LTAR DU ‘DOD DO,,

They believe similarly that the nature of the result would have to be the nature of both the causes & conditions, and vice versa—for this is what they believe about the nature of every individual manifestation.


[1214]
DE’I PHYIR SA MYUG PHAN TSUN THA DAD PA KHO NAR ‘DOD PAS MYU GU MYU GU LAS SKYE BAR MI ‘DOD KYANG, MYU GU NI SA BON DANG DE’I RANG BZHIN LAS SKYE BAR SMRA BA NA, RANG BZHIN GNYIS GCIG YIN PAS RANG GI RANG BZHIN LAS KYANG SKYE BA DANG MYU GU MI GSAL BA RGYU DUS NA YOD PA SKYE BA NI BDAG SKYE’I ‘DOD TSUL LO,,

As such they would say that the seed and the sprout can only be distinct from one another—and they would not agree that the sprout had grown from the sprout.  Nonetheless, if you do say that the sprout grows from the seed and from its nature, then since the two natures are one, you would have to say that the sprout had grown from its own nature; and that what grows is a sprout that existed at the time of its cause, but in a way which wasn’t manifest.  This is the way then in which they believe that when something grows, it grows from itself.


[1215]
GRANGS CAN GYI KHYAD PAR ‘GA’ ZHIG NI SKYE BAR MI SMRA BAR RGYU LAS SNGAR MI GSAL BA PHYIS GSAL BAR ‘DOD MOD KYANG DON ‘DRA’O,,

It is admittedly the case that there are some kinds of Numerists who don’t speak of something growing; rather, they phrase it as something manifesting from its cause which wasn’t manifest earlier.  But this amounts to the same thing as the other.


[1216]
‘DIS SPYI GSAL NGO BO GCIG TU ‘DOD PA YANG DE LTAR YIN GYI, SANGS RGYAS PAS DNGOS PO DANG BUM PA NGO BO GCIG TU ‘DOD PA DANG GTAN MI ‘DRA’O,,

This by the way describes the belief of this school that to be the particular is to be the general; but this is entirely different from the way in which the Buddhists would say that to be a water pitcher is to be a functioning thing.


[1217]
DE LTAR MYU GU’I NGO BO’AM RANG BZHIN GANG YIN THAMS CAD SA BON GYI DUS SU YOD NA, MYU GU’I NGO BO LAS DON GZHAN PA’I MYU GU GSAL BA NYID KYANG MI SRID PAS RGYU DUS NAS MYU GU’I RANG BZHIN NAM NGO BOR MA ZAD, MYU GU NYID KYANG YOD DGOS PAS, DE’I TSE DE GRUB PA’I ‘OG TU SLAR YANG SKYE BA LA DON GTAN MED DO,,

Thus we can say that—if every form of some essence or nature which the sprout possesses is present at the same time as the seed—then it is impossible for there to be any particular of a sprout which is a different entity from the essential nature of the sprout.  Not only that, but since the sprout itself must also be present already, then at that point—when it has already come into being—there is absolutely no point to its growing once again, after that time.



Things grown need not grow again

	[1218]
[VI.9]
Jātasya janmani punaḥ parikalpyamāne,
naivāṅkurādaya iha prabhavaṃ labheran.
Bījasya ca prabhava eva bhaved bhavāntaṃ,
tenaiva tasya hi kathaṃ ca bhaved vināśaḥ.

[VI.8c-VI.9a]
,SKYES PAR GYUR PA SLAR YANG SKYE BAR
RIGS PA’ANG MA YIN NYID,
,SKYES ZIN SLAR YANG SKYE BAR YONGS SU
RTOG PAR ‘GYUR NA NI,
,MYU GU LA SOGS RNAMS KYI SKYE BA
‘DIR RNYED MI ‘GYUR ZHING,

		If something had already grown,
		It would as well be totally illogical
		For it to grow once more.

		And suppose you fantasize
		That something already grown
		Could ever grow again;

		It would then be the case
That we could never observe
		Sprouts & such growing here.
				


[1219]
GNYIS PA NI, SKYES ZIN PAR GYUR PA SLAR YANG STE SKYES ZIN PA’I ‘OG TU LDABS NAS, SKYE BAR RIGS PA MA YIN PA NYID DO,,

Here is the second section from above: explaining that it would contradict logic if a result were to grow from a cause that were such that to be the cause were to be the result.  If something had already grown, then it would be totally illogical for it to be planted, and to grow, once more—that is, after the point that it had already grown.


[1220]
‘ANG GI SGRAS NI RANG GI RANG BZHIN LAS SKYE NA DON MED DU ‘GYUR BAR MA ZAD PA’O,,

The words “as well” are meant to say, “not only would it be pointless for something to grow from its own self-nature…”


[1221]
GAL TE GSAL BA’I PHYOGS ‘DZIN NA’ANG ‘BRAS BU GSAL BA RGYU DUS NAS YOD NA NI KHAS BLANGS DANG ‘GAL LA, MED NA NI ‘BRAS BU’I GSAL BA DANG DE’I RANG BZHIN GNYIS GCIG THA DAD DPYAD LA DGAG GO

Even if we were to consider this from the point of view of being the particular of a general, it would be a contradiction of what one has accepted to say that a result which was a particular could be present starting from the time of the cause.  And if it were not present, then that would prevent us from examining the question of whether the result as a particular, and its self-nature, were the same thing or separate things.


[1222]
,BDAG SKYE RIGS PA DANG ‘GAL ZHES PA DAM [f. 95a] BCA’ TZAM DU ZAD PAS DE ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA STON PA NI,

Even if all we do is to assert that something growing from itself would contradict logic, we should present the particular logic which denies this idea.


[1223]
SKYES ZIN PA’I SA BON SLAR YANG LDABS NAS SKYE BAR YONGS SU RTOG PAR ‘GYUR BA STE ‘DOD NA NI, RGYU MTSAN GANG GIS SA BON LDABS NAS SKYE BA BKAG NAS, MYU GU SKYE BAR ‘DOD PA SLAR YANG SA BON DE SKYE BA LA GEGS CI ZHIG YOD DE MED PAS, MYU GU DANG LA SOGS PAS SDONG BU DANG SBUBS ‘CHA’ BA SOGS KYI SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN ‘DIR GTAN RNYED PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

And so suppose that you fantasize (which is to say, believe) that we take a seed which has already grown, and plant it again, and then it grows.  What reason could you ever give then for saying that—once you had planted a seed, and it had grown and then stopped, and then from that the sprout had grown (all according to you)—the seed was prevented from growing once more?  There could in fact be no such reason.  And as such, it would then have to be the case, in the whole world here, that we could never observe, at all, instances where sprouts & such (which is meant to include things like the trunks of trees, and the channels inside them) ever grew.



Things would grow themselves forever

	[1224]
[VI.9b]
,SA BON SRID MTHAR THUG PAR RAB TU
SKYE BA NYID DU ‘GYUR,

The seed could only
Continue to grow,

Until the very end
Of the universe.


[1225]
SKYON GZHAN YANG SA BON DE NYID BAR MA CHAD PAR SRID PA’I MTHAR THUG PAR RAB TU SKYE BA NYID DU ‘GYUR TE, SKYES ZIN PA DE NYID SLAR YANG SKYE DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And there is yet another problem: That same seed could only continue to grow, without interruption, until the very end of the universe.  Because there was some need for something that had already grown to grown once more.


[1226]
DE NI ‘BRAS BU’I RIGS ‘DRA RNAMS MI SKYE BA DANG, RGYU’I RIGS ‘DRA RNAMS BAR MA CHAD DU SKYE BA’I SKYON GNYIS BSTAN NAS RIGS PA DANG ‘GAL BA BRJOD PA’O,,

These sections express contradiction by demonstrating two problems with the proposed ideas: how results of the same type could never grow at all; and how causes of the same type would have to grow without interruption.



A thing cannot act to destroy itself

	[1227]
[VI.9c]
,JI LTAR DE NYID KYIS DE [f. 204b] RNAM PAR ‘JIG PAR
BYED PAR ‘GYUR,

How could the presence
Of the one ever act [f. 204b]
To destroy the other?


[1228]
GSUM PA NI, CI STE MYU GU SKYE BA LE PHAN ‘DOGS PA’I RKYEN CHU DANG, DPYID KYI DUS LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYIS NI, SA BON SBANG RO LTA BUR RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA BYED CING, MYU GU SKYED PAR BYED LA,

Here is the third section from above, refuting replies which attempt to deny these problems.  So suppose someone thinks the following:

Now let’s consider what happens when a sprout grows.  Conditions which contribute to this growth—things like water, or spring having arrived—bring about a change in the seed, in the way that malt is changed during the process of fermentation.  And then it produces the sprout.


[1229]
MYU GU YANG RANG SKYED PA PO SA BON DANG LHAN CIG TU GNAS PAR ‘GAL BA’I PHYIR, SA BON ‘GAG PAR BYED CING ‘BYUNG BAS RIGS PA DANG ‘GAL BA’I SKYON GNYIS SMRAS PA’I NYES PA’I SKABS MED LA,

And it’s a contradiction to say that the sprout could be there at the same time as the seed which produced it.  Therefore the seed is put to a stop and then the thing occurs; there is no possible place here for the problems that you raised when you criticized our view by pointing out two kinds of contradiction.


[1230]
SA MYUG KYANG RANG BZHIN NAM NGO BO GZHAN MA YIN PAS BDAG LAS MI SKYE BA YANG MA YIN NO SNYAM NA,

And since the seed and the sprout are not such that to be one is not to be the other, in their nature or essence, then it’s further not the case that the sprout has not grown from itself.


[1231]
‘DI YANG MI RUNG STE GANG GI PHYIR SA MYUG GNYIS KYI RANG BZHIN GNYIS RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU GCIG YIN PAS [f. 95b] JI LTAR NA MYU GU DE NYID KYIS SA BON DE RNAM PAR ‘JIG PAR BYED PAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR TE, MYU GUS MYU GU ‘JIG PAR MI BYED PA BZHIN NO SNYAM DU BSAMS SO,,

That too though is a mistaken idea.  The reason is that—if the two natures of the two things, the seed & the sprout, were in every aspect the same—then how could the presence of the one (the sprout) ever act to destroy the other, the seed?  In fact, it could never do so, for in our opinion, to our way of thinking, it would be as though the sprout had destroyed the sprout itself.


[1232]
‘DI ‘DRA BA’I GNOD PA MTHONG YANG MI LDOG PA NI, MYU GUS SA BON ‘JIG PA NI RNAM ‘GYUR GYI STENG NAS YIN PAS, RANG GIS RANG ‘JIG PA DANG GA NA ‘DRA SNYAM DU RGOL BA BLUN PAS YIN LA, NGO BO’AM RANG BZHIN THAMS CAD PHAR YIN TSUR YIN DU SONG NA RNAM ‘GYUR SO SOR YANG MI ‘GRUB PAS GNOD PA SPANG MI NUS SO,,

The opponent here can see this kind of problem coming up, and refuses to change their position, saying that when the sprout destroys the seed it happens only at the level of the manifestation—and thus there’s no way that it’s as if the sprout had destroyed itself.  This kind of thinking though is foolish, for it cannot avoid the problem that—if all the essences or natures are such that to be one is to be the other, and vice versa—then you could never say on top of that that the manifestations were different from each other.



Seed & sprout all the same

[1233]
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, SA MYUG GNYIS LA DBYIBS SOGS THA DAD MED PAR THAL BAS DGAG ,DE’I NYES SPONG GI LAN DGAG ,GNAS SKABS GNYIS KYI RE RER GNYIS KA ‘DZIN MI ‘DZIN MTSUNGS PAR THAL BAS DGAG PA’O,,

This brings us to our second major section from above: a denial that a cause could at any rate be such that to be it were to be its result.  This explanation will be made in three steps: denying such a possibility by showing how the pair of the seed & the sprout could then never have different shapes, and so on; countering a response which attempts to avoid this problem; and then finally denying this possibility by showing how it would then have to be the same whether we held or didn’t hold to both the seed and sprout, as individual entities at two separate stages.


	[1234]
	[VI.10]
Saṃsthāna varṇa rasa vīrya vipāka bhedāḥ
syur nāṅkurasya tava kāraṇato vibhinnāḥ,
Prāgātma bhāvam avadhūya tad anya rūpam
āpadyate yadi tadāsya kathaṃ hi tattvam.

	[VI.10a]
,BYED RGYU SA BON GYI LAS THA DAD MYU GU’I
DBYIBS DANG NI,
,KHA DOG RO NUS SMIN PA’I THA DAD KHYOD LA
MED PAR ‘GYUR,

		According to you, the sprout
		Could have no shape, or color,
		Or taste or properties,

		Or ripening that was different
		From that of the seed
		Which had given it birth.


[1235]
DANG PO NI, SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE MYU GU SKYED PAR BYED PA’I RGYU SA BON GYI KHA DOG DANG DBYIBS LA SOGS PA LAS THA DAD PA’I MYU GU’I RING THUNG SOGS KYI DBYIBS DANG, SNGO SER SOGS KYI KHA DOG DANG, MNGAR SKYUR SOGS KYI RO DANG NUS MTHU DANG, SMIN PA RNAMS KYI THA DAD PA KHYOD LA MED PAR ‘GYUR TE, SA MYUG GNYIS KYI NGO BO DANG RANG BZHIN LA RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU KHYAD PAR MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here is the first.  There is yet another problem with saying that to be the seed is to be the sprout.  If that were the case, then the sprout could have no qualities (color, shape, and so on) that were different from those of the seed which had given it birth.  That is, the sprout would never possess a different shape—its length, or whatever; or color—whether it be green, yellow, or whatever; or taste—sweetness or sourness and such; or particular functional properties; or a particular manner of ripening.  And that’s because, according to you, there is no difference of any kind between the essence, and the nature, of this pair: the seed & the sprout.


[1236]
DE LTAR THAL BA LAS THA MI DAD PAR DMIGS PA YANG MA YIN PA’I PHYIR, DE GNYIS GYI NGO BO KUN NAS GCIG PA YANG MA YIN NO ZHES BZLOG PA ‘PHEN PA MDZAD DE, BZLOG PA ‘PHEN PA DANG BZLOG PA RANG RGYUD ‘PHEN PA LA KHYAD PAR SHIN TU CHE’O,,

And if this absurd consequence held true, then we could never observe the seed & the sprout displaying anything but qualities that weren’t different.  The statement of absurdity thus implies the denial, which states: “And so neither can we say that these two are such that to be one is to be, in every shape & manner, the other.”  There is a massive difference then between such a statement implying a denial, and a denial implying a statement of principle.


[1237]
DE LA NUS MTHU NI GZHANG ‘BRUM GYI SMAN LUS DANG NYE BA TZAM GYIS NAD DE SEL BA [f. 96a] DANG, RTZI SMAN SOGS ‘GA’ ZHIG BCANGS PA TZAM GYIS NAM MKHA’ LA ‘GRO BA LTA BU’O,,

When we say “functional properties” here, what we’re talking about is where the plant, for example, is a medicinal herb for treating ailments such as a hemorrhoid: it has the ability to cure the problem just by being being applied closely to the body.  Another example is where—if we simply hold certain elixir herbs or such in our hand, we are able to fly in the sky.


[1238]
RNAM PAR SMIN PA NI RKYEN MI ‘DRA BA LAS RDZAS KYI KHYAD PAR ‘GYUR BA STE, DPER NA ‘O MAS BCUS PA SOGS LAS SKYU RU RA DANG, PI PI LING SOGS LA RO MNGAR POR ‘GYUR BA LTA BU’O,,

When we say here “a particular manner of ripening,” we’re referring to a case where—if the plant receives different treatments—then it takes on a particular quality.  An example would be where we apply milk to myrobalan or peppercorns or the like, and their taste changes to sweetness.



Not stages of a single thing

	[1239]
	[VI.10b]
,GAL TE SNGAR GYI BDAG GIS DNGOS PO BSAL NAS
DE LAS GZHAN,
,NGO BOR ‘GYUR NA DE TSE DE YI DE NYID
JI LTAR ‘GYUR,

Suppose the self-nature
In the previous one fades away,

And transforms into
The essence of the other—

And at that point,
Its is that very one.

But how could that be?


[1240]
GNYIS PA NI, CI STE SA BON GYI GNAS SKABS BTANG NAS MYU GU’I GNAS SKABS GZHAN DU GYUR PAS, SA MYUG GNYIS GNAS SKABS THA DAD PA TZAM YIN PA’I PHYIR SA BON DE NYID MYU GUR ‘GYUR BA YIN NO ZHE NA,

Which brings us to our second step here: countering a response which attempts to avoid the problem we’ve described.  Here, someone comes and makes this claim:

The way it works is that an entity releases the stage of being a seed, and then enters another stage, of being a sprout.  These two—the seed & the sprout—are thus but different stages of the same thing; as such, what really happens is that the seed itself manifests as the sprout.


[1241]
GAL TE SNGAR GYI SA BON GYI BDAG GI DNGOS PO’I GNAS SKABS BSAL NAS, GNAS SKABS DE LAS GZHAN MYU GU’I GNAS SKABS KYI NGO BOR ‘GYUR NA, DE LTAR ‘DOD PA DE’I TSE SA BON DE YI RANG BZHIN NYID MYU GU’I RANG BZHIN DE NYID YIN ZHES

Now suppose the self-nature at the previous stage—the time of the seed—fades away, and transforms into the essence of the “other” stage: the stage of the sprout.  And suppose you assert that, at that point, its (the seed’s) essential nature is none other than the very nature of the sprout.


[1242]
JI LTAR RIGS PAR ‘GYUR TE, DE’I GNAS SKABS KYI DNGOS PO DE NYID DE’I DNGOS PO NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE’I NGO BO LAS DON GZHAN PA’I DE’I DNGOS PO MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

But how could that be the correct?  Because the the precise entity of that stage is that very entity; and there is no other entity which is not such that to be that entity is to be it.


[1243]
DES NA SA MYUG ‘DI GNYIS KYI NGO BO RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU THA MI DAD PA NYID NYAMS PA YIN NO,,

And in that case you’d lose the idea that the essential natures of both the seed & the sprout were, in every possible respect, inseparable.


[1244]
CI STE SA MYUG GI DBYIBS LA SOGS PA THA DAD KYANG, RDZAS THA MI DAD PAS MI ‘GAL LO SNYAM NA,

And suppose you think to yourself, “But what if we say that—even though the shape and so forth of seed & the sprout are different—the two are not such that to be one is not to be the other.  In that case, there would be no contradiction.”


[1245]
DE NI MI RIGS TE DBYIBS LA SOGS PA MA BZUNG NA SA MYUG GI RDZAS KYANG MI ‘DZIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And yet that line of thinking is incorrect: without holding to qualities such as their shape & such, there is no way that we can hold to the very substance of the seed or sprout.



Held or not held, together

	[1246]
	[VI.11]
Bījād ananya iha te yadi cāṅkuraḥ syād
gṛhyeta naiva hi sa bījam ivāṅkurākhyaḥ,
Gṛhyeta vā tad api nāma yathāṅkuro’yaṃ
tattvāt tayor iti na caitad ato’bhyupeyam.

,GAL TE KHYOD KYI SA BON MYU GU ‘DIR GZHAN
MA YIN NA,
,SA BON BZHIN DU MYU GU ZHES BYA
DE GZUNG MED PA’AM,
,YANG NA DE DAG GCIG PAS JI LTAR MYU GU
‘DI BZHIN DU,
,DE YANG GZUNG DU YOD ‘GYUR DE PHYIR ‘DI NI
KHAS MI BLANG,

		Suppose that, as you put it,
		The seed & the sprout here
		Were not not the other.

		Then just as the seed,
		Neither could the sprout
		Be something that we held.

		Or else we could also say that,
		Since these two are the same,
		Then just as the sprout
Is something that is held,

The other too would have to be—
And so we refuse to accept this idea.			
	

[1247]
GSUM PA NI, SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE GAL TE KHYOD KYI LTAR SA BON DANG MYU GU’I NGO BO GNYIS LA ‘JIG RTEN ‘DIR NGO BO GZHAN PA YOD PA MA YIN NA, JI LTAR MYU GU’I GNAS SKABS SU SA BON GZUNG DU MED PA DE BZHIN DU, MYU [f. 96b] GU YANG GZUNG DU MED PAR ‘GYUR TE,

We have reached then our third step: denying this possibility by showing how it would then have to be the same whether we held or didn’t hold to both the seed & the sprout, as individual entities at two separate stages.  And so there is another problem with your position.  Suppose it were true that, as you put it, the essential nature of these two—the seed & sprout—were not, here in the world, such that to be one was not to be the other.  We can in general observe that, at the sprout stage, the seed can no longer be held by our perceptions; and just in that same way, in your model, neither could the sprout at that point be something that our perceptions held.


[1248]
‘AM ZHES PA YANG NA SA MYUG DE DAG GI NGO BO RNAM PA KUN TU GCIG PAS JI LTAR MYU GU’I GNAS SKABS SU, MYU GU ‘DI GZUNG DU YOD PA DE BZHIN DU, SA BON DE YANG DBANG PO’I SHES PAS GZUNG DU YOD PAR ‘GYUR BA LAS,

The expression “or else” here is meant to convey, “we could also say”: that since the essential nature of these two—the seed & the sprout—is supposed to be in every respect the same, then just as the sprout is something that is held by our perceptions during the period of the sprout, then the other too—the seed—would have as well to be something that could be held, at that same point, by our perceptions, in the form of our awareness of our senses.


[1249]
MED PA DE’I PHYIR NYES PA DE GNYIS SPONG BAR ‘DOD PAS, SA MYUG GNYIS KYI NGO BO LA GZHAN MED PA ‘DI NI KHAS BLANG BAR MI BYA’O,,

But the fact is that, rather, the seed is not something held at this point; and so—desirous of avoiding these two problems—we refuse to accept this idea that the seed & sprout are not such that when something is one it cannot be the other.


[1250]
RIGS PA DE RNAMS LEGS PAR RTOGS NA CHOS CAN THAMS CAD PHAN TSUN DU NGO BO THA DAD PA LA, DE RNAMS KYI CHOS NYID THAMS CAD PHAR YIN TSUR YIN GYI GCIG TU ‘DOD PA DANG, GNAS SKABS SNGA MA’I DUS KYI CHOS NYID DE NYID GNAS SKABS PHYI MA’I DUS KYI CHOS NYID DE NYID DU ‘DOD PA’I LOG RTOG THAMS CAD LDOG PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

If a person is able to grasp this line of reasoning well, they avoid a pair of misconceptions which say that—starting from the point of particular objects not being such that to be one were to be the other—each & every example of the true nature of these objects is one, in the sense that to be one is to be the other; or that the true nature of an object at an earlier stage is precisely the same true nature of the same object at a later stage.



Cause & effect in the everyday world

[1251]
GNYIS PA NI, DE’I PHYIR DE LTAR DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAR ‘DOD PA’I GRANGS CAN GYI LUGS, SANGS RGYAS PA’I LUGS LAS GZHAN DU BRTAGS PA’I BDAG SKYE BKAG NAS, GRUB MTHA’I LUGS GZHAN DU BLO MA SBYANGS PA’I ‘JIG RTEN PA’I THA SNYAD DU YANG, BDAG LAS SKYE BAR RTOG PA ‘DI MI ‘THAD DO ZHES STON PA NI,

This brings us to the second point from above: demonstrating that things could not be said to grow from themselves even in the parlance of those who have not been influenced by any particular school of philosophy.  And so we have denied, as explained, the system of the Numerists, who believe they have realized the true nature of things; and yet it is nothing but what the Buddhists would describe as things coming from themselves: nothing but a figment of these other thinkers’ minds.  Here next then we describe how—even in the language of the everyday world, among people who have had no training in any specific school of thought—this idea that things could grow from themselves is an incorrect one.  The root text covers it in these lines:


	[1252]
	[VI.12]
Loko’pi caikyam anayor iti nābhyupaiti
naṣṭe’pi paśyati yataḥ phalam eṣa hetau,
Tasmān na tattvata idaṃ na ca lokataś ca
yuktaṃ svato bhavati bhāva iti prakalpam.

	[VI.12a]
,GANG PHYIR RGYU ZHIG NA YANG DE YI ‘BRAS BU 
MTHONG BA’I PHYIR,
,DE DAG GCIG PA YIN ZHES ‘JIG RTEN GYIS KYANG
KHAS MA LEN,

		Not even in the everyday world
		Would people accept the idea
		That they were one & the same.

		This is because,
		Even if the cause ends,
		Its result can still be observed.


[1253]
GANG GI PHYIR RGYU SA BON ZHIG NA’ANG SA BON DE YI ‘BRAS BU MTHONG BA’I PHYIR, SA MYUG DE DAG NGO BO GCIG PA YIN ZHES ‘JIG RTEN GYIS KYANG KHAS MI LEN NO,,

Not even in the everyday world would people accept the idea that they—the seed and the sprout—were one & the same: that to be one was to be the other.  This is because, even if the cause—the seed—ends, its (the seed’s) result can still be observed.



Nothing but a fanciful idea

	[1254]
[VI.12b]
,DE PHYIR DNGOS PO BDAG LAS ‘BYUNG ZHES RAB TU
BRTAGS PA ‘DI,
,DE NYID DANG NI ‘JIG RTEN DU YANG RIGS PA
MA YIN NO,

		Thus it is that
		The fanciful idea
		That objects grow from themselves

		Is illogical, both in the way
		Things are, and in
		The everyday world as well.


[1255]
GSUM PA NI, GANG GI PHYIR DON DAM PA DANG ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB KYI PHYOGS GNYIS KA LTAR YANG BDAG LAS SKYE BA RIGS PA DANG ‘GAL BA DE’I PHYIR, PHYI NANG GI DNGOS PO RNAMS BDAG LAS ‘BYUNG BA YIN ZHES RAB TU BRTAGS PA ‘DI, ,DE NYID [f. 97a] DON DAM DANG NI ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB TU’ANG RIGS PA MA YIN NO,,

Which brings us to our third point from before—a summary of the denials we have made.  Thus it is—from both the point of view of the ultimate, and of the deceptive (that of the everyday world); it doesn’t matter which—that the idea that things could grow from themselves is a logical contradiction.  The fanciful idea that “both outer & inner objects grow from themselves” is simply illogical, both from the point of view of the way things are (that is, ultimately), and from a deceptive point of view as well: that of the everyday world.


[1256]
DE’I PHYIR ‘PHAGS PAS BDAG SKYE ‘GOG PA NA DON DAM PA DANG KUN RDZOB KYI KHYAD PAR MA SBYAR BAR BDAG LAS MA YIN ZHES BDAG SKYE SPYIR BKAG GO

And so it is that—when the Realized One denied that things could grow from themselves—he denied this possibility in a general way, without making any distinction between it happening in an ultimate way, or in a deceptive way.


[1257]
,DES NA SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN ‘BYED KYIS DNGOS PO RNAMS NI DON DAM PAR BDAG LAS SKYE BA MA YIN TE, YOD PA’I PHYIR SEMS PA CAN BZHIN NO ZHES KHYAD PAR DU BYED PA DE’I DON DAM PAR ZHES PA’I KHYAD PAR DON MED DO ZHES BSAM PAR BYA’O,,

As such, we can consider it pointless when Master Bhavaviveka adds the distinction of this being impossible “ultimately”; expressing this distinction in the words,

It is not the case that—ultimately speaking—
things grow from themselves,  
	
	Because they exist;

	They are like living beings.



Avoiding problems well spoken

[1258]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second section from before: denying that things could grow from themselves, by using the logic employed in Master Nagarjuna’s Wisdom.


	[1259]
[VI.13]
Janyasya caiva janakasya ca karmaṇaś ca
kartuś ca janmani bhavet svata iṣyamāṇe,
Aikyaṃ na caikyam anayor iti nābhyupeyaṃ
janma svato vihita vistara doṣa sakteḥ.

,BDAG LAS SKYE BAR ‘DOD NA BSKYED PAR BYA DANG
SKYED BYED DANG,
,LAS DANG BYED PA PO YANG GCIG NYID ‘GYUR NA
DE DAG NI,
,GCIG NYID MA YIN PAS NA BDAG LAS SKYE BAR
KHAS BLANG PAR,
,BYA MIN RGYA CHER BSHAD PA’I NYES PAR THAL BAR
‘GYUR PHYIR RO,

		If we accept that a thing
		Could grow from itself,
		It would be the case that

		The thing being produced;
		And the thing doing the producing;
		The very act; and the agent
		Would have to be one & the same.
	
		They are though not the same;
		And so the idea that something
		Could grow from itself
		Is not something that we
		Should ever accept.

		After all, the problems
		Described at length
		Would then result.


[1260]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE, ,’BRAS BU BDAG LAS SKYE BAR ‘DOD NA, BSKYED PAR BYA BA ‘BRAS BU DANG, SKYED PAR BYED PA RGYU DANG, GANG ZHIG BYA BA’I LAS DANG, GANG GIS BYED PA’I BYED PA PO YANG GCIG NYID DU ‘GYUR NA, DE DAG NI GCIG NYID MA YIN PAS NA, BDAG LAS SKYE BAR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA BA MIN TE, BSTAN BCOS ‘DI DANG RTZA SHE LAS RGYA CHER BSHAD PA’I NYES PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

There are still other problems with the idea of the result coming from a cause that was one with it.  If we accept that a result could grow from itself, then it would be the case that the result (the thing being produced); and the cause (the thing doing the producing); and the very action of this production; and the agent (the one performing the action) would have to be all one & the same thing.  The fact though is that they are not one & the same; and so the idea that something could grow from itself is not something that one should ever accept.  Because after all, all the problems with this idea described at length in the present classical commentary, and in Wisdom, would then result.


[1261]
DE LA SKYON DANG PO NI RTZA SHE LAS,
,RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GCIG NYID DU,
,NAM YANG ‘THAD PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,
,RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GCIG NYID NA,
,SKYED DANG BSKYED PA GCIG TU ‘GYUR,

The first of these problems is described in Wisdom with the following lines:

It could never be correct
That the cause and its result
Could be one & the same.

If the cause and result
Really were the same,

Then what does the producing
And what is produced
Would have to be the same.


[1262]
ZHES GSUNGS TE RGYU ‘BRAS NGO BO GCIG NA PHA DANG BU DAG GAM, MIG DANG DE’I RNAM SHES DAG KYANG GCIG NYID DU ‘GYUR ZHES PA’O,,

What this is saying is that—if a cause and its result were such that to be one were to be the other—then parents would be one & the same with their children; and the organ of the eye would be one & the same with the visual consciousness which resulted from it.


[1263]
SKYON GNYIS PA NI RTZA SHE LAS,
,GAL TE SHING DE ME YIN NA,
,BYED PA PO DANG LAS GCIG ‘ GYUR,
ZHES GSUNGS PA’O,,

The second of the problems is described in these lines, also from Wisdom:

If the wood were the fire,
Then the agent and action
Would be one & the same.


[1264]
DE LTAR BKAG PA NA PHA DANG BU DANG BYED PA PO DANG LAS GNYIS KYANG NGO BO GCIG TU THAL ZER NA ‘DOD LA, SPYIR GCIG TU THAL [f. 97b] ZER NA MA KHYAB BO ZHES SMRA MOD KYANG, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR GYI RANG BZHIN GCIG TU ‘DOD NA RNAM ‘GYUR YANG GCIG TU ‘PHUL NUS PA’I RIGS PAS SPONG MI NUS SO,,

When you are doing this kind of refutation, and someone says “Well, in that case, parents would have to be the same person as their children; and the agent of a particular action would have to be that action”—the reply we’d give is “Agreed!”  When we say though in general that they would have to be the same, someone could admittedly reply “It doesn’t necessarily follow.”  The fact remains though that it is impossible, logically, to deny the implication that—if someone agrees that the seed & the sprout share, as described above, a single identity—then all of their manifestations would have as well to be totally the same.


[1265]
DE’I PHYIR JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I SKYON GYIS ‘JIGS PAS BDEN GNYIS PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR RTOGS PAR ‘DOD PAS, BDAG SKYE KHAS BLANG BAR MI BYA’O ZHES GSUNGS LA, BDAG LAS SKYE BA YOD MED KYANG GCIG YONGS SU GCOD PA CIG SHOS RNAM PAR BCAD PA MED NA MED PA’I DNGOS ‘GAL YIN PAS BDAG LAS SKYE BA MED PA NI NGES PAR KHAS BLANGS GOS {%DGOS} SO,,

And so in dread of the problems described above, and desirous of realizing the two kinds of reality in a manner which is unmistaken, we must say, “The idea that something could grow from itself is not something that we can accept.”  Whether or not things did in fact grow from themselves, there is a principle of direct, comprehensive contradiction at work here, where when you eliminate one possibility the other cannot have been eliminated.  As such, we must indeed accept the idea that things cannot grow from themselves.



The only option left?

[1266]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, PHYOGS SNGA MA BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG BA’O,,

This brings us to our second major point from above, which is denying that things could grow from something other than themselves.  Here first we will state the position of others with whom we disagree; and then show how we disprove this position.


[1267]
DANG PO NI, RANG SDE DNGOS POR SMRA BA RNAMS NA RE RANG LAS SKYE BA DON MED PAS BDAG SKYE MI RIGS SHING, DE MED PAS GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BA YANG MI RIGS SO,,

Here is the first.  Schools that belong to the Functionalist group would say:

There is no point served, if it were the case that something grew from itself; as such, the idea that something could in fact grow from itself is mistaken.  And if that’s impossible, then so would it be for things to grow both from themselves, and from other things.


[1268]
RGYU MED NI GCIG TU THA CHAD PAS DGAG PAR YANG RIGS NA, GZHAN DAG LAS LTA GA LA ZHIG CES GZHAN SKYE ‘GOG PA MI RIGS TE,

Saying that things could grow without any cause at all is the worst idea of all; and so it too is something we would have to deny.  Given all this, it would be a mistake to try to deny the remaining possibility, that things grow from something other than themselves: it would be a mistake to say, “And how on earth could things grow from something other than themselves?”


[1269]
RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GZHAN DU GYUR PA’I RKYEN BZHI DNGOS PO RNAMS KYI SKYED BYED DU GSUNGS PA’I GSUNG RAB LA LTOS NAS, MI ‘DOD BZHIN DU YANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA KHAS BLANG BAR BYA’O,,

This group looks at references from scripture which state that four different types of conditions which exist, by definition, as something other than their results function to produce things.  And so whether they want to or not, they find themselves in a position where they have to say that things do in fact grow from something other than themselves.


[1270]
RKYEN BZHI PO DE GANG LA ‘JOG PA LA, SDE PA KHA CIG NI RGYU’I RKYEN NI MDZOD LAS, RGYU ZHES BYA BA RGYU LNGA YIN ZHES BYED RGYU MA GTOGS PA RGYU LNGA DANG,

How are these four conditions described?  Here is how a number of schools of thought proceed.  First there is the (1) “causal condition,” which in the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge is described as referring to five of the six traditional types of causes: all but the “effective” type of cause.  As this work itself puts it,

The one we call “causal”
Consists of five of the causes.


[1271]
DMIGS PA’I RKYEN NI, DMIGS PA CHOS RNAMS THAMS CAD DO, ZHES RNAM SHES DRUG GI DMIGS YUL GYI CHOS THAMS CAD DANG,

The (2) “object condition” is described as all the entities in the universe which serve as objects of focus for the six categories of consciousness.  As the Treasure House again puts it,

The one we call “object”
Includes all entities there are.


[1272]
DE MA THAG RKYEN NI, 
,SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG SKYES PA [f. 98a] RNAMS,
,THA MA MIN MTSUNGS DE MA THAG
,CES LHAG MED DU ‘JUG PA LAS GZHAN PA’I SEMS SEMS BYUNG SNGAR SKYES RNAMS DANG,

The (3) “immediately-preceding condition” refers to instances of main mind, and mental functions, which grow previous to a current mental state; the one case where the mind enters nirvana without remainder is excepted.  Here the Treasure House says: 

The “immediately-preceding” one
Refers to previous states

Of main mind & mental functions
That share a mental link,
Except those for the final one.


[1273]
BDAG PO’I RKYEN NI, BYED RGYU ZHES BYA BDAG POR BSHAD, ,CES BYED RGYU LA BSHAD PA LTAR ‘DOD LA,

The description for the (4) “dominant” condition is said to match the explanation for the “effective” cause; again, the Treasure House:

What we call
The “effective” cause
Is explained as the “dominant.”


[1274]
RGYU DRUG NI MDZOD LAS,
,BYED RGYU LHAN CIG ‘BYUNG BA DANG,
,SKAL MNYAM MTSUNGS PAR LDAN PA DANG,
,KUN TU ‘GRO DANG RNAM SMIN DANG,
,RGYU NI RNAM PA DRUG TU ‘DOD,
CES SO,,

The six classical types of causes are listed as follows, also from the Treasure House:

They say that the causes
Number six in kind:

The effective cause;
The simultaneous;
The generic; those that share
A mental link;
The omnipresent; and
Those that ripen.


[1275]
SDE PA KHA CIG NI, SGRUB PAR BYED PA NI RGYU YIN ZHES MTSAN NYID BSTAN PA LAS NA, GANG ZHIG GANG GI SKYED BYED SA BON GYI NGO BOR GNAS PA DE NI DE’I RGYU’I RKYEN NO,,

Certain schools of thought give the definition of a cause as “anything which brings about another thing”; and so we can say that they view a causal condition as any entity whose nature is to be a seed which functions to produce any particular object.


[1276]
RGAN PO LDANG BA LTAR SEMS SEMS BYUNG SKYE BZHIN PA RNAMS RTEN ‘KHAR BA DANG ‘DRA BA’I DMIGS PA GANG GIS SKYED PA DE NI DE’I DMIGS PA’I RKYEN NO,,

And then they would say that an object condition refers to any particular object of perception which acts as the basis for the arisal of an instance of main mind, or a mental function; which helps these to grow—similar to the way in which a cane is used by an elderly person to stand from a sitting position.


[1277]
RGYU ‘GAGS MA THAG PA NI ‘BRAS BU SKYE BA’I DE MA THAG PA’I RKYEN YIN TE, DPER NA SA BON ‘GAGS MA THAG PA MYU GU ‘BYUNG BA’I RKYEN YIN PA BZHIN NO,,

An immediately-preceding condition is one where its result grows just after the cause has ended; for example, the instant when the seed has just ended is a condition for the sprout to appear.


[1278]
RANG ‘GREL LAS SA BON ‘GAGS MA THAG PA MYU GU’I MTSUNGS PA DE MA THAG PA’I RKYEN {%MA} YIN PA LTA BU’O, ZHES GSUNGS SHING TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG DE MA THAG RKYEN ‘GOG PA’I SKABS SU, MYU GU’I MTSUNGS PA DE MA THAG PA’I RKYEN BKAG LA, SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS KYANG DE BZHIN DU BZHED PAS ‘DI NI GZUGS LA YANG MTSUNGS PA DE MA THAG PA’I RKYEN ‘DOD PA’I LUGS SO,,

The autocommentary contains a reference where it says “This is similar to the case where the instant when the seed has just ended cannot be said to be an immediately-preceding condition involved in a mental link.”  A Clarification of the Verses also denies, for a sprout, an immediately-preceding condition involved in a mental link; this is inside the section where it disproves the idea of an immediately-preceding condition.  Master Buddha Palita takes the same position; and so we can say that the system we are describing here is one that does accept the idea of an immediately-preceding condition involved in a mental link, even for physical objects.


[1279]
GANG ZHIG YOD NA GANG ‘BYUNG BA ‘DI NI DE’I BDAG PO’I RKYEN NO,,

The dominant condition of a thing then is described as any entity which is present when another thing occurs.


[1280]
TSIG GSAL LAS SNGAR SKYES PA DANG LHAN CIG SKYES PA DANG PHYIS [f. 98b] SKYE BA LA SOGS PA YANG ‘DI DAG GI NANG DU ‘DU BAR GSUNGS SHING RANG ‘GREL LAS KYANG DANG PO MA GTOGS PA DE BZHIN DU GSUNGS PA NI, SHES RAB SGRON MA LAS, SDE PA GZHAN GYIS BRTAGS PA’I RKYEN MDUN DU SKYES PA DANG YOD PA DANG MED PA RNAMS ZHES BSGYUR BA DANG DON GCIG LA ‘GYUR YANG DE LTAR LEGS SO,,

A Clarification of the Verses says that things which have already grown; and things that are growing at the moment; and things that will grow later on—and so on—are also subsumed by the conditions described here.  The autocommentary as well says the same thing for all the conditions except for the first.  These statements are best understood in the same sense as they appear in the translation of the Lamp of Wisdom where it refers to “conditions that other groups imagine to be: the one that comes in front; the one that exists; and the one that doesn’t exist.”


[1281]
DE’I DON NI ‘GREL BSHAD LAS GNAS BRTAN PA’I SDE PAS THA SNYAD BTAGS PA MDUN DU SKYES PA’I RKYEN NI, DBANG PO RNAMS KYI MNGON SUM GYI MDUN DU SKYES PA DMIGS RKYEN NO,,

The meaning here, according to the explication, is that the condition named by the Elder School as the “condition in front” is a reference to a condition which has appeared in front of the direct perception by the sense organ; that is, the object condition.


[1282]
YOD PA’I RKYEN NI RGYU DANG BDAG PO’I RKYEN NO, ,MED PA’I RKYEN NI DE MA THAG PA’I RKYEN LA BSHAD DO,,

The expression “condition that exists” here is explained as a reference to the causal and dominant conditions.  “Condition that doesn’t exist” then is a reference to the immediately-preceding condition.


[1283]
DE ‘DRA BA’I THA SNYAD TZAM MI MTHUN PA RNAMS NI MTSAN NYID LA BRTAGS NA BZHI PO ‘DIR ‘DU LA, DBANG PHYUG LA SOGS PA NI RKYEN MA YIN PAS RKYEN LNGA PA NI YOD PA MA YIN NO, ,ZHES NGES PAR ‘DZIN TE

All of these types are different only in name; if we dig into their defining characteristics, we discover that they are all taken in by the list of four conditions.  The descriptions are also meant to help us come to a definite conclusion that, as we see, “there is no fifth type of condition; for creator gods & the like are not conditions that can make things grow.”


[1284]
MDZOD LAS,
,BZHI YIS SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG RNAMS,
,GSUM GYIS SNYOMS PAR ‘JUG RNAM GNYIS,
,GZHAN NI GNYIS PO DAG LAS SKYE,
,DBANG PHYUG SOGS MIN RIM SOGS PHYIR,
ZHES BSHAD PA BZHIN DU ‘DOD DO,,

As the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge puts it,

	Four produce the mind
	And mental functions,

	And three two kinds
	Of balanced meditation;

	The others are produced
	From two of them.

	Things though are not produced
	By things like a creator god,
	For they arise in stages, and such.



Denying schools that say
things can grow from themselves

[1285]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GZHAN SKYE ‘DOD PA’I PHYOGS SPYIR DGAG PA DANG, SEMS TZAM PA’I LUGS BYE BRAG TU DGAG PA’O,,

Having stated the position of others on how things grow from something other than themselves, we turn now to showing how we disprove this position.  This will include two sections: a general denial of schools which accept that something can grow from something else; and then a more specific denial of the explanation of this point by the Mind Only school.


[1286]
DANG PO LA LNGA, GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA DNGOS, BKAG PA LA ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA SPANG BA, DE LTAR BKAG PA’I YON TAN BSTAN PA, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA ‘GAR YANG MED PAR BSTAN PA, BDEN PA GNYIS CHAR DU’ANG RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA BKAG PA’I YON TAN [f. 99a] BSTAN PA’O,,

We’ll cover the first section in five parts:
	
 The actual denial of the idea that things could grow from
something other than themselves
 Overcoming objections which say that this denial in any way
contradicts the beliefs of the everyday world
 Demonstrating the advantages of the denial
 Demonstrating that there is no possible instance where
it would be correct to say that things could grow through
any nature of their own
	 Demonstrating the advantages of denying that things could grow
		through any nature of their own, relative to both forms
		of reality


[1287]
DANG PO LA GSUM, GZHAN SKYE SPYIR DGAG PA, GZHAN SKYE BYE BRAG TU DGAG PA, ‘BRAS BU LA MU BZHIR DPYAD NAS GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA’O,,

The first of these parts has three steps of its own:

	 A general denial that things could grow from something
other than themselves
	 A more particular denial that things could grow this way
	 A denial that things could grow from something other than 
		themselves, accomplished by examining four possible
		permutations.


[1288]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, HA CANG THAL BAS DGAG ,SKYON SPONG GI LAN DGAG PA’O,,

The first of these steps covers two points of its own: denying this kind of growth because it would be absurd; and then denying a response which attempts to avoid this problem.


[1289]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, HA CANG THAL BA DNGOS DANG, DE DAG GI MTHA’ DPYAD PA’O,,

And then finally the first of these points will cover two topics: the actual demonstration of absurdity, followed by a logical examination of the points.



The absurdity of a thing
growing from something
other than itself

[1290]
DANG PO NI, GZHAN SKYE ‘DI NI GZHAG PAR NUS PA MA YIN TE, RIGS PA DANG LUNG DANG ‘GAL BA’I PHYIR RO,,

And so here is that first point.  This idea that something could grow from something else is not something that anyone could ever be able to establish as true, for it contradicts both logic and scripture.


[1291]
PHYI MA NI SA LU LJANG BA’I MDO LAS, MING DANG GZUGS KYI MYU GU DE YANG BDAG GIS MA BYAS GZHAN GYIS MA BYAS ZHES PA LTA BU’I LUNG PHYI MA LTA BU MANG PO DANG ‘GAL BA’O,,

As for latter of these two, the idea contradicts many references found in scripture, such as the latter half of the statement from the sutra entitled A Sprout of Rice where it says, “The sprout of name & form is not created by itself; nor is it created by something other than itself.”


	[1292]
[VI.14]
Anyat pratītya yadi nāma paro’bhaviṣyaj
jāyeta tarhi bahulaḥ śikhino’ndhakāraḥ,
Sarvasya janma ca bhavet khalu sarvataś ca
tulyaṃ paratvam akhile’janake’pi yasmāt.

,GZHAN LA BRTEN NAS GAL TE GZHAN ZHIG ‘BYUNG BAR 
‘GYUR NA NI,
,’O NA ME LCE LAS KYANG MUN PA ‘THUG PO
‘BYUNG ‘GYUR ZHING,
,THAMS CAD LAS KYANG THAMS CAD SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE
GANG GI PHYIR,
,SKYED PAR BYED PA MA YIN MA LUS LA YANG
GZHAN NYID MTSUNGS,

		Suppose it were the case
		That something other
		Could grow, based on
		Something other;

		Well then we would get
		A thick darkness
		Even from flames.
	
		And all objects
		Would have to grow
		From all other objects;

		For the reason that
		Each & every thing
		That did not act
		To produce the thing

		Would be exactly the same,
		In being different.
	

[1293]
DE LA RIGS PA’I DBANG DU BYAS NAS BRJOD PA, GAL TE RANG GIS NGO BOS GRUB PA’I RGYU GZHAN LA BRTEN NAS RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA’I ‘BRAS BU GZHAN ZHIG ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR NA NI, 

Turning now to the logic here, suppose it were indeed the case that a result which was something other than the cause—and which existed in & of itself—could grow based on a cause which was something other than the result, and which also existed in & of itself.


[1294]
DE LTA YIN PA ‘O NA SEL BYED ME LCE RAB TU ‘BAR BA LAS KYANG BSAL BYA MUN PA ‘THUG PO ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR ZHING,

If that were the case, then well even when bright flames—the agent which dispels darkness—burst forth, we would get a thick darkness, the object of the dispelling.


[1295]
GZHAN YANG RGYU YIN MIN THAMS CAD LAS KYANG ‘BRAS BU’I DNGOS PO YIN MIN THAMS CAD SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE, CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA,

Moreover, it would also be true that all objects—whether they are things which are results or not—would have to grow from all other objects, whether they are causes or not.  And why would these be the case?


[1296]
GANG GI PHYIR ‘BRAS BU DE SKYED PAR BYED PA MA YIN PA MA LUS PA LA’ANG RGYU ‘BRAS SU ‘DOD PA GNYIS DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID MTSUNGS PAR YOD PA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES GZHAN GYIS KHAS BLANGS PA’I GTAN TSIGS LA BRTEN PA’I HA CANG THAL BA GNYIS SO,,

They would be this way for the reason that each & every thing that did not act to produce a result would also be exactly the same, in being different from what we agreed to be the two of cause & effect.  And so we come up with two completely absurd consequences that arise from the argument accepted by the other party here.


[1297]
THAL BA DE GNYIS BSHAD NA JI LTAR SA LU SKYED PA’I SA BON RANG ‘BRAS SA LU’I MYU GU LAS, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN PA [f. 99b] DE BZHIN DU, SA LU’I MYU GU SKYED BYED MA YIN PA ME DANG SOL BA DANG, NAS KYI SA BON LA SOGS PA YANG SA LU’I MYU GU LAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN PA NI GZHAN SKYE SMRA BA RNAMS KYI ‘DOD TSUL LO,,

Let’s look into these two absurdities.  Suppose that the seed which produced a sprout of rice were, by definition, something other than the sprout which was its result.  Things that were not agents in the production of a rice sprout then—things like a fire, or a lump of coal, or a barley seed—would also be, according to our other party here, objects which were, by definition, other than the rice sprout.  This is what those who support the idea of things growing from things that are other than them are agreeing to.


[1298]
GZHAN YIN TSUL GNYIS PO DE MTSUNGS PAR ‘DOD NA, JI LTAR SA LU’I SA BON GZHAN DU GYUR PA LAS SA LU’I MYU GU SKYE BA DE BZHIN DU, ME SOL SOGS LAS KYANG SA LU’I MYU GU SKYE BAR ‘GYUR DGOS SO,,

If we accept that the manner in which things are “other” or “different” than each other is equivalent in the two cases, then—in the same way in which a rice sprout grows from a rice seed which is something other than it—a sprout would also have to grow from things like a fire, or a lump of coal.


[1299]
YANG JI LTAR SA LU’I MYU GU GZHAN DU GYUR PA, SA LU’I SA BON LAS SKYE BA BZHIN DU, BUM SNAM SOGS KYANG SA LU’I SA BON LAS SKYE BAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES MTSUNGS PA BYED PA’O,,

We’d also have to say that—just as a rice sprout which is something other than the rice seed grows from that seed—then things like water pitchers and bolts of cloth would also have to grow from the rice seed.  This then is a second statement of absurdity equivalent to the first.


[1300]
‘DI NI RTZA SHE LAS,
,RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GZHAN NYID DU,
,NAM YANG ‘THAD PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,
,RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GZHAN NYID NA,
,RGYU DANG RGYU MIN MTSUNGS PAR ‘GYUR,
ZHES GZHAN SKYE LA HA CANG THAL BA GSUNGS PA’I RIGS PA’O,,

All this is a kind of reasoning, which derives from Arya Nagarjuna’s Wisdom, to express how completely absurd it would be if things grew from other things that were different from them.  As the Arya puts it,
	
	It could never be correct to say
	That causes and results
	Were something perfectly different
	One from the other.

	If causes and results
	Were indeed completely different,
	Then things that were not causes
	Would be just the same as the causes.


[1301]
THAL BA GNYIS KA LA BZLOG PA ‘PHEN PA ‘GREL PAR BSHAD DO,,

The autocommentary describes both of these absurd statements as the type which implies the truth of the very opposite of what the opponent is asserting.



The source of the absurdity

[1302]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GZHAN SKYE LA HA CANG THAL BA ‘JUG PA’I RGYU MTSAN, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA KHAS LEN PA YI ‘GAL BA’O,,

Having completed our demonstration of absurdity, we move on to the second topic here: a logical examination of the relevant points.  This itself comes in two steps: the reason why the idea that things could grow from something else leads to the absurdity; and then the contradiction that arises from accepting the opposite of the absurdity.


[1303]
DANG PO NI, ‘DIR GZHAN SKYE KHAS LEN PA LA HA CANG THAL BA’I SKYON ‘JUG PA’I RGYU MTSAN LA, BOD KHA CIG RGYU ‘BRAS LA SNGA PHYI BAS KHYAB CING, GZHAN LA DUS MNYAM DGOS PA’I GNAD KYIS YIN ZER BA NI

Here is the first.  Let’s look into the reason why accepting the idea that things could grow from something else leads into the absurdity.  Some Tibetan thinkers have claimed that this absurdity turns on the fact that—whereas cause & effect must always involve one thing coming before another—if we accept that things grow from something other than themselves, then the cause and its effect would have to be simultaneous.


[1304]
SHIN TU MI RIGS TE, DE LTAR BKAG PA’I SKYON THAMS CAD RANG LA MTSUNGS PAR ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE LA KHAS BLANGS MED DO ZHES PAS BSNYON NA, DE’I RGYU MTSAN ‘TSAL BA’I NGAL BA DON MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This position though is totally mistaken.  First of all, all the objections that are raised in doing the refutation this way would apply just as well to our own position.  And if you backtrack from the position you took and then say “we are free of all opinions on the subject,” then the exercise of attempting to identify why the absurdity applies becomes one of fruitless futility.


[1305]
YANG [f. 100a] BOD MANG POS RTOG GE BAS DU BA KHYAD PAR BA YOD PA LA ME YOD PAS KHYAB PA DANG, BYAS PA LA MI RTAG PAS KHYAB PA SGRUB PA NA, YUL DUS THAMS CAD DU MI ‘KHRUL PA SGRUB PA YIN LA,

There are other Tibetan thinkers, logicians, who would make yet another claim:

There are cases where we establish that—whenever a particular instance of smoke is present—then fire must also be there; or that whenever something is a thing that was created, then it must also be a changing thing.  And when we do establish these facts, then we establish that they they necessarily hold true in all places, and all times.


[1306]
DE SGRUB PA’I TSE NI TSANG MANG DANG BUM PA LTA BU NYI TSE BA GCIG GI STENG DU BSGRUBS NAS, DE NAS DE DANG YUL DUS GZHAN GYI KHYAB PA GNYIS RIGS MTSUNGS PA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS,

And when we establish that, then we establish in turn that these relationships must hold true in every single random case, or point in time: in the kitchen, or with water pot.  Again, when they hold in a single case, then by reason of logical equivalence they would hold as well in every other place or time.


[1307]
KHYAB PA DE GNYIS YUL DUS THAMS CAD KYI STENG DU MI ‘KHRUL BAR SGRUB PAR ‘DOD PA LA, DE LTA NA GZHAN TZAM DU MTSUNGS PA’I RTAGS KYIS HA CANG THAL BA ‘PHEN TE, ‘DI ‘DRA BA NI LDOG PA GCIG PA’I DPUNG ‘PHUL LO, ZHES ZER RO,,

But it would be absurd then to say that—just because these necessary relationships would hold true in every single location or moment—they would hold equally true for any other two objects we chose, simply because they were different from each other.  In that case you’d simply piling up logically necessary opposites.


[1308]
‘DI YANG GZHUNG GI DON MA NGES SHING RTOG GE’I ‘JUG PA LA RNAM PA MA SHAR BA’I GTAM YIN TE, DU BA KHYAD PAR BA DANG BYAS PA GNYIS YUL DUS KYIS KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR, SPYIR ME DANG MI RTAG PA LA MI ‘KHRUL BAR BSGRUBS PAS,

This kind of talk though simply reflects a failure to grasp the point of the scripture here; and an inability to adhere to logical form.  Even if we fail to specify a particular location or point in time for a particular instance of smoke, or for the quality of being made, it still holds true that they will always imply—in general—fire; or the quality of being changing.


[1309]
ME YOD PA DANG MI RTAG PA YIN PA LOG KYANG, RTAGS SU BKOD PA GNYIS MI LDOG PA SRID DAM SNYAM PA’I DOGS PA LEGS PAR GCOD NUS LA,

That in itself is enough to prevent, perfectly, the uncertainty where someone wonders whether—even if the presence of fire, or the quality of being changing, are cancelled—it might still be possible that the items put forth as the reason in each case could not be cancelled.


[1310]
CHOS DE GNYIS RGYU ‘BRAS YIN PA LOG KYANG GZHAN TZAM YIN PA ZHUGS PA DU MA ZHIG YOD PAS, DE GNYIS MTSUNGS PA’I GO SKABS GA LA YOD,

There are, moreover, a great many cases where we can demonstrate that two objects share no cause-and-effect relationship, and yet are still such that they are other than each other.  How then could there be a case where the two relationships were equivalent?


[1311]
DES NA ‘DI NI DPUNG ‘PHUL ZHES PA’I MING NYID KYIS RIGS PA MI SHES PA’I SUN ‘BYIN DU GSAL BAR BYAS TE GZHAN DU RGYAS PAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,

We can thus say that the phrase itself here—“piling up logically necessary opposites”—clearly indicates that the refutation being attempted here is one set forth by a person who has no understanding of logic.  I have already covered this point, at length, elsewhere.


[1312]
‘O NA ‘DI JI LTAR YIN ZHE NA, TSIG GSAL LAS, RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM GYIS KUN RDZOB GRUB PAR KHAS LEN GYI, PHYOGS BZHI KHAS [f. 100b] BLANGS PA’I SGO NAS NI MA YIN TE, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR DANG, DE YANG RIGS PA MA YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

“Well then,” one may ask, “what does the absurdity actually turn upon?”  Let’s begin with a reference from A Clarification of the Verses:
