What we say is that something is established as being deceptive reality simply by reason of this dependence upon conditions—it’s not that we say it’s due to accepting these four possibilities.  Because if that were the case, then working things would have to possess some nature of their own; whereas that is something illogical.


[1313]
RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM ZHIG KHAS BLANGS NA NI, RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU GNYIS PHAN TSUN LTOS BA’I PHYIR NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PA MA YIN PAS, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BAR ‘GYUR BA MA YIN NO,,

And if we do accept this idea of depending upon conditions, then these two—causes & effects—would have to be interdependent.  In that case, they could no longer exist in & of themselves; and it would not be the case that we would then become thinkers who assert that these working things have some nature of their own.


[1314]
ZHES RANG GIS SKYE BA KHAS LEN MI LEN GYI KHYAD PAR GNYIS DANG, DE GNYIS KYI RGYU MTSAN DU PHYOGS BZHI’I SKYE BA KHAS BLANGS NA, RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA DGOS PAR GSUNGS PAS,

What this is saying is that—if we recognize a difference between accepting or not accepting the growth of things, and if we accept the idea that the difference between the two turns upon accepting that things must grow in one of the four ways—then we would have to be someone who asserts that these things possess some nature of their own.


[1315]
GZHAN SKYE KHAS BLANGS NA RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA KHAS LEN DGOS PA DANG, RTEN ‘BREL GYI SKYE BA TZAM ZHIG KHAS BLANGS NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA KHAS LEN MI DGOS PAR GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

And so what the reference is really stating, quite clearly, is that—if we accept the idea that things grow from something other than themselves—then we have to accept the idea that things could grow through some nature of their own; and that if rather we simply accept a kind of growing where things depend on each other, then we needn’t accept the idea that they could grow through such a nature.


[1316]
DE LTAR NA GZHAN SKYE’I GZHAN NI GZHAN TZAM ZHIG MIN GYI, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN PAS DE KHAS LEN PA LA HA CANG THAL BA ‘PHEN GYI, GZHAN TZAM KHAS BLANGS PA LA ‘PHEN PA GTAN MIN NO,,

We can thus say that the phrase “something other than itself” in the expression “the idea that something could grow from something other than itself” doesn’t just refer to something other.  Rather, it’s a reference to something other which could exist through some nature of its own; and thus we can build a statement of complete absurdity based on accepting it.  It is not at all the case though that you could build this absurdity based on the other party accepting that things could grow from something that was simply other.


[1317]
‘OG NAS KYANG SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI THA DAD KYANG RGYUD GCIG TU ‘DOD PA LA,
,GANG DAG RANG MTSAN NYID KYIS SO SO BA,
,DE DAG RGYUD GCIG GTOGS PAR RIGS MA YIN,
ZHES RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SO SO BA YIN NA, SNGA PHYI RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA MI RIGS PAR GSUNGS PA DANG ‘DI GNYIS RIGS PA ‘DRA’O,,

Further on we’ll be agreeing, in addition, to the idea that successive moments in the flow of a thing—despite the fact that they are distinct from one another—can nonetheless together constitute a flow of the thing.  As the text puts it,

It would be incorrect to say
That two parts which were separate
Through some nature of their own

Could ever be included
Into the flow of a single thing.

This statement—that if successive moments of a thing were distinct from one another through some nature of their own, then it would be illogical to say that they were included into the flow of a single thing—is based upon the same sort of reasoning that we see here with something “other.”


[1318]
DE YANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN NA LTOS PA’I ‘BREL BA ‘GOG NUS LA, ‘BREL MED DON GZHAN DU SONG NA ‘BRAS BU GCIG [f. 101a] RANG GI RGYU LAS SKYE NA, RGYU MIN PA THAMS CAD LAS KYANG SKYE BA DANG, RGYU GCIG GIS RANG GI ‘BRAS BU SKYED NA RANG GI ‘BRAS BU MIN PA’I ‘BRAS BU’I DNGOS PO THAMS CAD SKYED PAR HA CANG THAL BA ‘JUG PA’O,,

Further, if something really were something other than something else through some nature of its own, then that would thereby have the power to disprove the concept of a dependent relationship, and the two objects involved would come to be things that were disparate entities with no connection at all.  And in that case, whenever a particular result grew from its particular cause, it would as well grow from each & every object in the universe that was not its particular cause.  It would also then be the case that—whenever a particular cause produced its particular result—then it would as well produce all resulting entities that were not that particular result.  Thus this position would indeed lead to certain complete absurdities.


[1319]
DES NA ‘DI ‘DRA BA’I RIGS PA LEGS PAR MI GO BA NI, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR GYI ‘DI ‘DRA CIG ‘GOG PA’I DGAG BYA ‘DZIN PA’I TSAD ‘DZIN DANG, ‘DI TZAM ZHIG KHAS LEN PA’I RTEN ‘BYUNG GI RNAM GZHAG GNYIS SO SOR LEGS PAR MA PHYED PA’I SKYON YIN PAS, DGAG BYA ‘GOG PA’I SKABS SU DGAG BYA’I TSAD ‘DZIN BSHAD PA DRAN PAR BYA’O,,

And so we can say that—if a person lacked a clear understanding of the sort of reasoning employed here—then they would fall into the error of failing to distinguish, perfectly, between the exercise where we take the measure of that thing which our logic is meant to deny, denying the existence of the particular object that we described earlier; and a presentation of the particular form of dependence which we do agree to.  As such, I would ask the reader to reflect again upon our explanation of how to take the measure of the object whose existence we do deny, back in the section where we disproved this object.



Demonstrating absurdity
is not automatically
to accept its opposite

[1320]
GNYIS PA NI, GAL TE SNGAR BSHAD PA’I THAL BA GNYIS LAS BZLOG PA’I DON KHAS LEN NA, TSIG GSAL LAS, THAL BAR ‘GYUR BA BZLOG PA’I DON DANG YANG PHA ROL PO NYID ‘BREL BA YIN GYI, KHO BO CAG NI MA YIN TE, RANG LA DAM BCA’ BA MED PA’I PHYIR RO, ,ZHES DANG,

This brings us to the second step from above: the contradiction which arises from accepting the opposite of the absurdity.  One may begin with the following question, in three parts:

Well, assume that what we are supposed to accept is the point which is the opposite of the two absurdities which have just been presented.  How then, first of all, can A Clarification of the Verses then make the statement that “And if we examine the point which is the opposite of the absurdity, we would have to say that it relates to the position of the other party; and not to our own.  And that’s because we take no position on the matter at all.”


[1321]
RANG BZHIN MED PAR SMRA BAS RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BA LA THAL BA BSGRUBS PA NA, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA’I DON CAN DU THAL BAR GA LA ‘GYUR TE, ZHES DANG,

And how can the work further then state, “Why on earth would it be the case that—when those who deny that things have any nature of their own demonstrate an absurd consequence of the beliefs of those who say that things do have such a nature—they would then necessarily have to be thinkers who support the point which is the opposite of this absurdity?”


[1322]
DE’I PHYIR THAL BA SGRUB PA NI PHA ROL PO’I DAM BCA’ BA ‘GOG PA TZAM GYI ‘BRAS BU CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA’I DON DU ‘GYUR BA YOD PA MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA RNAMS JI LTAR DRANG SNYAM NA,

How finally can the same text say, “As such the demonstration of absurdity here is meant only to have the effect of denying the position of the other party; it is not the case that there is some point which is the opposite of the absurdity and which is meant to be included into this effect.”


[1323]
SKYON MED DE DE LTAR GSUNGS PA NI BDAG SKYE ‘GOG PA’I SKABS KHO NA YIN PAS, DBU MA PAS ‘PHANGS PA’I THAL BA KUN LA MIN GYI, BDAG SKYE ‘GOG PA’I [f. 101b] THAL BA GNYIS LA YIN NO,

And yet there are no such issues here.  These statements apply only to the present context, where we are denying that things could grow through some kind of self-nature.  They are not meant to apply to all absurd consequences ever drawn from other thinkers’ positions by members of the Middle Way school; rather, they apply only here, to these two absurd consequences pointed out as we deny that things could grow through such a self-nature.


[1324]
DE’I THAL CHOS NI SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED DU THAL BA TZAM MIN GYI, SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED YIN LA, THAL CHOS DE BZLOG PA’I DON SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON BCAS DANG THUG BCAS NI GRANGS CAN KHO NA ‘DOD KYI, RANG LA DE’I DAM BCA’ BA MED PA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS, DE KHAS BLANGS PA’I GRUB MTHA’ DANG ‘GAL BA MED CES PA’I DON TE LUNG DANG PO’I DON NO,,

The point of the absurdity is not solely to say that the growing of things would then have to be pointless, and endless; but rather to say that their repeated growth would be pointless and endless.  The idea that would be the opposite of these two absurdities would be that the repeated growth of things did have a point, and did come to an end—and that would be accepted only by the Numerists.  What the first citation you’ve given then is actually saying is that—because we ourselves take no position on this matter—there is no danger of our contradicting the other position that our school does take.


[1325]
SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS KYIS KYANG YANG SKYE BA DON MED CES YANG GI SGRA SMOS SHING, TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG YANG GI SGRA SMOS LA, ‘DIR YANG SLAR YANG SKYE BAR YONGS SU RTOG PAR ‘GYUR NA NI, ZHES GSUNGS PAS YOD PA DANG SLAR YANG SKYE BA GNYIS ‘GAL GYI YOD PA DANG SKYE BA MI ‘GAL LO,,

Master Buddha Palita does insert the expression “once again” here—“it would be pointless for this thing to grow once again”; and we see the “once again” mentioned as well in A Clarification of the Verses.  And here in Master Chandrakirti’s root text we see, once again, “Suppose you fantasize that it could grow again.”  The point then is that the contradiction here lies between the pair of existing and growing over again; it is not the case that the contradiction is between existing & growing.


[1326]
DE BZHIN DU YOD PA DANG SLAR YANG SKYE BA THUG BCAS ‘GAL GYI, YOD PA DANG SKYE BA THUG BCAS GNYIS MI ‘GAL LO,,

Just so, existing and growing over again—but not endlessly—are contradictory; although there is no contradiction between the pair of existing & growing, but not endlessly.


[1327]
LUNG GNYIS PA’I DON NI RANG BZHIN MED PAR SMRA BA DBU MA PAS, RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BA GRANGS CAN LA SNGAR BSHAD PA’I THAL BA GNYIS ‘PHANGS PA NA, RANG LA BZLOG DON ‘PHEN PA KHAS LEN ‘DOD MED LA, DE MED KYANG RANG DBANG MED PAR BYED PAR YANG MIN PAS, THAL BA DE GNYIS LAS BZLOG PA KHAS MI LEN ZHES PA’I DON NO,,

The point of the second citation above is to express how those who say that nothing has any nature of its own—the followers of the middle way—might address the Numerists, drawing the two absurd consequences just described; but even as they do, it is not the case that they themselves would then accept the point which is the opposite of these absurdities.  And even assuming they would not want to, there is further no necessity that they would have to do so, despite themselves.  As such, what’s being said is that they would not in fact accept the points opposite to the absurdities listed.


[1328]
LUNG GSUM PA’I DON NI THAL BA GNYIS KYI THAL CHOS BZLOG PA’I DON SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON BCAS DANG THUG BCAS KYI RTAGS KYIS BDAG SKYE MED PA MI SGRUB KYANG DGOS PA MED PA MIN TE, GRANGS CAN MI ‘DOD PA’I SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED BSGRUBS PAS, GRANGS CAN GYIS DAM [f. 102a] BCAS PA’I BDAG LAS SKYE BA RNAM PAR BCAD PA TZAM ZHIG SGRUB PA’I DGOS PA CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO ZHES PA’I DON NO,,

What the third citation is saying is the following.  The opposites of the quality being expressed in the two absurdities are (1) that there would be some point to things growing once again after they had already grown once; and (2) that such repeated growing would not be endless.  Presented as reasons, they cannot, admittedly, establish that the growth of things does not occur through any kind of self-nature.  But neither do they serve no purpose; for they do have the benefit of establishing that something which the Numerists would not want to accept—that the growth of something was pointless, and that it would be repeated endlessly—would have to be the case.  And as such, they do disallow the growth through some self-nature which the Numerists do assert.


[1329]
HA CANG THAL BA GNYIS LA NI THAL BA’I BZLOG DON RANG NYID KYIS KHAS LEN PAS, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA’I DON LA RANG GIS KHAS LEN PA DANG MI LEN PA GNYIS SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Our readers should understand then that we might first accept that there is a point which is the opposite of that which is made by these two absurdities; but that, by the same token, there are two possibilities here: one where we would ourselves accept this point that was the opposite of the absurdity, and another where we would not.



A response to absurdity

[1330]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, SKYON SPONG GI LAN, LAN DE DGAG PA’O,,

This brings us to our second point from above: denying a response which attempts to avoid the problem.  We proceed in two steps: a presentation of this response, and then denying it.


	[1331]
[VI.15]
Śakyaṃ prakartum iti kāryam ato niruktaṃ
śaktaṃ yad asya janane sa paro’pi hetuḥ,
Janmaika santati gatāj janakāc ca tasmāc
chālyaṅkurasya na tathā ca yavādi taś cet.

,RAB TU BYA BAR NUS PA DE PHYIR ‘BRAS BUR
DES {%NGES} BRJOD CING,
,GANG ZHIG DE SKYED NUS PA DE NI GZHAN NA’ANG
RGYU YIN LA,
,RGYUD GCIG GTOGS DANG SKYED PAR BYED LAS SKYE BA
DE YI PHYIR,
,S’A LU’I MYU GU NAS LA SOGS LAS DE LTA
MIN ZHE NA,

		Now suppose someone says
		“We specify anything
		Which can be created,
		As such, as the result.

		And anything which is
		Capable of producing
		Is a cause, even if
		It is something other.

		A rice sprout grows
		From what is incorporated
		Into a single flow,

		And from something
		That does function
		To produce it.

		As such, it is not something
		That can grow, in the same way,
		From barley or the like.”			


[1332]
DANG PO NI, ‘DIR SMRAS PA RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID KYANG YOD LA, THAMS CAD LAS THAMS CAD ‘BYUNG BA YANG MIN TE, RGYU ‘BRAS SO SOR NGES PA MTHONG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here is the first.  Now suppose someone comes and says the following:

First of all, it is certainly the case that there is a difference—and a difference which exists in & of itself—between a cause and its result, where one is something other than the other.  Even so, it is not the case that all objects would then arise from all other objects.  And this is because we can see with our own eyes that certain causes are always connected to certain results.


[1333]
DE YANG ‘DI YIN TE GANG GI PHYIR DNGOS PO GANG ZHIG GANG GIS RAB TU BYA BAR NUS PA DE NYID DE YI ‘BRAS BUR NGES PAR BRJOD PA YIN LA, DE’I PHYIR ‘BRAS BU NGES SO,,

And here’s how this works.  We specify any particular thing which can be created by any other particular thing as the result of that same thing.  As such, the result is specific to its cause.


[1334]
DE PHYIR ZHES PA ‘GREL PA DANG MI MTHUN NO,,

Shortening the “as such” to “and so” here fails to match the autocommentary.


[1335]
RGYU GANG ZHIG ‘BRAS BU DE SKYED PAR NUS PA DE NI NGO BOS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN NA’ANG RGYU YIN LA, DE’I PHYIR RGYU NGES SO,,

They continue with:

And anything which is a cause and which is capable of producing a result is a cause, even if it happens to be something which exists by its own essence, and is other than the result; as such, the cause is specific.


[1336]
DES NA GZHAN KHYAD PAR BA KHO NAS RGYU ‘BRAS SU ‘JOG GI ,GZHAN NYID KYI SPYI GZHAN TZAM GYIS NI RGYU ‘BRAS SU MI ‘JOG GO

Therefore, things are established as causes and effects of each other only by virtue of being a particular thing which is other than the other; it is not as if we establish things as cause & effect only by virtue of their being distinct from each other—as displaying some general form of otherness.


[1337]
,GZHAN YANG SA LU’I MYU GU NI RANG DANG RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA SA LU’I SA BON LAS SKYE’I, RGYUD MI GCIG PA NAS KYI SA BON SOGS LAS MI SKYE’O,,

Moreover, the case is that a rice sprout grows from the rice seed which is incorporated with it into a single flow; it’s not as if a sprout could grow from a seed or whatever which were not included into the same flow.


[1338]
RGYUD GCIG KYANG SKYED BYED MIN PA SKAD CIG MA PHYI MAS SNGA MA MI SKYED PAS, RGYUD GCIG PA’I SNGA MAS PHYI MA SKYED PAR BYED PA LAS SKYE BA DE YI PHYIR, SA LU’I MYU GU NI NAS LA SOGS PA LAS NAS KYI MYU GU LA SOGS PA SKYE BA DE [f. 102b] LTAR SKYE BA MIN PAS THAMS CAD LAS THAMS CAD MI SKYE’O ZHE NA,

Even if they are incorporated into a single flow, a later instant of an object—which is not something which is functioning to produce the certain thing—cannot produce an earlier instant of the same object.  Rather, the case is that the object of the later instant grows from the object of the earlier instant included into the same flow—from something that does function to produce it.  As such, a rice sprout is not something that can grow from a barley seed or the like, in the same way that a barley sprout or such does.  Thus it is not the case that everything there is grows from everything else there is.



Entirely other,
with none of
four qualities

[1339]
GNYIS PA NI, SA LU’I SA MYUG SO SOR NGES PA ‘DI GO RGYU MTSAN GANG LAS YIN ZHES RGYU ‘BRAS NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SMRA BA ‘DI LA ‘DRI BAR BYA’O,,

This brings us to the second step from above, where we deny this response.  Here we ask the following question to those who say that causes and results exist in & of themselves: “What exactly is the reason you give for this position you’ve expressed—that the seeds and the sprouts of rice are specific to each other?”


[1340]
SMRAS PA NGES PA MTHONG BA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

And suppose the other side answers: “Well yes, we’ll tell you why: We can see, with our own eyes, that the two are specific to each other.”


[1341]
YANG CI’I PHYIR DE LTAR NGES PA MTHONG ZHES DE LTAR BRGAL ZHING BRTAGS PA NA,

And suppose we question them on this point, and dig deeper into it, asking: “Well just why is it that you can see, with your own eyes, that they are specific to each other?”


[1342]
GANG GI PHYIR NGES PA MTHONG BA DE’I PHYIR NGES PA MTHONG NGO ZHES DE TZAM ZHIG SMRA BA

And then all they can reply is, “Well, we can see that the cause & effect are specific to each other, because we can see that they’re specific to each other.”


[1343]
‘DIS NI NGES PA’I RGYU MA BSTAN PAR BSHAD ZIN PA’I NYES PA CUNG ZAD KYANG SPANG BAR MI NUS SO, ZHES GSUNGS TE,

And our answer to this is, “But this reply doesn’t help even the least bit to address the problem we’ve already raised—that it doesn’t present any reason why the two are specific to one another.”


[1344]
RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GZHAN YIN KYANG NGES PA MTHONG BA MI ‘GAL BA’I RGYU MTSAN MA BSTAN PAS SKYON SPONG GI LAN MIN ZHES PA’O,,

What we’re saying then is that this is not a response which eliminates the problems we’ve raised; it doesn’t provide any reason why it would not be a contradiction to say that—even though the seed and the sprout are, by definition, something other than each other—we still observe that they are particular to one another.


[1345]
GZHAN YANG RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID RGYU ‘BRAS YIN MIN KUN LA THUN MONG BA KHYAD PAR DU YONGS SU MA BCAD PA SHIN TU GRAGS PA ‘DI NYID, PHYIR RGOL ‘DI’I ‘DOD PA LA GNOD BYED DO ZHES BSHAD PA NI,

Moreover, it is absolutely common knowledge that if two things were other than each other in a way that existed by definition, then that difference could not be denied in the specific instance of the common group of each & every other object, whether they were cause & effect or not.  This fact, the root text says next, draws into question the entire position here of the other party.


	[1346]
[VI.16]
Iṣṭā yathā na janakā na ca śakti yuktā
naivaika santati gatāḥ sadṛśā na caiva,
Śālyaṅkurasya yava kesara kiṃ śukādyā
no śāli bījam api tasya tathā paratvāt.

,JI LTAR NAS DANG GE SAR DANG NI KENG SHU
KA LA SOGS,
,S’A LU’I MYU GU’I SKYED PAR BYED PAR ‘DOD MIN
NUS LDAN MIN,
,RGYUD GCIG KHONGS SU GTOGS MIN ‘DRA BA MA YIN
NYID DE BZHIN,
,S’A LU’I SA BON YANG NI DE YI MIN TE
GZHAN NYID PHYIR,

		Take barley; and filaments;
		The flame of the forest;
		Or anything of the like.
	
These are not at all things
That we could ever agree
Act to produce a rice sprout,
Nor do they possess the capacity;

They are not included in a single flow,
Nor are they the same.

Just so, neither is the rice seed
For it; because it is entirely other.


[1347]
JI LTAR TE DPER NA NAS DANG PAD+MA LA SOGS PA’I ZE’U ‘BRU GE SAR DANG KENG SHU KA’I ME TOG LA SOGS PA RNAMS GZHAN YIN PA’I PHYIR,

Let’s take, for example, a grain of barley; the filaments for the anther of a lotus or similar flower; the bloom of a flame-of-the-forest tree, or anything else of the like.  All these are things that are other than rice.


[1348]
SA LU’I MYU GU’I SKYED PAR BYED PAR ‘DOD PA MIN PA DANG, SA LU’I MYU GU SKYED PA’I NUS PA DANG LDAN PA MIN PA DANG, RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA MIN PA DANG RIGS ‘DRA BA’I SNGA MA MA YIN PA NYID

Therefore they are (1) not at all things that we could agree act to produce a rice sprout; (2) nor do they possess the capacity to ever produce such a sprout.  They are (3) not things that are included into a single flow with a rice sprout; (4) nor are they preceding entitites that are of the same type as this kind of sprout.


[1349]
DE BZHIN DU, SA LU’I SA BON YANG NI SA LU’I MYU GU DE LA LTOS PA YI KHYAD PAR BZHI DANG LDAN PA MIN TE, RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Just so, neither is the rice seed something which possesses these four qualities relative to it—to the rice sprout—because it is, in & of itself, something entirely other than the sprout.


[1350]
‘DI YANG ‘BREL MED DON GZHAN LA KHYAD PAR BZHI YOD MED KYANG [f. 103a] GZHAG PAR MI NUS PA’I RIGS PA’O,,

This is a type of logic for demonstrating that—whether those four qualities held or not—we cannot establish a cause & effect relationship with things that are completely different and unrelated.



A more particular denial
of otherness

[1351]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, RGYU ‘BRAS SNGA PHYI BA LA GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA, RGYU ‘BRAS DUS MNYAM PA LA GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA’O,,

Which brings us to our second step from before: a more particular denial that things could grow from something other than themselves.  This we present in two parts of its own: denying that things could grow from something other than themselves, in the case of a cause and its effect which are successive; and then denying that things could grow from something other in a case where cause & effect were simultaneous.


[1352]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, DNGOS KYI DON DANG, BKAG PA LA RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O,,

The first of these, in turn, comes in two points: the actual point; and then refuting attempted rebuttal of our denial.


	[1353]
[VI.17]
Astyaṅkuraś ca na hi bīja samāna kālo
bījaṃ kutaḥ parata yāstu vinā paratvam,
Janmāṅkurasya na hi sidhyati tena bījāt
saṃtyajyatāṃ parata udbhavatīti pakṣaḥ.

,MYU GU SA BON DANG NI DUS MNYAM YOD PA
MA YIN TE,
,GZHAN NYID MED PAR LA {%SA} BON GZHAN PA NYID DU
GA LA ‘GYUR,
,DES NA MYU GU SA BON LAS SKYE ‘GRUB PAR [205a]
‘GYUR MIN PAS,
,GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YIN ZHES BYA BA’I PHYOGS ‘DI
GTANG BAR BYOS,

		It is not the case
		That the sprout and seed
		Exist at the same time;
	
		If they cannot be
		Totally other,
		Then how could the seed
		Be something entirely other?

		Neither, therefore,
		Is it the case
		That the birth of a sprout
		From a seed could be [f. 205a].

		As such, we implore you
		To relinquish this position,
		Where you claim that things
		Grow from something other.			


[1354]
DANG PO NI, DE LTAR RE ZHIG PHYIR RGOL GZHAN LA GRAGS PA’I RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN GRUB GRUB LTAR BRJOD NAS SUN ‘BYIN BYAS SO, ,DE NI RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS LA NGO BOS GRUB PA’I GZHAN MI SRID PAR BSHAD PA,

Here’s the first; we will begin with describing how, as if it were possible, things could exist as something other than other things, in a way which existed in & of itself—as the other party here declares it would be.  And then we’ll demolish this idea.  That in itself would involve explaining why it’s impossible for causes and their results to be, through some essence of their own, other than each other.


[1355]
‘DI NA BYAMS PA DANG NYER SBAS YOD BZHIN PA DAG KHO NA PHAN TSUN LTOS NAS, ‘DI NI ‘DI LAS ZHES GZHAN NYID DU MTHONG GI ,MYU GU SA BON DANG NI DUS MNYAM DU YOD PA MA YIN TE, SA BON RNAM PAR MA ‘GYUR BAR MYU GU MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here we can say that John and Joe, first of all, are entities which exist.  And then—only with regard to them—we say that, relative to each other, we can observe that “this one is something completely different from that one.”  It is not though the case that the sprout exists at the same time as the seed; for there is no such thing as a sprout which is present before the seed is transformed.


[1356]
SA BON LA MYU GU LAS NGO BOS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID MED LA, DE MED PAR SA BON MYU GU LAS GZHAN PA NYID DU GA LA ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR RO,,

As for the seed as well, there exists none which is something totally other than the sprout, in a way where this is true in & of itself.  And if that cannot be, then how on earth could the seed ever be something entirely other than the sprout?  Meaning—it could never be so.


[1357]
NGO BOS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID MED PA DES NA MYU GU SA BON LAS SKYES PA NGO BO NYID KYIS ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR BA MIN PAS DNGOS PO RNAMS GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YIN ZHES BYA BA’I PHYOGS ‘DI GTANG BAR BYOS SHIG

And since there could never be any quality where things were other than each other in a way that existed in & of itself, it is therefore neither the case that the birth of a sprout from a seed could be something that existed through some essential nature of its own.  As such, we would implore you to relinquish this position, where you claim that things are such that they grow from something other than themselves.


[1358]
,’DI NI SA BON MYU GU LAS THA DAD PA DE RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YIN NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA LA DUS NAM YANG LDOG PA MED PAS, SA BON GYI DUS NA’ANG MYU GU LAS RDZAS THA DAD DU ‘GYUR LA, DE LTAR DE GNYIS DUS MNYAM DU ‘GYUR BA LAS DE MED PA’I PHYIR,

The point being made here is this.  Suppose that the fact that a seed was distinct from a sprout were something that existed through some nature of its own.  Now a thing that existed through its own nature could never be stopped; as such, even in the seed’s time it would be substantially distinct from the sprout—whereas if that were the case, then the seed & sprout would have to be simultaneous, while in fact they are not.


[1359]
DE GNYIS LA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN MED CES STON PA YIN GYI, RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS THA SNYAD DU NGO BO THA DAD DU ‘DOD PA [f. 103b] ‘GOG PA MIN TE, DGAG BYA LA GTUG PA SHES DGOS SO,,

All this is teaching us that—with regard to these two—there is no quality of being other than each other, in a way which exists through some essence of its own.  What we are not denying here though is the belief that causes & effects are, in name only, entities that are discrete from each other.  You need to try understand here that the argument is meant to address that non-existent thing which emptiness is empty of.



The mistaken metaphor
of the arms of a scale

[1360]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point here: refuting attempted rebuttal of our denial.  


	[1361]
	[VI.18]
Antadvayasya namanonnamane tulāyā
dṛṣṭe yathā na khalu naiva samāna kāle,
Syātāṃ tathā janaka janya nirodha jātī
yadyekadā tad asad atra vinaika kālam.

,JI LTAR SRANG GI MDA’ GNYIS MTHO BA DANG NI
DMA’ BA DAG
,DUS MNYAM MA YIN PAR NA {%NI} MIN PAR MTHONG BA
DE BZHIN DU,
,BSKYED PAR BYA DANG SKYED BYED DAG GI SKYE ‘GAG
‘GYUR ZHE NA,
,GAL TE GCIG TSE YIN NA ‘DIR DUS GCIG MED
DE YANG MIN,

Now the others may claim:
“We can observe
How the arms of a scale
Rising & descending,

These two, are not such
That they do not occur
At the same time.

The growth & the ending
Of what is produced,
And what does the producing,
Occur too in a similar way.”

This idea though is not correct;
Even given that these two
Are concurrent,
There would not be here
Simultaneity.				


[1362]
MYU GU SA BON DANG NI DUS MNYAM YOD PA MA YIN TE, ZHES SMRAS PA NI RIGS PA MA YIN TE, JI LTAR TE DPER NA SRANG GI MDA’ GNYIS KYI GCIG MTHO BA DANG NI CIG SHOS DMA’ BA DAG DUS MNYAM MA YIN PAR NI MIN PA STE DUS MNYAM PAR MTHONG BA DE BZHIN DU, BSKYED PAR BYA BA MYU GU DANG SKYED BYED SA BON DAG GI RIM PA BZHIN DU SKYE BA DANG ‘GAG PA’I BYA BA GNYIS DUS GCIG YIN PA’I PHYIR,

Now the other party may come then and make the following claim:

It’s incorrect for you to say that “It is not the case that the sprout & seed exist at the same time.”  What’s actually the case is that that the gradual growth of what is produced—the sprout—and the gradual ending of what does the producing—the seed—are two events which occur within the same time.  This is similar to the way, similar to the metaphor, in which we observe that the rising of one of the two arms of a scale takes place simultaneous to the descending of the other arm; these two actions are not such that they do not occur at the same time.


[1363]
SA MYUG GNYIS KYANG DUS MNYAM PAR ‘GYUR RO, ,DE’I PHYIR GZHAN NYID YOD PAS NYES PA MED DO ZHE NA,

As such, the seed and the sprout too are things that occur at the same time; and this means that there does exist this condition of being perfectly other than each other.  And that in turn means that our position is free of the problems you’ve raised.


[1364]
SRANG GI DPES SA MYUG GNYIS KYI SKYE ‘JIG GI BYA BA GNYIS DUS GCIG TU RTOG NA DE NI MI RUNG STE, GAL TE SRANG GI DPER MGO MJUG GNYIS DUS GCIG YIN PAS MTHO DMAN GYI BYA BA GNYIS GCIG TSE STE DUS GCIG YIN NA, DE LTA NA’ANG DPES MTSON PA’I DON DNGOS ‘DIR NI SA MYUG DUS GCIG PA MED PAS MI RIGS SO,,

In reply, we would say though that this idea—that a scale can be used as a metaphor for conceptualizing the way in which the actions of a sprout and a seed growing & ending take place—is simply not correct.  Even suppose it’s a given that, in the metaphor of the scale, the two sides of the scale are simultaneous; and that, therefore, these two actions of one arm of the scale rising, and the other descending, are concurrent (which is to say, simultaneous).  Still it would not be the case that here in the actual situation represented by the metaphor, there would be any simultaneity of seed & sprout—that would be mistaken.



How there is no simultaneity

[1365]
JI LTAR MED PA DE LTAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

Showing how this would not be the case is the purpose of the lines that come next.


	[1366]
[VI.19]
Janmonmukhaṃ na sad idaṃ yadi jāya mānaṃ
nāśonmukhaṃ sad api nāma niruddhya mānam,
Iṣṭaṃ tadā katham idaṃ tulayā samānaṃ
kartrā vinā janir iyaṃ na ca yukta rūpā.

,GAL TE SKYE BZHIN PA DE SKYE LA PHYOGS PAS
YOD MIN ZHING,
,’GAG BZHIN PA NI YOD KYANG ‘JIG LA PHYOGS PAR
‘DOD GYUR PA,
,DE TSE ‘DI NI JI LTA BUR NA SRANG DANG
MTSUNGS PA YIN,
,SKYE BA ‘DI NI BYED PO MED PAR RIGS PA’I
NGO BO’ANG MIN,

		Suppose that,
		In the act of growing,
		It is still approaching growth;
		And as such it is not
		Something that exists.

		There is though that
		Which is in the act of ending;
		But we treat it as something
		Approaching its destruction.

		How then in this moment
		Could it be that these
		Were the same as the scale?

		If the agent were absent,
		Then for this growing to exist
		Would be contrary
		To the very concept of logic.


[1367]
GAL TE SKYE BZHIN PA ZHES PA DE NI, DA LTA SKYE BA LA MNGON DU PHYOGS PA YIN PAS, MYU GU’I NGO BOR MA ‘ONGS PA’I PHYIR DA LTA YOD PA MIN ZHING, ‘GAG BZHIN PA NI YOD KYANG ‘JIGS LA MNGON DU PHYOGS PAR ‘DOD PAR GYUR PA’I PHYIR DA LTAR YOD PA’O,,

When it says here “Suppose it is in the act of growing,” the reference is to the sprout approaching, in the present moment, birth.  And because the sprout is at that point, its existing with the identity of a sprout is still something future; thus, the sprout is not something that exists in the present moment.  Now there is though that seed which is in the act of ending; but since we treat it as something approaching its destruction, we can say that it exists in the present moment.


[1368]
GANG GI TSE MYU GU SKYE BA LA PHYOGS PA’I DUS SU SA BON DA LTAR BA DANG, MYU GU MA ‘ONGS PA YIN PA DE’I TSE, SA MYUG GNYIS PO ‘DI NI JI LTA BUR NA SRANG GI MTHO DMAN GNYIS DANG MTSUNGS PAR [f. 104a] ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR TE,

So let’s consider this moment, in which the sprout is approaching growing; and in which the seed is in the present time, and the sprout in the future time.  How could it be then that these two—the seed & the sprout—were the same as the two arms of a scale; a pair where one is rising and the other is descending?  The fact is that they would not be the same.


[1369]
SRANG GI MGO MJUG GNYIS NI DA LTAR BA YIN PA’I PHYIR, DE’I MTHO BA DANG DMA’ BA’I BYA BA GNYIS KYANG DUS GCIG TU YOD KYI, SA MYUG GNYIS LA NI DUS GCIG PA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s because—since the two sides of the scale are in the present time—the two actions of one arm rising and the other arm descending exist simultaneously; whereas in the case of the pair of the seed & the sprout, we have no simultaneity.


[1370]
DE DAG GIS NI BYA BA GNYIS DUS GCIG PAS SA MYUG GNYIS KYANG DUS GCIG PA DANG, DE’I DPER SRANG MDA’I MTHO DMAN GNYIS BKOD PA’I DPE MA GRUB PAR BSTAN GYI, BYA BA GNYIS LA DUS GCIG PA SRID NA DUS DER CHOS GNYIS KYANG NGES PAR DUS MNYAM ZHES STON PA MIN NO,,

What the lines here are indicating is only the incorrectness of the ideas that—just because the two actions are simultaneous—then the pair of the seed & the sprout must also be simultaneous; and that the metaphor of the arms of a scale rising & dropping could apply here.  They are not making the assertion that—if it is possible for two actions to be simultaneous—then the two objects involved must also be simultaneous.


[1371]
CI STE CHOS SA MYUG GNYIS LTA BU DUS GCIG PA MED KYANG DE GNYIS KYI BYA BA LA DUS GCIG PA YOD DO SNYAM NA,

The following thought then might occur to someone:

Now even if there is no simultaneity with the two objects—with things like the seed & the sprout—there can though exist simultaneity with actions involving the two.


[1372]
DE YANG MI RUNG STE RGOL BA DE DAG GIS CHOS LAS BYA BA DON GZHAN DU KHAS MA BLANGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, ‘DI NI BYA BA GNYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ‘GOG PA’I SKABS YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This too though is mistaken, since these particular disputants do not accept the idea that action has an existence separate from the objects involved in the action; and, after all, this is a section of the text where we are disproving the idea that the two actions could exist through some nature of their own.


[1373]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE SKYE BA’I BYA BA LA LTOS PA’I BYED PA PO MYU GU NI, SKYE BA LA PHYOGS PA’I DUS SU MA ‘ONGS PA YIN PAS, DUS DER YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

And there is yet another problem here: the agent of the action, relative to the act of growing, is in fact the sprout—which in the moment of the growing is still future, and so is not something which exists in this moment.


[1374]
DER DE MED NA YANG RTEN BYED PA PO MYU GU MED PAR BRTEN PA SKYE BA’I BYA BA ‘DI NI YOD PAR RIGS PA’I NGO BO’ANG MIN PAS ‘GAG PA DANG DUS GCIG PAR MED PA’I PHYIR, BYA BA GNYIS DUS GCIG PAR MI RIGS SO,,

And if it is not something which exists yet—that is, if the basis of the action, the sprout (the agent), were absent—then for what rests upon this basis, this act of growing, to exist would be contrary to the very concept of logic.  As such, the growing could not be simultaneous to the ending; and therefore it would be incorrect to say that the two actions were simultaneous.


[1375]
GAL TE ‘PHAGS PA SA LU LJANG PA’I MDO LAS, SRANG MDA’I MTHO DMAN GYI TSUL DU SKAD CIG GANG KHO NA LA SA BON ‘GAGS PA DE NYID LA MYU GU SKYE’O, ZHES SRANG GI DPE ‘DI NYE BAR BKOD PA MA YIN NAM, DE’I PHYIR SA MYUG GNYIS [f. 104b] SRANG MDA’I MTHO DMAN DANG ‘DRA BAR ‘DOD PA ‘GOG PAR MI RIGS SO ZHE NA,

Someone may respond then with the following:

But doesn’t the sutra called A Sprout of Rice also utilize the metaphor of a scale, describing how in the very moment that the seed ends, the sprout grows, in the same way that the arms of a scale rise & descend?  Since that is indeed the case, isn’t it incorrect for you to deny that the pair of the seed & the sprout are similar to the rising & descending arms of the scale?


[1376]
BKOD PA NI BDEN MOD KYI DE NI GZHAN SKYE DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA BSTAN PA’I PHYIR YANG MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PAS, GAL TE SKYE BA ‘DI NI ZHES PAS SKYE BA BKAG PA NI RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA’I SKYE BA TZAM BKAG GI ,SA BON LAS MYU GU SKYE BA TZAM ‘GOG PA GTAN MIN NO,,

We would have to admit that the metaphor is, in truth, presented in that sutra.  Remember though that “this is speaking neither of things growing from something other than themselves; nor is it speaking of growth which occurs by definition.”  As such, when the part about “suppose this growing” denies that things grow, it is only denying that things could grow through some essential nature of their own.  We are absolutely not denying that, in general, sprouts grow from seeds.


[1377]
‘O NA MDO DE LAS SA MYUG GNYIS DUS GCIG PA SRANG MDA’I MTHO DMAN GYI TSUL DU MI STON NA, DPE DE DUS MNYAM PA CI ‘DRA ZHIG LA DGONGS ZHE NA,

One might respond to this, in turn, with—

Well suppose you’re right, and that this sutra is not describing a simultaneity of the two of a seed and a sprout which is analogous to the rising and descending of the arms of a scale.  What kind of synchronicity then is this metaphor in the sutra meant to refer to?


[1378]
‘GREL PAR CIG CAR DU BRTEN NAS ‘BYUNG BA MA BRTAGS PAR GRUB PA SGYU MA LTA BU GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU GSUNGS PAR BSHAD PA’I CIG CAR DU BRTEN NAS ‘BYUNG BA ZHES PA NI, BYA BA GNYIS CIG CAR DU YOD PA LA BYA DGOS TE, MDO DER SRANG MDA’I MTHO DMA’I DPES DUS MNYAM PA GCIG STON DGOS PA LA, SO {%SA} MYUG GNYIS DUS MNYAM PA LA BSHAD DU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Remember that the autocommentary goes on to say, “It is so that people can come to see clearly that—when these things occur altogether, and we choose not to examine how they occur altogether in a dependent relationship—then they exist in the same way that an illusion does.”  This statement must be read as describing how the two actions occur altogether.  That is, while it is true that the sutra must be explained as using the metaphor of the arms of a scale to describe a type of simultaneity, it would be mistaken to describe it as explaining why the two of seed and sprout were simultaneous.


[1379]
DES NA BYA BA GNYIS GCIG PA BKAG BA NI, RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I BYA BA GNYIS YIN GYI, BYA BA GNYIS SPYIR DUS MNYAM PA YOD PA BKAG PA MIN NO,,

Therefore the denial that the two actions occur at the same time is made with reference to the two as existing by definition; it is not the case that—in general—the idea that the two actions could be happening simultaneously is being refused.


[1380]
DE LA SKYE BA ‘DOD PHYIN CHAD RGYU ‘GAG PA DANG ‘BRAS BU SKYE BA LA MNGON DU PHYOGS PA GNYIS DUS MNYAM PA CIG DGOS SO,,

That is, once we agree that something grows, we must as well agree that the cause approaching its ending and the result approaching its growing are happening at the very same time.


[1381]
DE NI SKYE BA TZAM DANG THA SNYAD DU SKYE BA KHAS LEN PA LA MI RIGS PA MED KYANG, DON DAM PA DANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA KHAS LEN PA LA ‘GAL BA YIN TE, SNGA MA LA NI RGYU ‘BRAS KYI SKYE ‘GAG GI BYA BA [f. 105a] GNYIS DUS MNYAM YANG, RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS DUS MNYAM MI DGOS LA, PHYI MA LA NI BYA BA DUS MNYAM NA RGYU ‘BRAS KYANG DUS MNYAM DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

The point being made here is that there is nothing at all wrong with accepting the idea of growing per se; or the idea of something growing in a nominal manner.  It would though be a contradiction to agree to the idea of growing that could occur in an ultimate way, or by definition.  In the former case, the two actions of the growing & stopping of the cause and the result would be simultaneous; nonetheless, this doesn’t have to imply that the cause and the result themselves are simultaneous.  In the latter case, cause & results would have to be simultaneous, if the actions involved were themselves simultaneous.


[1382]
‘DI LTAR ‘BRAS BU SKYE BA’I BYA BA NI ‘DI SKYE ZHES PA’I BYED PA PO MYU GU SOGS LA BRTEN DGOS PAS RTEN DANG BRTEN PA’O,,

When we talk here about a basis and something relying upon this basis, what we’re saying is that the result—the action of growing (“this growing”)—is something that must depend upon an agent doing the growing: such as the sprout.


[1383]
RTEN BRTEN PA DON DAM PAR GRUB NA NI RANG BZHIN GZHAN DU ‘GYUR BA MI ‘THAD PAS, DUS NAM GYI TSE YANG BYA BA RTEN DGOS PAS MYU GU SOGS SKYE BA LA PHYOGS PA’I DUS SU YANG, SKYE BA’I BYA BA’I RTEN DU MYU GU YOD DGOS PAS RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS DUS MNYAM DU ‘GYUR BA SOGS KYIS GNOD PAS MI ‘THAD DO,,

If the basis and what rests upon this basis existed in an ultimate way, then it would be incorrect to say that they possessed a nature which was different from each other.  Therefore, at the point in time when the action had to rely upon its own basis, then even at the juncture where the sprout or such was approaching its growth, there would have to be a sprout there to act as the basis which supported the action of growing.  This model would be drawn into question by a situation where, for example, the cause and its result were thus simultaneous; as such, it would have to be incorrect.


[1384]
THA SNYAD PA’I SKYE BA LA LAN CIG RTEN BRTEN PAR SONG NA DUS THAMS CAD DU ‘GRO MI DGOS PAS MI MTSUNGS SO,,

In a case where the growing was going on in a nominal manner, it would not have to hold that—if things in a single instance shared a relationship where one was a basis and the other was something resting upon that basis—this relationship would have to continue on in every possible other time.


[1385]
SA BON DANG DUS MNYAM PA’I MYU GU SKYE BA’I BYA BA NI, MYU GU SKYE BA LA PHYOGS PA’I BYA BA YIN LA, DE DANG MYU GU GNYIS SPYIR RTEN BRTEN PA YIN PA DANG, BYA BA DE’I DUS SU MYU GU MED KYANG BYA BA YOD PA MI ‘GAL BA NI,

When we say that the action of a sprout growing is simultaneous to the seed, we are talking about an action where the sprout is approaching growing.  It is no contradiction to say at this point that the two of this action and the sprout itself are, generally, acting as a basis & what rests upon this basis; while at the same time the action does exist, even though no sprout exists in the moment of this action.  And here’s why.


[1386]
DPER NA SPYIR ‘BREL YUL KHEGS NA ‘BREL PO LDOG PA DANG, SA BON ‘BREL YUL DANG MYU GU ‘BREL PO YIN PA DANG, MYU GU’I DUS NA SA BON LOG KYANG MYU GU MI LDOG PA MI ‘GAL BA BZHIN NO,,

It is for example no contradiction to say that if you cancel the thing that another thing shares a relationship with, then the thing that has the relationship is also stopped; and that here the seed is what the relationship is had with, while the sprout is what has the relationship; and that even if you stop the seed, in the time of the sprout, that the sprout need not be stopped.


[1387]
DE ‘DRA BA’I TSUL GYIS RIGS PAS PHAR LA BKAG PA DANG, BKAG PA’I RIGS PA RANG LA MI LDOG PA LEGS PAR SHES NAS DBU MA’I LUGS SKYON MED ‘JOG SHES NA DBU MA PA YIN GYI,

You need to have a good understanding of how to employ this method of using logic to disprove another’s position, even as you avoid having the logic you used to do the disproving being used against your own position afterwards.  That is, if you know how to set forth the position of the middle way without making any mistakes, you are a true member of the Middle Way school.


[1388]
‘GOG PA’I TSE LTAR SNANG ‘BA’ ZHIG SMRAS NAS, DE NYID TSUR LA BZLOG [f. 105b] PA’I TSE BSNYON ‘DINGS PA LA RE NA, KHO BO CAG SMYON PA DANG LHAN CIG TU MI RTZOD DO, ZHES TSIG GSAL LAS GSUNGS PA LTAR BYA’O,,

If rather you put your hopes in people who are deranged—who attempt to disprove the ideas of others but who, at the same time, employ only arguments which can be turned back upon their own positions—then all we can do is repeat the words of the Clarification of the Verses: “For our part, we refuse to debate with those who have lost their sanity.”



Simultaneous others
could never grow

GNYIS PA NI,

[1389]
This brings us to the second point in our more particular denial that things could grow from something other than themselves.  This is where we deny that things could grow from something other than themselves, in a case where cause & effect were simultaneous.


	[1390]
	[VI.20]
Cakṣur dhiyaḥ svajanakaiḥ khalu cakṣur ādyaiḥ
saṃjñādibhiś ca sahabhāvibhir ekakālaiḥ,
Anyatvam asti yadi kiṃ bhavanena satyāṃ
nāsyāḥ satītvam atha ced vihito’tra doṣaḥ.

,GAL TE MIG GI BLO LA RANG GI SKYE BYED
DUS GCIG PA,
,MIG LA SOGS DANG LHAN CIG ‘BYUNG BA ‘DU SHES
LA SOGS LAS,
,GZHAN NYID YOD NA YOD LA ‘BYUNG BAS DGOS PA
CI ZHIG YOD,
,CI STE DE MED CE NA ‘DI LA NYES PA BSHAD ZIN TO,

Suppose the eye and such
Which are what produce
And are simultaneous to
The awareness of the eye;

As well as the discrimination
And the like which occur
In conjunction,

Are—relative to it—
Perfectly other.

What purpose
Could possibly be served
By the occurrence of something
That already existed?

Suppose you say
That there is none;
We have already described
The problem with that case.				


[1391]
‘DIR SMRAS PA SA MYUG DUS MNYAM PA MED PAS, NGO BO NYID KYIS GZHAN NYID MED PA’I PHYIR GZHAN LAS SKYE BA MI RIGS NA,

Some people come and present something like this:

You’ve shown how it’s wrong to say that things grow from other things, because there is no such thing as things that are completely other than each other, through some essential nature of their own—which itself is true because there is no such thing as a seed & a sprout which are simultaneous.


[1392]
RGYU ‘BRAS DUS MNYAM PA YOD PA DER GZHAN NYID YOD PAS GZHAN SKYE YOD DE, DPER NA MIG GI RNAM SHES DANG DE DANG DUS MNYAM PA’I TSOR BA LA SOGS PA RNAMS LTA BU’O,,

But let’s take a situation where there is a simultaneity between the cause & the result; in this case, there can exist a complete difference between the two, and then there can be the growth of something from something other than itself.  We can take, for example, where feelings or the like are simultaneous to our visual awareness.


[1393]
MIG DANG GZUGS SOGS DANG TSOR BA SOGS LHAN CIG ‘BYUNG BA RNAMS DUS MNYAM PA KHO NAR MIG GI RNAM SHES SKYED PA DE BZHIN DU, MIG SOGS DANG SEMS KYANG DUS MNYAM KHO NAR TSOR BA LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYI RKYEN YIN NO ZHES KHA CIG SMRA’O,,

Only in a case where the organ of the eye; and a visible object, or the like; and feelings and such occur altogether—only in a case where they are simultaneous—can visual awareness then grow.  Just so, it is only in a case where the eye and so forth, and the main mind, are as well simultaneous that they can serve as conditions for feelings & the like.


[1394]
GAL TE MIG GI BLO STE RNAM SHES LA RANG GI SKYED BYED RANG DANG DUS GCIG PA MIG LA SOGS PA DANG, DE DAG DANG LHAN CIG ‘BYUNG BA’I ‘DU SHES LA SOGS PA RNAMS RKYEN NYID DU RTOG NA, DE’I TSE ‘DU SHES SOGS LA BLTOS NAS GZHAN NYID YOD DU CHUG KYANG,

Suppose then that we do imagine that the eye and such which are what produce and which are simultaneous to the “awareness of the eye”—meaning the visual consciousness; as well as the capacity of discrimination and the like which occur in conjunction with this eye and so forth; are actually its conditions.  And suppose as well that we allow, at this point in time, that this consciousness exists—relative to the discrimination and so on—as something perfectly other.


[1395]
RGYU DUS NAS YOD PA LA SLAR YANG ‘BYUNG BAS DGOS PA CI ZHIG YOD DE CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PAS SKYE BA MED DO,,

What purpose though could possibly be served by the repeated occurrence of something that already existed in the time of the cause?  There is not the slightest point to it; as such, it doesn’t grow!


[1396]
CI STE SKYE BA MED PA’I SKYON SPANG BAR ‘DOD NAS RGYU DUS SU ‘BRAS BU DE MED DO ZHE NA, DE’I TSE SNGA PHYI BA ‘DI LA NGO BOS GRUB PA’I GZHAN MED PA’I NYES PA SNGAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,

Suppose then that the other party, hoping to avoid this problem that the awareness wouldn’t grow, says that there is no result in the time of the cause.  In that case there would come the problem that we already described earlier—with the case of a cause & result which were sequential—where there were no things that were other than each other, in a way where they existed through some essence of their own.


[1397]
DE LTAR NA RIGS PA ‘DIS NI RGYU ‘BRAS SU ‘DOD PA LA GZHAN NYID YOD KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MI SRID LA, DE’I PHYIR GZHAN LAS SKYE BA MI SRID PAR STON ZHING, RIGS PA SNGA MAS NI RGYU ‘BRAS LA SKYE BA SRID KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GZHAN YIN [f. 106a] PA MI SRID LA, DE’I PHYIR GZHAN SKYE MI SRID PAR STON TO,,

As such, what this reasoning is indicating is that you can accept cause & effect, and that there is such a thing where these are completely separate from one another, and yet still it is impossible for things to grow through some nature of their own—and so it is impossible for things to grow from something other than themselves.  The previous reasoning is indicating that—although it is possible for things to grow with cause & effect—it is impossible for these to be other than each other in a way that exists through some nature of its own; and that for this reason it is impossible for a thing to grow from something other than itself.


[1398]
DES NA GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YOD CES PA NI BRJOD BYA’I DON GYIS STONG PAS SONG SONG NAS, DE LTAR BRJOD PA’I SGRA ‘BA’ ZHIG LHAG MAR LUS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And so you can keep on repeating that there is such a thing as things growing from something other than themselves; but what you’re describing is devoid of any meaning at all—and thus what you’re saying is just another piece of sound in the world, and nothing more.



None of four possibilities

[1399]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third point from above: A denial that things could grow from something other than themselves accomplished by examining four possible permutations.


	[1400]
[VI.21]
Janyaṃ paraṃ ca janayej janakaḥ sa hetuḥ
sad vātha cāsad ubhayaṃ vigata dvayaṃ vā,
Sac cet kim asya janakair asato’pi kiṃ tair
dvaite’pi taiḥ kim atha kiṃ vigata dvaye taiḥ.

,SKYED PAR ‘BYED PA BSKYED BYA GZHAN SKYED PA DE
RGYU YIN NA,
,YOD PA’AM ‘ON TE MED DANG GNYI GA GNYIS BRAL
ZHIG SKYED GRANG,
,YOD NA SKYED BYED CI DGOS MED LA’ANG DES NI
CI ZHIG BYA,
,GNYIS NYID LA DES CI BYA GNYIS DANG BRAL LA’ANG
DES CI BYA,

		Suppose something produces
		Something produced;
		And what it produces
		Is something other.

		Let’s calculate whether
		That exists; or else does not;
		Or both; or is devoid of either.

		Suppose it existed;
		Then what need would there be
		For what acted to produce it?

		And if on the other hand
		It did not exist,
		Then what would it do for it?

		If both, what would it do?
		And if it were devoid,
		What again could it do?


[1401]
SKYED PAR BYED PA BSKYED BYA RANG LAS GZHAN SKYED PA DE RGYU YIN NA, RGYU DES ‘BRAS BU RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA’AM, ‘ON TE MED PA DANG, YOD MED GNYIS KA DANG, YOD MED GNYIS KA DANG BRAL BA ZHIG SKYED GRANG STE BRTAG GO

Suppose you have something that produces another thing—something produced—and that what it produces is something other than itself.  Let’s calculate, let’s examine, whether—when something is a cause like this—this cause produces a result which exists through some nature of its own; or else one which does not exist such; or one which both does & does exist thus; or one which is devoid of either existing or not existing, in this manner.


[1402]
,DE LA RE ZHIG ‘BRAS BU RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD NA DE LA SKYED BYED KYI RKYEN CI ZHIG DGOS TE MI DGOS TE, RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA SKYE NA SKYES ZIN SLAR YANG SKYE BAR ‘GYUR LA, DE YANG MI RIGS PAR BSTAN ZIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Suppose, in the first place, that the result here existed through some nature of its own; in that case, what need would there be for a condition that acted to produce it?  There would in fact be no such need; for if something grew which existed by nature, then something that had already grown would have to grow all over again—and we have already described how that would be illogical.


[1403]
‘BRAS BU MED PA LA’ANG RKYEN DES CI ZHIG BYA STE, BONG BU’I RVA LTAR MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And even if the result did not exist, then what would the condition ever do for it?  For it would not exist—it would be like rabbit antlers.


[1404]
YOD MED GNYIS KA TSOGS PA NYID LA RKYEN DES CI ZHIG BYA STE, DE GNYIS TSOGS PA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And suppose the result were a combination of both something that existed, and something that didn’t exist.  What would the condition ever do for it then?  After all, something which combined both would already be an impossibility.


[1405]
YOD MED GNYIS KA DANG BRAL BA DE LA’ANG RKYEN DES CI ZHIG BYA STE, DE GNYIS GANG YANG MIN PA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And what, finally, could a condition do for a result that was devoid of both existence & non-existence?  For a thing which was neither of these would as well be an impossibility.



What the world sees is proof

[1406]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, ‘JIG RTEN GYI GRAGS PAS GZHAN SKYE KHAS BLANGS NAS ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA SPANG BA, ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD DU YANG GZHAN SKYE MED PAS ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA SPANG BA’O,,

We’ve reached now our second topic from above: overcoming objections which say that the denial that things could grow from something other than themselves in any way contradicts the beliefs of the everyday world.  We cover this in two steps: overcoming objections relating to the everyday world which say that—in the conventions of the world—the idea that things grow from something other than themselves is accepted; and then overcoming such objections which say that there is no growth of things from something other than themselves, even in the parlance of the world.


[1407]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PA’I RTZOD PA DANG, DES MI GNOD PA’I LAN BSTAN PA’O,,

The first of these steps has two parts of its own: arguments which present how we’ve contradicted the beliefs of the everyday world; and the presentation of a reply to these arguments, which shows how we have not in fact contradicted these beliefs.


	[1408]
[VI.22]
Yuktyā kim atra khalu varṇitayā kriyeta
lokaḥ sthitaḥ svadṛśi yena mataḥ pramāṇam,
Lokaś ca nāma parataḥ parabhāvam eti
tenāsti janma parataḥ kim ihopapattyā.

,GANG GIS RANG LTA LA GNAS ‘JIG RTEN TSAD MAR
‘DOD PAS NA,
,’DIR NI RIGS PA SMRAS PA NYID KYIS LTA KO
CI ZHIG BYA,
,GZHAN LAS GZHAN ‘BYUNG BA YANG ‘JIG RTEN PA YIS
RTOGS ‘GYUR TE,
,DES NA GZHAN LAS SKYE YOD ‘DIR NI RIGS PA
CI ZHIG DGOS,

		Those who remain
		With their own viewpoints
		Consider the world accurate;

		What could possibly be here
		The use of articulating
The point with this logic?

		What people of the world
		Perceive is that things issue
		From things which are
Other than them.

What purpose would
The logic for this be—
For the fact that things do grow
From things that are other?


[1409]
DANG PO NI, GAL TE GZHAN SKYE GRUB PA’I PHYIR DU RIGS PA GANG SMRAS PA DE NI, BUD SHING SKAM PO MAR GYIS BRAN PA LTAR KHYOD KYI BLO GROS KYI MES MA LUS PAR [f. 106b] BSREGS PAS, KHYOD KYI SHES RAB KYI ME SBOR BA’I RIGS PA’I BUD SHING BSKUL BA DES CHOG GI DA DE BSKUL MI DGOS SO,,

Here is the first.  The other party may come and make the following statement:

Any argument that someone could present to prove the idea that things grow from something other than themselves is like pouring ghee on dry wood: the flames of your intellect consume everything.  It’s enough that you have the fuel of the firewood of clear thinking, to feed the fire of wisdom; we need no further fuel than that.


[1410]
‘O NA RIGS PA MA BSTAN PAR GZHAN SKYE ‘DOD PA’I DON MI ‘GRUB PA MA YIN NAM ZHE NA,

And you may ask us: “But if you cannot present any logic to help, how are you going to prove this idea—the belief you have that things could grow from something other than themselves?”


[1411]
DE NI MA YIN TE GANG ZHIG ‘JIG RTEN LAS GRUB PA DER NI, RIGS PA GZHAN GYIS CI YANG BYA BA MED DE, ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA NI SHIN TU STOBS DANG LDAN PA’I PHYIR RO ZHES BSHAD PA,

The fact is that no such logic is needed.  Once something has been established in the everyday world, there’s nothing else to be achieved throught the use of further reasoning.  And that’s because what the world sees with its own eyes has overwhelming authority.

And so the purpose of the lines that come next in the root text is to express this sentiment.  


[1412]
GANG GIS ‘JIG RTEN PA THAMS CAD RANG GI LTA BA KHO NA LA GNAS NAS, ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA TSAD MAR ‘DOD PAS NA SHIN TU STOBS DANG LDAN ZHING, NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I RGYU GZHAN LAS ‘BRAS BU GZHAN ‘BYUNG BA YANG ‘JIG RTEN PA RNAMS KYIS MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR TE,

Suppose then that someone comes & says,

Those—meaning all the people of the everyday world—who remain only with their own viewpoints consider what the world sees as accurate perception; that is, this is what they consider authoritative.  And what people of the world perceive, directly, is that results issue from causes which are other than them, and which exist in & of themselves.


[1413]
RIGS PA’I ‘THAD PA YANG NYE BAR ‘GOD PA NA, MNGON SUM DU GYUR MA GYUR GNYIS LAS GNYIS PA LA ‘GOD PA YIN LA, DANG PO NI, MNGON SUM TSAD MAS GRUB PA’I PHYIR DE LA ‘THAD PA ‘GOD PA MA YIN NO,,

When a person presents a justification utilizing logic, this could either be done in a case where direct perception is involved, or where it is not.  In the first of these two choices, things have already been established by virtue of a direct form of accurate perception; as such, we do not in this case present logical justifications.


[1414]
DE’I PHYIR GZHAN SKYE YOD PA ‘DIR NI, DE YOD PAR SGRUB PA’I RIGS PA GZHAN SMRAS PA NYID KYIS LTA KO CI ZHIG BYA,

Given that—here in this exercise of establishing the existence of things growing from things that are other than themselves—what could possibly be the use of  articulating the point with this additional logic for its existence?


[1415]
DES NA GZHAN SKYE’I SGRUB BYED KYI ‘THAD PA GZHAN MED PAR YANG, DNGOS PO RNAMS GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ‘GRUB PAS, GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YOD PA ‘DIR NI RIGS PA GZHAN BSTAN PAS DGOS PA CI ZHIG YOD DE MED DE, MNGON SUM GYIS GRUB PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

As such—even though there is no other justification used to establish, logically, the fact that things grow from things other than themselves—we nonetheless establish that entitites do, indeed, grow from other entities.  What purpose then would be served by presenting any further logic for this—for the fact that things do grow from things other than themselves?  There would be no such purpose, for this fact is established by our own direct perception.



Contradicting what the world says—or not

[1416]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to the second part from above: a reply to these arguments, meant to show that we have not in fact contradicted the beliefs of the world.


[1417]
GANG ZHIG GSUNG RAB KYI DON PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR MA RTOGS SHING, ‘KHOR BA THOG MA MED PA NAS DNGOS PO BDEN ‘DZIN GYI BAG CHAGS [f. 107a] BZHAG PA SMIN PA LAS BYUNG BA’I DNGOS PO LA BDEN PAR MNGON PAR ZHEN PA YUN RING MO NAS ‘DRIS PA’I MDZA’ BO DANG BRAL BA STE,

And so there are those who have yet to grasp the meaning of the highest of all words in an unerring way; in their hearts, the deep seeds for believing that things are real have been sown, for time with no beginning, here in the cycle of pain.  These seeds have ripened, and produced a craving for believing that things are real—and these people must learn to leave behind this friend, who has been so close to them, for so very long.


[1418]
‘BRAL BAR BYED PA’I THABS RANG BZHIN MED PA’I TSUL YANG DANG YANG DU THOS PA DANG BRAL BA, ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA’I RDOL THABS TE BLA BRDOL LA BRTEN PA ‘DI NI, ‘JIG RTEN GYI BYUNG TSUL MANG PO CIG MA BSHAD PAR ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA’I BLA BRDOL LAS BZLOG PAR MI NUS PAS, 

The way to leave the friend behind is to hear teaching, again & again, on how things have no nature of their own—but these friends have had no such teaching.  And now they babble about what contradicts what the world sees; they are delivering themselves to meaningless chatter.  In so doing, they will never be able to battle the blather that truly hurts the world—they are missing the many details of what really brought this world of pain into being.


[1419]
YUL ‘DI ‘DRA BA ZHIG LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD DO ZHES DE’I GNOD YUL KHYAD PAR CAN DANG, YUL ‘DI ‘DRA BA LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS MI GNOD DO ZHES MI GNOD PA’I YUL KHYAD PAR CAN BSTAN DGOS SO,,

And so what we need to do, here & now, is to identify for them that specific part of the world they are contradicting when we say “the world contradicts this particular aspect”; and the specific part of the world they are not contradicting, when we say “the world does not contradict this aspect.”


[1420]
DE LA BDEN PA GNYIS KYI RNAM DBYE BSTAN PA SNGON DU ‘GRO BA DGOS PA LA LNGA, BDEN PA GNYIS KYI SPYI’I RNAM GZHAG, SKABS KYI DON LA SBYAR BA, BDEN GNYIS SO SO’I NGO BO BSHAD PA, BKAG PA LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PA LA GNOD BYED BSTAN PA, ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PA’I GNOD TSUL BSTAN PA’O,,

To accomplish this, we must first give a presentation of a certain division of things—into two kinds of reality.  We’ll make this presentation in five steps:

 A general presentation of the two realities
 How to apply this presentation to the present topic
 A separate explanation of the nature of each of the two realities
 A demonstration that there are contradictions in the idea that 
	our denial of growth from something other is contradicted
	by the perceptions of the world
 A presentation on the way in which the perceptions of the world
	would in fact be contradicted.


[1421]
DANG PO LA BZHI, BDEN GNYIS SU DBYE BAS CHOS RNAMS LA NGO BO GNYIS GNYIS YOD PAR BRJOD PA, BDEN GNYIS KYI RNAM BZHAG GZHAN BSTAN PA, ‘JIG RTEN LA BLTOS TE KUN RDZOB KYI DBYE BA BSHAD PA, ZHEN YUL LA ‘KHRUL BA’I ZHEN YUL THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

The first of these has four parts of its own:

	 A statement about how all objects each possess two different
		natures, given the division into two realities
	 A description of other ways in which the two realities
		are set forth
	 An explanation of the divisions of deceptive reality,
		relative to the everyday world
	 Demonstrating that—when we are mistaken towards the
		object we think we see—this object that we believe in
		does not even exist nominally.



The two natures
of every existing thing

[1422]
DANG PO NI,

We begin with the way in which objects have two natures.


	[1423]
[VI.23]
Samyag mṛṣā darśana labdha bhāvaṃ
rūpa dvayaṃ bibhrati sarva bhāvāḥ,
Samyag dṛśāṃ yo viṣayaḥ sa tattvaṃ
mṛṣā dṛśāṃ saṃvṛti satyam uktam.

,DNGOS KUN YANG DAG BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA YIS,
,DNGOS RNYED NGO BO GNYIS NI ‘DZIN PAR ‘GYUR,
,YANG DAG MTHONG YUL GANG DE DE NYID DE,
,MTHONG BA BRDZUN PA KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR GSUNGS,

All objects involve
Two different natures:
Objects discovered
By seeing what is pure
And what is a lie.

It was declared that the one
Which serves as the object
When we see the pure
Is suchness;

And that seen to be a lie
Is deceptive reality.


[1424]
‘DI NA BDEN GNYIS KYI RANG GI NGO BO PHYIN CI MA LOG PA MKHYEN PA’I BCOM LDAN ‘DAS RNAMS KYIS ‘DU BYED SEMS PA SOGS NANG DANG MYU [f. 107b] GU SOGS PHYI ROL GYI DNGOS PO KUN TE THAMS CAD KYI RANG GI NGO BO RNAM PA GNYIS NI ‘DZIN PAR ‘GYUR BAR NYE BAR BSTEN TE, DE GANG ZHE NA, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA’I NGO BO DANG DON DAM BDEN PA’I NGO BO’O,,

For this, let us consider the Conqueror, who possesses high & unerring knowledge of the nature of each of the two realities.  He imparts to us the understanding of how all objects—each & every one of them—involve two different types of natures of their own, whether they are inner entitites such as the thought to apply an antidote; or outer entitites such as a sprout.  What are these two natures?  One nature belongs to deceptive reality; and the other belongs to ultimate reality.


[1425]
‘DIS NI MYU GU LTA BU GCIG GI NGO BO LA YANG PHYE NA KUN RDZOB YIN PA DANG, DON DAM PA’I NGO BO GNYIS YOD PAR STON GYI MYU GU’I NGO BO GCIG NYID SO SKYE DANG ‘PHAGS PA LA BLTOS NAS BDEN PA GNYIS SU BSTAN PA GTAN MIN NO,,

The point we are making here is that—if we take a single object such as a sprout, and make a division of its essential nature—then we would find that it possesses a nature both of being a deceptive object, and of having an ultimate side.  What we are absolutely not saying here though is that a single nature of a sprout possesses two realities, relative to common beings & realized beings.


[1426]
DE LTAR BYAS NA NGO BO MED PA’I CHOS MI SRID PAS, GZHI GRUB PA YIN NA NGO BO GCIG DANG THA DAD LAS MI ‘DA’ LA, NGO BO YOD PA KHAS LEN KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I NGO BO MED PA MI ‘GAL LO,,

Given all this, then—since an existing entity without any essential nature at all is an impossibility—we can say that once a thing exists, it possesses either one single essential nature, or else some separate natures: there is no other possibility.  At the same time, it is no contradiction to say that an object possesses an essential nature, but lacks any essential nature which exists through some nature of its own.


[1427]
DE LA MYU GU LA SOGS PA’I DNGOS PO’I NGO BO DON DAM PA NI, YANG DAG PA’I DON MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA RNAMS KYI YE SHES KYI KHYAD PAR GYI YUL NYID KYIS BDAG GI RANG GI NGO BO RNYED PA YIN GYI, RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI MA YIN TE, ‘DI NI NGO BO GNYIS BSHAD PA’I GCIG YIN NO,,

Let’s look at the ultimate nature possessed by objects such as a sprout.  This is an essential nature of these objects which is discovered by the exceptional wisdom of those who see, directly, pure reality: and it is discovered through a self-nature of this one object.  Even given that, this ultimate nature though is not something which exists in & of itself.  This then is one of the two natures we’ve alluded to.


[1428]
YE SHES KYI KHYAD PAR ZHES PA NI ‘PHAGS PA’I YE SHES GANG YIN GYIS RNYED PA MIN PAR YE SHES KYI KHYAD PAR TE BYE BRAG PA ZHIG LA BYED DE, DE YANG JI LTA BA ‘JAL BA’I YE SHES KYIS RNYED PA’O,,

When we speak here of an “exceptional” or particular form of wisdom, what we’re saying is that this nature is something which is discovered by the wisdom which is one that belongs to a realized being; that is to say, we are referring to a particular type or genre of wisdom in general.  We can also say that this nature is “discovered by the wisdom which takes the way things really are under consideration.”


[1429]
YE SHES DES RNYED PA’AM GRUB PAR BSTAN PA NA DES GRUB RGYU ZHIG BYUNG NA BDEN GRUB BO ZHES ‘DZIN PA DGAG PA’I PHYIR, RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PAS

When we say that this nature is “discovered” or established by this wisdom, we say in the same breath that it is not something which exists in & of itself; this is to prevent the idea that—if there is some way of establishing it—then this nature should exist in truth.


[1430]
‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG GI YE SHES KYIS DON DAM BDEN PA GZHAL NA, BDEN GRUB TU ‘GYUR BAS DE SHES BYA MA YIN PA SLOB [f. 108a] DPON ‘DI’I LUGS SU SMRA BA NI,

Some people say that—if a realized being in a meditation on emptiness is able to bring ultimate reality under their consideration—then this reality would then have to exist truly; and that therefore it is not something which can ever be known.  They say that this is the position being taken by the master here.


[1431]
LUGS ‘DIS MNYAM GZHAG GIS RNYED KYANG BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR BSHAD PA’I DON YE MA RTOGS BZHIN DU MKHAS PA’I LUGS NYAMS SU ‘JUG PA’O,,

People who describe it this way have failed, totally, to realize the point of the explanation that something can be discovered by this particular meditation and yet still not exist in truth; and in the midst of this failure, they are actually undermining the ways of the wise.


[1432]
DON DAM LAS GZHAN KUN RDZOB PA’I NGO BO NI, SO SO SKYE BO MA RIG PA’I RAB RIB KYI LING TOG GIS BLO’I MIG MA LUS PAR KHEBS PA RNAMS KYIS BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA’I STOBS LAS, BDAG GI NGO BO YOD PA RNYED PA YIN TE,

What then is the essential nature of that which is other than the ultimate—what is it for something to be deceptive?  Let’s look at common beings: people whose eyes—whose minds—are entirely wrapped within a coating of cataracts.  When they perceive something which is a lie, the power of this perception makes them “discover” that things have some essential nature of their very own.


[1433]
BYIS PA RNAMS KYI MTHONG BA’I YUL DU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA DE BZHIN DU RANG GI NGO BO YOD PA NI MIN TE NGO BO GNYIS KYI GCIG YIN NO,,

And so this is another one of the two natures we’ve been talking about: as an object being perceived by those who are still infants, it appears to exist by definition; and yet at the very same moment, it is anything but something which could possess some essential nature of its own.


[1434]
DE LTAR DON DAM BDEN PA RNYED PA LA RNYED MKHAN ‘PHAGS PAR GSUNGS PA NI GTZO BO YIN PA LA DGONGS KYIS, SO SO SKYE BO DBU MA’I LTA BA RGYUD LDAN GYIS KYANG MI RNYED PAR BZHED PA MIN NO,,

And so where the scriptures say that “when someone discovers ultimate reality, the person doing the discovery is a realized being,” the statement is meant only to describe the main discoverer—therefore this statement is not expressing a position which says that ultimate reality is not discovered by a normal person who possesses an understanding of the view of the middle way.


[1435]
KUN RDZOB RNYED PA LA RNYED MKHAN SO SKYE RANG DGA’ BA LA GSUNGS PA YANG, KUN RDZOB PA’I MTSAN GZHI PHYI NANG GI DNGOS PO RNAMS MA RIG PA’I GZHAN DBANG GIS MTHONG BA’I GTZO BO LA DGONGS KYI, ‘PHAGS PA’I RGYUD KYI THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS DNGOS PO DE RNAMS MI RNYED PAR BZHED PA MIN NO,,

As far as people who “discover” the deceptive, the discoverer here has been described in scripture as any average, normal person.  This statement though is meant to refer to primary act of observing typical examples of deceptive reality—inner & outer entities—under the thrall of misunderstanding.  It, in turn, is not expressing some position where we say that nominal types of accurate perception in the mind of a realized being never discover such entitites.


[1436]
KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA’I MTSAN GZHI BUM PA LA SOGS PA RNYED PA DBU MA’I LTA BA MA RNYED PA LA YANG YOD MOD KYANG, GZHI DE KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA YIN PAR TSAD MAS RNYED PA LA NI, SNGON DU DBU MA’I LTA BA RNYED PA CIG NGES PAR DGOS TE, 

It is admittedly the case that—with reference to discovering typical examples of deceptive reality, water pitchers & the like—the discovery can also be made by those who have yet to discover the viewpoint of the middle way.  Nonetheless, if we’re talking about discovering, with an accurate perception, that any particular object belongs to deceptive reality, a person must certainly have, previously, discovered the viewpoint of the middle way.


[1437]
GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR GRUB NA BRDZUN PAR ‘GRUB DGOS SHING, BRDZUN PAR DNGOS SU ‘GRUB PA LA GZHI DE [f. 108b] LA SNGON DU BDEN GRUB TSAD MAS KHEGS DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Establishing that any particular object belongs to deceptive reality requires that it be established as something which is a lie; and to establish, directly, that something is a lie requires having denied—earlier, and through the use of an accurate perception—that it exists in truth.


[1438]
DES NA BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA’I STOBS LAS ZHES PA NI, GANG ZAG RANG DGA’ BA DE RNAMS KYIS BRDZUN PA MTHONG YANG DE DAG GIS BRDZUN PAR ‘GRUB MI DGOS TE,

And so in the expression above about the power of perceiving that something is deceptive making something else happen, it’s not necessarily the case that—when some average person perceives something which is deceptive—they thereby establish that it is deceptive.


[1439]
DPER NA SGYU MA’I LTAD MO BAS SGYU MA’I RTA GLANG MTHONG BA NA BRDZUN PAR MTHONG YANG, SNANG BA DE BRDZUN PAR ‘GRUB MI DGOS PA BZHIN NO,,

A person watching a magic show, for example, can see an illusory horse or elephant, and are thus seeing something deceptive; but that doesn’t necessarily mean that they thereby establish that what appears to them is deceptive.


[1440]
DES NA KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR ‘JOG BYED BRDZUN PA MTHONG BAS RNYED PA’I DON NI, SHES BYA BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I DON ‘JAL BA’I THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS RNYED PA’O,,

As such, when we refer to a perception of deception which allows us to establish that a particular object belongs to deceptive reality, the meaning of the word “discover” here is that we have utilized a nominal form of accurate perception to bring under consideration the misleading nature of an entity which is deceptive.


[1441]
SNGAR BSHAD PA’I RANG BZHIN NAM NGO BO DE GNYIS LAS KYANG, YANG DAG PA’I DON MTHONG BA STE ‘JAL BA’I RIGS SHES KYIS RNYED PA’I YUL GANG YIN PA DE NI, DE NYID DE DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA STE, ‘DI NI RAB RIB ZHES SOGS KYI SKABS SU BSHAD PAR BYA’O,,

Earlier on, we made reference to two different kinds of nature, or essence; there is one of them which serves as the object which is discovered by the exploration of the nature of things which takes under its consideration—which sees—pure reality.  This is the one which is suchness, or ultimate reality.  We’ll be covering this point when we reach the lines of the root text which include the phrase, “due to some cataracts.”


[1442]
SHES BYA BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS RNYED PA NI KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PAR STON PAS GSUNGS TE, DON DAM PA DANG KUN RDZOB RNYED PA’I GZHI GNYIS SO SOR GSUNGS KYI GCIG LA RNYED TSUL GNYIS BYUNG BA MIN NO,,

Existing entities which are seen to be a lie—which are discovered by a nominal form of accurate perception—are what the Teacher declared to be deceptive reality.  He described two separate bases or objects for discovering the ultimate & the deceptive; but it is not the case that there are two different ways of discovery for either one of the two realities individually.



Other presentations of the two realities

[1443]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second point from above: a description of other ways in which the two realities are set forth.


[1444]
BDEN PA GNYIS KYI DBYE GZHI LA ‘DOD TSUL MI ‘DRA BA MANG MOD KYANG, ‘DIR SHES BYA LA BYA STE YAB SRAS MJAL BA’I MDO BSLAB BTUS SU DRANGS PA LAS,

Now there are admittedly many positions we see taken with regard to what it is we are dividing when we divide out two realities.  Here though we are referring to all perceivable objects in the universe as the basis of this division.  As we read in The Sutra of the Meeting between the Father and his Son, as this is quoted in The Compendium—


[1445]
‘DI LTAR DE BZHIN GSHEGS PAS KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA GNYIS THUGS SU CHUD DE, SHES PAR BYA BA YANG KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA ‘DIR ZAD DE, DE YANG BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS STONG PA NYID DU RAB [f. 109a] TU GZIGS RAB TU MKHYEN, LEGS PAR MNGON DU BYAS PAS DE’I PHYIR THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA ZHES BYA’O, ZHES GSUNGS TE,

This is how the One Thus Gone knows these two—the deceptive & the ultimate—to be.  All the things in the universe which can be perceived are subsumed by two realities: the deceptive & the ultimate—and there are no other realities beyond these two.  And it is because the Conqueror sees, perfectly, emptiness; and because he knows it, perfectly; and because he has made it perfectly real, for himself, that he is called “The Omniscient One.”


[1446]
SHES PAR BYA BA YANG ZHES PAS SHES BYA DBYE GZHI DANG, ‘DIR ZAD DO ZHES PAS BDEN GNYIS SU GRANGS NGES PA DANG, BDEN PA GNYIS KA DE BZHIN GSHEGS PAS THUGS SU CHUD PA’I PHYIR THAMS CAD MKHYEN PAR BSTAN TO,,

When the selection says here “all the things in the universe which can be perceived,” this is a reference to the basis of the division here: what we are calling “all perceivable objects in the universe.”  Where it says “there are no other beyond these two,” the point is that there are precisely two types of reality: no less, and no more.  And the Buddha is informing us that someone is considered “omniscient” when they have grasped, perfectly, both of these truths.


[1447]
DES NA DON DAM BDEN PA SHES BYA MA YIN PA DANG, BLO GANG GIS KYANG MA RTOGS PA SPYOD ‘JUG GI DGONGS PAR ‘CHAD PA NI LOG PAR ‘CHAD PA’O,,

As such, it is a mistaken explanation when people say that the intention of A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life is to say that ultimate reality is not a perceivable object; or that this reality cannot be perceived by any state of mind at all.


[1448]
KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA DANG DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA GNYIS SU ‘BYED PA NI DBYE PA’I NGO BO’O,,

Given that perceivable things are what we are dividing, the very nature of the division then is into the two of deceptive reality, and ultimate reality.


[1449]
PHYE BA’I DON LA YANG MI ‘DRA BA DU MA ZHIG ‘DUG KYANG, ‘DIR NI GNYIS KA LA NGO BO YOD LA, DE LA NGO BO GCIG DANG THA DAD GANG YANG MIN PA MI SRID PA’I PHYIR DANG,

The exact nature of the divisions can also be described in many different ways, but the point here is that both divisions have a particular nature.  And the nature of these natures is that they are either such that to be one is to be the other, or not—there is no other possible choice.


[1450]
CHOS CAN RNAMS BDEN STONG LAS NGO BO THA DAD NA BDEN GRUB TU ‘GYUR PA’I PHYIR, NGO BO GCIG LA LDOG PA THA DAD PA BYAS PA DANG MI RTAG PA LTA BU STE, BYANG CHUB SEMS ‘GREL LAS, 

Now if certain given objects were such that to be them were not to be empty of any true nature, they would perforce have to exist in reality.  As such, we would have to say that the two realities share the same nature, but in different manifestations—they are, for example, like being a thing which is made, and being a changing thing.  As A Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment puts it,


	[1451]
,KUN RDZOB LAS NI THA DAD PAR,
,DE NYID DMIGS PA MA YIN TE,
,KUN RDZOB STONG PA NYID DU BSHAD,
,STONG NYID KHO NA KUN RDZOB YIN,
,MED NA MI ‘BYUNG NGES PA’I PHYIR,
,BYAS DANG MI RTAG DAG BZHIN NO,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

There is no such thing
As suchness divorced
From the deceptive.

The deceptive is explained
As emptiness itself,
And only emptiness
Can be the deceptive.

Given the certainty
That one cannot occur
In the absence of the other,

They are like the qualities
Of being made, and of changing.


[1452]
RKANG PA DANG PO BZHI’I DON NI KUN RDZOB LAS NGO BO THA DAD PAR DE KHO NA NYID YOD PA MIN TE, KUN RDZOB PA RNAMS BDEN PAS STONG PA YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, BDEN STONG NYID KYANG GZHI KUN RDZOB LA ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’O,,

The point of the first two thirds of this quotation is that there exists no thusness which is divorced from the deceptive—for what deceptive things are, are those things which are devoid of being true; while at the same time the truth of emptiness is established relative to a certain basis, which happens to be those things which are deceptive.


[1453]
DE NAS GNYIS [f. 109b] KYIS NI DE LTAR YIN DANG MED NA MI ‘BYUNG BA’I ‘BREL PA NGES LA, DE YANG BDAG GCIG PA’I ‘BREL PA YIN PAS BYAS MI RTAG BZHIN DU NGO BO GCIG PAR BSTAN NO,,
