The rest of the verse is to indicate that this is indeed the way things are, and that the relationship where one cannot occur without the other is absolutely certain; and since this is, further, a relationship where to be one is to be the other, then—like the qualities of being made, and of being a changing thing—they share a relationship of identity.


[1454]
PHYE BA SO SO’I NGOS ‘DZIN NI SNGAR TSAD MA GNYIS KYIS RNYED PA SO SO’I MTSAN NYID DU BSHAD PA BZHIN NO,,

The identification of the individual divisions is similar to where we said, before, that their individual definitions amount to those objects which are discovered by the two instances of an accurate perception.


[1455]
GAL TE ‘DI DANG SPYOD ‘JUG GNYIS MTHUN PAR ‘CHAD NA DE NYID LAS,
,KUN RDZOB DANG NI DON DAM STE,
,’DI NI BDEN PA GNYIS SU ‘DOD,
,DON DAM BLO YI SPYOD YUL MIN,
,BLO NI KUN RDZOB YIN PAR BRJOD,
CES GSUNGS PA ‘DI JI LTAR BSHAD PAR BYA ZHE NA,

One may counter with the following question:

You’ve mentioned that this explanation fits the one given in A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life; but how then do you explain the verse there which says—

The deceptive, and the ultimate;
These are the two kinds of reality
Which we accept.

The ultimate is not a place
Where the mind can ever go;
For the mind is described
As deceived.


[1456]
DE LA RKANG PA DANG PO GNYIS KYIS BDEN GNYIS KYI DBYE BA BSTAN LA, PHYE BA SO SO’I NGO BO NGOS ‘DZIN PA NA DON DAM BDEN PA’I NGOS ‘DZIN NI, DON DAM ZHES PA GCIG GIS DANG, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA’I NGOS ‘DZIN KUN RDZOB CES PA GCIG GIS STON NO,,

The first part of this verse is meant to present the division into two realities.  As for the identification of the two parts of the division, the one mention of “the ultimate” is meant to introduce ultimate reality; whereas the mention of “the deceptive” is to introduce deceptive reality.


[1457]
RKANG PA SNGA MAS DON DAM BDEN PA BLO’I YUL MIN PAR DAM BCAS PA RKANG PA PHYI MAS SGRUB PAR ‘DOD PA NI, GZHUNG DE DAG GI DON DU GTAN MI SNANG NGO,,

The belief that the first part of the verse presents an assertion that the ultimate could never be an object perceived by the mind; and that this assertion is somehow proven by the latter part of the verse, doesn’t in my opinion represent the point of these lines in any conceivable way at all.


[1458]
DES NA BDEN GNYIS KYI NGOS ‘DZIN ‘DI NI YAB SRAS MJAL BA BSLAB BTUS SU DRANGS PA LAS, DE LA KUN RDZOB NI ‘JIG RTEN GYI SPYOD PAR DE BZHIN GSHEGS PAS GZIGS SO, ,DON DAM PA GANG YIN PA DE NI BRJOD DU MED PA STE, SHES PAR BYA BA MA YIN, RNAM PAR SHES PAR BYA BA MA YIN PA, YONGS SU SHES PAR BYA BA MA YIN PA, MA BSTAN PA, ZHES SOGS GSUNGS PA’I DON SPYOD ‘JUG TU BKOD PA’O,,

Thus we can say that this identification of the two realities represents the point of citations such as the following—of The Meeting of the Father & the Son from The Compendium—inserted into the The Guide:

The One Thus Gone sees that deception represents the way of life of the world; whereas the ultimate is something beyond any description: it is not something you could ever know; no one could ever perceive it; none could grasp it, none could teach it.


[1459]
DE LA DON DAM BDEN PA SHES [f. 110a] PAR BYA BA MA YIN PAR BSHAD PA’I DON NI, ‘OG NAS BDEN PA GNYIS LA ‘JUG PA’I MDO DRANGS PA’I DON ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA LTAR DU BLO’I YUL DU MI ‘GYUR BA YIN NO,,


What does it mean here, when they say that ultimate reality is not something we could ever know?  The point is that—as we will see below, when we explain the import of a citation of the Sutra on Entering the Two Realities—it could never be the object of the mind.
	

[1460]
DE LTAR MI ‘JOG PAR BLO GANG GI YANG YUL MIN NA, RGYAL BAS KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA STONG NYID KYI RNAM PA CAN THAMS CAD MNGON DU GYUR PAS THAMS CAD MKHYEN PAR ‘JOG PAR BSHAD PA DANG ‘GAL TE, ‘OG TU YANG MANG DU ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

If it were not as we see it established there—and if ultimate reality then could never be the object of any state of mind at all—it would contradict the explanation that we establish the Victors as omniscient by virtue of the fact that, to them, both deceptive reality and all the forms of ultimate reality—the emptiness—that they display are objects perceived directly.


[1461]
KUN RDZOB BDEN PA’I NGOS ‘DZIN NI BLO RKYANG PA DER ‘JOG PA’I DON MIN GYI BLO’I YUL YIN LA, DE YANG ‘JIG RTEN GYI SPYOD PAR ZHES GSUNGS PAS, ‘JIG RTEN TE THA SNYAD PA’I SHES PA BRDZUN PA ‘JAL BA’I SPYOD PAR TE SPYOD YUL DU RNYED PA’I DON YIN PAS, BLO’I YUL KUN RDZOB PAR ‘DOD PA’I DON DE BZHIN DU BYA’O,,

As for the identification of deceptive reality, the point is not that we are talking about it being established to the one mind by itelf; rather, it is both the object of the mind and—given the mention of “the way of life of the world”—it is that thing which is discovered by the “worldly” state of mind, a reference to nominal perception: a state of mind which holds a lie under its consideration, as the object of its way of life.  As such, when we hold that an object of the mind is deceptive, this is how we should think of the point.


[1462]
SHES BYA LA BDEN PA GNYIS SU PHYE BA NI, SHES BYA LA DE GNYIS SU GRANGS NGES PAR STON PA YIN TE, ‘DI LA LUNG NI SNGAR DRANGS PA’I YAB SRAS MJAL BA DANG, ‘PHAGS PA DE KHO NA NYID NGES PAR BSTAN PA’I TING NGE ‘DZIN LAS KYANG,
,GANG ZHIG KUN RDZOB DE BZHIN DON DAM STE,
,BDEN PA GSUM PA GANG YANG MA MCHIS SO,
ZHES GSAL BAR GSUNGS SHING,

When we say that all perceivable things may be divided into two realities, what’s being indicated is that all things we can perceive are subsumed by these two realities—no more, and no less.  Scriptural support for this position is clearly expressed in the Sutra of the Meeting of the Father & the Son quoted above, and also in the Exalted Concentration which Reveals the Way of Suchness:

There is only the deceptive,
And just so the ultimate;

There is no third kind
Of reality at all.


[1463]
RANG ‘GREL LAS KYANG, DE BZHIN DU BDEN PA GZHAN GANG CUNG ZAD CIG YOD PA DE YANG CI RIGS PAR BDEN PA GNYIS KYI KHONGS SU GTOGS PA KHO NAR NGES PAR BYA’O,,

The autocommentary also states:

In the same way, it is an absolute certainty that the slightest bit of any other reality there may be can only be subsumed by these two realities, whichever it may be.


[1464]
ZHES SA BCU PA LAS BDEN PA’I MING CAN MANG DU GSUNGS PA THAMS CAD BDEN GNYIS SU [f. 110b] ‘DUS PAR GSUNGS SHING, DER BSHAD PA’I PHYE STE RTOGS PA’I BDEN PA NI PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED KYI RNAM PAR BZHAG PA LA BSHAD PA’I PHYIR NA, SLOB DPON ‘DIS KYANG BDEN PA GNYIS SU GRANGS NGES PAR BZHED DO,,

What this is saying is that the many references to reality in The Ten Levels are all included into the two realities.  And since he explains the “reality that is grasped by making divisions” which is described in that teaching to be a presentation of the heaps, categories, and gateways, this master is also taking the position that the truths number two—never more, never less.


[1465]
RIGS PA NI GZHI GANG ZHIG BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I DON DU YONGS SU BCAD NA, MI SLU BA’I DE KHO NA NYID YIN PA RNAM PAR GCAD DGOS PAS, SLU MI SLU NI PHAN TSUN SPANGS TE GNAS PA’I DNGOS ‘GAL LO,,

When we say that something is “reasonable,” what we’re saying is that we have a certain object, and that we have eliminated the possibility that it is in any way false, or misleading.  And for it to be false, we would have to eliminate any possibility that it was the way things are: that it was not misleading.  As such, the two qualities of being misleading or not to be misleading stand in mutual contradiction—where when something is one, it cannot be the other.


[1466]
DE YIN NA NI SHES BYA THAMS CAD LA KHYAB PAR BYED PAS GNYIS DANG GNYIS MA YIN GYI PHUNG GSUM SEL BA YIN TE DBU MA SNANG BA LAS, PHAN TSUN SPANGS TE GNAS PA’I MTSAN NYID KYI CHOS DAG NI, CIG SHES {%SHOS} DGAG PA GZHAN SGRUB PA MED NA MED PA YIN PA’I PHYIR, GNYIS KA MA YIN PA’I PHYOGS SU RTOG PA YANG RIGS PA MA YIN NO, ZHES DANG,

And if something is this way, then it subsumes all the perceivable things there are; being either the two, or not the two, eliminates any third possibility between them.  As Light on the Middle Way puts it,

When two things are characterized by existing in a mutually exclusive relationship, then there exists no case where—if you eliminate the one—you do not establish the other.  As such, it would further be illogical to imagine that there existed an option where something were neither.
 

[1467]
GANG ZHIG YONGS SU GCOD PA GANG RNAM PAR BCAD PA MED NA MED PA DE GNYIS NI, PHAN TSUN SPANGS TE GNAS PA’I MTSAN NYID YIN NO, ,GANG DAG PHAN TSUN SPANGS TE GNAS PA’I MTSAN NYID YIN PA DE DAG NI, RNAM PA THAMS CAD LA KHYAB PAR BYED PA DAG YIN NO,,

And it says:

What characterizes a relationship of mutual exclusion is a relationship where it cannot be the case that if you eliminate one possibility you have not eliminated the other.  And two things which exhibit this mutually exclusive relationship also subsume all possibilities.


[1468]
GANG DAG RNAM PA THAMS CAD LA KHYAB PAR BYED PA YIN PA DE DAG NI, PHUNG PO GZHAN SEL BAR BYED PA DAG YIN TE, DPER NA LUS CAN DANG LUS CAN MA YIN PA LA SOGS PA’I BYE BRAG LTA BU’O,

Further, any two things which are such that they subsume all possibilities further eliminate any additional possibility.  An example would be the feature of being something which does possess a physical body, and the feature of being something which does not.


[1469]
ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR TE, ‘DI NI DNGOS ‘GAL GZHAN THAMS CAD LA YANG SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Understand that these descriptions apply as well to every other instance of a relationship of mutual exclusion.


[1470]
PHUNG GSUM SEL BA’I DNGOS ‘GAL CIG [f. 111a] STON RGYU MED NA NI, YOD MED DAM GCIG DANG DU MA SOGS GANG ‘DOD CES MTHA’ GNYIS SU KHA TSON BCAD PA’I BRTAG PA BYAS NAS ‘GOG SA MED LA, YOD NA DNGOS ‘GAL GCIG ‘GOG PA NI CIG SHOS SGRUB PA MED NA MED PA YIN PAS, DBU MA THAL ‘GYUR BA LA DNGOS ‘GAL MED ZER BA NI, DGAG GZHAG GI RNAM GZHAG MA CHAGS PA’O,,

If we were unable to demonstrate this principle of mutual exclusion—where all third possibilities are eliminated—then we could never reach a place where we denied an idea by using an examination where we divided things into two opposing possibilities: existing or not existing; one or many; and so on.  And if we were able to show this exclusion, then there would be no possibility where if we denied one part of a direct of some mutual exclusion, we established its pair.  And if there were no such possibility, then the claim that those of the Consequence branch had no case of mutual exclusion here would represent a failure to follow the principles of denial or assertion.


[1471]
DNGOS ‘GAL GCIG RNAM PAR BCAD NA CIG SHOS YONGS SU GCOD PA DANG, GCIG ‘GOG NA CIG SHOS SGRUB DGOS PA LA DBU MA THAL RANG LA KHYAD PAR YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

If two things stand in direct contradiction to one another and eliminating one of the two possibilities eliminates the other; or if disproving one had to establish the other; then we would have to say that there was no distinction between the Consequence and Independent groups within the Middle Way school.



Deception within deception

[1472]
GSUM PA NI,

Next is the third part from above: an explanation of the divisions of deceptive reality, relative to the everyday world.

	[1473]
[VI.24]
Mṛṣā dṛśe’pi dvividhā matā hi
spaṣṭendriyā doṣavad indriyāś ca,
Sad indriya jñānam apekṣya mithyā
jñānaṃ mataṃ doṣa vad indriyāṇām.

,MTHONG BA BRDZUN PA’ANG RNAM PA GNYIS ‘DOD DE,
,DBANG PO GSAL DANG DBANG PO SKYON LDAN NO,
,SKYON LDAN DBANG CAN RNAMS KYI SHES PA NI,
,DBANG PO LEGS GYUR SHES LTOS LOG PAR ‘DOD,

We take the position
That those which see the lie
Are also of two types:

Where the powers are clear,
And where the powers
Are defective.

We take the position
That states of mind
Belonging to those
With powers
Possessing a defect,

Relative to states of mind
With powers which are sound,
Are mistaken.	


[1474]
KUN RDZOB LA YUL YUL CAN GNYIS LAS THOG MAR ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PA LA LTOS NAS YUL CAN LA YANG DAG PA DANG LOG PA GNYIS SU STON PA NI,

When the deceptive is described in terms of objects & subjects, what’s presented first among these two is the perceptions of the world—that is, relative to these perceptions, the subject state of mind is said to come in two forms: the correct, and the mistaken.


[1475]
SHES BYA LA BDEN PA GNYIS SU PHYE BAR MA ZAD BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA’I YUL CAN LA’ANG, YANG DAG PA DANG LOG PA GNYIS SU ‘DOD DE,

The point here is that—not only are all perceivable objects divided into two realities—but we take the position that the subject states of mind, those which see the lie, are also divided into two types: those which are correct, and those which are mistaken.


[1476]
DBANG PO GSAL BA STE ‘PHRAL GYI ‘KHRUL RGYUS MA BSLAD PA’I DBANG PO DANG, DE LA BRTEN PA’I SHES PA DANG, DBANG PO SKYON LDAN TE ‘PHRAL GYI ‘KHRUL RGYUS BSLAD PA’I YUL CAN GNYIS SO,,

These two consist of subject states of mind where the powers are “clear”—referring to powers which are not infected by any adventitious condition which would cause them to be mistaken, along with states of mind founded upon such powers; and then subject states of mind where the powers are defective: those which are infected by just such an adventitious condition.


[1477]
DE LA SKYON DANG LDAN PA’I DBANG PO CAN RNAMS KYI BSLAD PA’I SHES PA NI, DBANG PO LEGS PAR GYUR PA STE ‘PHRAL GYI ‘KHRUL RGYUS MA BSLAD PA’I SHES PA LA LTOS NAS, LOG PA’I SHES PAR ‘DOD CING, SNGA MA NI YUL PHYIN CI MA LOG PA ‘DZIN PAR ‘DOD DO,,

Let’s consider states of mind belonging to those with powers possessing a defect—that is, consider their state of mind, which is infected.  Relative to powers which are sound—that is, relative to states of mind which are not infected by some adventitious condition which would cause them to be mistaken, we take the position that these other states of mind are mistaken.  Our position further states that the former—the unaffected states of mind—are to be considered unmistaken.


[1478]
KHYAD PAR DE GNYIS KYANG DBU MA’I LUGS MIN GYI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PA [f. 111b] LA LTOS NAS YIN NO,,

These two distinctions are, moreover, made relative to a state of mind in the normal, everyday world; it is not some kind of distinction that depends upon the teachings of the middle way.


	[1479]
[VI.25]
Vinopaghātena yad indriyāṇāṃ
ṣaṇṇām api grāhyam avaiti lokaḥ,
Satyaṃ hi tal lokata eva śeṣaṃ
vikalpitaṃ lokata eva mithyā.

,GNOD PA MED PA’I DBANG PO DRUG RNAMS KYIS,
,GZUNG BA GANG ZHIG ‘JIG RTEN GYIS RTOGS TE,
,’JIG RTEN NYID LAS BDEN YIN LHAG MA NI,
,’JIG RTEN NYID LAS LOG PAR RNAM PAR BZHAG,

		Things which are held
		By the six senses where they

		Are not adversely affected
		Are those perceived
		By the everyday world;
 
		Relative to the world itself,
		These are real—the rest
		Are established as mistaken,
		Even just to the world [f. 205b].


[1480]
YUL CAN LA PHYIN CI LOG MA LOG GNYIS SU PHYE BA DE BZHIN DU, YUL YANG YIN PAR STON PA NI, ‘PHRAL GYI ‘KHRUL RGYU’I GNOD PA MED PAR DBANG PO DRUG GI SHES PA RNAMS KYIS GZUNG BAR BYA BA’I DON GANG ZHIG ‘JIG RTEN GYIS RTOGS PA DE NI,

The next lines are meant to show that—just as subject states of mind may be divided into the two of unmistaken, and mistaken—so too may objects.  Let’s consider those objects which are perceived by the world: entities which are held by awarenesses of the six senses where these are not adversely affected by any adventitious condition which would cause them to be mistaken.


[1481]
‘JIG RTEN NYID DE KHO NA LAS BDEN PA STE YANG DAG PA YIN GYI, ‘PHAGS PA LA BLTOS NAS YUL DE DAG BDEN PA DANG YANG DAG PAR ‘JOG PA NI MA YIN NO,,

Only relative to the world itself would these states of mind be real—that is, correct.  Relative to realized beings, however, such objects could not be considered true, correct.


[1482]
‘PHAGS PA ZHES PA DANG DBU MA’I LUGS ZHES PA NI ‘DIR DON ‘DRA’O,,

When we refer to “realized beings” here, we mean it in the same sense as “the system of the middle way.”


[1483]
LHAG MA STE GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS PA GANG ZHIG DBANG PO RNAMS LA GNOD PA YOD PA NA YUL DU SNANG BA DE NI, ‘JIG RTEN NYID LA BLTOS NAS LOG PAR RNAM PAR BZHAG GO

“The rest”—a reference to cases where certain objects appear to the senses and there is some potential problem going on, such as in the case of a reflection in a mirror—are established as being mistaken, even just relative to the everyday world.


[1484]
,NYID KYI SGRAS NI SHES PA DE RNAMS ‘KHRUL PAR ‘JOG PA LA NI, THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA NYID KYIS CHOG GI RIGS SHES LA MI LTOS PAR STON PA’O,,

The expression “even just” here is meant to indicate that it’s enough here—when we establish these states of mind as mistaken—to utilize even just a nominal form of accurate perception; it’s not that, rather, we would have to rely upon some exploration of the way things are.


[1485]
DE LA DBANG PO LA GNOD PA’I RKYEN NANG NA YOD PA NI RAB RIB DANG MIG SER LA SOGS PA DANG DA DU RA ZOS PA LA SOGS PA’O,,

Items that could be included among things that represent potential problems to the senses are cataracts or the effects of jaundice, or such; or else, for example, consuming datura.


[1486]
DA DU RA NI THANG PHROM STE, DE’I ‘BRAS BU ZOS NA THAMS CAD GSER DU SNANG BA’O, ,SOGS PAS NI RIMS LA SOGS PA BSDU’O,,

When we say “datura” here, we’re referring to the plant that we call tang-trom in Tibetan; when you eat it, everything you look at takes on a yellowish cast.  And when we say “or such,” we mean to include other ailments, such as plague.


[1487]
DBANG PO LA GNOD PA’I RKYEN PHYI NA YOD PA NI, ME LONG DANG BRAG PHUG LA SOGS PA NAS SGRA BRJOD PA DANG, SOS KA’I NYI MA’I ‘OD ZER BYE MA SKYE {%SKYA} BO’I YUL DANG NYE BAR GYUR PA LA SOGS PA STE, DE DAG NI DBANG PO LA GNOD PA’I RKYEN NANG NA MED KYANG, RIM PA BZHIN DU GZUGS BRNYAN DANG BRAG CHA DANG SMIG RGYU LA CHU [f. 112a] LA SOGS PAR ‘DZIN PA’I RGYUR ‘GYUR RO,,

There are also external conditions which can adversely affect the powers; examples would be a mirror; or calling into a cave; or situations such as approaching an object which is reflected in white sand under the rays of the summer sun.  Even though these are not conditions which would adversely affect the powers and which are also within us, nonetheless they can act as causes for us to perceive, respectively, a reflection; an echo; or a mirage that we take as water—and so on.


[1488]
DE BZHIN DU MIG ‘PHRUL MKHAN LA SOGS PAS SBYAR BA’I SNGAGS DANG SMAN LA SOGS PA YANG SHES PAR BYA’O,,

We can understand, in the same way, the spells and potions and such composed by an illusionist or the like.


[1489]
YID KYI DBANG PO’I GNOD PA NI SNGAGS DANG SMAN LA SOGS PA DE DAG DANG GRUB MTHA’ LOG PA DANG, GTAN TSIGS LTAR SNANG DANG GNYID KYI GNOD PA SOGS SO,,

Conditions which can adversely affect the power of the thought would be things like the spells, potions, and such just mentioned—as well as mistaken schools of thought; false logic; or the mental hindrance caused by sleep.


[1490]
GNYID NI DBANG PO DRUG GI NANG NAS YID KYI GNOD PAR GSUNGS PAS, RMI LAM DU DBANG SHES YOD PAR SLOB DPON ‘DI BZHED CES PA NI LOG PAR BSHAD PA CHEN PO’O,,

It is a huge misexplanation to claim that, since he clarifies the adverse affect of sleep here as referring to—from among “the six senses”—that of the mind, this master takes the position that we do possess sense powers during a dream.


[1491]
DE LTAR NA THOG MA MED PA NAS ZHUGS PA’I BDAG TU ‘DZIN PA GNYIS KYI MA RIG PA LA SOGS PAS BSLAD PA’I GNOD PA NI ‘DIR GNOD PA’I RGYUR MI GZUNG GI, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR GYI ‘PHRAL GYI DBANG PO LA GNOD PA’I ‘KHRUL RGYU RNAMS GZUNG NGO,,

As such, we are not in this particular section identifying “adverse effects” in the sense of those brought about by conditions such as misunderstanding in the form of the two ways in which we believe that objects are themselves—something which has gone on within us for time with no beginning.  Rather, as we put it earlier, we are identifying here the adventitious or short-term conditions which adversely affect the senses, and cause them to make errors.


[1492]
DE LTA BU’I GNOD PA MED PA’I SHES PA DRUG GIS GZUNG PA’I KUN RDZOB PA’I DON DANG, DE LAS BZLOG PA’I DON LA YANG DAG DANG LOG PAR ‘JOG PA NI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PA KHO NA LA LTOS NAS YIN TE, DE DAG JI LTAR SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU YOD PA LA ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PAS GNOD PA MED PA DANG YOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

When we speak of the deceptive objects which are perceived by six forms of consciousness which are not adversely affected; and when we posit the opposite types of objects, dividing them into correct and mistaken; we do so relative only to states of mind of the everyday world.  And that’s because we are deciding whether or not these objects exist in the way they appear depending upon whether states of mind belonging to the everyday world can draw them into question or not.


[1493]
‘PHAGS PA LA LTOS NAS NI YANG LOG GNYIS SU MED DE, JI LTAR GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU MED PA BZHIN DU, MA RIG PA DANG LDAN PA RNAMS LA SNGON PO LA SOGS PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA YANG, SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

There is no such division in this case of correct & mistaken perceptions when the reference is, rather, to how a realized being sees things.  Objects such as those reflected in a mirror, for example, do not exist in reality as they do in appearance; just so, it is the case that objects such as blue appear, to those who still possess misunderstanding, as though they existed by definition—but these things do not in fact exist the way they appear.


[1494]
DE’I PHYIR [f. 112b] SHES PA DE GNYIS LA ‘KHRUL MA ‘KHRUL YANG DBYER MED DO,,

Neither do we, therefore, make a division of these two states of mind into mistaken & unmistaken.


[1495]
‘O NA DBANG PO GZUGS CAN LA ‘PHRAL GYI GNOD PA YOD PAS YUL LOG PAR SNANG BA DANG, YID KYI SHES PA LA GNYID LA SOGS PA’I GNOD PA YOD PAS, RMI LAM DU MIR SNANG BA SOGS LA MI LA SOGS PAR ‘DZIN PA DANG, SAD DUS SU SGYU MA’I RTA GLANG GI SNANG BA LA RTA GLANG DANG SMIG RGYU CHUR SNANG BA LA CHUR ‘DZIN PA RNAMS

One may then raise the following issue—

Well then.  Let’s take a case where an object appears in a mistaken way to physical sense powers which do involve some kind of adventitious condition that would adversely affect them; or where the awareness of the thoughts is adversely affected by sleep, or anything of the like; or where, in the waking state, we take the appearance of an illusory horse or elephant to be a horse or elephant—or the appearance of water in the case of a mirage to be water.


[1496]
PHYIN CI LOG YIN PAR, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I BLO RANG DGA’ BAS KYANG RTOGS MOD KYANG, YID LA GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PA’I GNOD PA YOD PAS LOG PAR BZUNG BA’I DON RNAMS, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I BLO RANG DGA’ BAS PHYIN CI LOG TU MI RTOGS PAS, ‘JIG RTEN NYID LAS LOG PAR JI LTAR BZHAG CE NA,

We can admittedly come to realize, even just with some random state of mind from the everyday world, that things like these are mistaken.  In the case though where we take particular objects in the wrong way because our mind is adversely affected by mistaken schools of thought, it is not that we can realize—with just such a random state of mind from the everyday world—that such objects are mistaken.  How then can we say of these particular objects that, even just from the viewpoint of the everyday world, they are mistaken?


[1497]
‘DIR GNOD PA YOD MED DPYOD PA’I GNOD PA NI, LHAN SKYES KYIS PHYIN CI LOG TU ‘DZIN PA’I GNOD PA LA MI BYED PAS, GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PAS BTAGS PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO BSGYUR BA KHO NAS LOG PAR BTAGS PA’I GTZO BO SOGS YIN LA,

The answer is that—when we are looking into the question of whether or not there is some adverse effect going on—we are not referring to an adverse effect in the sense of an inborn state of mind holding to an object in a mistaken way.  When we speak of an object which is imputed by the ideas of a mistaken school, we are speaking for example primarily of an object imputed only by the thoughts of those who have been influenced by some school of thought.


[1498]
DE DAG PHYIN CI LOG TU ‘JIG RTEN PA’I BLO RANG DGA’ BAS MI RTOGS KYANG, DE KHO NA NYID LA MNGON DU MA PHYOGS PA’I THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS LOG PAR RTOGS NA, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PAS LOG PAR RTOGS PA YIN NO,,

It is not the case that just some random state of mind from the everyday world can come to a realization that such objects are mistaken; nonetheless, we can say that when we employ a nominal form of accurate perception which is not approaching the idea of suchness to realize that a particular object is mistaken, this object has been realized to be mistaken, by a state of mind which belongs to the everyday world.


[1499]
BDAG ‘DZIN LHAN SKYES GNYIS KYIS BZUNG BA’I DON LTA BU NI, GNOD PA MED PA’I DBANG POS BZUNG BA ZHES PA YIN LA, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I BSAM PA RANG DGA’ BA LA BLTOS NAS YANG DAG PA’AM BDEN PA YIN MOD KYANG THA SNYAD DU YANG MED DO,,

When though we take the example of something like an object which is perceived by the two versions of the innate form of the tendency to believe that things are themselves, we say that “it is perceived by powers which are free of being affected adversely.”  And in this case the object is admittedly “correct”—or real—relative to random thoughts of the everyday world; although in fact it does not exist at all, even in a nominal sense.


[1500]
GAL TE YANG DAG [f. 113a] PA’I KUN RDZOB MI ‘DOD PAS YANG LOG GNYIS SU MI BYED KYANG, MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA’I YUL DANG YUL CAN RNAMS LOG PA’I KUN RDZOB TU CI’I PHYIR MI ‘JOG CE NA,

One may then raise another question:

Suppose we refuse the idea of a deceptive object which is “correct”; and thus refuse the division of such objects into correct & incorrect.  Why though can’t we say that objects & subjects involved in the infection of the mind by misunderstanding may be established as a mistaken form of deceptive reality?


[1501]
KUN RDZOB NI THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS ‘JOG DGOS PA’I PHYIR LOG PA’I KUN RDZOB ‘JOG NA YANG DE LA BLTOS NAS ‘JOG DGOS NA, MA RIG PA’I BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD PA NI ‘KHRUL PAR THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MAS MI ‘GRUB PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Deceptive reality is something which must be established by a nominal form of accurate perception; as such, if we were to establish a mistaken form of deceptive reality, that too would have to be established relative to this type of perception.  It is not the case then that we could ever use a nominal form of accurate perception to determine that something infected by deep seeds of misunderstanding was mistaken.



Views inspired by sleep

[1502]
BZHI PA NI, DA NI BSHAD ZIN PA’I YID KYI GNOD PAS ZHEN YUL LA ‘KHRUL BA SPYIR BSTAN PA’I DON DE NYID, MTSAN GZHI BYE BRAG LA DPER BRJOD PA’I TSUL GYIS BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

This brings us then to our fourth point from above: demonstrating that—when we are mistaken towards the object we think we see—this object that we believe in does not even exist nominally.  And so now we will take this same general topic that we’ve discussed—the way in which, as we’ve already described, we make an error about what we think we see, due to some problem in our mind—and give an explanation where we apply to particular classic cases, in a metaphor.


	[1503]
	[VI.26]
Ajñāna nidrā pracalāya mānais
tīrthair yathāsvaṃ parikalpitā ye,
Māyā marīcyādiṣu kalpitāś ca
teṣām atattvaṃ khalu lokato’pi.

,MI SHES GNYID KYIS RAB BSKYOD MU STEGS CAN,
,RNAMS KYIS BDAG NYID JI BZHIN BRTAGS PA DANG,
,SGYU MA SMIG RGYU SOGS LA BRTAGS PA GANG,
,DE DAG ‘JIG RTEN LAS KYANG YOD MIN NYID,

The nature of the self—
As it is imagined
By those of lower views,

Inspired by the sleep
Of misunderstanding;

And those things imputed
In illusions, mirages, & the like,

Are nothing that
Could ever exist,
Even relative to the world.


[1504]
MI SHES PA’I GNYID KYIS YID RAB TU BSKYOD PA’I MU STEGS CAN YID LA PHYIN CI LOG GI GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PA DANG, GTAN TSIGS LTAR SNANG GI GNOD PA YOD PA ‘DI DAG NI, DE KHO NA NYID LA ‘JUG PAR ‘DOD PAS SKYE BO MA BYANG BA GNAG RDZI DANG BUD MED LA SOGS PA YAN CHAD LA GRAGS PA’I SKYE BA DANG, ‘JIG PA LA SOGS PA PHYIN CI MA LOG PA MA BZUNG BAR, ‘JIG RTEN PA RNAMS LAS PHUL DU BYUNG BAR ‘GRO BAR ‘DOD PAS,

Consider now those of lower views, whose minds are inspired by the sleep of misunderstanding—those with minds adversely affected by mistaken, undesirable schools of thought, or false forms of logic.  They wish to rise above the everyday world: they hope to engage in the way things really are.  But they want to do so without recognizing things like starting & stopping—in the way these are understood among those who have not applied themselves formally to philosophy, beginning for example from cowherds or women—as being unmistaken.


[1505]
DPER NA SHING LA ‘DZEG PAS YAL GA PHYI MA MA BZUNG BAR SNGA MA BTANG BAR LTAR, LTUNG BA CHEN POS LTA BA NGAN PA’I RI SUL DU LTUNG BAR ‘GYUR ZHING, BDEN GNYIS LEGS PAR MTHONG BA DANG BRAL BAS ‘BRAS BU THAR PA THOB PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

These people are like those who are climbing a tree and let go of the lower branch before they have clasped the higher—and thus suffer a great fall, where they drop into the ravine of undesirable viewpoints, and fail to see the two realities clearly.  As such, they are unable to attain the goal, of freedom.


[1506]
DE’I PHYIR MU STEGS CAN ‘DI RNAMS KYIS RANG RANG GI GZHUNG LAS ‘BYUNG BA’I BDAG NYID JI LTA BA BZHIN [f. 113b] DU YON TAN GSUM LA SOGS PA GANG BRTAGS PA NI, ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB TU YANG YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

This too is why the nature of the self—as it is imagined by these followers of lower views in their holy books, as having three qualities and so forth—is not something which exists even in the deceptive reality of the everyday world.


[1507]
‘DIS NI LUGS ‘DIS BLO ‘KHRUL PA CIG GI NGOR YOD PA LA, KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR ‘JOG ZER BA LEGS PAR BKAG GO

This in itself is enough to disprove, perfectly, the claim by this system that a thing is established as existing deceptively relative to the perceptions of a mistaken state of mind.


[1508]
,DE BZHIN DU SGYU MA DANG SMIG RGYU DANG GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS PA LA RTA GLANG DANG, CHU DANG BYAD BZHIN SOGS SU BRTAGS PA GANG YIN PA DE DAG KYANG, ‘JIG RTEN KUN RDZOB LAS KYANG YOD PA MIN PA NYID DO,,

In the same way, those things that are imputed to be horses & elephants; or water; or the object placed before a mirror and so forth—illusions, mirages, reflections & the like—are nothing that could ever exist, even relative to the world: to deceptive reality.


[1509]
DE LTAR NA THA SNYAD DU YOD PA LA NI TSAD MAS GRUB PA ZHIG DGOS SO,,

As such, for a thing to exist nominally, it must be something which is confirmed by an accurate perception.


[1510]
DE ‘DRA BA’I ZHEN YUL RNAMS THA SNYAD DU YANG MED KYANG SNANG YUL LA NI DE LTAR MI BZHED DO,,

When we say that things like this which we think are there don’t even exist in a nominal way, we are not saying that this is what we accept with regard to the object as it appears to us.


[1511]
DA LTA GZUGS SGRA SOGS LNGA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR DBANG SHES LA SNANG BA NI, MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA YIN PAS SHES PA DE DANG, GZUGS BRNYAN DANG BRAG CHA SOGS SNANG BA’I DBANG SHES RNAMS LA, PHRA RAGS TZAM MA GTOGS PA SNANG YUL LA ‘KHRUL MA ‘KHRUL LA KHYAD PAR MED CING, SNGO SOGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA DANG, GZUGS BRNYAN BYAD BZHIN DU YOD PA MI SRID KYANG,

Right now the five types of objects which include visible & audible forms are assuming an aspect—within our sense consciousnesses—where it seems as though they existed by definition.  This is something that is happening because these states of mind are infected by misunderstanding.  As such, when we compare these mental states to forms of sense consciousness which are assuming the aspect of things like a reflection in a mirror, or an echo, there is no difference between them where one is mistaken and the other is not—only some distinction of relative subtlety.  It is impossible for things like the color blue to exist by definition; and it is impossible for reflections to be the things standing before the mirror.


[1512]
BYAD BZHIN DU MED PA’I GZUGS BRNYAN YOD PA BZHIN DU, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA MIN KYANG SNGO SOGS YOD DGOS LA, DE YANG PHYI ROL GYI DON DU YOD PA BZHIN DU GZUGS BRNYAN YANG GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DU BZHED PA YIN TE, ‘OG NAS GZUGS BRNYAN GYIS DE SNANG BA’I DBANG SHES SKYED PAR YANG GSUNGS SO,,

And yet there can still exist a reflection in the mirror which does not exist as the object placed before the mirror; just so, blue & the like—despite the fact that they do not exist by definition—must still exist.  Moreover, we take the position that the reflection, just as it exists as an outer object, belongs to the door of sense composed of visible objects.  That is, it will be stated—further on—that the reflection acts to produce a sense consciousness which assumes its aspect.


[1513]
TSUL DE DAG NI MIG LA RTA GLANG DU SNANG BA’I SGYU MA DANG BRAG CHA SOGS [f. 114a] LA YANG SHES PAR BYA STE, LUGS DAM PA ‘DI YI RNAM GZHAG THUN MONG MA YIN PA’O,,

You should understand that these descriptions apply as well to cases such as where an illusion appears to the eye as though it were a horse or elephant; or where there is an echo.  This is a unique presentation of this highest of all systems of thought.



The blind do not disprove the seeing

[1514]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to the second part in our general presentation of the two realities: how we apply this presentation to the present topic.


	[1515]
[VI.27]
Na bādhate jñānam ataimirāṇāṃ
yathopalabdhis timirekṣaṇāṇām,
Tathāmala jñāna tiraskṛtānāṃ
dhiyāsti bādho na dhiyo’malāyāḥ.

,MIG NI RAB RIB CAN GYIS DMIGS PA YIS,
,RAB RIB MED SHES LA GNOD MIN JI LTAR,
,DE BZHIN DRI MED YE SHES SPANGS PA’I BLOS,
,DRI MED BLO LA GNOD PA YOD MA YIN,

The perceptions of eyes
Clouded with cataracts

Cannot draw into question
A state of mind
Without such cataracts;

And there is nothing about
A mind which has abandoned
The wisdom free of stain

Which could ever draw
Into question the state of mind
Which is free of stain—

These two cases then
Are the same.


[1516]
DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON THA SNYAD PA’I SHES PAS MI ‘JOG PA DE’I PHYIR, GZHAN SKYE ‘GOG PA NI ‘JIG RTEN PA’I LTA BA KHO NA LA GNAS NAS MI BYED KYI, ‘PHAGS PA’I DE KHO NA NYID KYI GZIGS PA KHAS BLANGS NAS DON DAM PAR ‘GOG PA YIN NO,,

There is a specific object—that is, suchness—which cannot ever be established by a nominal state of mind.  As such, the denial that things could grow from something other than themselves is not something which can be accomplished if we remain just in the viewpoints of the everyday world.  Only after we have accepted the vision of suchness attained by a realized being can we deny that this growth could ever exist in an ultimate way.


[1517]
GANG GI TSE GZHAN SKYE DGAG PA ‘DI LA DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR SBYOR BA YIN PA DE’I TSE, JI LTAR MIG NI RAB RIB CAN GYI SHES PAS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA DMIGS PAS, RAB RIB KYIS MA BSLAD PA’I SHES PA LA SKRA SHAD SOGS MI SNANG BA LA GNOD PA MIN PA

Suppose that as we deny that things could grow from things other than themselves, we apply the distinction that we are referring here to growing in an ultimate sense.  Think then of how a state of mind influenced by eyes clouded with cataracts perceives a strand of hair, or something similar.  This state of mind cannot draw into question the way in which no strand of hair or the like ever makes its appearance to a state of mind which is not infected by such cataracts.


[1518]
JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU, DRI MA STE ZAG PA MED PA’I YE SHES SPANGS PA STE DE DANG BRAL BA’I SO SKYE’I BLO MA RIG PAS BSLAD PAS, MA RIG PAS MA BSLAD PA’I DRI MA STE ZAG PA MED PA’I BLO LA GNOD PA YOD PA MA YIN PAS,

Consider secondly the mind of a normal person: a mind which has abandoned—which still lacks—that wisdom which is free of stain, or impurity; that is to say, a state of mind which is infected by misunderstanding.  There is nothing about this mental state which could ever draw into question the state of mind which is free of the stains—the impurities—brought about by the infection caused by misunderstanding.  These two cases then are exactly the same.


[1519]
DON DAM PAR GZHAN SKYE BKAG PA LA ‘JIG RTEN PA’I NGOR GZHAN SKYE GRUB TU CHUG KYANG MI GNOD DO,,

As such, when we undertake to deny that things could grow—in an ultimate sense—from things other than themselves, it would not draw our position into question even if we allowed that the growth of things from things other than themselves were confirmed in the eyes of the everyday world.


[1520]
DE’I PHYIR PHA ROL PO NI DAM PA MKHAS PA DAG GIS BZHAD GAD DU BYA BAR ‘OS SO,,

Given all this, it would not be inappropriate for “the holy”—for sages—to consider the other party at this point to be a laughing stock.



Seeing deceptive reality is real

[1521]
GSUM PA LA GNYIS, KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA BSHAD PA DANG, DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA BSHAD PA’O,,

This brings us to our third point from before: a separate explanation of the nature of each of the two realities.  This consists of two parts of its own—an explanation of deceptive reality; and an explanation of ultimate reality.


[1522]
DANG PO LA GSUM, KUN RDZOB PA GANG GI NGOR BDEN LA GANG GI NGOR MI BDEN PA DANG, KUN RDZOB TZAM DE GANG ZAG GSUM LA SNANG BA DANG MI SNANG BA’I TSUL DANG, SO SKYE DANG ‘PHAGS PA LA LTOS TE DON DAM PA DANG KUN RDZOB TU ‘GYUR TSUL LO,,

We’ll cover the first of these in three steps:

 An examination of the state of mind to which deceptive reality
	is real, and the state of mind to which it is not real;
 An examination of which of the three types of individuals
basic deception can appear to, or not appear; and
 A description of the way in which things can become either
	ultimate or deceptive, relative to a common being, or
	a realized being.


[1523]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, DNGOS KYI DON DANG, NYON MONGS KYI RNAM [f. 114b] GZHAG THUN MONG MA YIN PA BSHAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these will have two parts of its own: a description of the actual point, followed by an explanation of this unique presentation on the negative emotions.


	[1524]
[VI.28]
Mohaḥ svabhāvāvaraṇād dhi saṃvṛtiḥ
satyaṃ tayā khyāti yad eva kṛtrimam,
Jagāda tat saṃvṛti satyam ityasau
Muniḥ padārthaṃ kṛtakañ ca saṃvṛtiḥ.

,GTI MUG RANG BZHIN SGRIB PHYIR KUN RDZOB STE,
,DES GANG BCOS MA BDEN PAR SNANG DE NI,
,KUN RDZOB BDEN ZHES THUB PA DES GSUNGS TE,
,BCOS MAR GYUR PA’I DNGOS NI KUN RDZOB TU’O,,

Dark ignorance draws a veil
Over the nature of things,
And from that fact is deception.

		Due to this, things
		That are a false construct
		Appear as though
		They were real.

		These were described
		By the Able One to be
		A deceptive reality:

		Objects which make up
		This false construct
		To the deceptive.


[1525]
‘DIS SEMS CAN RNAMS DNGOS PO JI LTAR GNAS PA’I RANG BZHIN LTA BA LA SGRIB PA STE RMONGS PAR BYED PA’I PHYIR NA GTI MUG STE, MA RIG PA DNGOS PO’I NGO BO RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN PA LA, RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR SGRO ‘DOGS PAR BYED PA YIN LUGS KYI RANG BZHIN MTHONG BA LA SGRIB PA’I BDAG NYID CAN NI KUN RDZOB BO,,

Dark ignorance is given its name from the fact that it leaves living beings in the dark: it draws a veil over our ability to see how things really exist—their nature.   Misunderstanding enables us to see things as more than they actually are: it makes us believe that the essential nature of things—which is anything but these things’ existing through some nature of their own—is for them to exist through just such a nature.  “Deception” then is that entity whose nature is to veil our ability to see the true nature of things: the way they truly are.


[1526]
‘DI NI KUN RDZOB BDEN PA ZHES PA’I BDEN PA, KUN RDZOB PA GANG GI NGOR ‘JOG PA’I KUN RDZOB NGOS ‘DZIN PA YIN GYI, KUN RDZOB PA SPYI NGOS ‘DZIN PA MIN NO,,

The “reality” in the expression “deceptive reality” is meant to identify deception in terms of the particular party deceived.  We are not here identifying deception in general.


[1527]
NGOS ‘DZIN DE YANG LANG KAR GSHEGS PA LAS,
,DNGOS RNAMS SKYE BA KUN RDZOB TU,
,DAM PA’I DON DU RANG BZHIN MED,
,RANG BZHIN MED LA ‘KHRUL PA GANG,
,DE NI YANG DAG KUN RDZOB ‘DOD,

As for this approach in identifying the deceptive, A Journey to Langka says—

Everything in the world
Starts in a way which is deceptive;

Things have no nature
Of starting in a way
Which is ultimate.

When we make a mistake
About the lack of a nature to things,

We say we’ve been deceived
About what is actually there.


[1528]
CES DON DAM PAR RANG BZHIN MED PA LA RANG BZHIN YOD PAR ‘KHRUL BA’I BLO KUN RDZOB PA YIN PAR GSUNGS PA’I DON NO,,

What’s being said here is that “deception” is a reference to that state of mind which makes this mistake of thinking that things which ultimately have no nature do have one.


[1529]
KUN RDZOB DE NI KUN RDZOB KYI SKAD ‘DOD SGRIB BYED LA YANG ‘JUG PAS SGRIB BYED DO,,

The Sanskrit word here for “deception,” sanvirti, can also be translated as that which veils; as such, we can describe the deception here as “that which veils.”


[1530]
DES GANG LA SGRIB NA YANG DAG KUN RDZOB ‘DOD CES PAS YANG DAG PA’I DON LA SGRIB PAS KUN RDZOB BAM SGRIB BYED DU ‘DOD CES PA STE, YANG LOG GNYIS KYI NANG NAS YANG DAG KUN RDZOB TU STON PA MIN NO,,

What is it that this reality veils?  Given the wording “deceived about what is actually there,” what we’re referring to is deception—a veil—in the sense of what covers & conceals actual reality.  This is not meant to be a reference to a “correct” form of deceptive reality, in the division of that reality into correct & mistaken.


[1531]
RKANG PA DANG POS BSTAN PA’I KUN RDZOB DANG, RKANG PA PHYI MA GNYIS KYIS BSTAN PA’I KUN RDZOB GNYIS GCIG TU MI BYA STE, DANG PO NI, RANG GIS DNGOS PO RNAMS SKYE BA SOGS SU GANG DU KHAS LEN PA’I KUN RDZOB YIN LA, PHYI MA NI DNGOS PO RNAMS GANG GI NGOR BDEN PA’I BDEN ‘DZIN GYI [f. 115a] KUN RDZOB YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

We are not to take the mention of “deception” in the first half of the verse in the same way that we take the “deceive” in the second half.  The first refers to a kind of deceptive reality involved for example in the growing of things—this is something that we would accept.  The second refers to how things deceive us when they seem to be real, to our tendency to hold things as real.


[1532]
KUN RDZOB BDEN ‘DZIN DE’I MTHUS SNGON PO LA SOGS PA GANG ZHIG ,RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED BZHIN DU DER SNANG BAR BCOS PA’I BCOS MA SEMS CAN RNAMS LA BDEN PAR SNANG BA DE NI,

Due to the power of this deception, in the form of our tendency to believe that things are real, there comes a construct where things like the color blue appear to exist through some nature of their own—in the very moment that they cannot.  This false construct is something which appears, to living beings, as though it were real.


[1533]
SNGAR BSHAD PA’I ‘JIG RTEN GYI PHYIN CI LOG GI KUN RDZOB PA DE’I NGOR BDEN PAS ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA ZHES THUB PA DES GSUNGS TE, GSUNGS TSUL NI SNGAR GYI MDO DER GSUNGS PA’O,,

As such, the construct was spoken by the Able One to be a “deceptive reality for the everyday world”—since to deception in the form of this mistaken state of mind of the everday world, as we’ve described that up to here, it is taken to be real.  How the Buddha said this is as we see it spoken in the sutra citation given above.


[1534]
GANG ZAG GSUM PO GANG GI NGOR MI BDEN PA’I RTOG PAS BCOS PAS BCOS MAR GYUR PA’I DNGOS PO NI DE’I KUN RDZOB PA’I NGOR MI BDEN PAS KUN RDZOB TZAM ZHES BYA’O,,

Let’s consider the objects which make up this false construct—this construct of our imagination, which is a construct that, to the perceptions of three particular types of individuals, is unreal.  Since these objects are, to their deceptive perceptions, unreal, they can be called “basic deception.”


[1535]
RTEN ‘BYUNG GZUGS BRNYAN DANG BRAG CHA SOGS CUNG ZAD CIG NI BRDZUN YANG MA RIG PA DANG LDAN PA RNAMS LA SNANG LA, SNGON PO LA SOGS PA’I GZUGS DANG SEMS DANG TSOR BA SOGS CUNG ZAD CIG NI BDEN PAR SNANG STE, CHOS RNAMS KYI YIN LUGS KYI RANG BZHIN NI MA RIG PA DANG LDAN PA RNAMS LA RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MI SNANG NGO, ,DE’I PHYIR RANG BZHIN DE DANG GANG ZHIG KUN RDZOB TU YANG BRDZUN PA NI KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA MA YIN NO,

A bit of the things that occur in dependence—that is, things like reflections in mirrors, or echoes—are lies; but they do make their appearance to those possessed of misunderstanding.  So too a little bit of physical forms like the color blue; and things like the mind and our feelings, appear really.  But the nature of things, in the sense of the way things actually are, cannot in any manner make its appearance to those who still have misunderstanding.  As such, a nature to things—and forms of the deception which are themselves a lie—do not constitute deceptive reality.


[1536]
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON BSHAD NA CUNG ZAD CIG CES PA NI, NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS ‘GA’ ZHIG TU BSGYUR BA LTAR BDE’O,,

In explaining the point of this statement, it would be more comfortable if we utilized Natktso’s translation, switching the “little bit” to “some number of.”


[1537]
GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS BRDZUN YANG SNANG BA NI BRDZUN PAR SNANG BA YIN LA, DE NI BYAD BZHIN DU SNANG BA DANG DES STONG PA GNYIS TSOGS PA’I BRDZUN PA YIN PAS, DE’I BDEN STONG NI BYAD BZHIN DU BDEN PAS STONG PA YIN GYI, GZUGS [f. 115b] BRNYAN RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I BDEN STONG GI DON MED DO,,

Reflections & the like can lie to us; but still they do make their appearance, in a lying way.  This is a kind of lie where there is a combination of two things: something appearing to be the object which was placed in front of the mirror; and this something’s being void of actually existing as that object.  As such, when we speak of “voidness of reality” here what we are talking about is the fact that the reflection is void of any existing, in reality, as the object reflected.  We are not referring here to a voidness of reality in the sense of the reflection being empty of any true existence, in the form of existing by definition.


[1538]
DE’I PHYIR GZUGS BRNYAN BYAD BZHIN GYIS STONG PAR GRUB KYANG, GZUGS BRNYAN RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BDEN PA YIN PA LA ‘GAL BA CI YANG MED PA’I DNGOS PO YIN PAS KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA YIN NO,,

As such, we can establish that the reflection is devoid of being the object placed before the mirror; but this is a case of a thing where there is absolutely no contradiction for this object to exist as real in the perceptions of a deception which holds that the reflection exists by definition.  As such, this thing then is, as well, a case of deceptive reality.


[1539]
DES NA GZUGS BRNYAN KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA MIN PAR GSUNGS PA NI, BRDA LA BYANG BA’I ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BYAD BZHIN GYI GZUGS BRNYAN LTA BU DE, BYAD BZHIN YIN PA DE BRDZUN PAS

Let’s look then at the statement that a reflection in the mirror is not deceptive reality.  What this is meant to refer to is something like the idea of a reflection of an object standing before a mirror—to the deceptive perceptions of the everyday world, a world where people are already familiar with the meaning of the particular words being used—actually being this object: that would be a lie.


[1540]
DE LA LTOS PA’I KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA MIN PA LA DGONGS KYI, MTHONG BA BRDZUN PA’I KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR GSUNGS, ZHES PAS BSHAD PA’I KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR MI ‘JOG PA GA LA YIN,

Relative to this situation, it’s being said, the reflection is not a case of deceptive reality.  “It was declared” though “that the one seen to be a lie is deceptive reality”—given these words, how could you ever say the reflection couldn’t be described as belonging to deceptive reality?


[1541]
DE LTA MA YIN PAR KUN RDZOB TU BDEN PAR MED NA KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN PAR ‘GAL NA, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PAR GSUNGS PA DANG, BDEN GRUB ‘GEGS PA DANG BDEN MED SGRUB PA THAMS CAD THA SNYAD DU BYED PA’I RNAM GZHAG THAMS CAD DANG ‘GAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

If it were not this way, and if there were nothing at all that constituted reality in a deceptive form, then it would be a contradiction for the reflection to be an instance of deceptive reality.  And if that were the case, it would contradict the entire structure of things existing in name: everything about statements that things which existed by definition could never exist even nominally; the denial of things existing in truth; and the proof that nothing exists in truth.


[1542]
DE’I PHYIR GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS ‘JIG RTEN PA’I SHES PA RANG DGA’ BAS KYANG ‘PHRUL {%’KHRUL} PAR SHES PA’I YUL RNAMS KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MIN GYI KUN RDZOB TZAM MO, ZHES ZER BA NI BDEN GNYIS KYI GRANGS NGES DANG, ‘JIG RTEN PA LA LTOS PA’I BDEN BRDZUN DANG, DBU MA PAS ‘JOG PA’I BDEN BRDZUN LA GO BA MA CHAGS PA’I GTAM DU SNANG NGO,,

Given all this, let’s look at the claim that “Objects like a reflection in a mirror, which are understood to be mistaken even by some random state of mind in the everyday world, do not constitute deceptive reality; rather, they are just basic deception.”  It would appear that such statements are the chatter of people who have failed to form an understanding of how the types of reality are fixed at two, no more and no less; and of the concepts of truth & falsity relative to the beliefs of the everyday world; and of these same two concepts as they are set forth by those who follow the middle way.


[1543]
RANG BZHIN NI MA RIG PA DANG LDAN PA LA THAMS CAD DU MI SNANG NGO ZHES GSUNGS [f. 116a] PA YANG, MA RIG PA MA SPANGS PA’I ‘PHAGS PAS DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PAR BZHED PAS NA, MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA’I SHES PA LA DGONGS LA,

Consider as well the statement that “A nature to things is not something that makes its appearance, in every aspect, to those who still possess misunderstanding.”  Given the fact that we accept the idea that a realized being who has yet to rid themselves of misunderstanding can realize thusness directly, such statements are intended to refer to a state of mind which is infected by misunderstanding.


[1544]
‘PHAGS PA SLOB PA’I RJES THOB KYI YE SHES DANG, SO SKYE’I DE KHO NA NYID KYI LTA BA RNAMS, MA RIG PA DANG DE’I BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD PA YIN PAS MNGON SUM DU MI SNANG YANG, SPYIR DON DAM BDEN PA SNANG BAR ‘DOD DGOS SO,,

The wisdom of a realized being who is still learning, during the “aftermath” period subsequent to the direct perception of emptiness; as well as correct views about suchness possessed by common beings; are still infected by misunderstanding, and by the deep seeds for this misunderstanding.  As such, they may not take on an aspect of ultimate reality directly; but still we would take the position that—in general—they do take on this aspect.


[1545]
DE LTAR NA RE ZHIG SRID PA’I YAN LAG GIS BSDUS PAS NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA’I DBANG GIS, KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA RNAM PAR GZHAG GO ZHES GSUNGS PAS NI, CHOS RNAMS BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA’I MA RIG PA GANG ZAG DANG CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN DU GRAGS PA NI, YAN LAG BCU GNYIS KYI MA RIG PAR BZHED PAS SHES SGRIB TU MI BZHED DO,,

There is a statement that, “In a preliminary assessment, then, we posit a deceptive form of reality due to the type of misunderstanding which involves negative emotions and which is counted among the links of the cycle of pain.”  Given these words, the form of misunderstanding which holds things to be real—what we commonly know as the tendency to hold that the person & things are themselves—is accepted as being the form of misunderstanding included into the twelve links of dependence.  And as such, it would not be accepted as being an obstacle to omniscience.


[1546]
MA RIG PA BDEN ‘DZIN DE’I DBANG GIS KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA ‘JOG CES PA NI, BDEN PA KUN RDZOB PA GANG GI NGOR ‘JOG PA’I ‘JOG TSUL STON PA YIN GYI, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN PA’I BUM SNAM SOGS BDEN ‘DZIN DES ‘JOG CES PA MIN TE, BDEN ‘DZIN DES BZHAG PA NI RANG GIS THA SNYAD DU YANG MI SRID PAR BZHED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

What does it mean when we say that “We posit a deceptive form of reality due to this type of misunderstanding—this particular tendency to hold things as being real”?  What this sentence is indicating is the way in which we posit realities depending on whether the object involved exists in the perceptions of a true or a deceptive state of mind.  The point being made is not that particular examples of deceptive reality such as a water pitcher or a bolt of cloth are established by this tendency to see things as real.  This is because we take the position that any object whose existence was established by this tendency to perceive things as real would be an impossibility, even in a nominal sense.


[1547]
DES NA KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA ZHES PA’I ZUR GYI BDEN PA GANG GI NGOR ‘JOG PA’I KUN RDZOB DANG, BUM SOGS KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR ‘JOG PA’I KUN RDZOB RNAMS MING MTSUNGS PAS, DON YANG GCIG TU ‘KHRUL BA MANG DU BYUNG SNANG BAS LEGS PAR PHYED PAR BYA’O,,

Given all this, let’s look at this word “reality,” as a component in the expression “deceptive reality.”  “Deception” in the sense of the state of mind in whose perceptions the deceptive is established; and “deception” in the sense of the state of mind which helps us establish that things like water pitchers exist in a deceptive manner, are exactly the same names.  It appears that, because of this, there have been many mistakes made where people took the meaning of the two to be the same as well.  Work hard then to make a proper distinction between these two.


[1548]
‘O NA BUM SOGS ‘DI RNAMS SANGS MA RGYAS PA’I GANG ZAG THAMS CAD KYI [f. 116b] KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BDEN PA YIN NAM, GANG ZAG ‘GA’ ZHIG GI KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR MI BDEN PA YANG YOD CE NA,

One may then ask the following question:

Well then.  Is it the case that all these things—water pitchers & the like—are real in the perceptions of all beings who have yet to become enlightened?  Or can they not be real, in the deceptive perceptions of certain individuals?


[1549]
KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PAR ‘JOG PA’I GZUGS SGRA SOGS DE YANG, NYAN RANG DANG BYANG SEMS NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA SPANGS PA, ‘DU BYED GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS DANG ‘DRA BAR GZIGS PA RNAMS LA NI, BCOS MA’I RANG BZHIN YIN GYI BDEN PA NI MA YIN TE, BDEN PAR MNGON PAR RLOM PA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,

Let’s consider objects such as visible or audible form, as these are established to be part of deceptive reality.  Their nature is further one of a false construct, and not of truth, in the high perceptions of those listeners, self-made buddhas, and bodhisattvas who have rid themselves of misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions; as well as in the perceptions of those who have seen that all factors are similar to a reflection in a mirror, or the like.  To people such as these, these things have a nature of being a false construct, but not of being true—for these individuals are free of any mistaken fantasy that the things could be real.


[1550]
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON BSHAD NA, GANG GI NGOR MI BDEN PA’I GANG ZAG NI GSUM STE, NYAN RANG DANG BYANG SEMS SO,,

Let’s explain what this statement is talking about.  First of all, the reference is to three different individuals in whose perceptions these things are not real.  These are the listener, the self-made buddha, and the bodhisattva.


[1551]
DE YANG NYAN RANG DANG BYANG SEMS GANG YIN LA MI BYED PAS KHYAD PAR SMOS PA NI, ‘DUS BYAS THAMS CAD GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG YANG DER SNANG BAR MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA NI KHYAD PAR GCIG GO

This is further not a reference to just any listener, self-made buddha, or bodhisattva—and here’s the difference.  One distinction is based on the fact that all things brought about by causes & conditions are like a reflection in a mirror, devoid of any nature of their own; and yet they do appear to have such a nature—and these are people who have realized this in a direct manner.


[1552]
,DE TZAM NI BYANG SEMS SA BDUN PA BA MAN CHAD DANG, NYAN RANG ‘PHAGS PA SLOB PA RNAMS LA’ANG YOD PAS DE GCAD PA’I PHYIR DU, GANG ZAG GSUM PA LA MA RIG PA SPANGS PA ZHES GSUNGS PAS DAG PA SA’I BYANG SEMS DANG, NYAN RANG DGRA BCOM PA GNYIS LA BYA STE DE GSUM GYI NGOR MI BDEN PA’O,,

This distinction in itself also applies to bodhisattvas on the seventh bodhisattva level on down, and to listeners & self-made buddhas who are realized beings but not yet enlightened.  In order to clarify that these people are not whom we’re talking about, we add the qualifier for these three individuals that—as stated—they have “rid themselves of misunderstanding.”  As such, the wording here is actually meant to refer to bodisattvas who have reached one of the levels of purity; and to listeners & self-made buddhas who are already enemy destroyers.  It is to the perceptions of these three that these things are unreal.


[1553]
GANG ZHIG MI BDEN PA NI DE YANG ZHES PA PHYI NANG GI CHOS RNAMS SO,,

And what are “these things” that are unreal?  Remember the reference to “further” above, meaning that we are referring to all outer & inner phenomena.


[1554]
MI BDEN PA’I RGYU MTSAN NI BDEN PAR RLOM PA STE BDEN ZHEN MED PA’I PHYIR TE, BDEN ‘DZIN GYI MA RIG PA ZAD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And what is the reason that these things are “unreal” at this point?  It’s because these individuals no longer possess any belief in things as real: they are free of any mistaken fantasy that things could be real.  Which is to say, they have put an end to misunderstanding in the form of believing that things are real.


[1555]
DES NA PHYI NANG GI CHOS RNAMS GANG ZAG GSUM PO DE’I KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR SGRUB PA YIN NO,,

Thus it is then that we establish that—to the perceptions of the deceptive state of mind of these three individuals—outer & inner phenomena cannot be determined to be real.


[1556]
DE LTAR ‘GREL PAS DE RNAMS KYI NGOR KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MIN PAR YE MA BSGRUBS PAR BDEN PA [f. 117a] MIN ZHES BSGRUBS PA LA, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MIN PAR BSGRUBS PAR ‘DZIN PA NI, HA CANG YANG BLO’I ‘JUG PA RTZINGS PAS SLOB DPON GYI DGONGS PA RANG GI BLO’I DRI MAS SBAGS NAS ‘CHAD PA’I LUGS NGAN PA’O,,

Let’s look then at the conclusion drawn in the autocommentary that these things are not real, in not being established in any way—to their perceptions—as not being deceptive reality.  Taking this to be an assertion that what they see is not deceptive reality represents a total insensitivity to the actual meaning; it is a distasteful system of explanation where people have polluted the true intent of this master with the stench of their own way of thinking.


[1557]
DE LTAR SGRUB PA YANG GANG ZAG DE GSUM LA MIN GYI, DE GSUM GYI NGOR BDEN PA MIN PA GANG ZAG GZHAN BDAG CAG RNAMS LTA BU LA SGRUB PA YIN NO,,

How we establish things as we said is not that we refer to these three individuals themselves, but rather to something not being real to the perceptions of the three.  It is determining the case for other persons—such as you & me.


[1558]
GANG ZAG DE GSUM MIN PA’I ‘OG MA RNAMS LA NI LHAN SKYES KYI BDEN ‘DZIN YOD PAS, DE RNAMS KYI KUN RDZOB GANG YIN THAMS CAD KYI NGOR GANG YANG BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR SGRUB MI NUS SO,,

People other than these three types—those at lower levels—still possess the inborn form of the tendency to believe that things are real.  We would never be able to establish that the things that are deceptive for them lacked any true existence, to anyone’s perceptions at all.


[1559]
SNGAR BSHAD PA DE LTA MIN PAR DE DAG GI NGOR KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA MIN PA BSGRUB NA NI, SHIN TU MA ‘BREL BA’I SGRUB BYED DU ‘GYUR TE, BLO DE’I NGOR GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR ‘GRUB PA LA GZHI DE BRDZUN PAR ‘GRUB DGOS PAS DE LA BDEN ZHEN MED PA RGYU MTSAN DU ‘GOD PA NI BZHAD GAD KYI GNAS SO,,

Suppose it were not the way we’ve explained it up to here: suppose to their perceptions things that were not deceptive reality could be established.  The assertion then would lose any pertinence to anything at all.  That is, in order to establish—to such a state of mind—that any particular object belonged to deceptive reality, we would have to prove that the object was lying to us.  As such, positing—as our reason here—the idea that such individuals have no belief in reality deserves no more than our laughter.


[1560]
BLO DE’I NGOR GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR ‘GRUB PA LA GZHI DE BRDZUN PAR ‘GRUB DGOS PA’I RGYU MTSAN NI, BUM SOGS LA KUN RDZOB BDEN PA ZHES PA’I TSIG ZUR GYI BDEN PA ‘JOG PA NA BLO DANG DON GNYIS LAS, DON LA BDEN PAR MI ‘JOG PAR, BDEN ‘DZIN KUN RDZOB PA’I NGO BO NYID DU BDEN PAR GZHAG DGOS PAR MTHONG BA NA, KHYAD PAR DE MA SBYAR NA BDEN PAR MI ‘GRUB CING BRDZUN PA YIN PAR MTHONG DGOS PA’I GNAD KYIS YIN NO,,

Now what is the reason that—in order to establish that a certain object is, to this particular state of mind, deceptive reality—we would have to establish that the object was lying to us?  Consider how we establish the word “reality,” in the expression “deceptive reality,” in the case of something like a water pitcher.  Does it refer to the state of mind, or to the object of this mind?  We are not in fact establishing the object as reality; rather, we need to establish reality here in the sense of establishing that the tendency to believe that things are real itself constitutes the essence of the deception.  Once we see the need to do so, we can perceive that—without applying this distinction—the object does not exist in reality, and is lying to us.  The need is the key here.



A unique presentation
on the negative emotions

[1561]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: an explanation of this unique presentation on the negative emotions.


[1562]
LUGS ‘DI LA NYON MONGS KYI NGOS ‘DZIN MNGON PA GONG ‘OG [f. 117b] NAS BSHAD PA DANG MI MTHUN PA THUN MONG MA YIN PA CIG YOD PA DE SHES PA GAL CHE BAR SNANG BAS DE BSHAD NA,

The present system has a way of identifying the negative emotions which is unique—that is to say, it is not shared with the explanation of these emotions found in the higher & lower divisions of the system called Higher Knowledge.  It seems to me that a knowledge of this presentation is quite important, and so I will cover it here.


[1563]
DNGOS PO BDEN ‘DZIN LA GANG ZAG DANG CHOS LA BDEN ‘DZIN GNYIS YOD LA, DE NYID BDAG ‘DZIN GNYIS SU’ANG BZHED PA NI SNGAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,

There are two versions of the tendency to believe that things are real: these are the pair of holding that the person is real, and then holding that things are real.  This is, as we’ve explained above, what we mean when we say that we assert that there are two ways of holding that things are themselves.


[1564]
BDEN ‘DZIN DE ‘JUG ‘GREL DANG, BZHI BRGYA PA’I ‘GREL PA GNYIS KAR NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PAR BSHAD LA, MA RIG PA DE NYAN RANG DGRA BCOM GYIS SPANGS PA DANG, BZHI BRGYA PA’I ‘GREL PAR MI SKYE BA’I CHOS LA BZOD PA THOB PA’I BYANG SEMS KYIS SPANGS PAR BSHAD DO,,

The tendency to believe that things are real is explained—in both the autocommentary to Entering the Middle Way and in the commentary to the 400 Verses—to be misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions.  Listener and self-made buddha types of enemy destroyers have rid themselves of that form of misunderstanding; and the commentary to the 400 Verses explains that a bodhisattva who has attained the state called “mastery over unborn things” has as well rid themselves of this misunderstanding.


[1565]
DE’I PHYIR NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA NI, BDAG MED PA’I DE KHO NA NYID RIG PA’I MI MTHUN PHYOGS DANG, DE YANG RIG PA DE MED PA TZAM DANG, DE LAS GZHAN PA TZAM LA MI BYED KYI, ‘GAL ZLA MI MTHUN PHYOGS GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR SGRO ‘DOGS PA’O,,

As such, the form of misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions represents the opposite of understanding where we grasp suchness, in the form of things not being themselves.  This “misunderstanding” refers not to a simple lack of understanding, nor even something other than understanding—but constitutes a direct and contradictory opposite to understanding.  Which is to say, this state of mind sees things where they are not: it believes that the person, and things, exist through some nature of their own.


[1566]
DE LTAR BYAS NA CHOS KYI BDAG TU SGRO ‘DOGS PA NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PAR ‘JOG PA DANG, NGA DANG NGA YI BA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA GNYIS ‘JIG LTAR ‘JOG PA RNAMS MNGON PA BA DANG MI MTHUN NO,,

As such, we can here establish “misunderstanding involved with negative emotions” as being the tendency to see a self-nature to entities which they don’t in fact possess.  And then we can establish, as being the view of destruction, the two tendencies to see “me” and “mine” as existing by definition.  This way of doing it is not shared with the presentation of the Higher Knowledge schools.


[1567]
MNGON PA BA’I LUGS KYIS NI MDZOD ‘GREL GYI GNAS DGU PA LAS BSHAD PA LTAR, GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA’I RDZAS SU YOD PAR ‘DZIN PA ‘JIG LTA NGAR ‘DZIN DANG, BDAG GI BA RNAMS GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD DE’I DBANG BSGYUR BYAR ‘DZIN PA NI, ‘JIG LTA BDAG GIR ‘DZIN PAR ‘JOG PA YIN TE CHES MI MTHUN [f. 118a] NO,,

And how do these Higher Knowledge schools make their presentation?  We can refer to the explanation that we see in the ninth chapter of the autocommentary to the Treasure House.  Here, first we establish the tendency to hold to some “me” as the view of destruction in the form of holding that the person is substantial, in the sense of being self-standing.  And then there is the view of destruction in the form of holding to some “mine”—which is established as the belief that the things belonging to this “me” are things which are under the control of a person who is themselves substantial.  As such, the two presentations are not at all shared.


[1568]
GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA’I RDZAS YOD DU ‘DZIN PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA LA YANG YOD MOD KYANG, GANG ZAG PHUNG PO DANG MTSAN NYID MI MTHUN PA’I GZHAN DU YOD PAR ‘DZIN PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA LA MED DO,,

Now we would admit that the tendency to hold the person as being substantial, in the sense of being self-standing, can also be possessed by a person whose mind has not been influenced by the teachings of some particular school of thought.  It is not the case though that someone whose mind has not been influenced in this way would ever hold that the person is other than the parts to the person, in the sense of being an entity with characteristics inconsistent with those of these parts.


[1569]
DE LTAR NA MTHAR ‘DZIN PAR LTA BA YANG GNYIS SO,,

Given all this, we can say that there are also two versions to the viewpoint which holds to philosophical extremes.


[1570]
GAL TE GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYOGS LA, DE LTAR ‘DZIN PA DE RNAMS NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA DANG, BDAG ‘DZIN GNYIS SU JI LTAR SGRUB CE NA,

One may ask the following question:

Let’s look at systems of thought which accept the idea that there do exist a person, and things, which exist by definition.  How do people who hold such views establish misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions, and the two ways of holding that things are themselves?


[1571]
GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA NI, DE ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA RNAMS KYIS KHEGS PAR ‘GYUR ZHING, DE’I TSE DE LTAR ‘DZIN PA DE ZHEN YUL LA ‘KHRUL PA’I BDEN ‘DZIN DU ‘GRUB LA, DE GRUB NA GANG ZAG DANG CHOS GNYIS BDEN GRUB TU ‘DZIN PA BDAG ‘DZIN GNYIS SU ‘GRUB BO,,

They refute the idea that the person & things could exist through some nature of their own by employing different forms of reasoning which disproves it.  They would establish, at this point, the tendency to hold these things this way as being a tendency to hold that things are real where we are mistaken about the object that we think we see.  Once this is established, they establish that the tendencies to hold the person and things as being real are what constitute the two forms of holding that things are themselves.


[1572]
DE RNAMS GRUB NA BDEN ‘DZIN DE DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON RIG PA’I ‘GAL BA MI MTHUN PHYOGS SU ‘GRUB PAS, MA RIG PAR ‘GRUB CING, DE MA ZAD PAR {%BAR} DU ‘JIG LTA YANG MI ‘DZAD PAR SGRUB NUS PAS, NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PAR ‘GRUB PAS NYON MONGS KYI RNAM GZHAG THUN MONG MA YIN PA ‘JOG SHES PA SHIN TU GAL CHE’O,,

Once these things are established, they can establish that the tendency to see things as real constitutes the direct, contradictory opposite of understanding suchness.  With this, they have established what constitutes misunderstanding.  Since we can prove that—until we finish this off—we could never finish off the view of destruction either, then once we have established what misunderstanding involved with negative emotions is, we can posit a unique presentation on the negative emotions.  Understanding all this is extremely important.


[1573]
‘DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA NYON MONGS GZHAN RNAMS KYANG BDEN ‘DZIN GYI GTI MUG LAS ‘JUG TSUL NI, BZHI BRGYA PA LAS,
,LUS LA LUS DBANG JI BZHIN DU,
,GTI MUG KUN LA GNAS ‘GYUR TE,

How do we describe the way in which desire & the rest—the other negative emotions—engage in their objects by way of that dark ignorance where we still hold that things are real?  As the 400 Verses puts it,

Dark ignorance abides
In all of them,

Just as the powers of the body
Reside throughout it.


[1574]
ZHES PA’I ‘GREL PA LAS, GTI MUG NI DE RNAMS JI LTAR BDEN PAR RTOGS PA [f. 118b] LAS RMONGS PA NYID KYI PHYIR, DNGOS PO BDEN PA’I RANG GI NGO BOR LHAG PAR SGRO ‘DOGS PAR RAB TU ‘JUG GO

The commentary to the 400 explains this as follows.  

Dark ignorance is completely ignorant of how to understand these things as they really are.  As such, it delves into objects seeing in them more than is there: believing that they they possess some essential nature of being real.


[1575]
,’DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA DAG KYANG GTI MUG GIS KUN TU BRTAGS PA’I DNGOS PO’I RANG BZHIN KHO NA LA, SDUG PA DANG MI SDUG PA LA SOGS PA’I KHYAD PAR SGRO ‘DOGS PAR ‘JUG PA

And then emotions such as desire as well engage, exclusively, in a nature to things which has been imputed to them by this dark ignorance, ascribing features such as being beautiful or being ugly—giving these details more reality than they have.


[1576]
NYID KYI PHYIR, GTI MUG LAS THA MI DAD PAR ‘JUG PAR ‘GYUR ZHING, GTI MUG LA BRTEN PAR YANG ‘GYUR TE, GTI MUG GTZO BO NYID KYI PHYIR RO,

And for this very reason, none of these emotions engages in their objects divorced from dark ignorance—they all rely upon this ignorance.  For dark ignorance, surely, is the lord of them all. 


[1577]
ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR BSHAD NA, ‘JUG GO ZHES PA YAN GYIS GTI MUG BDEN ‘DZIN DU STON NO,,

Using this citation as the basis of our explanation, we can say that the first of the three sections here is meant to indicate that what “dark ignorance” refers to is our tendency to believe that things are real.


[1578]
CHAGS SOGS RNAMS GTI MUG LAS THA MI DAD PAR ‘JUG PA NI, GTI MUG DANG MTSUNGS LDAN DU ‘JUG GI DE DANG BRAL BAR MI ‘JUG PA’O,,

When it says that none of the emotions such as attachment engages in its object divorced from dark ignorance, what it means is that they engage in their objects even as they share a mental link with this kind of ignorance; that is, they do not engage in their objects without it.


[1579]
DE’I RGYU MTSAN NI CHAGS SOGS NAS ‘JUG PA NYID KYI PHYIR ZHES PA YIN NO,,

And the reason why we can say this is expressed in the words, “for this very reason,”—because of the simple fact that attachment & the rest are engaging in the objects.


[1580]
DE LA YUL LA YID DU ‘ONG MI ‘ONG GI KHYAD PAR SGRO ‘DOGS PA NI CHAGS SDANG GNYIS SKYE BA’I RGYU TSUL MIN YID BYED YIN PAS, CHAGS SDANG GNYIS KYI ‘DZIN STANGS STON PA MIN NO,,

Now what does it mean when we say that these emotions are “ascribing features such as being attractive or being unattractive to their objects, giving these things more reality than they have”?  Given that attending to objects in an incorrect manner is the cause for both attachment & repulsion to grow, these words are not meant to describe the way in which the pair of attachment & repulsion hold their object to be.  


[1581]
DES NA GTI MUG GIS KUN BRTAGS PA KHO NA LA ZHES SOGS NI, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHO NA’I YID DU ‘ONG MI ‘ONG SGRO BTAGS PA LA BRTEN NAS CHAGS SDANG GNYIS ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’O,,

And thus the words “engage, exclusively, in a nature to things which has been imputed to them by this dark ignorance.”  What this is saying is that attachment & repulsion can only engage in objects that are attractive or unattractive in a way which makes them more real than they are: these objects are exclusively those that would be existing through some nature of their own.


[1582]
GTI MUG GIS BTAGS PA’I BDEN GRUB KHO NA CHAGS SOGS KYI DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI NANG NAS DMIGS PAR STON PA MIN TE, BDAG ‘DZIN LHAN SKYES GNYIS KA’I DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI DMIGS PA GZHI GRUB PA YIN LA, CHAGS SOGS KYANG GTI [f. 119a] MUG DANG MTSUNGS LDAN YIN PAS DMIGS PA MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This is not to say though that it is only the real existence imputed by dark ignorance which can serve as one of the things belonging to the two sets of objects perceived by attachment or the like.  For objects in the form of the two aspects of objects perceived by both the inborn forms of the tendency to believe that things are themselves are in fact existing entitites.  And since the attachment or whatever shares a mental link with the dark ignorance, the objects of the two are also shared.


[1583]
TSUL MIN YID BYED DE GNYIS KYIS DRANGS PA’I YUL LA ‘DOD PA’I RNAM PA CAN DANG, MI ‘DOD PA RGYAB KYIS PHYOGS PA’I RNAM PA CAN NI, CHAGS PA DANG SDANG BAR ‘GYUR BAS,

And so there are two kinds of “attending to objects in an incorrect manner” here; and the objects they elicit take on an aspect of being desirable, or being the opposite: undesirable.  This then is what leads to the attachment or the repulsion.


[1584]
GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA’I RDZAS YOD DU ‘DZIN PAS DRANGS PA’I ‘DOD MI ‘DOD KYI RNAM PA CAN TZAM ZHIG ,’DOD CHAGS DANG ZHE SDANG DU ‘JOG PA MIN PA’I PHYIR, CHAGS SDANG GNYIS KYANG ‘JOG TSUL MI ‘DRA’O,,

When we hold objects to be substantial, in the sense of being self-standing, this again elicits in those objects an aspect of being desirable or undesirable; but this in itself is not enough to call the attendant emotions desire or hatred.  As such, the way we establish something as being attachment or repulsion in this case would as well be different.


[1585]
GTI MUG LA BRTEN PAR YANG ‘GYUR TE ZHES PA NI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I GTI MUG SNGON DU SONG BAS CHAGS SOGS ‘DREN PA’I DON NO,,

Now when the citation states that “they all rely upon this ignorance,” the point is that dark ignorance where we hold that things exist by definition comes first, and then this elicits the attachment or whatever it may be.


[1586]
LUS LA LUS DBANG ZHES PA’I DPE NI, DBANG PO GZHAN BZHI LA LUS DBANG ZUR DU BZHAG PA’I RTEN MED PA BZHIN DU, NYON MONGS GZHAN THAMS CAD KYANG GTI MUG LA BRTEN NAS ‘JUG CING, DE DANG MI ‘BRAL BAR ‘JUG PA’I DON NO,,

Let’s return to that metaphor of the “powers of the body throughout the body.”  What this refers to is the fact that the other four physical powers have no home base apart from the power of the body.  Just so, all the other negative emotions too rely, upon dark ignorance, in order to engage in their various objects—and cannot engage divorced from this ignorance. 


[1587]
DES NA GTI MUG BCOM PA NYID KYIS NYON MONGS THAMS CAD ‘JOMS PAR ‘GYUR BAS, ‘DI’I GNYEN PO RTEN ‘BYUNG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA’I GTAM NYID LA GUS PAR BYA BAR GSUNGS SO,,

As such, the one & only way to destroy all our negative emotions is to destroy dark ignorance.  And because of that, the text is saying, we should honor this one antidote to the ignorance: the teachings upon dependence, the fact that things are empty of existing through any nature of their own.


[1588]
DNGOS PO BDEN ‘DZIN ‘DI NI ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BA’I MA RIG PAR YANG STONG NYID BDUN CU PA LAS GSUNGS SHING, RIGS PA DRUG CU PA LAS KYANG, 
,GANG YANG RUNG BA’I GNAS RNYED NA,
,NYON MONGS SBRUL GDUG G-YO CAN GYIS,
,ZIN PAR ‘GYUR RO GANG GI SEMS,
,GNAS MED DE DAG ZIN MI ‘GYUR,

The Seventy Verses also states that this tendency of holding things to be real constitutes the misunderstanding which is the root of the cycle of pain.  And the Sixty Verses says as well,

If some opportunity
Or another is found,

Then the deadly, devious viper
Of the negative emotions
Will catch us.

Those who never go
To this place
Will never be caught.


[1589]
ZHES BDEN [f. 119b] ‘DZIN GYI DMIGS GTAD GANG YANG RUNG BA’I GNAS SHIG RNYED NA, NYON MONGS PA’I SBRUL GYIS ‘DZIN PAR GSUNGS SHING,

What this is saying is that—when you come to any place at all where the tendency to believe things are real is seeing things—then you can be caught by the viper of the negative emotions.


[1590]
YANG DE NYID KYI MJUG THOGS SU,
,GNAS DANG BCAS PA’I SEMS LDAN LA,
,NYON MONGS DUG CHEN CIS MI ‘BYUNG,
,ZHES GSUNGS PAS ‘DI NI ‘PHAGS PA’I BZHED PA DAM PA’O,,

In its very next words, the Sixty then says:

Why wouldn’t the great venom
Of the negative emotions

Rise within a person
Who possesses a state of mind
With an opportunity?


[1591]
RKANG PA PHYI MA GNYIS KYI MTSAMS SBYOR DU, GANG DAG GZUGS LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYI RANG BZHIN DMIGS KYANG, NYON MONGS PA RNAMS SPONG BAR ‘DOD PA DE DAG LA NI, NYON MONGS PA SPONG BA MI SRID PA NYID DO ZHES BSTEN {%BSTAN} PA’I PHYIR GSUNGS PA ZHES DANG,

In tying these latter lines to the rest, we see the following:

Suppose a person perceives some kind of nature to things like physical form or the like.  They may even be someone who truly hopes to rid themselves of the negative emotions—but for them, eliminating these emotions will be a complete impossibility.


[1592]
PHYI ‘GREL LAS KYANG, DNGOS POR DMIGS PA YIN NA NI ‘DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA’I NYON MONGS PA RAB ‘BYAMS NGES PAR BZLOG TU MED PA RNAMS ‘BYUNG NGO,,

Subsequent comments here repeat—

And if they are seeing things as things, then ignorant liking & the rest—a whole myriad of negative emotions—will spring forth; and they will not be something that could ever be stopped.


[1593]
JI LTAR ZHE NA, RE ZHIG GAL TE DNGOS PO DE YID DANG MTHUN PA YIN NA NI, DE’I TSE DE LA RJES SU CHAGS PA BZLOG PAR DKA’O, ,CI STE MI MTHUN NA NI DE’I TSE DE LA KHONG KHRO NGA {%BA} DANG TSIG PA ZA BA BZLOG PAR DKA’O, ZHES GSUNGS SHING,

And how is that?  If at the moment these things fit the mind, then it will be difficult to stop desire for them.  If they do not, then it will be difficult to stop repulsion, and anger, for them.


[1594]
YUL DE YID DU ‘ONG MI ‘ONG GANG YANG MIN PA ZHIG NA’ANG MA RIG PA SKYE BAR ‘GREL PA LAS GSUNGS TE, YUL DE RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA CIG RGYUD LA ‘JUG BZHIN PA NA, YANG NA ‘DOD CHAGS, YANG NA ZHE SDANG SKYE DE GNYIS MIN NA’ANG GTI MUG GI RIGS ‘DRA ‘JUG PAR BZHED LA,

The commentary also says that misunderstanding will still arise even in a case where the object is neither attractive nor unattractive; for it takes the position that, so long as any tendency to hold things as existing by definition is operating within the mind, then desire or repulsion will arise and—even if neither does, at the moment—then a continued form of the dark ignorance will be in operation.


[1595]
SPYOD ‘JUG LAS KYANG,
,DMIGS PA DANG NI BCAS PA’I SEMS,
,’GA’ ZHIG LA NI GNAS PAR ‘GYUR,
,STONG PA NYID DANG BRAL BA’I SEMS,
,’GAGS PA SLAR [f. 120a] YANG SKYE ‘GYUR TE,
,’DU SHES MED PA’I SNYOMS ‘JUG BZHIN,

The Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life puts it this way:

It resides in any number
Of states of mind
Which still hold to this object;

And even stopped
It will rise again,
In a mind devoid of emptiness.

It’s just like the concentration
Where we stop discrimination.


[1596]
