ZHES GSUNGS TE PHYOGS ‘DI LA SLOB DPON ‘DI GNYIS DANG SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS GSUM ‘PHAGS PA’I DGONGS PA ‘GREL PA LA KHYAD PAR MED DO,

On this issue, there is no difference at all in the way these three masters—the two mentioned here, and Buddha Palita—comment upon the thinking of the Arya.


[1597]
‘DI’I GNAD KYIS MI RTAG SOGS BCU DRUG GI LAM TZAM GYIS MYA NGAN LAS ‘DA’ BAR BSHAD PA NI DGONGS PA CAN YIN LA, LAM DE’I DBANG DU BYAS PA’I NYON MONGS KYI NGOS ‘DZIN RNAMS KYANG LHAG MA DANG BCAS PA YIN NO,,

Given this particular crucial point, the explanation that it is only through the path of the 16 aspects of impermanence and so on that we can achieve nirvana is shown to be figurative.  Methods of identifying the negative emotions relative to this path also refer to nirvana where something is still left over.


[1598]
DE DAG LA BRTEN NAS NGA RGYAL SOGS KYANG SHES PAR NUS LA, THUN MONG MA YIN PA’I MA RIG PA DANG ‘JIG LTA DANG MTHAR LTA LA YANG KUN BRTAGS DANG LHAN SKYES GNYIS KA SHES PAR BYA STE TSIG MANGS SU DOGS NAS MA BRIS SO,,

Based on our presentation so far, you can understand the situation with other negative emotions, such as pride.  You can also understand that there are learned & innate forms of this unique form of misunderstanding; and to the view of destruction; and to extreme views.  It is only out of fear for going on too long that I will avoid describing these details here in the present work.


[1599]
DE BZHIN DU CHOS RNAMS BDEN GRUB TU ‘DZIN PA’I RNAM RTOG LA SGOM SPANG CHE ‘BRING DGUR BYAS NAS, GNYEN PO SGOM LAM DGU DANG SBYOR BA YANG,

In the same manner, there has been presented a division of the misperception where we hold all objects to exist in truth into nine different states of mind that we must rid ourselves of during the path of habituation, based on whether they are greater or middling.  These are then matched to nine different antidotes during this path of habituation.


[1600]
GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD DU ‘DZIN PA’I RNAM RTOG LA SGOM SPANG CHE ‘BRING DGUR BYAS NAS, SGOM LAM DGU DANG SPANG GNYEN DU SBYOR BAR BSHAD PA BZHIN DU,

These are similar to explanations in which misperceptions where we hold that object states & subject states are of a different substance are also divided into nine elements that we must rid ourselves of on the path of habituation; again, with greater or middling versions.  And then these are matched to nine components of the path of habituation itself, as antidotes which would allow us to rid ourselves of the nine misperceptions.


[1601]
RE ZHIG LA CHOS KYI BDAG MED PHRA RAGS GNYIS KA RDZOGS PAR RTOGS MI NUS PA’I GDUL BYA ‘GA’ ZHIG GI NGOR GSUNGS PA’I DRANG BA’I DON DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Understand, again, that these though were not meant literally; they are pronouncements that were only meant for a number of disciples who, at that moment, were incapable of grasping, completely, both the subtle and gross forms of the lack of a self-nature to things.



Deception makes its appearance

[1602]
GNYIS PA NI,

Here is our second point from above, which is how the simple deception either makes its appearance, or does not make its appearance, to three different types of individuals.


[1603]
DNGOS PO ‘DI DAG KYANG BYIS PA RNAMS LA NI RANG BZHIN MED BZHIN DU DER SNANG BAS SLU BAR BYED LA, DE DAG LAS GZHAN SNGAR BSHAD PA’I GANG ZAG GSUM LA NI, BCOS MAR GYUR PA’I DNGOS PO’I RTEN [f. 120b] CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA NYID KYIS NI KUN RDZOB TZAM DU ‘GYUR GYI BDEN PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

These things, moreover, make their appearance to infants as though they had some nature of their own, even as they possess no such nature; that is, they deceive these people.  But to people other than these—which is to say, to the three types of individuals we mentioned above—the things exist as simply deceptive, through occurring in the dependent relationship of entities which are artificial.  They do not occur in any way which is true.


[1604]
DE YANG SHES SGRIB KYI MTSAN NYID CAN GYI NYON MONGS CAN MA YIN PA’I MA RIG PA TZAM KUN TU SPYOD PA’I PHYIR, MA RIG PA DANG DE’I BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD PA’I SNANG BA DANG BCAS PA’I SPYOD YUL CAN GYI RJES THOB LA GNAS PA’I ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS LA SNANG GI, ‘PHAGS PA SNANG BA MED PA’I SPYOD YUL MNGA’ BA MNYAM GZHAG LA GNAS PA RNAMS LA NI SNANG BA MIN NO,,

These things make their appearance to realized beings who are in the aftermath period; to those who minds are engaging in objects where there is still an appearance infected by misunderstanding and its deep seeds.  And this is because they still engage habitually through simple misunderstanding which is not involved with nedgative emotions; rather, it displays the defining characteristics of an obstacle to omniscience.  It is not though the case that these same objects make their appearance to realized beings who possess an object of engagement where there is no impression of self-existence; that is to say, to such beings who are still in that particular deep, balanced meditation.


[1605]
‘O NA LUGS ‘DIS SHES SGRIB GANG LA BYED CE NA,

At this point, one may ask—

Well then, in this system what is it that they consider an obstacle to omniscience?


[1606]
‘JUG ‘GREL LAS, DE LA MA RIG PA’I BAG CHAGS NI SHES BYA YONGS SU GCOD PA’I GEGS SU GYUR PA YIN LA, ‘DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA’I BAG CHAGS YOD PA NI LUS DANG NGAG DAG GI ‘JUG PA DE LTA BU’I RGYU YANG YIN TE, MA RIG PA DANG ‘DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA’I BAG CHAGS DE YANG RNAM PA THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA DANG, SANGS RGYAS KHO NA LA LDOG PAR ‘GYUR GYI, GZHAN DAG LA NI MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR TE,

The case here is as we see it described in the autocommentary:

As for this, the deep seeds for misunderstanding act as an obstacle to separating out all knowable things; when we still possess the deep seeds for desire and the rest, they further act as a cause for engagement of this type by the two of body & speech.  The deep seeds for misunderstanding and desire and the like prevent only the state of omniscience, and enlightenment; but they do not stop the others.


[1607]
LUS DANG NGAG GI ‘JUG PA NI DGRA BCOM PA LA YOD PA SPRE’U LTAR MCHONG BA DANG, GZHAN LA RMANGS MO ZHES ZER BA’I LUS NGAG GI GNAS NGAN LEN STON PAS BKAG KYANG MA LOG PA LTA BU YIN NO,,

When the text here mentions that “engagement of body & speech” are possessed by an enemy destroyer, it refers to slight negative tendencies such as hopping like a monkey, or calling somebody a “housmaid.”  These were prohibited by the Teacher but in these cases the person has not been able to fully stop doing them.


[1608]
YANG ZHES PAS CHAGS SOGS KYI BAG CHAGS SHES BYA GCOD PA’I GEGS SU YANG BSTAN PAS, NYON MONGS PA’I BAG CHAGS RNAMS SHES SGRIB YIN TE, DE’I ‘BRAS BU GNYIS SNANG ‘KHRUL PA’I CHA THAMS CAD KYANG DER BSDU’O,,

When the text here says “further” act, it is indicating that deep seeds such as attachment and the like are as well obstacles to separating out all knowable things.  Thus we can say that the deep seeds for what is involved with negative emotions are obstacles to knowledge.  And as for their results, all states where we make errors due to the discrepancy between what is actually there and what appears to be there can be included here.


[1609]
NYON MONGS KYI SA BON LA BAG CHAGS SU BZHAG PA [f. 121a] CIG DANG, NYON MONGS KYI SA BON MIN PA’I BAG CHAGS GNYIS LAS SHES SGRIB TU ‘JOG PA NI PHYI MA STE, NYON MONGS KYI SA BON THAMS CAD ZAD PAS BDEN ‘DZIN MI SKYE YANG, BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD PAS SNANG YUL LA ‘KHRUL PA’I BLO SKYED PA’O,,

Deep seeds can be divided into two types: those which can be classified as seeds for negative emotions, and those which are not seeds for negative emotions.  Those that we classify as obstacles to knowledge are the latter.  That is, when we have finished off all our seeds for negative emotions, the tendency to hold things as real no longer arises; but because we are still infected by deep seeds, we do experience the arisal of states of mind that are mistaken towards the object as it appears to them.


[1610]
SANGS MA RGYAS PA’I ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS NI SHES SGRIB KYI MA RIG PA MA SPANGS PAS, RJES THOB KYI SNANG BCAS KYI RTOG PA DANG, MNYAM GZHAG TU SNANG MED DU ‘GYUR BA’I RES ‘JOG YOD LA,

Realized beings who are not yet enlightened have not yet eliminated misunderstanding in the form of an obstacle to knowledge; as such, they can experience an alternation of their mental state between perceptions—during the aftermath period—where they still have the appearance of things existing in truth; and those during that deep meditation, where this appearance is no longer there.


[1611]
SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS NI CHOS THAMS CAD KYI DON DAM PA DANG KUN RDZOB PA’I RNAM PA MNGON PAR TE MNGON DU GYUR PAR RDZOGS PAR TE MA LUS PAR, BYANG CHUB PA STE RTOGS PA’I PHYIR SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG GI RNAM RTOG GI RGYU BA THAMS CAD GTAN LOG PAS, MNYAM GZHAG DANG RJES THOB KYI SNANG BA’I RTOG PA YOD MED RES ‘JOG PA MED DO,,

For those who are enlightened, both the ultimate aspects of all existing entities, and their deceptive aspects as well, are evident: are experienced in a completely manifest manner—meaning that they are enlightened in their entirety, in their realizations.  And this means that the entire circulation of wrong ideas with their mind & mental functions is shut down completely, and permanently.  As such there is no alternation—in their case—between ideas of self-existence or a lack of these ideas, depending on whether they are in that deep meditation, or in the aftermath period.


[1612]
GTAN ZHES PA’I TSIG GIS ‘PHAGS PA GZHAN LA MNYAM GZHAG TU LOG PA NI RES ‘GA’ BAR STON LA, DE’I PHYIR MNYAM RJES RES ‘JOG PA YOD DO,,

When we use the word “permanently” in this last section, it is meant to indicate that—for other realized beings—the stopping of those thoughts during the deep meditation is a state which then fluctuates; and this is why we say that they alternate between deep meditation and its aftermath.


[1613]
DES NA SHES SGRIB KYI MA RIG PA SPYOD PA’I PHYIR, ZHES PA NI SNANG BA YOD PA’I RGYU MTSAN MIN GYI, MNYAM RJES SU SNANG BA YOD MED RES ‘JOG TU ‘BYUNG BA’I SGRUB BYED DO,,

Therefore when we speak of “misunderstanding engaging in the form of an obstacle to knowledge,” it’s not because there is an appearance of things as being self-existence; rather, we are simply establishing that things are alternating at that point: one possesses, and then doesn’t possess, an appearance of things as self-existent, in states inside of the deep meditation and then subsequent to that state.


[1614]
SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG GI RGYU BA NI RNAM RTOG LA BZHED PA YIN TE, TSIG GSAL LAS, RNAM PAR RTOG PA NI SEMS KYI RGYU BA YIN NA DE DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR, DE KHO NA NYID DE NI RNAM PAR RTOG PA MED PA YIN NO,,
JI SKAD DU MDO LAS, DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA GANG ZHE NA, GANG LA [f. 121b] SEMS KYI RGYU BA YANG MED NA, YI GE RNAMS LTA SMOS KYANG CI DGOS ZHES GSUNGS SO, ZHES BSHAD DO,,

It’s being accepted that when in this case we talk about “the circulation of mind & mental functions,” it involves wrong ideas; as A Clarification of the Verses explains it—

If wrong ideas involve the circulation of the mind, then with suchness there are no wrong ideas, since at that point we are free of any such circulation.  As sutra itself puts it, “What then is ultimate reality?  It is a state where there is not even any circulation of the mind; what need mention then that there could be no syllables there?”



Ultimate reality, to a common being

[1615]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third step from above: a description of the way in which things can become either ultimate or deceptive, relative to a common being, or a realized being.


[1616]
DE LA SO SO’I SKYE BO RNAMS KYI DON DAM PA GANG YIN PA DE NYID, ‘PHAGS PA SNANG BA DANG BCAS PA’I SPYOD YUL CAN RNAMS KYI KUN RDZOB TZAM YIN LA, DE’I RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI DE RNAMS KYI DON DAM PA’O, ZHES GSUNGS PA’I

Let’s consider then what is ultimate reality to common beings; that same thing is nothing more than deceptive reality to realized beings who are engaging in an object of perception while still seeing it appear to them as self-existent.  And yet still, whatever nature these things have of being emptiness “is, for them, ultimate reality.”


[1617]
SNGA MA’I DON NI, SO SKYES DON DAM PAR GRUB PAR BZUNG BA’I BUM SOGS DE NYID, SNGAR BSHAD PA’I ‘PHAGS PA GSUM MNYAM GZHAG LAS LANGS PA’I RJES THOB SNANG BA CAN RNAMS KYI KUN RDZOB TZAM YIN PAR BSTAN PAS,

What the first part of this last statement is saying is that those same objects which common beings hold to exist in an ultimate way—water pitchers and the like—are nothing more than deceptive objects for perceptions of the three types of realized beings described before who have come out of their deep meditation on emptiness, and to whom objects are appearing in a self-existent way.
 

[1618]
DE RNAMS KYI NGOR BDEN PA TZAM GCOD KYI KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN PA MI GCOD CING, SO SKYES BUM SOGS LA DON DAM DU GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I ZHEN YUL ‘PHAGS PA LA KUN RDZOB TU ‘GYUR BAR STON PA MIN TE DE MI SRID PA’I PHYIR RO,,

To their perceptions, deceptive reality in the form of the simple exclusion of a thing having real existence is not itself prevented; and we are not saying that, to a realized being, the things that common beings believe are there when they hold a water pitcher or the like to exist ultimately are present in a deceptive way—for that would be impossible.


[1619]
GZHUNG PHYI MA’I DON NI RTEN ‘BREL KUN RDZOB PA’I RANG BZHIN CHOS NYID ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYI DON DAM PAR STON PAS BUM PA LA SOGS PA’I GZHI GCIG NYID, SO SKYE LA LTOS NAS KUN RDZOB DANG, ‘PHAGS PA LA LTOS NAS DON DAM MO, ZHES GZHUNG LAS PHYIN CI LOG TU BZLOG STE SMRA BA NI, BLO GANG GI NGOR KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR SONG BA DE’I NGOR BDEN PA KHEGS DGOS PA MA SHES PA’I GTAM MO,,

The point of the latter part of that last statement is to indicate that the very nature of things—in the form of dependent events being the nature of the deception—is what the ultimate is, for realized beings.  As such, let us consider the position where someone states that nothing more than a single instance of a water pitcher, or the like, could at the same time be deceptive to a common being, and ultimate to a realized being.  This is a reversal of the whole idea of scripture at this juncture; this kind of talk reflects a failure to understand the idea that—once something represents deceptive reality appearing to a particular state of mind—this necessarily disallows the idea that the same object could represent truth to the same state of mind.


[1620]
SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYI DON DAM PA NI RANG BZHIN NYID YIN ZHING, DE YANG SLU BA MED PA NYID KYIS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA YIN LA, DE NI DE RNAMS KYIS SO SO RANG GIS RIG PAR BYA BA YIN NO, ZHES [f. 122a] GSUNGS SO,,

As the scripture itself states,

What represents the ultimate for the Enlightened Ones is the one true nature of things; and this is the ultimate form of reality, for it can never deceive us.  And this is what that one thing which these beings, each one, realize really is.


[1621]
RANG BZHIN NYID YIN ZHING ZHES PA’I NYID KYI SGRA NI NGES GZUNG YIN LA, DES GANG GCOD PA NI ‘PHAGS PA GZHAN RNAMS KYI DON DAM BDEN PA NI MNYAM GZHAG TU SNANG MED KYI RANG BZHIN DANG, RJES THOB TU SNANG BCAS KYI RANG BZHIN DU ‘JOG PA LTA BU’I RES ‘JOG MIN PAR, DUS RTAG TU RANG BZHIN LA MNYAM PAR BZHAG PA’I CHOS NYID YIN ZHES PA’O,,

The “one true” in the expression here, “it is the one true nature of things,” is meant in a sense of unique identification; that is, it is meant to exclude something else: a kind of alternating back and forth, where—for other realized beings—ultimate reality might be said to have a nature of not appearing to be self-existent during that deep meditation, and then appearing to be self-existent during the aftermath of the meditation.  And so what the expression is meant to say is that it is the very nature of things for someone who is at all times, for all eternity, within that deep meditation on the way things are.


[1622]
DE YANG ZHES SOGS KYI DON NI DON DAM BDEN PA’I BDEN PA DE BDEN GRUB MA YIN PAR BSTAN PAR BZHED NAS, DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA’I NGOR SLU BA MED PAR GNAS PA BDEN PA’I DON DU BSHAD DO,,

Moreover, the part in this citation which begins with “and this is” is meant by the author to indicate that the reality in ultimate reality is not something which exists really: what he’s saying is that what it means to be “real” is where—to the perceptions of these beings as they view suchness—things exist in a way where they are no longer deceiving anyone.



Not, in fact, indescribable

[1623]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, RTZA BA’I TSIG DON BSHAD PA DANG, DE LA RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: an explanation of that reality which is ultimate.  We proceed in two steps: an explanation of the words of the root text at this point, and then a refutation of argument concerning their meaning.  Here is the first.


[1624]
DE NI DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA BSTAN PAR ‘DOD PAS, DON DAM BDEN PA DE NI SGRAS BRJOD DU MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, SGRA DE’I RJES SU ‘BRANG BA’I SHES PA’I YUL MA YIN PA NYID KYI PHYIR, DNGOS SU BSTAN PAR MI NUS PAS NYAN ‘DOD PA RNAMS LA DE’I RANG BZHIN GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU SO SKYE RANG GIS MYONG BA’I DPE BSHAD PA,

What this is talking about is the following.  What we hope to present is the idea of a reality which is ultimate; but ultimate reality is not something that one can describe in words; neither will it act as an object of the state of mind which follows upon such words.  As such, this reality is not something that we could describe in a direct manner; and so to elucidate its nature to those who wish to hear more about it, we will need to employ an example which is something that common beings have some experience of.


[1625]
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I SHES BRJOD KYI YUL MIN PA’I DON NI DNGOS SU BSTAN PAR MI NUS PAS ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR TE, DE YANG NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS MNGON SUM DU BSTAN PAR MI NUS ZHES ‘BYUNG BA’O,,

When this kind of statement indicates that ultimate reality cannot be an object of either knowledge or expression, it’s in effect saying, “Because it cannot be directly indicated.”  In fact, Naktso’s translation at this point says “It is not something which can be indicated directly.”


[1626]
DE’I DON NI DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON GZHAN LAS SHES PAR BYA BA MIN PAR GSUNGS PA’I ‘GREL PA TSIG GSAL LAS, JI LTAR RAB RIB CAN DAG GIS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA’I NGO BO PHYIN CI LOG PA [f. 122b] MTHONG BA NA, RAB RIB MED PAS BSTAN DU ZIN KYANG, RAB RIB MED PA LTAR SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA RANG GI NGO BO MA MTHONG BA’I TSUL GYIS, RTOGS PAR BYA BA JI LTAR GNAS PA BZHIN RTOGS PAR MI NUS KYI,

The point here is explained by A Clarification of the Verses, commenting upon statements that the meaning of suchness is not something that can be learned from others:

Suppose that those with cataracts see, mistakenly, something with the nature of a strand of hair, or the like.  Someone who has no such cataracts can explain the situation to them, but still they will not be able to stop themselves from seeing the thing as having the nature of a hair or the like.  As such, we say that a person is unable to understand something in the same way it exists for someone who does understand the thing; but rather…


[1627]
ZHES RAB RIB CAN LA RAB RIB MED PAS SKRA SHAD MED DO ZHES BSTAN KYANG, RAB RIB MED PAS MTHONG BA ‘DRA BA’I SKRA SHAD MED PA MI RTOGS PAR GSUNGS PAS, NYAN PA POS DE LTAR MA RTOGS KYANG SKRA SHAD MED PA MI RTOGS PA MIN NO,,

What this is saying is that a person who has no cataracts can say to a person who still does have them, “There’s no strand of hair there!”—but the latter person will not be able to realize the lack of a hair there in the same way that the person with no cataracts sees this.  We can say though that even though the person listening to the correct explanation cannot realize this object in the same way, it’s not though the case that they have no realization at all then that there is no hair there.


[1628]
DE DPER BYAS NAS DE KHO NA NYID BSTAN PA MA RIG PA’I RAB RIB KYI BSLAD PA DANG BRAL BAS MTHONG BA ‘DRA BA CIG MI RTOGS KYANG, SPYIR DE KHO NA NYID MI RTOGS PA MIN PAR BZHED PAS NA,

We use this situation then as a metaphor for teaching someone about suchness.  Even though this person will not realize the actual situation in the same way as a person who is free of any perceptual infection by the cataracts of misunderstanding, we would still say that they are not—generally speaking—a person who has no understanding of suchness at all.


[1629]
DON DAM BDEN PA NI ZAB MO’I DON CAN GYI NGES DON GYI LUNG DANG, DE LTAR STON PA’I NGAG GIS BRJOD MI NUS PA DANG, DE’I RJES SU ‘BRANG BA’I BLOS KYANG RTOGS MI NUS PA MIN TE, DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON SHES BRJOD KYI YUL MIN PAR GSUNGS PA THAMS CAD LA YANG DE BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Thus then we can say that it is not the case that ultimate reality is not something which can be described through teachings which address the profound nature of things in a literal manner; or that this reality could never be elucidated in speech which describes it in this way; or that it would be impossible to grasp with a state of mind following after such descriptions.  You should understand then all such references—those which say that the meaning of suchness is not an object perceivable through thought or description—in the same way as we have described it here.


The ultimate reality of the Buddhas

	[1630]
	[VI.29]
Vikalpitaṃ yat timira prabhāvāt
Keśādi rūpaṃ vitathaṃ tad eva,
Yenātmanā paśyati śuddha dṛṣṭis
tat tattvam ityevam ihāpyavaihi.

,RAB RIB MTHU YIS SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA’I,
,NGO BO LOG PA GANG ZHIG RNAM BRTAGS PA,
,DE NYID BDAG NYID GANG DU MIG DAG PAS,
,MTHONG DE DE NYID DE BZHIN ‘DIR SHES KYIS {%GYIS},

	Suppose that a person,
	Due to some cataracts,
	Thinks they see something
	As different than it really is:

	They perceive a strand
	Of hair, or something of the like.

	And now suppose a person
	With clear eyes looks down
	Where those actual things
	Are supposed to be.
	
	They are the one
	Who sees the real;

	Understand the case here
	As being the same.


[1631]
MIG RAB RIB KYIS BSLAD PA’I MTHU YIS RAB RIB CAN GYIS RANG GI LAG GI BSE RU LA SOGS PA’I BZA’ BTUNG GI SNOD KYI NANG DU, SKRA SHAD DANG LA SOGS PAS SBRANG MA LA SOGS PA MTHONG BA NA,

Suppose then that—due to the fact that a person’s eyes are infected with some cataracts—a person who possesses such optical defects looks into a cup of horn held in their hand (or any similar vessel for eating or drinking), and perceives there a strand of hair “or something of the like” (which words indicate anything similar perceived inside the cup; say, a fly or the like).


[1632]
SKRA SHAD DANG SBRANG MA SOGS YIN PAR NGO BO LOG PA GANG ZHIG RNAM PAR BRTAGS PA NA, DE BSAL BAR ‘DOD NAS SNOD DE LA YANG DANG YANG DU BSGRE BZLOG BYED PA’I TSEGS THOB PAR RIG STE,

When they think that they see something then, as different than it really is—when they see the hair or the fly or whatever it may be—then naturally they would want to get it out of the cup, and so it would be completely appropriate for them to go to the trouble of turning the cup upside down and knocking it against the table repeatedly, to get the unwanted thing out.


[1633]
MIG DAG PA’I RAB RIB MED PAS DE’I GAN DU PHYIN NAS, SKRA SHAD SOGS DE DAG NYID KYI BDAG NYID GZHI GANG DU MTHONG BA DER MIG GTAD [f. 123a] KYANG SKRA SHAD KYI RNAM PA DE DAG MA DMIGS SHING, SKRA SHAD DE’I RTEN CAN TE KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS GANG YANG RTOG PAR MI BYED DO,,

And then suppose that a person with clear eyes—someone without any cataracts—walks over to this other fellow and looks down to the spot where the first person thought they saw one of those actual things: the strand of hair or the like.  


[1634]
YANG GANG GI TSE RAB RIB CAN GYIS RAB RIB MED PA LA, SKRA SHAD MTHONG NGO ZHES RANG GI BSAM PA STON PAR BYED PA DE’I TSE,

And suppose then that the person with the cataracts expresses what they think to the person who has no cataracts: “I see a strand of hair there.”


[1635]
RAB RIB CAN GYI RNAM RTOG BSAL BAR ‘DOD PAS DE’I NGOR BYAS NAS, ‘DI NA SKRA SHAD MED DO ZHES DGAG PA LHUR BYED PA’I TSIG SMRA MOD KYANG, SMRA BA PO ‘DI LA SKRA SHAD LA SKUR PA ‘DEBS PA MED DO,,

This other person will naturally then want to clear up the misperception that the one with the cataracts is having, and will do their very best to say something to help them stop their mistake: “But look, actually there’s no strand of hair there at all.”  We could not though in this case say that the speaker was trying to deny a hair that was actually there.


[1636]
RAB RIB CAN GYIS MTHONG BA’I SKRA SHAD KYI DE KHO NA NYID NI, RAB RIB MED PAS MTHONG BA DE YIN GYI, RAB RIB CAN GYIS MTHONG BA DE MIN NO,,

The one who sees the real nature—the suchness—of the hair that the person with the cataracts perceives is the person without the cataracts; it is not in fact something that the person with the cataracts is capable of perceiving.


[1637]
DPE GNYIS PO DE BZHIN DU DON GYI SKABS ‘DIR SHES PAR GYIS SHIG

Understand the case here as being the same, as we’ve described it with the referents of our two examples.


[1638]
,SHES PAR BYED TSUL NI, MA RIG PA’I RAB RIB KYIS GNOD PA BYAS PA STE BLO BSLAD PAS DE KHO NA NYID MA MTHONG BA RNAMS KYIS, PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED LA SOGS PA’I RANG GI NGO BO DMIGS PA NI, PHUNG SOGS DE DAG GI NGO BO KUN RDZOB PA STE RAB RIB CAN GYIS SKRA SHAD DMIGS PA LTA BU’O,,

And just how should we accomplish this understanding?  Those who are being hurt by the cataracts of misunderstanding—those whose minds are infected—cannot see the real nature of things: their suchness.  When they look upon the nature of the parts of a person; and the categories of things; and the doors of sense and all of the like, they see the nature of these things that deceives.  They are just like those people with cataracts, who perceive a strand of hair.


[1639]
PHUNG PO LA SOGS PA DE NYID MA MTHONG BAS DMIGS PA DE DAG NYID, MA RIG PA’I BAG CHAGS SHES SGRIB DANG BRAL BA’I SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS,

But let’s consider, instead, those who do not see these same parts to a person, and the rest.  Here we are talking about the Buddhas, who are considering these same objects, but free of the obstacles to knowledge: free of the deep seeds for misunderstanding.


[1640]
RAB RIB CAN MA YIN PA’I MIG GIS SKRA SHAD MA MTHONG BA’I TSUL DU, PHUNG SOGS KYI RANG BZHIN GANG DU GZIGS PA’I YUL DE NI SANGS RGYAS DE RNAMS KYI DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA’O,,

They are considering these things just as the person whose eyes have no cataracts, and who sees no strands of hair.  They look at the same thing—the same parts of the person and so on that were seen as having some nature of their own—and perceive it as the ultimate reality of the Buddhas.



Knowing by failing to see

[1641]
GNYIS PA NI,

This then brings us to our second point from above: refuting rebuttal upon the points we’ve made.


[1642]
GAL TE RAB RIB MED PA’I MIG GIS SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA TZAM YANG MA MTHONG BA BZHIN DU, SANGS [f. 123b] RGYAS KYIS MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA’I BLO LA SNANG BA’I PHUNG SOGS KUN RDZOB PA MA GZIGS NA, DE RNAMS MED PAR ‘GYUR TE, YOD NA NI SANGS RGYAS KYIS GZIGS DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO, ,PHUNG SOGS KUN RDZOB PA RNAMS MED NA NI SANGS RGYAS THOB PA YANG MED PAR ‘GYUR TE, DANG POR SEMS BSKYED PA’I GANG ZAG NI MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

One may come then with the following argument:

A person whose eyes are free of any cataracts doesn’t perceive even the false appearance of a strand of hair.  And a Buddha could never perceive the deceptive forms of the parts to a person and so on which make their appearance to a state of mind which is infected by misunderstanding.  And that’s simply because—if anything does in fact exist—then it has to be seen by an Enlightened Being.  But if, on the other hand, the deceptive forms of the parts to a person and so on didn’t exist at all, then there would exist no such thing as someone achieving enlightenment.  And that in turn is because a person who first attains the Wish to achieve enlightenment for all living beings is someone who is still infected by misunderstanding.


[1643]
SKYON ‘DI MED TSUL BSHAD NA, SANGS RGYAS KYI YE SHES KYIS SHES BYA MKHYEN TSUL NI GNYIS TE, DON DAM BDEN PA’I SHES BYA THAMS CAD MKHYEN TSUL DANG, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA’I SHES BYA THAMS CAD MKHYEN TSUL LO,,

If we were to explain how this problem is not one which is really there, we can begin by saying that there are two different ways in which the wisdom of an Enlightened Being knows all knowable things.  They know all knowable things within ultimate reality; and they know all knowable things within deceptive reality.


[1644]
DE LA DANG PO NI, PHUNG PO LA SOGS PA KUN RDZOB PA’I SNANG BA RNAMS MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS, DE RNAMS KYI DE KHO NA NYID MKHYEN PA’O,,

In the first way of knowing here, the Enlightened Beings fail to see the deceptive appearance of the parts to a person and so on; and in this manner then they know the true nature of these things.



How Buddhas know the deceptive

[1645]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to how Buddhas know all existing objects of deceptive reality.


[1646]
MI SNANG YANG RTOGS PA’I SHUGS RTOGS SANGS RGYAS LA GZHAG TU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR, SNANG NAS MKHYEN DGOS PAS JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PA’I YE SHES DE’I NGOR, YUL DANG YUL CAN GNYIS SU SNANG BA’I TSUL GYIS MKHYEN PA’O,,

Now it would be inappropriate to say—with Enlightened Beings—that they perceived an object by implication of another perception, even though that object was not appearing to them.  As such, they have to perceive things through those objects making an appearance to them.  As such, we have to say that—to the perceptions of an Enlightened Being where they see the total number of different entities in the universe—they perceive these entities by means of both the objects and their subjects appearing to them, as two.


[1647]
SANGS RGYAS KYI JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PA DE MA RIG PA’I BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD NAS PHUNG SOGS SNANG BA MIN KYANG, GANG ZAG GZHAN GYI SHES PA MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA LA SNANG BA SANGS RGYAS LA SNANG DGOS TE, SNANG BA DE MED PAR MI RUNG LA KUN RDZOB DE YOD NA JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PAS DMIGS DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

It is not the case that the knowledge of an Enlightened Being which knows all the things to be known assumes the appearance of the parts to a person and so forth due to some infection by the deep seeds of misunderstanding.  Nonetheless, the way it has to work is that the appearance that makes itself known to the perceptions of other individuals whose minds are infected by misunderstanding makes its own appearance to these Buddhas.  This is because it would be wrong to say that there were no such appearance at all; while at the same time—if the deceptive is something that exists—then it must be perceived by the knowledge of an Enlightened Being which perceives the total quantity of knowable objects.


[1648]
RAB RIB DANG BRAL BA’I MIG SHES LA, RAB RIB CAN LA SNANG BA’I SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA MED KYANG, SNANG BA DE MED MI DGOS PAS SANGS RGYAS DANG MI ‘DRA’O,,

There is no such thing as something making its appearance as the strand of hair that appears to a person who has cataracts, as one which appears to a person whose visual consciousness is free of such cataracts.  Nonetheless, it is not the case that the appearance would have to be something that did not exist; thus the case is different from that with an Enlightened Being.


[1649]
[f. 124a] GNYIS SNANG ‘KHRUL PA’I BAG CHAGS MA ZAD KYI BAR DU JI LTA BA DANG, JI SNYED PA MNGON SUM DU ‘JAL BA GNYIS NGO BO GCIG TU SKYE MI NUS PAS, MNYAM RJES RES ‘JOG TU ‘JAL DGOS PAS YE SHES SKAD CIG MA GCIG GI STENG NAS DE GNYIS ‘JAL BA MI ‘ONG NGO,,

Until the day when we are able to finish off those deep mental seeds for the mistake—for the discrepancy between what appears and what is actually there—it can never be the case that our direct encounter with the way that all things exist, and with the total quantity of things that exist, could ever arise as a case where to be one were to be the other.  That is, we would have to commune with these two in alternation, between states of deep meditation and the periods subsequent to those states.  Thus then there would be no instance where we communed with both, within a single millisecond of wisdom.


[1650]
‘KHRUL PA’I BAG CHAGS MA LUS PAR SPANGS PA NA, YE SHES SKAD CIG MA RE RE’I STENG DU YANG YE SHES GNYIS NGO BO GCIG TU SKYE BA RGYUN MI CHAD PAS, DUS GCIG TU SHES BYA GNYIS MNGON SUM DU  ‘JAL MI ‘JAL GYI RES ‘JOG MI DGOS SO,,

While we have yet to eliminate each & every one of the deep seeds for the mistake, then even relative to each individual instant of wisdom there is an unbroken flow of the two forms of wisdom arising as a single entity; as such, it is not necessary that in any particular moment we alternate, in the sense of both directly engaging in, and not directly engaging in, a particular object of knowledge.


[1651]
DES NA,
,MKHYEN PA’I SKAD CIG GCIG GIS KYANG,
,SHES BYA’I DKYIL ‘KHOR KUN KHYAB CAN,
ZHES GSUNGS PA YANG MI ‘GAL LO,,

This then is why we can say that our presentation is not in contradiction with the lines that say—

	Even a single instant
	Of their knowledge

	Extends over the entire realm
	Of every knowable thing.


[1652]
YE SHES GNYIS NGO BO GCIG YIN KYANG YUL GNYIS LA LTOS PA’I MKHYEN TSUL MI ‘DRA BA GNYIS ‘ONG BA LA ‘GAL BA CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PA NI,

And there is not the slightest contradiction in saying that—even though two instances of wisdom are such that to be one is to be the other—relative to two different objects we could see two disparate manners of knowing.


[1653]
SANGS RGYAS BCOM LDAN ‘DAS NYAG GCIG GI KHYAD CHOS SU ‘DUG PA LA, DE KHO NA NYID KYI MKHYEN TSUL GCIG PU SANGS RGYAS KYI MKHYEN TSUL DU BYAS NAS, JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PA SANGS RGYAS KYI THUGS RGYUD LA MED PAR GDUL BYA’I RGYUD KYIS BSDUS ZHES,

This is in fact a particular feature only of a Conquering Buddha.  Yes, we do see people who say that the way an Enlightened Being perceives suchness, taken by itself, is the way that Buddhas know things; and that no Buddha possesses, in their mindstream, a knowledge of all the separate knowable things there are—that this is actually included into the mind of the particular disciples.


[1654]
SANGS RGYAS KYI JI SNYED PA MKHYEN PA LA SKUR PA ‘DEBS PA DANG, KHA CIG JI LTA BA MKHYEN PA YANG SANGS RGYAS KYI THUGS RGYUD LA MED CES YE SHES GNYIS KA LA SKUR PA ‘DEBS PAR SNANG NGO,,

It would appear though that people who take this position are discounting the the way in which a Buddha knows all the different things there are; while those who go further and say that neither is there any knowledge of the way things are in the mindstream of an Enlightened Being are discounting both forms of wisdom.


[1655]
‘DI’I LHAG MA ‘GA’ ZHIG ‘BRAS BU’I SKABS SU BSHAD PAR BYA’O,,

I will cover a few remaining points in this regard, when we get to the section about results.


[1656]
GAL TE GNYIS SNANG THAMS CAD NUB PA RNAM PA DE LTA BU’I RANG BZHIN NI [f. 124b] MTHONG BA MED PA MA YIN NAM, DES NA JI LTAR SANGS RGYAS DE DAG GIS DON DAM BDEN PA GZIGS SHE NA,

One may come then with the following question—

Let’s consider a case where all instances of the discrepancy between what appears and what is actually there have subsided, for a particular person; aren’t you saying then that this type of situation is not something where that discrepancy is not perceived?  Isn’t this exactly how Enlightened Beings see ultimate reality?


[1657]
DE KHO NA NYID KYI GZIGS NGOR GNYIS SNANG NUB PAS GNYIS KYI TSUL GYIS MI GZIGS PA NI BDEN MOD KYI, ‘ON KYANG MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS DE DAG GIS GZIGS SO ZHES BRJOD DO,,

It is true that—to the state of mind perceiving suchness—all appearances of the discrepancy have subsided; and that therefore these beings do not see things in these two different modes.  What we say though is that they do their seeing by way of not seeing.


[1658]
‘DI RTZOD PA’I LAN DU ‘GRO TSUL NI, JI LTA BA MKHYEN PA’I YE SHES DES PHUNG SOGS KYI DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, PHUNG SOGS RNAMS GZIGS NGO DER MA GRUB PA DE DAG GI DE KHO NA NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, PHUNG SOGS MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS DE DAG GI DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS DGOS PA’I PHYIR TE,

How exactly does this point function to address that last objection?  First of all, the wisdom of a Buddha which perceives the way in which all things exist sees—directly—the true nature of the parts to the person, and so on.  And the way that these parts and the like do not exist to these perceptions is in fact the true nature of those entities.  Finally, these beings have to perceive the true nature of these objects through their way of not seeing these parts, and the rest.


[1659]
RANG ‘GREL LAS, DNGOS PO BYAS PA CAN LA MA REG PAR RANG BZHIN ‘BA’ ZHIG MNGON SUM DU MDZAD PAS, DE NYID THUGS SU CHUD PA’I PHYIR SANGS RGYAS ZHES BRJOD DO,

The autocommentary puts it this way:

They make no contact with entities that involved having been produced; rather, the only thing they have a direct knowledge of is their true nature.  It is in fact because they grasp this, that we can call them “Buddhas.”


[1660]
ZHES SANGS RGYAS KYI DON DAM MKHYEN PA’I YE SHES KYIS CHOS CAN LA MA REG PAR CHOS NYID ‘BA’ ZHIG THUGS SU CHUD PAR GSUNGS TE, PHUNG SOGS MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS DE DAG GI DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PAR GSUNGS PA DANG DON GCIG GO

What this is saying is that the ultimate knowledge of a Buddha comprehends the real nature of an object at hand without making contact with the object which possesses that nature.  This is the same point we are making when we say that they see the true nature of the parts to the person and so on by way of not perceiving them.


[1661]
,MTHONG BA MED PA NI MTHONG BA DAM PA’O ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON YANG, CI YANG MI MTHONG BA MTHONG BAR MI BZHED KYI, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR SPROS PA MA MTHONG BA NI SPROS BRAL MTHONG BAR ‘JOG PAS, MTHONG MA MTHONG GZHI GCIG LA BYED PA MIN NO,,

As they say, “Not seeing at all is the very highest form of seeing”; and here’s what that means.  We are not taking the position that not seeing is seeing; rather, as we pointed out before, we are establishing the not seeing of false projections as being seeing things without such projections.  It’s not that we can say both “you see it” and “you don’t see it” with regard to one object at one time.


[1662]
DE LTAR YANG SDUD PA LAS,

The Brief Presentation of the Perfection of Wisdom says it this way—


	[1663]
,GZUGS RNAMS MI MTHONG TSOR BA DAG KYANG
MI MTHONG ZHING,
,’DU SHES [f. 125a] MTHONG BA MED LA SEMS PA
MI MTHONG ZHING,
,GANG LA RNAM PAR SHES DANG SEMS YID
MTHONG MED PA,
,’DI NI CHOS MTHONG YIN ZHES DE BZHIN
GSHEGS PAS BSTAN,

	They see no body,
	And they see no feelings;

	They see no discrimination,
	And see no thinking;

	Neither do they see awareness,
	Or the mind, or the thoughts.

	And then this is what
	The Ones Gone Thus

	Teach as being
	Seeing what things are.


	[1664]
,NAM MKHA’ MTHONG ZHES SEMS CAN TSIG
TU RAB BRJOD PA,
,NAM MKHA’ JI LTAR MTHONG STE DES ‘DI
BRTAG PAR GYIS,
,DE LTAR CHOS MTHONG BA YANG DE BZHIN
GSHEGS PAS BSTAN,
,MTHONG BA DPE GZHAN GYIS NI BSNYAD PAR
NUS MA YIN,

		People in the world
		Say things like
		“I see the sky.”

		We have to consider
		The case here

		As the same as how
		You could see the sky—

		For this is the way
		That the Ones Gone Thus

		Describe the seeing
		Of the way things are.

		This seeing
		Could never be described
		By using any other example.


[1665]
ZHES MI MTHONG BA PHUNG PO LNGA DANG, MTHONG BA NI CHOS ZHES GSUNGS LA, DE NI DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON TE, SUS RTEN ‘BREL MTHONG BA DES CHOS MTHONG NGO ZHES GSUNGS PA BZHIN NO,,

What this is saying that we don’t see then is the five parts to a person; whereas what we do see is things—the way things are.  This is a reference to suchness, or the true nature of things.  It’s similar to when they say, “A person who has seen how things are created in dependence has seen the way of things.”


[1666]
DE YANG DPER NA NAM MKHA’ NI THOGS PA’I REG BYA BCAD TZAM YIN LA, DE MTHONG NGAM RTOGS PA NI DGAG BYA SGRIB THOGS YOD NA DMIGS SU RUNG BA LAS MA MTHONG BA LA BYED PA DANG ‘DRA STE, DER YANG MTHONG BA’I NAM MKHA’ DANG MA MTHONG BA NI SGRIB THOGS SO,,

The sky—or space—for example, consists of the simple exclusion of solidity, of tangible objects.  To “see” or to “realize” this space consists of not seeing what would obscure the space if it were present; that is, something solid; and the case here is similar.  That is, in this case, what we see is empty space; and what we don’t see is any solid object which might obstruct that space.


[1667]
DPE DE BZHIN DU MTHONG BA MIN PAR SNGON PO MTHONG BA BZHIN DU DE KHO NA NYID MTHONG BA NI RKANG PA THA MAS BKAG GO

As we see in this example, seeing suchness by not seeing in the same way that would apply in the case of seeing something blue is denied in the final lines above.


[1668]
,MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS GZIGS PA’I SHES BYED DU BDEN PA GNYIS LA ‘JUG PA LAS, LHA’I BU GAL TE DON DAM PAR NA DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA LUS DANG NGAG DANG, YID KYI YUL GYI RANG BZHIN DU ‘GYUR NA NI DE DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA ZHES BYA BA’I GRANGS SU MI ‘GRO STE, KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA NYID DU ‘GYUR RO,,

In support of this way that we see things by not seeing, we can refer to the Sutra on Entering the Two Realities:

O child of the pleasure beings, if ultimate reality were—in some ultimate way—such that it could act as the object of our actions or words or thoughts, then it could not be counted as what we refer to when we use the phrase, “ultimate reality.”  And that’s because then it would be deceptive reality.


[1669]
‘ON KYANG LHA’I BU DON DAM PAR NA DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA NI THA SNYAD THAMS CAD LAS ‘DAS PA, ,BYE BRAG MED PA{%, Kang} [f. 125b] MA SKYES PA MA ‘GAGS PA, SMRA BAR BYA BA DANG{%, Kang} SMRA BA DANG, SHES PAR BYA BA DANG, SHES PA DANG BRAL BA’O,

What we can say though, o child of the pleasure beings, is that in an ultimate way ultimate reality is beyond all expression; and it it has no particulars.  It never started, and it will never stop.  It is beyond something to say, or saying itself; it is beyond something to know, or knowing itself.


[1670]
ZHES GSUNGS PA DRANGS PA’I MDO SNGA MA’I DON NI, DON DAM PA GZIGS PA’I NGOR DON DAM BDEN PA DE, PHUNG SOGS KUN RDZOB PA MA MTHONG BA’I TSUL GYIS GZIGS PA MIN PAR,

Here is what the first paragraph of sutra citation just listed is saying.  Suppose that, to the state of mind perceiving the ultimate, ultimate reality was not something that we perceived by way of not seeing deceptive objects, such as the parts to a person.


[1671]
PHUNG SOGS LUS KYI DANG NGAG GI SPYOD YUL DANG, YID KYI YUL DU ‘GYUR BA LTAR YUL DU ‘GYUR NA NI, DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I NGOR SPROS PA DANG MA BRAL BAS,

That is, suppose that the ultimate were perceived through the parts of the person and so forth by somehow being the object that our physical actions or verbal speech engaged in; or else the object of our thoughts.  In this case, it would not be true that—to the perceptions of the mind perceiving suchness directly—that state of mind was free of all projections of reality.


[1672]
DON DAM BDEN PAR MI ‘GYUR GYI KUN RDZOB KYI SPROS PAR ‘GYUR RO ZHES PA STE, DE LTAR BYAS NA MA GZIGS PA’I TSUL GYIS GZIGS PA’I SHES BYED DU ‘GRO’O,,

And that would mean that what was perceived could not be ultimate reality; rather, it would be a deceptive projection.  As such, this citation serves as supporting evidence of the idea that we see by means of not seeing.


[1673]
MDO GNYIS PA’I DON NI DON DAM PA MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I NGOR NI, DON DAM BDEN PA BYE BRAG MED PA NI KHYAD PAR MI ‘DRA BA MANG PO MED PA’O,,

And what is the meaning of the second portion of the citation here?  What it’s saying is that—to the perceptions of a state of mind which is perceiving ultimate reality directly—ultimate reality has no particulars; that is, it has no great number of dissimilar features.


[1674]
GZHAN GSUM NI GO SLA’O,,

The remaining three portions of the citation are easily understood.


[1675]
GZIGS NGO DER SMRA BA’I BYA BYED DANG BRAL BA NI SLA’O,,

Saying that undertaking the action of speaking within the perceptions of that state of mind is completely absent is also easily understood.


[1676]
DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I YE SHES DE DON DAM SHES PA DANG, DON DAM BDEN PA DE’I SHES BYAR ‘JOG THUB KYANG, YE SHES DE’I NGOR BYA BYED DE GNYIS DANG BRAL BA MI ‘GAL BA NI,

We can say that the wisdom which directly sees the way things are is perceiving the ultimate; and that what it perceives is ultimate reality.  And yet still it is no contradiction to say that—to the perceptions of this particular state of wisdom—there is a complete absence of the two of the object of an action, and the action itself.


[1677]
BYA BYED GNYIS NI THA SNYAD PA’I BLO KHO NA’I NGOR ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR TE, DPER NA RIGS SHES RJES DPAG YUL CAN DANG, DON DAM BDEN PA YUL DU ‘JOG NUS KYANG, YUL DANG YUL CAN GYI BYA BYED GNYIS RIGS NGOR MA ‘JOG PA BZHIN NO,,

This is due to the fact that the two of an object to an action, and the action itself, can only be established in the perceptions of a nominal state of mind.  We can, for example, say that a perception based on logic possesses an object of deduction; or that ultimate reality could act as its object of perception.  We could not though establish, to the perceptions of such a deduction, objects of action or actions themselves, between the subject and its object.


[1678]
DE NAS LHA’I BU DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA NI RNAM PA THAMS CAD KYI MCHOG DANG LDAN PA{%,} [f. 126a] THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA’I YE SHES KYI YUL GYI BAR LAS ‘DAS PA YIN TE, JI LTAR DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA’O ZHES BRJOD PA LTAR NI MA YIN NO,,

“Neither could we then say” something like “o child of the pleasure beings, ultimate reality represents the highest of all the kinds of things; it is far beyond everything up to serving as the object of the wisdom which knows all things…as the reality which is ultimate.”


[1679]
CHOS THAMS CAD NI BRDZUN TE SLU BA’I CHOS SO, ZHES DRANGS PA’I DON NI, YIN TE’I BAR GYIS DON DAM BDEN PA THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA’I YE SHES KYI YUL LAS ‘DAS PAR BSTAN PA

That is, here then is the meaning of the words, “All existing objects are a lie; they are only things that deceive us.”  Everything up to “they are [beyond]” is meant to say that ultimate reality is beyond being the object of the wisdom which knows all things.


[1680]
DE’I YUL LAS ‘DAS TSUL, JI LTAR NAS MA YIN NO’I BAR GYIS STON TE,

Just how these things are beyond being the object of this wisdom is indicated in the wording of the sentence here that includes “similar to” and “they are not.”


[1681]
JI LTAR ‘DI DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA’O ZHES BRJOD PA NA SGRA DE’I RJES ‘BRANG GI RTOG PA LA, YUL YUL CAN SO SO BA GNYIS SU CHAD PAR SNANG BA LTAR THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA’I JI LTA BA MKHYEN PA DE LA DE LTAR SNANG BA’I TSUL GYIS DE’I YUL LAS ‘DAS PA STE, GNYIS SNANG GI CHOS THAMS CAD NI BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I CHOS YIN PAS, DE KHO NA NYID KYI MI SLU BA ‘BA’ ZHIG GZIGS PA’I NGOR DE MED CES PA’O,,

What the “similar to” is meant to say here is that—when we utter the expression “ultimate reality”—in our thoughts we get the impression of a separate object & subject, cut off from each other.  One part of the mind which knows all things though—the knowledge of how all things are—is completely beyond any such impression passing through it.  That is, all entities involved with the disparity between what appears to us and how we take it are a lie, and deceive us.  As such, these particular objects cannot exist to the perceptions of a state of mind which is seeing those things which are exclusively undeceiving; which is to say, suchness—the way things really are.


[1682]
DE RNAMS THAMS CAD DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I NGOR PHUNG SOGS KUN RDZOB PA MI SNANG BA’I KHUNGS SO,,

The points we’ve listed from this entire section of scripture then provide an authoritative source for the principle that deceptive objects—such as the parts to a person and so on—can never present themselves to the perceptions of a state of mind in which we are seeing suchness directly.


[1683]
DE’I PHYIR DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA’I NGOR, DNGOS PO DANG DNGOS PO MED PA LA SOGS PA’I GNYIS CHOS KYI SPROS PA THAMS CAD SRID PA MA YIN TE, SPROS PA DE DAG GI RANG GI NGO BO DER MA DMIGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

As such, we can say then that none of the projections of duality—such as that consisting of existing & non-existing objects—can ever possibly present themselves to the perceptions a mind which is perceiving, directly, the way things really are.  And this is because none of these projections can ever exist in some particular way that they are.


[1684]
DE LTAR NA DE KHO NA NYID BSAM PA LA DNGOS SU NA ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KHO NA TSAD MA YIN GYI, ‘PHAGS PA MA YIN PA NI DNGOS SU TSAD MA MA YIN PAS, GZHAN SKYE ‘PHAGS PA’I DON DAM GYI GZIGS NGOR BKAG PA LA [f. 126b] ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PA MA YIN NO,,

Given all this, we can say that relative to considering the true nature of things, it is only realized beings who can be described as being, in a direct way, accurate.  Those who are not realized beings are not then—in this direct way—accurate.  And as such, disallowing the idea that things starting from things other than themselves could ever present itself to the ultimate perceptions of a realized being is not a concept that could ever be drawn into question by the everyday world.



The world is wrong

[1685]
BZHI PA NI,

This brings us to our fourth point from above: a demonstration that there are contradictions in the idea that our denial of growth from something other is itself contradicted by the perceptions of the world.


	[1686]
	[VI.30]
Lokaḥ pramāṇaṃ yadi tattva darśī
syāl loka evetya paraiḥ kim āryaiḥ,
Kim ārya mārgeṇa bhavec ca kāryaṃ
mūḍhaḥ pramāṇaṃ na hi nāma yuktaḥ.

,GAL TE ‘JIG RTEN TSAD MA YIN NA NI,
,’JIG RTEN DE NYID MTHONG BAS ‘PHAGS GZHAN GYIS,
,CI DGOS ‘PHAGS PA’I LAM GYIS CI ZHIG BYA,
,BLUN PO TSAD MAR RIGS PA’ANG MA YIN NO,,

Suppose that people
Of the world were accurate;

These people of the world then
Would have to see the real nature.

If that were so,
Then there would be no need
For other realized beings.

And what use then
Would be served by
The path of the realized?

Neither do these simple fools
Enjoy any accurate perception
At all.


[VI.31]
Lokaḥ pramāṇaṃ na hi sarvathā tas
tattvādhikāre na ca lokabādhā,
Syāl loka bādhā yadi laukikārtho
loka pratītyaiva nirākriyeta.

[VI.31a]
,RNAM KUN ‘JIG RTEN TSAD MIN DE YI PHYIR,
,DE NYID SKABS SU ‘JIG RTEN GNOD PA MED,

Those of the world
Are not, in any way,
An accurate perception.

For this reason,
The world cannot draw
Anything into question,

With regard to
The way things are.


[1687]
CI STE GZHAN SKYE DON DAM PAR BKAG PA LA ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA BRJOD PAR ‘DOD PAS,

Now some people have come up with objections that they think will show that the parlance of the everyday world works against our denial that things could grow from things that are other than them, in an ultimate way.


[1688]
DE KHO NA NYID RNAM PAR DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU DE KHO NA NYID LA ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA YANG TSAD MAR KHAS LEN NA DE LTA YIN DANG

They would also accept that—at a point where we are examining the idea of suchness—the way that people of the world see the way things really are is accurate.


[1689]
GAL TE ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA DE KHO NA NYID LA TSAD MA YIN NA NI, ‘JIG RTEN RANG DGA’ BAS DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA STE RTOGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE YANG ‘KHOR BA THOG MA MED PA NAS YIN PAS,

Suppose then, in such a case, that the way people of the world see the idea of suchness is something which is accurate.  In that case, people of the world just in their everyday mode would have to see this real nature of things directly; which is to say, they would have to realize it.  Further, that would have to have been the case for time with no beginning.


[1690]
MA RIG PA SPANGS PAR KHAS BLANG DGOS PAS DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA LA ‘PHAGS PA GZHAN GYIS CI ZHIG DGOS TE MI DGOS LA, ‘PHAGS PA’I LAM TSOL BA YIS KYANG CI ZHIG BYA STE DGOS PA MED DO,,

And if that were so, then we would have to say that they had already eliminated misunderstanding within themselves.  And in that case, we would have to question why other realized beings would ever have to get involved with trying to realize suchness at all—for indeed there would be no need.  And what use then would be served by the pursuit of the path of the realized ones either?  There would be no need for it.


[1691]
‘JIG RTEN RANG DGA’ BA’I BLUN PO NI, DE KHO NA NYID LA TSAD MAR RIGS PA’ANG MA YIN NO,,

Neither then is it the case that people of the world just in their everyday mode—these simple fools—enjoy any accurate perception of the way things really are, at all.


[1692]
DE’I PHYIR DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU DE KHO NA NYID LA RNAM PA KUN TE THAMS CAD DU ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA TSAD MA MIN PA DE YI PHYIR, DE KHO NA NYID KYI SKABS SU ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA MED DO,,

And so we can say that—at that point where we are examining the way things really are—the way that those of the world see suchness is something which is not, in any way at all, an accurate perception.  For this reason then, the way of the world cannot draw anything into question, with regard to the way things really are.


[1693]
RNAM KUN ‘JIG RTEN TSAD MIN ZHES PAS LUGS ‘DIS TSAD MA GTAN MI ‘DOD PAR STON PAS, LUGS DE YANG DAG PA MA YIN NO ZHES SMRA BA DANG,

Some people say that the words of the root text here—“those of the world do not, in any way, have an accurate perception”—indicate that, in the current system, no form of accurate perception at all is accepted; and then they go on to say that, therefore, this is not a correct system at all.


[1694]
KHA CIG LUGS DE LEGS SO ZHES SMRA BA GNYIS KAS KYANG SLOB DPON ‘DI’I BZHED PA MA RTOGS BZHIN DU SMRAS PAS,

Still others applaud the opinion that there is no accurate perception.  But both of these positions are expressed through a total failure to grasp what our master here actually believes.


[1695]
RANG GI DE NYID STON PA TZAM DU ZAD DE, ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA DE KHO NA NYID LA RNAM PA KUN TU TSAD MA MIN PAR BSTAN PA LA, SPYIR TSAD [f. 127a] MA MI BZHED PAR GO ‘DUG PA’I PHYIR RO,,

What these debaters are actually demonstrating is nothing more than their own version of the way things really are.  Because they have taken lines that were meant to express how people of the world view the way things really are in a way which is not accurate at all; and understood this as a blanket denial of accurate perception itself.


[1696]
TSAD MA DANG GZHAL BYA YANG TSIG GSAL LAS GSUNGS PA LTAR NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA BKAG NAS, LTOS ‘JOG GI TSAD MA DANG GZHAL BYA ‘JOG PAR BSHAD PA LTA BUR BYED DGOS TE ‘OG TU ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As for the concepts of accurate perception and the objects under its consideration, we need to deny—in the same way as we seen this done in A Clarification of the Verses—that they could ever exist through any nature of their own.  And then we need to go further and do things like explaining how it is that we ourselves posit an accurate type of perception which could establish that things exist in reliance; and what the object under its consideration would be like.



The world
contradicts the world

[1697]
LNGA PA NI,

Here then is our fifth point from above—where we present how the perceptions of the world would in fact be contradicted themselves.


	[1698]
[VI.31b]
,’JIG RTEN DON NI ‘JIG RTEN GRAGS NYID KYIS,
,GAL TE SEL NA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD ‘GYUR,

Suppose that
The state of things
In the everyday world

Were itself disallowed
By the very conventions
Of this same world;

This same person
Would be contradicted
By the world.


[1699]
‘O NA JI LTAR ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PAR ‘GYUR ZHE NA,

“Well then,” one may begin.  “Just how is it that those ideas are contradicted by the world itself?”


[1700]
‘JIG RTEN NYID LAS GRAGS SHING GRUB PA’I DON NI, ‘JIG RTEN GYI GRAGS PA NYID KYIS GAL TE SEL NA, GANG ZAG DE LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Consider, in reply, the state of things as this is generally considered, and established, in the everyday world itself.  Suppose this were itself disallowed by the very conventions of this same world; in this case, we could say that this same person was contradicted by the world.


[1701]
DE NI DPER NA KHA CIG GIS NGA’I RDZAS PHROGS SO ZHES SMRAS PA DANG, GANG ZAG GZHAN CIG GIS DE LA DRIS PA RDZAS DE CI ZHIG YIN,

Suppose, for example, that someone comes up to somebody else and says, “Some people stole my things.”  And then the other person there asks, “Well what things, exactly, were taken?”


[1702]
DES BUM PA’O ZHES SMRAS PA LA, GZHAN DES BUM PA NI RDZAS MA YIN TE, GZHAL BYA YIN PA’I PHYIR RMI LAM GYI BUM PA BZHIN NO, ZHES SUN ‘BYIN PA

And the person says, “They took a water pitcher.”  And then their friend overthrows that whole assertion with, “But a water pitcher is not a thing; after all, it’s not something you could ever have under consideration.  It’s just the same as a water pitcher in a dream.”


[1703]
DE LTA BU LA SOGS PA’I YUL LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD KYI, GANG GI TSE ‘PHAGS PA’I DON DAM GYI GZIGS PA LA BRTEN TE, SKYE BO DON DAM LA MKHAS PA TSAD MAR BYAS NAS DE KHO NA NYID GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA DE’I TSE, ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

It is true that the perceptions of the everyday world could work to deny this sort of object; but suppose instead that we consider the case relative to the vision of ultimate reality possessed by a realized being.  Taking a person who has mastered the ultimate as someone who is accurate, then in a case where we seek to establish just what the real nature of things is, we cannot say that there is any contradiction with what the world says is so.


[1704]
MKHAS PAS PHYOGS ‘DIS GZHAN YANG DPYAD PAR BYA’O ZHES GSUNGS PA NI, NGA NI BUM PA’I BDAG PO DANG LHAS BYIN NI ‘PHROG MKHAN MA YIN TE, ZHES PA DANG, NGA’I ZHING STENG DU SKYES SO BYAS PA NA CI ZHIG SKYES ZHES ‘DRI BA LA

We see then the statement, “The wise should apply this position as well to their examination of other cases.”  That is, suppose we say “I am the owner of this pitcher,” and “John over there is the one who stole it.”  Or suppose we say “I grew that in my field,” and somebody asks us, “What is it that you grew?”


[1705]
MYU GU’O ZHES BYAS PA NA, MYU GU NI SKYE BA MED DE GZHAL BYA YIN PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA DANG, RMI LAM GYI GANG ZAG [f. 127b] DANG MYU GU BZHIN ZHES SMRA BA DA LTA DBU MA’I RIGS PA CHEN POR ‘DOD PA RNAMS LA ‘JIG RTEN GYIS GNOD PAR BSTAN NO,,

And then we reply to them, “It was a sprout of a plant.”  And they answer, “Hey, sprouts are not something that ever grows.  And that’s because they are something you can consider, in your mind.”  And: “They are just like a person that you meet in a dream, or a sprout in a dream.”  Which is to say, just normal people of the world can overthrow those nowadays who claim to utilize magnificent reasoning of the middle way.



Overcoming objections about what
the everyday world believes

[1706]
GNYIS PA NI,

Next is our second section from above: overcoming objections relating to the everyday world which say that there is no growth of things from something other than themselves, even in the parlance of the world.


	[1707]
[VI.32]
Uptvāpi lokaḥ khalu bīja mātraṃ
bravīti putro janito mayaiṣaḥ,
Uptas taruś ceti paraiti yasmāj
janmān yatas tena na lokato’pi.

,GANG PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN SA BON TZAM BTAB NAS,
,BDAG GIS BU ‘DI SKYED CES SMRA BYED CING,
,SHING YANG BTZUGS SO SNYAM DU RTOG DES NA,
,GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN LAS KYANG MED,

		Because the world
		Makes the declaration,

		“I was the one who
		Gave birth to this child,”

		And people think
		To themselves,
		“I planted the tree,”
		
		Things growing from things
That are other than them

Is not something that we see
Even in the everyday world.


[1708]
DE LTAR ‘JIG RTEN GYI GRAGS PA’I NGOR GZHAN SKYE KHAS BLANGS NAS KYANG ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA SPANGS TE, DA NI ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA LA YANG GZHAN SKYE MED PAS ‘JIG RTEN GYI LTA BA LA GNAS NAS KYANG GZHAN SKYE DGAG PAR ‘DOD PA LA ‘JIG RTEN GYI GNOD PA MED DO, ZHES BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

As such, we can say that—since the idea that things grow from other things is accepted even in the normal parlance of the world—any argument against this idea by that world is prevented.  What comes next here is an explanation which says, “But now let’s look here, at how even in the view of the world at large, the idea that one thing could grow from another thing is denied; and how, as such, even if we adhere to the views of the world, we then agree that the idea that one thing could grow from another is mistaken—and that there is no position of the world at large that could prevent this view.”  This is the idea that we seek to present in these next lines of the root text.


[1709]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN PA RNAMS PHO’I DBANG PO CAN ‘GA’ ZHIG STON PA NA, BU ‘DI BDAG GIS BSKYED CES SMRA BAR BYED LA, DE LTAR BYED KYANG PHA ‘DIS PHO’I DBANG PO CAN ZHIG RANG GI LUS LAS BTON NAS, BU DE’I MA’I KHONG DU ‘JUG PA NI MA YIN NO,,

The reason all this is true is because there are people of the world—some number of them, who possess the sexual organ of a male—who might make a declaration where they say, “I was the one who gave birth to this child.”  Despite them saying so, it is not the case though that the father was involved in such a way that the child issued forth from the body of a person possessing a male organ, and then entered into the cavity of its mother.


[1710]
‘O NA CI ZHE NA, BU DE’I LUS KYI SA BON DU GYUR PA’I MI GTZANG BA TZAM ZHIG MA DE’I MNGAL DU BTAB PA STE LDUGS PA’O,,

“Well then,” you might ask, “what was, rather, the case here?”  What happened was that the filth which constituted the seed for the body of the child was deposited into the womb of the mother: sprinkled around in there.


[1711]
GANG GI PHYIR PHA ‘DI BU DE’I LUS KYI RGYU BLUGS NAS RANG GI BU STON PAR BYED PA DE’I PHYIR, SA BON DANG BU GNYIS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘DZIN PA MA YIN NO, ZHES BYA BAR ‘JIG RTEN DU GSAL BAR NGES SO,,

And so the father points to the child as his child, since it was he who deposited the cause for the child’s body.  As such, it is beyond question that—in the world—the case is clear: neither of the two, the seed nor the child, is being considered something other which exists in & of itself.


[1712]
DE’I PHYIR SA BON GYI MI GTZANG BA DANG BU GNYIS DANG, NAS KYI SA BON DANG MYU GU GNYIS LA SOGS PA LA GZHAN LAS SKYE BAR ‘DZIN PA ‘JIG RTEN LAS KYANG MED DO,,

As such, holding the view that the two—the impure substance of the seed, and the child; or other things like the pair of the seed for a sprout, and the sprout itself—grow from something other than themselves is not something that even the world accepts.


[1713]
GAL TE RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘DZIN NA NI, GANG ZAG GZHAN LTAR BU DE BSTAN NAS ‘DI NGAS BSKYED DO ZHES STON PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

If the world did adhere to something other which did exist in & of itself, then it would never happen that—as we saw with that other person—people pointed to a child and said “I was the one who gave them birth.”  


[1714]
DE BZHIN DU SHING [f. 128a] SDONG PO’I SA BON TZAM BTAB NAS DE LAS SHING SDONG SKYES PA NA, SHING SDONG ‘DI NGAS BTZUGS SO SNYAM DU RTOG PA DES NA, ‘JIG RTEN GYI NGOR GZHAN SKYE MED PA SOGS SNGA MA BZHIN DU SBYAR RO,,

The case is the same, when someone plants a simple seed for a tree, and a trunk does indeed grow from that.  That is, people think to themselves, “I was the one who planted the tree with this trunk”; and this is why—as we did with the previous case—we can say things like “There is no instance where, in the perceptions of the world, one thing can grow from another thing.”


[1715]
BTAB PA’I SA BON GNYIS SHING SDONG DANG BU MA YIN KYANG, DE GNYIS BTAB PA LA BRTEN NAS SHING SDONG DANG BU SKYES PA NA, DE GNYIS BSTAN NAS ‘DI BDAG GIS BSKYED CES ‘JOG NUS TE, NA BA DANG SOS PA’I LAG PA GANG ZAG DE MA YIN KYANG, LAG PA NA BA DANG SOS PAS GANG ZAG DE NA BA DANG SOS PAR ‘JOG NUS PA BZHIN NO,,

The two seeds that were planted are neither the trunk of the tree, nor the child; but due to the planting of the two, the trunk and the child grow.  Once you have pointed to the two, you are able to establish the fact that “I gave birth to this.”  A hand that is ailing, or which has healed, is not the person who has the hand; but we are able to establish that a person is either ailing, or healed, through either the ailing or recovery of the hand itself.


[1716]
DE LTAR ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD LA GZHAN SKYE MED KYANG, GZHAN SKYE YOD PA ‘JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BAS ‘GOG NUS PA MIN TE, RGYU ‘BRAS RANG BZHIN GYIS NGO BO THA DAD PA ‘GOG PA NI DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I RIGS PA LA NGES PAR LTOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Thus we can say that—even though in the parlance of the world they may not talk about the fact that things have to grow from other things—there is nothing in the way that the world sees things that could succeed in disproving it.  And this is because—when we deny that causes and effects could be separate through any nature of their own—we definitely need to rely upon reasoning which is analyzing the way things really are.
 

[1717]
DE’I PHYIR GRUB MTHA’ SMRA BA GZHAN GYIS GZHAN SKYE KHAS BLANGS PA’I DON NI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN SKYE YIN GYI, NGO BO GZHAN DU GRUB PA TZAM MA YIN LA, DE TZAM ‘JIG RTEN GYI NGOR MA GRUB PA YANG MIN NO,,

As such, when those who profess other schools of thought say that they accept the idea that things grow from other things, what they are referring to actually is a growing from other things which could exist by definition.  It is not simply the fact that the essence of the things is that they exist as other than each other; just that much is not something that cannot be established to the perceptions of the everyday world.


[1718]
GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN LAS KYANG MED, CES PA’I DON NI, ‘JIG RTEN RANG DGA’ BAS SA MYUG LA SOGS PA’I NYER LEN GYI RGYU ‘BRAS LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘DZIN PA MED CES PA TZAM MIN GYI,

But then our verse here says, “Things growing from things that are other than them is not something that we see even in the everyday world.”  This is not simply saying that just normal people of the everyday world never hold that things like the soil and the sprout—examples of cause & effect where the cause turns into the result directly—exist as entities that are other than each other by definition.


[1719]
THA SNYAD DU YANG GZHAN SKYE MED PAR STON PAR YANG SHES PAR BYA STE, GNYI GA LAS SKYE BA ‘GOG PA’I ‘GREL PAR YANG, DE LA JI LTAR GONG DU BDAG [f. 128b] DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PAR YANG MI RIGS SO ZHES BSTAN PA DE BZHIN DU TSIG GAL GNYIS SU SMRA BA LA YANG JI SKAD DU BSHAD PA’I RIGS PAS MI SRID DO, ZHES THA SNYAD DU YANG GZHAN SKYE MED PA GSAL BAR GSUNGS PA DANG,

Rather, it is saying that we are to understand, further, that there is no growing of one thing from another here even in a nominal sense.  The growing of things from either here is denied in the autocommentary as well, in the words—

On this point, we have above demonstrated that the growing of things both from themselves and from something other than themselves is illogical for the everyday world, from both the deceptive and the ultimate points of view.  In the same vein, we see prior to this point, in the root text, two mentions of the wording starting with “suppose”—which is meant to indicate that it would be impossible to establish either option with the indicated reasoning.

What this is saying, very clearly, is that there is no concept of things growing from something other than themselves here, even nominally.


[1720]
TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG, GAL TE BDAG DANG GZHAN DANG GNYI GA DANG RGYU MED PA LAS DNGOS PO RNAMS SKYE BA YOD PA MA YIN NA, JI LTAR BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS MA RIG PA’I RKYEN GYIS ‘DU BYED RNAMS ZHES GSUNGS,

A Clarification of the Verses also says—

If there is no such thing as things growing from either themselves, or from something other than themselves, or from both, or from no cause at all, then how is it that the Conquering Buddha himself made the statement that “Fresh karma springs from the factor of misunderstanding”?


[1721]
ZHES PA’I LAN DU, BSHAD PAR BYA STE, ‘DI NI KUN RDZOB YIN GYI DE KHO NA NYID NI MA YIN NO, ZHES MA RIG PAS ‘DU BYED SKYED PA SOGS NI KUN RDZOB TU YIN GYI DON DAM PAR MA YIN PAR GSUNGS SO,,

And then the same text answers itself:

I will explain this to you, by saying “This refers to the deceptive; it is not, however, referring to the way things really are.”  And what this is saying is that—when fresh karma is triggered by misunderstanding—it’s all happening in a deceptive manner, and not in an ultimate way.


[1722]
CI KUN RDZOB KYI RNAM PAR GZHAG PA BRJOD PAR BYA BA YIN NAM ZHES PA’I LAN DU, RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM GYIS KUN RDZOB GRUB PAR KHAS LEN GYI, PHYOGS BZHI KHAS BLANGS PA’I SGO NAS NI MA YIN TE,

And the same work concludes with:

And you may ask, “What do you mean, when you say this is all happening in a deceptive way?”  In response we can say that we accept that something exists in a deceptive way as soon as we mention no more than “this particular factor.”  It is not though because we are accepting any one of the four options at this point.


[1723]
ZHES KUN RDZOB TU RKYEN ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS ‘DI ‘BYUNG GI SKYE BA KHAS LEN PA LA YANG, PHYOGS BZHI’I SKYE BA KHAS MI LEN PA GSAL BAR GSUNGS PAS, LUGS ‘DI LA GZHAN SKYE KUN RDZOB TU MI ‘GOG CES PA NI, LUGS ‘DI LEGS PAR MA RTOGS PA’I BSHAD PA’O,,

What this is saying is that we do accept a growing where—in a deceptive sense—"this particular thing has occurred due to that particular factor.”  But it goes on to state, quite clearly, that we do not accept a growing that could occur through any of the four classical options here.  Some people have said that—therefore–the present system does not deny that things could grow from other things, in a deceptive manner; but this statement reflects an inability to understand the present system clearly.



Things growing from other,
in the everyday world

[1724]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to our third part from above: demonstrating the advantages of denying that the idea that things could grow from something other than themselves in any way contradicts the beliefs of the everyday world.


	[1725]
[VI.33]
Yato na bījāt paratāṅkurasya
satyaṅkure bījam ato na naṣṭam,
Eko yato nāsti tato’pi bījaṃ
satyaṅkure’stīti na vācyam eva.

	,GANG PHYIR MYU GU SA BON LAS GZHAN MIN,
,DE PHYIR MYUG TSE SA BON ZHIG PA MED,
,GANG PHYIR GCIG NYID YOD MIN DE PHYIR YANG,
,MYUG TSE SA BON YOD CES BRJOD MI BYA,

And for what reason?
A sprout is not something
Which exists as something
Other than the seed;

Therefore, by the time
Of the sprout, the seed
Has gone out of existence;
That no longer exists.

For the reason that
They are not such
That they exist
As one single thing,

Because it’s not,
We never speak of a seed
Which is present,
By the time of the sprout.


[1726]
DE’I PHYIR DE LTAR DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PAR JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I TSUL LA, RTEN ‘BYUNG RTAG CHAD MED PAR GRUB PA’I SGO NAS RTAG CHAD KYI MTHAR MI LTUNG BA’I YON TAN BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA, 

For all these reasons, then, we have established that the way in which things occur in dependence is free of the extremes of lasting forever or simply discontinuing, in the way we have explained how things are free of existing through any nature of their own.  And then now we seek to demonstrate the benefits of avoiding, thus, falling into these extremes of things lasting forever, or discontinuing; which is why we continue on here to explain the following point.


[1727]
GAL TE MYU GU SA BON LAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I [f. 129a] GZHAN YIN NA NI, SA MYUG GNYIS RGYU ‘BRAS SU MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR,

That is, if a sprout were something other than its seed in a way where the sprout existed through some nature of its own, it would be inappropriate to say that the seed and the sprout were a cause and its effect.


[1728]
THE TSOM MED PAR MYU GU YOD BZHIN DU YANG SA BON RGYUN CHAD PAR ‘GYUR TE, DE LA NI SA MYUG ‘BREL MED DU SONG NAS, MYU GU YOD KYANG SA BON GYI RIGS BRGYUD MA CHAD PA LA MI PHAN PA’I PHYIR TE,

And for that reason—beyond any shadow of a doubt—at any point where the sprout is already in existence, the flow of the seed must already have discontinued.  And at that point as well, the seed and the sprout must have lost any connection between them.  As such, even if the sprout is present, it doesn’t at all assist in the continued existence of the seed as a particular type of thing.


[1729]
DPER NA BA MEN YOD PAS BA LANG SHI NAS RIGS BRGYUD CHAD PA MIN PA LA MI PHAN PA DANG, SO SKYE YOD PAS ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS RANG NYID KYI SRID PAR ‘KHOR BA RGYUN BCAD PA MIN PA LA MI PHAN PA BZHIN NO,,

For example, just because we have an ox standing there, it doesn’t at all help prevent the fact that a particular cow has discontinued as that type of thing, once the cow dies.  And just because you have a common being standing there, it doesn’t help prevent the fact that particular realized beings have managed to cut off the flow of their own personal circling within the world of pain.


[1730]
DE LTAR YIN PA LA RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR MYU GU SA BON LAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN MIN PA’I PHYOGS LA, DE GNYIS RGYU ‘BRAS SU MI ‘GAL BA DE’I PHYIR MYU GU YOD PA’I TSE SA BON ZHIG PA STE DE’I RIGS BRGYUD CHAD PA MED PAS CHAD PA SPANGS SO,,

Why—for what reason—is this the case?  Suppose we take the position that a sprout is not something which exists as something other than the seed—at least as something which is other through some nature of its own.  The fact is that it is no contradiction to say that these two exist as cause & effect; which means that, therefore, we can say that by the time that the sprout is in existence, the seed has gone out of existence.  It’s not though that the the seed type in itself has undergone any discontinuation here; that it no longer exists.  As such, we avoid the extreme of saying that things have stopped altogether.


[1731]
MYU GU’I DUS SU SA BON ‘GAGS PA LAN MANG DU BSHAD PAS, SA BON ZHIG PA’I DON ‘GREL BAS SA BON RGYUN CHAD PA LA BSHAD CING, SA BON MI ‘JIG PA BKAG PAR GSUNGS PAS, SA BON GYI RGYUN CHAD PA ZHES PA DE’I RIGS BRGYUD CHAD PA LA BZHED DO,,

The fact that—by the time of the sprout—the seed has come to a stop is described repeatedly; and so the autocommentary undertakes to explain what we mean when we say that the seed has ended, as saying that it is the discontinuation of the flow of the seed.  It speaks of a seed which has not ended being stopped; as such, the position being taken is that the expression “discontinuation of the flow of the seed” refers to the discontinuation of the continued existence of the seed as a particular type of thing.


[1732]
GANG GI PHYIR SA MYUG GNYIS GCIG NYID DU YOD PA MIN PAS SA BON DE NYID MYU GUR ‘PHOS PA MIN PA’I PHYIR, MYU GU’I DUS NA SA BON MI ‘JIG PA BKAG PA DE’I PHYIR YANG, MYU GU’I TSE SA BON YOD CES BRJOD PAR MI BYA BAS RTAG PAR YANG BKAG PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

For the reason that the pair of the seed and sprout are not such that they exist as one single thing, it is not the seed itself which shifts into being the sprout.  That’s because we’ve already denied the idea that—by the time that the sprout is present—the seed could not have gone out of existence.  And for this reason too we never speak of a seed which is present, by the time of the sprout.  Thus we avoid as well the extreme of saying that things would remain the same forever.


[1733]
DE LTAR BSHAD PA NI RGYA CHER ROL PA LAS,
,SA BON YOD NA MYU GU JI BZHIN TE,
,SA BON GANG YIN MYU GU [f. 129b] DE NYID MIN,
,DE LAS GZHAN MIN DE YANG MA YIN TE,
,DE LTAR RTAG MIN CHAD MIN CHOS NYID DO,
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON NO,,

Explaining things this way is what sutra called Playing Everywhere means when it says,

	How could there be a sprout
	When a seed is there?
	Whatever a seed is,
	Is not what that sprout is.
	
	But neither is it
	Something other than it;
	Thus it is that the
	Very nature of things
	
	Is not that they stay forever,
	Or that they have somehow
	Stopped.


[1734]
DE DAG GI DON NI SA BON YOD PAR GYUR NA SA BON GYI RGYU CAN MYU GU YANG JI LTA BA BZHIN DU ‘BYUNG NGO,,

What these lines are saying is that—if a seed exists—then a sprout which possesses this seed as its cause can also, correctly, occur.


[1735]
DE ‘BYUNG BA NA SA BON LAS GZHAN NYID DU STE NAS ‘BYUNG BA MI RUNG BAS, SA MYUG GNYIS NGO BO GCIG GO SNYAM NA,

And if the sprout does occur, then it would be incorrect to say that it could have occurred in any other way except from its cause.  And suppose that, because of this fact, you think to yourself that seed and the sprout must be such that to be one is to be the other.


[1736]
MYU GU SA BON LAS GZHAN NAS ‘BYUNG BA MIN KYANG SA BON DE NYID MYU GUR ‘PHOS PA MIN NO,,

The sprout does not occur through anything other than the seed; but that doesn’t mean that what’s happening is that the same seed is shifting into the sprout.


[1737]
DE’I RGYU MTSAN CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, MYU GU DE SA BON LAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DANG, RANG BZHIN GCIG PA NYID DE YANG MIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And why is that?  Because the sprout is not something that exists through some nature of its own which is other than the seed; nor is it something which is such that to be it is to be no other than the seed.


[1738]
DE ‘DRA BA’I PHYOGS GNYIS CAR YANG BKAG PA NA MYU GU’I RANG BZHIN DE RTAG CHAD DANG BRAL BA’I CHOS NYID DU GSAL BAR BYAS SO,,

If we disprove that the sprout could ever fit either of these two possibilities, then we have made perfectly clear that the nature of this sprout is an actual nature of things where they are free of either staying the same forever, or simply blinking out of existence.


[1739]
DON ‘DI NYID MDO DE NYID LAS,
,’DU BYED RNAMS NI MA RIG RKYEN CAN TE,
,’DU BYED DE DAG DE NYID DU YOD MIN,
,’DU BYED MA RIG ‘DI GNYIS STONG PA STE,
,RANG BZHIN GYIS NI G-YO BA DANG BRAL BA,
ZHES BYA BAS BSHAD DE,

This point is clarified in the same sutra, in the following words—

Incidents of fresh karma
Are things that have
Misunderstanding as their cause;

These cases of fresh karma
Are not something that exist
In and of themselves.

Fresh karmas and misunderstanding,
These two, are empty;

They are free of any shifting
Through any nature of their own.


[1740]
RKANG PA DANG POS NI ‘DU BYED MA RIG PA LA BRTEN NAS ‘BYUNG BA’I GTAN TSIGS DANG, GNYIS PAS NI ‘DU BYED DE KHO NA NYID DU YOD PA MIN ZHES PA’I BSGRUB BYA DANG, GSUM PAS NI RGYU ‘BRAS GNYIS KA STONG PAR BSTAN LA, BZHI PAS NI STONG TSUL STON TE, G-YO BA NI MNGON PAR ‘DU BYED PA YIN LA, DE DANG BRAL BA NI ‘DU BYED ‘DU BYED KYIS STONG PA’O,,

The first of the four sections here presents the logical statement, that fresh karma occurs through its dependence upon misunderstanding.  The second of the four presents the assertion to be proven, which is that fresh karma is not something which could exist in & of itself.  The third presents the idea that both cause and effect are empty; and then the fourth section describes the way in which they are empty.  Here, the word “shifting” connotes occurrence through conscious undertaking; and mentioning “free of” is meant to indicate that fresh karma is empty of any such undertaking.


[1741]
DE YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG BRAL LO ZHES DGAG BYA’I KHYAD PAR BSTAN TE, DE KHO NA NYID DU MED PA DANG DON ‘DRA’O,,
