And then when it’s saying here that “things are devoid of existing through any nature of their own”—which is to indicate the logical feature of what it is we deny.  This is similar to saying that these things are devoid of existing in & of themselves.


[1742]
[f. 130a] MDO DE’I DON BSTAN BCOS RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,GANG LA BRTEN TE GANG ‘BYUNG BA,
,DE NI RE ZHIG DE NYID MIN,
,DE LAS GZHAN PA’ANG MA YIN PA,
,DE PHYIR RTAG MIN CHAD MA YIN,
,ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

The point of these sutra citations is also covered in Wisdom:

Once something occurs
Through relying on anything else,

We cannot at that point say
It exists in & of itself.

But neither is it
Something other than that;

And that’s why we can say
That things neither last forever,
Nor do they simply discontinue.



A seeing emptiness
that destroyed things

[1743]
BZHI PA LA GNYIS, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PAR ‘DOD PA DGAG PA DANG, DE LTAR BKAG PA LA RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O,,

Here then is our fourth point from above, demonstrating that there is no possible instance where it would be correct to say that things could grow through any nature of their own.  Here we proceed in two steps: denying the belief that things could exist by definition; and then disproving any argument against this denial.


[1744]
DANG PO LA GSUM, ‘PHAGS PA’I MNYAM GZHAG DNGOS PO’I ‘JIG RGYUR THAL BAS DGAG ,THA SNYAD BDEN PA RIGS PAS DPYAD BZOD DU THAL BAS DGAG ,DON DAM PA’I SKYE BA MI KHEGS PAR THAL BAS DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first step here has three parts of its own.  We will first make our denial by showing that the deep meditation of a realized being would then have to act as a cause for the destruction of the entity.  Secondly we will make the denial by demonstrating that it would have to be the case that nominal reality could stand up under logical analysis.  And then thirdly we’ll make the same denial by showing that, in the same case, we could never deny that things started in any ultimate way.  And so here is the first of those three points.


	[1745]
[VI.34]
Svalakṣaṇaṃ ced bhavati pratītya
tasyāpavāde sati bhāvanāśāt,
Syāc chūnyatā bhava vināśa hetur
yuktaṃ na caitan na tato’sti bhāvaḥ.

,GAL TE RANG GI MTSAN NYID BRTEN ‘GYUR NA,
,DE LA SKUR BAS DNGOS PO ‘JIG PA’I PHYIR,
,STONG NYID DNGOS PO ‘JIG PA’I RGYUR ‘GYUR NA,
,DE NI RIGS MIN DE PHYIR DNGOS YOD MIN,

Suppose they existed
By definition; if that
Were something depending,
In a manner discounting these,

Entities would have to be
Destroyed; and as such,

Emptiness must act
As a cause
For the destruction
Of the entities.

Yet neither is that
Reasonable; as such,

It could never occur
That objects could exist.


[1746]
JI LTAR RANG BZHIN GYIS CHOS ‘GA’ YANG SKYE BA MED DO ZHES BYA BA ‘DI NI GDON MI ZA BAR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA DGOS SO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR DON ‘DI NGES PAR KHAS BLANG DGOS ZHES SMRA BAR RIGS KYI, ‘DI LA KHAS LEN GZHAG TU MI RUNG NGO ZHES BZLOG STE SMRA BAR MI BYA’O,,

As they say, “We must, beyond any shadow of a doubt, accept the idea that ‘There is no starting of any entity at all by means of any nature of its own’.”  That is, it would be appropriate at this point to follow this advice and say, “This is an idea that we must indeed agree to.”  Which is to say, it would be inappropriate to say the opposite: “We don’t see any way that this could be considered something we should agree to.”


[1747]
DE LTA MA YIN TE GAL TE GZUGS DANG TSOR BA LA SOGS PA’I RANG GI MTSAN NYID DE RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I RANG BZHIN, RGYU DANG RKYEN LA BRTEN NAS SKYE BAR ‘GYUR NA NI, RNAL ‘BYOR PAS CHOS RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PAR MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I TSE, DNGOS PO’I RANG BZHIN DE LA SKUR PA BTAB PA’I TSUL GYIS STONG PA NYID RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR TE,

And that is indeed the case, since—well, suppose it were not.  Suppose that physical form and feelings and the rest had a nature of existing by definition; which is to say, through some nature of their own.  If that nature were something that started by depending upon causes & conditions, then when a deep practitioner perceived, directly, that entities were empty of existing through any nature of their own, then they would be perceiving emptiness itself in a manner where they were discounting the very nature of all these entities.


[1748]
MNYAM GZHAG GIS GZUGS SOGS RNAMS MA DMIGS PA DGOS LA, DE RNAMS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB NA MNYAM GZHAG GIS DMIGS DGOS PA LAS MA [f. 130b] DMIGS PA’I PHYIR, DE’I TSE DNGOS PO DE RNAMS MED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And the simple fact is that—when we are in this particular deep meditation—we would then have to be focusing upon physical form and the like; and if these things existed by definition, then the meditation would have to be perceiving that fact.  But in fact, it does not.  And for this reason then, those entities—at that moment in time—would have to be non-existent.


[1749]
DE MED NA NI DNGOS PO DE RNAMS MNYAM GZHAG GI SNGAR YOD PA PHYIS MED PA’I ‘JIG PA STE ZHIG PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And if they were in fact non-existent, then entities which were existent previous to the meditation would have to be absent after the meditation: there would have had to be some kind of destruction, where they ended.


[1750]
DE’I PHYIR DE LTAR ‘JIG PA LA MNYAM GZHAG NYID RGYUR ‘GRO DGOS PAS, THO BA LA SOGS PA BUM PA LA SOGS PA’I ‘JIG RGYU YIN PA DE BZHIN DU, STONG PA NYID MTHONG BA YANG DNGOS PO’I RANG BZHIN ‘JIG PA DANG DE LA SKUR BA’I RGYUR ‘GYUR BA ZHIG NA,

As such, the case where they end in such a way must be one where the deep meditation itself has acted as the cause; which means that it must be similar to the way in which a hammer or the like acts as a cause for the destruction of a clay water pitcher, or something of that ilk.  Which is to say, seeing the fact of emptiness must in turn act as a cause for the destruction of the nature of the entities involved; for discounting them.


[1751]
DE NI RIGS PA YANG MIN PA DE’I PHYIR DNGOS PO RNAMS KYI RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI YOD PA MIN PAS, DUS THAMS CAD KYI TSE RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA KHAS BLANG BAR MI BYA’O,,

And yet neither is that a reasonable thing to say happened; as such, it could never occur that objects could exist by definition.  And thus we could never accept that things had started through any nature of their own, at any particular point in time at all.


[1752]
‘DI LA DBU MA PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SKYE BA KHAS LEN PA RNAMS, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB KYANG BDEN GRUB TU MI ‘GRO BAR ‘DOD PA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS, GZUGS SOGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB NA DE KHO NA NYID MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PAS DMIGS MI DGOS SO, ZHES SMRA MOD KYANG,

Now there are certain members of the Middle Way school who accept the idea that the starting of things could exist by definition; and they would say that a thing’s existing by definition does not necessitate that it exists in truth.  And then for this reason they would say that it’s not necessarily the case that—if physical form and the rest exist by definition—then that would have to be perceived by someone who was seeing, directly, the way things really are.


[1753]
DE TZAM NAS BDEN GRUB YIN PAR SNGAR YANG BSHAD CING, SLAR YANG ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA’I RIGS PAS NYES PA SPONG MI NUS SO,,

From this standpoint alone they would have to be accepting, as we explained earlier, that things existed in truth; and it’s not as though we would be able to disabuse them of their mistake by repeated any further logic.


[1754]
‘DIR ‘GREL PA LAS, DKON BRTZEGS LAS ‘OD SRUNGS GZHAN YANG DBU MA’I LAM CHOS RNAMS LA YANG DAG PAR SO SOR RTOG PA NI, GANG STONG PA NYID KYIS CHOS RNAMS STONG PAR MI BYED DE, CHOS RNAMS NYID STONG PA NYID DANG, ZHES GSUNGS SHING,

On this point, the autocommentary says—

We see, in the Pile of Jewels, “O Kashyapa, we can say moreover that—when we use the path of the middle way to comprehend entities so thoroughly—it’s not as if the fact of emptiness is making those things empty: rather, the very nature of those things is their very emptiness; and…”


[1755]
MTSAN MED DANG SMON MED DANG MNGON PAR ‘DU BYA BA MED PA DANG, MA SKYES PA DANG MA [f. 131a] BYUNG BA LA YANG DE BZHIN DU GSUNGS PA DRANGS TE,

We see as well a comparable section referred to with the pronouncement that nothing has any signs; there are no wishes for the future; nothing has been put together; nothing has been born; and nothing has ever happened.


[1756]
CHOS RNAMS LA RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I RANG BZHIN YOD NA, CHOS DE RNAMS RANG NGOS NAS STONG PAR MA SONG BAS CHOS RNAMS NYID STONG PA DANG ZHES PA MI ‘THAD LA,

If things did have a nature to them which existed by definition, then we could never say that these same things were, from their side, empty.  And then it would be incorrect to say things like we just saw: “The very nature of those things is their emptiness.”


[1757]
RANG NGOS NAS NGO BO NYID KYIS YOD PA MA BKAG PAR, GZHAN ZHIG GIS STONG PA’I SGO NAS STONG BAR BSTAN DGOS PAS, STONG PA NYID KYIS CHOS RNAMS STONG PAR MI BYED CES PA DANG ‘GAL BAS

And if we weren’t going to deny that things could exist, from their own side, through some nature of their own, then we would have to demonstrate that they were empty through being empty of some other thing.  And then we would contradict the statement that “it’s not as if the fact of emptiness is making those things empty.”


[1758]
DBU MA’I LAM GYIS CHOS RNAMS KYI RANG BZHIN LA SO SOR RTOG PA NA, CHOS RNAMS RANG NGOS NAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PAR STON PAR YIN PAR BSTAN NO,,

And so all this would mean that what’s being said is that—when we use the path of the middle way to make a thorough investigation of the nature of things—what we’re learning is that things are empty of existing through any nature where they could be coming from their own side.


[1759]
MDO ‘DIS NI RNAM RIG PAS GZHAN DBANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAS MI STONG BA DANG, DE GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD PA MED PAS STONG ZHES PA YANG BKAG LA,

This sutra is also serving to deny the idea of the Mentalists that those entities which arise at the pleasure of their causes & conditions are not empty of existing by definition; and the idea that these things are empty because there cannot exist any state of mind holding to an object, and any object being held by it, which are such that it is not true that to be one is to be the other.


[1760]
BRGYA PA LAS,
,STONG MIN STONG LDAN MTHONG MIN TE,
,MYANG ‘DAS BDAG GIR GYUR CIG CES,
,LOG LTAS MYA NGAN MI ‘DA’ BAR,
,DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA RNAMS KYIS GSUNGS,
ZHES DANG,

As The Hundred puts it,

	Its not as though we see
	Something that’s not empty
	As having emptiness;

	For Those Gone Thus
Have stated that
The statement that
“I’ve made nirvana my own”

Is a wrong view which means
You have not reached nirvana.


[1761]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,STONG NYID LTA BA THAMS CAD NI,
,NGES PAR ‘BYIN PAR RGYAL BAS GSUNGS,
,GANG DAG STONG PA NYID LTA BA,
,DE DAG BSGRUB TU MED PAR GSUNGS,
ZHES PAS KYANG SNGAR GYI MDO’I DON DE NYID ‘CHAD DO,,

Wisdom also says—

	The victorious Buddhas have stated
	That emptiness functions
	To destroy all of those views.

	And they say as well
That those with a view
	Of emptiness can never
	Be sustained.	

These lines as well are expressing the same point as the sutra listed above.	


[1762]
CHOS RNAMS RANG GI NGO BOS STONG ZHES PA’I BSAM DON YANG DE NYID YIN GYI, BUM PA BUM PAS MI STONG BAR BDEN PAS STONG PA NI, GZHAN STONG YIN PAS BUM PA BUM PAS STONG PA NI RANG STONG YIN NO ZHES SMRA BA NI GTAN NAS MI [f. 131b] RIGS TE,

The thought behind the expression “All entities are empty of any essential nature” is, also, exactly that.  We do see people saying things like “The fact that things are empty of any real existence of their own, in the form of a water pitcher not being empty of being a water pitcher, is other-emptiness.  As such, the fact that a water pitcher is empty of being a water pitcher is self-emptiness.”  This idea though is completely irrational.


[1763]
BUM PA BUM PAS STONG NA BUM PA LA BUM PA MED DGOS NA, RANG LA RANG MED NA GZHAN SU LA YANG MED PAS BUM PA GTAN MED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

That is, suppose that—if a water pitcher is empty of being a water pitcher—then that water pitcher must be non-existent.  In this case, the pitcher could not exist in any way at all; because if the pitcher itself has no possibility of having the pitcher itself with it, then it couldn’t ever be with anything else either.


[1764]
DE’I TSE DNGOS PO GZHAN THAMS CAD KYANG DE DANG ‘DRA BAS, DE LTAR SMRA MKHAN YANG MED PAR ‘GYUR ZHING, ‘DIS STONG PA DANG ‘DIS MI STONG ZHES PA’I RNAM GZHAG GANG YANG MI SRID PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

In such an instance, then all other entities too would be similar; which means that the person expressing the opinion itself would also have to not exist.  And then it would be completely impossible to ever put forth any positions where we said that something was empty of one thing, or not empty of something else.


[1765]
DE ‘DRA BA’I STONG PA DE KHA CIG YANG DAG TU SMRA LA, GZHAN DAG CHAD STONG DU ‘DOD PA GNYIS KA YANG RTEN ‘BREL RTAG CHAD KYI MTHA’ DANG BRAL BAR RGYAL BA RGYAL SRAS KYIS LAN CIG MA YIN PAR BSGRUBS PA LAS PHYI ROL TU GYUR PA YIN NO,,

And so some people say that these kinds of emptiness are correct forms of emptiness; while others say that they represent an emptiness of things simply discontinuing.  Both of these parties though have left behind what the Victors and the children of these Victors have established—have “sustained,” and certainly no single time—as dependent events, free of the extremes of all things remaining forever unchanging, or simply discontinuing.


[1766]
KHYAD PAR DU KUN RDZOB BDEN PA THAMS CAD KHO RANG KHO RANG GIS STONG PAR GTAN LA ‘BEBS DGOS ZER NAS, DE CHAD STONG DU ‘DOD PA NI MI RIGS PA KHO NA STE, GRUB MTHA’ BZHI PO SU YANG LTA BA DE CHAD LTA YIN PAR SHES NAS, DE RANG GI RGYUD LA SKYED PAR BYED PA SU YANG MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Let’s look more particularly at the claim here that we must establish all instances of deceptive reality through saying that they are empty of being themselves.  The belief that this then represents the emptiness of things simply discontinuing is nothing but mistaken.  It doesn’t matter which of the four classical schools a person might belong to; everybody in all the schools realizes that this is simply the view that things would, indeed, have simply discontinued.  As such, there is not a single person in all these schools that would attempt to engender this viewpoint within their own mindstream.


[1767]
DES NA DGAG GZHI DE DGAG BYA’I NGO BOR MED PA DANG, GZHI DE DGAG BYAS STONG TSUL YANG YIN PAS STONG PAR ‘DRA BZHIN DU, CHOS RNAMS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NI RANG GI NGO BOS STONG PA’I DON YIN LA,

As such, we can say that the object which we assert lacks a certain quality represents an absence of sharing any essence of that quality; and we can also say that this is equivalent to the way in which this object is empty of the particular quality that we deny about it.  These two are both ways in which we can describe the object as “empty.”  Similarly, the fact that entities are empty of existing in any way by definition is exactly what it means when we say they are empty of any essence of their own.  
 

[1768]
DE LAS GZHAN PA’I STONG TSUL RNAMS RANG GI NGO BOS STONG PA MIN PA’I RGYU MTSAN NI, STONG TSUL SNGA MA TSAD MAS GRUB ZIN BYED PA MA NYAMS PA’I RING LA, GRUB MTHAS GZHI DE BDEN PA’AM DE’I DON DU YOD PAR ‘DZIN PA’I SGRO ‘DOGS SKYE MI SRID LA, PHYI MA RNAMS KYI DON TSAD MAS GRUB [f. 132a] CING BYED PA MA NYAMS KYANG, GRUB MTHA’ BDEN PA’AM BDEN PA’I DON DU SGRO ‘DOGS PA MI ‘GAL BA’O,,

And what then is the reason why we say that ways in which things could be empty that are different than these particular ways do not represent an emptiness of some kind of self-essence?   Suppose that those previous ways in which we described things as being empty had already been confirmed by accurate perception; and we were all still sitting in a place where none of those confirmations had in any way declined.  It would in that state be impossible for us to hold a school of thought which took those same examples of things to exist in truth; neither would it be possible for there to grow, within our minds, that form of overestimation where we held that things could exist in this same kind of truth.  The idea in the latter cases here would be that a certain point had been confirmed by an accurate perception, and that the working of this perception had in no way declined; and yet this would not preclude overestimation through a learned philosophical school which said that a certain object was real; or even described what it was to be real.



Normal reality
cannot stand up
under true analysis

[1769]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above, where we deny the belief that things could exist by definition, through demonstrating that it would have to be the case that nominal reality could stand up under logical analysis.


[1770]
‘DIR SMRAS PA DON DAM PAR SKYE BA MED PAS BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA DGAG LA RAG MOD, GZUGS DANG TSOR BA SOGS TSAD MA GNYIS KYIS DMIGS PA DE DAG GI RANG BZHIN NI GDON MI ZA BAR GZHAN LAS SKYE BAR ‘GYUR RO, ,CI STE DE LTAR MI ‘DOD NA BDEN PA GNYIS SU CI STE BRJOD DE BDEN PA GCIG KHO NAR ‘GYUR RO, ,DE’I PHYIR GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YOD DO ZHES ZER RO,,

Now suppose that someone comes with the following claim about what we have said here—

Admitted that the assertion that nothing can start in an ultimate way is something that depends upon disproving that things could start either from themselves, or from something other than themselves.  But let’s take things like physical form and feelings—objects that are confirmed by either one of the two types of accurate perception.  The nature of these things is, beyond any possible debate, that they grow from things that are other than themselves.  In the event that we deny this, then how can we say that there are two types of reality?  It would all have to be but a single reality.  Thus it is that we can say that there certainly does exist the fact of things growing from things other than themselves.


[1771]
‘DI LTAR RGOL BA NI DON DAM PAR SKYE BA MED PA DANG, THA SNYAD DU GZHAN SKYE ‘DOD PAR SNANG BAS DBU MA RANG RGYUD PA ‘GA’ ZHIG GO 

Those who offer this kind of argument would appear to be accepting the idea that there is no growing of things in an ultimate sense, but that things do grow from other things, in a nominal sense.  As such they can only be members of the Independent group within the Middle Way school.


[1772]
,RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA’I GZHAN SKYE KUN RDZOB TU MI ‘DOD NA BDEN PA GCIG KHO NAR ‘GYUR ZHES PA NI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA KUN RDZOB TU MED NA YANG DAG KUN RDZOB MED PAR ‘GYUR LA, DE’I TSE KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MI SRID PAS DON DAM BDEN PA GCIG PUR  ‘GYUR ZHES PA’I DON NO,,

Some would say that “If we don’t accept the idea that things could grow—in a deceptive way, and through some nature of their own—from things other than themselves, then there will only be a single reality.”  What this is saying is that—if, deceptively, there is no birth of things by definition—then we cannot say that there exists any correct form of the deceptive.  In that case then it would be impossible for there to exist any deceptive reality; and there could only exist, they would say, the single reality: the ultimate one.


[1773]
DE’I LAN DU ‘DI BDEN MOD KYI DON DAM PAR NI BDEN PA GNYIS YOD PA MA YIN TE, DGE SLONG DAG BDEN PA DON DAM PA ‘DI NI GCIG STE, ‘DI LTA STE MI SLU BA’I CHOS CAN MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA’O, ,’DU BYED THAMS CAD NI BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I CHOS CAN NO ZHES ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

In response we can say that this assertion is true; but that it was never the case that two realities existed, in any ultimate sense.  After all, Lord Buddha himself said,

O monks, there is only one reality which is ultimate; and here’s the way it is: the one thing that cannot deceive us is nirvana.  All factors in the world are things that lie—things that deceive us.


[1774]
DE DAG GI DON NI RANG GIS KHAS LEN PA’I BDEN PA’I DON NI MI SLU BA YIN PAS, MI SLU BA’I BDEN PA KHO NAR ‘GYUR BAS DE ‘DIR [f. 132b] BDEN MOD CES GSUNGS SO,,

The import of these points is that what we accept as the meaning of “truth” is something which does not deceive us; and we would have to say then that there is only that one truth—the one which does not deceive us.  We would have to say that this is, admittedly, true.


[1775]
DON DAM PAR NI ZHES PA NI DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA’I NGOR NI, KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA GNYIS MED DE, DE’I NGOR NI DON DAM BDEN PA NYAG GCIG TU GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’O,,

And when we say “ultimately speaking,” what we are saying is that—to the perceptions of someone who is seeing the way things really are—there are no two realities: no deceptive and ultimate versions.  And so what this is all saying is that—to the perceptions of such a person—there is only that one & only reality, the ultimate one.


[1776]
BDEN PA DAM PA NI DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA’O,,

The highest truth then is the ultimate truth.


[1777]
YE SHES DE’I NGOR KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MED PA NI SLU BA’I CHOS CAN DU GSUNGS PAS SHES SO,,

And when we say that deceptive reality does not exist in the perceptions of this particular wisdom, we should understand that what’s being said then is that this reality is an example of something which deceives us.


[1778]
DON BSDU NA CHOS RNAMS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB NA ‘DU BYED RNAMS BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I CHOS CAN DU MI ‘GRUB PAS, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MED PA’I PHYIR BDEN PA GNYIS MED PAR ‘GYUR LA, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED PA’I PHYOGS LA NI, KUN RDZOB DANG DON DAM BDEN PA GNYIS KA YOD CES PA’I DON NO,,

To summarize, we can say that if things existed by definition, then it would not be the case that the various factors were things that were lying to us: deceiving us.  And in this case, there would be no deceptive form of reality; which means that there would then be no two realities.  And what this is all really saying is that—when we take the position that there is nothing in the universe that exists by definition—then there can exist the two realities: deceptive and ultimate.


[1779]
GAL TE SNGAR GYI LUNG GIS MYANG ‘DAS GCIG PU BDEN GYI, ‘DU BYED GZHAN BRDZUN PAR GSUNGS PAS ‘DUS BYAS RNAMS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB KYANG, MYANG ‘DAS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA MA YIN NAM SNYAM NA,

Now someone might think to themselves the following:

Well then, the lines you just quoted were saying that only nirvana is true; and that other things, factors, were false.  Wouldn’t this then imply that—although produced things are not things which exist by definition—nirvana, or ultimate reality, does exist by definition?


[1780]
DE’I BDEN PA NI MDO NYID LAS MI SLU BA’I CHOS CAN ZHES GSUNGS PAS MI SLU BA’I DON DU BSHAD KYI, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I BDEN PA NI MA YIN NA, ,’DU BYED THAMS CAD NI BRDZUN PA SLU BA’I CHOS CAN ZHES GSUNGS PAS KYANG SNGA MA’I BDEN PA MI SLU BA’I DON DU SHES SO,,

That type of reality is described in the sutra itself as being something that never deceives us; as such, this is what’s being explained as the meaning of “never deceives.”  But if saying that a truth existed by definition were not what “never deceives” refers to, then we would have to understand that “all the factors there are lie to us: they deceive us” was what it meant for the first truth to be something that did not deceive us.


[1781]
RIGS PA DRUG CU PA’I ‘GREL PA LAS KYANG, ‘DUS BYAS LOG PAR SNANG NAS BYIS PA SLU BAR BYED PA BZHIN DU, MYANG ‘DAS DON DAM PAS DE LTAR SNANG NAS MI SLU BAS MYANG ‘DAS BDEN PA DANG, GZHAN RNAMS MI BDEN [f. 133a] PAR GSUNGS PAR BSHAD PAS, BDEN MI BDEN GNYIS SU PHYE BA NI SLU MI SLU’I DON YIN PAR GDON MI ZA BAR ‘DOD PAR BYA’O,,

The commentary to the Sixty Verses describes how composed things appear in a wrong way and deceive infants; whereas—since nirvana is ultimate—it does not appear in this way, and does not deceive.  As such then, nirvana is described as being real, and the others as not being real.  We can thus say that the position being taken here is that the division into two realities is being made according to whether or not things are deceiving us.


[1782]
RIGS PA DRUG CU PA’I ‘GREL PA LAS MYANG ‘DAS KUN RDZOB TU BDEN PAR GSUNGS PA NI, MYANG ‘DAS DON DAM PA’I BDEN PAR YOD PA KUN RDZOB PA’I NGOR ‘JOG PA’I DON YIN GYI, THA SNYAD DU DE BDEN PAR BZHED PA MIN NO,,

When the commentary to the Sixty Verses says that nirvana is, in a deceptive way, real, what it means is that—to deceptive perceptions—nirvana is established as existing as reality which is ultimate.  The work is not though saying that, in nominal terms, that is being accepted as real.


[1783]
DE LTAR NA KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA NI DON DAM BDEN PA LA ‘JUG PA’I THABS YIN PA’I PHYIR, BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA MA DPYAD PAR ‘JIG RTEN PA’I LUGS KYIS THA SNYAD BYED PA BZHIN DU, DBU MA PAS KYANG KHAS LEN PAR BYED DO,,

We can say then that deceptive reality can serve as a means for people to engage in ultimate reality.  And so it’s similar to the way that people use terms in the way of the everyday world—without checking to see if things have grown from themselves, or from something other than themselves.  The way that those of the middle way accept things is similar.


	[1784]
[VI.35]
Arvāṅ na tattvātmakarūpato’mī
sthitiṃ labhante pravicāryamāṇāḥ,
Yataḥ padārthā na tato vicāraḥ
kāryo hi loka vyavahāra satye.

,GANG PHYIR DNGOS PO ‘DI DAG RNAM DPYAD NA,
,DE NYID BDAG CAN DNGOS LAS TSU ROL TU,
,GNAS RNYED MA YIN DE PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN GYI,
,THA SNYAD BDEN LA RNAM PAR DPYAD MI BYA,

In a selected case,
We might make an examination
Of these things, and then

We might not be able
To discover whether

Entities involved with suchness
Existed, in their nature,
Towards us.

As such,
In the nominal reality 
Of the everyday world,

No one undertakes
Those kinds of examination.


[1785]
‘DI LTAR GANG GI PHYIR GZUGS DANG TSOR BA LA SOGS PA’I DNGOS PO ‘DI DAG NI, CI BDAG LAS SKYE BA ZHIG GAM, CIG {%CI; our carving is wrong} GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ZHIG CES DE LTA BU LA SOGS PAR RNAM PAR DPYAD PA NA,

And so in a selected case we might make an examination of these things—physical form and feelings and the like—to determine whether we should say for example that “what they have grown from was themselves,” or “what they have grown from was something other than themselves.”


[1786]
DE KHO NA NYID KYI BDAG NYID CAN GYI DON DAM PAR MA SKYES PA DANG MA ‘GAGS PA LAS, TSU ROL TE GZHAN DU GYUR PA’I CHA SKYE BA LA SOGS PA CAN LA GNAS PA RNYED PA MA YIN TE,

And then we might not be able to discover whether—as opposed to demonstrating any of the starting or stopping in an ultimate sense, which we would see with entities involved with suchness itself—they existed in a way of coming towards us; which is to say, possessing some nature of growing or the like, where they displayed an aspect of evolving into something else.


[1787]
DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN THA SNYAD KYI BDEN PA LA BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS ZHES BYA BA DE LTA BU LA SOGS PA’I RNAM PAR DPYAD PAR MI BYA BAR, ‘JIG RTEN PAS MTHONG BA ‘DI YOD NA ‘DI ‘BYUNG NGO ZHES BYA BA ‘DI TZAM ZHIG GZHAN ‘JIG RTEN LA RAG LAS PA’I THA SNYAD LA ‘JUG PA’I SGO NAS KHAS BLANG BAR BYA STE,

As such, in the nominal reality of the everyday world, no one undertakes those kinds of examination, where we try to make determinations like “from itself,” or “from something other than itself,” or the like.  People in the world say things like “If there’s something in front of us that we can see, then it must have happened”; and “but these other things, they are something else.”  And what we’re saying is that we accept things relying upon the application of terms as we see them in the everyday world.


[1788]
‘PHAGS PA LHAS,
,JI LTAR KLA KLO SKAD GZHAN GYIS,
,GZUNG BAR MI NUS DE BZHIN DU,
,’JIG [f. 133b] RTEN PA YI MA GTOGS PAR,
,’JIG RTEN GZUNG BAR NUS MA YIN,
ZHES DANG,

As Master Aryadeva puts it,

	The words that barbarians speak
	In another language
	Are not something that
	The rest of us could grasp.

	Just so, those of the world
	Are unable to grasp
	Anything but that
	Which belongs to the world.


[1789]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,THA SNYAD LA NI MA BRTEN PAR,
,DAM PA’I DON NI RTOGS MI ‘GYUR,
,DAM PA’I DON NI MA RTOGS PAR,
,MYA NGAN ‘DAS PA THOB MI ‘GYUR,
ZHES DANG,

Wisdom says as well—

Without relying on terms,
There’s no way
That we could realize
The ultimate meaning of things.

And if we fail to realize
This ultimate meaning of things,
There’s no way that we could ever
Achieve the state of nirvana.


[1790]
RTZOD ZLOG LAS,
,THA SNYAD KHAS NI MA BLANGS PAR,
,NGED CAG ‘CHAD PAR MI BYED DO,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

Stopping All Argument, finally, puts it this way:

It’s not that we are saying
That we refuse all terms.


[1791]
‘DIR DPYAD MA DPYAD NI DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYAD MA DPYAD YIN LA, DE YANG DPYOD LUGS JI TZAM ZHIG NAS DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYAD PAR ‘GRO BA SHES PA GAL CHE BAS

When we talk about “examining” or “not examining” here, what we’re referring to is examining the way things really are, or not.  Now in this regard, it is very important that we understand just what manner of examining things constitutes examining the way things really are.


[1792]
CUNG ZAD BSHAD NA THAL ‘GYUR BA’I LUGS KYIS NI, THA SNYAD GDAGS PAS MA TSIM PAR MYU GU SKYE ZHES PA LTA BU LA, DE LTAR BTAGS PA’I BTAGS DON BDAG GAM GZHAN LAS SKYE ZHES TSOL BA NAS DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PAR ‘JOG GO

As such, I will offer just a brief explanation of that point here.  According to the system of the Consequence group within the Middle Way school, it constitutes an examination of the way things really are if—when for example we call something a “sprout”—we aren’t content to leave things at applying the term.  Rather, we dig into it to see whether we can say that the thing which we have applied this kind of term to is something that has grown from itself, or from something other than itself.


[1793]
,DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD KYIS GANG NAS ‘ONGS GANG DU ‘GRO ZHES PA DANG, PHYI DANG NANG GANG NA YOD CES SOGS KYI DPYAD PA RNAMS DANG GTAN MI ‘DRA BA SHES PAR BYA’O,,

As such, you should understand that the case here is totally different from instances such as where, for example, in the parlance of the everyday world we examine where it is that a thing has come from, and where it is headed to; or we check to see whether something is sitting outside, or inside.


[1794]
RANG RGYUD PA RNAMS KYIS NI DE TZAM NAS DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PAR MI ‘JOG GI ,SNGAR BSHAD PA BZHIN GYI SHES PA LA SNANG BA’I DBANG GIS YOD PAR BZHAG GAM, DE’I DBANG GIS BZHAG PA MIN PA’I DON GYI SDOD LUGS NAS GRUB PA YIN DPYOD PA NAS,

This in itself though is not enough—according to those who belong to the Independent group within this same Middle Way school—to say that we are examining the way that things really are.  They would investigate whether, first of all, things are established as existing by force of their making their appearance to a state of mind, as we described it before.  Or else they would try to see if things were not established in this manner; but, rather, simply from the way that the object itself existed in the world.


[1795]
DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PAR ‘GRO STE, DGAG BYA’I NGOS ‘DZIN MI ‘DRA BA’I GNAD KYIS, DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD MTSAMS KYANG MI ‘DRA BA GNYIS ‘ONG NGO,,

This, for them, would then constitute that analysis of the way things really are.  As such, we can say that the crucial point here is the two different ways in which the two groups identify what it is that emptiness denies; and then from this are derived the two different ways of defining the point at which something becomes an analysis of the way things really are.


[1796]
DE LTAR MA GO BAR DPER NA GNAS ‘DIR LHAS BYIN DON LA MA ‘ONGS PA LA, [f. 134a] DANG PO ‘ONGS PAR ‘KHRUL DE NAS ‘ONGS MA ‘ONGS BRTAGS PA NA, MA ‘ONGS PAR SHES PA LTA BU LA BYAS NAS,

Some though fail to understand this point.  We can look at the example of first making an error of thinking that John has arrived to the place where we are, when in fact he has yet to come.  We then check whether he has arrived or not, and realize that he hasn’t.


[1797]
MA DPYAD PA’I RNAM GZHAG THAMS CAD LOG PA’I DON CAN KHO NA DANG, DPYAD PA’I RNAM GZHAG RNAMS MA LOG PAR ‘DOD PA NI DBU TSAD GANG GI YANG LUGS MA YIN TE, GNYIS KA’I LUGS KYIS MA DPYAD PA’I RNAM GZHAG LA TSAD MAS GRUB PA DU MA ZHIG ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR RO, ,RGYAS PAR GZHAN DU BSHAD ZIN PAS MA SPROS SO,,

Just so, all determinations that we make about things without any real examination result in nothing other than erroneous conclusions.  And claiming that different ways of making the examination are not mistaken is not the position of any school which counts itself part of the Middle Way; since, for that matter, there are many points in positions not examined by either system which can indeed be confirmed by accurate perception.  I have in the past expanded on these points significantly elsewhere; and so I will not present more detail on them here.


[1798]
DE LTAR DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I RIGS PAS KUN RDZOB PA RNAMS LA DPYOD NA NI, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I THA SNYAD THAMS CAD NYAMS PAR ‘GYUR BAR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

This then is the way in which you should understand the way in which—when we examine deceptive objects using the logic which examines the real nature of things—all expressions of the everyday world collapse.



A tiny bit, on the point

[1799]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to the third of our three parts here: making the same denial that things could exist by definition, by showing that—in the same case—we could never deny that things started in any ultimate way.


	[1800]
[VI.36]
Tattvādhikāre hi yayaiva yuktyā
svasmāt parasmāc ca na janma yuktam,
Yuktyā tayaiva vyavahārato’pi
na yujyate kena tavāstu janma.

,DE NYID SKABS SU RIGS PA GANG ZHIG GIS,
,[206a] BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA RIGS MIN PA’I,
,RIGS DES THA SNYAD DU YANG RIGS MIN PAS,
,KHYOD KYI SKYE BA GANG GIS YIN PAR ‘GYUR,

Use the same rationale
As at the point of
	The way things are:

	That it would be illogical [f. 206a]
	To say that a thing
	Could have grown

	Either from itself,
	Or from something different.

	This very same reasoning
	Applies in nominal cases
	As well, to show that
	It could not be logical.

	What kind can you point to,
	For the growing?


[1801]
CI STE YANG DE LTAR DNGOS PO LA BDEN PAR MNGON PAR ZHEN PA THAMS CAD GCOD PA NA, BRED SHA ‘THON PA THA SNYAD KYI BDEN PA LA BDEN PAR ZHEN PA ‘DI GANG KUN BYANG GNYIS KYI ‘CHING GROL GYI RGYUR ‘GYUR BA, RDZAS TE RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I BDAG NYID ‘GA’ ZHIG TU SKYE BAR ‘GYUR BA CIG BYA DGOS SO ZHES SMRA NA, DE SKAD DU SMRA BA LA NI TSIG TZAM ZHIG LHAG MAR LUS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Well now, how is it?  Suppose that, as we’ve described it, people start to eliminate all of their tendencies to grasp to things existing in reality.  Then though their faces take on a certain look of panic, and they start feeling a strong belief that nominal reality though must be real.  That is, they begin to say that there must exist objects which act as causes behind the bondage and the liberation going on with the negative side of things, and the enlightened side of things.  And they feel that these causes must be creating some number of entities which are substantial; that is, which exist by definition.  But these kinds of proclamations end up just being all words, and nothing else.


[1802]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, JI LTAR DE KHO NA NYID DON DAM PA LA DPYOD PA’I SKABS SU, JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I RIGS PA GANG ZHIG GIS GZUGS SOGS BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA RIGS PA MIN PA DE BZHIN DU, THA SNYAD DU YANG RIGS PA DE NYID KYIS SKYE BAR RIGS PA MIN PAS, KHYOD KYI RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA TSAD MA GANG GIS ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR [f. 134b] RO,,

And why can we say that?  The fact is that the case here is just the same as it was at the point where we were examining the way things really are; that is, the ultimate.  We can use the same rationale that we expressed there, and say that it would be illogical to say that physical form or the like could have grown either from itself, or from something other than itself.  This very same reasoning applies in nominal cases as well, to show that it could not be logical to say that things were growing.  Thus the question remains, of what kind of accurate perception you can point to in order to establish things’ growing through some nature of their own.  Because, in fact, no such perception exists.


[1803]
DE’I PHYIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA NI BDEN PA GNYIS CAR DU YANG YOD PA MA YIN NO ZHES MI ‘DOD BZHIN DU YANG, GDON MI ZA BAR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA’O ZHES GSUNGS PAS,

What this is saying is that, therefore, your growing of things by definition is something that can exist with neither one of the two realities, at all.  This is a fact that—even though you dearly want to avoid agreeing to it—you must in the end come to accept.


[1804]
DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I RIGS PAS MI SNYAD DU YANG SKYE BA ‘GOG PA’I SKYE BA NI, MTSAMS SBYOR DU RDZAS KYI BDAG NYID KYI SKYE BA LA BSHAD CING, DON BSDUR SNGAR LTAR BSHAD PAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA ZHES DGAG BYA LA KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA KHO NA LA YIN GYI, SKYE TZAM LA NI GTAN MIN TE, THA SNYAD PA’I DON LA DON DAM PA’I DPYAD PA BYAR MI RUNG BAR LAN DU MAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Now let’s consider a growing where you use reasoning which is examining the way things really are, to deny growing even in a nominal sense.  If we were to fill out the wording here, it would be saying that the kind of growing we’re talking about is a growing which consists of some kind of substantial entity.  And to address this briefly, what they’re talking about is just the same kind of growing by definition that we spoke about earlier; it’s just that they’ve added some additional qualifier to the object we deny.  We are not though referring at all to a simple case of growing; for it has been stated over & over that it’s disallowable to apply an examination into the ultimate, when the object under consideration exists only nominally.


[1805]
DE KHO NA NYID LA DPYOD PA’I RIGS PAS THA SNYAD DU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SKYE BA MI KHEGS NA, DON DAM PAR GRUB PA’I SKYE BA YANG MI KHEGS PAR BZHED PA NI RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA TZAM NAS BDEN GRUB TU ‘GYUR BAS, DE LA THA SNYAD DU ZHES SBYAR MA SBYAR ‘DRA BAR BZHED PA’O,,

Some would take the position that—if we cannot use reasoning which is examining the way things really are to deny a case of growing which exists by definition in a nominal sense—then neither could we deny a case of growing which exists ultimately.  But taking this position is, then, to take the position that—since something exists in truth as soon as it exists by definition—it would be the same whether or not you went on to add the qualifier “in a nominal sense.”


[1806]
DE LTAR NA DGAG BYA LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS DANG, RANG BZHIN GYIS DANG, RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS ZHES SOGS KYI KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA NI MTHA’ YAS PA CIG MDO SDE DANG, YAB SRAS GNYIS DANG SLOB DPON ‘DI’I GZHUNG LAS ‘BYUNG LA, DE ‘DRA BA DE ‘GOG PA’I TSE DBU MA PA KHA CIG PHYOGS SNGAR BYAS PA NI SNGAR BSHAD PA DANG,

We see an infinite number of qualifiers applied to the object we deny here: “by definition”; “by nature”; “through some essence of its own,” and so on.  And these occur in the collection of sutras; as well as in the major writings of the father and his spiritual son—and in those of our master here.  And so consider the denial when it’s made as we’ve described it here—where certain members of the Middle Way school take the part of the disputant, and the case with them is as we’ve just been describing it.


[1807]
TSIG GSAL LAS KYANG, ‘DI NI DE KHO NA LTAR GDON MI ZA BAR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA STE, DE LTA MA YIN NA KUN RDZOB ‘THAD PA DANG LDAN PA MA YIN NAM, DES NA ‘DI DE KHO NA NYID DU ‘GYUR GYI KUN RDZOB TU MI ‘GYUR RO, ZHES [f. 135a] THA SNYAD DU BTAGS PA TZAM GYIS MI CHOG PAR BTAGS DON BTZAL BA’I DPYAD PA BYAS NAS THA SNYAD PA’I DON ‘JOG PA BKAG PA NA,

On this point we see A Clarification of the Verses also denying that we could establish the meaning of things existing nominally through a process where—without being satisfied just with describing this existence as something being labelled with terms—we go further and carry out an analysis where we search out the product of the labeling process:

This can only be accepted—beyond any shadow of a doubt—as referring to the way things are.  If that were not the case, then we ask you: wouldn’t it then be correct to say that it was the deceptive here?  As such, this can only be a reference to the way things really are, and not to the deceptive.


[1808]
DE LTA NA DON DAM PAR YOD PAR ‘GYUR BA DANG, GZUGS SOGS KUN RDZOB PAR MI ‘GYUR ZHES GZUGS SOGS DON DAM DU GRUB PAR KHAS MI LEN PA DANG, KUN RDZOB PAR ‘JOG PA CIG LA ‘PHEN LA, DE YANG DNGOS POR SMRA BA LA MIN PAS DBU MA RANG RGYUD PA YIN PAR SHIN TU GSAL LO,,

In this case what you’re saying is that things do exist in an ultimate way, but that physical form and the like don’t exist in a deceptive way.  Which is to say, by implication, that there must be someone else who takes the position that form and the rest cannot exist in an ultimate way, and must then be said to exist in a deceptive way.  And there is no one among the Functionalists who would fit this description; which means that it’s very clear that you are referring to someone who belongs to the Independent group with in the Middle Way school.


[1809]
‘DIR SLOB DPON GYIS KHA CIG ‘PHAGS PA’I ZHAL SNGA NAS, BDAG LAS MA YIN GZHAN LAS MIN, ZHES SOGS KYI GZHUNG GIS SKYE BA SOGS BKAG PA NI, GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD PA’I KUN BRTAGS KYI SKYE BA SOGS BKAG PA YIN GYI, GZHAN DBANG BDEN PA BKAG PA MIN PAR ‘DOD PA

At this point, the Master starts talking about how some people refer to the lines from The Realized One which include “Things don’t grow from themselves”;  that is, how these words deny growing and the like.  They believe that what this is denying is a growing to imagined entities, where the object held by a perception and the perception holding it could ever be such that to be one was not to be the other.  They would not say though that this was a denial that things under the control of others could ever be real.


[1810]
‘DI YANG, DE LTAR ‘GREL PA’I GTAN TSIGS MED PAR MI ‘GRUB PAS, DE SKAD DU SMRA BA LA NI BRGAL ZHING BRTAG PAR BYA BA KHO NA’O, ZHES BSHAD PA’I PHYOGS SNGA SMRA BA NI, SNGA RABS PA KHA CIG SLOB DPON BLO BRTAN LA SOGS PA YIN PAR SMRA MOD KYANG, DE’I GZHUNG NA DE LTAR BSHAD PA MI SNANG NGO,,

At this point, the autocommentary says that “since without a proper syllogism the point could not be made, making this statement is simple argumentation, and conjecture.”  Now admitted that some thinkers of the earlier generation here in Tibet have expressed the opinion that the opponent in the argument here is Master Sthiramati, or someone like that; but I have not observed in his writings any such explanation.


[1811]
BZHI BRGYA PA’I ‘GREL PAR SLOB DPON CHOS SKYONG GIS BZHI BRGYA PA’I LTA BA SEMS TZAM DU BKRAL BAR BSHAD PAS DE LA SBYAR NA ‘GRIG GO

In his commentary to the 400 Verses, Master Dharmapala explains the viewpoints of the 400 as commenting upon the Mind Only school; and it would seem acceptable to apply that here.


[1812]
,’O NA ZAB MO’I MDO’I DON SEMS TZAM DU ‘GREL PA RNAMS KYIS ‘PHAGS PA’I GZHUNG RNAMS KYI DON JI LTAR DU ‘GREL ZHE NA,

“Well then,” one may ask.  “How is it that those who interpret the meaning of sutras on the profound as following the ideas of the Mind Only comment upon the meaning of the works of the Realized One?”


[1813]
SLOB DPON DBYIG GNYEN LA SOGS PA’I CHEN PO RNAMS KYI GZHUNG NA, KLU SGRUB KYI GZHUNG [f. 135b] GI DON ‘DI LTAR ‘GREL PA YIN ZHES GSAL BAR MI SNANG YANG,

Now it is not the case that we see clear references in the great books of great masters like Vasubandhu which interpret the import of Nagarjuna in this way.


[1814]
RNAM BSHAD RIGS PA LA SOGS PAR DGONGS ‘GREL GYI MDO LA BRTEN NAS SHER PHYIN GYI MDO DRANG DON DU ‘CHAD PAR SNANG BAS,

There do appear though references in works like Reasoning in Explanation which—basing their arguments on What I Really Meant—explain the sutras of the perfection of wisdom as being figurative.


[1815]
DE BZHIN DU ‘CHAD PAR MNGON TE ‘PHAGS PA’I GZHUNG ‘GOG PA NI MI SRID LA, SGRA JI BZHIN PAR ‘CHAD NA NI SHER PHYIN GYI MDO SGRA JI BZHIN PAR MI ‘CHAD PA MI MDZAD CIG, SGRA JI BZHIN PA DRANG DON DU BSHAD NA DE’I DON SEMS TZAM DU ‘CHAD DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And they might indeed appear to be making their explanation this way.  It is flatly impossible to refute the great classics of the Realized One; but don’t think that if you interpret them as being literal, you can’t also explain the sutras of the perfection of wisdom as being literal.  And that’s because—if you interpret what is meant literally as something which is figurative—then you would have to read the Realized One’s works as being Mind Only.


[1816]
‘ON KYANG CHOS THAMS CAD DON DAM PAR MA GRUB PA DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PAR BSHAD PA RNAMS SGRA JI LTA BA BZHIN DU RIGS PAS ‘GRUB PAS, SGRA JI BZHIN PA LA GNOD PA MED PA’I PHYIR, DRANG DON DU ‘GREL MI NUS PA LA DGONGS NAS, BRGAL ZHING BRTAG PAR BYA BA KHO NA’O ZHES GSUNGS TE,

The fact though is that explanations which say that nothing in the universe exists in an ultimate way; and that nothing exists by definition; can be established, by correct reasoning, as being literal.  Given this, people have thought that—since there is nothing to prevent us from taking the points literally—there is no way that we can explain them as being figurative.  And thus we come up with statements like “this is simple argumentation, and conjecture.”


[1817]
SGRA JI BZHIN PA’I BZLOG PHYOGS LA GNOD BYED DANG, DRANG THAD LA SGRUB BYED MTHA’ YAS PA CIG STON PA NI, GZHUNG GI DON RNAM PA GZHAN DU DRANG DU MI RUNG BAR SGRUB PA YIN PAS ‘DIR MDO TZAM LAS MA GSUNGS SO,,

Once we present problems with doing the opposite of taking something as literal, and once we have offered innumerable arguments in support of leaving off taking them as figurative, then we have established that it would be incorrect to interpret the meaning of a text as referring to something other than what it says directly.  As such, I have said no more than a tiny bit on the point here.



Illusions in the world

[1818]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second point from before: disproving any argument against our denial that things could exist by definition.


[1819]
GAL TE RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SKYE BA BDEN LA {%PA scan is wrong = LA} GNYIS CAR DU YANG MED NA, GZUGS LA SOGS PA RNAMS MED PAR ‘GYUR LA, DE LTA NA GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I NGO BO MIG LA SOGS PA’I SHES PA LA ‘JIG RTEN DU DMIGS PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, DE LTA MA YIN NA RI BONG GI RVA LA SOGS PA YANG MIG LA SOGS PA’I SHES PA LA SNANG BAR ‘GYUR TE, RGYU MTSAN KUN NAS MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

One may begin with the following question—

Suppose then that it really is the case that a growing of things by definition exists with neither one of the two realities.  In this case, physical form and the rest could would have to be non-existent.  And in that case, then things that have the essential nature of form and the like could never be something that the awarenesses of the eye and such ever perceive, here in the everyday world.  And if that were the case, then even things like rabbit horns could make their appearance to the awarenesses of the eye and the like.  And that’s because the reasoning would be equivalent, in every respect.


	[1820]
[VI.37]
Śūnyāḥ padārthāḥ pratibimbakādyāḥ
sāmagryapekṣā na hi na prasiddhāḥ,
Yathā ca śūnyāt pratibimbakādeś
cetas tadākāram upaiti janma.

,DNGOS PO STONG PA GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS PA,
,TSOGS LA LTOS RNAMS MA GRAGS PA YANG MIN,
,JI LTAR DER NI GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS STONG LAS,
,SHES PA DE YI RNAM PA SKYE ‘GYUR LTAR,

		Things which are empty—
		A reflection in a mirror,
		And so on—
	
		Rely upon the coming together;
		And we cannot say
		This is something
		The world itself wouldn’t say.

		It’s just the same
		As there: a reflection
		And the like are empty,

		And from these grow
		Awareness which assumes
		The likeness of it.


	[VI.38]
Evaṃ hi śūnyā api sarva bhāvāḥ
śūnyebhya eva prabhavaṃ prayānti,
Nocchedinas te na ca śāśvatāś ca
satya dvaye’pi prakṛter abhāvāt.

[VI.38a]
	,DE BZHIN DNGOS PO THAMS CAD STONG NA YANG,
,STONG NYID DAG LAS RAB TU SKYE BAR ‘GYUR,
,BDEN PA GNYIS SU’ANG RANG BZHIN MED PA’I PHYIR,

		All functioning things—
		Even though they are empty—

		Quite certainly grow,
Just as these, from those
Of emptiness.


[1821]
[f. 136a] DE’I LAN BSHAD PA, DNGOS PO STONG PA STE BRDZUN PA GZUGS BRNYAN DANG LA SOGS PAS SGRA BRNYAN LA SOGS PA RNAMS, ME LONG DANG BYAD BZHIN DANG BRAG PHUG DANG, SGRA PHYUNG BA SOGS KYI RGYU RKYEN GYI TSOGS PA LA LTOS PA STE BRTEN NAS SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN NA MA GRAGS PA YANG MIN TE GRAGS SO,,

In answer to this concern, let’s take things which are empty—which is to say, false; let’s take a reflection in a mirror and things that are covered in the wording “and so on”: things like echoes and such.  These are phenomena which rely upon the coming together of causes & conditions, such as a mirror and something standing in front of it; or the hollow of a cave, and a sound that someone emits.  That is to say, they grow in dependence—and we cannot say that this is something that the world itself wouldn’t say; that is, the world does say it.


[1822]
JI LTAR ‘JIG RTEN LA GRAGS PA DER NI GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS PA STONG BA STE BRDZUN PA LAS, MIG LA SOGS PA’I SHES PA GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS PA DE YI RNAM PA CAN SKYE BAR ‘GYUR BA TAR {%LTAR},

The case here is just the same as we see it spoken of there in the world; that is, in that instance things like a reflection in the mirror and the like are empty—which is to say, false—and from these false things can grow kinds of awareness such as that of the eyes and such: awareness which assumes the likeness of the reflection and so on.


[1823]
BRDZUN PA’I GZUGS BRNYAN LAS BRDZUN PA’I RNAM PA CAN GYI SHES PA SKYE BA DE BZHIN DU, DNGOS PO THAMS CAD RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG NA’ANG, DES STONG PA’I RGYU DAG LAS DES STONG PA’I ‘BRAS BU RAB TU SKYE BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Just as a type of awareness can grow which has assumed the false form of the reflection which is itself false, all the functioning things there are—even though they are empty of existing by definition—quite certainly grow, as results that are empty of that existence flowing from causes that are also empty of it.


[1824]
‘DIR GZUGS BRNYAN LAS NI DE ‘DZIN PA’I MIG SHES SKYE BAR GSUNGS PAS, GZUGS BRNYAN DNGOS PO YIN ZHING SHES PA DANG NGO BO THA DAD PAS NI, PHYI ROL GYI DON YIN LA DE YANG MIG SHES KYI DMIGS RKYEN YIN PAS, GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DU BZHED PA YIN TE, ZLA GNYIS DANG SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA DANG SGYU MA SOGS DANG, SGRA BRNYAN SOGS LA YANG DE BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

When this says that the visual awareness which grasps to a reflection has grown from a reflection, what it’s saying is that the reflection itself is an actual thing, and that it is not such that to be the awareness of it is to be the reflection.  As such, the reflection is an outside object, and is serving as an “object factor” for the arisal of the visual consciousness.  Thus then the reflection is accepted here as belonging to the door of sense of visible form.  You should understand appearances such as the doubled moon, and the hair in the sink—as well as illusions and echoes and the like—as being the same.


[1825]
DE LTAR NA DBANG SHES ‘KHRUL PA LA SNANG BA’I BYAD DANG ZLA GNYIS DANG SKRA SHAD SOGS NI, DBANG PO LA ‘PHRAL GYI GNOD PA MED PA’I SHES PA LNGA LA SNANG BA’I RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

And so what’s being said here is that when our sense perceptions are mistaken, and an object which is actually just a reflection in the mirror appears to us—or we see things like the two moons, or a hair lying there—it is similar to the case with our five sense perceptions when they are not affected by any adventitious defect, but things appear to them to exist by definition.


[1826]
BYAD BZHIN SOGS MI SRID KYANG DER SNANG BA NI  [f. 136b] RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI {%carving: add also MI} SRID KYANG DER SNANG BA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

A reflection which is actually the object reflected is an impossibility; but it can seem as though it is.  It is an impossibility for something to exist by definition; but it can seem as though it does—the cases are similar.


[1827]
GZUGS BRNYAN DANG SGRA BRNYAN LA SOGS PA NI GZUGS DANG SGRA LA SOGS PA DANG ‘DRA BAS, DES NA GZUGS SOGS LNGA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA PHYI ROL TU MI ‘JOG KYANG DER SNANG BA’I GZUGS SOGS PHYI ROL TU ‘JOG PA BZHIN DU, GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS BYAD BZHIN YIN PA SOGS PHYI ROL TU MI ‘JOG KYANG, GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS PHYI ROL TU ‘JOG STE DE GNYIS PHYI ROL TU ‘JOG MI ‘JOG MTSUNGS PA YIN NO,,

Reflections in a mirror, and echoes in a cave, and other such things are similar to actual visible forms, and sounds, and the like.  As such, even though we do not say that visible forms and the other four exist as outside objects which exist through some nature of their own, we can say that the visible form and such which appear to be this way are on the outside.  Similarly, we do not say that reflections and the like which are the actual image standing before the mirror and such exist on the outside; but we can say that the reflection and such themselves are on the outside—that is, the case here is the equivalent, when we are making the determination of whether these two are outside objects, or not.


[1828]
GZUGS BRNYAN BYAD BZHIN GYIS STONG PA TZAM GYI BRDZUN PA NI, STONG NYID STON PA’I LUNG RIGS GANG LA YANG BLO KHA MA PHYOGS PA’I ‘JIG RTEN PA’I RGAN PO BRDA BYANG THAMS CAD KYIS ‘GRUB PAS, DE LTAR RTOGS PA DE RIGS SHES RAGS PA CIG TU ‘DOD PA NI MI RIGS PA KHO NA’O,,

The concept of falseness in the form of a reflection in the mirror being simply empty of existing as the object standing in front of the mirror is something that even old geezers in the everyday world who understand the words we are using can establish as fact, without directing their minds in any way to forms of scripture and logic which present the concept of emptiness.  As such, portraying this kind of understanding as a coarse version of logical thinking is simply in error.


[1829]
GAL TE DE LTA NA NI GZUGS BRNYAN BRDZUN PAR GRAGS PA DE GRUB KYANG, DBU MA PAS BZHAG PA’I BRDZUN PAR MI ‘GRUB PAS, SNGA MA DE PHYI MA’I DPER JI LTAR ‘GYUR ZHE NA,

One may come with the following question—

If that’s the way it is, and there really does exist a reflection which everyone admits is false, then it wouldn’t be false in the same was as the those of the Middle Way school describe it.  How then can you say that the former stands as an illustration of the latter?


[1830]
SKABS ‘DIR GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS DPER BKOD PA NI ‘JIG RTEN PAS GRUB ZIN DPER ‘GOD PA YIN GYI, DBU MA PAS BRDZUN PAR BZHAG PA GRUB ZIN PA CIG DPER ‘GOD PA MIN NO,,

When we present the reflection in a mirror and so on as examples in this particular context, we are only putting them forth as instances which are already accepted in the everyday world.  We are not putting them forth as examples of something which those of the Middle Way have already completed demonstrating as false.


[1831]
DE YANG BYAD BZHIN DU SNANG BA’I GZUGS BRNYAN LTA BU DE LA SNANG BA’I STENG NAS CHA ‘DI TZAM ZHIG BYAD BZHIN DU SNANG LA, ‘DI TZAM ZHIG BYAD BZHIN DU MI SNANG NGO ZHES RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU DBYE MI NUS LA,

It is not, moreover, the case in any way at all that we could ever make a distinction here where we say that—with something like a reflection that appears to actually be the object standing in front of the mirror—this particular part is appearing as that object; and this particular other part is not appearing as the object.


[1832]
BYAD BZHIN GYI GANG SNANG GI CHA THAMS CAD NAS SNANG BA LTAR DU YOD [f. 137a] PAS STONG YANG, RANG GI RGYU LA BRTEN NAS SKYE BA MI ‘GAL BA DPER BYAS NAS DE BZHIN DU SNGON PO RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA NA YANG, SNGON PO’I STENG NAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR SNANG MI SNANG GI CHA GNYIS DBYER MED PAR SNANG LA,

Rather, the reflection is appearing in a way where it is empty of existing as the object in front of the mirror in all of the parts of it which are making their appearance.  And yet there is still no contradiction in saying that this reflection is growing through reliance upon its particular causes.  And we can go ahead and use this as an illustration for describing how the color blue might act.  That is, the blue may appear as though it exists by definition; but it appears this way in a manner where we could never divide out a part of the blue which is appearing as though it exists by definition, and another part which does not appear as though it exists by definition.


[1833]
DE LTAR SNANG BA YANG GANG SNANG GI CHA THAMS CAD NAS SNANG BA LTAR DU YOD PAS STONG YANG, RANG GI RGYUS BSKYED PA DANG RANG GIS ‘BRAS BU BSKYED PA MI ‘GAL BAR SGRUB PA YIN TE,

And even though the blue does appear this way, it is empty of actually being the way that it appears to be, in all of its various parts making such an appearance.  Nonetheless, we have shown how it is no contradiction here to go further and say it has been produced by its causes; and is in turn producing its own results.


[1834]
BYAD BZHIN KYI GZUGS BRNYAN LA DER GANG SNANG GI CHA THAMS CAD NAS SNANG BA LTAR DU MED KYANG GZUGS BRNYAN MED PAR MI ‘GRO BA CIG ‘JOG SHES NA, SNGON PO LA YANG RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA’I CHA THAMS CAD NAS SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU MED KYANG, SNGON PO YOD PAR NGES PAR ‘JOG NUS PA CIG ‘ONG NGO,,

The reflection of an object in the mirror is not something which exists in the way it appears, in each and every one of the parts of it which appear to actually be that object.  But this in no way requires us to say that there is no reflection there at all.  If we understand how we can say all this, then in the case of the color blue as well we can say that it does not, in reality, exist in the way that it appears to exist, in any single one of the multiple parts of it which appear to exist by definition.  At the same time though, there certainly does exist a color blue there; and we can in this way learn to establish that fact, with complete certainty.


[1835]
ZHIB MO’I BLOS GZUGS SOGS KYI STENG NAS ‘DI ‘GOG ‘DI MI ‘GOG CES PA’I RNAM PA GNYIS GZUGS BRNYAN GYI DPE STENG NAS PHYED PA NI, DBU MA’I LTA BA SNYED PA LA MED MI RUNG DU DGOS PAS TSIM SLA MI NYAN NO,,

And so we make distinctions here based upon the example of a reflection in the mirror, where with delicate mental distinctions we say—with reference to visible form and the like—that this thing is something we are refusing; but that other thing is not something that we are refusing.  This kind of work is something that you actually cannot do without, in your search for the viewpoint of the middle way.  As such, I urge you not to listen to people who buy easy explanations.


[1836]
DES NA ‘GREL PA LAS KYANG GZUGS BRNYAN RANG BZHIN MED PA’I RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU RNAM PAR BZHAG PA YANG, SHES BZHIN DU MKHAS PA SU ZHIG GZUGS DANG TSOR BA LA SOGS PA RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU LAS THA DAD PA MED PAR GNAS PA RNAMS YOD PA TZAM ZHIG TU DMIGS PAS, RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PA NGES PAR BYED, DE’I PHYIR YOD PAR DMIGS KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED DO,

Thus it is too that the autcommentary says,

We can use a reflection in the mirror to describe cause & effect which have no nature of their own.  Wise ones who are keeping their wits about them though observe that things like physical form and feelings exist in a way where they are in no way divorced from the principles of cause & effect—although they might simply appear to be, and thus certainly be thought to exist through some nature of their own.  As such, the wise perceive these things as existing, but not as having grown through some nature of their own.


[1837]
ZHES [f. 137b] YOD TZAM DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA DANG, SNGAR SKYE BAR BSTAN LA ‘DIR RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR BSTAN PAS, SKYE BA DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA GNYIS SO SOR ‘BYED PA SHIN TU GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

What this is saying is that things do, simply, exist; but have no existence through any nature of their own; and that things which we said earlier to grow, do not however grow through any nature of their own.  As such there is being described here—extremely clearly—the idea that we need to learn to distinguish between these two ideas: of things growing, and of things growing through some nature of their own.


[1838]
DE DAG MA PHYED NA DNGOS PO YOD PHYIN CHAD RANG GI NGO BOS YOD PA DANG, RANG GI NGO BOS MED PHYIN CHAD YE MED DU SONG NAS SGRO ‘DOGS DANG SKUR ‘DEBS KYI MTHA’ GNYIS LAS MI ‘DA’ STE,

If we fail to make such a distinction, then we would have to say that—once an entity exists—then it would have to exist through some essence of its own.  And we would have to say as well that—once an object did not exist through any essence of its own—then it could not exist at all.  That is, we could never get beyond the two extremes of overrating the relative existence of a thing, and underrating the same thing.


[1839]
BRGYA PA’I ‘GREL PA LAS, DNGOS PO DNGOS PO YOD PAR SMRA BA’I LTAR NA NI JI SRID DU DNGOS PO DE’I YOD PA NYID YIN PA DE SRID DU, DE LTAR RANG GI NGO BO YANG YIN PA NYID LA, GANG GI TSE RANG GI NGO BO DANG BRAL BA DE’I TSE DE LA DNGOS PO DE RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MED PA’I PHYIR, BONG BU’I RVA DANG ‘DRA BAS GNYIS SU SMRA BA LAS MA ‘DAS PA’I PHYIR, ‘DI’I MNGON PAR ‘DOD PA THAMS CAD ‘GRIG DKA’ BAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES SO,,

The commentary to The Hundred puts it this way—

According to those who say that things exist, the essential nature of a thing is also there, just as long as the existence of that same thing is there; and at any point where that same thing loses its essential nature, then the thing itself can no longer exist in any form at all: it becomes the exact equivalent of a rabbit horn.  As long as they think this way, then these people are never anything more than those who assert a discrepancy.  As such, it is quite difficult to reconcile all the beliefs that people like this hold.


[1840]
DES NA RANG GI NGO BOS MED PAS YOD MTHA’ THAMS CAD DANG, DE NYID LA RANG BZHIN MED PA’I RGYU ‘BRAS ‘JOG NUS PAS MED MTHA’ THAMS CAD LAS GROL BA NI SLOB DPON SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS DANG ZLA BA’I ZHABS KYIS ‘PHAGS PA’I DGONGS PA BKRAL BA’I KHYAD CHOS SU SNANG BAS, YOD PA GNYIS DANG MED PA GNYIS PHYED PA SHIN TU GAL CHE’O,,

As such, a position where we can avoid every form of the extreme of things existing, because they can never exist through any nature of their own; and where at the same time we can avoid every form of the extreme of things not existing, because we are unable to posit cause & effect with no nature of its own, in the true way of things; would appear to be a unique feature of the way in which Master Buddha Palita, and the honored Chandrakirti, have interpreted the true thought of the Realized One.  As such, it is crucial that we learn to distinguish between two forms of existing, and two forms of not existing.


[1841]
GZUGS BRNYAN GYI DPES GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA NI, YAB SRAS MJAL BA LAS,
,ME LONG SHIN TU YONGS DAG LA,
,JI LTAR RANG BZHIN MED PA YI,
,GZUGS BRNYAN SNANG BA DE BZHIN DU,
,LJON PA CHOS RNAMS SHES [f. 138a] PAR GYIS,
ZHES GSUNGS TE,

Establishing all these points with the example of the reflection of something in a mirror hearkens back to the sutra called The Meeting of the Father & Son:

You should understand
Trees and the rest of things

As being like the reflection
Of something in a mirror
Which is crystal clear:

They have no nature
Of their own.


[1842]
BRDZUN PA’I DPE GZHAN RNAMS KYI DPE DON SBYOR TSUL YANG SNGAR BZHIN DU SHES PAR GYIS SHIG

You can understand other examples of falseness by applying the relevant metaphors and their referents as we have done up to here.



Easily escaping extremes

[1843]
,LNGA PA LA GNYIS, RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA SPANG SLA BA’I YON TAN DANG, LAS ‘BRAS KYI ‘BREL BA CHES ‘THAD PA’I YON TAN NO,,

Here is our fifth point from above, where we demonstrate the advantages of denying that things could grow through any nature of their own, relative to both forms of reality.  This we present in two points, describing first the advantage that both the views that things could never change, or that they could simply discontinue, are thus easily prevented; and then secondly the advantage of showing that the connection between karma and its consequences is eminently correct.


[1844]
DANG PO NI,

Here then is the first.


	[1845]
	[VI.38b]
,DE DAG RTAG PA MA YIN CHAD PA’ANG MIN,

These things
Neither last forever
Nor simply discontinue.


[1846]
GANG GI PHYIR DNGOS PO THAMS CAD GZUGS BRNYAN LTAR RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAS STONG PA DE NYID KYI PHYIR, DON DAM PA DANG KUN RDZOB BDEN PA GNYIS SU’AM GNYIS CAR DU’ANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PA’I PHYIR, GZUGS SOGS DE DAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I RTAG PA MA YIN LA, DER MA ZAD CHAD PA’ANG MIN TE, CHAD PA NI MYUG TSE SA BON ZHIG PA MED PA’I SKABS SU BSHAD PA LTA BU’I CHAD PA DANG,

Due to the fact that all entities are similar to reflections in a mirror, they are empty of existing through any nature of their own.  And for this very reason, they can exist through a nature of their own neither with regard to ultimate reality, nor deceptive reality.  And this then is why these things—physical form and the rest—are neither things that could last forever, and which exist by nature; nor things that could simply discontinue, in the same way.  And when we say “discontinue” here, what we’re referring to is a kind of discontinuation such as where a seed could ever not have ended at the time of its sprout.  


[1847]
RTZA SHE LAS,
,SNGON BYUNG DA LTAR MED CES PA,
,DES NA CHAD PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR,

As Wisdom puts it,

They say that
What happened before
Is not there now;

And for this reason
Things must have
Discontinued.


[1848]
ZHES DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHAS BLANGS PAS SNGAR YOD KYI DNGOS PO PHYIS MED PA’AM, ZHIG PA’I MI RTAG PAR ‘DOD NA’ANG CHAD LTAR ‘GYUR TE, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR KHAS LEN NA DE RTAG MI RTAG GANG DU ‘DOD KYANG, RTAG CHAD KYI MTHAR LTUNG BA’I LTA BAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

What this refers to is where we accept that idea that things could exist through any nature of their own; and where something that was there before is not there afterwards—which is to say, it has stopped.  This constitutes agreeing to the thing being changing; but it amounts to things simply discontinuing.  Once you accept the idea that a thing could exist through any nature of its own, it doesn’t matter whether you assert that it’s unchanging  or changing; you are still holding a viewpoint where you have fallen into the extremes of things lasting forever, or simply discontinuing altogether.  This is what’s being said in these lines.


[1849]
‘DIR ‘GREL PAR RTZA SHE LAS, STON PAS SPRUL PA ZHIG SPRUL LA NGES KYANG GZHAN ZHIG SPRUL PA DE BZHIN DU, BYED PA PO DANG LAS DANG DES BYAS PA RNAMS KYANG DE RNAMS DANG ‘DRA BAR GSUNGS PAS, RANG BZHIN MED PA LAS RANG BZHIN MED PA RNAMS SKYE BAR BSTAN TO, ZHES [f. 138b] GSUNGS PAS NI, RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA LA BYA BYED THAMS CAD ‘JOG PAS CHAD LTA MED PAR STON PA’O,,

At this point in the autocommentary they talk about how we can ascertain that the Teacher has sent out an emanation, but then that emanation can emanate yet another.  And what it’s saying is that the agent of an action; and the action itself; and what that does are similar.  The wording here is “Things without any nature of their own grow from things with no nature of their own.”  What these words are indicating is that—in a case where we establish the working of things while nothing exists through any nature of its own—we avoid the view that things could have simply discontinued.


[1850]
‘DIR KUN RDZOB TU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA MA BKAG NA SHIN TU PHRA BA’I BDAG MED MI RTOGS PAS, SHIN TU PHRA BA’I RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA RGYUD LA MI SKYE BA YANG BYA DKA’ BAS, RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA MA LUS PAR SPONG BA NI, DGAG BYA DE KUN RDZOB TU BKAG PA’I YON TAN NO,,

If we are unable to disprove the idea that—from a deceptive point of view—things could ever exist through some nature of their own, then we will never grasp the extremely subtle form of the lack of self-existence.  It is an extremely difficult task to prevent the viewpoint of the extremely subtle forms of staying forever and simply discontinuing from growing within our mind; and it is one of the great features of blocking the object which we deny when we speak of no-self-nature even deceptively, when our goal is to eliminate, within ourselves, each and every case of the views that things could stay forever, or simply discontinue.


[1851]
DE KUN RDZOB TU YOD PA KHEGS NA DON DAM LA LTOS PA’I RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BAR MI LTUNG BAR MA ZAD, KUN RDZOB LA LTOS NAS RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA’I DRI MAS MI GOS PAS NA, RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA SPONG SLA BA’I YON TAN YOD DO,,

If we can prevent the belief that this could exist deceptively, then we will never fall into the viewpoints that things could either last forever, or simply discontinue, relative to the ultimate.  Not only that, but if we can prevent ourselves from being sullied by the stench of the viewpoint that things could either last forever or simply discontinue, relative to the deceptive, then there is the added benefit that we find in easier to eliminate, completely, these views of lasting or discontinuing.



How does karma
connect to a consequence?

[1852]
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MI ‘DOD PA LA KUN GZHI SOGS KHAS BLANG MI DGOS PAR BSTAN PA DANG, LAS ‘GAGS PA LAS ‘BRAS BU ‘BYUNG BA’I DPE BSTAN PA DANG, DE LTAR BSTAN PA LA RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O,,

Which brings us to our second point from above: The advantage of showing that the connection between karma and its consequences is eminently correct.  Here we proceed in three steps: a demonstration that it is not the case that if we deny that things could exist through any nature of their own, we must then accept things like foundation consciousness; the presentation of a metaphor to illustrate how a karmic consequence can come from the karma itself having stopped; and then finally disproving any debate that may arise about this presentation.


[1853]
DANG PO LA GSUM, MTSAMS SBYOR GYI GZHUNG BSHAD PA DANG, RTZA BA’I TSIG DON BSHAD PA DANG, DE LAS ‘PHROS PA’I DON BSHAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these three steps has three parts of its own: explaining that part of the text which provides a segue here; explaining the words of the root text; and explaining additional points that those issues themselves raise.  Here is the first of these.


[1854]
DE LTAR BDEN PA GNYIS GAR YANG RANG BZHIN MED PAS RTAG PA DANG CHAD PAR LTA BA RGYANG RING DU SPANGS PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU MA ZAD KYI, 

Not only is it the case that we are able to banish, to a great distance, the views that things could last forever or simply discontinue—for the reason that these things have no nature of their own, relative to both of the two forms of reality.  


[1855]
LAS RNAMS ‘GAGS NAS YUN RING DU LON YANG LAS RNAMS KYI ‘BRAS BU DANG ‘BREL BA NI, KUN GZHI RNAM PAR SHES PA DANG SEMS KYI RGYUN DANG CHUD MI ZA BA DANG THOB PA LA SOGS PAR YONGS SU RTOG PA MED PAR YANG ‘THAD PA YIN NO,

Even if an extended period of time has gone by after particular karmas have come to an end, they still have a connection to the results of those karmas.  And this connection is something which is correct, even without imaginary ideas about a foundation consciousness; or the flow of the mind; or the way in which nothing ever just fades away; or retainers, or others of the like.


[1856]
ZHES RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PA’I PHYOGS [f. 139a] LA RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BA RGYANG RING DU BSRINGS PA’I YON TAN YOD PAR MA ZAD KUN GZHI LA SOGS PA KHAS MA BLANGS KYANG LAS ‘BRAS KYI ‘BREL BA SHIN TU ‘THAD PA’I YON TAN YOD PAR BSTAN NO,,

What this is saying is that—yes—with those who take the position that things cannot exist by definition, even nominally, there is that benefit that they are able to banish, to a great distance, the viewpoints either that things could last forever as they are, or else simply discontinue.  But that’s not all; there is also the benefit that the connection between karma and its consequences is, for them, something which is extremely correct, even if they refuse to accept concepts such as foundation consciousness, or the like.


[1857]
‘PHAGS PA’I GZHUNG ‘GREL TSUL LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA RDUL TZAM MED KYANG, BYA BYED THAMS CAD BZHAG PAS CHOG PA’I ‘GREL TSUL GYI LUGS THUN MONG MA YIN PA ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS, RNAM PAR DAG PA’I GRUB MTHA’ ‘GREL BYED GZHAN DANG THUN MONG MA YIN PA MANG DU YOD DE,

As far as commenting upon the classic of the Realized One, this is a truly unique way of doing it; where we say that—even though there does not exist even the tiniest bit of anything which could ever exist by definition—still we can go ahead and posit the entire system in which things do what they do.  And based upon this kind of presentation, there are many other points here that are not held in common even with other commentators who belong to quite accurate schools of thought.


[1858]
DE GANG ZHE NA RE ZHIG GTZO BO RNAMS BRJOD NA, TSOGS DRUG LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I KUN GZHI RNAM SHES DANG, RANG RIG ‘GOG LUGS THUN MONG MA YIN PA DANG, RANG RGYUD KYI SBYOR BAS PHYIR RGOL GYI RGYUD LA DE KHO NA NYID KYI LTA BA SKYED PA KHAS MI LEN PA GSUM DANG,

And what are those points?  Well, if we were just to mention some of the main ones, we could point first to the three of—

	1) A foundation consciousness which was not such that
		to be it was automatically to be the group of six
		different types of consciousness;

	2) A unique way of denying apperception; and

	3) The denial that one can—with the “independent” form of
		reasoning—inspire the view of the way things really
		are, in the mind of an opponent.


[1859]
SHES PA KHAS LEN PA BZHIN DU PHYI ROL GYI DON YANG KHAS BLANG DGOS PA DANG, NYAN RANG LA DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PA YOD PA DANG, CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN NYON MONGS SU ‘JOG PA DANG, ZHIG PA DNGOS PO YIN PA DANG, DE’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS DUS GSUM GYI ‘JOG TSUL THUN MONG MA YIN PA SOGS YIN NO,,

And then there are also:

	4) The fact that—just as one accepts awareness—you must also 
		accept the existence of outside objects.

	5) The idea that listeners and self-made buddhas do realize
		the fact that things have no nature of their own.

	6) The determination that the tendency to grasp to a
		self-existence of things is a negative emotion.

	7) The idea that the fact of something having ended is
		itself a functioning thing.

	8) The concept that—due to that being the case—the 
		three times can be defined in a unique way.


[1860]
DE’I DANG PO NI SKABS ‘DIR BSTAN LA, RANG RIG KHAS MI LEN PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MI ‘DOD PA LA THUG TSUL NI ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

The first of all these is presented at this juncture; and we will go on to explain how our refusal to accept apperception stems from our denial that things could exist through any nature of their own.


[1861]
RANG RGYUD MI BZHED PA DE LA THUG TSUL NI RGYAS PAR GZHAN DU BSHAD ZIN LA, MDOR BSDUS SHIG ‘DIR YANG ‘CHAD DO,,

We have already explained elsewhere, in detail, how our refusal to accept an “independent” logical statement also stems from the same thing.  But we will give just a brief recap of that here.


[1862]
PHYI ROL KHAS LEN PA ‘DI [f. 139b] LA THUG PA NI ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR LA, LNGA PA YANG ‘DI LA THUG TSUL NI SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS KYIS NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD LAS CHOS THAMS CAD BDAG MED DO ZHES GSUNGS PA’I MED RGYU’I BDAG NI, NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA BSHAD PA LTAR ‘DIR YANG BZHED DE, DE YANG BDAG MED MTSAN NYID RDZOGS PA’I DON NO,,

The way in which our accepting the existence of outside objects comes down to this is something we will be explaining.  The fifth point also comes down to this same concept; Master Buddha Palita has made that reference to “the lack of a self-nature to all things, covered in the collections of the listeners.”  The self-nature lacking here is explained as referring to things existing through some essence of their own; and that idea is accepted here as well.  This is moreover the point of saying that things have no self-nature; it describes this concept definitively.


[1863]
DE’I PHYIR GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED MTSAN NYID RDZOGS PA YANG GANG ZAG RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED PA LA BYA DGOS LA, DE JI BZHIN DU RTOGS PA LA NI CHOS KYI BDAG MED JI BZHIN PA YANG RTOGS DGOS PA’I GNAD DO,,

Therefore when you describe the lack of a self-nature to the person in its definitive form, you have to tie it to how the person cannot exist through any essential nature of their own.  And the crucial point here is that you have to understand how to describe the lack of a self-nature to things in the same way that you have grasped that other fact.


[1864]
DE LTA YIN NA CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN NYON MONGS SU NGES PAR ‘DOD DGOS PAS NYON MONGS KYI NGOS ‘DZIN LA PHRA RAGS GNYIS DANG, MI RTAG SOGS BCU DRUG GI LAM TZAM GYIS GROL MI GROL GYI ‘DOD TSUL GNYIS DANG, SHES SGRIB MTSAMS GANG NAS SPONG BA MI ‘DRA BA SOGS KYI KHYAD PAR MANG PO ZHIG YOD DO,,

Since that’s the case, we most certainly have to accept the tendency to believe in a self-nature to things as being a negative emotion; and this means that there are relatively more subtle, and relatively less subtle, ways of identifying just what a negative emotion is.  There are quite a few distinctions to be drawn here; such as two different opinions about whether or not a person can be liberated solely through the path of the 16 aspects of impermanence and the rest, and different ideas about the point at which we are able to eliminate obstacles to omniscience.


[1865]
‘O NA DANG POR THEG CHEN DU ZHUGS PA’I DE KHO NA NYID KYI LTA BA LEGS PAR GTAN LA PHEBS PA ZHIG DANG, NYAN RANG DU LHUNG PA GNYIS GZHI MTHUN SRID PA NI DBU MA PA GNYIS KAS KYANG ‘DOD DGOS LA, DE LTA NA DE ‘DRA BA DES CHOS KYI BDAG MED BSGOMS PAS MNGON SUM DU ‘GYUR BA DANG, DE LTAR MTHONG ZIN GOMS BAR BYED PA CIG KYANG ‘DOD DGOS SO,,

But first of all here we can say that we need to describe, accurately, how both of the groups within the school of the Middle Way would have to agree to the concept of one person who had just entered the greater way—and succeeded in establishing, accurately, the view of suchness—who at the same time could conceivably drop into the ways of the listeners, or the self-made buddhas.  And they would have to agree that, in such a circumstance, the person who had done so could have a direct experience—since they had been meditating on the lack of a self-nature to things; and they could as well undertake to accustom themselves to what they had finished seeing.


[1866]
DE LTA NA LAM DES CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN KUN BRTAGS MTHONG LAM NAS SPONG BA DANG, BDAG ‘DZIN DE LHAN SKYES, DE’I SGOM LAM NAS KYANG SPONG BA ‘DOD DGOS [f. 140a] PAS, DNGOS PO RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I DBU MA PA’I LUGS LA YANG CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN LA NYON MONGS CAN YIN MIN GNYIS ‘DOD DAM SNYAM NA,

One might wonder about something here.  In such a case, we would have to agree that a person could use this particular path to eliminate the learned form of grasping to a self-nature to things at the point of the path of seeing; and then could eliminate the innate form of grasping to this self-nature at the point of the path of habituation.
