GANG ZAG DE’I BLO YI MTHONG BA LA LTOS NA NI, MIG SHES DANG SKRA BSHAD {%SHAD} KYI RNAM PA STE SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA’I YUL GNYIS CHAR YANG YOD PA YIN LA, DON GSAL MTHONG BA STE RAB RIB MED PA’I MIG GIS MTHONG BA LA LTOS NA NI SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA DANG, DE SNANG BA’I SHES PA GNYIS KA’ANG BRDZUN PA STE MA SKYES PA YIN TE, SNANG BA TZAM GYI YUL YANG MED PAR SHES PA YOD PA NGES PAR DKA’ BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Relative to what the mind of this person sees, the visual consciousness and the aspect of the strand of hair—the object which appears as though it were a strand of hair—do both indeed exist.  Relative though to the sight of someone who is seeing objects clearly—that is, to the sight of an eye which has no cataracts—both the appearance of something as a strand of hair and the state of mind which holds this appearance are false; which is to say, neither one has actually grown.  That is, it would be difficult to say that one ascertained the existence of a state of mind if there were not even any object which was just appearing to be there.


[2160]
‘DI NI GDON MI ZA BAR DE LTAR NGES PAR ‘DOD DGOS SO,,

And one would have to agree that—beyond any shadow of a doubt—this could be ascertained as such.


	[2161]
[VI.55]
Jñeyaṃ vinā syād yadi nāma buddhis
tat keśa deśānuga locanasya,
Vitaimirasyāpi ca keśa buddhiḥ
syād eva na tvevam ato’sti naitat.

,GAL TE SHES BYA MED PAR BLO YOD NA,
,SKRA DE’I YUL DANG MIG NI RJES ‘BREL PA’I,
,RAB RIB MED LA’ANG SKRA SHAD BLOR ‘GYUR NA,
,DE LTA MA YIN DE PHYIR DE YOD MIN,

		Suppose a state of mind
		Were there in the absence
		Of an existing object;

		The object of that strand
		Would have an eye which
		Was connected with it;

		And one who had
		No cataracts would also
		Have a state of mind
		With a strand of hair—

		And for this reason
		It is not the case;
		It is not something
		Which could exist.


[2162]
DE LTA MA YIN TE GAL TE RAB RIB CAN LA SHES BYA SKRA SHAD MED PAR SKRA SHAD KYI RNAM PA CAN GYI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I BLO SKYE BA YOD NA

And suppose it were not this way; suppose a state of mind were there—that it started—with the person who had the cataracts, which existed through some nature of its own and held the appearance of a strand of hair even in the absence of any strand of hair which was an existing object.


[2163]
GANG DU RAB RIB CAN GYIS SKRA SHAD DE MTHONG BA’I YUL DER [f. 160b] MIG NI RJES SU ‘BREL BA STE GTAD PA’I RAB RIB MED PA LA’ANG RAB RIB CAN DANG ‘DRA BAR SKRA SHAD MTHONG BA’I BLO SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE, YUL MED PAR MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

The object which was such that the person with the cataracts saw it as a strand of hair would have to have an eye which was connected with it; that is, which was attending to it.  And in that case, even a person who had no cataracts would also give rise to a state of mind where they saw a strand of hair, in the same way that the the person with the cataracts did.  And this is because the object is equally a non-entity, in both cases.


[2164]
‘DI NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN LAS SKYE NA, GZHAN YIN TSAD THAMS CAD LAS SKYE BAR ‘PHEN PA BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I SHES PA CIG SKYE NA, YUL SKRA SHAD MED PAR MTSUNGS PA LA, RAB RIB CAN LA DE MTHONG BA SKYE LA, RAB RIB MED PA LA DE MTHONG BA MI SKYE BA MI ‘THAD DE, SHES PA DE RAB RIB LA MI LTOS PAR ‘PHUL NUS PAS ‘BREL MED DU ‘GRO BA’I PHYIR RO,,

If something could grow from something other than it which existed through some nature of its own, then that implies that it could grow as well from each & every other object in the universe which was other than it.   Just so, if it were possible for one state of mind to grow which existed through some nature of its own, then it would be incorrect to say that—in a case where the strand of hair were equally absent—the sight of it would grow in a person who had cataracts but the sight of it would not grow in a person who had no cataracts.  That is, since there would be the potential for this state of mind to make itself known without any dependence upon cataracts, everything would happen without any connection to anything.


[2165]
RAB RIB MED PA LA SGRA SHAD DU SNANG BA’I BLO SKYE BA DE LTA MA YIN PA DE’I PHYIR PHYI ROL MED PAR RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I SHES PA DE YOD PA MIN NO,,

And so it is not the case that a state of mind which holds the appearance of a strand of hair could start with the person who had no cataracts; and for this reason, that state of mind which exists through some nature of its own—in the absence of outer objects—is not something which could ever exist.



Denying others on deep seeds

[2166]
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, BAG CHAGS SMIN MA SMIN NYID LAS DON SNANG GI RNAM SHES SKYE BA DANG MI SKYE BA DGAG PA, SLAR YANG PHYI ROL MED PAR RNAM SHES YOD TSUL BRJOD PA DGAG PA, SEMS TZAM GYI LUGS BKAG PA LA LUNG GI GNOD PA MED PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

This brings us to our second section from above: denying the referent of the metaphor in a case where awareness arises from the power of a deep seed.  Here we proceed in three steps: denying that an awareness that takes on the image of the object and which comes from either the ripening or the lack of ripening of a deep seed could ever grow, or not grow; once more denying the description of how there could be an awareness, in the absence of outer objects; and showing how there is no problem from scripture when we deny the system of the Mind Only.


[2167]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, GZHAN LUGS BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these has two parts of its own: a presentation of the position of the opponent; and a denial of this position.  Here is the first.


[2168]
GAL TE SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA’I SKRA SHAD LTA BU’I YUL GYI YOD PA NYID RNAM SHES SKYE BA’I RGYU YIN NA, RAB RIB MED PA LA YANG SKRA SHAD SNANG BAR ‘GYUR BA ZHIG NA DE NI MIN NO,,

Suppose one were to say that—if the very existence of an object similar to a strand of hair that appeared as a strand of hair were the cause of an awareness growing—then the strand of hair would appear as well even to a person with no cataracts.  Our answer then would be “That’s not the case.”


	[2169]
[VI.56]
Dhī śakti pāko’sti na śuddha dṛṣṭer
yatas tato dhīr na hi jāyate’sya,
Na jñeya sadbhāva viyoga taś cet
tac chaktyabhāvān na hi siddham etat.

[VI.56a]
,GANG PHYIR MTHONG BA DAG LA BLO NUS NI,
,SMIN MED DE PHYIR DE LA BLO MI ‘GYUR,
,SHES BYA YOD DNGOS BRAL BAS MIN ZHE NA,

		Suppose this were
Your position:

“It is not the case
		That there would be
		Any ripening
		
		Of the potential
		For a state of mind
		With those who saw.

		For this reason then,
		It is not the case
		That a state of mind could
		Ever come with these

		Because it was devoid
		Of any entity
		Which possessed
		An existing object.”


[2170]
‘O NA CI ZHE NA,

“So then,” one might ask, “how does it work?”  Well, suppose you took the following position—


[2171]
RNAM SHES SKYE BA’I BAG CHAGS SNGAR BZHAG PA DE SMIN PA DANG MA SMIN PA DE DAG RNAM PAR SHES PA SKYE BA DANG MI SKYE BA’I RGYU YIN TE,

A deep seed for the growth of awareness was planted earlier on; and the ripening—or the not ripening—of that seed is the cause for the growth, or the failure to grow, of that awareness.


[2172]
DE’I PHYIR GANG ZAG GANG LA SKRA’I RNAM PA CAN GYI SHES PA SNGA MA GZHAN GYIS BZHAG PA’I [f. 161a] BAG CHAGS SMIN PA YOD PA DE KHO NA LA, SKRA SHAD KYI RNAM PA CAN GYI SHES PA ‘BYUNG GI

As such, it is only a person who is experiencing the ripening of a deep seed that was planted by another, previous state of mind that possessed an image of a hair that will have an awareness arise with the image of a strand of hair.


[2173]
,GANG GI PHYIR RAB RIB MED PAR YUL MTHONG BA DAG LA SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA’I BLO YI NUS PA BAG CHAGS NI SMIN PA MED PA DE’I PHYIR RAB RIB MED PA DE LA SKRA SHAD MTHONG BA’I BLO SKYE BAR MI ‘GYUR BA YIN GYI, SHES BYA SKRA SHAD DU YOD PA’I DNGOS PO DANG BRAL BAS BLO DE MI SKYE BA MIN NO ZHE NA,

It is not however the case that there would be any ripening of a deep seed—the potential for a state of mind that took on the aspect of a strand of hair—with those who saw the object but had no cataracts.  And for this reason then, it is not the case that a state of mind where they saw a strand of hair could ever come to grow with these individuals who had no cataracts.  It is not though the case that this state of mind would fail to grow because it was devoid of any entity which possessed an existing object which was a strand of hair.  

Suppose then that this were your position.



The present has no potential on its own

[2174]
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, DA LTAR BA LA NUS PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG ,MA ‘ONGS PA’I NUS PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG, ‘DAS PA LA NUS PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Which brings us to our second part from above: a denial of our opponent’s position.  We’ll cover this point in three steps: a denial that the present could possess a potential that existed through some nature of its own; a denial that the potential of the future could exist through some nature of its own; and a denial that the potential of the past could exist through some nature of its own.  Here is the first.


	[2175]
	[VI.56b]
,NUS DE MED [207a] PAS ‘DI NI ‘GRUB MA YIN,

	Since there is no such thing
	As a potential like this
	Which exists [f. 207a],

	That is not something
	Which could be established.


[2176]
GAL TE NUS PA ZHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA CIG YOD NA NI, DE’I TSE NUS PA DE SMIN MA SMIN LAS RNAM SHES ‘BYUNG MI ‘BYUNG YOD DU CHUG NA YANG, NUS PA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA DE MED PAS, ‘DI NI ‘GRUB PA MA YIN NO,,

If what we call “potential” here were one that could exist through some nature of its own, then admittedly we could say that awareness would occur, or not occur, when that potential had ripened, or not yet ripened.  But since there is no such thing as a potential like this which exists in & of itself, then that is not something which could be established.


	[2177]
[VI.57]
Jātasya śakter na hi sambhavo’sti
nājāta rūpasya ca śaktir asti,
Viśeṣaṇaṃ nāsti vinā viśeṣyaṃ
vandhyā sutasyāpi ca tat prasaṅgaḥ.

	[VI.57a]
,SKYES LA NUS PA SRID PA YOD MA YIN,
,MA SKYES NGO BO LA YANG NUS YOD MIN,

	It is not a possibility
	That there could exist
	A potential to what
	Had already grown;

	Neither could there exist
	Any potential that had
	A nature of
Not having yet grown.


[2178]
JI LTAR MI ‘GRUB CE NA,

“And just how is it,” one may ask, “that this could not be established?”


[2179]
NUS PA ‘DI RTOG PA NA RNAM SHES DA LTAR BA’I ‘BREL PA CAN ZHIG GAM, RNAM SHES ‘DAS PA DANG MA ‘ONGS PA’I ‘BREL BA CAN ZHIG TU ‘GYUR GRANG,

When you imagine this kind of potential, do you think of it as something which has a connection to a present state of consciousness, or something which has a connection to a consciousness which is past or future?


[2180]
DE LA RE ZHIG SKYES PA STE DA LTAR BA LA NUS PA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA SRID PA NYID YOD PA MA YIN LA, MA SKYES PA MA ‘ONGS PA’I NGO BO LA YANG NUS PA YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

On this question, to start with, we would say that it is not at all a possibility that there could exist a potential to the present—to what had already grown—which also existed in & of itself.  Neither could there exist any potential that had a nature of being future; that is, of not having yet grown.


[2181]
DE LA RE SHIG {%ZHIG} RNAM SHES DA LTAR BA LA NUS PA ‘DOD PA NA,

And let’s say, for a moment, that you assert that the present form of this awareness had some potential.


[2182]
RNAM SHES DANG NUS PA GNYIS KA DUS MTSUNGS SU ‘GYUR LA, DE’I TSE NUS PA DANG NUS PA CAN GNYIS LA NUS PA’I RNAM SHES ZHES RNAM DBYE DRUG PA YIN PA DE’I TSE, DE GNYIS DON GZHAN DU MI RIGS PAS [f. 161b] NUS PA’I RNAM SHES NI NUS PA NYID DU YOD PA MI RIGS TE,

In this case, both the awareness and that potential would have to be the same, as far as the time in which they existed.  In that case, then the sixth grammar case—“the consciousness of the potential”—would apply to both the potential itself, and to what possessed the potential.  And in that case, it would be illogical to say that the two were two different things.  As such, it would be incorrect to say that the consciousness of the potential existed as the potential itself.


[2183]
YOD NA NI ‘BRAS BU LA RANG LAS GZHAN PA’I RGYU MED PA CAN DU ‘GYUR ZHING, MYU GU SKYES PA NA YANG SA BON MI ‘JIG PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

If it did exist in that way, then the result would be something that lacked a cause which was other than it; and once the sprout had grown, then the seed could never stop.


[2184]
GANG GI TSE NUS PA DANG NUS PA CAN GNYIS LA NUS PA LAS RNAM SHES ZHES RNAM DBYE LNGA PA YIN PA DE’I TSE NI, RNAM PAR SHES PA SKYES PA DUS MNYAM PA’I NUS PA LAS ‘BYUNG BAR MI RIGS TE, RGYU’I DUS NA ‘BRAS BU YANG YOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And then suppose that the relationship between the two of the potential and that which possessed the potential were expressed by the fifth grammar case: “the consciousness which came from the potential.”  In this case, it would be incorrect to say that the consciousness’ having taken birth arose from a potential which were simultaneous with it.  This is because the result would also be present during the time of its cause.


[2185]
DE LTAR NA RE ZHIG RNAM SHES DA LTAR BA LA DE’I RGYU’I NUS PA YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

As such, we would have to say for the moment that the potential of its cause could not be present with the present form of the consciousness.



Denying a self-existent
potential for the future

[2186]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which bring us to our second step from above: a denial that the potential of the future could exist through some nature of its own


[2187]
RNAM SHES MA SKYES PA LA NUS PA YOD NA NI, RNAM PAR SHES PA’I NUS PA ZHES SBYAR BA NA, NUS PA KHYAD PAR GYI GZHI DANG RNAM SHES KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS YIN NO,,

Suppose that the consciousness yet to arise had some potential.  When you phrase it like this—“The consciousness potential”—then the potential becomes the basis of the particular feature and the consciousness becomes the feature that this basis possesses.


[2188]
DE LA RNAM SHES MA SKYES PA MA ‘ONGS PA NI, RNAM PAR SHES PA’O ZHES SGRUB PA’I NGO BOR BSTAN PAR MI NUS LA, RNAM PAR SHES PA MA YIN ZHES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I DGAG PA’I NGO BOR BSTAN PAR MI NUS SO,,

Suppose here though that the consciousness had not yet grown; that it was future.  In this case you could not speak of it as having an established existence: “The consciousness.”  But neither could you speak of it as “not being consciousness”: as having a nature where you denied that it could exist through some nature of its own.
 

[2189]
GANG GI TSE RNAM SHES MA ‘ONGS PA DA LTAR RNAM SHES SU MED PA DE’I TSE, NUS PA ‘DI NI RNAM SHES ‘DI’I NUS PA’O ZHES BYA BAR GANG GIS NUS PA KHYAD PAR DU BYED PAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR RO,,

And suppose there is a point in time when a future consciousness does not yet exist as a present consciousness.  At that point, how could you distinguish then a potential where you said “This particular potential is the potential of this particular consciousness”?  In fact, you could not.


	[2190]
	[VI.57b]
,KHYAD PAR MED PAR KHYAD PAR CAN YOD MIN,
,MO GSHAM BU LA’ANG DE NI YOD PAR THAL,

	There would exist none
	Characterized by
	A certain feature,

	In the absence of
	A feature.

	This would also
	Have to exist
	With the child
	Of a barren woman.


[2191]
DE LTAR NA KHYAD PAR RNAM SHES MED PAR DES KHYAD PAR DU BYAS PA CAN GYI NUS PA YOD PA MA YIN TE, DE LTA MA YIN NA MO GSHAM GYI BU LA’ANG DE’I NUS PA NI YOD PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As such, there would exist no potential which could be characterized by a certain feature, in the absence of any consciousness that was its feature.  And if this were not the case, then it would also have to be the case that this kind of potential also existed with the child of a barren woman.


[2192]
GAL TE RNAM SHES GANG ZHIG NUS PA LAS SKYE ‘GYUR DE SNYING LA BSAMS NAS, RNAM SHES ‘DI YI NUS PA ‘DI YIN ZHING NUS PA ‘DI LAS RNAM SHES ‘DI ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR [f. 162a] RO, ,ZHES DE LTAR KHYAD PAR DANG KHYAD GZHI’I DNGOS POR ‘GYUR TE,

Suppose that deep in your heart you are thinking of a certain consciousness which is going to grow from the potential, and then you speak of “such-and-such a potential of such-and-such a consciousness,” and “such-and-such a consciousness that will arise from such-and-such a potential.”  That is, suppose there comes to be an entity where there is a feature and some locus for the basis.


	[2193]
[VI.58]
Bhaviṣyatā ced vyapadeśa iṣṭaḥ
śaktiṃ vinā nāsti hi bhāvitāsya,
Parasparāyāśrayaṇī ca siddhir
asiddhir eveti vadanti santaḥ.

,GAL TE ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR BAS BSNYAD ‘DOD NA,
,NUS PA MED PAR ‘DI YI ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR MED,
,PHAN TSUN DON LA BRTEN PA’I ‘GRUB PA NI,
,GRUB MIN NYID CES DAM PA RNAMS KYIS GSUNGS,

		Suppose you assert
		That you apply a term
		To that which is
		Yet to come.

		But there cannot exist
		Any which could arise
		In the absence
		Of a potential.

These are things
Which occur in a
Codependent relationship;

The holy ones
Would say that
That is something
Which could only never exist.


[2194]
‘JIG RTEN NA ‘BRAS CHAN TSOS SHIG CES PA DANG, SNAL MA ‘DI LA RAS YUG THOGS SHIG CES ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR GYI ‘BRAS CHAN DANG, SNAM BU LA BSAMS NAS DE SKAD SMRAS PA DANG,

Suppose one comes with the following comment:

In the everyday world, we say things like “Could you cook that fluffy rice?” or “Could you weave some cloth from that thread?”  When we speak thus, we are actually thinking of fluffy rice that is going to be there, and cloth that is going to be there.


[2195]
MDZOD LAS KYANG,
,MNGAL DU ‘JUG PA GSUM DAG STE,
,’KHOR LO SGYUR DANG RANG BYUNG GNYIS,

And in the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge too we read—

	There are three ways in which
	They enter into the womb:

	An emperor of the wheel,
	And the two who are self-born.


[2196]
ZHES ‘KHOR SGYUR SOGS SU ‘GYUR RGYU ZHIG MNGAL DU ‘JUG PA LA, DE DAG MNGAL DU ‘JUG PAR BSHAD PA BZHIN ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR BA’I RNAM SHES LA BSAMS NAS RNAM SHES KYI NUS PA ZHES BSNYAD PAR ‘DOD DO ZHE NA,

That is, we are talking about how someone who is to become a wheel emperor enters the womb, referring to them as if it were a wheel emperor entering the womb.  And so what we assert is that we apply a term here in the same sense, referring to “the potential for the consciousness” where we are talking about a consciousness which is yet to come.


[2197]
DE YANG SNYING PO MED DE, RES ‘GA’ ZHIG TU YOD PAR ‘GYUR NA NI, ‘BRAS BU DE DA GZOD ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR GYI, RTAG TU DUS NAM GYI TSE YANG MI ‘BYUNG BAR NGES PA MO GSHAM GYI BU LA SOGS PA DANG, ‘DUS MA BYAS KYI NAM MKHA’ LA SOGS PA NI, DA LTA DANG DUS PHYIS GANG DU YANG MI ‘BYUNG NGO,,

This position though is hollow.  If you are talking about something that at for some time being is existent, then the result would have already made its appearance.  But there are also things like the child of a barren woman that will never make their appearance.  And items such as empty space which is not a produced thing never come into being anyway—whether we are talking about now, or some later time.


[2198]
DE’I PHYIR GAL TE RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I NUS PA YOD NA RNAM SHES ‘BYUNG DU CHUG KYANG, GANG GI TSE DA LTA MA ‘ONGS PA’I RNAM SHES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA NI DUS NAM YANG MED PAS, DE SKYED PA’I NUS PA GTAN MED PA DE’I TSE, MO GSHAM GYI BU LA SOGS PA BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I RNAM SHES SKYED PA’I NUS PA MED PAR RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I RNAM SHES ‘DI YI ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR BA MED DO,,

And so we can say that—if there did exist a potential that existed through some nature of its own—we could allow that consciousness might then occur.  But in a situation where there is never, upon any occasion, any present or future consciousness which could exist through a nature of its own, there cannot exist at all any potential which could trigger it.  And in this case, there cannot exist any consciousness that existed through its own nature and which could arise in the absence of a potential that triggered a consciousness that existed through some nature of its own: the whole thing would be like the child of a barren woman, or something of that ilk.


[2199]
DBU MA PAS MYU GU SKYE BA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA ‘GOG PA’I SKABS MANG POR, MYU GU SA BON GYI DUS SU MED KYANG SKYE NA, RI BONG GI RVA LA SOGS PA YANG SKYE BAR [f. 162b] ‘GYUR RO, ,ZHES HA CANG THAL BA ‘PHEN PA’I

In many contexts where those of the Middle Way school deny that the growing of a sprout could happen by definition, they say things like “If the sprout could be absent at the time of the seed and yet still grow, then the horn of a rabbit or the like would also grow.”  That is, they point to an absurd consequence that would be necessitated.


[2200]
GNAD NI RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I MYU GU NI SKABS GCIG TU MED NA DUS NAM YANG MED DGOS PAS, GZHI MA GRUB DANG KHYAD MED DU ‘GRO BA’I RGYU MTSAN GYIS YIN GYI, SPYIR MYU GU SA BON GYI DUS NA MED KYANG SKYE NA, RI BONG GI RVA YANG SKYE BAR THAL ZHES ‘GOG PA GTAN MIN NO,,

The point of such statements is to say that—if there were any single occasion upon which a sprout that existed by definition were absent—then it would have to always be absent.  And then there wouldn’t be any difference from saying that it never existed in the first place.  This is the rationale being employed at this point; it is not the point though to say that—generally speaking—if a sprout were absent in the time of the seed but were still able to grow, then a rabbit horn would also have to grow.  This is not at all the denial being made here.


[2201]
RIGS PA ‘DIS NI ‘BRAS CHAN LA SOGS PA YANG BSHAD PA YIN TE, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA LTAR NA, ‘BRAS CHEN SOGS ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR YANG GTAN MED DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

We can use this same reasoning to explain the fluffy rice and so on.  That is, if their growing were something that happened through some nature of its own, then the fluffy rice or whatever to come would also have to be entirely non-existent.


[2202]
GZHAN YANG RNAM SHES ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR YOD PA LA LTOS NAS DE’I NUS PA ‘JOG LA, NUS PA LAS RNAM SHES ‘BYUNG NGO ZHES NUS PA LA LTOS NAS RNAM SHES ‘JOG NA, PHAN TSUN GYI DON LA BRTEN PA’I ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Moreover, the potential for a consciousness is posited relative to a consciousness which is yet to occur; and we posit the consciousness relative to the potential; we say: “The consciousness is going to rise from the potential.”  As such, these are things which occur in a codependent relationship.


[2203]
DE ‘DOD DO ZHE NA, DE LTAR NA RNAM SHES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MIN PA NYID CES DAM PA MKHYEN RAB MNGA’ BA RNAMS KYIS GSUNGS SO,,

And if you say that all this seems like something you could agree to, then in that case the holy ones—which is to say, those who possess supreme intellect—would say that, in that case, a consciousness which could exist through some nature of its own is something which could only never exist.


[2204]
‘GREL PAR RING THUNG DANG PHA ROL TSUL {%TSUR} ROL LTA BU’I LTOS ‘GRUB RNAMS NI BTAGS PAR YOD PAR ‘GYUR GYI, GRUB PA RANG BZHIN PA MED PAR GSUNGS PAS DE DAG LA GRUB PA SPYIR ‘GOG PA MIN GYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ‘GOG PA’I KHYAD PAR RNAMS SHES PAR BYA’O,,

In the autocommentary, they talk about how things like long & short—and “over there” & “over here”—exist as designated relative to each other; but since it is said that their existence is not one which has any quality of being natural, it is not the case that we are denying, in general, that they could have any existence at all.  As such, you need to understand the details of how we deny that things could exist through any nature of their own.


[2205]
DE LTAR SMRA NA NI KHO BO CAG GI SMRA BA’I RJES SU ‘BRANG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

When you can describe things like this, then you can say that you are a follower of the way that we describe things.


[2206]
DE LTAR NA RNAM SHES MA ‘ONGS PA LA YANG NUS PA MED DO,,

And as such, we can say that future consciousness has no potential either.



Denying a past on its own

[2207]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third and final step from above: a denial that the potential of the past could exist through some nature of its own.

	[2208]
[VI.59]
Niruddha śakteḥ paripākataḥ syād
yadyanya śakteḥ parasambhavaḥ syāt,
Santānināṃ tatra mitho’sti bhedaḥ
sarvasya sarva prabhavas tataḥ syād.

,GAL TE ‘GAGS PA’I NUS SMIN LAS ‘GYUR NA,
,GZHAN GYI NUS PA LAS GZHAN ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR,
,RGYUN CAN RNAMS DER PHAN TSUN THA DAD YOD,
,DE PHYIR THAMS CAD KUN LAS ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR,

	Suppose that
	Some potential
	From the stopping
	Ripens, and from that
	There comes this.

	Something other
	Is arising from
	A potential which
	Is something other.

	In a case where
	Things have the flow
	There exist those
	Distinct from one another;

	In that case
	Everything would happen
	From everything.


[2209]
DA NI ‘DAS PA LA YANG NUS PA MED DO ZHES BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

Now the next part of our text then is dedicated to showing how the past has no potential either.


[2210]
GAL TE SKYES NAS ‘GAG BZHIN PA’I RNAM SHES KYIS RANG DANG MTHUN PA’I ‘BRAS BU’I DON DU, KUN GZHI RNAM SHES LA BAG CHAGS KYI NUS PA’I [f. 163a] KHYAD PAR BZHAG PA,

Suppose that a consciousness which has grown—and is now in the act of stopping—deposits some type of potential, in the form of a deep seed, into the foundation consciousness—towards creating a result which corresponds to it.


[2211]
RNAM PAR SHES PA ‘GAGS PA’I NUS PA SMIN PA LAS ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR GYI RNAM SHES ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR NA NI,

And suppose it is the case then that some potential from the stopping of the consciousness ripens, and from that there comes this arisal of the consciousness which was yet to come.


[2212]
RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN GYI NUS PA LAS ‘BRAS BU’I RNAM SHES GZHAN ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And so something other—a resulting consciousness—is arising from a potential which is something other, and which exists through some nature of its own.


[2213]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, GANG GI PHYIR RGYUN CAN SKAD CIG MA RNAMS RIM CAN DU ‘BYUNG BA DER, KHYOD LTAR NA SNGA PHYI PHAN TSUN NGO BO NYID KYIS THA DAD PA YOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And why is that?  It is for the reason that—in a case where the moments, the things that have the flow, are occurring, one by one, in a stream—there exist those that come before and those that come later, and which are distinct from one another, by their very nature.


[2214]
DE YANG RGYUN GYI BYINGS LAS TA NU NI RGYAS PA LA’O ZHES PA LA RKYEN BYIN PAS BRGYUD PAS NA RGYUN NO, ZHES PAR ‘GYUR TE,

Here also we can point out that—regarding the Sanskrit root for “stream” here—“tanu refers to a spreading.”  That is, if we enhance the basic source syllable we can say “it’s a stream due to the flowing.”


[2215]
CHU KLUNG GI RGYUN LTAR RGYUN CHAGS PAR RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU ‘BREL BAR ‘JUG PA NA, SKYE ‘CHI BRGYUD PAS BAR STONG MED PAR RNAM PAR MA CHAD PAR GNAS PA, ‘DU BYED KYI SKAD CIG DUS GSUM PA’I NYE BAR LEN PA CAN LA BYA STE, SKAD CIG MA RNAMS GANG GI CHA SHAS YIN PA’I CHA CAN YIN GYI SNGA PHYI BAR MA CHAD PA TZAM MIN NO,,

And so suppose we have causes and their effects going on in a connection, in a continued series which resembles the flow of a stream of fresh water.  As such, a flow of birth and death goes on with a single break inbetween, uninterrupted.  The moments of fresh karma take as their precursor the object across the three times; it is the whole which possesses the moments as its parts; but then again it’s not as if there is no disconnect between the moments, earlier & later.


[2216]
DE NI RGYUN GYI CHA SHAS RDZAS KYI SKAD CIG MA RNAMS LA YOD PAS NA, RGYUN GYI YAN LAG RDZAS KYI SKAD CIG MA RNAMS LA RGYUN CAN ZHES BRJOD DE,

Here the components of the flow are the seconds of the material; and so the parts of the flow are described as the seconds of the material referred to collectively as “what comes in a flow.”


[2217]
RGYUN GYI CHA SHAS DANG YAN LAG RNAMS CHA CAN GYI RGYUN DE’I YIN PAS RGYUN LA DE’I NYE BAR LEN PA ZHES BRJOD DE, DPER NA BUM PA NI BUM PA’I MCHU DANG MGRIN PA LA SOGS PA’I NYE BAR LEN PA YIN PA BZHIN NO,,

The parts of the flow, and its components, belong to the flow which represents the whole.  As such, we speak of the flow as their “precursor.”  For example, it’s like the way in which a vase is the precursor of the spout, the neck, and the other parts of a vase.


[2218]
SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI DE DAG PHAN TSUN GZHAN DANG GZHAN DU THA DAD CING, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID DU PHA ROL POS KHAS BLANGS PA YIN NO,,

The other party here accepts the idea that the earlier and later seconds are discrete, each one from the other; and that they are invariably others from each other which exist by definition.


[2219]
DE LTAR NA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN GYI NUS PA LAS GZHAN ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As such, we can say then that one thing which is other comes from a potential which is also other and which exists by definition.


[2220]
GAL [f. 163b] TE DE NI ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR SKYON MA YIN NO SNYAM NA, DE’I PHYIR DNGOS PO THAMS CAD RANG LAS GZHAN PA’I DNGOS PO KUN LAS ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And now suppose you think to yourself that there would be no problem with accepting the position just described.  Well, in that case everything there is would happen from everything else there is which is different from it.


	[2221]
[VI.60]
Santānino yadyapi tatra bhinnāḥ
santāna bhedo’sti hi naiva teṣām,
Tato na doṣā iti sādhyam etat
abheda santāna gater ayogāt.

,GAL TE DER NI RGYUN CAN THA DAD KYI,
,DE DAG LA RGYUN THA DAD MED DE’I PHYIR,
,NYES MED CE NA ‘DI NI BSGRUB BYA ZHIG
,THA MI DAD RGYUN SKABS MI RIGS PHYIR RO,

	Suppose then
	There is the composite
	Flow of those
	That are different
	From each other.

	But suppose you say
	That the flow for those
	Could never involve
	Separate things;

	And so there is
	No such problem.

	This idea though
	Is something that
	You would still
	Have to prove.

	It is illogical to say
	That there could be
	Any opportunity

	For a flow of things
	That were not separate.	


[2222]
GAL TE YANG SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI RIM GYIS ‘JUG PA DER NI RGYUN CAN RDZAS KYI SKAD CIG MA RNAMS PHAN TSUN NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I THA DAD DE GZHAN NYID YOD MOD KYI,

Suppose then that we do accept the idea that there in the progressive flow of the earlier & later seconds there are seconds of the material, the composite flow, which are different from each other, by their very nature. 


[2223]
DE LTA NA’ANG SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI BA DE DAG LA RGYUN NI THA DAD PA MED PA STE GCIG PA KHO NA YIN PA DE’I PHYIR, THAMS CAD THAMS CAD LAS SKYE BAR THAL BA’I NYES PA MED DO ZHE NA

But suppose you say that “Even in that case too though the flow for those things—the earlier & later seconds—could never involve separate things; rather, it could only be singular.  And so there is no such problem, where everything would have to grow from everything else.”


[2224]
SNGA PHYI RGYUD GCIG YIN PA ‘DI NI GZHAN SKYE LA HA CANG THAL BA SPONG BA’I LAN DNGOS GZHI’O,,

This idea though—of a single flow with earlier & later parts—is the most basic response for denying the idea that things arising from other things is far too much.


[2225]
SNGA PHYI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SO SO BA LA RGYUD GCIG GRUB NA, SKYON MED DU CHUG KYANG RGYUD GCIG PA ‘DI MA GRUB PAS NA RGYUD GCIG PA ‘DI NI BSGRUB PAR BYA BA ZHIG GO

Let’s say that a single flow is composed of earlier and later parts that are separate and which exist through some essential nature of their own.  Even if you allow that there is no problem here, they could never constitute a single flow.  As such, this idea of a single flow is something that you would still have to prove.


[2226]
,CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, SNGA PHYI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I THA DAD RNAMS LA THA MI DAD PA’I RGYUN TE RGYUD GCIG PA’I GO SKABS MI RIGS PA’I PHYIR TE,

And why is that?  Because it is illogical to say that there could be any opportunity for a single stream, a flow, of things that were not separate with these separate parts of earlier and later that existed in and of themselves.


	[2227]
[VI.61]
Maitropaguptāśrayiṇo hi dharmā
na hyeka santāna gatāḥ paratvāt,
Svalakṣaṇenāpi pṛthak pṛthag ye
te’pyeka santāna gatā na yuktāḥ.

,BYAMS PA NYER SBAS LA BRTEN CHOS RNAMS NI,
,GZHAN NYID PHYIR NA RGYUD GCIG GTOGS MIN TE,
,GANG DAG RANG MTSAN NYID KYIS SO SO BA,
,DE DAG RGYUD GCIG GTOGS PA RIGS MA YIN,

	John is leaning on Joe;
	Still, they are entities
	That are essentially different;
	
As such, they are not
Sharing a single flow.

For those that were
Separate things that
Existed by definition,

It would not be logical
That they were sharing
A single flow.


[2228]
DPER NA BYAMS PA DANG NYER SBAS LA BRTEN PA STE RGYUD DU GTOGS PA NI, GANG ZAG SO SO’I GZHAN NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR NA, RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA MIN PA

Suppose for example that John is leaning on Joe, and in that sense their flows are intertwined.  Still though they are essentially different from one another: they are separate people.  As such, we would not say that they were sharing a single flow.


[2229]
DE BZHIN DU, SNGA PHYI BA GANG DAG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I SO SO BA DE DAG NI, RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA STE GCIG PA NYID RIGS PA DANG LDAN PA MA YIN NO,,

The same would hold true with those earlier and later parts that were separate things that existed by definition.  It would not be something that was logical to say that they were all one and the same: that they were sharing a single flow.


[2230]
DE LTAR NA GZHAN SKYE LA HA CANG THAL BA ‘PHANGS PA’I SKYON SPONG LA, SA LU’I SA MYUG RGYUD GCIG YIN LA NAS KYI SA MYUG DANG RGYUD MI GCIG PAS THAMS CAD LAS THAMS CAD MI SKYE ZHES ZER BAS, SKYON SPONG MI NUS PA’I GNAD PHA ROL POS, RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I [f. 164a] GZHAN KHAS BLANGS PA LA THUG PAR BSTAN PAS,

As such, people have to say the following sort of thing to avoid the problem that is raised by the idea that things grow from things other than themselves—the problem that it would all be too much.  That is, for this they make the claim that “The seed & the sprout for a rice plant constitute a single flow; but they are not a single flow with the seed & the sprout for a barley plant; as such, it is not the case that everything grows from everything else.”  The fact that this does not allow them to avoid the problem comes down to one crucial point: that these other parties accept the idea that one thing could be other than another thing by definition.  And we have shown them this.


[2231]
GZHAN TZAM LA ‘PHEN PA MIN PAR SHIN TU GSAL BA LA LDOG PA GCIG PA’I DPUNG ‘PHUL SOGS BYED PA DANG, RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN CES GSUNGS PA DGAG BYA’I KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA MA GO BAS,

Here those other parties though have misunderstood how totally clear it is that none of these problems comes up when we accept something which is a simple other; they continue to toss out examples where they pile up items as if they were all stuck together into one thing.  It seems as though they are just completely incapable of understanding it when we apply the term for the thing whose existence we deny to something which is other, by saying that it would exist “through some nature of its own.”


[2232]
DPAL LDAN ZLA BA NYID KYIS SKYON SPONG MI NUS PAR GSUNGS PA’I RGYU MTSAN BZHAG NAS MA GSUNGS PA’I RTOG BZO BYED PA NI YANG DAG PA’I GRUB MTHA’ SLOD PA’O,,

They throw out to us, as one of their reasons, the idea that the glorious Chandrakirti himself made statements in which he was unable to avoid certain problems; and in this way they make up ideas that this Master never did express, polluting what is in actuality the very purest school of thought.



The Mind Only on outer objects

[2233]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GZHAN GYI LUGS BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Which brings us to our second step from before: once more denying the description of how there could be an awareness, in the absence of outer objects.  Here we will first state the position of our opponent; and then deny that position.  Here is that statement.


	[2234]
[VI.62]
Cakṣur dhiyo janma yataḥ svaśakter
ājāyate’nantaram eva tasyāḥ,
Śakteḥ svavijñāna samāśrayasya
rūpīndriyaṃ cakṣur iti pratītiḥ.

,MIG BLO SKYE BA RANG NUS GANG ZHIG LAS,
,DE MA THAG TU KUN NAS SKYE ‘GYUR ZHING,
,RANG GI RNAM SHES RTEN GYI NUS DE LA,
,DBANG PO GZUGS CAN MIG GCES {%CES}
BYA BAR RTOGS,

The growing of
Awareness of the eye
Springs forth from
That potential which
Occurs just after that.

And its consciousness
Is the support for a potential;

They think of this and say,
“This is the eye,
A physical sense power.”


[2235]
DE SKAD BSTAN PA YIN DANG SLAR YANG SEMS TZAM PAS RANG GI LUGS BRJOD PA GTZO BOR BYAS PA NYID KYIS RANG GI ‘DOD DON ‘GRUB PAR BSAMS SHING SMRAS PA,

And so this is the presentation; and then once again the followers of the Mind Only hope to focus on describing, primarily, their own position—thus then they consider ways of establishing it and present the following.


[2236]
MIG GI BLO STE RNAM PAR SHES PA SKYE BA’I RANG GI NUS PA BAG CHAGS GANG ZHIG KUN GZHI LA, RNAM SHES GZHAN GYIS RANG ‘GAG BZHIN PA NA, DE MA THAG TU ‘JOG PAR BYED LA,

Let’s look at how the awareness of the eye—which is to say, that consciousness—has the deep seed for it, that potential for it to grow, planted into the foundation consciousness.  This is done by another instance of consciousness as it is in the act of ending, and occurs just after that.


[2237]
DE SMIN PA LAS DUS PHYIS SNGA MA DE’I RNAM PA’I RJES SU BYED PA’I MIG GI RNAM SHES SKYE BAR ‘GYUR ZHING, RANG GI STE MIG GI RNAM SHES DE NUS PA’I SKAD CIG BAR MED PA GANG ZHIG LAS SKYE BA’I NUS PA’I SKAD CIG PAR {%BAR} MED PA RTEN DU GYUR PA DE LA, GTI MUG GIS ‘JIG RTEN RNAMS DBANG PO GZUGS CAN MIG YIN NO SNYAM DU RTOGS KYI, RNAM SHES LAS THA DAD PA’I MIG DBANG NI YOD PA MIN NO,,

When this deep seed ripens, a later awareness of the eyes springs forth, in a form which follows upon that of the former one.  And then “its”—meaning the eye’s—consciousness becomes the support for a potential which occurs without even a moment’s interval, from the potential that also occurred without even a moment’s interval, for the consciousness itself.  And then out of dark ignorance, people of the world get an idea where they consider this support and think to themselves, “this is the eye, a physical sense power”—even though it’s not the case that there exists any power of the eye which is separate from consciousness itself. 


[2238]
DE BZHIN DU DBANG PO GZUGS CAN LHAG MA LA YANG SBYAR BAR BYA’O,,

You can apply the same explanation to the remainder of the physical sense powers.


[2239]
DE LA MIG SHES SKYE BA’I RGYU BAG CHAGS NI DE’I RGYU’I RKYEN YIN LA, MIG GI [f. 164b] DBANG PO NI MIG SHES KYI BDAG PO’I RKYEN NO,,

Here the deep seed which acts as the cause for the arisal of the visual consciousness is the causal factor for it; whereas the sense power of the eye is the dominant factor.


[2240]
‘DIR MIG DBANG MIG SHES KYI DNGOS RGYUR BSTAN PA NI, MIG SHES SKYE BA’I BAG CHAGS SMIN PA’I SKABS LA DGONGS KYI MIG DBANG GANG YIN LA MIN NO,,

When they describe here the sense power of the eye as the direct cause of the consciousness of the eye, what they have in mind is the point at which the deep seed for the visual consciousness ripens; it is not a reference to the power of the eye itself.


[2241]
DE YANG DBUS MTHA’ LAS,
,DON DANG SEMS CAN BDAG RNAM RIG
,SNANG BA’I RNAM PAR SHES PA NI,
,RAB TU SKYE BO {%SKYE’O} DE DON MED,

Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes puts it this way—

States of consciousness proliferate
Where awareness gives an impression

Of object, person, and self;
No object here exists.


[2242]
CES DON GZUGS SOGS DANG, SEMS CAN DBANG PO LNGAR SNANG BA’I RNAM SHES SKYE’O ZHES GSUNGS PA NI KUN GZHI RNAM SHES YIN LA SLOB DPON BLO BRTAN GYIS KYANG DBANG PO GZUGS CAN RNAMS KUN GZHI’I DMIGS PAR BSHAD PAS, SEMS TZAM PA KUN GZHI KHAS LEN PA RNAMS KYIS KUN GZHI LA DBANG PO GZUGS CAN DU SNANG BA MIG DBANG SOGS SU ‘DOD DO,,

The word “object” here refers to visible form and the rest.  And then they would say that “an awareness arises which appears to be the five powers of a living being”; which is a reference to foundation consciousness.  Here Master Sthiramati explains that the physical sense powers are the object of perception for the foundation consciousness; as such, we can say that members of the Mind Only school who accept a foundation consciousness would assert that what appears to the foundation consciousness as the physical powers is what constitutes the power of the eye and so on.


	[2243]
[VI.63]
Bahir vinā rūpam iha svabījān
nīlādi nirbhāsitayodbhavantīm,
Vijñaptim akṣi prabhavām abuddhvā
grāhyaṃ jano bāhyam avaiti cittāt.

,’DI NA DBANG PO LAS BYUNG RNAM PAR RIG
,PHYI GZUNG MED PAR RANG GI SA BON LAS,
,SNGO SOGS SNANG NYID ‘BYUNG BAR MA RTOGS NAS,
,SKYE BOS PHYI ROL BZUNG BAR SEMS KHAS LEN,

		Here awareness
		That arises from
		The sense powers

		Comes from
		Seeds for it
		In the absence
		Of outer objects.

		Beings though fail
		To understand that
		What arises is just

		The appearance
		Of blue and the like,
			
		Believing that
		What is mind 
		Constitutes outer
		Objects of perception.


[2244]
RNAM SHES LAS THA DAD PA’I MIG DBANG SOGS MED PAR BSTAN NAS, GZUGS KYANG RNAM PAR SHES PA LAS DON GZHAN PA MED PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR SMRAS PA,

Having described how there is no power of the eye or such which is separate from consciousness itself, we have the following description of how form itself is has no existence as an object which is separate from awareness either.


[2245]
‘JIG RTEN ‘DI NA DBANG PO LNGA LAS BYUNG BA’I RNAM PAR RIG PA LNGA, SNGON PO LA SOGS PA’I PHYI ROL GYI GZUNG BA MED PAR RNAM SHES RANG GI SA BON KUN GZHI LA BZHAG PA SMIN PA LAS, SNGO SOGS SU SNANG BA NYID ‘BYUNG BAR MA RTOGS NAS, SKYE BOS SEMS SNGO SOGS SU SNANG BA LA PHYI ROL GYI GZUNG BAR KHAS LEN PA STE MNGON PAR ZHEN NO,,

Here in the world then we have five different types of awareness that arise from the five different sense powers.  Consciousness comes from the ripening of the seeds for it that were planted in the foundation consciousness; and this happens in the absence of any outer objects of perception such as blue or the like.  Beings though fail to understand that what arises is just the appearance of blue and the like; and so they have a strong attraction towards believing that what is actually the mind appearing as blue and the like constitutes outer objects of perception.


[2246]
DE’I PHYIR RNAM SHES LAS DON GZHAN PA’I PHYI ROL MED DO,,

As such, we can say that there exist no outer objects which are separate things from consciousness itself.


	[2247]
[VI.64]
Svapne vinārthāntaram eva rūpaṃ
yathā tadākāram udeti cetaḥ,
Svaśakti pākād iha jāgrato’pi
tathāsti bāhyena vinā manaś cet.

,RMI LAM NA NI GZUGS DON GZHAN MED PAR,
,RANG NUS SMIN LAS DE YI RNAM CAN SEMS,
,’BYUNG BA JI LTA DE BZHIN SAD LA’ANG ‘DIR,
,PHYIR ROL MED PAR YID NI YOD CE NA,

		In a dream,
		There are no physical objects
		Which are other entities.

		The potential for them ripens,
		And from that arises
		A state of mind
		With the aspects of those.

		In this very same way,
		Here when we are awake
		As well, there are none outer;
		What we have is the thought.

		Suppose you take this position.
		

[2248]
BSHAD PA’I RNAM PA GCIG TU NA, RMI LAM NA NI GZUGS DON GZHAN DU GYUR PA MED PAR RANG GI BAG CHAGS KYI NUS PA SMIN PA LAS, GZUGS SGRA SOGS DE’I RNAM PA CAN GYI SEMS ‘BYUNG BA JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU, [f. 165a] SAD PA’I SKABS LA’ANG ‘DIR PHYI ROL GYI DON MED PAR YID NI YOD DO ZHE NA,

This explanation can take a different twist.  In a dream, there are no physical objects which are other entities.  Rather, the potential of a deep seed for them ripens, and from that arises a state of mind with the aspects of those visible forms, sounds, and the rest.  In this very same way, here during the period when we are awake as well there are no outer objects here; what we have is the thought.  Now suppose this is the position that you take.



Denying Mind Only objects

[2249]
GNYIS PA NI,

Here secondly we deny the position just stated.


	[2250]
[VI.65]
Nīlādi nirbhāsam udeti cetaḥ
svapne yathā mānasam akṣyabhāve,
Kasmād ihāndhasya tathākṣyapāye
svabīja pākād udayaṃ na yāti.

,JI LTAR MIG MED PAR NI RMI LAM DU,
,SNGO SOGS SNANG BA’I YID SEMS ‘BYUNG DE LTAR,
,MIG DBANG MED PAR RANG GI SA BON NI,
,SMIN LAS LONG BA LA ‘DIR CIS MI SKYE,

		In a dream,
		A state of mind
		Comes up which is
		The thought,
	
		And takes on
		An aspect of blue
		Or whatever it may be,

		Even though
		There is no sense power
		Of the eye there.

		A deep seed
		Within it ripens;

		In this case,
		Why wouldn’t a person
		Who was blind
		Come to see?


[2251]
DE NI MI RIGS TE, JI LTAR MIG DBANG MED PAR RMI LAM DU SNGO SOGS SNANG BA’I YID SHES KYI SEMS ‘BYUNG BA DE LTAR DU, MIG DBANG MED PAR RNAM SHES RANG GI SA BON BAG CHAGS NI SMIN PA LAS, SAD PA’I LONG BA LA YANG MA LONG BA LTA BU’I GZUGS MTHONG BA SOGS CI’I PHYIR MI SKYE STE RMI LAM DANG SAD PA GNYIS KAR YANG MIG DBANG MED PAR MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And yet, that position must be wrong.  In a dream, a state of mind comes up which is actually consciousness of the thought, but which takes on an aspect of blue or whatever it may be, even though there is no sense power of the eye there.  And suppose it were the same for consciousness, which in the absence of a sense power of the eye has a seed—a deep seed—within it which ripens.  In this case, why wouldn’t it be the case that—in the waking state—a person who was blind would come to see visible forms just the same as a person who was not blind?  After all, the two cases are similar: they have no sense power of the eye, in both the cases: in the dream, and while awake.


[2252]
‘DI YANG PHYI’I GZUGS SOGS MED PAR RNAM SHES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA SKYE NA, RMI LAM DANG SAD PA GNYIS KA LA KHYAD MED PA’I GNAD KYIS YIN NO,,

And there is another crucial point to back this up: If an awareness that existed through some nature of its own could arise even in the absence of outer visible form and the like, then there would be no difference between the dream state and the waking state.


[2253]
CI STE SAD PA’I LONG PA LA YID KYI SHES PA GZUGS SOGS GSAL BAR SNANG BA RMI LAM GYI DE LTA BU MI ‘BYUNG BA’I RGYU NI, MIG MED PA MA YIN GYI ‘O NA CI ZHE NA, DE ‘DRA BA’I YID KYI SHES PA ‘BYUNG BA’I NUS PA MA SMIN PA YIN NO,,

But then a question may arise.  In the waking state, the consciousness of the thought for a blind person can take on a vivid aspect of visible form or the like; whereas the same sort of thing does not happen in a dream.  If the reason for this, you may ask, is not the absence of an eye, then what could it be?  What has happened is that the potential for such a consciousness of the thought to occur has not yet ripened.


	[2254]
[VI.66]
Svapne’sti ṣaṣṭhasya hi śakti pāko
na jāgrato’stīti sacet tava syāt,
Yatheha ṣaṣṭhasya na śakti pākaḥ
svapne tathāsann {%?} iti kiṃ na vetsi.

,GAL TE KHYOD LTAR RMI LAM DRUG PA YI,
,NUS PA SMIN YOD SAD PAR MED GYUR NA,
,DRUG PA’I NUS SMIN JI LTA ‘DIR MED PA,
,DE LTAR RMI TSE MED CES CIS MI RIGS,

		Suppose that,
		As you would have it,

		There does exist the
		Ripening of the potential
		For the sixth
		Within a dream;

		And suppose that
		This were absent
		During the waking state.

		Why then wouldn’t it be
		Correct to say that

		Here there was no ripening of
		The potential for the sixth,

		And just so no such thing
		During the dream?


[2255]
DE’I PHYIR NUS PA SMIN PA YOD PA DER DE ‘DRA BA’I YID SHES ‘BYUNG BA YIN LA DE YANG GNYID KYI RKYEN GYIS RMI LAM KHO NA NA YOD KYI SAD PA LA NI MA YIN NO SNYAM NA,

And suppose you think to yourself the following.  It is in the presence of the ripening of the potential that this type of consciousness of the thought occurs.  And due to the factor of the sleep, this is present only in a dream; it is not something that comes during the waking period.


[2256]
DE NI MI RIGS TE, GAL TE KHYOD LTAR RMI LAM NA DRUG PA YID SHES KYI NUS PA SMIN PA YOD LA, SAD PA LA MED PAR GYUR NA DRUG PA YID SHES GZUGS SOGS SU GSAL BAR SNANG BA’I NUS PA SMIN PA SAD PA’I SKABS ‘DIR LONG BA LA MED PA JI LTA BA DE LTAR RMI LAM GYI TSE MED CES CIS MI RIGS TE RIGS SO,,

This idea though is mistaken.  Suppose that, as you would have it, there does exist the ripening of the potential for “the sixth”—that is, the consciousness of the thought—within a dream.  And suppose that this were absent during the waking state.  Why then wouldn’t it be correct to say that—just as for a blind person there is here in the waking state no ripening of the potential for the sixth (the consciousness of the thought) to take on a clear aspect of visible form and the rest—there could, just so, be no such thing during the dream state?  It would in fact be perfectly correct to say so.


[2257]
‘DI YANG DGAG BYA LA GTUGS PA’I LUGS SO,,

This again is a position which boils down to the object that we deny.


[2258]
GAL TE RIGS PA MED PAR TSIG TZAM GYIS DE SKAD SMRA NA, KHO BO CAG GIS KYANG SNGAR LTAR SMRAS PAS CHOG [f. 165b] GO

And if you claim that you are taking your position not out of logic but just nominally, well then you should be satisfied with whatever statements we ourselves made previous to this.


[2259]
,RMI LAM MTHONG BA LA NI SAD PA’I SKABS KYI LONG BA LTAR RNAM SHES KYI RTEN DBANG PO BYED PA DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR, NUS PA’I MING CAN GYI MIG GI DBANG PO LA RNAM SHES BRTEN PA’I RNAM PA’I RJES SU BYED PA, YID SHES KYI NUS PA SMIN PA YONGS SU ‘GYUR BA LAS BYUNG BA’I YID KYI RNAM SHES CAN MA YIN NO,,

When we see things in a dream, it’s the same as with a blind person during the waking period.  That is, they lack any of the functionality of the sense power acting as a support for consciousness.  As such, what we have is a sense power of the eye which is referred to with the name of “a potential,” and which assumes the aspect of a support for consciousness.  It’s not as if we are possessed of a consciousness of the thought which has sprung from a transformation resulting from the ripening of some potential for this same consciousness.


	[2260]
[VI.67]
Akṣyor abhāvo’sya yathā na hetuḥ
svapne’pi middhaṃ na tathaiva hetuḥ,
Svapne’pi tad rūpam ato’bhyupeyaṃ
cakṣur mṛṣā gocara bodhi hetuḥ.

,JI LTAR MIG MED ‘DI YI RGYU MIN LTAR,
,RMI LAM DU YANG GNYID NI [207b] RGYU MA YIN,
,DE PHYIR RMI LAM DU YANG DE DNGOS MIG
,BRDZUN PA’I YUL CAN RTOGS PA’I RGYUR KHAS BLANG,

		As they do when
		There is no eye,
		For this they are not
		Acting as a cause.

		Just so, in a
		Dream as well,
		Sleep could not be
		The cause [f. 207b].

		For that reason,
		You would accept
That in a dream
As well as that,

There were
False entities
Having objects

As the cause
For the perception
Of the eye.


[2261]
DE’I PHYIR MIG MED PA SAD PA’I LONG BA ‘DI LA DON SNANG GI BAG CHAGS SMIN PA RGYU MIN PA JI LTA BA DE LTAR RMI LAM DU YANG GNYID NI DON SNANG GI BAG CHAGS SMIN PA’I RGYU MA YIN TE, PHYI ROL MED PAR SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA SKYE NA BAG CHAGS SMIN PA LA MI LTOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

As such, it’s not as if things are happening here as they do when there is no eye: where, for this person who is blind during the waking state, the ripening of a deep seed for the mind to take on the appearance of the object is not acting as a cause.  Just so, in a dream as well, sleep could not be a cause for the ripening of the deep seed of the mind taking on the aspect of the object.  And that’s because—if it were the case that a state of mind that existed through some nature of its own could grow in the absence of outer objects, then it wouldn’t have to rely upon the ripening of some deep seed.


[2262]
GANG GI PHYIR BAG CHAGS BRDZUN PA LAS RMI LAM GYI DON SNANG GI SHES PA BRDZUN PA SKYE BA DE’I PHYIR, RMI LAM DU YANG SAD PA’I SKABS DE LTA BU’I YUL GYI DNGOS PO GZUGS SOGS SU SNANG BA’I RNAM PAR SHES PA BRDZUN PA DANG, RMI LAM GYI MIG RTOGS PA STE RNAM PAR SHES PA’I RGYU STE RTEN DU GYUR PA KHAS BLANG BAR BYA’O,,

Suppose then that a false state of mind which takes on the aspect of an object in a dream arises from a false version of a deep seed.  For that reason then, you would also have to accept the idea that in a dream as well—just as in that waking state—there would be a false consciousness that was taking on the aspect of visible form and such: these types of entities acting as the same sort of objects.  And these would act as the cause—which is to say, the support—for the consciousness or perception of the eye in the dream.


[2263]
‘DI NI ‘GREL PAR RMI LAM NA YUL YONGS SU GCOD PA NA GSUM ‘DUS PAR DMIGS PA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS SHING, YANG RMI LAM NA GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DANG MIG DANG, DE GNYIS KYIS BSKYED PA’I MIG GI RNAM SHES MED PAR YANG GSUNGS PA

On this point, we see in the autocommentary the statement that “When we descry an object in a dream, we are having a perception where the three have convened.”  We also see statements that—in a dream—there is no door of sense of visible form; or eye; or the consciousness of the eye triggered by these two.


[2264]
BZHIN DU, RMI LAM NA MIG SHES SOGS LNGA’I YUL DBANG RNAM SHES GSUM MED KYANG, RMI LAM RMI BZHIN PA’I GANG ZAG GI NGOR DE GSUM DU DMIGS PA YOD PAS RMI LAM GYI MIG DANG, RMI LAM GYI MIG SHES DANG, RMI LAM GYI GZUGS GSUM PO KHAS BLANG BAR STON GYI,

Just so, we can say that—even though, in a dream, there are none of the three of the object, the power, or consciousness for the five of the consciousness of the eye and so on—there do exist things perceived as these three to the perceptions of the person dreaming the dream.  As such, what these references are saying is that we would have to accept the three of a dream eye; a dream consciousness of the eye; and dream visible form.


[2265]
DE GSUM MIG SOGS SU GRUB PAR ‘DOD PA MIN TE, SGYU [f. 166a] MA’I RTA GLANG DANG SGYU MA’I MI KHAS LEN KYANG, DE DAG RTA GLANG DANG MIR ‘DOD MI DGOS PA BZHIN NO,,

It’s not saying though that we would have to say that these three actually existed as an eye or the like.  That is, we would have to agree that there do exist illusory horses and cows, and illusory people; but that doesn’t mean that we would have to agree that they were horses, or cows, or people.


	[2266]
[VI.68]
Yaṃ yaṃ parīhāram ayaṃ bravīti
taṃ taṃ pratijñāsamam asya paśyan,
Nivārayed vādam amuṃ na Buddhā
vastu kvacin nāma sad ityuśanti

[VI.68a]
,’DI YIS LAN NI GANG DANG GANG BTAB PA,
,DE DANG DE NI DAM BCA’ MTSUNGS MTHONG BAS,
,RTZOD ‘DI SEL BYED

		Whatever response it is
		That these might make,
		We can see that this
		Assertion is equivalent.

		As such,
		This particular argument
		Actually clears the beliefs.


[2267]
DE’I PHYIR DE LTAR NA SEMS TZAM PA ‘DI YIS DBU MA PA LA LAN NI GANG DANG GANG BTAB PA DE DANG DE NI, DAM BCA’ BA STE BSGRUB BYA MA GRUB PA DANG MTSUNGS PAR MTHONG BAS, RTZOD ‘DI STE RNAM PAR RIG PA TZAM DU SMRA BA ‘DI SEL BA STE ZLOG PAR BYAD {%BYED} DO,,

And so thus, given this we can say that whatever response it is that these proponents of the Mind Only school might make to those of the Middle Way, we can see that this assertion is equivalent to a logical proof which doesn’t hold.  As such, this particular argument actually “clears” the beliefs of those who say that there is nothing but awareness; which is to say, it blocks them. 


[2268]
DE DAG DPER BRJOD NA DBU MA PAS SAD PA’I SKABS KYI YUL DBANG RNAM SHES GSUM RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA YIN TE, DMIGS PA YIN PA’I PHYIR RMI LAM BZHIN NO, ZHES BKOD PA NA

And so let’s say for example that those of the Middle Way were to set forth the logic that these three, when we are awake—the object, the sense power, and the consciousness—are empty of existing through any nature of their own, simply because they are observed: they are like a dream.


[2269]
SEMS TZAM PAS SAD PA’I RNAM SHES NI PHYI ROL GYI DON GYIS STONG STE, RNAM SHES YIN PA’I PHYIR RMI LAM GYI RNAM SHES BZHIN NO ZHES DANG,

Those of the Mind Only would reply by saying that our consciousness, when we are awake, is devoid of any outer object; for the simple reason that it is consciousness.  It is like, they would say, our consciousness in a dream.


[2270]
SAD PA’I SKABS SU DMIGS PA’I YUL NI BRDZUN PA YIN TE, YUL YIN PA’I PHYIR RMI LAM GYI YUL BZHIN NO, ZHES DANG,

They would also say that, when we are awake, the object under our consideration is deceptive, simply because it is an object.  And again, that is because it is like an object in a dream.


[2271]
DE BZHIN DU KUN BYANG GI GZHI GZHAN DBANG MED NA KUN BYANG MED PA YIN TE, RTEN MED PA’I PHYIR, RUS SBAL GYI SPU’I GOS BZHIN NO, ZHES SMRA’O

They would also say that—if there were no dominated entities to serve as the basis of both the negative and the enlightened side of things—then there could in fact be no vast negativity or pure enlightenment themselves; it would be, they say, like clothing woven from the hairs that grow on the shell of a turtle.


[2272]
DE BZHIN DU RAB RIB KYI DPES KYANG BRJOD PAR BYA’O, ZHES PA RNAMS SO,,

And they would also say, “We further use the example of eyes with cataracts, in describing these cases.”


[2273]
DE LA SBYOR BA DANG PO GNYIS NI, DPE MA GRUB PAS SGRUB BYED BSGRUB BYA DANG MTSUNGS PA YIN TE, RMI LAM NA YID KYI SHES PA LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I CHOS KYI SKYE MCHED KYI GZUGS YOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

As for the first two logical sentiments expressed here, we can say that since the example cited isn’t correct, what is being used to prove the idea and the idea that they are trying to prove end up being equivalent.  And that’s because, in a dream, there does exist form of the sense door of phenomena which is essentially separate from consciousness of the thought.


[2274]
SBYOR BA GSUM PA NI, KUN BYANG GI RTEN RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA CIG SGRUB ‘DOD PA YIN PAS DE LA NI, RTEN TZAM MED PA MA GRUB PA YIN LA, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA BSAMS NA NI MA NGES PA’O,,

As for the third logical thought expessed above, they seek to establish that there is a foundation to the negative side of things—and to the enlightened side of things—which could exist by definition.  Proving this foundation in its simple form is simply an argument that is not proven to be true; whereas if what they have in mind is specifically something that could exist by definition, then the proof is inconclusive.



Scripture can deny Mind Only

[2275]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to our third step from before: showing how there is no problem from scripture when we deny the system of the Mind Only.


	[2276]
	[VI.68b]
…SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS NI,
,’GAR YANG DNGOS PO YOD CES MA BSTAN TO,

	The Buddhas have not
	Ever taught the idea,

	In any at all, that
	Entities could exist.


[2277]
DE [f. 166b] LTAR SEMS TZAM PA’I LUGS BKAG PA LA RIGS PAS MI GNOD PAR MA ZAD, LUNG GIS GNOD PA SRID PA MA YIN TE, GANG GI PHYIR YANG DAG PAR RDZOGS PA’I SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS NI, RANG GI LUGS LA GSUNG RAB ‘GAR YANG DNGOS PO BDEN PAR YOD CES MA BSTAN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Now not only is it the case that our denying the system of the Mind Only school is, therefore, something that cannot be disproven by logic; moreover, it is further a position where there is no problem with it from scripture.  And this is because the total and perfectly enlightened Buddhas have not—in expressing the position that they themselves adhere to—ever taught the idea, in any at all of the teachings they have given, that entities could exist in reality.


[2278]
DE YANG LANG KAR GSHEGS PA LAS,
,SRID PA GSUM NI BTAGS PA TZAM,
,NGO BO NYID KYIS DNGOS PO MED,
,BTAGS PA DNGOS PO’I NGO BOR NI,
,RTOG GE BA DAG RTOG PAR ‘GYUR,

As the Journey to Langka puts it,

	The three realms of existence
	Are nothing but labels;
	Nothing at all exists
	Through some essence of its own.

	Seeing some essence to things
	That exist only in labels
	Is just an idea thought up
	By some who think it is logic.


	[2279]
,RANG BZHIN MED CING RNAM RIG MED,
,KUN GZHI MED CING DNGOS MED NA,
,BYIS PA NGAN PA RTOG GE BA,
,RO DANG ‘DRA BAS ‘DI DAG BRTAGS,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,


	Things have no nature;
	There is no awareness;
	There is no foundation consciousness;
	There exists no thing at all.

	Those unruly infants,
	Those so-called logical thinkers,
	So similar to dead bodies,
	Have made it all up.


[2280]
RKANG PA DANG POS SRID GSUM BLOS BTAGS PA TZAM DU YOD PAR BSTAN LA, RKANG PA GNYIS PAS NI DE’I DON BSTAN TE, DE YANG NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I DNGOS PO MED PAR BSTAN PAS, NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED PA YIN GYI DNGOS PO YE MED MIN ZHES PA’O,,

The first line here [in the Tibetan; the first two lines in the English] are meant to indicate that the three realms into which the entire universe is divided exist only as something labeled by the mind.  The second line [third and fourth in the English] are meant to explain what this means; that is—by showing how there can be no entity which exists in & of itself—we are saying that there is nothing which exists in & of itself, but not that nothing exists at all.


[2281]
DE LTAR BLOS BTAGS PA TZAM LA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I DNGOS POR DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON MA RNYED PA’I RTOG GE PAS ‘DOD DO ZHES PA NI, BTAGS PA ZHES PA GNYIS KYIS STON NO,,

And what the two mentions of “labels” are meant to indicate is that the idea that what is—in actuality—merely a creation of the mind could exist as an entity which existed in & of itself is only something that could be asserted by a person trying to think logically who had yet to discover the true meaning of suchness.


[2282]
NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED PAR SPYIR BSTAN PA STE, BYE BRAG TU PHYE STE STON PA NI, R’U PA ZHES PA RANG BZHIN DANG GZUGS GNYIS KA LA ‘JUG PA LAS ‘DIR GZUGS CAN LA BYA STE, RNAM RIG CES PA’I ZLA STOBS KYIS SO,,

Saying that things don’t exist in & of themselves is the general presentation; if we were to break things down more particularly, we would point out that the Sanskrit word rūpa can refer both to “nature” and to “form”; and that here, it is meant to allude to things which possess physical form.  This physicality is indicated here in the lines in the form of what they call a “contrasting poeticism,” with the word “awareness.”


[2283]
DNGOS MED CES PA’I DNGOS PO NI SHES PA DANG GZUGS CAN GYI DNGOS PO MED PAR BSTAN ZIN PAS, ‘DIR NGO BO LA YIN LA DE YANG DNGOS PO BDEN PA BKAG PA’I NGO BO DANG, DNGOS POR MED PA GZHAN RNAMS LA BYA’O,,

As for the line which says “there exists no thing at all,” the fact is that we have already in the lines previous presented the idea that there exist no mental or physical entities.  The reference at this point then is to existing in essence; and here we mean “essence” in the sense we see it when we deny that things are real—and to other connotations of the expression that nothing exists in actual fact.


[2284]
RO DANG ‘DRA TSUL [f. 167a] NI DE KHO NA NYID DPYOD NUS PA’I SEMS MED PA’O,,

How is it then that the thinkers referred to are “similar to dead bodies”?  The point is that they have no awareness—in the sense of being able to explore the concept of suchness.


[2285]
LUNG DES NI KHAMS GSUM GYI GZHAN DBANG RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR ‘DOD PA BKAG GO

The entire citation then is meant to deny an entire universe of three realms where dominated entities could be said to exist through some nature of their own.


[2286]
,GAL TE LUNG DE DAG GIS GCIG GZHAN DBANG LA CIG SHOS KUN BRTAGS GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD KYI NGO BO NYID KYIS STONG PA BSTAN PAS MI GNOD DO SNYAM NA,

Suppose the following thought were to occur to someone:

The actual purpose of these lines is to say that the one type of things, dominated entities; and then the other type of things, imagined entities, are empty of an essential nature where objects and subject states of mind are essentially different from one another.  As such, the citation does not draw our position into question.


[2287]
DE ‘DRA DE NI YANG DAG PA’I STONG NYID DU RIGS PA MA YIN TE, BLO GROS CHEN PO GCIG LA GCIG MED PA’I STONG PA NYID NI STONG PA NYID THAMS CAD KYI THA SHAL YIN NO ZHES LANG KAR GSHEGS PA LAS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Saying that this sort of description represents pure emptiness though would not be logical.  And that’s because the Journey to Langka itself includes that part that says,

O one of great understanding, that emptiness which is said to apply to one thing but is lacking in another thing is the very worst of all attempted explanations of emptiness.


[2288]
BA LANG NI RTA YIN PAS STONG PA’I PHYIR YOD PA MIN NO ZHES BRJOD PA NI RIGS PA YANG MA YIN TE, RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS YOD PA’I PHYIR, ZHES BYA BA LA SOGS PA BRJOD PAR BYA’O ZHES ‘GREL PAR GSUNGS SO,,

The autocommentary also notes—

You would have to say things like: “It would be incorrect to say that, because a cow is empty of being a horse, it didn’t exist at all.  After all, it exists in & of itself.”


[2289]
BDAG NYID KYIS ZHES PA LA NAG TSOS RANG GI BDAG NYID YOD PA’I PHYIR RO ZHES BSGYUR BA LEGS SO,,

Where this version of the autocommentary says “in & of itself,” the translation by Naktso reads “because its very self is there”; this is a good way of rendering it.


[2290]
GCIG LA CIG SHOS MED PA’I STONG PA ‘DI DPER BRJOD DE DANG ‘DRA BAR ‘GYUR TSUL NI BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYI RANG BZHIN GYIS DBEN PA’I STONG NYID GSUNGS PA NI SEMS CAN RNAMS THOG MA MED PA NAS GZUGS SOGS KYI DNGOS PO LA BDEN PAR GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I MNGON ZHEN BZLOG PA’I PHYIR DU YIN PA LA,

Now let’s consider this approach, where—as in the example just cited—we speak of emptiness as one thing lacking another.  When the conquering Buddhas make statements like this, about an emptiness where things are devoid of any nature, the reason they do so is to stop the belief of living beings, for time with no beginning, where they grasp to the idea that entities such as form and the like could exist as real.


[2291]
DE LA GZUGS SOGS SU SNANG BA’I GZHAN DBANG ‘DI NYID BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR BSTAN DGOS PA LA, DE LTAR MI STON PAR GZHAN DBANG ‘DI GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD PAR MI BDEN NO ZHES BSTAN PA NA, BA LANG MED PA’I RGYU MTSAN DU BA LANG LTAR MED CES ZER BA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

To this point, one has to demonstrate that dominated entities which appear as form or the like cannot exist in reality.  And suppose that we do not present it that way, and only indicate that these dominated things are not real in the sense of objects & subjects which are essentially different.  This would be like saying—as a reason for asserting that a cow doesn’t exist—that “it doesn’t exist, because it’s similar to the case with a cow.”


[2292]
DES NA DBU [f. 167b] SEMS SU YI LUGS LA YANG SEMS CAN RNAMS GANG LA MNGON PAR ZHEN PA’I GZHI, PHYI NANG GI CHOS SU SNANG BA ‘DI DAG LA BYED PA LA NI MI ‘DRA BA MED LA, DE RNAMS STONG PAR STON PA NI GZHI DE LA MNGON ZHEN ZLOG PA’I PHYIR DU YIN PA YANG ‘DRA MOD KYANG, ZHEN TSUL LA MI MTHUN TE

Thus we can say that—whether we are speaking about the system of the Middle Way, or to that of the Mind Only—there is no difference in the fact that we are referring to the way that outer & inner entities make their appearance: we are speaking of that foundational state of things which living beings are holding on to.  When we clarify that these things are empty, the statement in each of the two systems is similar in that we are attempting to put a stop to how people hold on to this foundation; and yet the way in which each system describes the holding on that people do is incompatible.


[2293]
SEMS TZAM PAS NI GZUNG ‘DZIN GNYIS PHYI NANG DU RGYANGS CHAD DU SNANG BA LA SNANG BA LTAR DU, GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD DU ZHEN PA YIN LA, DE’I GNYEN POR SNANG BA GZHAN DBANG ‘DI CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NAS, GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD DU YOD PA ‘GOG PA YIN PAS DGAG GZHI DE DGAG BYA DE YIN PA ‘GOG PA YIN NO,,

That is, the Mind Only would say that the belief that people hold to here is that objects and their subjects are essentially separate, as they appear to be when it seems that—for the objects and subjects—those which are inside of us and those which are outside look to exist at a significant distance away from each other.  And then as an antidote for this perception, we take what it is that appears—dominated entities—and take them as the subject under logical consideration, and then disprove that it could display any reality where objects & their subjects were essentially separate.  Thus, the denial is done by taking this foundational state of things that we deny itself as the object we are denying, and work to deny that.


[2294]
DBU MA PA LTAR NA ZHEN TSUL NI SNANG BA LA THA SNYAD PA’I BLOS BZHAG PA MIN PA’I BDEN GRUB TU ZHEN PA YIN LA, DE’I GNYEN POR SNANG BA ‘DI CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NAS, DE ‘DRA BA’I BDEN PAR MED CES ‘GOG STE, 

Those of the Middle Way describe the belief with which we hold to things in a different way.  They say that we hold that things exist in reality—which is to say, we believe that what appears to us is not being established by a nominal state of mind.  And then as an antidote for this belief, we start by taking this way that things appear to us as the subject under our logical consideration.  Then we deny this appearance by saying, “This is not something which exists as real, in the way we have described that.”


[2295]
DE YANG DGAG GZHI DE DGAG BYA YIN PA ‘GOG PA YIN TE, SEMS CAN GYIS ZHEN PA NA GZHI DE LA DGAG BYA DE DON GZHAN DU YOD PAR ‘DZIN PA MIN PAR, GZHI DE DGAG BYA DE’I NGO BOR ZHEN PA’I PHYIR DANG, STONG PA YANG JI LTAR ZHEN PA DE LTAR DU YOD PAS STONG PAR BSTAN DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This denial is a refusal that the objects which make up the foundation state where we are accomplishing our denial could in fact exist as what we are denying about them.  This is not to say that when living beings are engaging in what they believe, they hold this foundation state to exist in some other way than that expressed by the object that we deny; rather, they actually hold that this state exists, in its very essence, as expressed by the object that we deny.  Moreover, we have to demonstrate as well that emptiness itself is also empty of existing in the way that we might believe it to.


[2296]
DE’I PHYIR DA LTAR GYI SNANG GZHI RNAMS BDEN PAS STONG PA CHAD STONG DU BYAS TE, ‘DI DAG BOR NAS SNANG BA GZHAN CIG LA STONG GZHIR BYAS TE, DGAG BYA DE YIN PAS STONG PAR MI STON PAR DNGOS PO YOD PAS STONG PAR STON PA NI,

As such, the foundational state we are talking about here—the one that appears to us—is what we are saying is empty: what we are eliminating to arrive at emptiness.  But suppose that a person were to reject these elements, and take something completely different to be that foundational state which we are saying is empty.  That is, suppose a person decided not to describe emptiness as being the lack of the object denied, as we have described it.  Suppose—rather—that what entities were empty of was their very existence.


[2297]
DBU SEMS SU’I YANG LUGS MIN LA, SEMS CAN GYI RGYUD KYI THOG MA MED PA’I MNGON ZHEN LA DE ‘DRA BA’I DGAG BYA ‘DZIN PA’I BLO ‘DUG MI [f. 168a] ‘DUG KYANG KHA NANG DU LOG LA RTOGS SHIG

This then would be a system that belonged neither to the Middle Way nor to the Mind Only.  And so we would ask people like this to turn their thoughts inside of themselves, to see whether they are able to discover, or not discover, that kind of belief in things which has existed in the minds of living beings for time with no beginning; and check to see just what kind of object to be denied that your thoughts may be grasping to.


[2298]
,DE NAS DPAL LDAN CHOS KYI GRAGS PAS,
,’DI LA’ANG RJES SU BRJOD PA YOD,
,DES NA NGAN PA’I MUN PAS KHYAB,
CES GSUNGS TE, ‘DI ‘DRA BA RNAMS SHIN TU BDO BA’I DUS SU SNANG BA RNAM DPYOD CAN GYIS SHES PAR BYA’O,,

And thus it is that the glorious Dharmakirti has said,

They even say
It could be this way;

As such, we can say
They are smothered in dark.

The point here is that those who are possessed of true discernment should be aware that we are living in times when these kinds of ideas have spread quite widely.


[2299]
‘DIR ‘GREL PA LAS, YAB SRAS MJAL BA’I MDO LAS DBANG PO NYER GNYIS RANG BZHIN MED PAR GTAN LA PHAB PA DRANGS PA LAS, ‘DI LTAR MING DU GDAGS PAR BAS KYI, DON DAM PAR NI MIG DANG DBANG PO MI DMIGS SO, ZHES PA DANG,

We see this in the autocommentary, at the point were it is citing the way in which the sutra known as The Meeting of the Father & Son sets forth how the 22 powers have no nature of their own.  Here it says, “Things then are like this, existing as labelled in names; but there exists no eye, and no sense power, in any ultimate sense.”


[2300]
DE BZHIN DU CHOS THAMS CAD KYANG NGO BO NYID KYIS DMIGS SU MA MCHIS PA STE, ZHES CHOS RNAMS MING DU BTAGS PA TZAM DU ZAD KYI DON DAM PAR DANG, NGO BO NYID KYIS MA MCHIS PAR GSUNGS PAS,

Along the same lines we see, “It is not a possibility that any existing entity could be present through some essence of its own.”  What this is saying is that all existing things are nothing more than labelled in names, and that is the end of it; it is not possible for things to exist ultimately, or through some essential nature of their own.


[2301]
DGAG BYA LA KHYAD PAR SBYOR BA LA DE GNYIS RNAM GRANGS PA DANG, RANG GI RNAM GZHAG ‘JOG PA’I PHYOGS THAMS CAD MING DU BTAGS PA TZAM GYIS BYED PAR GSUNGS SHING,

Given this description, the two qualifications applied to the object we are denying are synonymous; and what’s being said is that all the positions being taken to establish a system are accomplished through simple creation by labels.


[2302]
RMI LAM NA DGA’ RTZED BYED PA’I YUL DE RNAMS RMI LAM NA YANG DES DE DAG MA RNYED NA SAD PA’I TSE LTA CI SMOS ZHES GSUNGS SHING DE ‘DRA MANG BAS RMI LAM GYI MI DANG, SAD DUS KYI MI LA MI YIN MIN KHYAD PAR MED CES SMRA BA NI,

And so we see those references where they talk about how there are places where we take our sport in a dream; but how, even in the dream, one cannot find them—and so how much more is this the case, when we are awake?  And then people say, since there are so many such allusions in the scriptures, that there is no difference between a person in a dream and a person during the waking hours.


[2303]
SHIN TU MI ‘THAD DE DGA’ RTZED KYI GROGS BYED PA’I SEMS CAN DE RNAMS RMI LAM GYI DUS SU YANG SEMS CAN DE DAG TU MA RNYED PAR GSUNGS SHING, SAD DUS SU DE DAG RNYED PA GZHAG DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This though is incorrect in the extreme.  There are, after all, statements in scripture about how—even during the dream—beings who join into the play of enjoyment cannot be located as beings.  And they describe how we would have to say that, during the waking hours, we would be able to find them.


[2304]
DES NA RMI LAM DU MIG SHES LA SOGS PA’I DBANG SHES YOD PA ‘DI’I LUGS SU SMRA BA NI [f. 168b] NOR PA CHEN POR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

As such, you should understand that when people say that according to this system there do exist consciousness of the eye and such inside a dream, this is a massive error.


[2305]
DE LTAR NA SEMS TZAM PA NGES DON MTHAR THUG PA RTOGS PA’I SHES RAB KYI RTZAL MED PAR GRUB PA’I MTHAR SBYAR BA ‘DI BSAL BAR BYA BA KHO NA’O,,

And so we can say that this attempt to depict the Mind Only as a school of thought that completely lacks any dexterity in the wisdom needed to perceive the ultimate intended meaning is an idea that should only be refused.



No contradiction with the repulsive

[2306]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third section from before: a demonstration that there is no contradiction between this particular denial, and the meditation on the repulsive.


[2307]
GAL TE PHYI YI YUL MED PAR GZUGS SGRA SOGS GSAL BAR SNANG BA’I SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED NA, BLA MA’I MAN NGAG LAS MI SDUG PA SGOM PA’I RNAL ‘BYOR PA RNAMS KYIS, SA GZHI KENG RUS KYIS GANG BAR MTHONG BA DE JI LTAR ‘THAD DE, KENG RUS NI MED KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I RNAM SHES NI YOD PA’I PHYIR RO SNYAM NA,

One may come next with the following thought:

Well then, suppose it is the case that—even in a total absence of outer objects—the consciousness which so clearly takes on the aspect of visual form, sound, and the rest does not exist as something with some nature of its own.  How then can it be correct for those great pracitioners who are following the advices of their spiritual teachers, and meditating upon the repulsive, to see the entire surface of the earth covered with skeletons?  Because it must then be the case that—even though these skeletons don’t actually exist—there is present some awareness which exists through a nature of its own.


	[2308]
[VI.69]
Pūrṇāṃ mahīṃ saṅkalayā ca yogī
gurūpadeśād api yat paraiti,
Tatrāpi paśyet trayam apyajātaṃ
mithyā manaskāra tayopadeśāt.

,RNAL ‘BYOR PA YIS BLA MA’I MAN NGAG LAS,
,KENG RUS KYIS GANG SA GZHI MTHONG BA GANG,
,DER YANG GSUM CHAR SKYE BA MED PAR MTHONG,
,LOG PA YID LA BYED PA BSTAN PHYIR RO,

		There is that case
		Where high practitioners
		Follow the advice
		Of their spiritual teachers,
		
		And see the entire
		Surface of the earth
		Covered with skeletons.

		There also they see,
		In the absence
Of all three arising.

And that’s because
It has been described
As a mistaken
Bringing to the mind.
		

[2309]
MI SDUG PA SGOM PA’I RNAL ‘BYOR PA YIS BLA MA’I MAN NGAG LAS, KENG RUS KYIS SA GZHI GANG BAR MTHONG BA GANG YIN PA DER YANG YUL DBANG RNAM SHES GSUM CHAR RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR MTHONG STE, TING NGE ‘DZIN DE NI LOG PA STE DE KHO NA NYID MA YIN PA YID LA BYED PAR BSTAN PA STE MDO LAS GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

In reply, let’s consider that case where high practitioners meditating on the repulsive follow the advices of their spiritual teachers, and see the entire surface of the earth covered with skeletons.  There also they see these things even in the absence of all three—the object, the sense power, and the consciousness—arising through some nature of their own.  And that’s because this meditative focus has been described—spoken—in the sutras as being mistaken; which is to say, it consists of bringing to mind something which is not actually the way things are.


[2310]
KENG RUS SNANG BA’I SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, DE’I SNANG BA YANG DE LTAR ‘GYUR BAS YID BYED DE DE KHO NA NYID KYI YUL CAN DU ‘GYUR RO,,

If awareness that had taken on the aspect of skeletons existed through some nature of its own, then the aspect that it takes on would also have to be the same.  And in that case, this particular way of focusing the mind would have to have, as its object, something that represented the way that things actually are.


[2311]
‘DI NI GDON MI ZA BAR DE LTAR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA’O,,

This fact is something that you would also be compelled to accept, as we have just described it.


	[2312]
[VI.70]
Yathā’kṣi buddhau viṣayākṛtis te
tathāśubhāyāṃ manaso yadi syāt,
Tad deśa buddher itarasya tadvat
syād eva bodho na mṛṣā ca tat syāt.

,KHYOD KYI DBANG BLO’I YUL RNAMS JI LTA BA,
,DE LTAR MI SDUG YID KYI YANG ‘GYUR NA,
,DE BZHIN YUL DER BLO GTAD CIG SHOS KYIS,
,RTOGS ‘BYUNG DE NI BRDZUN PAR YANG MI ‘GYUR,

		Suppose you have
		Objects of the awareness
		Of a sense power,
		And the same
		For all of them.

		Just so,
For certain others
There should also
Be a perception,
A mind of the repulsive,

When they direct
Their minds towards
The same objects:
The perception 
Should also occur.

Neither would this
Be deceptive.


[2313]
DE LTA MA YIN NA KHYOD KYI ZLOS GAR GYI LTAD MO LA SOGS PA LTA BA NA YUL DER MIG GTAD PA RNAMS LAS JI LTAR GANG ZAG GCIG LA DBANG PO’I BLO MIG GI RNAM PAR SHES PA YUL DE’I RNAM PA CAN SKYE BA DE BZHIN DU STE DE ‘DRA BA’I RNAM PA CAN LTAD MO BA GZHAN RNAMS LA YANG SKYE BA

If this were not the way it is, then let’s consider a case where you have a group of audience members who are sitting watching a dance performance, or something of the like.  The visual consciousness of one of these people—their awareness of their sense power—arises in the aspect of this particular object of perception.  But at the same time, a state of mind also arises in all those other spectators which is the same, meaning that it takes on a very similar aspect.
