[2314]
JI LTA BA DE LTAR DU, MI SDUG PA’I YID CAN GYI RNAL ‘BYOR PA [f. 169a] LTAR CIG SHOS TE RNAL ‘BYOR PA MA YIN PAS, RNAL ‘BYOR BAS KENG RUS MTHONG BA’I YUL DER BLO GTAD PA STE KENG RUS LA SOGS PA’I YUL LA LTA ‘DOD PA RNAMS LA YANG KENG RUS RTOGS PA STE MTHONG BA SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE, SNGON PO SOGS KYI RNAM SHES BZHIN NO,,

Just so—in the same way—we can have a case where there is a certain other individual who is not a deep practitioner; which is to say, they are not like the deep practitioner whose mind has taken on an aspect of the repulsive.  It should be the case then that if they decide they would like to look upon the skeletons (or whatever else it may be)—if they were to direct their minds towards the same objects where the deep practitioner perceives skeletons—then a perception of the skeletons, that sight, should also arise in them.  It would be just the same as the perception of blue and the like.


[2315]
‘DIR ‘GREL PA DANG BSTUN NA,
,KHYOD KYI DBANG BLO’I YUL GTAD JI LTA BA,
,DE LTAR MI SDUG YID CAN DE BZHIN DU,
,YUL DER BLO GTAD CIG SHOS RNAMS LA YANG,
,SKYE ‘GYUR DE NI BRDZUN PAR YANG MI ‘GYUR,
ZHES PA’I ‘GYUR CIG THOB PAR SNANG NGO,,

If we were to match these thoughts up to the autocommentary at this point, then it would seem that we could come up with a translation of the same lines as follows—

You direct your awareness
Of the powers of sense
In a certain way,

And they take on thus
A certain aspect;

Just so,
When the mind is directed
Towards a certain object,
Then it should arise
For the other ones as well;

Neither would this be
Deceptive.


[2316]
TING NGE ‘DZIN ‘DI BRDZUN PAR TE LOG PA’I DON YID LA BYED PAR YANG MI ‘GYUR RO,,

Neither is it the case that this meditative concentration would be deceptive; which is to say, you would not be directing your mind towards something mistaken.


[2317]
RNAL ‘BYOR PA YIN MIN MGO MTSUNGS MDZAD PA YANG, SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YIN NA KENG RUS KYI MAN NGAG SGOM PA LA LTOS PA ‘GOG NUS PA’I GNAD KYIS YIN NO,,

This is true because of a crucial point here.  Even if we were to say that the two observers were the same—in either being a deep practitioner, or not—in a case where their states of mind existed through some nature of their own, we would be able to deny that they were relying on a meditation upon the advices for the practice of the skeletons.


	[2318]
[VI.71]
Toyaṃ vahantyām api pūya buddhiḥ
pretasya nadyāṃ timirākṣa tulyā,
Saṃkṣepatas tvartham amuṃ paraihi
jñeyaṃ yathā nāstyapi dhīs tatheti.

[VI.71a]
,RAB RIB DANG LDAN DBANG PO CAN MTSUNGS LA,
,CHU ‘BAB RLUNG {%KLUNG} LA YI DAGS {%DVAGS}
	RNAG BLO YANG,

	For cases equivalent
To a state of mind 
With a sense power
That has cataracts,

There is also
The state of mind
Of pus for those
Craving spirits

Towards a stream
Of fresh water.


[2319]
DE BZHIN DU RAB RIB DANG LDAN PA’I DBANG PO CAN DANG MTSUNGS PA’I SGYU MA DANG GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS DPER ‘GOD PA LA YANG LAN GDAB TSUL SHES PAR BYA LA, CHU ‘BAB PA’I KLUNG LA YI DVAGS RNAMS LA RNAG KHRAG GI BLO SKYE BA LA YANG SNGA MA BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

You can understand, in the same way, how to reply as well to cases where someone sets forth—as an example—an illusion, or a reflection in a mirror, as being equivalent to a state of mind with a sense power that has cataracts.  And you should also understand, in the same way, the illustration of when a state of mind arises in craving spirits wherein they perceive a stream of fresh water as being pus & blood.


[2320]
DE LA CHOS KYI SKYE MCHED KYI GZUGS LNGA NI DNGOS POR SMRA BA’I GRUB MTHAS BTAGS PA MIN GYI, MDO LAS GSUNGS SHING RANG NYID KYANG DE LTAR DU BZHED DO,,

Now the five types of form relating to the sense door of all things are not something simply imputed by the school of thought known as the Functionalists.  Rather, they have been stated in sutra, and we also accept them as being such.


[2321]
DE’I PHYIR KENG RUS MED KYANG DE GSAL BAR SNANG BA NI, GZUGS BRNYAN DANG ‘DRA BAR GZUGS CAN DU ‘DOD DGOS LA, ‘DI YID SHES KHO NA LA SNANG BA YIN PAS, GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED MIN LA, SKYE MCHED [f. 169b] GZUGS CAN LHAG MA DGU YANG MIN PAS CHOS KYI SKYE MCHED KYI GZUGS KUN BRTAGS PA ZHES ‘BYUNG BA’O,,

As such, even though the skeletons don’t really exist, we do have to accept that the vivid aspect of them does exist; and that it involves form, in the same way that a reflection in the mirror does.  And so despite the fact that the image of the skeletons is not, like the reflection in a mirror, something possessed of form, neither does it belong to any of the remaining nine doors of sense of form.  And this means that it constitutes form within the sense door of all things, and can be referred to as an imaginary form.


[2322]
MIG SHES LA SKRA SHAD DU SNANG BA NI GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DO,,

When a strand of hair makes its appearance to the consciousness of the eye it belongs, like a reflection in a mirror, to the sense door of visible form.


[2323]
YI DVAGS LA CHU KLUNG RNAG KHRAG TU SNANG BA NI DE’I MIG SHES LA SNANG BA YIN PAS GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DU GZHAG DGOS SO,,

When a stream of clear water appears, to a craving spirit, as though it were pus & blood, it is making its appearance to the consciousness of the eye.  As such, we would have to  categorize it too as belonging to the sense door of visible form.


[2324]
THEG BSDUS LAS KYANG,
,YI DVAGS DUD ‘GRO MI RNAMS DANG,
,LHA RNAMS JI LTAR RIGS RIGS SU,
,DNGOS GCIG YID NI THA DAD PHYIR,
,DON MA GRUB PAR ‘DOD PA YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS SHING,

The Compendium of the Greater Way puts it this way:

Since a single entity
Is separate things

To a craving spirit,
And a human,
And a worldly god,

Each according
To their type,

We assert that
It cannot exist
In fact.


[2325]
‘DI LA THEG BSDUS SU DNGOS PO GCIG GANG YIN DANG, SO SOR MTHONG TSUL GSAL BAR MA BSHAD DO,,

This compendium though does not clearly state what the one entity is, nor the individual ways in which it is seen.


[2326]
DE’I BSHAD SBYAR DGE BSNYEN BTZUN PAS MDZAD PAR, CHU KLUNG GI DNGOS PO LA RANG RANG GI LAS KYI RNAM SMIN GYI DBANG GIS YI DVAGS KYIS RNAG LA SOGS PAS GANG BAR MTHONG BA DANG, DE NYID LA DUD ‘GRO NYA LA SOGS PAS GNAS KYI BLOS GNAS PAR BYED PA DANG,

The explanation of this work by the layperson with lifetime vows named “Holy One” though does give the following explanation—

Each one, according to the power of their own karmic ripening, sees the stream of fresh water in a different way.  The craving spirit sees it filled with pus and the like.  An animal like a fish or the like sees the very same object as being their home, and they want to reside in it.  


[2327]
MI RNAMS KYIS NI MNGAR BA DANG DVANGS PA DANG BSIL BA’I CHUR RTOG CING KHRUS BYED DO, ,’THUNG NGO DER ‘JUG GO ,NAM MKHA’ MTHA’ YAS SKYE MCHED LA SNYOMS PAR ZHUGS PA’I LHA RNAMS KYIS NI NAM MKHAR MTHONG STE, GZUGS KYI ‘DU SHES RNAM PAR BSHIG PA’I PHYIR RO ZHES BSHAD DO,,

Human beings perceive it as water which is sweet and clear and cool, and relate to it by saying, “I’ll take a bath in it,” or “I’ll take a drink from it.”  Those worldly gods who are deep in meditation upon the absorption known as “Limitless Space” see the same thing as empty space, for their conception of it as form has dissolved completely.


[2328]
‘DI LA ‘DI SNYAM DU ‘GRO BA DE DAG GI MTHONG BA NI THA SNYAD PA’I TSAD MA YIN LA, GZHI GCIG MI MTHUN PA DE DAG TU TSAD MAS GRUB NA RNAG KHRAG DANG RNAL KHRAG MA YIN PA GNYIS MI ‘GAL ZHING, TSAD MAS GRUB PA LA YANG YID BRTAN MED PAR ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA,

One may feel the following concerns about this citation:

The way that these different beings see things is a nominal form of accurate perception; and if these incompatible perceptions of a single base object are all confirmed with an accurate perception, then it must be the case that being blood and pus, and not being blood and pus, are not two incompatible states.  It also throws into the question the whole process of confirming things with accurate perception.


[2329]
‘DI LA GZHUNG DON DE LTAR GO BAS [f. 170a] DE BZHIN DU BZHAG NA TSAD MA LA YID BRTAN MI ‘GYUR BAR ‘GYUR NA, DE YANG MI RUNG BAS JI LTAR YIN ZHES ‘DRI NA RTOG LDAN GYI DRI BA YIN NO,,

If we understand the the quotation in that manner and decide that things must be this way, then it would indeed seem as though accurate perception itself were drawn into question.  That in itself would be unacceptable, and so it is an insightful question to ask what’s going on here!


[2330]
DE LTAR GO BA DE’I DON YIN PAR BZUNG NAS TSAD MAS GRUB PA LA YID BRTAN MED DO ZHES SMRA NA NI, DON ‘DI KHO BOS ‘DI LTAR RTOGS SO ZHES PA GCIG KYANG GZHAG TU MED CING, TSAD MA THAMS CAD LA SKUR PA ‘DEBS PAS NA SHIN TU MI ‘THAD PA’O,,

But if you do take this interpretation of the matter as what the lines are referring to, and say that they draw into question the principle of things being confirmed with accurate perception, it doesn’t seem as though you have a single concept to point to which you from your side would say represented your stand on the question.  And it would be a massive error to discount each and every form of accurate perception.


[2331]
‘O NA JI LTAR ZHE NA THOG MAR DPE BSHAD PAR BYA STE, LCAGS GONG MES BSREGS PA’I DMAR ‘BAR BA LA REG KYANG MI ‘TSIG PA’I RIG SNGAGS DANG LDAN PA ZHIG GIS,

“Well then,” you might return, “how do we resolve the question?”  To start with, let’s consider a certain metaphor.  Let’s say that we have thrust a length of high-quality steel into the fire, and it has turned red-hot.  Then along comes a person who has mastered the secret spell that allows a person to grasp the steel without being burned.


[2332]
LCAGS GONG DE LAG TU BLANGS PA NA LUS SHES KYIS LCAGS DE’I REG BYA ‘DZIN KYANG, DE LA REG BYA DE SHIN TU TSA ZHING SREG PA’I RNAM PA CAN DU MI SKYE BA NI, RIGS SNGAGS BZLAS PA’I CHUS LAG PA BKRUS PA SOGS KYI RKYEN GYIS YIN NO,,

When they take the piece of steel up into their hand, their tactile consciousness is aware of the tactile sensation of the metal.  But this sensation does not arise in the aspect of being hot and burning; and this is something that occurs due to the factor of the person having, for example, dipped their hand in water over which they have repeated the secret words.


[2333]
DE ‘DRA BA’I RIG SNGAGS ZLOS PA DANG BRAL BA LA NI, LCAGS GONG GI REG BYA DE SHIN TU TSA ZHING SREG PA’I RNAM PA CAN DU SKYE’O,,

For a person who is without the skill of repeating these kinds of secret words, the touch of the length of steel takes on an aspect of being hot and burning.


[2334]
DE LTAR NA MI SREG PA DANG SREG PA’I REG BYA GNYIS KA LCAGS GONG GCIG PU DE’I REG BYAR NI BYA DGOS LA, LUS SHES TSAD MA GNYIS GCIG GIS GRUB PA’I REG BYA CIG SHOS KYIS GRUB PA NI MIN PAS GNYIS KA TSAD MAR KHAS BLANGS KYANG TSAD MA GCIG GIS GRUB PA CIG SHOS KYIS ‘GOG PA MIN NO,,

As such, we would have to say that both tangible objects—not being burning, and being burning—must be tangible objects of the single length of steel.  And we can say that, of these two different accurate perceptions of the awareness of the tangible, one is confirming a tangible object which by the other is not confirmed; and that, as such, we would have to accept both as being accurate.  It is not though the case that the confirmation by one accurate perception would have to invalidate the other.


[2335]
DE BZHIN DU GZHI GANG DU CHU KLUNG ‘BAB PA’I GZHI DER CHU KLUNG DE’I CHA SHAS SHIG YI DVAGS RNAMS LA SNGON LAS KYI DBANG GIS RNAG KHRAG TU SKYES PA DANG, CHU KLUNG GI CHA SHAS GZHAN ZHIG MI LA SNGON LAS KYI DBANG [f. 170b] GIS RNAG KHRAG TU MI SNANG BA’I BTUNG BA DANG, KHRUS KYI CHUR SKYE BA NA

And so we can point to any particular location where a clear stream happens to be flowing.  One part of the stream—due to the previous karma of a particular craving spirit—arises as pus and blood.  Another part of the stream—due to the previous karma of a particular human being—arises as water to drink, or water in which to wash oneself.


[2336]
DE GNYIS KA CHU KLUNG GCIG GI CHA SHAS RE YIN PAS, YI DVAGS KYI MIG SHES TSAD MAS GRUB PA’I DON DANG, MI’I MIG SHES TSAD MAS GRUB PA’I DON GNYIS KYANG DNGOS PO SO SO BA YIN PAS DE GNYIS GCIG GIS GRUB PA’I DON DE NYID, CIG SHOS KYIS DE’I BZLOG PHYOGS SU GRUB PA GA LA YIN,

Each one of the two represents a section of a single stream of water; and we can also say that the object as confirmed by the accurate perception of the craving spirit’s visual consciousness, and the object as confirmed by the accurate perception of the human being’s visual consciousness—these two—are discrete entities in their own right.  How then could one ever assert that these two were such that the very object confirmed by one were the incompatible opposite of that confirmed by the other?


[2337]
DE BZHIN DU BSHES SPRINGS LAS,
,YI DVAGS RNAMS LA SOS KA’I DUS SU NI,
,ZLA BA’ANG TSA LA DGUN NI NYI MA’ANG GRANG,

The same point is made in A Letter to a Friend:

For craving spirits,
Even the light of the moon
Is hot, in the summer;

And even sunlight
In the winter feels cold.


[2338]
ZHES GSUNGS PA YANG YI DVAGS RNAMS LA SNGON LAS KYI DBANG GIS SOS KA ZLA ‘OD REG BYA SHIN TU TSA BA DANG, DGUN GYI TSE NYI ‘OD KYI REG BYA GRANG BAR SKYE YANG, ZLA NYI’I ‘OD KYI STENG NAS MI LA GRANG DRO’I RNAM PA CAN DU SKYE BA MI ‘GAL LA,

What this is saying is that the touch of moonlight in the summer feels—due to their previous karma—unbearably hot to craving spirits; while at the same time the touch of sunlight can arise as something cold for them, in the winter.  Nor is it any contradiction to say that a feeling of cold or of heat arises from the moonlight or sunlight, for a human.


[2339]
DE GNYIS NI TSAD MA GCIG GIS TSA BAR GZHAL BA’I REG BYA NYID, CIG SHOS KYIS GRANG BAR ‘JAL BA MIN ZHING, GNYIS KA’ANG ZLA NYI GCIG GI ‘OD KYI REG BYAR ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR, DNGOS PO GCIG CES KYANG GSUNGS PAS GZHUNG DON ZHIB TU MA DPYAD PAR GO BA RAGS PA RE SHAR BA NA DES TSIM PA’I THAG GCOD MA SNGA ZHIG

As for these two, it is not the case that the very same sensation is experienced by the one accurate perception as being hot; and by the other as being cold—although it is the case that we can say of both that they are a sensation relating to a single moon, or a single sun.  And because of that, we do see the phrase here, “a single entity.”  It would be best though if we did not make any premature decision to be satisfied with a rough understanding on this point, without digging deeper.



A summary of the denial

[2340]
,GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to the second part of our more specific denial of the explanation on these points by the Mind Only school: the summary of just such a denial.


	[2341]
[VI.71b]
,MDOR NA JI LTAR SHES BYA MED DE BZHIN,
,BLO YANG MED CES DON ‘DI SHES PAR GYIS,

	To summarize,
	There is nothing
	In the universe;

	Just so, there is
	No state of mind.

	This is the point
	We need to understand.


[2342]
SNGAR RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA RNAMS KYI DON MDOR BSDU NA SHES BYA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PA JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU SHES BYA’I RNAM PA CAN GYI BLO YANG RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS SKYES PA MED CES DON ‘DI SHES PAR GYIS SHING GCES GSUNGS PAS,

Suppose then we were to summarize the points that we have covered in detail so far.  The fact is that there is nothing in the universe which exists through some nature of its own.  Just so, there is no state of mind which takes on the aspect of these existing entities which could arise in & of itself.  This, the root text is telling us, is the point which we need to understand.


[2343]
SHES BYA DANG SHES PA LA RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD MED KYI KHYAD PAR MED PAR STON PA YIN LA, SKRA SHAD MED NA DER SNANG BA’I SHES PA YANG MED CES PA DANG, SGYU MA LA RTA GLANG DU ZHEN PA’I [f. 171a] ZHEN YUL MED NA DER ‘DZIN PA’I SHES PA YANG MED CES SOGS NI, SLOB DPON ‘DI’I LUGS GTAN MIN NO,,

What this is indicating is that there is no difference between knowable things and the awareness which knows them, as far as existing through some nature of their own, or not.  And what this is saying is that—if there is no strand of hair—then neither is there any state of mind which is taking that strand as its aspect.  It is absolutely not the position of this master though to say that—if the object that one was thinking was there when we perceived a horse or cow in an illusion didn’t really exist—then the state of mind that was grasping to it didn’t exist either.


[2344]
‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PAR BSTOD PA LAS KYANG,
,MA SHES PAR NI SHES BYA MIN,
,DE MED RNAM PAR SHES MED PA,
,DE PHYIR SHES DANG SHES BYA DAG
,RANG BZHIN MED PAR KHYOD KYIS GSUNGS,
ZHES PA DANG,

As A Praise of the One Who Went Beyond the World says it,

	In the absence of knowing,
	There is nothing to know.

	And when that is missing,
	There can be no knowing.

	Thus it is that you stated
	That nothing possesses
	Any nature of its own.


[2345]
DE BZHIN DU,
,RNAM SHES SGYU MA DANG MTSUNGS PAR,
,NYI MA’I GNYEN GYIS GSUNGS PA YIN,
,DE YI DMIGS PA’ANG DE BZHIN TE,
,NGES PAR SGYU MA’I DNGOS DANG ‘DRA,
ZHES GSUNGS TE,

And along the same lines we see,

	The Cousin of the Sun proclaimed
	That consciousness was just the same
	As an illusion.

	And what this consciousness
	Focuses upon is just the same:

	It is, with certainty,
	Like an illusory object.


[2346]
SHES PA ‘DI ‘DRA ZHIG GIS SHES ZHES ‘JOG RGYU MED NA, SHES BYA YUL DU ‘JOG MI NUS SO, ,’DIS YUL ‘DI ‘DRA ZHIG SHES ZHES ‘JOG RGYU MED NA SHES PAR YANG ‘JOG MI NUS PAS, SHES BYA DE MED PAR RNAM PAR SHES PA YANG MED DO,,

What this is saying is that—it we cannot say that such-and-such a state of mind is doing the knowing, then we cannot say that such-and-such an existing entity is the object that it knows.  If we cannot say “It is this which is knowing such-and-such an object,” then we cannot establish that there has been any knowing itself.  And so as such, if there exists here nothing to be known, then neither can there exist here anything to do the knowing.


[2347]
SHES PA DANG SHES BYA LTOS ‘JOG YIN PA DE’I PHYIR, DE GNYIS KA RANG BZHIN MED PAR KHYOD KYIS BSTAN ZHES GSUNGS PAS, DE GNYIS LA BDEN GNYIS GANG DU YANG GCIG MED LA CIG SHOS YOD PA’I RNAM DBYE MED PA ‘PHAGS PA’I BZHED PA’O,,

And what these lines are saying is, “What you taught us is that—since things to be known and the states of mind to know them are established in mutual dependence—then neither one has any nature of its own.”  As such, the position that the Realized One takes is that there can never be any distinction between these two where you could say that one of the two realities did not exist, but that the other one did.


[2348]
BYANG CHUB SEMS ‘GREL LAS,
,SHES PAS SHES BYA RTOGS PA STE,
,SHES BYA MED PAR SHES PA MED,
CES GSUNGS PA YANG SNGAR DRANGS PA’I BSTOD PA DANG DON ‘DRA BAS DON SHES YOD MED MTSUNGS PA’I KHUNGS SO,,

The Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment also says,

What the mind does
Is to perceive
Things known by the mind.

Wherever there is nothing
To know,
There can be no mind knowing.

These lines convey the same point as the words of praise just quoted; as such, both are reputable sources for the idea that objects and the states of mind which perceive them are—in this way—equivalent.



An attempted proof
of the dominated

[2349]
GNYIS PA LA BZHI, GZHAN DBANG GI SGRUB BYED RANG RIG DGAG PA, SEMS TZAM PA’I LUGS BDEN PA GNYIS CHAR LAS NYAMS PAR BSTAN PA, DES NA KLU SGRUB KYI LUGS KHO NA’I RJES SU ‘BRANG BAR RIGS PA, GZHAN [f. 171b] DBANG DANG ‘JIG RTEN PA’I THA SNYAD ‘GOG PA GNYIS MI MTSUNGS PAR BSTAN PA’O,,

Here next is the second general part of this discussion: denying the accurate perception which is supposed to prove that dominated things exist through some nature of their own.  We proceed in four steps: a denial of apperception, which is used to establish dominated entities; a demonstration that the Mind Only system fails from the viewpoint of both of the realities; a description of how—therefore—it is appropriate to follow the system of Arya Nagarjuna, exclusively; and showing that denying dominated entities and denying the verbiage of the world are not equivalent.


[2350]
DANG PO LA BZHI, GZHAN DBANG GI SGRUB BYED DRIS NAS DE MI ‘THAD PAR BSTAN PA, DE ‘THAD PA’I GZHAN GYI LAN DGAG PA, RIGS PA GZHAN GYIS KYANG RANG RIG MI ‘THAD PAR BSTAN PA, GZHAN DBANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MO GSHAM KYI BU DANG MTSUNGS PAR BSTAN PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these steps has four parts of its own.  These are (1) a request for proof to substantiate the existence of dominated entities, and then a demonstration that the attempted proof is incorrect; (2) a denial of the response by others that the proof is indeed correct; (3) a demonstration that apperception is illogical even according to other proofs; and (4) establishing that dominated entities which existed through some nature of their own would be the equivalent of the child of a barren woman.


	[2351]
[VI.72]
Grāhyaṃ vinā grāhakatā viyuktaṃ
dvayena śūnyaṃ paratantra rūpam,
Yadyasti kenāsya paraiṣi sattām
agṛhyamāṇaṃ ca sad ityayuktam.

,GAL TE GZUNG MED ‘DZIN PA NYID BRAL ZHING,
,GNYIS KYIS STONG PA’I GZHAN DBANG DNGOS YOD NA,
,’DI YI YOD PA GANG GIS SHES PAR ‘GYUR,
,MA BZUNG BAR YANG YOD CES BYAR MI RUNG,

		Suppose that there exist
		No objects to be held,
		Devoid then of any
		Holding itself;

		And that there
		Could exist
		Dominated entities
		That were empty
		Of the two.

		How is it then
		That you can perceive
		The existence of these?

		It would be wrong
To say there did exist
Something there,
Even though it wasn’t held.


[2352]
DE LTAR PHYI ROL MED PAR RNAM SHES PA MI SRID PAR BSTAN NAS, DA NI PHYI ROL MED PAS KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PA’I GZHAN DBANG GI DNGOS PO TZAM ZHIG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

We have demonstrated, then, that a kind of consciousness which could have no outer objects would be impossible.  We will now give an explanation which is meant to deny that the simple form of entities which are dominated—meaning, when we do not distinguish these as not being outer objects—could exist through any nature of their own.


[2353]
GAL TE PHYI ROL GYI GZUNG BA MED PAS DE LAS DON GZHAN PA’I ‘DZIN PA NYID DANG BRAL ZHING, GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD PA GNYIS KYIS STONG PA’I GZHAN DBANG GI DNGOS PO YOD NA, GZHAN DBANG ‘DI YI YOD PA DE KHYOD KYI SHES PA GANG GIS SHES PAR ‘GYUR ZHES DRI BAR BYA’O,,

Let’s suppose that since there exist no outer objects to be held, they are then devoid of any holding itself which could exist as an entity other than them.  And let’s also say that there could exist dominated entities that were empty of involving subject states of mind—and the objects that they hold—where these two are substantially separate.   We need to ask you then how it is that you can perceive the existence of these dominated entities.


[2354]
DE LA SHES PA DE NYID KYIS SHES PA DE NYID ‘DZIN PAR NI MI ‘THAD DE, RANG LA RANG GI BYED PA ‘JUG PA ‘GAL PA’I PHYIR RO,,

On this point, it would be incorrect to say that this perception could perceive this same perception—since it would be a contradiction for something to engage in an action upon itself.


[2355]
‘DI LTAR RAL GRI’I SO DE NYID KYIS DE NYID MI GCOD LA, SOR MO’I RTZE MO DE NYID KYIS DE NYID LA MI REG CING, LEGS PAR BSLABS PA’I G-YER ZHING YANG ZOR CAN GYIS KYANG RANG GI PHRAG PA LA ZHON PAR MI NUS SHING, MES RANG GI BDAG NYID MI SREG LA, MIG GIS RANG GI BDAG NYID LA LTA BA MA YIN NO,,

The blade of a sword, for example, cannot cut itself; nor can the tip of a finger touch itself.  Not even the most supple and airy gymnast can ride on their own shoulders; fire cannot burn itself; and the eye is not something which can see itself.


[2356]
‘DIR SHES PA DE NYID KYIS SHES PA DE NYID ‘DZIN PA MI ‘THAD PAR BSHAD PA’I GZHAN GYI LUGS KHYAD PAR BA NI ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And so here we will explain the particular position of others which states that a particular state of mind could hold that same particular state of mind; and show how this is incorrect.


[2357]
SHES PA DE NI RANG LAS DON GZHAN PA’I SHES PAS [f. 172a] KYANG ‘DZIN PA MA YIN TE, SEMS TZAM PA RANG GI GRUB MTHA’ DANG ‘GAL BA’I PHYIR TE, GAL TE ‘BRAS BU’I GNAS GYUR MA THOB PA’I SKABS SU RNAM PAR RIG PA DON GZHAN CIG RNAM PAR RIG PA’I SNANG YUL YIN NA RNAM PAR RIG PA TZAM NYID DU SMRA BA NYAMS PAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES SEMS TZAM GYI GZHUNG LAS ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

It is not by the way the case that this particular state of mind is being held by a state of mind which is different from it; for that would contradict the Mind Only’s own school of thought.  This is because we see, in the great books of the Mind Only themselves, sentiments like “You would lose your status as a person who is professing that things are awareness alone, if you were to say that, even before this entity had reached that point where it had become a result, one state of awareness could act as the object which that same state of awareness were taking as its aspect of focus.”


[2358]
DE’I PHYIR SEMS TZAM PA LTAR BYAS NA DE LTAR ‘DZIN PA RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MED LA, SHES PAS MA BZUNG BAR YANG YOD CES BYA BAR MI RUNG NGO ZHES DBU MA PAS SMRAS PA NA, SEMS TZAM PA NA RE, GAL TE YANG SHES PA DON GZHAN GYIS MI ‘DZIN KYANG RANG RIG NI YOD DO,,

As such, if we were to follow the thinking of the Mind Only, this kind of holding could not in any way exist.  To this, the Middle Way then would say, “Well then, it would be wrong to say there did exist something there, even though it wasn’t held by the mind.”  And then the Mind Only in turn would reply that “Even in a case where such an object were not held by a state of mind as a separate object, still we could point to apperception.”


	[2359]
[VI.73]
Tenaiva tasyānubhavo na siddhaḥ
siddhaḥ smṛter uttara kālataś cet,
Asiddha siddhyartham asiddham etan
nirucyamānaṃ na hi sādhanāya.

[VI.73a]
,DE NYID KYIS DE MYONG BAR ‘GRUB MA YIN,

		This particular one
		Is not something
		That could establish these,
		By experiencing them.


[2360]
DE’I PHYIR RANG RIG KHO NAS GZHAN DBANG DE ‘DZIN PA’I PHYIR DE YOD DO ZHE NA,

Suppose then that you say, “Dominated entities do exist, because they are perceived, if only by apperception.”


[2361]
SHES PA DE NYID KYIS DE MYONG BAR GRUB PA MA YIN NO,,

But then we would say that this particular state of mind is not something that could establish these, by experiencing them.


[2362]
‘DIR SEMS TZAM PAS RANG RIG JI LTA BU ZHIG KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYOGS SNGA MA’I KHUNGS CUNG ZAD BSHAD NA, RTOG GE ‘BAR BA LAS, SEMS TZAM PAS RNAM SHES NI GNYIS SU SNANG STE, RANG SNANG BA DANG YUL DU SNANG BA’O,,

Why don’t we pause here, and say something about the earlier sources for the Mind Only’s assertion of apperception: how they come to accept its existence.  We can start with the Blaze of Reasoning, which talks about how—

The Mind Only say that consciousness appears in two forms: one where it appears as itself, and another in which it appears as its object.


[2363]
YUL DU SNANG BA’I RNAM SHES NI PHYI ROL GYI YUL GYI RNAM PAR GYUR NAS, RANG SNANG BA’I RNAM SHES KYI YUL DU ‘GYUR RO ZHE NA, ZHES PA’I LAN DU, YUL DU SNANG LAS GZHAN GYUR PA’I, ,SEMS NYID JI ‘DRA BA ZHIG SNANG, ZHES

And then comes the question: “Is it that the consciousness which is taking the aspect of the object assumes this aspect of an outer object, and thus becomes the object of the consciousness which takes its aspect on?”  In reply, we have the lines—

How is it that
The mind itself,

As something other
Than what appears
As the object,

Makes its own appearance?


[2364]
YUL DU SNANG BA LAS GZHAN PA STE DE DANG BRAL BA’I RANG NYID DU SNANG BA NI MA MTHONG NGO, ZHES BSHAD PAS

What this is saying is, “We don’t see where the mind itself is making its appearance, independent from—other than—its appearance as the object.”


[2365]
SEMS TZAM PAS SHES PA KHA NANG LTA LA GNYIS SU SNANG BA THAMS CAD LOG PA DANG, DE ‘DRA BA’I SHES PA DE KHO RANG GIS KHO RANG RIG PA’I RANG RIG TU ‘DOD [f. 172b] LA, DE LTA NA’ANG SHES NGO DER RIG BYA DANG RIG BYED THA DAD PA’I SNANG BA MED PAR ‘DOD DO,,

Those of the Mind Only school believe that our awareness is focused inward, and that all appearance of a duality between subject & object can be stopped.  They also say that this type of awareness is apperception, where it knows itself by itself.  Even so though, according to them, there is no appearance of a separate known and knower here.


[2366]
BDEN GNYIS KYI RANG ‘GREL LAS KYANG RANG RIG ‘GOG PA NA, SHES PA NI GNYIS KYIS DBEN PA’I NGO BO RIG PAR ‘BYUNG BA YIN PA DANG, DE MED PAR SHES PAR ‘GYUR GYI DE LTA MA YIN NA MI RIGS PA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES GSUNGS TE,

The autocommentary to Distinguishing Between the Two Realities puts it this way:

If we deny the idea of apperception, we can understand how awareness can know things with a nature of being devoid of this duality; and how that could not exist.  If it were not this way, then the situation would be illogical.


[2367]
SEMS TZAM PAS GZHAN DBANG GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS GZHAN GYI KUN BRTAGS KYIS STONG PAR BSGRUBS PA NA, SHES PA GZHAN DBANG NI GNYIS SNANG GIS DBEN PA’I NGO BO RIG PAR ‘BYUNG BA’I RANG RIG GRUB NA, DE NAS GZHI DE GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS GZHAN DU MED PA SHES KYI, DE LTAR SNGON DU GZHI DE RANG RIG GIS MA GRUB NA, DE GZHIR BZUNG NAS KUN BRTAGS KYIS STONG PA MI ‘GRUB BO ZHES BSHAD DE,

That is, suppose that those of the Mind Only are trying to prove that dominated entities are devoid of constructs, in the sense of an object held and a holding consciousness which could be materially different from one another.  If they can establish a state of apperception which can perceive that the nature of the dominated entity of awareness is to be devoid of any duality of object & subject, then we could understand that this base entity had no quality where objects & subjects were materially different.  And they would say that if we take this as the base we could never establish that it was empty of these constructs.


[2368]
KHYOD KYI LTAR NA GZHAN DBANG GI SGRUB BYED GNYIS SNANG DANG BRAL BA’I RANG RIG GIS GRUB DGOS PA LA, DE MI ‘GRUB CES BKAG GO

That is, this master is making his denial by saying that—according to you—the support for dominated entities would have to be established by an apperception which was free of all duality; whereas it is not so established.


[2369]
,DE’I PHYIR DE ‘DRA BA’I RANG RIG BKAG PAS RNAL ‘BYOR BA SO SO RANG RANG GIS DE KHO NA NYID RIG PA’I RANG RIG BKAG PA DANG, ‘JIG RTEN PAS NGAS NGA RANG RIG CES PA’I THA SNYAD KYI DON GYI RANG RIG BKAG ZER BA NI BLUN PO’I GTAM MO,,

Some have said that—as such—when we deny such a kind of apperception, we are denying the apperception that individual deep practitioners might use to perceive suchness; and that we are also denying apperception in the sense it is meant by people in the world, when they use it in the phrase “I know myself.”  Such positions are of course just foolish talk. 



A response on the dominated

[2370]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GZHAN GYI LUGS BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

This brings us to our second part from above: a denial of the response by others that the proof of dominated entities is indeed correct.  Here we proceed in two steps—a statement of the position that others take, and then a denial of that position.  Here is the first.


[2371]
‘DIR KHA CIG GIS TE SEMS TZAM PAS MDO SDE PA’I PHYOGS KHAS BLANGS NAS RANG RIG BSGRUB PA’I PHYIR, JI LTAR ME NI SKYES PA NYID NA RANG DANG BUM PA LA SOGS PA DAG RIM GYIS GNYIS SU GSAL BA LA MI ‘JUG PAR CIG CAR GSAL BAR BYED LA,

On this point, some make the following assertion:

Those of the Mind Only accept the position of the Sutrists on this point, and give the following description to substantiate the existence of apperception.  Think of how—when a fire starts—it illuminates both itself and something like a vase at the same instant; it is not the case that it acts in stages, first illuminating itself and then only afterwards illuminating the vase or whatever it may be.


[2372]
BUM PA’O [f. 173a] ZHES BRJOD NA SGRA RANG LA DMIGS PA DANG, DE’I DON BUM PA LA DMIGS PA GNYIS SKYED PA DE BZHIN DU RNAM SHES KYANG SKYE BA NA SO SOR RIM GYIS GNYIS SU MI ‘JUG PAR RANG DANG YUL GNYIS KA CIG CAR RIG PAR BYED DO,,

When we say the word “vase,” two things are triggered: the term is focused both upon itself, and upon the vase which it refers to.  Consciousness works the same; it is not the case that—when it arises—it engages in two things one after the other.  Rather, it knows both itself and the object of perception at the very same moment.


[2373]
DE’I PHYIR RANG RIG PA NI YOD PA KHO NA’O,,

As such, we have to say that apperception most certainly does exist.


[2374]
GANG ZHIG RANG RIG MI ‘DOD PA DES KYANG NGES PAR RANG RIG KHAS BLANG DGOS TE, DE KHAS MI LEN NA SNGAR DON ‘DI MTHONG NGO ZHES DUS PHYIS YUL DRAN PA DANG, SNGAR NGAS MTHONG NGO SNYAM DU YUL GYI NYAMS SU MYONG BA YUL CAN DRAN PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

And if someone were to say that they could not accept the concept of apperception, we would reply that they most certainly should.  And that’s because—if we fail to accept it—then it would be impossible for us ever to recall, later, a particular object, saying “Oh yes, I saw that earlier on.”  That is, it would never happen that the subject state of mind recalled having experienced its object.


[2375]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, SNGAR NYAMS SU MA MYONG BA LA DRAN PA SKYE MI SRID PAS DRAN PA NI SNGAR GYI NYAMS SU MYONG BA’I YUL CAN YIN NA, KHYOD RANG RIG MI ‘DOD PA LTAR NA SNGAR GYI SNGO ‘DZIN LTA BU’I SHES PA YANG RANG DUS SU NYAMS SU MA MYONG BAS, PHYIS KYI DRAN PA YOD PAR MI ‘GRUB BO,,

And why is that?  It is impossible for us to have a memory of something that we have not experienced earlier on.  As such, memory is a subject state of mind which holds as its object a previous experience.  According to you all though—those of you who do not accept the concept of apperception—a previous perception such as having perceived a patch of blue could not have experienced this object within its own time, which means that you cannot say that there was a later memory.


[2376]
‘DIS NI SNGAR GYI SNGO ‘DZIN DE LA MYONG BA YOD PAR PHYIS DE DRAN PA’I RTAGS LAS SGRUB PA YIN TE, SNGAR GYI SNGO ‘DZIN LA RANG MYONG BA’I RANG RIG YOD DE ZHES SGRUB NA NI, GZHAN LA GRUB PA’I DPE MI SNYED PAS DE LTAR MI SGRUB BO,,

What this is saying is that the existence of an earlier experience with the perception of blue is proven from the logical reason that we have a memory of it later.  If we were to phrase it like “during that previous perception of blue, there was present an occurrence of apperception which experienced this perception, because…” one would be unable to find a common example that the other party accepted as valid; so this is not how this would be proven.


[2377]
SNGO ‘DZIN LA MYONG BA YOD PAR GRUB NA NI, DE’I MYONG BA LA RANG GIS DANG GZHAN GYIS MYONG BA GNYIS SU KHA TSON BCAD NAS DANG PO KHYOD LA MI RUNG LA, GNYIS PA RANG LUGS KYIS BKAG PA NA MYONG BA’I KHYAB BYED KHEGS PA NA, MYONG BA TZAM YANG MI ‘THAD PAR ‘GYUR RO 

If we are seeking to prove that there exists an experience of a perception of blue, then we can narrow the possibilities down to two: either this perception experiences itself, or something else experiences it.  According to you, the first would be incorrect.  But if the second were denied by our own system, then we would be denying the general entire category of the possibility of experience.  In this case then, any experience at all would become incorrect here.


[2378]
ZHES ‘GOG PA YIN TE, RANG RIG SGRUB PA’I RIGS PA DRAG SHOS YIN NO,,

The denial presented thus actually represents the very best attempt at a reasoning to establish the existence of apperception.


[2379]
SNGO ‘DZIN DE RANG LAS DON GZHAN PA’I SHES PAS KYANG MYONG BAR MI RIGS TE, DE RIGS NA GNOD PA [f. 173b] GNYIS LAS DANG PO THUG MED DU THAL BA NI,

If would moreover be illogical to say that this perception of blue was experienced by some kind of awareness which was a discrete object from it.  And that’s because—if it were said to be logical—then two problems would attain.  The first of these is the necessity that the situation would be an infinite regression, described as follows.


[2380]
SNGON PO YONGS SU GCOD PA’I SHES PA DE RANG GI MJUG THOGS SU ‘BYUNG BA’I SHES PA GZHAN GYIS YONGS SU GCOD NA, DE LA DE ‘JAL BYED KYI SHES PA DON GZHAN DGOS SAM MI DGOS,

We would start with a specific question.  Suppose you say that a state of mind which discerns the color blue is itself discerned by another state of mind which comes just after it.  According to you, would this second state of mind require another state of mind that took it under consideration, and was separate from it, or not?


[2381]
MI DGOS NA SHES PA SNGA MA LA YANG MI DGOS PAR ‘GYUR LA, DGOS NA DE LA YANG GZHAN DGOS PAS THUG PA MED PA’I SKYON DU ‘GYUR ZHING, THUG MED DU SONG NA NI SNGO ‘DZIN DANG PO LA MYONG BA MI GRUB PA’I SKYON YOD DO,,

If you say that this following state of mind were not required, then it wouldn’t be required either with the state of mind previous to it.  If it were required, then yet another state of mind would be required, and you’d have the problem that the process would become endless.  And if it did become endless, then you’d have the problem that there was nothing you could establish as experiencing the first perception of blue.


[2382]
GNYIS PA YUL GZHAN YONGS SU MI GCOD PAR THAL BA NI, SHES PA SNGA MA PHYI MAS GCOD NA NI GZUGS SGRA LA SOGS PA’I YUL GZHAN MI GCOD PA DANG, DE LA MI ‘PHO BAR ‘GYUR TE, RNAM PAR SHES PA’I RGYUN LUGS TE RGYU BA MTHA’ DAG SHES PA SNGA MA GZHAN DE’I YUL CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here’s that second problem, which is that it would have to be the case that there was no discernment of other objects.  If the previous state of mind were discerned by the later one, then things like visible form, and sound—other objects—would not be discerned.  There would be no moving over to them; since the flow of the consciousness—all of its motion—would be devoted to being the object state of mind for that other, earlier state of mind.


[2383]
DE NI KHYAB PA MA NGES PA MIN TE, SHES PA SNGA MA SNGA MA SHES PA PHYI MA PHYI MAS YONGS SU GCOD NA, SNGA MA DE GZUNG DON DU BYAS NAS PHYI MA DE SKYE DGOS LA, DE’I TSE NANG GI YAN LAG GI NYE BA’I GZUNG DON BOR NAS, RING BA’I PHYI ROL LA MI ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And this is not something where the necessity would be uncertain.  If it were the case that each earlier perception were discerned by each later perception, then each later instance would have to arise by taking each earlier instance as the object it held to.  And in this circumstance the awareness would not drop a closer object of perception that was an inner component, and engage rather in an outer object that was further.


[2384]
GAL TE SNGO ‘DZIN GYI RNAM SHES SNGA MA GCOD PA’I SNGO ‘DZIN GYI RNAM SHES PHYI MA DANG SNGON PO GCOD PA’I SNGO ‘DZIN GYI RNAM SHES GNYIS DUS GCIG TU SKYE BAS, YUL GZHAN LA MI ‘PHO BA’I SKYON MED DO SNYAM NA,

Here one may have the following thought:

Let’s consider the later example of a consciousness which is holding to a patch of the color blue, and which discerns an earlier consciousness which is holding to blue.  It would be arising at the same time as another consciousness which is holding to blue and discerning the blue itself.  As such, there is no such problem where it could not move on to another object.


[2385]
DE LTAR NA MIG GI RNAM SHES RIGS MTHUN RDZAS THA DAD PA GNYIS DUS GCIG TU GANG ZAG GCIG GI RGYUD LA SKYE BAR ‘GYUR LA, DE ‘DOD NA SEMS CAN RNAMS RNAM PAR SHES PA’I RGYUD GCIG PA STE RE RE BA’O ZHES GSUNGS PA DANG ‘GAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

If that were the case, then two different visual consciousnesses that were of the same type but substantially different from one another would arise within the mindstream of a single person at a single moment in time.  And if you agreed to that, then you would be contradicting statements that living beings are “of a single flow of consciousness; which is to say, a flow which is separate.”


[2386]
‘DIR [f. 174a] ‘GREL PA LAS RNAM PAR SHES PA AUD PA LA’I ‘DAB MA BRGYA ‘BIGS PA LTAR, RIM GYIS ‘BYUNG BA RNAMS CIG CAR DU ‘JUG PA LTA BUR MNGON PA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LA

Now at this point the autocommentary notes how “The way that consciousness works is similar to the way in which an arrow strikes a stack of lotus petals; although in actuality the point is passing through the petals one by one, it appears as though they are all being penetrated at the same moment.”


[2387]
‘GREL BSHAD KYIS, GAR MKHAN GYI KHANG PAR ZHUGS PA NA GAR MKHAN GYI GDONG DANG GLU LA SOGS PA YUL LNGA CIG CAR DU ‘DZIN PA’I RNAM SHES LNGA CIG CAR DU SHES PA MI SKYE ZHES PA’I LAN DU,

And the Explanation describes how, when we enter the home of an actor, it’s not the case that there arises in our mind a perception of five different states of consciousness, all at the same moment—where we perceive, altogether, five different objects of the actor’s face; their song; and so on.


[2388]
YUL LNGA ‘DZIN PA’I RNAM SHES RNAMS RIM GYIS ‘BYUNG YANG ‘JUG PA MYUR BAS CIG CAR DU SKYE BAR MNGON PA YIN NO, ZHES ‘CHAD PA NI

And so you can give the explanation that the states of consciousness that hold to the five different sense objects here occur one after the other; but because it is happening so quickly, it appears to us as though they are all occurring simultaneously.


[2389]
SHIN TU MI RIGS TE, RANG RIG SGRUB PA’I MDO SDE PA DANG SEMS TZAM PAS NI SEMS CAN RNAMS NI RNAM PAR SHES PA’I RGYUD RE RE BA’O,

And yet this would be wrong in the extreme, for the Sutrists and members of the Mind Only who seek to prove the existence of apperception would say that living beings have flows of consciousness that are discrete from one another.


[2390]
ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON RNAM ‘GREL LAS,
,DE RNAMS RIGS MTHUN PA NYID LAS,
,NUS PA NGES PAR ‘GYUR BA YIN,

The point here is described in A Commentary on Accurate Perception with the lines,

The potential they possess
Is certain, from the fact that
They are of the same type.


[2391]
ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR RNAM SHES RIGS MTHUN CIG CAR DU GANG ZAG GCIG LA MI SKYE BA LA ‘DOD KYI, RIGS MI MTHUN GYI RNAM SHES CIG CAR DU MI SKYE BA LA ‘DOD PA GTAN MIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

What this is saying is that we assert that multiple states of consciousness of one particular type cannot arise within a single person; but this is not at all a denial that different types of consciousness can arise within a single person at the same time.


[2392]
BOD MANG POS ZA ‘OG LA LTA BA’I TSE DKAR DMAR SOGS ‘DZIN PA’I SHES PA DU MA CIG CAR SKYE BA MA YIN NAM ZHES PA’I LAN DU, SHES PA DE RNAMS RIM GYIS ‘BYUNG YANG CIG CAR DU SKYE BAR SNANG BA YIN NO ZHES ZER BAS NI,

Many thinkers in Tibet have given the following answer to the question, “But isn’t it the case that many states of consciousness holding to different colors of white & red and so forth, arise altogether at the same time when we look at a length of multicolored silk?”  They would make the claim that these states of awareness come up on after the other, but only appear to be happening at the same time.


[2393]
RNAM PAR SHES PA’I RGYUD RE RE BA’O ZHES GSUNGS PA’I DON GTZO BO’I RNAM SHES RIGS MTHUN LA DGONGS PA YANG MA SHES SHING, MIG GI RNAM SHES GCIG GIS KHA DOG MI ‘DRA BA DU MA ‘DZIN PA [f. 174b] YANG MA SHES PAR, KHRA BO ‘DZIN PA’I MIG SHES KYANG MA RTOGS PAR SNANG NGO,,

Then they say this, it’s an indication that they fail to understand that statements about how consciousness represents a separate flow are meant to refer to the continuity of the single type, of primary consciousness.  The fact is that a single visual awareness does hold multiple, differing colors; but they fail to understand this—and it would further seem the case that they have not realized how this visual consciousness can perceive a checkered pattern.


[2394]
DES NA RNAM SHES RIGS MTHUN CIG CAR DU SKYE BAR BRTZAD PA’I LAN DU, DE RNAMS ‘JUG PA MYUR BAS RIM GYIS SKYE YANG CIG CAR DU SKYE BAR MNGON ZHES ‘CHAD DGOS PA ‘DRA BA ZHIG SNANG YANG

As such, it would appear that such people have to give the following response to the challenge of asking how it is that specific sustained flows of awareness can arise.  That is, they would have to make explanations like saying that the way these awarenesses engage is very quick, and so—even though they are arising one after the other—it appears as though they are coming up all together.


[2395]
RANG RIG SGRUB MKHAN DE GNYIS KYIS ‘JUG PA MYUR BA CIG CAR DU ‘KHRUL BA’I RGYU YIN PA YANG RNAM ‘GREL DU BKAG PAS NA, GZHUNG ‘DI DE GNYIS KYI LUGS SU ‘JOG DKA’ BAR SNANG STE

As for these two groups though who are trying to establish the existence of apperception, the fact is that the Commentary on Accurate Perception denies this idea about the speed of their engagement being the cause of mistaking these awarenesses as being simultaneous.  As such, it would seem that in the system of these two groups there is some difficulty in establishing the meaning of this classical source.


[2396]
PHAL CHER RGYA DPE MA DAG PA’I SKYON YIN NAM ‘ON KYANG BLO GROS DANG LDAN PA RNAMS KYIS DPYAD PAR BYA’O,,

It seems most likely to me that the difficulty here stems from problems with the original Sanskrit manuscripts being used; but all this is a point that those with sharper intelligence than my own should investigate further.


[2397]
DE’I PHYIR THUG PA MED PA’I DANG, YUL GZHAN MI GCOD PA’I SKYON SPANG BA’I PHYIR, GDON MI ZA BAR RANG RIG KHAS BLANG DGOS SO,,

And so to avoid those problems of things going into an endless progression; or of an inaibility to discern other objects, these thinkers must beyond any doubt accept the concept of apperception.


[2398]
DE’I PHYIR YUL DANG YUL CAN GNYIS KA DRAN PA PHYIS SKYES PA LAS, SNGAR SNGON PO MTHONG BA’I TSE YUL MYONG BA DANG YUL CAN MYONG BA YOD PAR DPOG PAR BYED DO,,

As such, we have to deduce the existence of both an experience of the object, and an experience of the subject, during an earlier incidence of seeing blue, when later on there has arisen a memory of both the object and the subject involved.


[2399]
DE LTAR RANG MYONG BA’I RANG RIG YOD NA YANG GZHAN DBANG YOD PAR RANG RIG DES ‘GRUB PAS, ‘DI NI YOD PAR GANG GIS SHES PAR ‘GYUR, ZHES DBU MA PAS DRIS PA LA LAN ‘DI NYE BAR BSTAN PA YIN NO, ZHES SMRA’O,,

And so what’s being said in this entire section is the following.  Thus—given that there exists a state of apperception which can experience itself—then this apperception can be used to establish the existence of dominated entities; and this is the reply which is presented in response to the question of those of the Middle Way school when they said, “What is it that allows you to say that this state of mind exists?”



Assumptions from recollection

[2400]
GNYIS PA LA GSUM, GZHAN LUGS DGAG PA DNGOS, RANG LUGS LA RANG RIG MED KYANG DRAN PA SKYE BA’I TSUL, DE LTAR BKAG PA LA RTZOD PA SPANG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Now that we have stated the position that others take here, we can continue on to the second step here: our actual denial of that position.  We will cover this point in three sections: the denial of the others’ position itself; an explanation of how—according to our own system—a memory can still arise, even in the absence of apperception; and responding to attempted rebuttal of this explanation.  Here is the first of these.


	[2401]
[VI.73b]
,GAL TE PHYI DUS DRAN PA LAS ‘GRUB NA,
,MA GRUB BSGRUB PAR BYA PHYIR BRJOD PA YI,
,MA GRUB ‘DI NI SGRUB PAR BYED PA MIN,

		Suppose we were
		To establish it
		From recollection
		At a later time.

		They are
		Bringing it up
		In order to substantiate
		
		That which has not yet
		Been established.

		The fact that this
		Does not exist
		Is not something
		Which serves to establish it.


[2402]
GAL TE RDZAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I DBANG DU BYAS NAS PHYIS KYI DUS KYI DRAN PA LAS, DRAN YUL GYI SHES PA SNGA MA RANG RIG PAR ‘GRUB NA, PHYIR RGOL LA RANG RIG MA GRUB PA BSGRUB PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU, BRJOD [f. 175a] PA YI DRAN PA RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR MA GRUB PA ‘DI NI, RANG RIG SGRUB PAR BYED PA MIN TE, SGRA MI RTAG PAR SGRUB PA LA MIG GI GZUNG BYA BZHIN NO,,

Suppose then that—with reference to a substance which existed by definition—we were to establish the existence of a previous case of apperception, an awareness of the original object we are now remembering, from the presence of a recollection at a later time.  Here, the opponent in the debate is bringing up a state of recollection in order to substantiate the existence of an apperception which has not yet been established.  And yet the fact that this recollection does not exist through any nature of its own is not something which serves to establish the apperception here; it would be like saying that sound is a changing thing because it is an object which the eye perceives.


[2403]
‘ON TE ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD KYI DBANG DU YIN NA NI, RANG RIG PA’I ‘BRAS BU’I DRAN PA MED DO,,

But if you are speaking from the point of view of the parlance of the world, we would say that recollection as a result of apperception doesn’t even exist.


[2404]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, GAL TE ‘DIR MI GRUB NA DU BA DE’I ‘BRAS BUR SHES PAR ‘GYUR BA BZHIN DU, RANG RIG GRUB NA DE LAS DRAN PA ‘BYUNG BA’I ‘BREL PA GRUB NA, DRAN PA LAS RANG RIG YOD PAR NGES PAR ‘GYUR BA ZHIG NA, RANG RIG DE DA DUNG DU YANG PHYIR RGOL LA MA GRUB PAS, RANG RIG GI ‘BRAS BU RANG RIG MED PAR MI ‘BYUNG BA’I DRAN PA GA LA YOD,

And why is that?  If the point were not made here, then it would be the same as when we deduce the presence of something from its result, of smoke.  If establishing apperception allows us establish a connection to a recollection that occurs from it, then we could confirm the existence of apperception from recollection; but in that case apperception would stil not have been confirmed to the opponent.  And as such, how could we ever say that there was a recollection which were a result of apperception, and which could never occur without apperception?


[2405]
‘BREL PA MED PAR MI ‘GRUB PA’I DPE NI, CHU TZAM DANG ME TZAM MTHONG BA LAS NOR BU CHU SHEL DANG ME SHEL DPOG PA NI MA YIN TE, DE GNYIS MED PAR YANG CHAR LA SOGS PA DANG, GTZUB SHING GTZUB PA SOGS LAS CHU DANG ME DAG ‘BYUNG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

What are some examples of a failure to occur without a connection?  We cannot for example deduce the presence of the precious stones water crystal or fire crystal from seeing only water, or only fire.  This is because water and fire can also occur in the absence of these minerals; for example, from rain or the like, or from “fire sticks” that are rubbed together to help start a fire.


[2406]
DE BZHIN DU ‘DIR YANG RANG RIG MED PAR DRAN PA JI LTAR ‘BYUNG BA NI ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

In the same way, here too we will be covering ways in which recollection can occur, even without apperception.


[2407]
DGAG PA ‘DI LA LAN DU DRAN PA DANG RANG RIG MED {%ME} DU BZHIN DU RGYU ‘BRAS SU BSGRUBS PA’I SGO NAS, DRAN PAS RANG RIG DPOG PA MIN GYI, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR DRAN PAS SNGAR GYI SHES PA LA MYONG BA YOD PAR DPOG LA,

For a reply to this denial, we can say that when you try to use a proof based on recollection and apperception being cause and effect in the way that fire and smoke are, it’s not the case that we can deduce apperception from recollection; rather, as we explained before, recollection helps us deduce the fact that the mind had a previous experience.


[2408]
DE LA RANG GIS DANG GZHAN GYIS MYONG BA GNYIS SU BCAD NAS BKAG PA NA, RANG GIS RANG MYONG BA ‘GRUB BO ZHES SMRA MOD KYANG SHES PAS RIG PA LA MDO SDE PA DANG SEMS TZAM PAS BZHAG PA DE GNYIS SU KHA TSON MA CHOD PA’I PHYIR TE,

Suppose we were to attempt making the denial here by eliminating both the possibility that the mind was experienced by itself, and by something else.  Now you could say that the determination was made by the mind’s knowing itself, but in fact when the Sutrists and the Mind Only present how it is that awareness knows things, they would not make the division into those two possibilities.


[2409]
MAR MES RANG GIS [f. 175b] RANG GSAL BAR MI BYED KYANG, DE LA GSAL BA MI LDOG PA BZHIN DU, SHES PAS PHYOGS SNGA MAS ‘DOD PA LTAR DU RANG GIS RANG MYONG BAR MI BYED KYANG DE LA MYONG BA TZAM MI LDOG PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Now a butter lamp does not illuminate itself by itself; nonetheless, neither can we say that it prevents this illumination.  Similarly, it is not the case that awareness—as the other side here has presented it—acts to experience itself, by itself.  This fact though does not prevent us from saying that it does experience things.


[2410]
GAL TE MAR MES RANG GIS RANG GSAL BAR BYED DO ZHE NA,

And suppose that you say that a butter lamp does illuminate itself, by itself.


[2411]
DE LTA NA MUN PAS RANG GIS RANG SGRIB PAR ‘GYUR LA, DE ‘DOD NA MUN KHUNG DU BUM PA MI MTHONG BA BZHIN DU, MUN PA YANG MI MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

In that case then, darkness would also obscure itself, by itself.  And if you agree to that, then you’d have to say that in a dark room we would not be able to see the darkness; just as in that same place we are unable to see a vase that is standing there.


[2412]
DE LTAR YANG RTZA SHE LAS,
,MAR ME RANG DANG GZHAN GYI DNGOS,
,GAL TE SNANG BAR BYED GYUR NA,
,MUN PA’ANG RANG DANG GZHAN GYI DNGOS,
,SGRIB PAR ‘GYUR BAR THE TSOM MED,
CES GSUNGS PA LTAR RO,,

As Wisdom puts it,

Suppose that a butter lamp
Acted to illuminate
Both itself and other things.

Beyond any doubt then
Darkness would as well
Obscure both itself
And other things too.


	[2413]
[VI.74]
Kāmaṃ sva saṃvedana siddhir astu
smartuḥ smṛter naiva tathāpi yuktā,
Ajñāna santāna javat paratvād
dhetur viśeṣān api caiṣa hanyāt.

,RANG RIG PA NI GRUB LA RAG MOD KYI,
,DE LTA’ANG DRAN PA’I DRAN PA RIGS MIN TE,
,GZHAN PHYIR MA SHES RGYUD LA SKYES PA BZHIN,
,GTAN TSIGS ‘DIS NI KHYAD PAR DAG KYANG ‘JOMS,

	In the end, your proofs
	Are going to rely upon
	It knowing itself;

	But it is still
	Not logical
	For recollection
	To recall,

	Because they are
	Other than each other.

	It’s the same as
	What could have arisen
	In the mindstream of one
	Who has not known;

	That logical statement
	Would also obviate details.


[2414]
CI STE DE LTAR RNAM PAR DPYOD PA BTANG NAS KYANG, SHES PAS RANG GI BDAG NYID RIG PA DANG, YUL RIG PAR BYED PA NI GRUB LA RAG MOD KYI STE GRUB TU CHUG KYANG, DRAN PA’I SHES PAS YUL DANG YUL CAN DE DAG DRAN PA NI RIGS PA MIN TE, PHYIS KYI DRAN SHES DANG SNGAR GYI YUL MYONG GI SHES PA GNYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID DU KHYED KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

You may undertake some different forms of examination, but in the end your proofs are going to rely upon the idea of a state of mind knowing itself—its own self—and also knowing the particular object.  But still it is not logical to say that the state of mind of recollection can recall both the subject and the object involved.  And this is simply because you have accepted the idea that both the later recollecting state of mind and the earlier awareness which perceived the object are objects that are other than each other and which exist through some nature of their own.


[2415]
‘DI LTAR BYAMS PA’I SHES PA’I RANG RIG PA DANG YUL MYONG BA NI, SNGAR NYAMS SU MA MYONG BAS NYER SBAS KYI SHES PAS DRAN PA MA YIN PA

For example we can take the apperception and the experience of the object that occur with the state of mind possessed by an individual named John.  These were not previously experienced by another individual by the name of Mary, and so cannot be something that her mind recollects.


[2416]
DE BZHIN DU, SNGAR MA SHES PA STE MA MYONG BA’I RGYUD LA SKYES PA BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN YIN PA’I PHYIR NA, RANG GI RGYUD DU GTOGS PA’I RNAM PAR SHES PA DUS PHYIS ‘BYUNG BAS KYANG SHES PA DANG DON DAG NYAMS SU MA MYONG BA’I PHYIR DRAN PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

The case here is the same as with what could have arisen in the mindstream of a person who has not known or had a certain experience.  Because this person constitutes an “other” who exists through their own nature, even if a state of awareness taken in by their mindstream were to occur later on, there would be no recollection here, since they had not undergone an experience of the state of mind and corresponding object.


[2417]
CI STE RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA RNAMS LA RGYU DANG ‘BRAS BU’I DNGOS [f. 176a] PO GNAS PA’I PHYIR DRAN PA YOD PAR ‘GYUR RO SNYAM DU SEMS NA, 

And suppose you think to yourself the following:

Those that are though included into a single mindstream exist as entities which are cause and effect; as such, recollection would then be there.


[2418]
DE YANG MI RIGS TE GANG GI PHYIR RANG MTSAN GYIS GZHAN YIN PA’I PHYIR ZHES GTAN TSIGS ‘DIS NI, RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA DANG RGYU ‘BRAS LA SOGS PA’I KHYAD PAR DE DAG KYANG NYE BAR ‘JOMS PAR BYED DE, ‘DI NI SNGAR BYAMS PA NYER SBAS LA BRTEN ZHES PA’I SKABS SU RGYAS PAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,

And so let’s consider a logical statement which states that this is also illogical, since the “other” here is one that exists by definition.  That would also obviate details such as these things being included into a single stream of awareness, or there being a connection of cause & effect.  We have already covered this in detail, back where we spoke about things that were relative either to John or to Mary.



Recollection according to
the autocommentary

[2419]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GZHUNG ‘DI NYID NAS BSHAD PA’I LUGS DANG, GZHUNG GZHAN NAS BSHAD PA’I LUGS SO, ,DANG PO NI,

This brings us to our second section from before: an explanation of how—according to our own system—a recollection can still arise, even in the absence of apperception.  Here first we will give the presentation on this topic as it is made in the current text; and then review how it is made in other classical texts.  Here is the first.


	[2420]
[VI.75]
Yenānubhūto viṣayas tato’sya
smartuḥ paratvaṃ na hi me’sti yasmāt,
Tato mayā dṛṣṭam iti smṛtiḥ syād
eṣā ca loka vyavahāranītiḥ.

,GANG PHYIR GANG GIS YUL MYONG GYUR DE LAS,
,DRAN PA ‘DI GZHAN NGA LA YOD MIN PA,
,DE PHYIR NGA YIS MTHONG SNYAM DRAN ‘GYUR TE,
,’DI YANG ‘JIG RTEN THA SNYAD TSUL LUGS YIN,

		First of all, in ours
		That recollection of
		Of having undergone
		An experience

		Could never be
		Something other.

		For this reason,
		It will happen
		That there will be
		A recollection

		Where we say to ourselves,
		“I have seen this.”

This too is the way
Of the world;
The way that the world
Speaks of things.


[2421]
GAL TE RANG RIG MI ‘DOD PA KHYOD KYI LTAR NA DRAN PA SKYE LUGS JI LTAR YIN ZHE NA,

Suppose now that one were to come with the following question: “Well, if you refuse to accept the idea of apperception, then just how is it—according to your view—that we can have a recollection of something?”


[2422]
GANG GI PHYIR SNGAR GYI SHES PA GANG GIS YUL MYONG BAR GYUR PA’I SHES PA DE LAS DRAN PA’I SHES PA ‘DI RANG MTSAN GYIS GZHAN DU GYUR PA NGA’I LUGS LA JI LTAR YOD PA MIN PA DE LTAR NI BSHAD ZIN LA,

First of all, we have already explained how, in our system, that state of mind or recollection which comes from a state of mind—a previous state of mind—which underwent an experience of a particular object could never be something that existed as something “other” which existed by definition.


[2423]
SA MYUG LTA BU’I NYER LEN GYI RGYU ‘BRAS LA RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘DZIN PA, ‘JIG RTEN GYI BLO RANG DGA’ BA LA MED PA YANG SNGAR BSHAD ZIN PAS SNGAR GYI YUL MYONG DANG PHYIS KYI DRAN PA’I RGYU ‘BRAS LA YANG, ‘JIG RTEN PA’I BLO LHAN SKYES LA RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘DZIN PA MED DO,,

There is not even any normal state of mind of a person in the everyday world which—with regard to cause & effect in the sense of a material cause such as a seed for a plant producing a sprout—would hold to the idea that these things were other than each other, by definition.  Further, as we have already explained, there is no tendency for the natural state of mind of people in the world to hold to things as being other than each other by definition, in the case of the cause & effect represented by the earlier experience of an object and a later recollection.


[2424]
DE MED PA TZAM DU MA ZAD SNGAR SNGO ‘DZIN GYIS MTHONG BA’I YUL PHYIS DRAN PA NA ‘DI NGAS SNGAR YANG MTHONG NGO ZHES THA SNYAD BYED DO,,

Not only is there no such thing, but people further apply a certain terminology to this type of thing, saying “I saw that before” when referring to an object seen by a perception of blue earlier, and then remembering that object later on.


[2425]
DE’I PHYIR MYONG DRAN GNYIS DANG DE’I DUS KYI YUL GNYIS RANG MTSAN GYIS THA SNYAD DU ‘DZIN PA ‘JIG RTEN PA RANG DGA’ BA LA MED PAR GSAL TE, DE LTA MA YIN NA RGYUD [f. 176b] GZHAN GYI MYONG BA LA YANG RANG GI DRAN PA SKYE BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As such, it is clear that it simply does not happen with normal people of the world that they consider both an original experience and a later recollection of it—along with the objects involved in each case—and think of them as existing nominally, by definition.  If this were not the way it is, then we ourselves could suddenly undergo a recollection of something that had been experienced by someone else.


[2426]
DE’I PHYIR SNGAR YUL NYAMS MYONG GI SHES PAS MYONG BA DANG BCAD PA DE, PHYIS DE DRAN PA’I SHES PAS MA MYONG BA DANG MA BCAD PA MIN PAS, ‘DI SNGAR YANG NGA YIS MTHONG SNYAM DU DRAN PA SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE,

For this reason, it is not the case that a state of mind which has undergone the experience of a certain object previously has this experience, and makes this discernment; and then when a later recollection of this occurs, it cannot experience or discern that.  As such, it will happen here that there will come to arise a recollection where we say to ourselves, “I have seen this thing before as well.”


[2427]
‘DI YANG ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD KYI TSUL GYI LUGS YIN GYI, THA SNYAD BTAGS PA TZAM GYIS MA TSIM PAR BTAGS DON ‘TSOL BA’I TSUL GYIS DPYAD NAS ‘JOG PAR NI MI BYA STE, BTAGS DON BTZAL NA MI RNYED BA’I BRDZUN BA’I DON CAN NYID KYI ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This too is the way of the world; the way that the world speaks of things.  It is not, rather, the case that those of the world refuse to be satisfied with the way in which things are simply referred to with terms, and then feel that they need to engage in some close examination accomplished by seeking out just what it is that the terms refer to.  And that’s because the very meaning—in the parlance of the world—of falsity is where you seek out what something refers to and find that it is missing.


[2428]
RANG ‘GREL LAS RDZAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I RANG RIG DANG DRAN PA BKAG PA’I ‘OG TU, ‘ON TE ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD KYI DBANG DU YIN NA NI, DE LTA NA YANG RANG RIG PA’I RGYU CAN GYI DRAN PA MI SRID PA NYID DO,

Subsequent to denying both apperception and recollection that could exist substantially—by definition—the autocommentary states, “But even if you were to restrict yourself to the terminology of the everyday world, still a recollection that had, as its cause, apperception would be completely impossible.”


[2429]
ZHES DON DAM DU MA ZAD THA SNYAD DU YANG RANG RIG BKAG LA, RANG RIG PA MED PAR DRAN PA JI LTAR ‘BYUNG BA DE LTAR STON PAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES RANG RIG MED KYANG MYONG BA LAS DRAN PA SKYE TSUL SKABS ‘DIR STON PAR GSUNGS SO,,

What this is saying is that apperception is denied not only in an ultimate sense, but in a nominal sense as well: “We will demonstrate thus how recollection occurs even without apperception.”  That is, they are saying that here in this section of the text, it will be explained how—even without apperception—we can have a recollection of an experience.


[2430]
DE LA NGAS MTHONG SNYAM DU DRAN PA NI YUL CAN DRAN PA DANG, SNGON PO LA SOGS PA ‘DI MTHONG SNYAM DU DRAN PA NI YUL DRAN PA’O,,

And so when we have a recollection where we say “I was seeing,” we are having a recollection of the subject in the perception; and when we think to ourselves “I saw a patch of blue” or whatever it may be, and have this recollection, it is a recollection of the object in the perception.


[2431]
DE YANG SNGAR NGA RANG GIS MTHONG BA DE NYID NGA RANG GIS DRAN SNYAM PA NI DRAN TSUL KHYAD PAR BA YIN LA, DRAN PA LA DE BYUNG NA SNGAR BYAMS PA LTA BU MTHONG BA’I YUL CAN SHES PA DE KHO RANG GIS KHO RANG MYONG BAR GSAL TE, DRAN PA NI MYONG BA JI LTA BA’I RJES SU BYED PA’I PHYIR RO SNYAM DU BSAMS SO,,

And when we say to ourselves, “I saw this previously, I remember that very thing,” this is a particular detail of recollection.  When this kind of thing happens in a recollection, we can say that it is becoming clear to someone like John that they must had a subject state of mind that was holding some object that they saw, and that they had some experience of themselves here.  That is, we always think to ourselves that a recollection is something that followed upon a certain original experience.


[2432]
RANG LUGS NI ‘JIG RTEN NA [f. 177a] SNANG BA’I DRAN TSUL DE KHAS LEN KYANG, DRAN TSUL DE LTAR ‘ONG BA DE SNGAR GYI YUL MYONG BA’I SHES PA DE KHO RANG GIS KHO RANG RIG PA’I DBANG GIS BYUNG BA MIN GYI, SNGAR GYI MYONG BAS BCAD PA DE NYID DRAN PAS KYANG GCOD PA’I YUL GCIG PA’I DBANG GIS BYAMS BA ‘DI SNGAR YANG NGAS MTHONG ZHES DRAN PA SKYE’O,,

Our own position says first of all that we do accept this description of how recollection occurs to us, as it is described in the everyday world.  Nonetheless, what we say is that for a recollection to occur in the way it’s described here, it is not something that could have occurred through the power of some kind of apperception, where the previous experience of the object somehow knew itself by itself.  Rather, what happens is that there has been the discernment of an object by a previous experience, and then we recollect that; and so it is due to the single object discerned that there can arise in John a recollection where he says to himself, “I saw this previously as well.”


[2433]
DES NA NGA RANG GIS MTHONG BA NGA RANG GIS DRAN ZHES PA LTA BU’I THA SNYAD NI RANG GIS KYANG KHAS LEN LA, DE KHAS BLANGS KYANG BKAG PA’I RANG RIG DANG MI ‘DRA BA YANG ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS SHES PAR BYA’O,,

As such, we can say that we also accept the kind of expression where we say to ourselves, “I myself recall what I myself saw”; but even accepting that, we need to realize that what we depend upon for this to happen is something other than the apperception which we have denied.


[2434]
GZHAN GYI LUGS KYIS MYONG DRAN DANG DE’I DUS KYI YUL GNYIS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN DU ‘JOG PAS, MYONG DRAN GNYIS YUL GCIG PA DANG DE GNYIS RGYUD GCIG TU ‘DOD MOS KYANG DER ‘JOG MI NUS PA NI SNGAR MANG DU BSHAD ZIN TO,,

The other party in the debate here posits things which are other than each other which also exist be definition, with both the original experience and the recollection; as well as with the two objects of each of these, in their own time.  And admittedly one may assert that the two of the experience and the recollection share the same object; and that the pair constitute part of a single stream of awareness; but we have gone in to some great detail already to show how one might fail to establish this.


[2435]
BYAMS PA ‘DI ZHES ZER YANG DE SKAD SMRA DUS KYI DUS DANG, DE’I DUS SU GANG NA GNAS PA’I YUL GYIS KHYAD PAR DU BYAS PA’I BYAMS PA SNGAR MTHONG SNYAM DU MI ‘DZIN PAR, BYAMS PA TZAM LA ‘DZIN PA NI RANG GI BLO LA BLTAS PAS SHES SO,,

We can say the name “John” without specifically holding to John in terms of a specific point in time—the time when we are speaking of him, or a distinction of a certain time in which the the object involved is existing, when we think of John that we saw earlier on.  Rather, we can just be considering John in general, as any of us knows by observing how our own thoughts work.



Recollection according to
other classics

[2436]
GNYIS PA NI,

With this we have reached our second step from above: a review of how recollection can still arise, even without apperception, as this presentation is made in classical texts other than the autocommentary.


[2437]
RANG RIG MED PAR DRAN PA SKYE TSUL GYI LUGS CHEN PO GNYIS YOD PA’I DPAL LDAN ZHI BA LHA’I LUGS NI, SPYOD ‘JUG LAS, GAL TE RANG RIG YOD MIN NA, ,RNAM SHES DRAN PAR JI LTAR ‘GYUR, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR RO,,

Now there are two great classical presentations of how recollection can arise, even in the absence of apperception.  We can point first to the system of the glorious Shantideva, which is broached as follows in A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life:

How can we recollect
A state of mind,

In the case that there exists
No apperception?


[2438]
‘DI’I PHYOGS SNGA MA’I LUGS NI SNGAR RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA NYID YIN NO,,

The position here of the other party is something that we have most certainly covered already, in some detail.


[2439]
PHYOGS SNGA MA’I THAL BA DANG BZLOG PA GNYIS KA LA’ANG KHYAB PA MED PA’I LAN ‘DEBS [f. 177b] PAS, RANG RIG MED KYANG DRAN PA SKYE TSUL JI LTAR YIN ZHE NA,

And so one may question us here, saying—

You have answered “that is not necessarily the case” to both the statement of necessity of the other party here, and to the position it implies.  How then, according to you, is it that a recollection can arise even in the absence of apperception?


[2440]
‘DZIN PA’I SHES PA LAS GZHAN GZUNG BYA’I DNGOS PO YUL DU GYUR PA BLOS MYONG BA NA, YUL MYONG BA’I SHES PA LAS RNAM SHES YUL CAN DRAN PA ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

When the mind experiences that which serves as the object—the entity which is perceived, as distinct from the perceiving awareness—we recollect the subject state of mind from the state of mind that experienced the object.


[2441]
GAL TE YUL GZHAN MYONG BA LAS YUL CAN DRAN PA SKYE BA NI RIGS PA MA YIN TE, HA CANG THAL BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

And suppose to this someone were to reply—

But saying that a recollection of a subject state of mind were to arise from the experience of some other object doesn’t seem logical; it would be excessive to think that.


[2442]
NYES PA MED DE YUL MYONG BA LAS YUL CAN DRAN PA SKYE BA NA, SHES PA SPANGS NAS DRAN PA MIN GYI, SNGAR GZUGS ‘DI MTHONG NGO ZHES YUL YUL CAN GNYIS ‘BREL BA LAS TE ‘BREL BAR DRAN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And yet there’s no problem here.  When a recollection arises of a subject state of mind, from an experience of the object involved, it’s not as if the recollection occurs by releasing the state of mind.  What happens is that our recollection occurs through a relationship: when you say, “Earlier on, I saw this particular visible object,” it happens through a connection between the object and the subject state of mind.


[2443]
DPER NA DGUN GYI DUS SU BYI BAS LUS LA RMUGS PA NA, BYI DUG ZHUGS YOD KYANG RMUGS PA MYONG GI DUG MA MYONG NGO,,

Suppose, for example, a rat bites the body of a hibernating bear, during the wintertime—and some poison enters the bloodstream from the bite.  This animal might experience the bite, but they may not experience the poison.


[2444]
DE LAS DUS PHYIS ‘BRUG GI SGRA THOS PA NA RMUGS PA’I TSE DUG ZHUGS PAR ‘DUG SNYAM DU DRAN KYANG, SNGAR GYI TSE DUG MA MYONG BA BZHIN NO,,

Some time later on, the bear hears the sound of thunder and awakens, and may have a memory in which they think to themselves, “That poison must have entered by body while I was hibernating.”  But they do not experience the poison of the previous time.


[2445]
DE LA BYI BAS RMUGS PA NI SNGO ‘DZIN GYIS YUL MYONG BA BZHIN NO,,

Being bitten by the rat is analogous to the experience of its object, by the perception of a patch of blue.


[2446]
RMUGS PA DANG DUS GCIG TU DUG ZHUGS PA NI YUL BZUNG BA DANG DUS GCIG TU YOD PA’I YUL CAN GYI MYONG BA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

The infection of the body by the poison which occurred simultaneous to the original bite is analogous to the experience of the subject state of mind that existed at the same time as when the object was perceived.


[2447]
DE’I TSE YUL CAN RANG GIS RANG MA MYONG BA NI, RMUGS PA’I TSE DUG MA MYONG BA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

The fact that—at that time—the subject state of mind did not experience itself by itself is analogous to the way in which the poison was not experienced, at the time of the bite.


[2448]
PHYIS RMUGS PA DRAN PA NI YUL MYONG BA DRAN PA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

Recollecting the bite later on is analogous to recollecting the original object.


[2449]
YUL MYONG DRAN PA NYID KYIS SNGAR GYI YUL CAN KHO RANG GIS KHO RANG MA MYONG YANG DRAN PA NI, RMUGS PA DRAN PA NYID KYI MTHUS SNGAR ZHUGS PA’I DUG MA MYONG BA DRAN PA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

And so a recollection occurs through the recollection of the experience of the object, even though the previous subject state of mind did not experience itself by itself.  This is analogous to the way in which—due to the single recollection of the hibernation—one recalls what was not experienced when the poison entered the body earlier on.


[2450]
‘DI NI RANG RIG MED PAR DRAN PA SKYE BA’I RIGS PA MKHAS PA’I DBANG POS MDZAD PA PHUL DU BYUNG BA ZHIG SNANG STE, SPYOD ‘JUG GI [f. 178a] BSHAD PA BYED PA RNAMS KYIS JI BZHIN DU MTHON PA ‘DRA’O,,

This reasoning for how recollection occurs even without apperception would appear to be one of the greatest achievements of this lord of all masters; and it seems to me that the commentators on A Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life have drawn out this point quite properly.


[2451]
‘DI NI SPYIR PHYIS KYI RNAM SHES KYI DRAN PA MI ‘THAD PAR THAL, SNGAR GYI RNAM SHES DES RANG GIS RANG MA MYONG BA’I PHYIR, ZHES PA LA KHYAB MA GRUB KYI LAN BTAB PA YIN PAS, SPYOD ‘JUG GI DGONGS PA NI THA SNYAD DU RANG RIG ‘GOG PA MIN ZHES PA NI RGYAL SRAS CHEN PO’I BZHED PA GTAN MIN NO,,

Generally speaking, this reasoning is a reply of “that’s not necessarily the case” to the argument that it must be incorrect to say that we have a later recollection of a state of mind, since earlier on this state of mind did not experience itself by itself.  As such, it is not at all the position of his great child of the Victors to say that it was not the intent of The Guide to deny apperception, in a nominal sense.



Rejecting rebuttal about
direct accurate perception

[2452]
GSUM PA LA GNYIS, MNGON SUM GYI TSAD MA GZHAN DANG RJES DPAG LA RTZOD PA SPANG BA DANG, YID SHES GZHAN GYI RTZOD SPANG NGO, ,DANG PO NI,

This brings us to our third section from before, which is responding to attempted rebuttal of our explanation of how a memory can still arise, even in the absence of apperception.  Here we proceed in two steps: rejecting rebuttal about another direct, accurate perception, and then the same for a deductive form of the same; followed by rejecting rebuttal concerning another consciousness of the thoughts.


[2453]
‘O NA RANG LUGS LA SNGO ‘DZIN SOGS KYI SHES PA THAMS CAD YOD PAR ‘DOD DGOS LA DE LTA NA, ‘DI YI YOD PA GANG GIS SHES PAR ‘GYUR, ,MA GZUNG BAR YANG YOD CES BYAR MI RUNG, ZHES GZHAN LA SMRAS PA LTAR RANG LA YANG SKYON DU ‘GYUR TE, SNGO ‘DZIN DE RANG GIS YOD PAR SHES NA RANG RIG KHAS BLANG DGOS LA, SHES PA DON GZHAN GYIS RIG PA YANG MI ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

One may come then with the following objection—

Well now, even in your own system, you would have to agree that all of these states of mind do actually exist—the perception of a patch of blue, and so on.  And the same criticism that you have leveled at others applies to you yourselves as well: “How do you know that this kind of perception exists?  You can’t just say that there are also things here that cannot be perceived.”  That is, if you respond that the perception of the blue itself perceives that it itself exists, then you would have to accept the idea of apperception.  And it would be incorrect to say that it was perceived by a perception that was something different.


[2454]
‘DI NI SHIN TU DKA’ BA’I GNAS SU ‘DUG PAS BSHAD PAR BYA STE, DE NI YUL DANG YUL CAN DRAN TSUL DPER BLANGS TE BSHAD NA RTOGS SLA’O,,

Given that this is such an extremely difficult point, let’s cover it here.  It can be easily understood if we use a metaphor to explain how we can recollect both an object and its subject.


[2455]
DE LA YUL DRAN PA NYID KYIS YUL CAN YANG DRAN PAS, YUL CAN DRAN PA ZUR PA MI DGOS PA BZHIN DU SNGO ‘DZIN LTA BU’I YUL SNGON PO GRUB PA NYID KYIS SNGON PO ‘JAL BYED ‘GRUB KYI, SNGON PO ‘GRUB TSUL LAS GZHAN PA’I SNGON PO ‘JAL BYED ‘GRUB TSUL MI DGOS SO,,

Here we can start by saying that the recollection of an object itself also recalls the original subject state of mind.  As such, there is no need for a different, additional recollection of that subject.  That is, the very establishment of the object—the patch of blue, say, for a perception of blue—establishes the state of mind which took the blue under consideration.  It is not though as if we would require some way of establishing the state of mind which took the blue under consideration which were different from the way we were establishing the blue itself.


[2456]
DE YANG SNGON POS SNGO ‘DZIN LA RANG ‘DRA’I RNAM PA GTAD PA SHAR BA NYID KYIS, SNGON PO ‘GRUB PA NI LUGS GZHAN DANG YANG ‘DRA’O,,

That is, when the blue directs the particular aspect that reflects it towards the perception of the blue, the very manifestation of this perception is sufficient to establish the existence of that blue—this much is similar in other schools of thought as well. 


[2457]
‘ON KYANG MI ‘DRA [f. 178b] BA NI SNGO ‘DZIN DE ‘GRUB PA NA GNYIS SNANG DANG BRAL BA’I ‘DZIN RNAM YAN GAR BA MYONG BA’I RANG RIG GI SGO NAS ‘GRUB PA YIN LA, DE YANG SHES PA THAMS CAD LA ‘DRA BAR LUGS GZHAN DAG ‘DOD LA,

A point on which the presentations diverge here though is where certain other systems would say that—when they establish the existence of the perception of the blue—they must do so by pointing to an apperception which experiences a discrete aspect of perceiving which is devoid of all duality between subject & object.  And they would say that this is the same for all other states of mind.


[2458]
‘DIR NI DBU MA SNYING PO DANG BDEN GNYIS RTZA ‘GREL LAS GSUNGS PA BZHIN DU DE ‘DRA BA’I ‘DZIN RNAM YAN GAR BA MI SRID PAR BZHED PAS, DE MYONG BA’I RANG RIG GIS MI ‘GRUB KYI, SNGON PO GRUB PA NYID KYIS SNGO ‘DZIN DE ‘GRUB STE,

On this, we would ourselves take the same position here as that expressed in Heart of the Middle Way and both the root text and commentary to the Two Realities—which say that it is impossible for there to be any such discrete aspect of perceiving.  As such, we cannot say that there is established any state of apperception which would further establish the subject here; rather, it is simply establishing that the blue itself is present, which establishes the presence of the perception of this blue.


[2459]
DPER NA YUL DRAN PA NYID KYIS YUL CAN DRAN PA YIN GYI, SNGAR YUL CAN KHO RANG GIS KHO RANG GZHAN DAG ‘DOD PA LTAR MYONG BA’I DBANG GIS DRAN PA DE ‘BYUNG BA MIN PA DANG ‘DRA’O,,

For example, the recollection of a particular object is what allows the recollection of the particular subject state of mind involved; the case here is similar to where it is not, as others would have it, that the previous subject state of mind experiences itself by itself, and then this allows the recollection to occur.


[2460]
DE LTAR BYA DGOS PA YANG TSIG GSAL LAS, TSAD MA’I GRANGS ‘JUG PA GZHAL BYA’I GZHAN GYI DBANG YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, GZHAL BYA’I RNAM PA’I RJES SU BYED PA TZAM GYIS RANG GI NGO BO YOD PAR RNYED PA’I TSAD MA DAG GI RANG GI NGO BO RNAM PAR ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR, ZHES GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

The fact that we have to proceed in this manner is clearly expressed as well in A Clarification of the Verses:

The number of accurate perceptions we recognize is determined by a different factor: that is, the number of objects that these perceptions can take under consideration.
