,SA RNAMS SNA TSOGS KUN GZHI STE,
,BDE GSHEGS SNYING PO DGE BA’ANG DE,
,SNYING PO DE LA KUN GZHI’I SGRAS,
,DE BZHIN GSHEGS RNAMS STON PAR MDZAD,
,SNYING PO KUN GZHIR BSGRAGS PA YANG,
,BLO GZHAN {%ZHAN} RNAMS KYIS MI SHES SO,,

In the sutra called The Paradise of the Clouds, we see the following—

The various levels
Are the foundation of all;

And the goodness
Which is the essence
Of Those Gone Thus

Is also a heart
Which the Ones Gone Thus

Have referred to
With the name,
“Foundation of all.”

And this essence
Which is known as the
Foundation of everything

Cannot be known
By any weaker
State of mind.


[2777]
ZHES GSUNGS SHING LANG GSHEGS LAS KYANG, DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA’I SNYING PO KUN GZHI RNAM PAR SHES PAR BSGRAGS PA RNAM PAR SHES PA BDUN DANG BCAS PA ZHES DE GNYIS MING GI RNAM GRANGS SU LAN DU MAR GSUNGS SO{%,}

In A Journey to Langka we see as well mention of “the heart of the Ones Gone Thus; that which is known as the ‘foundation consciousness,’ along with the seven types of consciousness.”  That is, the two are spoken of as synonyms many times.


[2778]
DE YANG DE GNYIS GCIG RTAG LA GCIG MI RTAG PAR BSHAD PAS SGRAS ZIN GYI DON GNYIS GCIG TU BSTAN PA MIN YANG GANG LA BSAMS NAS SNYING PO BSTAN PA’I DON DE NYID LA DGONGS NAS KUN GZHI BSTAN PAS DGONGS PA’I DON LA LTOS TE MING GI RNAM GRANGS YIN PAS DON GCIG GO

But now of these two, one is explained as being unchanging; and the other as being changing.  As such, it is not literally the case that the two connotations are being described as the same.  But if we look at the intention of the terms here, we can say that they are both meant to convey the idea of something essential.  And so when the term “foundation of everything” is used, the two are meant synonymously with reference to their intention—and as such, we can say they refer to the same thing.


[2779]
,DE LTAR NA SNGA MA DRANG DON DU BSTAN PA NYID KYIS PHYI MA YANG DRANG DON DU ‘GRUB BO,,

As such, we can say that—since the former is explained as being meant figuratively—the latter is established as being figurative as well.


[2780]
‘GREL PA LAS, DNGOS PO THAMS CAD KYI RANG BZHIN GYI RJES SU ZHUGS PA’I PHYIR STONG PA NYID KHO NA KUN GZHI RNAM PAR SHES PA’I SGRAS BSTAN PAR RIG PAR BYA’O, ZHES GSUNGS LA,

The autocommentary puts it this way:

You should understand that—since it follows upon the nature of every existing entity—it is emptiness alone which is indicated with the term, “foundation consciousness.”


[2781]
‘DI DANG RTAG BRTAN SOGS KYI SNYING PO DRANG DON DU BSTAN PA GNYIS LEGS PAR BSGRIGS NAS LUNG DES KUN GZHI DRANG DON DU BSTAN PA RTOGS DGOS PAR YOD DO,,

And so you have to set these two forth properly—demonstrating that this and that heart of things which is unchanging and stable were both meant figuratively; you need to come to the realization that this reference is stating that the idea of a foundation to everything is meant figuratively.


[2782]
BLO GROS CHEN PO STONG PA NYID DANG ZHES PA NAS CHUD PA ‘DI ZHES PA’I MJUG THOGS SU MDO NYID LAS, ‘DI NI MDO SDE GANG DU YANG RUNG STE, DE DAG TU DON ‘DI NYID KHONG DU CHUD PAR BYA’O, ZHES GSUNGS PA NI NGO BO NYID DANG PO GNYIS LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS [f. 199a] YOD MED KYI KHYAD PAR PHYE BA DRANG DON DU STON PA’I LUNG NGO,,

The very same sutra continues with the following words, just after that section that starts with “O you of great wisdom, these ideas of emptiness itself…” and continues down to “…inserted into all of their sutras.”  It says, “You should come to understand the meaning in those to be this very same one.”  This then is a reference which is indicating that making the distinction between the first two kinds of essential nature as things that exist by definition or not was itself something that was meant figuratively.



Figurative by logic

[2783]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: showing how logic takes these statements as figurative.


[2784]
DA NI RIGS PAS SEMS TZAM GSUNGS PA DRANG DON DU GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

And so now let us present an explanation which will clarify how we establish—by using logic—the fact that statements about “mind only” were intended only in a figurative way.


[2785]
DE LA BSOD NAMS BSAGS PA RNAMS CHOS NYID LA BDE BLAG TU ‘JUG PA’I THABS SU JI LTAR THOG MAR SBYIN SOGS KYI GTAM SBYOR BAR MDZAD PA DE BZHIN DU ZAB MO’I DON RDZOGS PA THOG MA NAS RTOGS PAR MI NUS PA’I GDUL BYA RNAMS SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS RIM GYIS RANG BZHIN MED PA RTOGS PA LA ‘DZUD PAR MDZAD DO,,

Now accumulating merit is the method for engaging, with ease, in the very nature of things.  Thus it was then that the Buddha first introduced students to descriptions of giving and the like.  In the same way, there are certain disciples who would not be capable, from the very start, of grasping in its entirety the import of that most subtle of all objects.  People like this then the Buddhas lead into the realization of how nothing has any nature of its own, by going step by step.


	[2786]
[VI.96]
Jñeyaṃ vinā jñāna nirākṛtiś ca
labhyā sukheneti vadanti Buddhāḥ,
Jñeyasya pūrvaṃ pratiṣedham eva
jñeye’sati jñāna niṣedha siddheḥ.

,SHES BYA MED NA SHES PA BSAL BA NI,
,BDE BLAG RNYED CES SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS GSUNGS,
,SHES BYA MED NA SHES PA BKAG ‘GRUB PAS,
,DANG POR SHES BYA DGAG PA MDZAD PA YIN,

		The Buddhas
		Have stated that
		If no objects exist,

		And then we
Clear away
The idea of a
State of mind,

		Then people can
		Come to this idea
		More easily.

		If there are no
		Objects of knowledge,

		We can deny
		Any perception,
		And establish that.

		Therefore
		At the beginning
		We focus on denying
		Objects of knowledge.


[2787]
DE ‘DRA BA LA SNGON DU SHES BYA PHYI ROL LA MED PA BSTAN NA, DE’I ‘OG TU SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA GSAL BA NI, BDE BLAG TU RNYED CES SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS GSUNGS SO,,

And so the Buddhas have stated that if, before we take such a step, we teach people that no objects exist on the outside—and only after that clear away the idea of any state of mind which could exist through some nature of its own—then they can come to this idea more easily.


[2788]
DE LTAR NA SHES BYA MED PA STE THOG MAR PHYI ROL BKAG PA YANG BDAG MED RDZOGS PAR RTOGS PA’I THABS YIN PA’I PHYIR,

As such, we can say that teaching people that there exist no objects of knowledge—denying, at the start, that there are any outer objects—was a strategy for helping these individuals to grasp the lack of a self-nature to things, in its entirety.


[2789]
SANGS RGYAS RNAMS KYIS DANG POR SHES BYA PHYI ROL DGAG PAR MDZAD PA KHO NA GSUNGS PA YIN TE SHES BYA MED NA STE PHYI ROL GYI BDAG MED PA RIG PA RNAMS SHES PA BKAG PA STE DE’I BDAG MED PA BDE BLAG TU ‘GRUB PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Thus it is then that the Buddhas say things, at the beginning, which focus only on denying the existence of outer objects of knowledge.  And that’s because—if there are no objects of knowledge—then we can go on to deny any perception or knowledge of what on the outside lacks any self-nature, and thus easily establish that lack of a self-nature to things.


[2790]
PHYI ROL RANG BZHIN MED PAR RIG PA RNAMS KYIS NI SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR RES ‘GA’ RANG KHO NAS RTOGS LA, RES ‘GA’ NI GZHAN GYIS CUNG ZAD BSTAN PA TZAM GYIS RTOGS SO,,

Those who understand that things on the outside have no nature of their own can, in selected cases, come to the realization that the mind cannot exist through any nature of its own.  Other types of people come to realize the same thing only after receiving some small amount of explanation from others.


[2791]
PHYI ROL MED PA DANG SHES PA RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA DRANG DON YIN PAR NI BYANG CHUB SEMS ‘GREL LAS GSAL BAR GSUNGS TE,
,’DI DAG THAMS CAD SEMS TZAM ZHES,
,THUB PA YIS NI GANG GSUNGS PA,
,BYIS RNAMS SKRAG PA SPANG DON [f. 199b] TE,
,DE NI DE BZHIN NYID MA YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS SHING,

The fact that the ideas that nothing exists on the outside, and that the mind could exist through some nature of its own, were only meant figuratively is clearly expressed in A Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment:

The Able One stated
That all of this
Was only the mind;

But this was only meant
To help the infants
Abandon their fear,

And was not meant
The way it was stated.


[2792]
‘PHAGS PA LHAS KYANG YE SHES SNYING PO KUN LAS BTUS LAS GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

Master Aryadeva also speaks of these things clearly in his Compendium of the Essence of Wisdom.



Distinguishing the figurative
from the literal

[2793]
GNYIS PA NI,

With this we have reached our second major section from above, which is showing the way in which we can understand which points in sutra are meant figuratively, and which meant literally.


	[2794]
[VI.97]
Evaṃ jñātvā prakriyām āgamasya
vyākhyātārthaṃ yac ca neyārtham uktam,
Sūtraṃ buddhvā nīyatāṃ yan na tattvaṃ
nītārthaṃ ca jñāyatāṃ śūnyatārtham.

,DE LTAR LUNG GI LO RGYUS SHES BYAS TE,
,MDO GANG DE NYID MA YIN BSHAD DON CAN,
,DRANG DON GSUNGS PA’ANG RTOGS
NAS [209a] DRANG BYA ZHING,
,STONG NYID DON CAN NGES DON SHES PAR GYIS,

		That is, we should
		Come to know
		The whole story
		Of the scriptures.

		There are certain sutras
		Which contain ideas
		That explain something
		Other than suchness.

		They were taught
		In a figurative way;
		We should realize that,
		And interpret them [f. 209a].

		And any which conveys
		The idea of emptiness
		Should be understood
		As something
		To be taken literally.


[2795]
SHES RAB CAN DAG GIS DE NYID RDZOGS PAR DNGOS SU MI STON PA’I DRANG DON GYI MDO GZHAN YANG DE BZHIN DU BSTAN PAR BYA’O ZHES BSHAD PA, 

The following lines are meant to say, “Those of you possessed of wisdom should explain the other sutras—those that have to be interpreted, those that teach suchness neither in its entirety, or directly—in the very same way.”


[2796]
SNGAR BSHAD PA DE LTAR LUNG GI DRANG NGES KYI LO RGYUS TE RNAM GZHAG SHES PAR BYAS TE, MDO SDE GANG DAG DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON MA YIN PA BSHAD PA’I DON CAN TE BRJOD BYA CAN,

That is, first of all we should come to know the whole story—that is, the entire treatment—of which scriptures thus are meant literally, and which figuratively.  And so there are certain groups of sutras which contain ideas, subject matter that explain something other than sheer suchness.  Let’s consider the topics that these sutras discuss.


[2797]
SKYE BA MED PA LA SOGS PAS KHYAD PAR DU BYAS PA’I RTEN ‘BYUNG DNGOS SU GSAL BAR MI BYED PA’I DRANG DON GSUNGS PA’ANG DRANG DON DU RTOGS PAR BYAS NAS DRANG BAR BYA ZHING STE, JI LTAR RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PA RTOGS PA LA ‘JUG PA’I RGYUR ‘GYUR BA DE LTAR BSHAD PAR BYA STE,

They were taught in a figurative way, where they clarify—directly—the topic of dependence characterized by things never starting, or the like.  And we should come first to realize that they were spoken figuratively; and then we should interpret them as necessary.  That is, these teachings are meant to be explained in a manner which would serve as a cause for entering the concept that there is nothing which exists through some nature of its own.


[2798]
‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PAR BSTOD PA LAS,
,’BYUNG RNAMS MIG GZUGS MA YIN NA,
,DE ‘BYUNG MIG GZUNG JI LTAR ZHES,
,GZUGS LA DE SKAD GSUNGS PA NA,
,KHYOD KYIS GZUGS KYI ‘DZIN PA BZLOG
,CES GSUNGS LA,

As A Praise of the One Who Went Beyond the World puts it,

	If the elements
	Are not form
	That the eye ever sees,

	Then how can you
	Even talk about
	Their occurrence
	Being held by the eye?

	Because when you talk
	About form in the way
	That you have,

	You deny that there
	Is anything at all
	Which could hold
	To that form.


[2799]
MDO LAS KYANG, MI RTAG DON NI MED DON ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

We also see lines in sutra itself which say, “The meaning of changing is that things do not exist.”


[2800]
LUNG SNGA MA SHES BYED DU ‘GRO TSUL NI BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS CHOS MNGON PAR, ‘BYUNG BA BZHI MIG GI YUL MIN PA’I REG BYA DANG, DE LAS BYUNG BA’I ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR GYI GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED MIG GI GZUNG BYAR GSUNGS LA,

Now how does the previous citation serve as support for the idea here?  The Conqueror has made the following statement in the teachings on higher knowledge:

The four elements consist of tangible entities which cannot serve as objects of the eye.  Those examples of the door of sense of form though which are products of the elements are objects which the eye can hold.


[2801]
DE GNYIS KA KHAS BLANG DGOS PA LA DE DAG GI DE KHO NA NYID STON PA NA DE RNAMS RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB NA ‘BYUNG BA MIG GI GZUNG BYA’AM, YANG NA YUL GZUGS MIG GI GZUNG BYA MIN [f. 200a] PAR KHAS BLANG DGOS PAR

In fact we have to accept both of these; but when we teach the suchness that they possess, we would have to say that—if they existed through some nature of their own—then we would have to accept that the elements were something that the eye could grasp; or else that the object of form were not something that the eye could grasp.


[2802]
SHES PA NA BSHAD TSUL SNGA MA DE RNAMS KYI DE KHO NA NYID STON PA MIN PAR SHES NAS DE KHO NA NYID GSAR DU RTOGS PA DANG, BSHAD TSUL SNGA MA DE LA ‘JUG PA’I THABS SU GSUNGS PAR SHES PA’O,,

If we understand this point, then we would understand that those previous ways of explaining things were not teaching suchness.  And then we would perceive suchness in a fresh way; and we would understand that the previous way of explaining things was just presenting a method of engaging in that understanding.


[2803]
LUNG GNYIS PA’I DON NI SNGA MA BZHIN DU DNGOS PO RNAMS SKYE BA DANG, ‘JIG PAR BSTAN PA NI RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PA’I DON DU YIN PAR GO BA’O,,

The meaning of the second citation can be understood as similar to the earlier one; that is to say, as indicating that teaching a starting and a stopping to things was meant in the sense of things that did not exist through any nature of their own.


[2804]
MDO GANG LAS GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG PA NYID KYI DON CAN TE DNGOS SU BRJOD PAR BYED PA CAN DE NGES PA’I DON DU SHES PAR GYIS SHIG

And you should understand that any sutra which conveys the idea—which is to say, serves to relate directly—that the person, and things in general, are completely empty of any nature of their own, should be understood as being a sutra which is to be taken literally.


[2805]
,DE LTAR YANG TING NGE ‘DZIN RGYAL PO LAS,
,STONG PA BDE BAR GSHEGS PAS BSHAD PA LTAR,
,NGES DON MDO SDE DAG GI BYE BRAG SHES,
,GANG LAS SEMS CAN GANG ZAG SKYES BU BSTAN,
,CHOS DE THAMS CAD DRANG BA’I DON DU SHES,

The King of Concentration sutra puts it the same way—

You should understand
That explaining emptiness
As it was done by the ones
Who have Gone to Bliss

Is a feature of those sutras
Which were meant as literal.

All of those teachings
In which living beings
And the person
And the individual
Were taught should be

Understood as being
Intended only figuratively.


[2806]
ZHES GSUNGS TE MDO SDE DAG GI BYE BRAG NI DRANG DON GYI MDO SDE DANG MI ‘DRA BA’I KHYAD PAR RO,,

When they speak of a “feature of those sutras” here, what they are referring to is a characteristic which sets them apart from the sutras which are to be taken figuratively.


[2807]
GANG ZAG BSTAN PA NI MTSON PA TZAM STE BYED PA PO DANG, LAS SU BYA BA DANG BYED PA RNAMS YOD PAR STON PA’O,,

And when they mention “the person” here it is only in a representative way; we can also say it refers to those sutras that speak about the agent of an action; the object of the action; or the action itself.


[2808]
‘DI NI MDO SDE LA DRANG NGES GNYIS SU ‘JOG TSUL GYI KHUNGS SO,,

This citation is in fact the ultimate source for separating the body of sutras into those two types: the ones which are figurative, and the ones which are literal.


[2809]
YANG DE NYID LAS,
,’JIG RTEN KHAMS NI STONG PHRAG TU,
,NGA YIS CHOS RNAMS GANG GSUNGS PA,
,YI GE THA DAD DON GCIG STE,
,YONGS SU BSGRAG PAR NUS MA YIN,

The same source also says—

	The teachings
	That I have given
	In all the worlds there are

	Are presented 
	In separate words
	With but a single meaning:

	They are not something
	Which someone else
	Could spread.


	[2810]
,DNGOS PO GCIG NI BSAM BYAS NA,
,DE DAG THAMS CAD BSGOMS ‘GYUR TE,
,SANGS RGYAS KUN GYIS CHOS MANG PO,
,JI SNYED RAB TU BSTAN PA RNAMS,

If you really think
About a single entity,
Then you are meditating
On all those that exist.

And so consider now
All of the many teachings
That all of the Enlightened Ones
Have worked so hard to give;


	[2811]
,CHOS RNAMS KUN GYI BDAG MED YIN,
,MI GANG DON LA MKHAS RNAMS KYIS,
,GNAS ‘DI LA NI BSLAB BYAS NA,
,SANGS RGYAS CHOS RNAMS [f. 200b] RNYED MI DKA’, 
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

	They consist of the lack
	Of a self, to any
	Of all the things there are.

	Those who are wise
	In the real meaning of things
	Should educate themselves
	In this single way of things;

	For them, it is
	Nothing difficult at all
	To find the teachings
	Of the Buddha.


[2812]
‘JIG RTEN ZHES PA’I RKANG PA BZHI NI MDO SDE JI SNYED CIG GSUNGS PA LA DON DAM PA DNGOS SU GSAL BAR BYED PA NI DE BZHIN NYID LA DNGOS SU GZHOL LA, DE LTAR MI STON PA’I DRANG DON RNAMS KYANG BRGYUD NAS DE BZHIN NYID LA GZHOL BAS, DON DAM LA GZHOL BAR DON GCIG PA’O,,

The four lines [in the Tibetan, nine in the English] which include “all the worlds” are meant to say that all of the sutras ever spoken in order to clarify, directly, the ultimate—however many such sutras there may be—flow directly into suchness.  And even those which don’t teach things this way—that is, all the sutras that were meant figuratively—also flow down indirectly to reach the very same place, of suchness.  As such, all sutras in the universe teach the same thing, since they all flow down into ultimate reality.


[2813]
DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN GYI KHAMS NA MDO SDE YOD TSAD LAM LA SLOB PA’I LAS DANG PO PAS RTZAD GCAD PAR MI NUS PAS MDO SDE GANG YIN PA GCIG GI DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON RTZAD GCAD CES PA YIN TE,

As such, we can say these lines are speaking to us as follows.  There is no person who is just starting out in their study of the path who could ever seek out the total amount of sutras that exist in this world.  As such, we should do our best to seek out just the meaning of suchness as it is presented in any one of these sutras.


[2814]
DE KHO NA NYID DNGOS SU MI STON PA RNAMS KYANG DE LA ‘JUG PA’I RGYUR BSHAD DGOS PA’I SHES BYED DU DRANGS PAS SHES SO,,

This is a point that you should understand because I have cited this sutra as support for the idea that even those sutras which do not convey suchness directly must be explained as providing the basis for us to enter into that same thing.


[2815]
DNGOS PO GCIG NI ZHES PA GNYIS NI CHOS CAN GCIG GI DE KHO NA NYID LEGS PAR SHES NAS BSGOMS NA CHOS CAN THAMS CAD KYI DE KHO NA NYID BSGOMS PAR ‘GRO BAS CHOS CAN RE RE NAS KYI CHOS NYID SO SOR SGOM MI DGOS PA’I DON NO,,

The two references to a single entity convey the fact that if we really understand the suchness of a single typical thing, and then meditate upon this understanding, then it will turn into a meditation upon the suchness of all the things there are.  The point here is that it won’t be necessary for us to meditate, individually, on the ultimate nature of each and every representative object.


[2816]
DNGOS PO GCIG BSGOMS NA THAMS CAD BSGOMS PAR ‘GYUR BA DE GANG YIN PA STON PA NI SANGS RGYAS KUN GYIS ZHES PA GSUM GYIS STON TE, DE LTAR GSUNGS PA NI CHOS KYI BDAG MED YIN ZHES PAS, CHOS CAN RGYA CHE BA’I SPYOD PHYOGS RNAMS LA GCIG GIS CHOG ZER BA MIN NO,,

How is this fact expressed, that by meditating on a single entity we begin to meditate on all those that there are?  It is expressed by the three lines [in the Tibetan, seven lines in the English] which begin with “and so consider now.”  This is all a reference to the lack of a self-nature to things; as such, it is not the case that the lines are saying that when we are dealing with a broad number of examples, just one of them would be sufficient.


[2817]
ZLA BA SGRON MA LAS, GRANGS NGES SU ‘JOG TSUL GSUNGS PA DE BZHIN DU BLO GROS MI ZAD PA LA SOGS PA’I MDO SDE DAG LAS RGYA CHER BSTAN PA YANG RTOGS PAR BYA ZHES GSUNGS TE, ‘DI RNAMS MTHA’ CHOD PAR DRANG NGES RNAM ‘BYED DU BSHAD ZIN TO,,

We are advised to “glean our understanding from how the Lamp of the Moon describes the manner of deciding what is literal, and what is figurative, as well as from the extensive presentation in sutras such as Never-Ending Wisdom.”  I have already given a definitive explanation of these points in my Distinguishing the Figurative from the Literal.


[2818]
PHYOGS TZAM ZHIG NI BRJOD PAR BYA STE ZHES PA NI DGONGS [f. 201a] ‘GREL LAS NGO BO NYID GSUM BSHAD PA DRANG DON DU ‘GREL NA RANG LUGS KYIS DE GSUM GYI ‘JOG TSUL JI LTAR YIN SNYAM PA LA DE’I PHYOGS TZAM STON PA’O,,

At this point in the autocommentary we see “I will explain this just a touch.”  What this is saying is that Master Chandrakirti intends to speak just a bit about the following question: If we explain the presentation of the three essential natures in What I Really Meant as something to be taken figuratively, then how does our own system present these same three?


[2819]
DPER NA SBRUL NI THAG PA BSDOGS PA’I RTEN ‘BREL LA LOG PAR BTAGS PA YIN TE SBRUL DE THAG PA DE LA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Let’s consider for example a case where there is a mistaken appellation, for the connection between a rope and a snake; that is, there is absolutely no snake there amidst the rope.


[2820]
SBRUL DNGOS LA NI YONGS SU GRUB PA YIN TE MED BZHIN DU KUN TU MA BTAGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

A genuine snake is something we could call “totality”—“completely established”—in the sense that it is in no way just called what it is, without being there at all.


[2821]
DE BZHIN DU RANG BZHIN GSHIS LUGS KYANG GZHAN DBANG ‘DUS BYAS LA NI DER MED BZHIN DU KUN TU BTAGS PA YIN TE,

In the same way, some original nature to things is something simply ascribed to dominated entities—productions of causes; whereas in truth there is no such thing there at all.


[2822]
RTZA SHE LAS,
,RANG BZHIN DAG NI BCOS MIN DANG,
,GZHAN LA LTOS PA MED PA YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS PAS GSHIS LUGS KYI NGO BO NYID NI BYAS PA CAN MA YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Wisdom puts it this way—

	Natures to things
	Could never be artifice;

	There can be no dependence
	Upon other things.

What this is saying is that an essence to things that was their original nature could never be something that was made.


[2823]
BZUNG BZHIN PA STE MTHONG BZHIN PA’I RTEN ‘BREL BYAS PA CAN GZUGS BRNYAN DANG ‘DRA BA LA GSHIS SU KUN BTAGS PA’I RANG BZHIN DE NI SANGS RGYAS KYI JI LTA BA GZIGS PA’I SPYOD YUL LA NI GSHIS LUGS DNGOS YIN TE,

And so let’s consider something that we were in the act of holding; which is to say, a dependence which we could observe—something made—which was similar then to a reflection in a mirror.  The original condition here of having a nature of being ascribed, as the object of activity for the way that a Buddha sees how things exist, is the actual original nature of things.


[2824]
DER NI MED BZHIN DU KUN TU MA BTAGS PA’I PHYIR TE, DNGOS PO RGYU RKYEN GYIS BYAS PA CAN LA YE SHES DES MA REG PAR RANG BZHIN ‘BA’ ZHIG MNGON SUM DU MDZAD PAS DE NYID THUGS SU CHUD PA’I PHYIR SANGS RGYAS ZHES BRJOD DE, ,MA REG PA’I MTHA’ BCAD PA NI ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

This is not something that is not at all ascribed even as it has no existence; for in fact we call a being “enlightened” when they comprehend suchness only as a nature of things which is perceived directly, without their wisdom ever making contact with entities which were produced by causes & conditions.  Where we draw the line with this “not making contact,” by the way, is something we will cover further on.


[2825]
DE’I PHYIR DE LTAR NGO BO NYID GSUM GYI RNAM GZHAG RTOGS PAR BYAS NAS MDO’I DGONGS PA BSHAD PAR BYA’O ZHES GSUNGS TE, BSHAD TSUL DES BYAMS ZHUS KYI LE’UR MTSAN NYID GSUM BSHAD PA’I DGONGS PA YANG SHES PAR BYAS LA, ,DGONGS [f. 201b] ‘GREL GYI NGO BO NYID GSUM BSHAD PA’I DGONGS PA DRANG DON YIN PA YANG SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Such it is then that we see, “I will make an explanation of the actual intent of the sutra, now that we have grasped the presentation of three essential natures in this way.”  From the way this explanation is made then we can as well understand the true intent of the explanation of the three defining characteristics in the Section Requested by Loving One.  And then we can also come to an understanding of how the true intent of the three essential natures taught in What I Really Meant was that they were only metaphoric.


[2826]
SEMS TZAM PAS GDAGS GZHI GZHAN DBANG LA GZUNG ‘DZIN NGO BO THA DAD PA GNYIS SU BTAGS PA KUN BRTAGS SU BYED PA NI BSAM PA’AM BRTAG PAR BYA DGOS TE, GZUNG ‘DZIN GNYIS NI GZHAN DBANG YIN GYI DE MIN PA’I GZHAN DBANG NI DNGOS POR MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Those of the Mind Only school ascribe separate essences of held and holder to the object of their ascription: dominated entities.  We need to think about—or examine—this form of conceiving of things; that is, the two of what is held and what does the holding are dominated entities; but in actual fact there is no kind of dominated entity which is other than these.


[2827]
BYAMS ZHUS NAS BSHAD PA’I NGO BO NYID GSUM DANG DGONGS ‘GREL GYI NGO BO NYID GSUM GYI RNAM GZHAG MTHA’ CHOD PAR NI DRANG NGES RNAM ‘BYED DU BSHAD ZIN TO,,

I have already made a definitive presentation, in Distinguishing the Figurative from the Literal, of the three essential natures found in the Section Requested by Loving One, and the three essential natures from What I Really Meant.



Denying things from themselves & other

[2828]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us then to our third major step from before: denying that things could grow both from themselves and from something other than themselves.


[2829]
DE LA BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA’I TSIG GAL GNYIS SU SMRA BA GCER BU PA RNAMS NI ‘JI BA’I GONG BU DANG DBYU GU DANG ‘KHOR LO DANG SKUD PA DANG CHU DANG RDZA MKHAN LA SOGS PA DAG LAS BUM PA ‘BYUNG BA NA,

Now on all this there is a position taken by the Naked Ones where they make an assertion of two contradictory statements, saying that things arise from both themselves and from something other than themselves.  They would start by noting that a pitcher comes from a lump of clay; the shaping stick; the wheel; a measuring thread; water; the potter, and other such things.


[2830]
RDZA BUM ‘JI BA’I BDAG NYID DU YOD PA KHO NA SKYE BA DE’I PHYIR BDAG LAS SKYE LA, RDZA MKHAN GYI BYA BA LA SOGS PA GZHAN DU GYUR PA DAG RDZA BUM GYI SKYED PAR BYED PA YIN PA’I PHYIR, GZHAN LAS KYANG SKYE BAR SEMS SO,,

They would say that since the pitcher itself has been made exclusively of clay, it has grown from itself.  And then again, the actions of the potter and so on—things other than the pitcher—have acted to produce it; and so as such, they would consider the vessel to have arisen from something other than itself as well.


[2831]
PHYI ROL LA JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU NANG LA YANG BDAG DANG GZHAN GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And they would say that—since the inside is similar to what’s going on on the outside—then it too must have arisen from both the pitcher itself, and something else as well.


[2832]
DE LA GANG ZAG DANG BDAG GCES PA’I SROG DANG, DBANG PO LA SOGS PA SROG MA YIN PA DANG, MNGON MTHO DANG NGES LEGS ‘GRUB PA’I CHOS DANG, DE LAS BZLOG PA’I CHOS MIN PA DANG, NYON MONGS PA’I ZAG PA DANG ‘CHAL KHRIMS ‘GOG PA’I SDOM PA DANG, LA SOGS PAS BDE BA DANG, SDUG BSNGAL BA DANG, SHES PA LAS SKYES SHING SHES PA’I RGYUR GYUR PA’I ‘DU BYA BA’I SHUGS TE, TSIG GI DON [f. 202a] DGU’I RNAM GZHAG BYAS NAS

They set forth nine different principles, which involve the person and the life which is cherished by the self; those things which are not the life, such as the powers and so forth; the teachings which help us achieve the higher rebirths and definite goodness; the opposite of these teachings, negative teachings; the impurities of the negativities; the commitments which help prevent immoral behavior; and “so on”—which would include pleasure, pain, the power that brings things together born from mind and supplying the causes for mind.


[2833]
BYAMS PA TSE RABS GZHAN DU YANG SROG GI BDAG NYID DU YOD PA KHO NAS DA LTAR GYI SKYE BA ‘DI LEN PA’I PHYIR BDAG LAS SKYE STE, BYAMS PA DANG SROG GNYIS GZHAN MIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Someone like John, when he passes on to his other lifetimes, takes on these births exclusively as the same entity of an individual which is alive; as such, he arises from himself.  Here, the pair John and his life are not considered different from one another.


[2834]
SROG NI SKYE BA GCIG NAS GCIG TU ‘GRO BA DANG LDAN PA’I PHYIR, LHA LA SOGS PA’I ‘GRO BAR RGYU BA YANG GZHAN GYIS ‘DOD DO,,

Life involves passing on from one rebirth to another; and so when it courses into births such as a worldly god or the like, it is—they say—by means of something which is other.


[2835]
YANG BYAMS PA RANG GI PHA DANG MA DANG, CHOS DANG CHOS MA YIN PA DANG, ZAG PA LA SOGS PA GZHAN DU GYUR PA LAS SKYE BA’I PHYIR GZHAN LAS KYANG SKYE’O,,

They would also say that John has arisen from things other than him: things like his father and mother; or from good teachings or bad teachings; or from impurity or other things of the like.  And so as such, he has arisen too from something other than himself.


	[2836]
[VI.98]
Dvābhyāṃ na cāpi jananaṃ khalu yukta rūpaṃ
doṣāḥ patanti vihitās tuta eva yasmāt,
Na lokato’pi na ca tattvata iṣṭam etad
ekaikato na jananasya yato’sti siddhiḥ.

,GNYIS LAS SKYE BA’ANG RIGS PA’I NGO BO
MA YIN GANG GI PHYIR,
,BSHAD ZIN NYES PA DE DAG THOG TU
‘BAB PA YIN PHYIR RO,
,’DI NI ‘JIG RTEN LAS MIN DE NYID
DU YANG ‘DOD MIN TE,
,GANG PHYIR RE RE LAS NI SKYE BA
‘GRUB PA YOD MA YIN,

		It is also not the nature
		Of clear thinking
		To say that things
		Could arise from
		A combination.

		Why is that?
		Because those same
		Problems already raised
		Would strike
		Like lightning.

		From the point
		Of the everyday world
		There are none;

		And speaking as well
		From the point of view
		Of suchness,

		Neither is this idea
		Something that
		We can accept.

		The reason
		That this is true
		Is that there
		Is no such thing

		As an arising
		Accomplished separately.


[2837]
DE’I PHYIR BDAG GZHAN RE RE KHO NA LAS SKYE BAR KHAS MI LEN PAS SNGAR BDAG GZHAN RE RE BA LAS SKYE BA BKAG PA NI KHO BO CAG LA MI GNOD DO ZHE NA,

And so this other group would say,

It is not in fact the case that we accept the idea that things arise either from themselves or from others; as such, your previous denial of these two separately—that things could arise from themselves, or from other things—does no damage to our position.


[2838]
RE RE BA LAS SKYE BA MI RIGS PAR MA ZAD RANG GZHAN GNYIS KA TSOGS PA LAS SKYE BA’ANG RIGS PA’I NGO BO MA YIN TE, GANG GI PHYIR NA SNGAR RE RE BA LA BSHAD ZIN PA’I NYES PA DE DAG GNYIS CHAR LAS SKYE BA’I PHYOGS LA YANG THOG TU ‘BAB PA NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR TE,

Not only is it illogical to say that things could arise from either one of the two separately; it is also not the nature of clear thinking to say that things could arise from some combination of the two, of themselves and other things.  And why is that?  Because those same problems that we have already raised with each of the two possibilities separately would quite certainly strike like lightning itself to the position that things could arise from both together.


[2839]
BYAMS PA SROG LA LTOS TE BDAG LAS SKYE BAR ‘DOD NA NI, SNGAR BSHAD PA’I SKYE BA DON MED SOGS KYIS DGAG LA, PHA MA SOGS LA LTOS TE GZHAN SKYE ‘DOD NA NI, HA CANG THAL BA SOGS KYIS DGAG GO

First of all, the position that John is born from himself because he depends upon the power of life was already denied previously, in the discussion of how such a starting would be pointless.  And saying that one has arisen from something other than oneself, if they have arisen in dependence upon parents or the like, was already denied by showing that it had unacceptable, extreme implications.


[2840]
,GONG DU JI LTAR BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB DANG, DON DAM PAR YANG MI RIGS SO ZHES BSTAN PA DE BZHIN DU ‘DIR YANG GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BA MI SRID DO ZHES MJUG BSDU BA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA, BDAG GZHAN GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BA ‘DI NI ‘JIG RTEN LAS KYANG YOD PA MIN LA, DE NYID DON DAM DU YANG ‘DOD PA MIN NO,,

Earlier on, we showed that it was illogical to say that things had arisen either from themselves or from something other than themselves, from both the point of view of the deceptive nature of the everyday world, and ultimately speaking as well.  In the same way, at this particular point in the text, our author presents a final conclusion to say that—first of all—from the point of the everday world there can exist none of this arising of things from both themselves and from things other than themselves.  And speaking as well from the point of view of the ultimate suchness of things, neither is this idea something that we can accept.


[2841]
GANG GI PHYIR BDAG GZHAN RE RE LAS [f. 202b] NI SKYE BA ‘GRUB PA YOD PA MA YIN PAS GNYIS KA LAS SKYE BA YANG RIGS PA MA YIN NO,,

The reason that this is true is that there is no such thing as an arising of things which is accomplished separately, either from the thing itself, or from things other than itself.  As such, it would be illogical then to say that something could arise from both together.



And never with no cause

[2842]
BZHI PA NI,

Which brings us to our fourth step from before: denying that things could grow without any cause at all.


[2843]
‘DIR NGO BO NYID LAS BYUNG BAR SMRA BA RGYANG PHAN PA NI, GAL TE SKYE BA RGYU LAS YIN NA ‘BRAS BU LA LTOS TE BDAG DANG GZHAN DANG GNYIS KAR GYUR PA ZHIG TU SKYE BAS SKYON DE DAG TU ‘GYUR NA BDAG GIS NI RGYU LAS SKYE BAR KHAS MA BLANGS PAS PHYOGS GSUM GA LA BSHAD PA’I NYES PA MED DE,

The non-Buddhist school named “The Outcasts” claims that things happen through some essence of their own.  They would say that—since the arising of something occurs through a cause—then from the point of view of the result, there has been an arising from itself; from something other than itself; and from both.  And they would say that "If the problems raised before apply here, then we refuse to accept that the result arises from a cause at all; and therefore we incur none of the faults you have raised with all three possibilities.”


[2844]
‘DI LTAR PAD+MA’I CHU BA DANG DE’I ‘DAB MA RNAMS KYI RTZUB PA DANG ‘JAM SHA DAG ‘GA’ ZHIG GIS BYED PAR MA MTHONG LA, DE’I ‘DAB MA DANG ZE’U ‘BRU DANG LTE BA RNAMS KYI KHA DOG DANG DBYIBS SNA TSOGS PA DAG BYED PAR MA MTHONG NGO,,

Here’s why we would say that.  Consider the stem of a lotus flower, and its petals.  One is scratchy, but the other is very soft.  But no one ever saw something that made them so.  No one has ever seen anybody who sat down and crafted the petals of the lotus, and the anthers, and the center; the various hues and curves.


[2845]
DE BZHIN DU PA NA SA DANG BAL PO SE’U LA SOGS PA’I SNA TSOGS PA YANG YIN NO,,

And the whole variety of things like the jackfruit, and the pomegranate, are just the same.


[2846]
DE LTAR PHYI ROL LA BZHIN DU RMA BYA DANG BYA TI TI RI DANG BYA GAG LA SOGS PA NANG GI BDAG NYID CAN DAG LA YANG ‘GA’ ZHIG GIS ‘BAD PAS GZUNG NAS KHA DOG DANG DBYIBS LA SOGS PA ‘GOD PAR MI DMIGS SO,,
