As the 400 Verses puts it,

	The teachings were never
	Granted by Those Gone Thus
	So that they could engage
	In simple disputation.

	But yes they did indeed
	Incinerate their opponents,
	Just because that is what
	Fire tends to do with wood.


[3043]
,CES ME BUS PA BTUNG BA BSKOL BA’I PHYIR DU BYAS KYI THAL BA DANG SOL BA’I PHYIR DU BYAS PA MIN KYANG, DE DAG KYANG ZHAR LA ‘BYUNG BA’I DPES GSUNGS SO,,

That is, when we make efforts to stoke a fire, it’s not that we’re hoping we can get more dust and ashes.  But that does tend to happen, as a side-effect of our exertions.  This is what the metaphor here is expressing.


[3044]
GAL TE RTZOD PA LA CHAGS PA’I PHYIR CHOS NYE BAR BSTAN NA NI, DE’I TSE THE TSOM MED PAR GZHAN GYI PHYOGS SKYON DANG LDAN PA LA SDANG ZHING RIGS PA DANG LDAN PA’I RANG GI PHYOGS LA RJES SU CHAGS PAR ‘GYUR BAS, KHRO CHAGS KYI RTOG PA LDOG PA MED DO,,

Suppose the reason that one grants these teachings is all out of some attachment to argumentation.  In this case, it’s beyond any doubt that we would start to feel aversion for the positions of the other side, defective as these positions are.  And then equally we would start to feel attachment to our own side, logical as it is.  And in this case, those wrong emotions of anger and attachment would become themselves unbeatable.


	[3045]
[VI.119]
Svadṛṣṭirāgo’pi hi kalpanaiva

	To our own viewpoints,

	In the same way—

	Falling into those

	We will be able
	To clear away

	To feel attachment
	And aversion—

[3046]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, ‘DI LTAR RANG GI LTA BA LA CHAGS PA DANG DE BZHIN DU GZHAN PHYOGS KYI LTA BA LA RGYUD ‘KHRUG PA GANG YIN PA DE NI, ‘CHING BA’I RTOG PA NYID YIN PAS KHRO CHAGS KYI RTOG PA MA LOG PAR ‘PHEL BAS BCINGS PA NYID DU ‘GYUR GYI THAR PA NI MIN NO,,

And why is that?  When we have attachment like this to our own viewpoints, and when—in the same way—our hearts feel disturbed by the views of other parties, we are falling into the very notions that enslave people.  And then rather than turning away from these useless ideas of anger and attachment, these instead increase within us.  And then they lead us to that same old enslavement—and there is no freedom for us.


[3047]
GANG GI TSE CHOS ‘DI RTZOD PA’I PHYIR DU BSTAN PA MA YIN PA DE’I TSE, DE’I PHYIR RANG PHYOGS LA ‘DOD CHAGS DANG, GZHAN PHYOGS LA KHONG KHRO BA RNAM PAR BSAL TE, RIGS PAS RNAM PAR DPYOD PA NI MYUR DU GROL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Suppose then that we are able to avoid the tendency of granting the teachings out of some desire to argue with others.  In this case, we will be able to clear away those tendencies to feel attachment to our own positions, and aversion towards those of others.  That is, when we are able to analyze things with clear thinking, we find ourselves liberated, with speed.

Those who are great beings

[3051]
BDAG GZHAN GYI PHYOGS LA CHAGS PA DANG KHRO BA’I PHYOGS LHUNG DOR NAS GZU BO’I BLOS MA DPYAD NA, GRUB MTHA’ LA DPYOD PAR SGOM PA DE NYID LA BRTEN NAS ‘KHOR BAR DAM DU ‘CHING BAR GSUNGS PA ‘DI NYID, BDAG CAG RNAMS LA THUGS BRTZE BAS MAN NGAG KHYAD PAR CAN BYIN PAR SHES PAR GYIS SHIG

Suppose we are unable to let go of this kind of prejudice, of attachment and hatred towards the positions we ourselves hold, and those of others—we are unable to think out things with an unbiased state of mind.  What this very citation is saying is that—when we accustom ourselves to just this kind of analysis of the various schools of thought—it will chain us ever more tightly to the circle of pain.  And so all of us should understand that we have thus been granted some very special words of advice, from a person who really loves us.


[3052]
,BDAG SKYE ‘GOG PA NAS ‘DI YAN CHAD KYIS CHOS KYI BDAG MED BSTAN PAR GSUNGS TE, DNGOS PO’I CHOS KYI BDAG MED BSTAN PA NI SHIN TU MANG LA, DNGOS MED KYI CHOS KYI BDAG MED KYANG BAR BAR DU BSTAN PA LA DGONGS SO,,

It’s been said that—now that we’ve denied the idea that things could arise from themselves—from this point on in the text what’s being presented is the lack of any self-existence to things.  The thinking here is that there are a great many presentations of how things that are functional have no nature of their own; but it is only from time to time that we see explanations of how existing entities with no function lack any such nature.



Freedom requires understanding the self

[3053]
GNYIS PA GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED RIGS PAS BSGRUB PA LA GSUM, THAR ‘DOD KYIS THOG MAR BDAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA NYID DGAG DGOS PAR BSTAN PA, BDAG DANG BDAG GI BA GNYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ‘GOG PA’I TSUL, BDAG DANG SHING RTA’I DPYAD PA DNGOS PO GZHAN LA YANG BSGRE BAR BSTAN PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

With this we have reached our second major part from above, on using reasoning to prove that the person has no self-nature.  This itself we will cover in three sections: (1) showing how those who wish to achieve freedom need, before anything else, to deny that the self is something that could exist through any nature of its own; (2) how it is that we deny the idea that either me or mine could exist through any nature of their own; and (3) the way in which we can apply our examination of the self, and of a wagon, to other entities as well.  Here is the first.


	[3054]
[VI.120]
Satkāyadṛṣṭi prabhavān aśeṣān
kleśāṃś ca doṣāṃś ca dhiyā vipaśyan,

		Is that what this

DE LTAR LUNG DANG RIGS PAS CHOS KYI BDAG MED BSTAN NAS, DE’I ‘OG TU GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

Having thus made our presentation—utilizing both scripture and logic—of the way in which entities have no self-nature, we turn now to an explanation meant to show how there is no self-nature to the person.


[3056]
‘DI NA RNAL ‘BYOR PA DE KHO NA NYID LA ‘JUG PAR ‘DOD CING NYON MONGS PA’I SKYON MA LUS PA SPONG BAR ‘DOD PA NI, ‘KHOR BAR ‘KHYAM PA ‘DI CI ‘DRA BA ZHIG GI RTZA BA CAN YIN SNYAM DU RTOG PAR BYED LA,

On this point, we have some advice for those deep practitioners who wish to engage in subject of suchness; and who seek to eliminate each & every one of the problems relating to the negative emotions.  They should be wondering just what serves as the very root behind the way we all wander in the circle of suffering.


[3057]
DE LTAR BRTAGS PA NA NYON MONGS PA NI ‘DOD CHAGS LA SOGS PA DANG, SKYON RNAMS NI SKYE RGA NA ‘CHI LA SOGS PA STE [f. 215a] DE RNAMS MA LUS PAR NGA DANG NGA’I ‘O SNYAM PA’I RNAM PA CAN DE GNYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I SHES RAB NYON MONGS PA CAN GYI ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA LAS BYUNG BAR BLO YIS MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR TE, DE DAG NI MA LUS PAR ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I ‘BRAS BU YIN NO,,

And when we examine this question, our intellect comes to see where it is that everything related to negative emotions—ignorant desire and the like—as well as all the rest of our problems (birth, aging, death, and so on) really comes from.  And the fact is that each & every one of these troubles comes the view of destruction, which is a kind of negative intelligence where we have thoughts about “me” and “mine” and hold these two to exist through some nature of their own.  That is, each and every one of those pains is a result of the view of destruction.


[3058]
DE LTAR MTHONG BA NA ‘JIG LTA SPONG BAR ‘DOD PA ‘BYUNG LA, DE’I TSE SHES RAB CAN ZHIG YIN NA NI DE SPONG BA DE YANG SNGAR CHOS DBYINGS BSTOD PA DANG BZHI BRGYA PA’I LUNG DRANGS PA LTAR ‘JIG LTAS JI LTAR BZUNG BA LTAR GYI BDAG YUL STENG NA MED PAR MTHONG BAS SPONG DGOS PAR MTHONG NAS,

When we do see this fact, then we start to feel a desire to eliminate this view of destruction.  At this point, if someone is a person of intelligence, they see what it is that they have to give up to accomplish this.  That is, they will follow the lines that we have cited previously from The Praise of the Realm of Reality and The 400 Verses, and come to recognize that the kind of self-nature which our perishable view holds to exist does not in the least apply to the objects of the world.


[3059]
‘JIG LTAS GZHI GANG LA ZHEN PA ‘DI’I DMIGS PA GANG YIN SNYAM DU BRTAGS PA NA, BDAG STE NGA ZHES PA’I NGA NI BDAG TU LTA BA ‘DI’I YUL DMIGS PA’O SNYAM DU RTOGS TE, NGAR ‘DZIN PA NI BDAG GI YUL CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

One may wonder then just what kind of aspect it is that the view of destruction assumes, when it begins to hold its beliefs about any particular object.  And what we come to realize is that what this view thinks it sees is what we have called “the self”—which is to say, a certain kind of “me.”  It is the “me” which the view of some self thinks it is focused upon.  And that is because the tendency to hold to “me” takes, as its object, a “self.”


[3060]
DE’I TSE NYES SKYON MA LUS PA SPONG BAR ‘DOD PAS RTZA BA ‘JIG LTA NYID SPANG BAR BYA BA YIN LA,

At this point, what we hope to do is to eliminate each & every problem there is: each and every fault.  Thus it is then that what we will have to eliminate is none other than this view of destruction.


[3061]
DE YANG DE’I DMIGS PA BDAG GI BDAG STE NGO BOS GRUB PA MED PAR KHONG DU CHUD PA LAS SPONG BAR ‘GYUR BAS, RNAL ‘BYOR PAS GANG ZHIG BDAG TU ‘DZIN PA’I YUL BDAG CES BYA BA ‘DI, NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB MA GRUB CI ‘DRA BA ZHIG CES THOG MAR BDAG KHO NA LA RTOG PAR BYED DO,,

This in itself is something that we have to eliminate by coming to a realization that my “me”—the object that this view focuses upon—has nothing about it which could exist through some essential nature of its own.  And so it is that that the deep practitioner is going to have to decide—at the beginning, only with regard to themselves—the question of whether this “self” that the tendency to hold to a self grasps on to is something that could exist though some essential nature of its own, or not.


[3062]
RNAL ‘BYOR PA YIS BDAG DE NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ‘GOG PAR BYED PA LAS, ‘JIG LTA SPANGS NA NYES SKYON KUN LDOG PAS NA, BDAG LA RNAM PAR DPYAD PA ‘DI NI THAR PA SGRUB PA’I THABS YIN TE,

The way it goes is that the deep practitioner works to stop the idea that the self is something that could exist through some nature of its own; this then eliminates the view of destruction, which in turn puts a stop to all the problems there ever were.  As such, the examination of whether a self exists or not is itself the method for attaining freedom.


[3063]
BSLAB BTUS LAS, GANG ZAG STONG PA NYID NI DE LTAR SHIN TU GRUB PA YIN NA, ,DE’I PHYIR RTZA BA CHAD PAS [f. 215b] NYON MONGS PA THAMS CAD KUN TU MI ‘BYUNG NGO,,

As the Compendium of All the Trainings puts it,

Suppose that a person is able to prove, beyond the shadow of a doubt, the emptiness of the person.  This has the effect of stopping each and everyone one of the negative emotions, completely—because it severs their very root.


[3064]
‘PHAGS PA DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA’I GSANG BA’I MDO LAS JI SKAD DU, ZHI BA’I BLO GROS ‘DI LTA STE DPER NA, SHING RTZA BA NAS BCAD NA YAL GA DANG LO MA DANG YAL GA PHRA MO THAMS CAD SKAM PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

As the exalted Sutra of the Secret of Those Gone Thus puts it,

O Peaceful Intellect, this is the way it is.  If—to take an example—you cut a tree from its roots, then the branches, the leaves, and the twigs all dry up on their own.


[3065]
ZHI BA’I BLO GROS DE BZHIN DU ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA NYE BAR ZHI NA, NYON MONGS PA DANG NYE BA’I NYON MONGS PA THAMS CAD ZHI BAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTA BU’O, ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

Here, o Peaceful Intellect, it is the same.  It’s similar to the way it’s been stated that—if you are able to put a final stop to the view of destruction—then everything to do with the negative emotions, and the secondary negative emotions, comes to a stop as well.


[3066]
‘DI LTAR GSUNGS PA LA MKHAS PA’I DBANG PO RNAMS DGONGS PA MTHUN PAS, THOG MAR ‘KHOR BA’I NYES DMIGS LEGS PAR SHES NAS SEMS PA DANG, 

The lords of the wise are of one mind regarding these kinds of statements.  That is, we start off by learning, thoroughly, all the various problems with this circle of pain—and then we think about them.


[3067]
DE NAS DE’I RTZA BA GANG YIN NGOS ‘DZIN PA DANG, DE NAS DE SPONG BAR ‘DOD PA NA SPONG THABS KYI THAD DU MA ‘PHYUGS PAR DE’I ZHEN YUL BKAG PA’I BDAG MED KYI LTA BA ZHIG NGES PAR RNYED NAS,

With this, we come to identify just what it is that serves as the very root of this circle.  If then we hope to eliminate this root, then we have to be sure that we make no errors regarding the proper methodology of doing so.  Which is to say, we will beyond any doubt have to ascertain that view of no-self which we can use to put a stop to the object that we think we see here: we will have to identify, with certainty, a correct view of how no self exists.


[3068]
DE’I DON LA ‘DRIS PAR BYED PA NI, THEG PA CHE CHUNG GANG LA YANG DGOS PA SHES PAR BYA’O,,

After that, we must accustom ourselves to what this view involves.  One should understand that all this is a necessity—whether we’re talking about the greater way, or the lesser way.


[3069]
GAL TE RIN CHEN ‘PHRENG BA LAS,
,JI SRID PHUNG POR ‘DZIN YOD PA,
,DE SRID DE LA NGAR ‘DZIN YOD,
,NGAR ‘DZIN YOD NA YANG LAS TE,
,LAS LAS KYANG NI SKYE BA YIN,

One may ask then about the following lines from the String of Precious Jewels—

	As long as we grasp to
	The parts of the person,
	Then we will continue
	To hold to a “me.”

	As long as we hold
	To a “me,” then
	There will be karma;
	And rebirth comes
	From karma.


[3070]
ZHES PHUNG PO BDEN ‘DZIN CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BAR BSHAD LA, ‘DIR ‘JIG LTA ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BAR BSHAD PA GNYIS ‘GAL TE, ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BA MI MTHUN PA GNYIS MI ‘THAD PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

“What this is saying,” you might begin, “is that holding that the parts to a person are real is the tendency to grasp to some self-nature of things which we are taught is the very root of the cycle of pain.  But that would contradict the explanation that the view of destruction is the root of this same cycle.  It seems to me that it would be incorrect to say that there were two different roots of the cycle of pain that were incompatible with each other.”


[3071]
SKYON MED DE ‘DI PA’I LUGS KYIS BDAG ‘DZIN GNYIS DMIGS PAS SO SOR ‘BYED KYI, ‘DZIN STANGS KYI RNAM PA MI ‘DRA BA MED DE,

And yet there is no such problem.  According to those who follow this system, the two forms of grasping to some self-nature are distinguished from one another by the object upon which they focus; it is not though the case that there is any difference between the two in the manner in which they hold their object.


[3072]
GNYIS KA YANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I RNAM PA CAN YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BA GNYIS ‘GAL BA NA YUL LA [f. 216a] ‘JUG PA’I ‘DZIN STANGS MI MTHUN PA GNYIS ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BAR ‘JOG PA LA BYED PA’I PHYIR,,

And that’s because both of them display an aspect where they hold their object to exist through some nature of its own.  And if the two roots of the circle of pain were to contradict each other, then one would have to establish the root of this cycle as consisting of two manners of engaging in an object which were internally inconsistent with each other.


[3073]
DES NA CHOS KYI BDAG ‘DZIN ‘JIG LTA’I RGYUR STON PA NA, MA RIG PA’I NANG TSAN GNYIS RGYU ‘BRAS SU STON ZHING, DE GNYIS KA NYON MONGS KYI RTZA BAR STON PA NA RANG DANG ‘DZIN STANGS MI MTHUN PA’I NYON MONGS GZHAN THAMS CAD KYI RTZA BAR STON PA YIN LA, TSUL DE YANG DE GNYIS KA LA YOD PAS MI ‘GAL TE, MA RIG PA’I RIGS ‘DRA SNGA PHYI GNYIS KA ‘KHOR BA’I RTZA BAR MI ‘GAL BA BZHIN NO,,

As such, when what you teach says that the tendency to hold to some self-nature to things is the cause of the view of destruction, what you’re saying is that two variations of misunderstanding are acting as cause & effect.  When you say that both of these are roots for negative emotions, then what you are saying is that they are roots of each and every other negative emotion which holds things in a manner which is inconsistent with the way that they do.  It would not be a contradiction for this way of things to apply to both, for it similar to the way in which earlier and later manifestations of misunderstanding can both represent the root of the circle of pain, without there being any contradiction.



The system of the Numerists

[3074]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, BDAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA DANG, BDAG GI BA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA’O,,

Which brings us to our second section from above: how it is that we deny the idea that either me or mine could exist through any nature of their own.  We proceed in two steps: denying that the self could exist through any nature of its own; and then denying that what belongs to the self could exist through any nature of its own.


[3075]
DANG PO LA DRUG ,GZHAN SDES BTAGS PA’I PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BDAG DGAG ,RANG SDES BTAGS PA’I PHUNG PO NYID BDAG TU ‘DOD PA DGAG ,DE GNYIS KYI LHAG MA’I PHYOGS RTEN DANG BRTEN PA SOGS GSUM DGAG ,DE NYID DANG GZHAN NYID DU MED PA’I GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD DGAG ,BDAG BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA TZAM DU BZHAG PA DPE DANG BCAS PAR BSHAD, DE LTAR BZHAG PA LA MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI RTOG PA SPANG SLA BA’I YON TAN BSTAN PA’O,,

The first step here we will cover with six different topics:

 (1) denying the position concocted by other groups, who believe that there is a self which could exist which was essentially separate from the parts to the person;

(2) denying the position concocted by some of our own groups, who believe that the parts to the person themselves represent the self;

(3) denying positions other than these two, which themselves involve three ideas including one about the basis and what relies upon this basis;

(4) denying a substantial form of the person that would be neither itself nor something other than itself;

(5) explaining, with the use of a metaphor, how it is that we establish that the self is something labelled through dependence; and

(6) a demonstration of how setting things forth in this manner has the advantage of making it easy to eliminate the notion where we hold to things in some extreme way.


[3076]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, PHYOGS SNGA MA BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these has two parts of its own: a statement of the position that the others take; and then disproving that position.  Here is the first.


[3077]
‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I DMIGS PA BDAG DE CI ZHIG CES DE NYID MI SHES PAS STON ZHIG CE NA,

Suppose that someone comes and poses the following question:

We would like to ask you just what the self which is the object of focus for the view of destruction could be; we personally can’t picture it, and hope you will enlighten us.


[3078]
‘DI LA GNYIS, GRANGS CAN GYI LUGS BRJOD PA DANG, BYE BRAG PA LA SOGS PA’I LUGS BRJOD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

In response we will cover this point in two stages.  That is, first we will describe the system of the Numerists.  And then secondly we’ll describe the system of the Detailers and so on.  Here then is the former.


	[3079]
[VI.121]
Ātmā tīrthyaiḥ kalpyate nityarūpo
‘kartābhoktā nirguṇo niṣkriyaś ca,
Kaṃcit kaṃcid bhedam āśritya tasya
bhedaṃ yātāḥ prakriyās tīrthikānām.

[VI.121a]
,ZA PO RTAG DNGOS BYED PO MIN PA’I BDAG
,YON TAN BYA MED MU STEGS RNAMS KYIS BRTAGS,

		That River system
		Imagines a consumer
		Which is a self that is
Unchanging & functioning;

Although not
The creator.

It does not have
The qualities, and
Performs no activity.	


[3080]
RE ZHIG DE ZA BA PO STE BDE SDUG SOGS LA LONGS SPYOD PA PO DANG, RTAG PA’I DNGOS PO [f. 216b] DANG RNAM ‘GYUR RNAMS KYI BYED PA PO MIN PA DANG, RDUL MUN SNYING STOBS KYI RANG BZHIN GYI YON TAN MED PA DANG, KHYAB PAR BYED PA NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR NA, BYA BA MED PAR MU STEGS GRANGS CAN RNAMS KYIS BRTAGS SO,,

Just to get a start here, that River system called the “Numerists” imagines a self which is a consumer—meaning the one who experiences pleasure and pain and the like.  They say that it is unchanging, but at the same time functioning; although it is not the creator of the expressions.  It does not have the nature of the three qualities of activity, darkness, and light.  It is the one thing which pervades all things, but it performs no activity.


[3081]
DE LA GRANGS CAN PA DAG NI,
,RTZA BA’I RANG BZHIN RNAM PAR ‘GYUR MIN LA,
,CHEN PO SOGS BDUN RANG BZHIN RNAM ‘GYUR ZHING,
,BCU DRUG PO NI RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA STE,
,SKYES BU RANG BZHIN MA YIN RNAM ‘GYUR MIN,
ZHES SMRA BAR BYED DO,,

Their own text on the topic says:

The fundamental nature is no creation;
The seven that include the great principle
Are both creator and creation.

Those sixteen are creations; and the soul
Is neither creator nor creation.


[3082]
DE LA ‘BRAS BU RAB TU BYED PAS NA RANG BZHIN NO,,

We call it the “fundamental nature” because it spews out results.


[3083]
SKABS GANG DU BYED CE NA, SKYES BU’I ‘DOD PA MTHONG BA’I DUS SU’O,,

When does it do this?  When it sees the soul’s desire.


[3084]
GANG GI TSE SGRA LA SOGS PA’I YUL NYE BAR LONGS SPYOD PA’I RNAM PA CAN GYI ‘DOD PA SKYES PA DE’I TSE SKYES BU’I ‘DOD PA YONGS SU SHES PA’I RANG BZHIN DANG SKYES BU SBYOR ZHING, DE NAS GTZO BOS SGRA LA SOGS PA ‘BYIN NO,,

A desire first arises in the soul, wishing to partake of sounds and so on.  The fundamental nature, which knows every wish of the soul, next joins with it; and then the primal nature gives forth the sounds and other objects.


[3085]
DE’I TSUL NI ‘DI YIN TE, RANG BZHIN LAS NI CHEN PO’O, ,DE LAS KYANG NGA RGYAL LO, ,DE LAS DBANG PO BCU GCIG DANG DE TZAM LNGA STE BCU DRUG PO’I TSOGS SO,,

Here’s the process through which this occurs.  It happens step by step: from the fundamental nature comes the great principle, and from that in turn comes the sense of self.  From the sense of self come the eleven powers, along with the five subtle elements—for a total of sixteen.


[3086]
BCU DRUG PA LAS KYANG ‘BYUNG BA LNGA NI DE TZAM LNGA LAS TE, SGRA LA SOGS PA LNGA LAS ‘BYUNG BA LNGA ‘BYUNG NGO ZHES BYA BA NI RIM PA YIN NO,,

From among the sixteen then, the five great elements derive from the five subtle elements; the order is indicated in the wording, “the five great elements come from sound and the rest of the five.”


[3087]
RNAM ‘GYUR MIN LA ZHES PA NI ‘BRAS BU RAB TU BYED PA KHO NA YIN GYI, CHEN PO LA SOGS PA LTAR RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA YANG NI MA YIN NO,,

When we say that something is “not a creation,” what we mean is that it only produces results, and is not itself a creation—as the great principle and the rest are.


[3088]
CHEN PO LA SOGS PA BDUN NI RAB TU BYED PA’ANG YIN LA RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA YANG YIN NO,,

The seven including the great principle are both creators and creations.


[3089]
CHEN PO LA SOGS PA YANG RANG GI RNAM ‘GYUR LA LTOS NAS RANG BZHIN YIN LA, RTZA BA’I RANG BZHIN LA LTOS NAS RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA YIN NO,,

The great principle and the others are creators from the perspective of the things which are their creations.  From the perspective of the root nature, though, they are creations.


[3090]
BLO’I DBANG PO LA SOGS PA BCU DRUG NI RNAM ‘GYUR KHO NA’O,,

The sixteen which include the sense power of the mind and so on are only creations.


[3091]
[f. 217a] SKYES BU NI RAB TU BYED PA’ANG MA YIN LA, RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA YANG MA YIN NO,,

The soul is neither a creator nor a creation.


[3092]
RNA BA LA SOGS PA’I DBANG PO LNGA YID KYIS BYIN GYIS BRLABS PAS YONGS SU GZUNG BA’I YUL SGRA LA SOGS PA DAG LA BLOS ZHEN PAR BYED LA, DE NAS BLOS ZHEN PAR BYAS PA’I DON LA SKYES BUS SEMS PAR BYED DO,,

The ear and the rest of the five powers, inspired by the mental sense power, cause the mind to yearn towards sound and the rest: the objects that they hold.  And then the soul turns its thoughts towards the objects that the mind has been yearning for.


[3093]
DE LTAR YUL LA SPYOD ‘DOD PAS YUL NYE BAR LONGS SPYOD CING, GANG GI TSE YUL LA CHAGS PA CHUNG BA NYID KYIS SKYES BUS YUL LA NYES DMIGS SU BLTAS PAS, CHAGS PA DANG BRAL BAR GYUR PA DE’I TSE RIM GYIS BSAM GTAN SGOM ZHING, DE LA BRTEN NAS LHA’I MIG GI MNGON ZHES THOB PA NA,

Out of a desire for these objects, the soul comes to partake of them.  At some point the desire for objects lessens, and the soul comes to see faults in these things.  Through becoming free of this desire, the soul cultivates meditative concentration—which leads to the achievement of the type of clairvoyance known as “the eyes of a god.”


[3094]
MIG DE’I SGO NAS GTZO BO LA LTA BAR BYED LA, DES BLTAS PA DANG, GTZO BO DE GZHAN GYI BUD MED LTAR NGO TSA BAR GYUR PAS, BDAG LA MI ‘GRO ZHING ‘BRAL BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

The soul then looks upon the primal nature with these new eyes.  When it does, then the nature—like a woman who is being stared at by a man other than her husband—becomes shy, and shrinks from view.  This nature then no longer comes to the self, and becomes disconnected from it.


[3095]
RNAM ‘GYUR GYI TSOGS THAMS CAD KYANG SKYE BA’I RIM PA LAS BZLOG PA’I SGO NAS GTZO BO DE NYID DU RAB TU THIM PA’I PHYIR, MI GSAL BA’I NGO BOR GYUR PA DE’I TSE SKYES BU NYAG GCIG GNAS TE, DE’I PHYIR GROL BA ZHES BYA’O,,

At this point the entire group of expressions—the creations—dissolves completely back into the primal nature, in reverse order to the process by which they were created.  The nature then is reduced to its own featureless essential form, and the soul simply rests in total isolation.  This is how this system describes liberation.


[3096]
BDAG DE NI RTAG TU YAN GAR BA’I NGO BOR GNAS PA’I PHYIR RTAG PA ZHES BYA’O,,

Since the self will rest then, forever alone in its essence, they speak of it as “unchanging.”


[3097]
GANG ZHIG NI BYED PA PO YIN LA GANG ZHIG NI BYED PA PO MA YIN ZHE NA, ‘DI LA RDUL MUN SNYING STOBS RNAMS NI YON TAN GSUM MO, ,DE LA RDUL NI G-YO BA DANG ‘JUG PA’I BDAG NYID CAN NO, ,MUN PA NI LCI BA DANG G-YOG PA’I BDAG NYID CAN NO, ,SNYING STOBS NI YANG BA DANG RAB TU GSAL BA’I BDAG NYID CAN NO, ,BDE BA DANG SDUG BSNGAL DANG GTI MUG ZHES PA NI ‘DI DAG KHO NA’I RNAM [f. 217b] GRANGS SO,,

Let’s talk about which of these are creators, and which are not.  The three qualities are activity, darkness, and light.  Activity has the nature of action and engagement.  Darkness has the nature of heaviness, and of smothering.  Light has the nature of lightness, and brightness.  When we speak of pleasure, pain, and dark ignorance, they are synonyms for these three.


[3098]
‘DI DAG CHA MNYAM PA’I SKABS NI GTZO BO STE, ‘DIR YON TAN DAG GTZOR GYUR CING RAB TU ZHI BAR GYUR PA’I PHYIR RO,,

“Primal nature” refers to a state of balance between these three, because the three qualities are both primary to that state and at rest in that state.


[3099]
DE DAG RNAM PAR MI ‘GYUR BA’I SKABS NI RANG BZHIN NO,,

We call it “fundamental nature” when these qualities are in a state where they no longer fluctuate.


[3100]
RANG BZHIN LAS NI CHEN PO STE, CHEN PO DANG BLO GNYIS NI RNAM GRANGS TE PHYI YUL DANG NANG GI SKYES BU’I GZUGS BRNYAN GNYIS KA ‘CHAR BA ZHIG GO ,CHEN PO LAS NI NGA RGYAL LO,,

From that fundamental nature comes the great principle.  “Great principle” and “intellect” refer to the same thing.  It reflects both the images of objects which are outside, as well as that of the soul, which is inside.


[3101]
NGA RGYAL NI GSUM STE RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA CAN DANG, SNYING STOBS CAN DANG, MUN PA CAN NO,,

From the great principle comes the sense of self, and from the sense of self come three groups of things which relate to the activeness, darkness, or light.


[3102]
DE LA RNAM PAR ‘GYUR BA’I NGA RGYAL LAS NI DE TZAM LNGA STE, GZUGS DANG SGRA DANG DRI DANG RO DANG REG PA DAG GO

From the sense of self relating to activity come the five subtle elements: sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible things.


[3103]
,DE TZAM DAG LAS NI ‘BYUNG BA RNAMS TE, SA DANG CHU DANG ME DANG RLUNG DANG NAM MKHA’ ZHES BYA BA DAG GO

From those subtle elements come the great ones, called “earth,” “water,” “fire,” “wind,” and “space.”


[3104]
,SNYING STOBS CAN GYI NGA RGYAL LAS NI LAS KYI DBANG PO LNGA PO DAG {%NGAG} DANG LAG PA DANG RKANG PA DANG RKUB DANG, ‘DOMS KYI DBANG PO DANG, BLO’I DBANG PO LNGA PO MIG DANG RNA BA DANG SNA DANG LCE DANG LPAGS PA’AM LUS KYI DBANG PO DANG, GNYIS KA’I BDAG NYID CAN GYI YID DE DE LTAR NA BCU GCIG GO

Eleven expressions come from the sense of self related to light.  They are five organs of action (speech, hands, legs, anus, and sexual organ) and the five sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin or body sense power).  The combination of the organs of action and the sense organs amounts to the mental sense power.


[3105]
,MUN PA CAN GYI NGA RGYAL NI NGA RGYAL GZHAN GNYIS KA’I ‘JUG PAR BYED PA’O,,

The sense of self related to darkness inspires the activities of the other two qualities.


[3106]
DE LA CHEN PO DANG NGA RGYAL DANG DE TZAM LNGA STE BDUN NI RANG BZHIN DANG RNAM ‘GYUR GNYIS KA’O,,

The group of seven made up of the great principle, the sense of self, and the five subtle elements are both creators and creations.


[3107]
DBANG PO BCU DANG YID DANG ‘BYUNG BA LNGA NI RNAM ‘GYUR KHO NA DANG,

The ten powers, the mind, and the five great elements are only creations.


[3108]
RTZA BA’I RANG BZHIN GTZO BO NI RANG BZHIN KHO NA’O ZHES PA NI GZHUNG LUGS SO,,

The root nature—the primal nature—is only a creator.  This is what their text is saying.



The system of the Detailers

[3109]
GNYIS PA NI,

Here then is the second point mentioned above: a description of the system of the Detailers and so on.


	[3110]
[VI.121b]
,DE’I DBYE CUNG ZAD CUNG ZAD LA BRTEN NAS,
,MU STEGS CAN RNAMS LUGS NI THA DAD ‘GYUR,

	Based upon various
	Minor distinctions,

	There have developed
	The different systems
	Of the River Schools.


[3111]
JI LTAR GRANGS CAN DAG GIS BDAG KHAS BLANGS PA DE BZHIN DU, BDAG DE’I DBYE BA CUNG ZAD CUNG ZAD LA BRTEN NAS MU STEGS CAN RNAMS KYI LUGS NI THA DAD PAR ‘GYUR TE,

Thus then do those of the Numerist School accept the idea of a self; and based upon various minor distinctions in this presentation of a self, there have developed the different systems of the River Schools.


[3112]
‘DI LTA STE BYE BRAG PA RNAMS NI BLO DANG BDE BA DANG SDUG BSNGAL DANG, ‘DOD [f. 218a] PA DANG SDANG BA DANG ‘BAD PA DANG CHOS DANG CHOS MA YIN PA DANG BYA BA’I SHUGS TE, BDAG GI YON TAN DGU SMRA BAR BYED DO,,

Here is how we describe these systems.  The Detailers profess that there are nine different attributes of the self; these include (1) mind; (2) pleasure; (3) suffering; (4) desire; (5) aversion; (6) endeavor; (7) teachings; (8) the opposite of the teachings; and (9) the power of action.


[3113]
DE LA BLO NI YUL ‘DZIN PA’O,,

(1) The mind is that which perceives objects.


[3114]
BDE BA NI ‘DOD PA’I YUL NYAMS SU MYONG BA’O,,

(2) Pleasure is that which undergoes desirable objects.


[3115]
SDUG BSNGAL NI DE LAS BZLOG PA’O,,

(3) Suffering is the opposite of that.


[3116]
‘DOD PA NI ‘DOD PAR GYUR PA’I DNGOS PO LA RE BA ‘CHA’ BA’O,,

(4) Desire is the aspiration to attain desirable entities.


[3117]
SDANG BA NI MI ‘DOD PA’I YUL LA RGYAB KYIS PHYOGS PA NYID DO,,

(5) Aversion is feelings of repulsion towards undesirable objects.


[3118]
‘BAD PA NI DON BSGRUB PAR BYA BA LA DE’I MTHAR THUG PAR SEMS KYI MKHAS PA NYID DO,,

(6) Endeavor consists of a special mental fluency in achieving the final ends of attempts to accomplish some goal.


[3119]
GANG LAS MNGON PAR MTHO BA DANG NGES PAR LEGS PA ‘GRUB PA DE NI CHOS SO,,

(7) Teachings are those things which allow us to achieve higher rebirths and final good.


[3120]
DE LAS BZLOG PA NI CHOS MA YIN PA’O,,

(8) The reverse of that is what we refer to when we speak of the opposite of the teachings.


[3121]
SHES PA LAS SKYES SHING SHES PA’I RGYUR GYUR PA NI ‘DU BYA BA’I SHUGS SO,,

(9) The power of undertaking action is born of understanding, and is also the cause of understanding.


[3122]
BDAG GI YON TAN DGU PO DE JI SRID DU BDAG LA ‘DU ZHING YOD PA DE SRID DU, DE DAG GIS SBYAR BA’I DGE BA DANG MI DGE BA’I LAS SGRUB PA’I PHYIR ‘KHOR BAR ‘GYUR LA,

As long as these nine attributes of the self are incorporated into ourselves—as long as they are present there—then we tend to undertake good deeds and bad karma utilizing the nine. This then causes us to circle in the wheel of pain.


[3123]
GANG GI TSE SKYES BU YANG DAG PAR RTOGS PA’I SHES PAS BLO LA SOGS PA’I YON TAN RNAMS RTZA BA DANG BCAS PAR GCOD PA DE’I TSE, RANG GI BDAG NYID LA GNAS SHING THAR BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

At some point, knowledge which has a perfect understanding of the individual is able to cut off mind and the other attributes, along with their roots.  When we arrive at this place, we are residing in our true self, and we reach freedom.


[3124]
BDAG DE YANG RTAG PA DANG, ‘BRAS BU’I BYED PA PO DANG, ‘BRAS BU LA LONGS SPYOD PA’I ZA BA PO DANG, YON TAN DANG BCAS PA DANG, KHYAB PA’I PHYIR NA BYA BA MED PAR YANG SMRA’O,,

This self is also described as being beyond all activity, for it is unchanging; it is the creator of all results; it is the consumer which undergoes all results; it is the one that possesses qualities; and it is overarching.


[3125]
BYE BRAG PA KHA CIG SKUM PA DANG, RKYONG BA NYID KYIS BYA BA DANG BCAS PAR KHAS LEN NO,,

There are some members of the Detailers who accept the idea that this self also involves the activities of perfect retraction and extension.


[3126]
RIG BYED DU SMRA BA DAG NI BUM PA LA SOGS PA THA DAD PA RNAMS KYI NAM MKHA’ GCIG YIN PA LTAR, RTEN LUS THA DAD PAS BRTEN PA BDAG GCIG NYID SNA TSOGS PA NYID DO ZHES PA LA SOGS PAR [f. 218b] KHAS LEN NO,,

Those who follow the ancient books of knowledge point to the way in which a water pitcher and other such separate objects share a single space.  In the same way, they say, there is a single grand self that rests upon all the separate bodies there are; and thus they can refer to that as “the multiplicity of things.”  And so they maintain these and other similar beliefs.


[3127]
‘GREL PAR BDAG GI KHYAD PAR CUNG ZAD CUNG ZAD LA BRTEN NAS MU STEGS CAN RNAMS KYI LUGS PHAN TSUN THA DAD PAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES GSUNGS PAS GZHUNG ‘DI’I LUGS KYIS GRANGS CAN DE’I DBYE BA LA BRTEN NAS, MU STEGS KYI LUGS SO SOR GYES PAR ‘CHAD PA NI DON MA GO BA’O,,

The autocommentary notes that “the systems of the River Schools are distinguished from each other by various slight differences in how they see the self.”  As such, people who say that the different divisions of the River Schools in general are based upon the divisions within the Numerists as described in this one classic text have not caught its import correctly.



Disproving others on the self

[3128]
GNYIS PA NI,

This then brings us to our second part from before: disproving the position that others have taken here.


	[3129]
[VI.122]
Itthaṃbhūtasyātmano nāsti sattvaṃ
nāhaṃkārasyāśrayaś caiṣa yuktaḥ,
Vandhyāputrasyeva jāter viyogān
no saṃvṛtyāpīṣyate sattvam asya.

,MO GSHAM BU LTAR SKYE BA DANG BRAL PHYIR,
,DE LTAR GYUR PA’I BDAG NI YOD MIN ZHING,
,’DI NI NGAR ‘DZIN RTEN DU’ANG MI RIGS LA,
,’DI NI KUN RDZOB TU YANG YOD MI ‘DOD,

		Because things
		Are devoid of arising,
		
Like the child
		Of a barren woman,

		It is not the case
With the self—
		They are not reality.

		This cannot
		Logically be
		The basis for

		Our tendency to
		Grasp to some “me [f. 210b].”

		We deny
		The existence
		In a deceptive sense
		As well.


[3130]
MU STEGS CAN RNAMS KYI GZHUNG LUGS RE RE LAS BDAG MI ‘DRA BA GANG ZHIG SMRAS PA DE NI, DE DAG GIS JI LTAR BTAGS PA DE LTAR GYUR PA STE DE KHO NA NYID DU YOD PA MIN STE, SKYE BA DANG BRAL PA STE MA SKYES PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’I RTAGS NI MU STEGS RANG GI RJES SU DPAG PA STE KHAS BLANGS PA’O,,

The various scriptural traditions within the River Schools thus then present different versions of the self.  But it is not the case that what they impute here is the way things actually are: it is not the case that it is indeed reality.  The reasoning which says that “things are devoid of arising, because they cannot have arisen” is just the River Schools expressing their own process of deduction: their own position.


[3131]
DPER NA MO GSHAM GYI BU LTAR RO,,

And then they would say, “It’s like the child of a barren woman.”


[3132]
RTAGS DES SMRAS PA’I CHOS CAN BKAG KYANG SKYON MED PA NI RTAGS DANG CHOS GNYIS KA RNAM BCAD TZAM YIN PA’I GNAD KYIS SO,,

They would hold the idea then that the expressed subject of the logical statement was voided by the reason presented—and for them there would be no problem with that.  And that’s because of the cogent point here that both the reason presented and the subject under consideration were both simple absences.


[3133]
DE LTAR GZHAN GYIS BRTAGS PA’I BDAG ‘DI NI NGAR ‘DZIN LHAN SKYES KYI RTEN DU’ANG MI RIGS TE, RTAGS DANG DPE NI SNGAR BZHIN NO,,

As such we can say that this self as perceived by these other schools of thought cannot logically be the one that provides the basis for the inborn version of our tendency to grasp to some “me.”  The reason for saying this, and the consistent example to support that reasoning, are as we have described them earlier.


[3134]
NGAR ‘DZIN GYI RTEN ZHES PA NI DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI NANG NAS DMIGS PA’I YUL MA YIN ZHES PA STE, DE’I YUL NI NGA TZAM DANG GANG ZAG SOGS YIN LA, DE YANG DNGOS POR ‘DOD PAS MA SKYES PA DANG ‘GAL BA’O,,

When we speak of “the support of our tendency to hold to some ‘me’,” we are referring to two possible objects of focus.  One of these can be called “the non-object of that focus,” which is the object of this tendency represented by the simple “me”; the person; or something of the like.  This is something that we accept as being a functional entity; and so it contradicts the concept of never arising.


[3135]
RNAM PA’I YUL NI GANG ZAG GI BDAG YIN PAS DE NI THA SNYAD TZAM DU YANG MA GRUB PA YIN PAS, MA SKYES PA DANG MI ‘GAL LO,,

Then there is the object as represented by the aspect here—which would refer to the self-nature of the person.  This is not something which can exist even in a nominal sense, and so it would not contradict the idea of things never arising.


[3136]
DE’I PHYIR ‘DI’I LUGS KYIS GANG ZAG GI BDAG THA SNYAD DU YOD PAR ‘DOD DO ZHES PA NI ‘DI PA’I GRUB MTHA’I ‘GANGS DANG, ‘JIG LTA’I DMIGS RNAM GYI YUL ZHIB TU MA PHYED PAR BYUNG RGYAL DU SMRA BA’O,,

Therefore those who say that “The way that this present system accepts the existence of the self-nature to the person, at least nominally, is its one most crucial concept” and then failing to distinguish this carefully from the object represented by the aspect of focus taken on by the view of destruction represents no more than blurting out whatever comes to their minds.


[3137]
DE LTAR BDAG YOD PA DANG NGAR ‘DZIN GYI YUL YIN PA [f. 219a] BKAG PA NI DGAG BYA LA DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR SBYAR BA’I DBANG DU BYAS PA’O,,

As such, the case is that when we deny the existence of a self, and that thing which the tendency to hold to a “me” takes as its object, this is all done relative to applying the additional qualification of speaking ultimately to the object we deny.


[3138]
DE KHO NAR MA ZAD KUN RDZOB TU YANG DE GNYIS ‘GOG PA YANG SHES PAR BYA STE, DE’I TSE BDAG YOD PAR MI ‘DOD CES PA NI BDAG RDZAS SU YOD PA MIN PA’O,,

And that’s not all; you should also understand that we are denying these two in a deceptive sense as well.  At that point, when we say that we deny the existence of a self, this does not consist of a self which exists substantially.


[3139]
RTAGS DANG DPE DE GNYIS KYIS DGAG BYA GNYIS ‘GOG PAR MA ZAD KYI, GZHAN YANG MU STEGS PAS BTAGS PA’I BDAG DE’I KHYAD PAR KUN KYANG YOD PA MA YIN NO ZHES BYA BAR RIG PAR BYA’O,,

It is not only the case that this reason and this consistent example—these two—are being used to disprove two different objects which we deny.  You should also understand that here we are saying as well that all the possible features of all the kinds of self imagined by the River Schools are things that could never exist.


	[3140]
[VI.123]
,GANG PHYIR BSTAN BCOS BSTAN BCOS LAS DE’I KHYAD,
,MU STEGS RNAMS KYIS GANG BSTAN DE KUN LA,
,RANG GRAGS MA SKYES GTAN TSIGS KYIS GNOD PA,
,DE PHYIR DE KHYAD KUN KYANG YOD MA YIN,

		It’s because
		All the features that
		These River Schools
		Describe both in

		Those classical commentaries
		And these classical commentaries

		Are themselves
		Drawn into question
		
		By the logic of things
		Never arising
		That they declare among
		Themselves so widely.

		These characteristics
		Are, none of them,
		Things that can exist.
	

[3141]
DE’I RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR NA GRANGS CAN GYI BSTAN BCOS DANG, BYE BRAG PA SOGS KYI BSTAN BCOS LAS BDAG DE’I KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS MU STEGS RNAMS KYIS GANG BSTAN PA DE KUN LA STE THAMS CAD LA, MU STEGS RANG LA GRAGS PA’I MA SKYES PA’I GTAN TSIGS KYIS GNOD PA DE’I PHYIR RO,,

And why is that?  It’s because every one of the features of the self as it is presented both in those classical commentaries of the Numerists, and in these classical commentaries of the Detailers and other such schools—all those qualities that these River Schools describe—are themselves drawn into question by the logic of things never arising that these schools declare among themselves so widely.


[3142]
DE YANG SNGAR BSHAD PA’I GRANGS CAN DANG BYE BRAG PA’I BDAG GI KHYAD PAR BSHAD PA KUN KYANG YOD PA MA YIN NO ZHES DGAG PAR BYA’O,,

With this then the characteristics of the self that we have heard up to here explained by the Numerists and the Detailers are, none of them, things that can exist.  This is the denial we are making here.


[3143]
PHYOGS ‘DIS NI BDAG TU SMRA BA THAMS CAD DU MA SKYES PA’I GTAN TSIGS DANG MO GSHAM GYI BU YI DPES, DE DAG GIS BTAGS PA’I BDAG GI NGO BO DANG KHYAD PAR RNAMS GSAL BAR RIG PAR BYA’O,,

You should understand then that this position completely discounts both the essential nature and the particular qualities of the self that these other schools imagine is there.  This is accomplished by presenting both the logic involving the way in which things cannot arise, and the consistent example of the son of a barren woman, to all the groups that profess the existence of some self.


	[3144]
[VI.124]
Skandhebhyo’nyo vidyate nāta ātmā
hitvā skandhāṃs tad grahasyāprasiddheḥ,
Lokasyāhaṃkāra buddher apīṣṭo
naivādhāro’tadvidām ātmadṛṣṭeḥ.

,DE PHYIR PHUNG PO LAS GZHAN BDAG MED DE,
,PHUNG PO MA GTOGS DE ‘DZIN MA GRUB PHYIR,
,’JIG RTEN NGAR ‘DZIN BLO YI RTEN DU YANG,
,MI ‘DOD DE RIG MIN PA’ANG BDAG LTA’I PHYIR,

		And this is why
		There is no self
		Separate from the
		Parts of the person:

		Because you could
		Never establish
		The capacity to hold
		To some that didn’t
		Involve the parts.

		Neither are we saying
		That it is the basis
		For the tendency
		To hold to some “me”

		That the world
		Thinks of;

		That is not something
		Which could ever
		Make sense.

		And that’s because
		Even then we could
		View something
		As the self.
	

[3145]
DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO GZHAN PA’I BDAG MED DE, PHUNG PO BZUNG BA MA GTOGS PAR BDAG DE YAN GAR DU ‘DZIN PA MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And this is why we can say that there is no self which is essentially separate from the parts of the person; and that’s because you could never establish the capacity to hold to some discrete self that didn’t involve holding to the parts of the person.


[3146]
DE NI BDAG PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD NA ‘BREL BA GNYIS KA MED PAS ‘BREL MED DU ‘GYUR LA,

What this is saying is that—if there were to exist some self that were essentially separate from the parts to the person—then neither of the two possible types of relationship would hold; meaning that there would be no connection to anything.


[3147]
DE’I TSE BUM PA MA BZUNG BAR SNAM BU YAN GAR DU ‘DZIN PA BZHIN DU ‘DZIN PA ZHIG ‘ONG DGOS NA, DE ‘GAR YANG MA MTHONG BA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’O,,

In this case then it would be similar to saying that to perceive a bolt of cloth discretely, you would have to go and be careful not to perceive a water pitcher.  If this were the way that holding things had to work, then—what we are saying is—you would never see holding with anything.


[3148]
DE LTAR YANG RTZA SHE LAS,
,BDAG [f. 219b] NI NYE BAR LEN PA LAS,
,GZHAN DU ‘THAD PA NYID MA YIN,
,GAL TE GZHAN NA LEN MED PAR,
,GZUNG YOD RIGS NA GZUNG DU MED,

On this point we see, in Wisdom, the following lines:

It would be totally
Incorrect to say
That the self was something
Other than the parts
That we have taken on.

If it were not this way,
And it were correct
To say that we could hold
To something without
Taking it, then we
Could never hold to anything.


[3149]
CES DANG,
,GAL TE PHUNG PO RNAMS LAS GZHAN,
,PHUNG PO’I MTSAN NYID MED PAR ‘GYUR,

We also read:

	If it were something other
	Than the parts to the person,
	There would be no definition
	Of it being the parts.


[3150]
ZHES GSUNGS TE NYE BAR LEN PA NI PHUNG PO’O,,

When the reference here is read simply as “what we have taken on,” you should understand that it is referring to the parts to the person that we have taken on.


[3151]
SKYON GZHAN YANG PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BDAG ‘DI ‘JIG RTEN SEMS CAN GYI THOG MA MED PA NAS KYI NGAR ‘DZIN GYI BLO YI RTEN TE DMIGS PAR YANG MI ‘DOD DE,

There is another problem here as well.  That is, neither are we saying that this supposed self which is essentially separate from the parts to a person is the basis or object of focus for the tendency to hold to some “me” that the world—which is to say, living beings—has tended to think of “me,” for time with no beginning.


[3152]
MU STEGS KYIS BTAGS PA LTAR GYI BDAG DE RIG PA MIN PA STE DE’I RNAM PAR MI ‘DZIN PA’ANG MNGON PAR ZHEN PA’I KHYAD PAR LAS BDAG DANG BDAG GI ZHES BDAG TU LTA BAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Which is to say, that self as it is imagined by the River Schools is not something which could ever make sense.  And that’s because, if it could, then that would mean that even if then we didn’t perceive any aspect of it, we could view something as the self—as being “self” or “something of the self”—simply by virtue of a strong wrong belief about it. 


[3153]
‘DI NI NGAR ‘DZIN BLO YI RTEN DU’ANG MI RIGS ZHES SNGAR BKAG PA DANG MI ZLOS TE, SNGAR NI BDAG RDZAS SU YOD PA TZAM BDAG LTA’I DMIGS PA YIN PA BKAG LA, ‘DIR NI PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA DMIGS PA YIN PA BKAG PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This by the way is not just a simple repetition of the denial that we made earlier, where we also said that it would be illogical to say that this self was the support for the tendency to believe in some “me.”  In that previous case, we were denying only that a self which existed in a substantial way could serve as the object of focus for the belief in a self.  What we’re denying now is that this object of focus could be something that was essentially separate from the parts to the person.


[3154]
CI STE GANG ZAG GANG DAG DA LTA BDAG DE RTAG PA DANG MA SKYES PA LA SOGS PAS KHYAD PAR DU BYAS PA MI SHES PA DE DAG LA YANG SNGON GOMS PA’I DBANG GIS BDAG DE’I YUL CAN NGAR ‘DZIN PA’I LTA BA YOD PAR ‘GYUR RO SNYAM NA,

One might wonder then about the following question:

Suppose we have a person who in the present moment does not perceive the self as being distinguished by characteristics such as being unchanging, or having never arisen.  Wouldn’t it be the case though that they too—by force of what they had become accustomed to in the past—could possess the view where they held that the subject aspect of the self was “me”?


[3155]
DE NI MA YIN TE GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PAS BLO BSGYUR BA KHO NA LA, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BDAG NGAR ‘DZIN GYI RTEN DU ‘DZIN PA YOD PA YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Our answer is that it would not be the case.  And that’s because it is only with those individuals whose minds have been influenced by inferior schools of thought that the tendency to hold to some “me” grasps onto, as its basis, a self which is essentially separate from the parts to a person.


[3156]
SEMS CAN GANG DAG LA SNGAR GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PA’I GOMS PA MED PA DE DAG LA YANG ‘DIR NGAR ‘DZIN ‘JUG PAR MTHONG STE, ‘DI LTA STE,

We do however also see here—with individuals who have not previously become accustomed to some inferior school of thought—the mind engaging in the tendency to hold to some “me.”  And here is how that works.


	[3157]
[VI.125]
Tiryakto ye kalpaśaḥ saṃpravṛddhā
nityājātaṃ te’pi paśyanti nainam,
Dṛṣṭvā teṣām apyahaṃkāra vṛttiṃ
skandhebhyo’nyas tena nātmāsti kaścit.

,GANG DAG DUD ‘GRO BSKAL MANG BRKYAL GYUR PA,
,DES KYANG MA SKYES RTAG ‘DI MA MTHONG LA,
,NGAR ‘DZIN DE DAG LA YANG ‘JUG MTHONG STE,
,DES NA PHUNG PO [210b] LAS GZHAN BDAG ‘GA’ MED,

		Consider too
Those beings
		Who have passed
		Their lives—

		Over the length
		Of many eons—
		As an animal:

		Those who may not
		Be perceiving it
		As never starting,
		And as unchanging.

		Even with these
		We can see
		Engaging in
		Grasping on
		To some “me.”

		We can say then
		That there does not
		Exist any kind
		Of a self at all

		Which could be
		Separate from the
Parts to a person.


[3158]
SEMS CAN GANG DAG DUD ‘GROR BSKAL PA MANG POR TSE BRGYAL {%BRKYAL} BAR GYUR PA SNGAR DE TZAM SONG DU ZIN KYANG, DA DUNG DU YANG DUD ‘GRO’I SKYE GNAS [f. 220a] LAS LDOG PAR MI ‘GYUR BA DES KYANG,

Consider here beings who have passed their lives—over the length of many eons—in an existence as an animal.  Despite the fact that they have spent so long this way in their past, that doesn’t mean that they too will necessarily be able to turn away from a birth as an animal in the time to come.


[3159]
MU STEGS KYIS BTAGS PA’I MA SKYES PA DANG RTAG PA’I BDAG ‘DI MA MTHONG BA DE DAG LA YANG, NGAR ‘DZIN ‘JUG PAR MTHONG BA STE SHES NAS,

The same applies to those who may not be perceiving any self as imagined by those of the River Schools; that is, a self which has never started, and which is unchanging.  Even with these individuals we can see—we can perceive—cases where they engage in grasping on to some “me.”


[3160]
SHES RAB CAN SU ZHIG MU STEGS PAS BTAGS PA’I BDAG RNAM PA DE LTA BU NGAR ‘DZIN GYI RTEN DU ZHEN PAR BYED,

What person then of intelligence would get attached to thinking that the support for this kind of a tendency to hold to a “me” would necessarily have to be supplied by the type of self concocted by the River Schools?


[3161]
DES NA PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO GZHAN PA’I BDAG ‘GA’ANG MED DO,,

In conclusion then we can say that there does not exist any kind of a self at all which could be essentially separate from the parts to a person.


[3162]
KYANG GI SGRAS NI DMYAL BA LA SOGS PAR SKYES PA RNAMS SDUD PA’O,,

When we said “they too” a few sentences back, we meant it to be read as including as well beings such as those who had taken birth in the hell realms, or the like.



Other groups on parts
being a self

[3163]
GNYIS PA LA LNGA, PHUNG PO BDAG TU ‘DOD PA LA GNOD BYED BSTAN PA, DE LTAR ‘DOD PAR MI RIGS PA’I SGRUB BYED BSTAN PA, PHUNG PO BDAG TU SMRA BA LA GNOD BYED GZHAN BSTAN PA, PHUNG PO BDAG TU GSUNGS PA SOGS KYI DGONGS PA BSHAD PA, GZHAN GYI LUGS ‘BREL MED DU BSTAN PA’O,, 

These brings us to our second topic from above: denying the position concocted by some of our own groups, who believe that the parts to the person themselves represent the self.  This we offer in five different sections—

1) A presentation of problems with the position that the parts to the person constitute the self;

2) A presentation of support for saying that this kind of belief is incorrect;

3) A presentation of other problems with saying that the parts to the person are the self;

4) An explanation of the actual intent behind statements that the parts to the person are the self, and so on; and

5) A demonstration that the position of others here is irrelevant to the case.


[3164]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, DNGOS KYI DON DANG, SKYON SPONG GI LAN DGAG PA’O,,

The first section has two parts of its own: the actual point; and then refuting the answer, where the other side attempts to deny the problems we’ve raised.


[3165]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, PHYOGS SNGA MA BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these, in turn, covers two sections of its own: a statement of the other side’s position, and then a denial of that particular position.


	[3166]
[VI.126]
Skandhā evālambanaṃ tvātma dṛṣṭeḥ
skandhebhyo’nyasyātmanaḥ siddhyabhāvāt,
Skandhān pañcāpyeka icchanti kecic
cittaṃ tvekaṃ niśrayāyātma dṛṣṭeḥ.

,PHUNG PO LAS GZHAN BDAG GRUB MED PA’I PHYIR,
,BDAG LTA’I DMIGS PA PHUNG PO KHO NA’O,
,KHA CIG BDAG LTA’I RTEN DU PHUNG PO NI,
,LNGA CHAR YANG ‘DOD KHA CIG SEMS GCIG ‘DOD,

		There is no self
		Which exists
		As separate from
		The parts to
		The person.

		As such,
		Seeing a self
		Takes as its
		Object of focus
		Only the parts.

		Some number
		Describe the support
		Of the view of a self
	
		As consisting
		Of all five
Of the parts.

		Some assert
		That it is only
		The mind.


[3167]
‘DIR RANG GI SDE PA DAG NA RE PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO GZHAN PA’I BDAG GRUB PA MED PA’I PHYIR BDAG TU LTA BA STE ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI NANG GI DMIGS PA NI PHUNG PO KHO NA YIN TE, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA DANG NANG GI PHUNG PO DMIGS PAR ‘JOG PA GNYIS SU NGES PA LAS SNGA MA MI RUNG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here certain of our own groups make the following argument:

There is no self which exists as essentially separate from the parts to the person; as such, the tendency to see a self—which is to say, the view of destruction, which has two objects of its focus—takes as its inner object of focus only the parts to the person.  And that’s due to the fact that the objects of focus here are fixed at two—no more, no less: one which is essentially separate from these parts to a person, and a second which is focused on the heaps inside; and it would be inappropriate here to include the former.


[3168]
DE’I PHYIR BDAG NI RANG GI PHUNG PO TZAM YIN NO ZER RO,,

As such—they say—the self consists of our own heaps, and nothing else.


[3169]
PHYOGS ‘DI NI GNAS MA BU’I SDE PA LA SOGS PA ‘PHAGS PA MANG POS BKUR BA’I SDE PA’I ‘O, ,DE LAS KYANG MANG BKUR BA KHA CIG BDAG LTA’I RTEN DU STE DMIGS PAR NI,

This particular position is one of the Vatsiputra and certain other sections within what is called the “Widely Respected Group,” itself named from a very honored, realized being.  Here is the way that some number of the members of the Widely Respected describe the support, or object of focus, of the view of a self.  


[3170]
RANG GI PHUNG PO LNGA CHAR YANG ‘DOD CING, BDAG [f. 220b] TU MNGON PAR ZHEN PA ‘DI YANG PHUNG PO LNGA PO DE LAS YIN NO ZHES SMRA STE,

They would state first that this object consists of all five of the parts to the person; and that when we say that someone is strongly attached to the idea of a self, this is something that comes from those same five parts.


[3171]
JI SKAD DU BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS DGE SLONG DAG DGE SBYONG NGAM BRAM ZE GANG SU DAG CIG BDAG GO SNYAM DU YANG DAG PAR RJES SU LTA BA DE DAG NI, NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA PO ‘DI KHO NA LA YANG DAG PAR RJES SU LTA’O, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTA BU’O,,

On this point they would reference the Conqueror himself, who made the following very clear statement on the matter:

Think, o monks, of any spiritual practitioner or brahmin who holds the complete form of this view where they think, “There is some kind of self here.”  What they are focusing on in this complete way is the five parts to a person that have been taken on; and nothing else.


[3172]
DE NYID KYI PHYIR DE DAG LA KHYED CAG GI LTA BA ‘DI NI ‘JIG PA’I BDAG NYID CAN GYI TSOGS PA LA YIN GYI BDAG GAM BDAG GI BA LA NI MA YIN NO, ZHES GSAL BAR MDZAD PA’I SLAD DU,

And it is for this exact reason that it is the view which all of you entertain towards these things which is the one directed towards the collection characterized by destruction; it is not directed at the self, or that which belongs to the self.


[3173]
BDAG DANG BDAG GI BA’I RNAM PAR ZHUGS PA’I LTA BA LA ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BAR GSUNGS SO, ZHES SMRAS TE, NYER LEN GYI PHUNG PO LNGA LA LTA’O

And so what this is saying is that what was described as the view of the collection of destruction is one which is focused upon the self, and what belongs to the self.  That is, it is focused upon the five parts to a person that we have taken on.


[3174]
ZHES GSUNGS PA LA BRTEN NAS BDAG LTA’I DMIGS PA PHUNG PO LNGAR KHAS BLANGS SO,,

And so—based on this statement—this group would say that the object of focus for the view of a self is the five parts to the person.


[3175]
MANG BKUR BA KHA CIG NI SEMS GCIG PU LA BDAG GO ZHES ‘DOD DE,
,BDAG NYID BDAG GI MGON YIN GYI,
,GZHAN NI SU ZHIG MGON DU ‘GYUR,
,BDAG NYID LEGS PAR THUL BAS NI,
,MKHAS PAS MTHO RIS THOB PAR ‘GYUR,
ZHES TSIGS SU BCAD PA LAS SEMS LA BDAG GI SGRAR GSUNGS SO,,

Some members of the Widely Respected Group assert that it is only the mind which is the self, given that the following lines speak of the mind as the “self”:

The self itself
Is the protector of the self;
Where else can we see one?

When they master
Restraining this self itself,

The wise attain
The higher forms of birth.


[3176]
‘DI GA LAS SHE NA, PHUNG PO LAS THA DAD PA’I BDAG MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, MDO GZHAN LAS KYANG, ,SEMS ‘DUL BAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR TE,
,SEMS ‘DUL BA NI LEGS PA STE,
,SEMS ‘DUL BA NI BDE BA ‘DREN,
ZHES BYA BA DE LAS SO,,

From where can we understand this?  First of all, there is no self which is separate from the parts to the person.  And other sutras state as well that it is the mind which we have to restrain:

	Restraining the mind
	Is a goodness;

	Restraining the mind
	Brings on happiness.


[3177]
DE’I PHYIR NGAR ‘DZIN PA’I GZHI SEMS LA BDAG CES GDAGS SO ZHE’O,,

That’s then why it is that when we speak of the basis for holding something to be “me,” we are referring to the mind as the “self.”


[3178]
RTOG GE ‘BAR BA LAS KYANG, ‘DI LTAR KHO BO CAG KYANG THA SNYAD DU RNAM PAR SHES PA LA BDAG GI SGRA DNGOS SU ‘DOGS TE, ‘DI LTAR RNAM PAR SHES PA NI YANG SRID PA LEN PA’I PHYIR BDAG [f. 221a] YIN NO, ZHES LUS DANG DBANG PO’I TSOGS DAG LA NYE BAR ‘DOGS PA’I PHYIR TE ZHES DANG,

The Blaze of Reasoning too says,

And so it is that we as well—at least in a nominal sense—use the word “self” directly to refer to consciousness.  That is, when they say that “Consciousness is the self in the sense that it takes on the next life,” what we are giving the name is the body, and the collection of the senses.


[3179]
DE YANG MDO KHA CIG LAS SEMS DUL NA BDE BA ‘THOB PAR GSUNGS LA, KHA CIG TU BDAG DUL BAS MTHO RIS THOB PAR GSUNGS PAS SEMS LA BDAG TU ‘JOG CES LUNG DANG,

Now we also see some sutras were it says that—if we are able to restrain the mind—then we will be able to achieve happiness.  In other sutras we see the statement that we can attain the higher rebirths if we are able to restrain the self.


[3180]
PHUNG PO LEN MKHAN NI BDAG YIN LA RNAM SHES KYIS YANG SRID LEN PA’I PHYIR RNAM SHES BDAG TU BZHAG GO ZHES RIGS PA’I SGRUB BYED SMRA’O,,

We also see statements of the supporting logic here: “The one who takes on the parts to a person is the self; and since it is our consciousness which takes on the next rebirth, then we can say that it is consciousness which must be the self.”


[3181]
SLOB DPON ‘DI KUN GZHI MI BZHED PAS LUS LEN PA’I RNAM SHES NI YID KYI RNAM SHES YIN TE, KUN GZHI MI ‘DOD PA GZHAN YANG DE DANG ‘DRA’O,,

Our present master does not accept the concept of a foundation consciousness; as such, the consciousness which takes on a body must be the consciousness of the thoughts.  This would follow in the same way for others as well who do not accept the idea of foundation consciousness.


[3182]
KUN GZHI ‘DOD PAS KUN GZHI RNAM SHES NYID GANG ZAG GI MTSAN GZHIR SMRA’O,,

Those who do accept foundation consciousness would describe this foundation type of consciousness as that thing which is referred to as the “person.”


[3183]
DE YANG LUGS DE DAG GIS NYAN RANG GIS GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD DU MED PAR RTOGS PAR ‘DOD KYANG, RNAM SHES GNYIS PO RDZAS YOD DU MED PAR RTOGS PAR MI ‘DOD PAS,

These particular systems would—moreover—accept the idea that listeners and self-made buddhas are capable of realizing that there is no person who exists in a substantial way.  Nonetheless, they would not agree that these could come to the realization that these two types of consciousness are not something which could exist in a substantial way.


[3184]
GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA’I RDZAS SU MED PAR SMRA BA NI GANG ZAG GI RANG GI LDOG PA NAS ‘DOD PA YIN GYI, GANG ZAG GI MTSAN GZHI RNAM SHES LA DE LTAR ‘DOD PA MIN NO,,

As such, when people assert that the individual is not something which could exist substantially, in a self-standing way, they are referring to the person in the abstract; they would not though agree to this idea that what we refer to as the “person” could be consciousness.



Denying others on the parts

[3185]
GNYIS PA NI,

Here is our second section from above: a denial of the other side’s position on the parts.


	[3186]
[VI.127]
Skandhā ātmā ced atas tad bahutvād
ātmānaḥ syus te’pi bhūyāṃsa evam,
Dravyaṃ cātmā prāpnuyāt tad dṛśaś ca
dravye vṛttau vaiparītyaṃ ca na syāt.

,GAL TE PHUNG PO BDAG NA DE PHYIR DE,
,MANG BAS BDAG DE DAG KYANG MANG BAR ‘GYUR,
,BDAG NI RDZAS SU ‘GYUR ZHING DER LTA BA,
,RDZAS LA ‘JUG PAS PHYIN CI LOG MI ‘GYUR,

		Suppose the five parts
		Were the self.

		In that case then—
		Since these are multiple—

		One would also
		Have multiple selves.

		The self would be
		Something substantial,

		And the one
		That acts to view these
		Engages in substance;

		As such, it is not something
		Which is mistaken.

	
[3187]
GAL TE RANG RGYUD KYI PHUNG PO LNGA BDAG YIN PA’I PHYOGS LTAR NA, DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO DE MANG BAS GANG ZAG GCIG LA YANG BDAG DE DAG KYANG MANG POR ‘GYUR RO,,

Suppose things were as this other position says it: suppose the five parts to the person taken in by our own being were themselves the self.  In that case then—since these parts to the person are themselves multiple—one single individual would also have multiple selves.


[3188]
GANG GI LTAR NA SEMS BDAG YIN PA DE’I LTAR NA MIG LA SOGS PA’I RNAM PAR SHES PA’I DBYE BAS SAM SKAD CIG RE RE LA, RNAM SHES DU MA SKYE BA DANG ‘GAG PA’I DBYE BAS MANG BA’I PHYIR BDAG KYANG MANG POR ‘GYUR RO,,

In the case that the mind was the self, then given that there are many divisions to the consciousness of the eye and so one—as well as many instants of each of these—then there would be many consciousnesses, with each one split into divisions of starting or stopping.  In this case then again, the self would have to be multiple in number.


[3189]
‘DIR ‘GREL PA LAS, BDAG MANG POR THAL BA PHYOGS SNGA MA GNYIS KYI DANG PO LA [f. 221b] ‘PHEN PA DANG, YANG NA SKYON GZHAN YANG GNYIS KA LA ‘PHEN PAR GSUNGS SO,,

The autocommentary notes that the logical necessity that the self would be multiple is implied by the first of the two previous positions.  We can also say that other problems are implied by both positions.


[3190]
‘DI NI MANG PO DANG NGO BO GCIG PAR ‘DOD PA TZAM LA ‘PHEN DU MI RUNG BAS, BDAG DANG PHUNG PO GNYIS THA DAD GTAN MED GCIG TU ‘DOD PA LA ‘PHEN PA’O,,

These are not implications that would logically hold only with the assertions of being multiple or essentially the same.  As such, these implications would hold with the two of the self and the parts to the person being a single thing where they were absolutely never separate.


[3191]
DE YANG DANG PO NAS GZHAN GYIS DE LTAR KHAS MA BLANGS PAS, NGO BO GCIG PA DANG THA DAD TZAM YIN PA BRDZUN PA LA SKYON MED KYANG, BDAG PHUNG GNYIS BDEN PAR KHAS LEN PA LA NGO BO GCIG NA DBYER MED KYI GCIG TU PHUL NAS, DE’I ‘OG TU BDAG MANG PO DANG PHUNG PO LNGA GCIG TU THAL BA ‘PHANG NGO,,

And the fact is too that the other side would never, from the very start, accept this kind of thing.  Therefore being essentially the same, or simply separate, would not be a problem in the case that things were false.  If though one were to accept that the two of the self and the parts to the person existed in truth, then saying that they were essentially the same would mean that they would have to be an inseparable single thing.  And then subsequent to that you would have to say that the self was multiple, and that the five parts to the person were singular.


[3192]
DE’I TSE ‘JIG RTEN SKYE BA NA GANG ZAG NYAG GCIG SKYE’O ZHES BYA BA’I LUNG LAS NA, PHA ROL POS BDAG MANG POR ‘DOD PA YANG MIN NO,,

We see though references which say that “When someone is born in the everyday world, it is only the one single person who is born.”  It is not then the case that the other side here is asserting that the self is somehow multiple.


[3193]
BDAG NI RDZAS SU ‘GYUR ZHING STE, GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I RDZAS ‘DAS PA LA SOGS PA’I DBYE BAS, THA DAD PAR ‘GYUR BA RNAMS KHO NA LA PHUNG PO NYID DU BRJOD PA’I PHYIR DANG,

As the line here puts it, “The self would be something substantial, and…”  Which is to say, suppose that we do assert the divisions of form and the rest into substance that was past, and so on.  As such, it would be only the separate entitites here that we could refer to as those very parts to the person.


[3194]
DE RNAMS KHO NA LA BDAG TU BSNYAD PA’I PHYIR BDAG RDZAS SU YOD PAR ‘GYUR NA, 

And since it is only those that we could refer to as the “self,” the self would have to be something that existed in a substantial way.  And yet we know from specific references that it’s not that the other side here would agree to the idea that the self existed in a substantial way.


[3195]
DGE SLONG DAG LNGA PO ‘DI DAG NI MING TZAM THA SNYAD TZAM BTAGS PA TZAM STE, GANG ‘DI LTA STE, ‘DAS PA’I DUS DANG MA ‘ONGS PA’I DUS DANG, NAM MKHA’ DANG, MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA DANG, GANG ZAG GO ZHES BYA BA DANG,

First of all, we have this statement from scripture:

O monks, these five exist only in name; they are something labeled, with no more than a term.  And what they are named is things like “the time which has already passed,” or “the time that is yet to come,” or “space,” or “going beyond grief,” or “the person.”


[3196]
DE BZHIN DU,
,JI LTAR YAN LAG TSOGS RNAMS LA,
,BRTEN NAS SHING RTAR BRJOD PA LTAR,
,DE BZHIN PHUNG PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS,
,KUN RDZOB SEMS CAN ZHES BYA’O,
ZHES BYA BA ‘DI LAS NA PHA ROL POS BDAG RDZAS SU ‘DOD PA YANG MA YIN NO,,

In the same way, we see:

	It’s just the same way
	That we refer to something
	As a “wagon,”

	Based upon the
	Collection of its parts.

	That is, we refer
	To a living being,
	In a deceptive way,

	Based upon their heaps.


[3197]
GZHAN YANG PHUNG PO DER LTA BA’I ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA RDZAS LA ‘JUG PA STE RDZAS SU GRUB PA’I YUL CAN YIN PAS, SNGON PO DANG SER PO LA [f. 222a] SOGS PA’I SHES PA LTAR PHYIN CI LOG NYID DU MI ‘GYUR RO,,

We can moreover say that the view of destruction that acts to view these parts to the person engages in substance; which is to say, it is a subject which takes as its object things which exist substantially.  As such, in the sense that it is aware of things like blue and yellow and the like, it is not something which is exclusively mistaken.


[3198]
DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG LTA SPONG BA NA RIGS ‘DRA RGYUN MA CHAD DU MI ‘BYUNG BA’I TSUL GYIS SPANGS PA MIN PA’AM, SNGO SER SOGS TZAM LA DMIGS PA’I SHES PA LTAR ‘JIG LTA LA DMIGS PA’I ‘DUN PA’I ‘DOD CHAGS SPANGS PA KHO NAS SPONG BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

This means that—when we do eliminate the view of destruction within ourselves—it is not as if we get rid of it in the manner that there is no longer an unbroken flow of matching instances.  Nor is it that we have eliminated it only by eliminating attachment focused upon the view of destruction, as would be the case with an awareness focused only upon blue or yellow or the like.


	[3199]
[VI.128]
Ātmocchedī nirvṛtau syād avaśyaṃ
nāśotpādī nirvṛteḥ prāk kṣaṇeṣu,
Kartur nāśāt tat phalābhāva eva
bhuṃjītānyenārjitaṃ karma cānyaḥ.

,MYA NGAN ‘DAS TSE NGES PAR BDAG CHAD ‘GYUR,
,MYA NGAN ‘DAS SNGON SKAD CIG DAG LA NI,
,SKYE ‘JIG BYED PO MED PAS DE ‘BRAS MED,
,GZHAN GYIS BSAGS LA GZHAN GYIS ZA BAR ‘GYUR,

		When we attain nirvana,
		The self would surely
		Have discontinued.

		In the instants
		Prior to nirvana,
		They would have been
		Going in & out
		Of existence.

		There could be
		No agent involved,
		And so there would be
		No such result.

		What was collected
		By one would be
		Consumed by another.


[3200]
GZHAN YANG RANG GI PHUNG PO BDAG YIN NA KHYOD KYI LTAR NA LHAG MED KYI MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA’I TSE PHUNG PO LNGA CHAR CHAD PAS, NGES PAR BDAG CHAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Moreover, there’s another issue here.  If the parts to the person that one possesses are the self, then according to you when we attain nirvana without any remainder, then all five parts to the person would have discontinued.  In that case then, the self itself would surely have discontinued as well.


[3201]
DE’I PHYIR MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI CHAD PA’I LTA BAR ‘GYUR TE, KHYED CAG GIS GANG BDAG TU BZUNG BA DE NYID LA RTAG CHAD DU ‘DZIN PA MTHAR ‘DZIN GYI LTA BAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And because of that then, what we have here would become the version of extreme view where we hold that everything has simply discontinued.  And that in turn is because you fellows have taken the position that the tendency to grasp to a self constitutes the extreme view of holding either that things would last forever, or that they have simply come to a complete stop.


[3202]
MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PAR ZHUGS PA’I SNGON GYI SKAD CIG DAG LA NI, PHUNG PO SKAD CIG RE RER SKYE ‘JIG BYED PA LTAR BDAG KYANG SKAD CIG RE RER NGO BO NYID KYIS SO SO BA’I SKYE ‘JIG BYED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

In the instants prior to entering into nirvana, the parts to the person would have been going in & out of existence with each passing moment.  And in that case, the self itself would be similar: in every passing instant, it would be going through discrete startings and stoppings that existed in & of themselves.


[3203]
DE’I PHYIR SKYE BA DRAN PA NA JI LTAR NGA’I LUS ‘DI SNGON BYUNG BAR GYUR TO, ZHES BYA BAR MI ‘DZIN PA DE BZHIN DU, DE’I TSE DE’I DUS NA NGA RGYAL PO NGA LAS NU ZHES BYA BAR GYUR TO, ZHES BYA BA ‘DI YANG GSUNG BAR MI ‘GYUR TE,

Thus then it would be similar to when we recall a past rebirth that we had: it’s not as if we are able to say, “I had a body like this in those days gone by.”  It’s not as if we say to ourselves, “In those days, in that life, I was that king whose name was ‘Nurse from Me’.”


[3204]
DE’I DUS KYI BDAG KYANG LUS LTAR ZHIG PAS, DA LTA MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, TSE ‘DIR SNGAR GYI BDAG LAS RANG BZHIN GYIS THA DAD PA’I BDAG GZHAN SKYES PAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s because you have taken the position that the self that I had in those days gone by would have ended just as the body did—and could no longer exist at present.  And that means you are saying that yet another self would have taken birth here in this life: one which was essentially separate from that previous self.


[3205]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,NYE BAR LEN NYID BDAG MA YIN,
,DE ‘BYUNG BA DANG ‘JIG PA YIN,
,NYE BAR BLANG BA JI LTA BUR,
,NYE BAR LEN PO YIN PAR ‘GYUR,
ZHES DANG,

Wisdom says as well,

What you took on
At your birth, itself,

Is not the self;
For that is something
Which comes about
And comes to an end.

And whatever applies
To what was taken on
Applies as well
To the one who took it.


	[3206]
,GAL TE PHUNG PO BDAG YIN NA,
,SKYE DANG ‘JIG PA CAN DU ‘GYUR,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

We also see:

	If the self
	Were the parts
	To the person,

	Then it would be
	Something that
Went through starting
And stopping too.


[3207]
SKAD [f. 222b] CIG SNGA PHYI BA RNAMS NGO BO NYID KYIS GZHAN YIN NA, DE’I TSE BYED PA PO’I BDAG MED PAS, LAS LA YANG GNAS PA’I RTEN MED PA’I PHYIR LAS KYANG MED PAS, LAS DE’I ‘BRAS BU DANG ‘BREL BA MED PA NYID DU ‘GYUR RO,,

Suppose then that successive moments, previous and subsequent, were other than each other, by their very essence.  In that case, there could be no self to the agent involved; and so there would moreover be no basis for the action itself to remain—which means there would be no action either.  And then there would be absolutely no connection to the result of such an action.


[3208]
GAL TE SKAD CIG MA SNGA MAS BYAS PA’I LAS KYI ‘BRAS BU SKAD CIG MA PHYI MA RNAMS SU LONGS SPYOD PAS SKYON MED DO SNYAM NA,

In response then one might have the thought that “Well, the result of the action taken by something in the previous instant would be experienced by things in the later instants; and so there would be no problem here.”


[3209]
DE’I TSE GZHAN GYIS BSAGS PA’I LAS KYI RNAM PAR SMIN PA GZHAN GYIS LONGS SPYOD PA’I PHYIR, RGYUD GZHAN GYIS BSAGS PA’I ‘BRAS BU LA GZHAN GYIS ZA BAR ‘GYUR RO,,

At that point though the ripening of a karma collected by one entity would we experienced by another; which means that the result of what was collected by a person in one mental stream would be consumed by a person in another.


[3210]
DE LTAR NA LAS BYAS PA CHUD ZOS PA DANG, MA BYAS PA DANG PHRAD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And in that case, it would be possible for a person to commit a karma and see the result simply fade away, without having to be experienced; and one would also meet up with the results of a karma that one had never originally committed.


[3211]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,GAL TE ‘DI NI GZHAN ‘GYUR NA,
,DE MED PAR YANG ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR,
,DE BZHIN DU NI GNAS ‘GYUR ZHING,
,DE MA SHI BAR SKYE BAR ‘GYUR,

Wisdom too puts it this way—

	If this were to become
	Something other,
	Then that would have
	To stop existing.

	We would stay as well
	In the very same way,
	And take a birth
	Without dying first.


	[3212]
,CHAD DANG LAS RNAMS CHUD ZA DANG,
,GZHAN GYIS BYAS PA’I LAS RNAMS NI,
,GZHAN GYIS SO SOR MYONG BA DANG,
,DE LA SOGS PAR THAL BAR ‘GYUR,

Things would simply stop,
And karma would fade away;

And the karmas committed
By one person would be
Experienced by another,
One by one.

These and other such things
Are the implications here.


[3213]
ZHES SNGA PHYI RANG BZHIN GYIS GZHAN YIN NA SNGA MA LA LTOS PA MI RUNG BAS SNGA MA DE MED PAR YANG ‘BYUNG BA DANG, SNGA MA’I BDAG DE DE BZHIN DU GNAS PAS, DER MA SHI BAR ‘DIR SKYE BAR ‘GYUR BA SOGS GSUNGS SO,,

What this is saying is that—if what came before and what came after were different from each other, by nature—then it would be wrong to say that the one was relying upon the previous.  And then that would have to occur even in the absence of what had come before.  The self of the previous time would have to remain in the very same manner, which means that a person would, for example, have to take their rebirth without having died first.



Refuting answers on the parts

[3214]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: Refuting the answer, where the other side attempts to deny the problems we’ve raised.


	[3215]
[VI.129]
Na syād doṣaḥ santatis tattva taś ced
ukto doṣaḥ santateḥ prāgvicāre,
Skandhā nātmā nāpi cittaṃ ca tasmād
ito lokasyāntavattvādyabhāvāt.

[VI.129a]
,DE NYID DU RGYUD YOD NA SKYON MED NA,
,SNGAR RNAM DPYAD TSE RGYUD LA NYES BSHAD ZIN,
,DE PHYIR PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG MI RIGS,

		Suppose it is the case
		That there is a stream
		That exists
		In & of itself;

		And so there is 
		No problem here.

		When we did
		Our examination earlier,
		We already explained
		The problems.

		As such, it is
		Illogical that the parts
		To a person,

		Or the mind,
		Are the self.


[3216]
GAL TE SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI DAG GZHAN YIN MOD KYI, DE LTA NA YANG RGYUD GCIG YIN PAS SKYON MED DO ZHE NA,

One may come with the following comment:

It is admittedly the case that those things of the prior and subsequent instants in time are different things from one another; but even then, they represent a single flow.  As such, there is no such problem as the one you have raised here.


[3217]
DE KHO NA NYID DU RGYUN CAN RDZAS THA DAD PA RNAMS LA RGYUD GCIG YOD PAS SKYON MED NA, DE YANG MI ‘THAD DE RANG BZHIN GYIS THA DAD PA RNAMS LA RGYUD GCIG YIN PA LA, SNGAR RNAM PAR DPYAD PA BYAS PA’I TSE NYES PA BSHAD ZIN TE, BYAMS PA NYE SBAS LA BRTEN CHOS RNAMS [f. 223a] NI, ZHES BYA BA DER RO,,

Suppose it is the case that there is no problem here, because things occurring in a stream that exists in & of itself exist as separate substances sharing a single flow.  This idea though must be mistaken, since when we did our examination earlier, we already explained the problems with things that are separate by nature acting in a single flow.  This in fact was back when we spoke about “John leaning on Joe.”


[3218]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,GAL TE LHA LAS MI GZHAN NA,
,DE LTA NA NI MI RTAG ‘GYUR,
,GAL TE LHA MI GZHAN YIN NA,
,RGYUD NI ‘THAD PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

Wisdom also states—

If a worldly deity
Is other than a human,

Then in that case
They must be changing.

If the deity and the human
Are other than each other,

Then it must be incorrect
To say there is a flow.


[3219]
DE’I PHYIR RANG BZHIN GYIS THA DAD PA RNAMS LA RGYUD GCIG PA NYID MI RIGS PAS, LAS MA BYAS PA DANG PHRAD PA DANG BYAS PA CHUD ZOS PA SOGS KYI THAL ‘GYUR LDOG PA MED DO,,

And so it is illogical to speak of a single flow when we are talking about two things that are separate from each other by nature.  As such, you have in no way succeeded in repulsing the ridiculous consequences we raised: that one would meet with the consequences of an action that they had never committed; and that the consequences of actions which one had indeed committed could just fade away on their own—or other ideas of the like.


[3220]
DE’I PHYIR RANG GI PHUNG PO RNAMS DANG RANG GI SEMS RANG GI BDAG NYID DU ‘DOD PA MI RIGS SO,,

As such, it is illogical to cling to your belief that the parts to a person are ones self itself; or that ones mind is ones self.



Support for denying that
the parts constitute the self

[3221]
GNYIS PA NI,

Here then is our second point from before: a presentation of support for saying that the kind of belief presented is incorrect.


	[3221]
[VI.129b]
,’JIG RTEN MTHA’ LDAN LA SOGS MED PHYIR RO,

		And that’s because
		There was none
		About the universe

		Having a beginning
		And an end,
		And so on.		


[3222]
JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I RIGS PAS PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG MIN PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU MA ZAD KYI GZHAN YANG ‘JIG RTEN MTHA’ DANG LDAN PA NYID DANG, LA SOGS PAS MTHA’ DANG MI LDAN PA DANG, GNYIS KA DANG GNYIS KA MA YIN PA DANG, ‘JIG RTEN RTAG PA DANG, MI RTAG PA DANG, GNYIS KA DANG GNYIS KA MA YIN PA DANG, DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA GRONGS PHAN CHAD ‘BYUNG BA DANG, MI ‘BYUNG BA DANG, GNYIS KA DANG GNYIS KA MA YIN PAR LTA BA BCU GNYIS DANG, LUS GANG YIN PA DE NYID SROG GO ZHES PA DANG, LUS KYANG GZHAN LA SROG KYANG GZHAN NO ZHES BYA BAR LTA BA GNYIS TE BCU BZHI PO DER LUNG BSTAN DU MED PAR ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR LUNG MA BSTAN GYI LTA BAR SDE PA THAMS CAD KYIS ‘DON PA’I PHYIR PHUNG PO BDAG TU MI RIGS SO,,

It is, further, illogical to say that the parts to the person are the self, because that idea in turn leads to what all the various groups agree are viewpoints on which no opinion was expressed.  And that’s because of the fact that the same logic which we just explained not only clarifies how the parts to the person, and the mind itself, cannot be the self; it also shows how there are fourteen different ideas which we accept as being ones about which no opinion was expressed.  These fourteen are the following; they begin with twelve different possible viewpoints—

(1) The question of whether the universe has a final beginning and an end, and “so on,” which includes the following—

(2) The question of whether the universe has no beginning & end;

(3) The question of whether the universe both has a beginning & end, and has no beginning & end;

(4) The question of whether the universe neither has a beginning & end, nor has no beginning & end;

(5) The question of whether the universe will last forever;

(6) The question of whether the universe will not last forever;

(7) The question of whether the universe will both last forever and not last forever,

(8) The question of whether the universe will neither last forever nor not last forever;

(9) The question of whether the Buddha still exists after he passes away;

(10) The question of whether the Buddha does not still exist after he passes away;

(11) The question of whether the Buddha both exists and does not exist after he passes away;

(12) The question of whether the Buddha neither exists nor does not exist after he passes away.
