And then on top of these, we add the two of:

	(13) The viewpoint that it is the body which is the self; and

(14) The viewpoint that the body is one thing, and the self is a different thing.


[3223]
GAL TE ‘JIG RTEN GYI SGRAS PHUNG PO RNAMS ‘DZIN NA, DE’I TSE PHUNG PO RNAMS SKYE ‘JIG BYED PA RANG GI LUGS YIN PA’I PHYIR, ‘JIG RTEN MI RTAG PAR LUNG BSTAN DGOS PA DANG,

If we take the term “the universe” in this context as referring to the parts of the person, then it would be our own position that these parts act to start and stop.  And in that case, the Buddha would indeed have had to express the opinion that the universe would not last forever.


[3224]
MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA’I ‘OG ROL TU KHYED LTAR NA PHUNG PO RNAMS MED PAS ‘JIG RTEN MTHA’ [f. 223b] DANG LDAN PA DANG, DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA GRONGS PHAN CHAD YOD PA MIN NO ZHES LUNG BSTAN DGOS PAR YANG ‘GYUR RO,,

And then—still, according to you—subsequent to ones reaching nirvana, there could be no parts to the person; which means that the Buddha should have expressed the opinion that the universe did indeed have a beginning and an end.  And he would have had to opine that the One Thus Gone did not exist after he passed away.


[3225]
DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN MTHA’ DANG LDAN PA LA SOGS PA LA LAN LUNG STON PA BKAG PA’I PHYIR, PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG GO ZHES MI RIGS SO,,

As such, it is illogical for you to say that the parts to the person are the self, given that you have denied that it would be possible to express an opinion in response to questions such as whether the universe has a beginning or an end, and so on.


[3226]
DE LA SROG NI BDAG GI RNAM GRANGS SO,,

When they say “life” in this context, by the way, they are considering it a synonym for “the self.”


[3227]
‘JIG RTEN NI BDAG LA BRTZAMS NAS ‘DRI BA’O,,

And questions about the universe are considered to start off from the self itself.


[3228]
DE YANG NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU LA BSAMS NAS ‘DRI NA NI, KHYAD GZHI MA GRUB PAS KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS LUNG BSTAN DU MED DO,,

If these questions about things are intended as starting off from an individual considered as something inner, then—since the basis that we are considering doesn’t exist at all—then it would be impossible to express an opinion about a quality that this basis supposedly possessed.


[3229]
BTAGS PA TZAM GYI BDAG GI SGO NAS LUNG BSTAN NA NI, DE’I TSE ‘DRI BA PO DE RNAMS DE ‘DRA BA’I BDAG MED RTOGS PA’I SKAL BA DANG MI LDAN PAS DE YANG LUNG BSTAN DU MED DO,,

And suppose, on the other hand, that you are talking about expressing an opinion concerning a self that exists only as something imputed.  In that case, we would have to say that the people asking the question did not have enough good karma to realize that there was no such self.  As such then—again—there could be no expressing an opinion.



Other problems with parts as the self

[3230]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third section from before: a presentation of other problems with saying that the parts to the person are the self.


	[3231]
[VI.130]
Ātmābhāvaṃ paśyato yoginaś ca
bhāvābhāvaḥ syādavaśyaṃ tadā te,
Nityātmā cet kṣipyate te tadānīṃ
skandhāś cittaṃ vā bhaven nāta ātmā.

,KHYOD KYI RNAL ‘BYOR BDAG MED MTHONG BA LA,
,DE TSE NGES PAR DNGOS RNAMS MED PAR ‘GYUR,
,RTAG BDAG SPANGS NA DE TSE DE YI PHYIR,
,KHYOD KYI SEMS SAM PHUNG PO BDAG MI ‘GYUR,

		When your deep
		Practitioner sees
		That things have no
		Self-nature,

		Then at that point
		Those entities
		Have no existence.

		Suppose we eliminate
		An unchanging self;

		At that point,
		As such,
		Your mind,
		And parts to
		The person,

		Could never be
		The self.


[3232]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE, GAL TE KHYOD KYI LTAR NA, RNAL ‘BYOR PAS BDAG MED PA MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA’I DUS SU, CHOS THAMS CAD NI BDAG MED PA’O ZHES BDAG MED PA’I RNAM PAR SDUG BSNGAL GYI BDEN PA MTHONG BA

There are still other problems here.  If things are the way you say they are, then at the point when a deep practitioner sees—directly—that things have no self-nature, then they have seen that aspect of the truth of suffering called “no self”: the point at which we say “nothing in the universe has any nature of its own.”


[3233]
DE’I TSE, NGES PAR PHUNG PO’I DNGOS PO RNAMS MED PAR MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR BAS BDAG MED PA MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR TE, PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

At that point, then definitely one sees that those entities known as the parts to the person have no existence—which is to say, they see the lack of a self-nature.  And that’s because the parts to the person, and the mind, are the self.


[3234]
DE LTAR ‘DOD PA YANG MA YIN PAS DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG MA YIN NO,,

And since this itself is again not something that we could agree to, the parts to the person are not the self.


[3235]
‘O NA PHUNG PO BDAG TU MI ‘DOD PA’I LUGS LA YANG, GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA’I TSE, BDAG GI MTSAN GZHIR ‘JOG PA’I GANG ZAG THAMS CAD MED PAR MTHONG DGOS PAR ‘GYUR TE, RGYU MTSAN MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,

One may come then with the following question:

Even according to the system where they disagree that the parts to the person are the self, something is supposed to happen when you see, directly, the fact that there is no self-nature to the person.  That is, you would have at this point to see that none of the persons normally cited as the defining example of the self even existed; for the logic here is equivalent.


[3236]
‘DI LA RIGS PA PHRA MO MA RTOGS NA LAN MI THEBS PAS BSHAD PAR BYA STE, PHA ROL POS PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG TU ‘DOD PA NI BDAG [f. 224a] DANG GANG ZAG RNAMS THA SNYAD KYI DBANG GIS BZHAG PA TZAM DU MA RTOGS PAR BTAGS DON BTZAL NAS BZHAG PA YIN LA, DE LTAR NA PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG YIN PA DE RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I BDAG TU ‘GYUR LA,

There is some subtle reasoning here that—if you cannot grasp it—will prevent you from giving a proper answer here; so we’d better explain it.  When the other side here holds that the parts to the person, or the mind, are the self, they are at the same time failing to realize that both the self and the person are things that are established only by force of terms.  And then on this basis they are looking for what it is that we gave the name, and making a decision about what it should be.  And then in this way the parts to the person and the mind that are supposed to be the self turn into a self that could exist through some essential nature of its own.


[3237]
BDAG MED PAR MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA’I TSE BDAG DE RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MED PAR RTOGS DGOS PAS, PHA ROL PO LA PHUNG PO DANG SEMS KYI DNGOS PO BDAG YIN PA DE THAMS CAD MED PAR MTHONG DGOS PA’I SKYON ‘JUG LA,

At that point when we see, directly, how there is no self, then we should be coming to a realization of how no such self could ever exist, in any way at all.  As such, our opponent here is incurring the logical fault of saying that one would have to see that none of these entities which were supposed to be the self—the parts to the person and the mind—even existed.


[3238]
MING DU BTAGS PA TZAM GYIS ‘JOG GI ,BTAGS DON BTZAL NAS ‘JOG PAR MI ‘DOD PA’I LUGS LA SKYON DE RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

The system though which says that all these things are established only in name—and which denies that, when you go looking for what it is you gave the name, you could ever find something—incurs none of these problems, in any manner at all.


[3239]
CI STE GANG GI TSE LAS DANG ‘BRAS BU ‘BREL BA’I DUS SU BDAG GI SGRA SBYOR BA DE’I TSE, PHUNG PO LAS DON GZHAN PA’I BDAG MI SRID PA’I PHYIR, PHUNG PO RNAMS KHO NA LA ‘JUG LA, GANG GI TSE BDAG MED PAR MTHONG BA DE’I TSE NI MU STEGS BYED GZHAN GYIS KUN BTAGS PA NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU NYID LA ‘JUG STE,

And now suppose someone comes with the following thought—

At that point when we talk about the connection between karma and its conseuqences, we apply the word “self.”  The term at this point can only apply to the parts of the person, since it is impossible for there to be any self which would be a separate thing from the parts to the person.  When we get to the point then where we see that there is no self, this can only apply to an inner being of the kind which has been concocted by those other, River Schools.


[3240]
DE’I PHYIR BDAG MED PAR MTHONG BA’I DUS SU YANG NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU DANG BRAL BA ‘DU BYED TZAM MTHONG BA YIN LA, DE LA NI PHUNG SOGS KYI DNGOS PO RNAMS MI MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR BA’I SKYON MED DO SNYAM NA,

As such, then, at that point in time when we see that there is no self, all that we are really seeing is that factor that things lack any inner being.  Thus then one would incur none of the faults of not seeing entities such as the parts to the person or the like.


[3241]
GAL TE BDAG MED MTHONG BA’I DUS SU RTAG PA’I BDAG NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU SPONG BA STE MED PAR MTHONG BA YIN NA NI, DE LTAR ‘DOD PA DE’I TSE SKABS GZHAN DU BDAG GI SGRA’I DON GZHAN LA DRANG DU MI RUNG BA DE’I PHYIR, KHYOD KYI PHUNG PO DANG SEMS BDAG TU MI ‘GYUR LA, DE LTA NA NI RANG PHYOGS NYAMS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Suppose then that it is the case that—when we perceive that there is no self—we eliminate the idea of an inner being which was some kind of unchanging self.  At that point where we take this kind of position, it becomes inappropriate for us—in other contexts—to interpret the word “self” as applying to other entities.  As such, then, your parts to the person, and your mind, could never be the self; and in such manner, your own position would be undermined.


[3242]
CI STE LAS ‘BRAS KYI [f. 224b] ‘BREL BA’I SKABS DE LTA BU’I YUL LA NI, MU STEGS KYI BDAG GI SGRA ‘DI ‘JUG PAR MI ‘DOD DE, DE’I PHYIR RANG GI PHYOGS NYAMS PA’I SKYON MED DO SNYAM NA,

One may return then with the following idea:

Well, we would deny that—in the context of the connection between karma and its consequences—this particular type of object could be referred to with the word “self” as it is used by the River Schools.  As such, there is no problem here that could draw into question our position.


[3243]
DE YANG MI RIGS TE, ‘DIR NI NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU BDAG YIN LA, GZHAN DU LAS ‘BRAS KYI SKABS SU NI PHUNG PO RNAMS YIN NO ZHES ‘DOD DGUR SPYOD PA LA RIGS PA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

That itself though is incorrect; for it is illogical for you to take a thousand different positions here, according to your own fancy, saying that this inner being is the self, but that in certain other contexts—such as the point at which we’re talking about karma & its consequences—the self happens to be the parts to the person.


[3244]
GAL TE LAS ‘BRAS KYI SKABS SU NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU LAS BYED PA PO DANG ‘BRAS BU MYONG BA POR MI SRID PA’I PHYIR RO SNYAM NA,

In response one may have another thought:

But at the point where we’re talking about karma & its consequences, it would be impossible for there to be any agent which committed the karma, and any individual who experienced the result of that karma, other than this inner being.


[3245]
PHUNG PO RNAMS LA YANG BDAG GI SGRA ‘DI ‘JUG PA MED DE {%DO} ZHES SNGAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,

But we have already explained this issue earlier, at the point where we said that the word “self” cannot apply to the parts of the person either.


[3246]
DE’I PHYIR GAL TE CHOS THAMS CAD NI BDAG MED PA’O ZHES BYA BA ‘DIR BDAG GI SGRA PHUNG PO RNAMS LA ‘JUG PAR MI ‘DOD NA, GZHAN LAS ‘BRAS KYI SKABS SU YANG MI ‘DOD PAR BYA DGOS SO,,

As such, suppose we disagree that the word “self” in the expression “nothing in the universe has any self” could apply to the parts of the person.  In that case, we would have to disagree in the same way that it could apply in the context of karma & its consequences.


[3247]
CI STE LAS ‘BRAS KYI SKABS SU BDAG GI SGRA PHUNG PO LA ‘JUG PAR ‘DOD NA NI, CHOS THAMS CAD BDAG MED DO ZHES PA ‘DIR YANG BDAG GI SGRA PHUNG PO LA ‘DOD PAR BYA DGOS SO,,

And suppose that you did agree that the word “self” could apply to the parts of the person, in the context of karma & its consequences.  In that case, you would have to agree that the word “self” referred to the parts of the person as well here in the context of saying that “nothing in the universe has any self.”


	[3248]
[VI.131]
Rūpādīnāṃ naiva tattvaṃ gataṃ syād
ātmābhāvaṃ paśyato yoginas te,
Rāgādīnāṃ rūpam ālambya vṛtteḥ
syād utpattis tat svarūpāvibodhāt.

,KHYOD KYI RNAL ‘BYOR BDAG MED MTHONG BA YIS,
,GZUGS SOGS DE NYID RTOGS PAR MI ‘GYUR ZHING,
,GZUGS LA DMIGS NAS ‘JUG PHYIR ‘DOD CHAGS SOGS,
,SKYE ‘GYUR DE YI NGO BO RTOGS MED PHYIR,

		When your
		Deep practitioner
		Sees that there
		Is no self,

		They must not
		Realize the nature
		Of form and the rest.

		They would still be
		Engaging in form
		While perceiving it,

		And subject to
		The arisal of
		Desire and the like;

		Because they had
		Not yet realized
		The essential nature.


[3249]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE, KHYOD KYI LTAR NA RNAL ‘BYOR PAS BDAG MED PA MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA YIS, GZUGS SOGS KYI DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAR MI ‘GYUR TE, DES DE’I TSE MU STEGS KYIS KUN BTAGS PA’I RTAG PA’I BDAG TZAM ZHIG MED PAR MTHONG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

And there’s yet another problem here.  According to your view, when a deep practitioner sees, directly, that there is no self, they must not realize the true nature of form and the rest.  And that’s because—at this point—they would only have seen that the self concocted by the River Schools didn’t exist.


[3250]
DE’I PHYIR GZUGS LA SOGS PA LA BDEN PAR DMIGS NAS ‘JUG PA’I PHYIR, GZUGS SOGS KYI YUL CAN GYI ‘DOD CHAGS SOGS DA DUNG YANG SKYE BAR ‘GYUR TE, GZUGS LA SOGS PA DE YI NGO BO STE YIN LUGS RTOGS PA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

As such, they would still be engaging in things like form and the rest while perceiving them, at the same time, as existing in truth.  And then they would still be subject to the arisal of desire and the like, with the subject state of mind holding to objects such as form and such.  And this would be true because they had not yet realized the essential nature of this form and the rest; which is to say, the way they really were.


[3251]
DPER NA ME TOG GI ZE’U ’BRU LA KHU BYUG YOD CES PA TZAM GYIS ZE’U ‘BRU’I MNGAR PO NYID [f. 225a] RANG GIS MA MYANGS PAR, DE’I MNGAR PO DMIGS PA MA YIN PA

You can go around saying, for example, that there are natural sugars in the anthers of a flower; but just saying that doesn’t mean that you have yourself experienced the real sweetness of those anthers.  And then we would say that the sweetness had still not been perceived.


[3252]
DE BZHIN DU RNAL ‘BYOR PAS PHUNG PO’I CHOS RNAMS RTAG PA’I BDAG DANG BRAL BAR MTHONG BA TZAM YOD DU CHUG KYANG, GZUGS SOGS DE’I RANG BZHIN SNGAR MA SHES PA PHYIS RTOGS PA CI YANG MI DMIGS SO,,

In the same way, we can say that there is a deep practitioner who has seen nothing more than the fact that these entities—the parts to the person—are devoid of any unchanging self; but at the same time they might not have later on perceived, in any way at all, some nature of the form and the rest that they had not understood previously.


[3253]
YANG ZE’U ‘BRU LA KHU BYUG MED PA TZAM GYIS ZE’U ‘BRU’I RO MNGAR PO MYANGS BZHIN DU RO DE MA DMIGS PA MA YIN ZHING, DER GTOGS PA’I MNGON ZHEN SPONG MI NUS PA BZHIN DU,

That is, one is saying further that we can be in the very act of experiencing the sweet taste of anthers and not be a person who is failing to perceive the taste there, just because there is no natural sugar on the anthers; and have thus been unable to give up the craving implied there.


[3254]
GZUGS SOGS KYI RANG GI NGO BO BDEN PAR DMIGS PAS RTAG PA’I BDAG MED PAR MTHONG BA LA, GZUGS SOGS LA DMIGS PA’I CHAGS SOGS SPONG BA’I RGYU CI ZHIG ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR RO,,

We can be perceiving some essence or reality in things like form and the like, and then see how nothing has any self which is unchanging; how then though could you say that there was some cause here that would help someone eliminate attachment and such focused on form and the like?  There could not be.


[3255]
RTAG PA’I BDAG MED PAR MTHONG BAS GZUGS SOGS KYI YUL CAN GYI CHAGS SOGS SPONG BAR ‘GYUR BA, GANG ZAG SU YANG NANG GI BYED PA’I SKYES BU BDEN SNYAM NAS BDE BA MYONG ‘GYUR GYI YUL STEN PAR MI BYED LA, NANG RTAG BDE SDUG BSNGAL BAR DOGS NAS MI ‘DOD PA’I YUL DANG PHRAD PA SPONG BAR YANG MI BYED DO,,

When we see that there is no unchanging self, subject states of mind holding to form and the like are able to eliminate craving and such.  Any person at all who thinks that some inner being though is real will not be able to partake themselves of an object which is going to cause an experience of happiness.  And if we have some suspicion that an inside which is unchanging could be happy or sad, we will never be able to give up meeting with objects that we didn’t want to meet with.


[3256]
DE’I PHYIR CHAGS SOGS SPONG BA’I RGYU MED PAS ‘KHOR BA LAS MI GROL TE, PHYI ROL PA BZHIN NO SNYAM PA’O,,

What I think then is that if we lack the cause that will help us eliminate craving and the rest, we will never be able to liberate ourselves from the circle of pain—in which case we would end up like the non-Buddhists.



Sutra on what we deny

[3257]
BZHI PA LA LNGA, BDAG TU GANG LTA BA THAMS CAD PHUNG PO KHO NA LA LTA PAR GSUNGS PA’I DON BSHAD PA, MDO GZHAN LA BRTEN NAS PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM BDAG MIN PAR BSHAD PA, PHUNG PO TSOGS PA TZAM GYI DBYIBS KYI BKOD PA BDAG YIN PA DGAG PA, PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM BDAG TU ‘DOD PA LA GNOD BYED GZHAN BSTAN PA, THUB PAS BDAG DE KHAMS DRUG LA SOGS PA [f. 225b] LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PAR GSUNGS PA’O,,

Which brings us to our fourth part from above: an explanation of the actual intent behind statements that the parts to the person are the self, and so on.  We’ll cover this topic in five different sections:

1) An explanation of the statement that all cases of viewing a self are viewing nothing but the parts to the person;

2) Relying on other sutras to explain how the simple collection of the parts to the person cannot be a self;

3) A denial that the outline of the simple collection of the parts to the person could be a self;

4) A demonstration of other problems with the position that the simple collection of the parts to the person could be a self; and

5) A description of how the Able Ones have stated that the self is merely something labeled upon the basis of things like the six elements.


[3258]
DANG PO LA GSUM, LUNG GI DGONGS PA DGAG BYA GCOD PA’I DGAG PHYOGS NAS YIN PAR BSTAN PA, SGRUB PHYOGS NAS YIN DU CHUG KYANG PHUNG PO BDAG TU STON PA MIN PA, DE DAG LA GZHAN GYI RTZOD PA SPANG BA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The first of these five sections has three parts of its own: (1) a demonstration that the intent of the scriptural reference is meant in a negative connotation, where we are eliminating what we deny; (2) how this reference is not saying that the parts to the person are a self, even if we allow that the reference was meant in a positive sense; and (3) refuting additional argument on these points.  Here then is the first of these.


	[3259]
[VI.132]
Skandhā ātmetyuktavān yena śāstā
skandhā evātmeti tasmān mataś cet,
Skandhebhyo’nyasyātmano’sau niṣedho
rūpaṃ nātmetyādisūtrāntarokteḥ.

,GANG PHYIR STON PAS PHUNG PO BDAG GO ZHES,
,GSUNGS PA DE PHYIR PHUNG PO BDAG ‘DOD NA,
,DE NI PHUNG LAS GZHAN BDAG ‘GOG PA STE,
,GZUGS BDAG MIN SOGS MDO GZHAN GSUNGS PHYIR RO,

		This is because
		Of statements
		By the Teacher:

		Suppose you assert
		That the parts
		To the person
		Are a self,

		Because of statements
		That the parts
		To the person
		Are the self.

		That is to deny
		A self different
		From the parts
		To the person.

		Other sutras express
		That form
		Is not the self,
		And so on.


[3260]
CI STE KHO BO CAG LUNG TSAD MAR BYED PA LA RTOG GE’I TSAD MAS GNOD PA MA YIN LA, LUNG GIS KYANG PHUNG PO KHO NA BDAG TU STON PAR BYED DE,

Well now, we for our part would say that the valid perceptions of logicians are not something which could ever draw into question the holy writ, which must be taken as valid.  And this writ teaches that it is nothing but the parts to the person which constitute the self.


[3261]
GANG GI PHYIR STON PAS DGE SLONG DAG DGE SBYONG NGAM BRAM ZE GANG SU DAG CIG BDAG GO SNYAM DU YANG DAG PAR RJES SU LTA BA DE DAG NI, NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA PO ‘DI DAG KHO NA LA YANG DAG PAR RJES SU LTA’O, ZHES GSUNGS PAS

And this in turn is because the Teacher has made the statement,

Consider now any monk or practitioner or Brahmin who entertains the opinion that something is the self.  These types of people can only be considering, in this case, those five parts to the person that have been taken on.


[3262]
PHUNG PO BDAG GO ZHES GSUNGS PA DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO BDAG TU ‘DOD NA, MDO DE NI PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG TU STON PA MA YIN NO,,

Suppose thus that you assert that the parts to the person are a self, because of statements that the parts to the person are the self.  The fact though is that that sutra is not meant to indicate that these parts are a self.


[3263]
‘O NA CI ZHE NA, STON PA’I DGONGS PA NI PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO GZHAN PA’I BDAG BDAG TU LTA BA’I DMIGS PAR ‘DOD PA NI, KHO NA LA ZHES PA’I NGES BZUNG GIS ‘GOG PA STE,

“Well then,” one may ask.  “What then does that statement refer to?”  What the Teacher has in mind here is to express the opinion that—when someone accepts a self which is essentially different from the parts to the person as being what the view of a self focuses upon—we are to deny this idea with that specification of “only.”


[3264]
KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA LA LTOS NAS MU STEGS KYI GZHUNG DGAG PA’I PHYIR DANG, KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PAR YOD PA’I BDAG PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And this is because—relative to deceptive reality—we deny the major texts of the River Schools; and because we teach that the idea of a self which exists in deceptive reality is mistaken.


[3265]
YANG ‘DI PHUNG PO RNAMS LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BDAG ‘GOG PA YIN PAR GANG LAS SHES SHE NA,

“How is it,” you may ask, “that we are to understand that this is a denial of a self which is essentially distinct from the parts to the person?”


[3266]
MDO GZHAN LAS GZUGS BDAG MIN NO ZHES SOGS KYIS GZUGS SOGS RNAMS BDAG YIN PA BKAG PAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This is due to the fact that—in other sutras—the understanding was expressed that “form is not the self”; and so on.  Which is to say, it was denied that form and the like could be the self.


	[3267]
[VI.133]
Rūpaṃ nātmā vedanā no na saṃjñā
no saṃskārā nāpi vijñānam uktam,
Sūtre’nyasmin yena tasmān na hīṣṭaḥ
skandhā evātmeti sūtropadeśaḥ.

,GANG PHYIR GZUGS TSOR BDAG MIN PA ‘DU SHES KYANG,
,MA YIN ‘DU BYED RNAMS MIN RNAM SHES KYANG,
,MIN PAR MDO GZHAN LAS GSUNGS DE YI PHYIR,
,MDOR BSTAN PHUNG PO BDAG CES BZHED MA YIN,

		This is because—
		In other sutras—
		It is stated that

		Neither form
		Nor feelings
		Are the self;

		Nor is
		Discrimination;
		Nor are
		The other factors;
		Nor is consciousness.

		As such,
		The statement
		In sutra is not
		An assertion
		
		That the parts
		To the person
		Are the self.


[3268]
MDO GZHAN LAS BKAG PA DE JI LTAR YIN ZHE NA,

“How then,” one may ask, “is the denial made in other sutras?”


[3269]
GANG GI PHYIR GZUGS DANG TSOR BA BDAG MIN PA DANG, ‘DU SHES KYANG BDAG MA YIN PA DANG, ‘DU BYED RNAMS KYANG BDAG MIN PA DANG, RNAM SHES KYANG BDAG MIN PAR MDO [f. 226a] GZHAN LAS GSUNGS PA

This is the case because—in other sutras—it is stated that neither form nor feelings are the self; nor is discrimination the self; nor are the other factors the self; nor is consciousness the self.


[3270]
DE YI PHYIR NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA PO ‘DI DAG KHO NA LA BDAG GO SNYAM DU YANG DAG PAR RJES SU LTA’O ZHES MDOR BSTAN PA ‘DI LAS NI, PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG GO ZHES BZHED PA MA YIN GYI, PHUNG PO RNAMS LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BDAG ‘DOD PA KHO NA’I TSIG GIS BKAG PA KHO NAR NGES SO,,

As such, we can say the following about the statement, in sutra, that “One should have this view of things: one should consider the five parts to the person that we have taken on, alone, as being the self.”  This is not an assertion that the parts to the person are the self; rather, this should definitely only be considered an expression of denial that there could be a self that was essentially separate from the parts to the person.


[3271]
GAL TE MDO DES KHO NA LA LTA ZHES PAS BDAG DON GZHAN BKAG MOD KYANG, PHUNG PO ‘DI KHO NA LA LTA’O ZHES PHUNG PO LNGA LA LTA BAR GSUNGS PAS, PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG LTA’I DMIGS PAR GSAL BAR STON PAS, MDO’I DGONGS PA PHUNG PO BDAG LTA’I DMIGS PA YIN NO SNYAM NA,

Suppose someone thinks to themselves as follows:

It’s admittedly the case that—when this sutra says “can only be”—it is denying that the self could be some other entity.  But then there is the statement that “they can only be considering the parts to the person”—saying that they consider those five parts to the person.  This is clearly a pronouncement that the parts to the person are what the view of a self focuses upon.  As such, the intent of the sutra is to say that the parts to the person are what the view of a self focuses upon.


[3272]
DE LTA YIN NA MDO GZHAN LAS PHUNG PO LNGA BDAG MA YIN PAR GSUNGS PA DANG ‘GAL BAR ‘GYUR TE, ‘JIG LTA LHAN SKYES NGAR ‘DZIN GYI DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI NANG NAS DMIGS PA YIN NA BDAG YIN DGOS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

If this though were the case, it would contradict the statement that we find in other sutras where they say that the five parts to the person are not the self.  And that’s because if—from among the two possible objects of focus of the tendency to grasp to “me”—we are talking about the object of the inborn view of destruction, it must be the self.


[3273]
DE LTAR GSUNGS PA’I MDO PHYI MA’I DON LA GNOD PA MED LA, BZLOG DON LA GNOD PA SNGAR MANG DU BSHAD CING, DA DUNG YANG ‘CHAD PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR, MDO SNGA MAS PHUNG PO RNAMS ‘JIG LTA’I DMIGS PAR STON PA MIN NO,,

There is no problem if we are talking about the meaning of the latter of the sutras which makes this kind of statement; and we have previously explained many problems with taking this to mean the opposite.  We will, in addition, speak additionally on this point.  As such we can say that the preceding statement from sutra is not meant to indicate that the parts to the person are the object of focus for the view of destruction.


[3274]
DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO LA LTA’O ZHES PAS NI PHUNG PO LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA’I BDAG DMIGS PAR STON PAR GSAL TE, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA DANG PHUNG PO NYID BDAG TU ‘DZIN PA’I DMIGS PA YIN PA KHEGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

As such, it’s clear that the statement that “it is focused on the parts to the person” is meant to refer to focusing on the self which is labeled, based on these parts.  And that’s because it’s denying that something essentially different from the parts to the person, or these parts themselves, could be the object of focus for the tendency to grasp to a self.


[3275]
MDO GANG LAS GZUGS SOGS RNAMS KYANG BDAG YIN PA BKAG PA DE LAS NI, BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA’I BDAG ‘JIG LTA’I DMIGS PA ‘DIS PHUNG PO LEN PA’I PHUNG PO’I NYE BAR LEN PA CAN RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA BKAG PAR RIG PAR BYA STE, [f. 226b] GZUGS SOGS BDAG MIN PAR GSUNGS PA DE NI DE KHO NA NYID LA SEMS PA’I SKABS YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

There are other sutras in which it is also denied that form and the rest could be the self; and from this we should understand that the self as labeled in dependence—what it is that the view of destruction focuses upon—serves to deny the idea that the one it is that takes on the parts to the person as these parts are taken could exist through any nature of its own.  That is, statements that form and the rest are not the self are made in the context of considering the topic of suchness.


[3276]
DE LTAR NYE BAR LEN PA PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MA DMIGS NA, BDAG DE’I NYE BAR BLANG BAR BYA BA PHUNG PO YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN NO, ZHES GZUGS SOGS LA YANG BDEN PAR ZHEN PA’I ‘DOD CHAGS DANG BRAL BA ‘THAD PA NYID DO,,

And so what we have here is the statement, “Suppose then that the one who does take these things on could not be someone who existed through some nature of their own.  We would have to say in that case that what they did take on—the parts to the person—could   never be entities that existed through some nature of their own either.”  In that case then it would be perfectly appropriate to say that we were free from the desire which is so hungry to believe that form and the rest are real.


[3277]
MDO SDE PHAN TSUN GYI GUNG LEGS PAR BSGRIGS NAS PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA DANG, PHUNG PO RNAMS BDAG ‘DZIN GYI DMIGS PA YIN PA BKAG NAS,

If we look at how these sutra references support each other as sources, we can see that the idea that the self could be something essentially separate from the parts to the person, or that these parts could be the object of focus for the tendency to believe in a self, are both denied.


[3278]
BDAG PHUNG PO LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA MING GI THA SNYAD KYI DBANG GIS BZHAG PA TZAM GYI GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED KYI ‘JOG TSUL THUN MONG MA YIN PA,

This method of describing the lack of a self to the person—where we describe the self as no more than something established through the power of terms, names labeled on the basis of the parts to the person—is truly unique.


[3279]
RANG GI SDE PA GONG ‘OG GI MKHAS PA MDO’I DGONGS PA ‘GREL BA DU MAS LEGS PAR ‘BAD KYANG GSAL BAR MTHON PA’I MDO’I DGONGS PA, LUNG RIGS PHYIN CI MA LOG PA’I LAM NAS BTON PA DANG,

The great masters of both the higher & lower schools of thought in our own system have made noble efforts to clarify the true intent of these sutras in a great many commentaries that they have composed.  They have thus been able to draw out, with clarity, the sutras’ intended meaning, extracting it by using the path of faultless reasoning and scriptural authority.


[3280]
DE LA BRTEN NAS CHOS GZHAN RNAMS KYANG DE DANG ‘JOG TSUL KHYAD MED PA’I CHOS KYI BDAG MED GSAL BAR BSTAN NAS,

Based on this work, they have gone on to elucidate the meaning of the lack of a self to things in general, establishing as well how these additional entities are to be described in a manner which in no way differs from that just described.


[3281]
SANGS RGYAS BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYI DGONGS PA SHIN TU PHRA BA’I GNAS RNAMS RJEN CHER DU STON PA’I MKHAS PA’I DBANG PO’I BZHED PA THUN MONG MA YIN PA ‘DI RNAMS LEGS PAR SHES PA LA ‘BAD PAR GYIS SHIG

Thus then are they lords among masters, who have taken this extremely subtle intent of the Buddha, the Conqueror, and laid it out completely bare for us.  And so I beg you to make massive efforts to learn, deeply, the truly unique positions of these thinkers.



Sutra never said
the parts were the self

[3282]
,GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second part from above, where we show how these scriptural references are not saying that the parts to the person are a self, even if we allow that they were meant in a positive sense.


[3283]
GAL TE NYE BAR LEN PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA PO ‘DI DAG KHO NA LA LTA’O ZHES PA ‘DI NI, SGRUB PHYOGS KYI SGO NAS PHUNG PO BDAG TU STON PA YIN KYANG, PHUNG PO RE RE NAS BDAG TU STON PA MIN NO,,

What then about statements that say, “It can only be considering the five parts to the person that we have taken on”?  This is expressing the point positively, describing the parts to the person as the self; but it is not saying that each separate part to the person is the self.


	[3284]
[VI.134]
Skandhā ātmetyucyamāne samūhaḥ
skandhānāṃ syān naiva tu skandha rūpaḥ,
No nāthatvaṃ no damaḥ sākṣitā vā
tasyāsattvāt syād ato no samūhaḥ.

,PHUNG PO BDAG CES BRJOD TSE PHUNG RNAMS KYI,
,TSOGS PA YIN GYI PHUNG PO’I NGO BO MIN,
,MGON MIN ‘DUL BA’AM DBANG PO NYID KYANG MIN,
,DE MED PHYIR DE TSOGS PA MA YIN NO,

		When it states
		That the parts
		To the person
		Are the self,

		It’s the collection
		Of the parts
		To the person.

		It is not though
		That the essence
		Of the parts is.

		It could not be
		The savior,
		Or the trainer,
		Or the absolute lord.

		Since that
		Would not exist,
		This could not be
		The collection.


[3285]
‘O NA CI ZHE NA,

“Well then,” you may ask, “just what is it saying?”


[3286]
‘DI LTAR PHUNG PO BDAG GO ZHES BRJOD PA’I TSE, PHUNG PO RNAMS KYI TSOGS PA BDAG TU BRJOD PA YIN GYI, PHUNG PO RNAMS KYI NGO BO STE RE RE BA BDAG TU STON PA MIN [f. 227a] TE,

When it states in this way that the parts to the person are the self, what it’s saying is that the collection of the parts to the person is the self.  It is not though meant to indicate that the essence of the parts to the person—which is to say, these parts taken individually—are the self.


[3287]
DPER NA SHING RNAMS NI NAGS TSAL LO ZHES BRJOD PA NA, SHING GI TSOGS PA NAGS TSAL YIN GYI, SHING RE RE BA NAGS SU ‘GYUR BAS SHING GI NGO BOR RE {%BO RE RE} BA NAGS SU BRJOD PA MIN PA BZHIN NO, ZHES GZHAN LA GRUB PA DPER BRJOD PA’O,,

Think for example when we use the expression “the forest of the trees.”  It’s the collection of the trees which is the forest; it is not though the case that each separate tree represents the forest, and that we are then referring to the essential nature of each tree and calling it a forest.  All this then is being used as an example meant to apply to other things.


[3288]
GAL TE TSOGS PA BDAG YIN PA ‘DOD DO ZHE NA,

And suppose someone comes and says that they agree that the collection of the parts is the self.


[3289]
DE LTA NA BDAG NI MGON DANG ‘DUL BA’AM DBANG PO NYID DU GSUNGS LA, KHYED LTAR NA TSOGS PA RKYANG PA DE MGON MIN ZHING, ‘DUL BA’AM DBANG PO NYID KYANG MIN TE, TSOGS PA TZAM DE NI RDZAS SU MED PA’I PHYIR NA, BDAG DE PHUNG PO’I TSOGS PA TZAM MA YIN NO,,

Thus it is then that the “self” has been described as the “savior,” or the “trainer,” or the “absolute lord.”  According to your view though the simple collection here could not be the savior, or else the trainer, or the absolute lord.  And that’s because—since that simple collection would not exist in a substantial way—this self could not be the simple collection of the parts to the person.


[3290]
BDAG MGON LA SOGS PAR GSUNGS TSUL NI, MDO LAS,
,BDAG NYID BDAG GI MGON YIN TE,
,BDAG NYID BDAG GI DGRA YANG YIN,
,LEGS DANG NGAN PA BYAS PA LA,
,BDAG NYID BDAG GI DBANG PO YIN,

How is it that the self was described as the savior and so on?  Sutra puts it this way:

	You yourself
	Are your own savior;

	And you yourself
	Are your own foe.

	You yourself
	Are the master of yourself,
	Who does you well,
	Or does you harm.


[3291]
ZHES BYA BA DE LAS MGON NYID DANG, DBANG PO NYID DU GSUNGS LA,

“This then is the type of source for referring to the one & only savior; and the one & only lord.”


	[3292]
,BDAG NYID LEGS PAR DUL BAS NI,
,MKHAS PAS MTHO RIS THOB PAR ‘GYUR, 
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

And we also see—

	The wise attain
	To the higher rebirths

	By succeeding in taming
	Themselves themselves.



Additional argument on these points

[3293]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to our third part here, refuting additional argument on the preceding points.


[3294]
CI STE TSOGS PA NI TSOGS PA CAN LAS NGO BO THA DAD DU MED PA’I PHYIR, ‘BRAS BU STE MGON BYED PA SOGS NI TSOGS PA CAN RNAMS KYI YIN PAR RTOGS PAR ‘GYUR BAS, MGON DANG ‘DUL BA DANG DBANG PO NYID RIGS PAR ‘GYUR RO SNYAM NA,

Suppose one were to entertain the following thought:

Now let’s consider the fact that the collection of parts cannot be separate from the thing that possesses this collection of parts.  As such, we can come to the realization that the result—which is to say, acting as a savior and so forth—is something that belongs to the one that possesses the collection of the parts.  As such, it is perfectly logical that we should have here the savior, or the trainer, or the absolute lord.


[3295]
BDAG GI SGRA RES ‘GA’ PHUNG PO TSOGS PA LA BYED LA, RES ‘GA’ TSOGS PA CAN PHUNG PO RNAMS LA NYE BAR SBYOR BA ‘DI LA, SNGAR DE LTAR ‘DOD DGUR BDAG GI SGRA SO SO LA SBYOR BA MI ‘THOB BO ZHES NYES PA BSHAD ZIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

But we have already long since explained the problems with this idea.  That is, suppose the appellation “self” applies at some points to the collection of the parts to the person, and then at other points applies to what is involved in the collection—which is to say, the parts themselves.  In this case then, as in your previous pile of assertions, they would not apply to the individual instances of the word, “self.”


	[3296]
[VI.135]
Kūṭasthānāṃ syād rathatvaṃ tadānīṃ
tasyāṅgānāṃ tulya ātmā rathena,
Skandhāṃś copādāya sūtre niruktas
tasmān nātmā skandha saṃhāta mātram.

[VI.135a]
,DE TSE DE YI YAN LAG TSOGS GNAS RNAMS,
,SHING RTA NYID ‘GYUR SHING RTA DANG BDAG MTSUNGS,

		At that point,
		When we pile
		The collection

		Of the various
		Components together,

		Then that would be
		A wagon itself.

		It’s the same,
		Whether you’re talking
		About a wagon
		Or a self.


[3297]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE, PHUNG PO’I TSOGS PA BDAG TU ‘DOD PA DE’I TSE [f. 227b] SHING RTA DE YI YAN LAG GI TSOGS PA PHYOGS GCIG TU GNAS PA RNAMS SHING RTA NYID DU ‘GYUR BA’I SKYON YOD DE, SHING RTA DANG BDAG GNYIS RANG GI YAN LAG TSOGS PA LA ‘JOG MI ‘JOG MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

There is also another problem here.  When we consider the collection of the parts to the person to be the self, then at that point we incur the problem that whenever we pile the collection of the various component parts to a wagon together in one place, then that would be a wagon itself.  And that’s because the question of whether or not we can posit something as the collection of its component parts is the same, whether you’re talking about a wagon or a self.


[3298]
MTSUNGS PAR BSTAN PA YANG MDO LAS,
,BDAG CES BYA BA BDUD KYI SEMS,
,KHYOD NI LTA BAR GYUR PA YIN,
,’DU BYED PHUNG PO ‘DI STONG STE,
,’DI LA SEMS CAN YOD MA YIN,

The fact that the question is the same is expressed in the following lines, from sutra—

	To say that something
	Is the self
	Is an idea of the devils,

	For this is what
	We call “the view.”

	The factors
	Are empty of
	The parts to the person;

	There was never any
	Living being here.


	[3299]
,JI LTAR YAN LAG TSOGS RNAMS LA,
,BRTEN NAS SHING RTA BRJOD PA LTAR,
,DE BZHIN PHUNG PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS,
,KUN RDZOB SEMS CAN ZHES BYA’O,
ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

	We refer to something
	As a “wagon”
	Based upon the collection
	Of its parts;

	In the same way,
	In deceptive terms
	We call someone
	
	A living being
	Based upon the
	Parts to the person.



Other sutras on simple collections

[3300]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second section here: relying on other sutras to explain how the simple collection of the parts to the person cannot be a self.


	[3301]
[VI.135b]
,MDO LAS PHUNG PO BRTEN NAS YIN GSUNGS PA,
,DE PHYIR PHUNG PO ‘DUS TZAM BDAG MA YIN,

		Sutra states that
		It is on the basis
		Of the parts
		To the person;

		As such, the simple
		Accumulation
		Of the parts

To the person
Is not the self [f. 211a].


[3302]
SNGAR BSHAD PA DE LTAR NA MDO LAS PHUNG PO TSOGS PA LA BRTEN NAS SEMS CAN DU GDAGS PA YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS PA DE YI PHYIR PHUNG PO ‘DUS PA STE TSOGS PA TZAM BDAG MA YIN NO,,

As we explained earlier on, sutra states that the living being is something ascribed on the basis of the collection of the parts to the person.  As such, the simple accumulation or collection of the parts to the person is not the self.


[3303]
DE NYID SGRUB PA’I NGAG GIS GSAL BAR BYED PA NI, GANG ZHIG LA BRTEN NAS GANG BRTAGS PA DE NI BTAGS PA NYE BAR LEN PA’I YAN LAG TSOGS PA TZAM MA YIN TE, BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA’I PHYIR ‘BYUNG BA LAS GYUR PA BZHIN NO,,

Here is a clarification of this very point, made through the use of supporting logic.  That is, any entity which is ascribed on the basis of something is not the simple collection of the component parts that were taken on.  The case is similar to one in which something has come from the elements, as it is labeled on their basis.


[3304]
JI LTAR ‘BYUNG BA DAG RGYUR BYAS NAS, ‘BYUNG BA LAS GYUR PA SNGON PO LA SOGS PA DANG, MIG LA SOGS PA BTAGS MOD KYI DE GNYIS ‘BYUNG BA ‘DUS PA TZAM NYID NI MA YIN NO,,

That is, what’s happening here is the same as where we have the elements acting as a cause.  That is, we apply the labels “blue” and the like—or “the eye” and such—upon that which has derived from the physical elements.  But we wouldn’t say that these entities are nothing more than the coming together of those elements.


[3305]
DE BZHIN DU BDAG PHUNG PO RGYUR BAS {%BYAS} NAS BTAGS PA’I RANG BZHIN CAN YANG, PHUNG PO TSOGS PA TZAM YIN PAR MI RUNG NGO ZHES PA’O,,

Here it’s the same.  The self is indeed something that has the nature of being labeled through the parts to the person having provided the cause; but what we are saying is that it would be improper to refer to the self as the simple collection of those parts.


[3306]
GAL TE MDO LAS PHUNG PO TSOGS PA LA BRTEN NAS ZHES GSUNGS NA, TSOGS PA GANG ZAG TU MI RUNG YANG, DE BZHIN PHUNG PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS, ZHES PA TZAM LAS MED PAS PHUNG PO TSOGS PA GANG ZAG GI RTEN DU ‘JOG PA’I KHUNGS MIN NO SNYAM NA,

With this, one may have the following thought:

We see the phrase, in sutra, that “just so, it is through its dependence upon the collection of the parts to the person.”  And although it would be inappropriate to say that the collection was the person, we do see the phrase, “in the same way, it depends upon the parts to the person”—and that’s all we see.  As such, it would seem inappropriate to point to these references as a source for saying that the collection of the parts to the person is the basis of the person.


[3307]
DE NI MA YIN TE DPE’I SKABS SU, JI LTAR YAN LAG [f. 228a] TSOGS RNAMS LA, ZHES YAN LAG TSOGS PA LA BRTEN NAS SHING RTAR BSHAD LA,

That though is not the case.  When we get to the example used here, we see “based on the collection of its parts”; referring to the fact that we speak of something as a wagon based upon the collection of its parts.


[3308]
DE’I PHYIR SHING RTA DANG DPE DON DU SGRIG PA NA, DE BZHIN PHUNG PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS, ZHES PA’I SKABS SU TSOGS PA DNGOS SU MA BRJOD KYANG DE GDON DGOS PAR SHIN TU GSAL BAS MKHAS PA’I DBANG POS, MDO’I TSIG ZUR RE’I NUS PA ‘DON LUGS YIN PAS ZHIB PAR GO NA BLO LA DGA’ BA SKYED PA’O,,

As such, when we set forth both the metaphor and its referent in the case of the example of the wagon, it’s extremely clear that there is something additional which we need to bring out, even though it’s not directly stated at the point where they say, “just so, it is through its dependence upon the parts to the person.”  And this is the idea of “a collection.”  As such, it is the custom among those lords among sages to draw out the force of each separate word in a phrase from the sutras.  And if we really understand this point in detail, it is only a reason for us to rejoice.


[3309]
BUM PA LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYIS MA NGES PA NYID DO ZHE NA,

One may then ask,

But isn’t this idea drawn into question with things such as water pitchers and the like?


[3310]
DE YANG YOD PA MA YIN TE, BUM PA LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYANG GZUGS LA SOGS PA TSOGS PA TZAM NYID YIN PAR MA GRUB PA’I PHYIR DANG, DER YANG BDAG DANG ‘DRA BAR BRGAL ZHING BRTAG PA MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This though is not the case.  This is first of all because it is not the case that water pitchers and the like are simply the collection of form and the rest.  And secondly, the examination and the final conclusions we draw with them are just the same as we do with the self.


[3311]
‘DIS NI BDAG RANG GI CHA SHAS RNAMS TSOGS PA LA GZHAG TU MI RUNG BA BZHIN DU, BUM PA LA SOGS PA YANG RANG GI YAN LAG TSOGS PA TZAM LA ‘JOG TU MI RUNG BA GNYIS ‘DRA BAR BSTAN NO,,

What this is indicating is that the case here is just the same as with the example of the self, where we say it cannot simply be posited as the collection of its parts.  And so there is a similar instance here where it would incorrect to say that water pitchers or the like could be posited as nothing more than the collection of their component parts.



Denying the outline as the self

[3312]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to our third part from above: a denial that the outline of the simple collection of the parts to the person could be a self.


[3313]
CI STE ‘PHANG LO LA SOGS PA TSOGS PA TZAM NI SHING RTA MA YIN TE, ‘O NA CI ZHE NA,

One may begin with the following question—

Well then, if the simple collection of the wheels and so on is not the wagon, what is?


	[3314]
[VI.136]
Saṃsthānaṃ ced rūpiṇāṃ tasya sattvāt
teṣām evātmeti saṃjñā tava syāt,
Cittādīnāṃ saṃhater ātmatā tu
na syād yasmāt saṃniveśo’sti naiṣām.

,[211a] DBYIBS SHE NA DE GZUGS CAN LA YOD PHYIR,
,KHYOD LA DE DAG NYID BDAG CES ‘GYUR GYI,
,SEMS SOGS TSOGS NI BDAG NYID ‘GYUR MIN TE,
,GANG PHYIR DE DAG LA DBYIBS YOD MA YIN,

		And suppose you say
		It’s the outline.

		This is
Something possessed
By physical things;

With you,
These would be
Referred to
As the “self.”

It would not
Be the case that
The mind and such
Were this same self;

That’s because
These are not things
Which possess
Any outline.		


[3315]
GANG GI TSE ‘PHANG LO LA SOGS PA TSOGS PA NA SHING RTA’I DBYIBS KHYAD PAR CAN DANG LDAN PAR GYUR PA DE’I TSE SHING RTA’I MING RNYED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And suppose you begin your answer with saying that—at the point when the collection of the wheels and so on takes on that distinctive outline of a wagon—then at that time it is granted the name of “wagon.”


[3316]
DE BZHIN DU SEMS CAN GYI RGYUD KYI GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I PHUNG PO RNAMS KYI DBYIBS KYI BKOD PA TZAM BDAG YIN NO ZHE NA,

And suppose you say,

It’s the same with the outline of the form and the rest of the parts included within the person of the particular living being; this then is what the “self” is.


[3317]
DBYIBS DE NI GZUGS CAN KHO NA LA YOD PA’I PHYIR, KHYOD LA STE LTAR NA GZUGS CAN DE DAG NYID DE KHO NA BDAG CES BYA PAR ‘GYUR GYI, 

But the fact is that this kind of outline is something possessed only by physical things; as such, “with you” (meaning, “according to you”) it is only these physical parts here that would be referred to as the “self.”


[3318]
SEMS DANG SOGS PAS SEMS BYUNG GI TSOGS LA NI, BDAG NYID DU ‘JOG PAR ‘GYUR BA MIN PAR ‘GYUR TE, GANG GI PHYIR NA SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG DE DAG LA DBYIBS YOD PA MA YIN PA’I [f. 228b] PHYIR TE, GZUGS CAN MA YIN PA’I PHYIR RO SNYAM DU BSAMS SO,,

It would not though be the case that you were positing the collection of the mind “and such” (which would include the mental functions) as being this same self.  And that’s because these mind and mental functions are not things which possess any outline—for they are not physical.  This is the thinking here.



Other problems with
parts as a self

[3319]
BZHI PA NI,

Which brings us to our fourth part from above: a demonstration of other problems with the position that the simple collection of the parts to the person could be a self.


	[3320]
[VI.137]
Nopādātuś caikatā yukta rūpā
svopādānaiḥ kartṛ karmaikataivam,
Syāt kartāsan karma cāstīti ced dhīr
no kartāraṃ yad vinā nāsti karma.

,LEN PO RANG NYER LEN GCIG RIGS DNGOS MIN,
,DE LTA NA LAS BYED PO GCIG NYID ‘GYUR,
,BYED PO MED LAS YOD SNYAM BLO YIN NA,
,MA YIN GANG PHYIR BYED PO MED LAS MED,

		The one doing
		The taking,
		Themselves,
		
		Would be
		What is taken;

		It is illogical
		To say that these
		Could be
		A single thing.

		In that case
		The action
		And the agent
		
		Would constitute
		A single entity.

		There cannot exist
		An agent;

		Suppose you
		Are thinking
		That it is
		The action.

		This cannot be
		The case,
		For the reason that
		
		There is no such thing
		As an action
		Without an agent.


[3321]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE ‘DIS NYE BAR LEN PAR BYED PAS NA, NYE BAR LEN PA PO RANG STE BYED PA PO BDAG DANG, ‘DI NYE BAR BLANG BAR BYA BAS NA NYE BAR LEN PA STE LAS SU BYA BA PHUNG PO LNGA’O, ,DE GNYIS GCIG PA’I DNGOS POR RIGS PA MIN PA NI TSOGS PA TZAM BDAG TU ‘JOG PAR MI RIGS PA’O,,

And there are still other problems here.  This in fact is what does the taking on; so that, in this case, the one doing the taking on themselves would be both the agent here—the self—and what it took on as well: what is taken (which is to say, the five parts to the person which are the object of the action here).  It is illogical though to say that these two could constitute a single thing; as such, it is also illogical to say that it is the simple collection alone which is the self.


[3322]
GAL TE GZUGS SOGS KYI PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM BDAG YIN PA DE LTA NA NI LAS DANG BYED PA PO RNAMS GCIG NYID DU ‘GYUR LA,

Suppose then that the simple collection of the parts here—form and the rest of the parts to the person—constituted the self.  In that case, the action undertaken, and the agent of that action, would constitute a single entity.


[3323]
‘DI NI ‘DOD PA YANG MA YIN TE, ‘BYUNG BA DANG ‘BYUNG ‘GYUR GYI GZUGS GNYIS DANG, BUM PA DANG RDZA MKHAN KYANG GCIG NYID DU ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

But neither is this something that you could agree to.  Because in this case, the pair of the elements and the products of the elements—as well as clay pot and the potter themselves—would be one & the same.


[3324]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,GAL TE SHING DE ME YIN NA,
,BYED PA PO DANG LAS GCIG ‘GYUR,
ZHES DANG,

As Wisdom puts it,

	If the firewood
	Were the fire,

	Then the agent
	And the action
	Would be one & the same.


	[3325]
,ME DANG SHING GIS BDAG DANG NI,
,NYE BAR BLANG BA’I RIM PA KUN,
,BUM SNAM SOGS DANG LHAN CIG TU,
,MA LUS PAR NI RNAM PAR BSHAD,
CES GSUNGS SO,,

And it states as well:

	Fire and firewood
	Explain all the steps

	Between the self
	And the things
	That we take on.

	The same applies
	To water pitchers,
	And bolts of cloth,

	And everything else
	That exists in combination.
	

[3326]
‘DIR ME DANG BUD SHING DAG GCIG NYID DU MI ‘DOD PA DE BZHIN DU, BDAG DANG NYE BAR LEN PA DAG LA YANG MI ‘DOD PAR BYA DGOS TE, DE GNYIS MTSUNGS PAR GSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

What this is saying is that we could never agree that a fire and the firewood were one and the same thing.  Neither could we ever say this about the two of the self and what the self took on.  The two cases, these lines are pointing out, are equivalent.


[3327]
CI STE BYED PA PO NYID DU ‘GYUR BA PHUNG PO TSOGS PA NYE BAR LEN PA PO NI ‘GA’ YANG MED DE, BYED PA PO ‘DI NI NYE BAR LEN PA LAS SU BYA BA PHUNG PO ‘DUS PA TZAM ZHIG YOD DO SNYAM DU BLO LA SEMS PA YIN NA, 

The point is that there cannot exist, at all, a collection of the parts to the person—what it is that we take on—which were as well the very agent of this action.  Which is to say, suppose you are thinking to yourself—suppose you have the idea—that the agent here is what is taken on: the simple assembly of the parts to the person, the object of the agent’s action.


[3328]
DE NI DE LTAR MA YIN TE, GANG GI PHYIR NA BYED PA PO MED NA RGYU MED PA’I LAS KYANG MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

This though simply cannot be the case, for the reason that there is no such thing as an action without a cause: where there is no agent.


[3329]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,DE BZHIN NYER LEN SHES PAR BYA,
,LAS DANG BYED PO BSAL PHYIR RO,
,BYED PA PO DANG LAS DAG GIS,
,DNGOS PO LHAG MA SHES PAR BYA,
ZHES GSUNGS TE,

Wisdom says it this way:

	Understand
	What is taken on
	In the very same way,

	Since the action
	And the agent
	Are distinct.

	You can understand
	The rest of all
	Functional things

	With the pair
	Of an agent,
	And an act.


[3330]
LAS DANG BYED PA PO RANG [f. 229a] BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA BKAG PA’I RIGS PAS NYE BAR BLANG BA DANG LEN PA PO YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA BKAG PA YANG SHES PAR BYA’O,,

You should understand that—using the same logic we employ to deny that the action & the agent could exist through some nature of their own—we deny that the agent of taking things on, and the one who does the taking, could exist either through any nature of their own.


[3331]
DNGOS PO LHAG MA NI TSIG GSAL LAS, BSKYED BYA SKYED BYED DANG ‘GRO BA DANG ‘GRO BA PO DANG, BLTA BYA LTA BYED DANG, MTSAN NYID DANG MTSAN GZHI DANG, ‘BYUNG BAR BYA BA DANG, {%no ,} ‘BYUNG BAR BYED PA DANG, YAN LAG DANG YAN LAG CAN DANG, YON TAN DANG YON TAN CAN DANG, TSAD MA DANG GZHAL BYA LA SOGS PA’I DNGOS PO MA LUS PA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA BKAG STE, PHAN TSUN LTOS PA’I GRUB PA NYID YIN PAR SHES RAB CAN GYIS SHES PAR BYA’O,

As for the rest of functioning things, we can follow the words of A Clarification of the Verses:

We deny that any functional entity at all could ever exist through some nature of its own, whether we’re talking about things that start or the things that start them; or goings or the one who goes; or what is viewed, and the the one who views it; or definitions or things defined; or the fact of things happening or what makes them happen; or the component parts of things or the wholes made up of those parts; or specific qualities and those that possess those qualities; or accurate perceptions and the objects which those perceptions hold under their consideration.  And this is all because those who possess wisdom understand that all these are nothing but things which occur in mutual reliance.


[3332]
ZHES GSUNGS PAS BYA BYED SPYI DANG, KHYAD PAR DU TSAD MA DANG GZHAL BYA’I BYA BYED RNAMS NGO BO NYID KYIS MA GRUB CING, LTOS ‘GRUB KYI TSUL GYIS KHAS LEN PA YIN TE,

Given this kind of statement, what we accept is that neither actions & agents in general—nor, more particularly, actions & agents in the form of accurate perceptions and the objects under their consideration—could ever exist through some essential nature of their own; but rather through a process of reliance.


[3333]
LTOS ‘GRUB ‘DI LA GNYIS KA PHAN TSUN LTOS PA’I THUN MONG MA YIN PA’I ‘JOG LUGS YOD PA RNAMS SHES DGOS PAR YOD DO,,

And as regards this process of reliance, you should understand the unique methods in which we establish both of the two here as sharing a mutual reliance.


[3334]
NYE BAR LEN PA ZHES PA ‘DIR DNGOS PO LA AU PA TRA ZHES PA SGRA’I BYINGS LA, L’U tA’I RKYEN BYIN NA NYE BAR LEN PAS NA, NYE BAR LEN PA ZHES BYA BA YIN LA,

When we talk about “things taken on” here, we are referring to working things as in the Sanskrit term, upatra.  And then if we take this root and do the lūṭa strengthening it goes towards taking something on, which is how we arrive at “taken on.”


[3335]
DNGOS PO YANG RANG GI SGRUB PAR BYED PA MED PAR ‘BYUNG BA MA YIN PAS, RANG GI SGRUB PAR BYED PA NYE BAR BLANG BA DANG, NYE BAR LEN PA PO GNYIS KA YANG NYE BAR LEN PA ZHES PAR ‘JOG GO

Working things are not entities that can occur in an absence of what produces them; and so we can speak of what produces them as both that taking them on, and as the entity it is which takes them on.


[3336]
,GAL TE L’U tA’I RKYEN GYIS ‘DIS NYE BAR LEN PA’I BYA BA TZAM BRJOD PA’I PHYIR, NYE BAR BLANG BAR BYA BA’I LAS JI LTAR BRJOD CE NA,

One may then raise the following question:

The function of the lūṭa strengthening here is only to convey the connotation of “that which is taken on”; how then do you derive the action of taking on out of it here?


[3337]
KRI {%KRi?} TA DANG L’U tA NI PHAL CHER RO, ZHES SGRA’I GZHUNG LAS ‘BYUNG BAS PHAL CHER DE LTAR YIN KYANG, LAS LA L’U tA’I RKYEN BYIN PA NA NYE BAR BLANG BAR BYA BA’I [f. 229b] LAS KYANG BRJOD PA MI ‘GAL LO,,

The texts on Sanskrit grammar mention, at this point, “kṛta and lūṭa, for the most part…”  What this is saying is that what you have noted is, for the most part, the case; but that if you do the lūṭa strengthening, it is no contradiction to say that we are also talking about the action of taking something on.


[3338]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,DE LTAR LEN LAS GZHAN MA YIN,
,DE NI NYER LEN NYID KYANG MIN,
,BDAG NI NYE BAR LEN MED MIN,
,MED PA NYID DU’ANG DE MA NGES,

Wisdom also puts it this way:

	It is not something
	Separate from the taking;

	Nor is it
	The taking on itself.

	Neither is the self
	Without taking on;

	Neither can it be
	Found amidst
	Its total absence.


[3339]
ZHES BDAG NYE BAR LEN PA LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA DANG, NYE BAR LEN PA NYID BDAG MIN PA DANG, BDAG NI NYE BAR LEN PA BZUNG BA LA LTOS PA MED PA’ANG MIN PA DANG, BDAG DE MED PA YANG MIN PAR GSUNGS SO,,

What this is saying is that the self is not essentially separate from the taking on, nor is the taking on itself not the self; and neither is the self something which has no reliance on what is taken on; but neither is the self something which cannot exist.


[3340]
DE’I PHYIR BYED PA PO MED PAR LAS KYANG YOD PA MIN NO,,

As such, there can be no action without an agent.


[3341]
YANG DON DAM PA STONG PA NYID KYI MDO GANG LAS BYED PA PO NI MA DMIGS KYI, LAS KYANG YOD LA RNAM PAR SMIN PA YANG YOD DO ZHES BRJOD PA’I MDO 

But then we also see, in the sutras about things ultimately being emptiness, the statement that no agent can be found; but still the action exists, and it has a ripening.


[3342]
DE LAS NI, BYED PA PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA BKAG PAR SHES PAR BYA’I, RTEN NAS GDAGS PAR BYA BA THA SNYAD KYI YAN LAG TU GYUR PA YANG BKAG GO ,ZHES BYA BAR NI SHES PAR MI BYA’O,,

What this says is that we should understand that the agent existing through some nature of its own is denied; but that we are not to entertain the understanding that we deny something which can be, nominally, the adjunct here: something which is labeled through reliance.


[3343]
DE SKAD DU YANG, MA RIG PA DANG RJES SU ‘BREL BA’I GANG ZAG ‘DI NI BSOD NAMS MNGON PAR ‘DU BYA BA YANG MNGON PAR ‘DU BYED DO, ZHES RGYA CHER GSUNGS SO,,

We also see statements, on a common basis, which say that “the person connected to the misunderstanding is both that thing which is assembled by the good deeds, and also that thing which does the assembling.”


[3344]
MDO GONG MA NGO BO NYID MED PAR SMRA BA LA MI ‘GRIG GI ,SEMS TZAM GYI TSUL LA ‘GRIG GO ZHES RNAM BSHAD RIGS PA LAS GSUNGS MOD KYANG, 

Now it is the case that Reasoning in Explanation says that the sutra reference above would not be allowable for those who say that nothing has any essential nature of its own; but that it would be allowable in the system of the Mind Only.


[3345]
LUGS MCHOG TU GYUR PA ‘DI’I GANG ZAG ‘JOG TSUL LA NI, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I BYED PA PO THA SNYAD TZAM DU YANG MED PA DANG, THA SNYAD DU LAS DANG RNAM SMIN KHAS BLANGS PA NA,

How is it that this highest of all systems establishes what the person is?  An agent which is essentially different from the heaps is something that could never exist, even nominally.  Nominally though karma and its consequences are accepted.


[3346]
MDO PHYI MAS GSUNGS PA BZHIN DU LAS KYI BYED PA PO GANG ZAG NGES PAR ‘DOD DGOS PAS DE YANG NYE BAR BLANG BYA’I GSEB NAS MI ‘JOG PAR, DE DAG GI NYE BAR LEN PA PO ‘JOG PA NI SHIN TU LEGS PA YIN NO,,

As the latter sutra reference puts it, we definitely have to accept someone, a person, who is the one who commits the karma.  As such, it is quite perfect if we establish this as the one who takes on those things; rather than dumping them in the middle of everything it is that we take on.



The self as the six elements

[3347]
LNGA PA NI,

Here then is our fifth point from above: a description of how the Able Ones have stated that the self is merely something labeled upon the basis of things like the six elements.


	[3348]
[VI.138]
Bhūmyambutejāṃsi samīraṇaṃ ca
vijñānam ākāśam iti pratītya,
Dhātūn ṣaḍ ātmā muninopadiṣṭaḥ
sparśāśrayāṃ ṣaṭ ca sa cakṣurādīm.

,GANG PHYIR THUB PAS BDAG DE SA CHU ME,
,RLUNG DANG RNAM SHES NAM MKHA’ ZHES BYA BA,
,KHAMS DRUG DANG NI MIG SOGS REG PA YI,
,RTEN DRUG DAG LA BRTEN NAS NYER
BRTEN {%BSTAN} ZHING,

	Because the Able One
	Has presented a teaching
	Which states that
	
	The self is something
	Which depends upon

	The six elements we know as
	Earth, water, fire, and wind;
	Consciousness, and space;

	As well as the six bases
	Of contact involving
	The eye and so on;


[VI.139]
Dharmān upādāya sa citta caittān
nirucyate yena tato na tattvam,
Tebhyo’sya no saṃhati mātratā ca
tasmād ahaṃkāra matir na teṣu.

,SEMS DANG SEMS BYUNG CHOS RNAMS
NYER BZUNG NAS,
,DES GSUNGS DE PHYIR DE NI DE RNAMS DANG,
,DE NYID MA YIN TSOGS TZAM NYID MIN TE,
,DE PHYIR NGAR ‘DZIN BLO DE RNAMS LA MIN,

And has also stated
That it is taken as
The entities

Of the mind and
The mental functions,

It would be inappropriate
To say that it constituted
These here, or any one
Of these same things;

Neither is it
The simple collection.

As such, the state
Of mind which has held
To “This is me” 
Is not upon these.


[3349]
PHUNG PO SOGS TSOGS TZAM NYID BDAG TU ‘DOD PA LA SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE,

Now there are also other problems with the position that the simple collection of the parts to the person and such are the self.
 

[3350]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR THUB PAS YAB SRAS [f. 230a] MJAL BA’I MDO LAS BDAG DE SA DANG CHU DANG ME DANG RLUNG GI KHAMS DANG, RNAM PAR SHES PA’I KHAMS DANG, SNA’I BU GA SOGS BU GA NAM MKHA’ YI KHAMS ZHES BYA BA’I KHAMS DRUG LA BRTEN NAS DANG,

This is the case because, for the reason that the Able One—in the sutra known as The Meeting of the Father & the Son—has presented a teaching which states that the self is something which depends, first of all, on the six elements.  These include the elements we know as earth, water, fire, and wind; the element of consciousness; and the element of space, which incorporates things like the cavity within the nose, and such.


[3351]
MIG GI REG PA’I SKYE MCHED DANG LA SOGS PAS YID KYI REG PA YI SKYE MCHED DRUG DAG LA BRTEN NAS NYE BAR BSTAN ZHING,

The Able One has taught as well that the self is something which depends upon the six different doors of sense with contact involving the eye, and “so on”—which also further refers to contact involving the thought.


[3352]
SEMS DANG DE DAG LAS GZHAN PA’I SEMS BYUNG GI CHOS RNAMS GDAGS GZHIR NYE BAR BZUNG BA LA BRTEN NAS BDAG TU ‘DOGS SO ZHES NGES PAR TE GSAL BAR GSUNGS PA DE’I PHYIR,

The Able One has also quite surely—which is to say, clearly—stated that the self is something which is labeled on the basis of (having taken as what is labeled) the entitites of the mind and the mental functions which are separate from those others.


[3353]
BDAG DE NI SA’I KHAMS LA SOGS PA’I YA GYAL DE RNAMS DANG, DE NYID MA YIN PA STE DE RNAMS RE RE NAS BDAG TU MI RUNG LA, DE RNAMS KYI TSOGS PA TZAM NYID KYANG BDAG TU ‘JOG PA MIN TE,

It would be inappropriate to say that this self constituted these various divisions here, such as the element of earth and the like; or that it was “any one of these same things”—which means, these elements taken separately.  But neither is it the case that we can posit the self as being the simple collection of these things.


[3354]
DE’I PHYIR THOG MA MED PA NAS ZHUGS PA’I NGA’O SNYAM DU ‘DZIN PA’I BLOS CHOS DE RNAMS KYI TSOGS PA DANG YA GYAL RNAMS LA DMIGS PAR BYED PA MIN NO,,

As such, we can say that the state of mind which for time with no beginning has held to, or thought, “This is me” is not something which is focused upon either the collection or the individual divisions of these various entities.


[3355]
MDO LAS GSUNGS TSUL NI, RGYAL PO CHEN PO SKYES BU GANG ZAG DE NI KHAMS DRUG DANG REG PA’I SKYE MCHED DRUG DANG, YID KYI NYE BAR RGYU BA BCO BRGYAD DO, ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

And how is it that sutra makes these statements?  We see the following:

O Great King, this individual—this person—consists of the flow of eighteen different things: the six elements, along with the six doors of sense in contact, and their awarenesses.


[3356]
NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS, KHAMS DRUG ‘DUS PA, REG PA’I GZHI DRUG PA, YID KYI NYE BAR SPYOD PA BCO BRGYAD PA’O, ZHES BSGYUR BA LEGS SO,,

The translation of Naktso here is preferred:

…the group of eighteen including the collection of the six elements; the six bases of contact; and the activities of the thought. 


[3357]
DE LA SKYES BU DANG GANG ZAG NI RNAM GRANGS SO,,

When the reference here mentions “individual” and “person,” they are meant as synonyms.


[3358]
KHAMS DRUG ‘DUS PA DANG GZHI DRUG PA DANG, BCO BRGYAD PA’O ZHES PA GSUM PO NI LDAN PA’I CHOS YIN PAS CHOS DE DAG NI LDAN CHOS DANG, GANG ZAG NI DE DAG GANG LA LDAN PA’I LDAN GZHI DANG, GANG LA BRTEN NAS GANG ZAG TU ‘DOGS PA’I GZHIR GSUNGS SO,,

When they speak here of the “collection of the six elements” and the six bases and the eighteen, these three are what is possessed in this case.  As such, these are the entitites which are possessed; and the person is being described as the basis which possesses these things—as the basis for labeling something “person.”


[3359]
YID KYI NYER RGYU BCO BRGYAD NI, YUL YID DU ‘ONG BA DRUG LA [f. 230b] TSOR BA BDE BA NYE BAR RGYU BA DRUG DANG, YID DU MI ‘ONG DRUG LA TSOR BA SDUG BSNGAL NYE BAR RGYU BA DRUG DANG, BAR MA DRUG LA TSOR BA BTANG SNYOMS NYE BAR RGYU BA DRUG GO

When they speak here of the “flow” of the mind in eighteen different parts, what they’re referring to is six flows of pleasant feelings with the six desirable objects of perception; six flows of unpleasant feelings with the six undesirable objects of perception; and six flows of neutral feelings with the six inbetween objects of perception.


[3360]
,TSOR BA BDE SDUG BTANG SNYOMS KYI DBANG GIS YID GZUGS SGRA SOGS LA YANG DANG YANG DU RGYU BAR BYED PA’I PHYIR, YID KYI NYE BAR RGYU BA ZHES BYA’O,,

The reason that we speak here of the “flow of the thought” is that the thought runs again and again to visible forms, audible objects, and the like; all due to the power of these feelings of pleasure, pain, and neutral sensation.


[3361]
DE LTAR PHUNG PO RNAMS NGAR ‘DZIN LHAN SKYES KYI DMIGS RNAM GNYIS KYI NANG NAS, DMIGS PA’I YUL YANG MA YIN LA, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA’I DE’I DMIGS PA YANG YOD PA MA YIN PA’I PHYIR,

Thus we can say that—from among the two different objects of focus for the inborn form of the tendency to perceive some “me”—the different parts to the person are not the object of focus.  But neither is it the case that there are some objects of focus here which are essentially separate from the parts to the person.


[3362]
NGAR ‘DZIN GYI DMIGS YUL RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MA YIN PAS, RNAL ‘BYOR BAS BDAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MA DMIGS PA LAS, BDAG GI BA YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I SNYING PO DANG LDAN PA MA YIN PA NYID DU SHES SHING,

The object of focus for the tendency to hold to some “me” is not something which could exist through some nature of its own.  As such, we should understand that when the deep practitioner fails to perceive any self that could exist through some nature of its own, what belongs to the self can only be something which could never have possessed any essence of existing through any nature of its own, either.


[3363]
‘DUS BYAS ‘KHOR BA MTHA’ DAG GI ‘CHING BA BSAL NAS YANG SRID PHYI MA LEN PA MED PAR NGES PAR MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA ‘THOB PAR ‘GYUR TE,

When we have cleared away all the produced entities of the fetters of this circle of suffering life, then it is a certainty that we can no longer take any additional rebirths—and we have attained nirvana.


[3364]
DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO LNGA’I YA GYAL DANG TSOGS PA DANG, DE DAG LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA GANG YANG BDAG LHA’I {%LTA’I} DMIGS PAR MI ‘JOG PA DANG, DE LTA NA’ANG BDAG LTA’I DMIGS  PA GANG ZAG LEGS PAR ‘JOG SHES PA DANG,

Thus it is that we are unable to say that what the view of a “self” focuses upon could be either the five parts to the person taken individually, or as a collection; or something which was essentially separate from these.  Nonetheless, we can quite perfectly posit the person as being what the view of a “self” focuses upon.


[3365]
RGYU MTSAN DE DAG LA BRTEN NAS GANG ZAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PAR ‘JOG PA’I RNAM PAR DPYOD PA ‘DI NI, THAR PA ‘DOD PA’I DBANG PO SHIN TU RNON PO LA CHES MDZES PA YIN TE, ‘DIS YID ‘PHROG PA ‘DRA BA GRUB PA’I MTHA’ GZHAN LA MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

We can also say that—based on all these reasons—this particular logical examination where we establish how the person is empty of existing through any nature of its own is something extremely beautiful for those individuals of sharp faculties who hope for freedom.  There is no presentation found in any other school of thought which can so completely steal our hearts as this one does.



The irrelevance of others’ position

[3366]
LNGA PA NI,

This brings us to our fifth point here, which is a demonstration that the position of others here is irrelevant to the case.


[3367]
NGA’O SNYAM DU ‘DZIN PA’I DMIGS PA’I YUL BDAG GI BTAGS DON BTZAL BA NA, KHA CIG PHUNG PO LNGA CHAR DANG, KHA CIG SEMS GCIG PU YIN NO ZHES SMRA BA’I

Here the position is stated as follows.  When we look for what it is that we name the “self”—that is, the object that holding to the thought of “me” is focused upon—some people say that it is all five parts to the person; while others say that it is the mind alone.


[3368]
PHYOGS LTAR NA, JI SRID DU RANG GI RGYUD LA PHUNG PO [f. 231a] RNAMS ‘BYUNG BA DE SRID DU GANG ZAG GI BDAG TU ‘DZIN PA ‘JUG PAR ‘GYUR TE, NGA’O SNYAM PA’I NGA’I BTAGS DON BTZAL NAS ‘JOG PA

According to these views, then so long as the parts to the person included in a particular person’s being are still occurring, then the tendency to hold to some self-nature of the person will continue to engage.  This then is how we establish what it is that we are referring to as “me” when we have the thought of “me.”


[3369]
LTAR NA, DE NYID GANG ZAG GI BDAG TU ‘DZIN PA’I GZHI STE RNAM PA’I YUL GYI DNGOS POR YOD PA’I PHYIR RO ZHES BSHAD PA,

According to this position, this then is the basis for holding to the self of the person; because there does exist an object of this state of mind which is a specific entity.


	[3370]
[VI.140]
Nityātmā ca kṣipyate’nātma bodhe
nāhaṃkārasyāśrayaś cāyam iṣṭaḥ,
Ātmābhāva jñena kiṃ tat svadṛṣṭer
utkhātaś cetyucyate’tīva citram.

,BDAG MED RTOGS TSE RTAG PA’I BDAG SPONG ZHING,
,’DI NI NGAR ‘DZIN RTEN DU’ANG MI ‘DOD PA,
,DE PHYIR BDAG MED SHES PAS BDAG LTA BA,
,DPYIS KYANG ‘BYIN ZHES SMRA BA SHIN TU MTSAR,

		At the point
		Where one perceives
		The lack of self,

		We have to eliminate
		The self which is
		Unchanging;

		And yet neither
		Do we accept
		That this is the basis
		For our grasping
		To a “me.”

		And so then
		We have this position
		Of understanding
		That this simple self
		Could never exist;

		And then we tear out
		This view of some self,
		With finality.

		It is exceedingly strange!


[3371]
GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED PA MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PAR ‘DOD PA’I TSE NA, RTAG PA’I BDAG TZAM ZHIG SPONG BA STE MED PAR MTHONG ZHING, RTAG PA’I BDAG ‘DI NI ‘JIG LTA LHAN SKYES KYI NGAR ‘DZIN GYI RTEN TE DMIGS PA DANG RNAM PA GANG GI YUL DU’ANG MI ‘DOD PA,

Now suppose we are talking about the point where one is desirous of perceiving the lack of self to the person, in a direct way.  Here the only thing we have to eliminate is the self which is unchanging; which is to say, we have to see that it is something which does not exist.  And yet neither do we accept that this unchanging self is the basis for the innate form of the view of destruction: our grasping to a “me.”  That is, we do not accept that it is the object here, whether you’re talking about that thing which we are focused upon, or the aspect which this focus takes.


[3372]
DE’I PHYIR RTAG PA’I BDAG TZAM MED PAR MTHONG BA’I SHES PA GOMS PAS, THOG MA MED PA NAS ZHUGS PA’I BDAG TU LTA BA DPYIS TE DRUNGS NAS KYANG ‘BYIN ZHES SMRA BA NI,

And so then we have this position that one accustoms themselves to the understanding where they see that this simple self which is unchanging could never exist; and then, with this, we also tear out this view where we have perceived, for time with no beginning, some self; we tear it out “with finality”—which is to say, from the very root.


[3373]
KYE MA MA LA KHYOD KYI ‘DI NI SHIN TU MTSAR RO,,

And all we have to say about this position of yours is that it is exceedingly strange!


[3374]
RTAG PA’I BDAG TZAM MED PAR MTHONG BAS THOG MA MED PA’I BDAG ‘DZIN SPONG BAR ‘DOD PA’I DON ‘DI NYID, PHAN TSUN ‘BREL PA MED PAR ‘JIG RTEN PA’I DPE’I SGO NAS GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

And so let’s consider the point that you make when you take the position that people can eliminate their habit of grasping to a self—a habit they have had for time with no beginning—by seeing no more than the absence of a self which is unchanging.  We are going to explain here a way of clarifying, through a worldly metaphor, that this position relates to things that have no mutual connection at all.


	[3375]
[VI.141]
Paśyann ahiṃ chidragataṃ svagehe
gajo’tra nāstīti nirastaśaṅkaḥ,
Jahāti sarpād api nāma bhītim
aho hi nāmārjavatā parasya.

,RANG KHYIM RTZIG PHUG SBRUL GNAS MTHONG BZHIN DU,
,’DI NA GLANG CHEN MED CES DOGS BSAL TE,
,SBRUL GYI ‘JIGS PA’ANG SPONG BAR BYED PA NI,
,KYE MA GZHAN GYI GNAM POR ‘GYUR NYID DO,

		Some saw
		That there was
		A snake living

		Inside the wall
		Of their own home;
		They live in it.

		And then
		Someone dispels
		All their worries
		By saying
		“There’s no elephant!”

		They are also able
		To stop being afraid
		About the snake.

		Oh my gosh!
		Others would consider
		This kind of person
		A real laughing stock!		


[3376]
GANG ZAG BLUN PO KHA CIG RANG GI KHYIM GYI RTZIG PHUG NA SBRUL GNAS PA MTHONG NAS ‘JIGS BZHIN DU GNAS PA LA, GZHAN ZHIG GIS KYE MI KHYOD MA ‘JIGS SHIG KHYIM ‘DI NA GLANG CHEN MED DO ZHES DOGS PA BSAL BA NA,

And so say there were some foolish persons who saw that there was a snake living inside the wall of their own home—they live then in a state of fear.  And then another person comes along and dispels all their worries by saying, “Hey there!  You have no reason to be scared!  There’s no elephant here in your house, at all!”


[3377]
KHYIM DER GLANG PO CHE MED PAR SHES PAS DE’I ‘JIGS PA LDOG PAR MA ZAD SBRUL GYI ‘JIGS PA’ANG SPONG BAR BYED PA NI, KYE MA’O MKHAS PA GZHAN GYI GNAM POR TE BZHAD GAD DU ‘GYUR BA NYID DO,,

And so once these people have learned that there’s no elephant there in their house, they not only stop being afraid about the elephant, but they are also able to stop being afraid about the snake.  Oh my gosh!  This kind of person is someone that other thinkers would consider a real laughing stock: a real joke.


[3378]
DE LTAR SBRUL GYI ‘JIGS PA’I RKYEN NYE BAR GNAS SU ZIN KYANG, BLUN PO GZHAN GYI TSIG LAS SBRUL LA YOD PA’I [f. 231b] ‘JIGS PA MA MTHONG BAS,

And so the situation you have here is that there is—close at hand—something which should rightfully make you afraid of a snake.  The fools here though—because of what they’ve been told by others—don’t see any reason to be afraid about the presence of a snake.


[3379]
DE’I ‘JIGS PA BZLOG THABS MI BYED PAR GLANG PO CHE MED PAR SHES PA LAS BAG PHAB STE SDOD PA NA SBRUL GYIS ‘DZIN PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And so they don’t take any action to try to remedy this particular fear, but rather sit full of relief, in the knowledge that there is no elephant here.  And then of course they are clasped by the snake.


[3380]
DE BZHIN DU GLANG PO CHE LTA BU’I RTAG PA’I BDAG TZAM MED PAR MTHONG BA GOMS PAS, SBRUL LTA BU’I THOG MA MED PA NAS ZHUGS PA’I BDAG ‘DZIN GYI ‘JIGS PA LDOG PAR BZUNG NAS BAG PHAB PAS NI,

Here it’s the same; the practitioner has perceived no more than the absence of an unchanging self, which is comparable to the elephant.  And they sit in relief that they have thus escaped any fear of the perception which is like the snake—the tendency to hold onto a self which has lived in their hearts for time with no beginning.


[3381]
PHUNG PO’I YUL CAN DU ‘DOD PA’I NGAR ‘DZIN PA’I ‘JIG LTA BSAL BAR MI NUS TE, DE’I PHYIR NGES PAR GANG ZAG ‘DI’I ‘KHOR BA NYAMS BAR {%PAR} MI ‘GYUR RO,,

This sense of relief though is not something which has the power to dispel the view of destruction, where they hold to a “me” in the form of believing in a subject involving the five parts to the person.  As such, it is a certainty that the circle of suffering—for this individual—will not subside.


[3382]
‘DIS NI RANG GZHAN GYI SDE PA DNGOS PO’I DE KHO NA NYID GTAN LA ‘BEBS PAR ‘DOD PA MANG POS, LHAN SKYES KYI BDAG ‘DZIN GYIS JI LTAR BZUNG BA’I YUL SUN ‘BYIN PA MI SHES PAS,

The point here is that there are many individuals—in both our own schools of thought, and others—who believe that they have managed to set forth just what constitutes the suchness of entities.  But actually they have no understanding of how to smash objects as they are held to exist by the inborn form of the tendency to grasp to some self.


[3383]
DE DOR NAS DE LAS GZHAN PA’I DE NYID GTAN LA ‘BEBS PA’I RNAM GZHAG THAMS CAD SNYING PO MED PA’I GNAS LA NGAL BA BYED PAR BSTAN TE,

And so what all this is describing is that these people have actually given up this particular kind of smashing, and instead are exhausting themselves in all these presentations that seek to set forth some other kind of suchness, and thus have no essential point at all.


[3384]
‘DI SHES PA SHIN TU GNAD CHE’O,,

It is absolutely crucial that you understand this point.



Denying that the basis
and what relies on it are involved

[3385]
GSUM PA LA GNYIS, RTEN DANG BRTEN PA DANG LDAN PA’I PHYOGS DGAG PA, BKAG PA RNAMS KYI DON BSDOMS TE BSTAN PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

These brings us to our third more general part from above: denying positions other than the previous two, which themselves involve three ideas, including one about the basis and what relies upon this basis.  We proceed in two steps: a denial of the position which says that both basis and what relies upon this basis are involved; and then a summary presentation of the denials.  Here is the first.


[3386]
DE LTAR BDAG PHUNG PO DANG RANG BZHIN GCIG DANG THA DAD GANG DU YANG MA GRUB PAR BSTAN NAS, BDAG PHUNG PO DANG PHAN TSUN RTEN DANG BRTEN PA NYID DU YANG NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED PAR BRJOD PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

Having thus presented how the self is neither essentially the same nor separate from the parts to the person, we will now make an explanation which is meant to express how the self and the parts to the person cannot exist, mutually, either exactly as a basis or what relies upon this basis, at least in a way where this exists through some essence of its own.


	[3387]
[VI.142]
Skandheṣvātmā vidyate naiva cāmī
santi skandhā nātmanītīha yasmāt,
Satyanyatve syād iyaṃ kalpanā vai
tac cānyatvaṃ nāstyataḥ kalpanaiṣā.

,PHUNG POR BDAG YOD MA YIN BDAG LA YANG,
,PHUNG PO DE RNAMS YOD MIN GANG PHYIR ‘DIR,
,GZHAN NYID YOD NA RTOG PA ‘DIR ‘GYUR NA,
,GZHAN NYID DE MED DE PHYIR ‘DI RTOG PA’O,

		The self is not something
		That exists in the parts
		To the person; neither
	
		Are the parts to the person
		Something which exists
		In the self.

		Why can we say this?
		Suppose here they
		Were perfectly separate.

		If these ideas were
		Indeed the case here,
		
		This would be
		A mistaken imagining,
		For the reason that

		There could be
		No possibility of
		Being essentially other.


[3388]
PHUNG POR TE DE LA BDAG NGO BO NYID KYIS BRTEN PA’I TSUL GYIS YOD PA MA YIN ZHING, BDAG LA YANG PHUNG PO DE RNAMS NGO BO NYID KYIS BRTEN PA’I TSUL GYIS YOD PA MIN TE,

Now the self is not something that exists in some manner of dependence, through some essence of its own, “in” the parts to the person; which is to say, upon these parts.  And neither are the parts to the person something which exists in some manner of dependency, through some essence of their own, upon the self.


[3389]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR NA PHUNG PO DANG BDAG ‘DIR NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I GZHAN NYID YOD NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I RTEN DANG BRTEN PA’I [f. 232a] RTOG PA GNYIS PO ‘DIR ‘GYUR NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GZHAN NYID DU GRUB PA DE MED PA DE’I PHYIR RTEN DANG BRTEN PAR NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA ‘DI PHYIN CI LOG GI RTOG PAS BZHAG PA TZAM STE,

And what is the reason why we can say this?  Suppose it were the case that the parts to the person and the self “here” (meaning, in a way in which they existed through some essence of their own) were perfectly separate from one another.
