If these two ideas—of a basis and something relying upon that basis that existed through some nature of their own—were indeed the case here, then for the reason that there could be no possibility of their being essentially other than each other by nature, we can say that this essential existence of a basis and something relying upon this basis is a proposal that is established by nothing more than a mistaken imagining.


[3390]
DPER NA ‘JIG RTEN NA ‘KHAR GZHONG DANG ZHO GNYIS NGO BO THA DAD PA LA RTEN DANG BRTEN PA MTHONG BA LTAR PHUNG PO DANG BDAG GNYIS LA DE LTAR MTHONG BA MED PAS RTEN DANG BRTEN PA’I NGO BOR RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED DO,,

In the everyday world, for example, we can see an example of a basis and something relying upon that basis where some yogurt—and the metal dish that might hold that yogurt—are essentially separate entities.  We do not though see this sort of thing with the pair of the parts to the person and the self.  As such, it is not the case that there is a relationship here of a basis and what depends upon that basis existing through some essential nature of their own.


	[3391]
[VI.143]
Iṣṭo nātmā rūpavān nāsti yasmād
ātmā matvarthīya yogo hi nātaḥ,
Bhede gomān rūpavān apyabhede
tattvānyatve rūpato nātmanaḥ staḥ.

,BDAG NI GZUGS LDAN MI ‘DOD GANG PHYIR BDAG,
,YOD MIN DE PHYIR LDAN DON SBYOR BA MED,
,GZHAN NA GNAG LDAN GZHAN MIN GZUGS LDAN NA,
,BDAG NI GZUGS LAS DE NYID GZHAN NYID MED,

		We do not accept
		That the self is something
		That could possess form;

		Why we say so
		Is that there is no
		Possibility of the self;

		Therefore the point of
		The connection possessed
		By them is not something
		That could exist.

		Suppose it were
		To something being other:
		“He is possessed of a blackie.”

		Suppose he was possessed
		Of a physical form where
		There was no separate thing.

		The relationship of the self
		To the form is neither the same;
		Nor are they essentially different.


[3392]
PHUNG PO DANG LDAN PA NYID KYANG BDAG LA NGO BO NYID KYIS JI LTAR YOD PA MA YIN PA DE LTAR BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

Here next we have an explanation of how the very possession of the parts to the person is not something that could ever exist with the self by its very nature.


[3393]
BDAG NI GZUGS KYI PHUNG PO DANG LDAN PA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAR MI ‘DOD DE, RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR NA BDAG PHUNG PO RNAMS LAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG DANG THA DAD PA NI BKAG ZIN PAS YOD PA MIN PA DE’I PHYIR, BDAG PHUNG PO DANG LDAN PA’I SBYOR BA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED DE,

We do not then accept the idea that the self is something that could possess the heap of form in a way where this occurred through some nature of its own.  Our reason for saying this, why we say it’s so, is that there is no possibility of asserting that the self is either—by nature—one with or separate from the parts to the person; we have already disproved these possibilities.  Therefore the connection possessed by the self and the parts to the person is not something that could exist through any nature of its own.


[3394]
‘DI LTAR LDAN PA’I RKYEN YANG LHA SBYIN GNAG STE BA LANG DANG LDAN NO ZHES PA LTA BU NI, GZHAN NA STE NGO BO THA DAD PA LA SBYOR LA, 

The fact that we could have this kind of factor here is something similar to the way in which we say that “John is possessed of a blackie” (referring to a kind of dark-colored cow).  Which is to say, suppose we made the reference here to something being other, or essentially separate.


[3395]
LHA SBYIN GZUGS DANG LDAN ZHES PA LTA BU NI NGO BO GZHAN MIN PA LA SBYOR BA YIN NA, BDAG NI GZUGS LAS DE NYID DE GCIG DANG, GZHAN NYID DE THA DAD PA MED PAS, BDAG GZUGS DANG LDAN PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ‘DI YANG MI SRID DO,,

And then suppose we posed a connection where we said that “John is possessed of a physical form,” where there was no essentially separate thing.  The relationship of the self to the form is neither that they are essentially the same, or one; nor are they essentially different, where they are things distinct from each other.  As such, neither is it a possibility that the self could be possessed of form in a way that existed through some nature of its own.


[3396]
DE DAG GIS NI PHUNG PO LHAG MA BZHI DANG LDAN PA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA YANG BKAG PAR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

You should understand that the points here further serve to deny that the self could be possessed of any of the remaining four parts to the person in a way that existed in & of itself.



How destruction is mistaken

[3397]
GNYIS PA NI, DA NI SNGAR BKAG ZIN PA’I PHYOGS RNAMS BSDOMS TE BSTAN PAS ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BAS PHYIN CI LOG LA DMIGS PAS RNAM PAS ZHUGS PA’I GRANGS BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

This brings us to our second part from above, which is a summary presentation of the denials.  Which means that we will now set forth the whole collection of the positions that we have up to here denied: we will give an explanation enumerating the different ways in which the view of the collection of destruction utilizes an aspect where it focuses in a mistaken way.


	[3398]
[VI.144]
Rūpaṃ nātmā rūpavān naiva cātmā
rūpe nātmā rūpam ātmanyasac ca,
Skandhān evaṃ viddhi sarvāṃś caturdhā
viṃśaty aṃśā eta iṣṭāḥ svadṛṣṭeḥ.

,GZUGS BDAG MA YIN BDAG NI GZUGS LDAN MIN,
,GZUGS LA BDAG MED BDAG LA’ANG GZUGS YOD MIN,
,DE LTAR RNAM BZHIR PHUNG KUN SHES BYA STE,
,DE DAG BDAG TU LTA BA NYI SHUR ‘DOD,

		Form is not
		The self;

		The self is not
		Possessed of form;

		Form does not
		Possess the self;

		And the self does not
		Possess form.

		You should understand
		All the parts to the person
		Just as that, as four
		Different types.

		These are accepted
		As the twenty
		Views as a self.


[3399]
GZUGS NI BDAG MA YIN PA LA BDAG TU LTA BA DANG, [f. 232b] BDAG NI GZUGS DANG NGO BO NYID KYIS LDAN PA MIN PA LA DER LTA BA DANG, GZUGS LA BDAG DANG BDAG LA GZUGS RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MIN PA LA DER LTA BA BZHI STE,

Let’s consider then these four: (1) the view that form is the self, even though it is not; (2) the view that the self is possessed of form, through some essence of its own, even though it is not; and the views that (3) either form possesses the self, or (4) the self possesses form, in a way that does not exist through some nature of its own.


[3400]
GZUGS PHUNG LA BSHAD PA DE LTAR ‘JIG LTAS LTA BA’I TSUL RNAM PA BZHIR TSOR BA LA SOGS PA’I PHUNG PO BZHI PO KUN LA BZHI BZHIR LTA BA SHES PAR BYA STE, DE DAG NI BDAG TU LTA BA ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I CHA NYI SHUR ‘DOD PA YIN NO,,

You should understand that—just as we have explained the case with the part of the person which is form—the view of destruction can be understand as being of four different types, with a view in four distinctions each for all of the four parts to the person such as feelings and the like.  These then are accepted as being the twenty different parts to the view of the collection of destruction as it views things as having a self.


[3401]
GAL TE BDAG GZUGS PHUNG DANG NGO BO THA DAD PAR LTA BA BSNAN NAS PHUNG PO RE RE LA RNAM PAR DPYAD PA LNGA LNGA SKABS SU BAB LA,

Someone may come with the following question—

Suppose we get to a point where we are engaging in five different examinations for each of the different parts to the person, having added the view that the self is essentially different from the part consisting of form.


[3402]
RTZA SHE LAS KYANG,
,PHUNG MIN PHUNG PO LAS GZHAN MIN,
,DE LA PHUNG MED DER DE MED,
,DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA PHUNG LDAN MIN,
,DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA GANG ZHIG YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS PA MA YIN NAM,

After all, doesn’t Wisdom state the following?

		They are not
		The parts to the person,

		Nor are they something
		Other than the parts.

		They have no parts,
		Nor are they there.

		Those Gone Thus
		Are not possessed of parts;

		Where could you ever find
		The Ones Gone Thus?


[3403]
DE’I PHYIR CHA NYER LNGAR ‘GYUR DGOS PA LA CHA NYI SHUR JI SKAD BRJOD CE NA,

As such, there should have been 25 different divisions here; why then do you mention but 20?


[3404]
‘JIG LTA’I CHA NYI SHU PO DE DAG NI MDO LAS RNAM PAR BZHAG LA, DE LTAR ‘JOG PA’I RGYU MTSAN NI SNGON DU PHUNG PO RNAMS MA BZUNG BAR ‘JIG LTAS BDAG TU MNGON PAR ZHEN PAR MI NUS PAS, RNAM PA BZHI BZHI’I SGO NAS PHUNG PO RNAMS LA DMIGS SHING BDAG LA ‘JUG GO

These twenty different divisions of the view of destruction are set forth in sutra.  The reason for positing them this way is that—without first holding to the parts to the person—the view of destruction would be unable to hold the strong belief in a self.  As such, we say that it focuses upon the parts to the person in four types each, and thus engages in the self.


[3405]
,DE’I PHYIR PHUNG PO RNAMS MA GTOGS PAR GZHAN DU BDAG TU ZHEN PA’I GZHI LNGA PA MU STEGS MA GTOGS PA LA MI ‘BYUNG BAS, CHA LNGA PA MA GSUNGS SO,,

As such, if we exclude the heaps, there is no other, fifth basis which one believes strongly is the self—that is, unless we include here the viewpoints of the River Schools.  This then is why no fifth part was described.


[3406]
RTZA SHE LAS PHYOGS GZHAN LNGA PA GSUNGS PA NI MU STEGS PA’I LUGS DGAG PA’I PHYIR RO, ZHES BYA BAR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

You can understand this from the statement that the fifth option mentioned in Wisdom “is a denial of the system of the River Schools.”


	[3407]
[VI.145]
,LTA RI BDAG MED RTOGS PA’I RDO RJE YIS,
,BCOM BDAG GANG DANG LHAN CIG ‘JIG ‘GYUR PA,
,’JIG TSOGS LTA RI LHUN STUG LA GNAS PA,
,RTZE MO MTHO BAR GYUR PA [211b] ‘DI DAG GO,

		The mountain of view
		Is destroyed with
		The diamond weapon
		
		Of realizing
		That no self exists.

		The self that was
		Will be destroyed
		Along with it.

		The high peaks
		That are found
		On the massive
		Central mountain

		Of the view
		Of the collection of
		Destruction are these [f. 211b].		
		

[3408]
DE LA ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I RI’I RTZE MO NYI SHU MTHO BA, YE SHES KYI RDO RJES BCOM NAS RGYUN DU ZHUGS PA’I ‘BRAS BU MNGON DU BYAS SO, ZHES GANG LUNG LAS GSUNGS PA NI,

Let’s consider then the statement in scripture which reads—

We take the diamond weapon of wisdom and use it to destroy the twenty lofty peaks of the mountain of the view of the collection of destruction; and with that, we bring about the spiritual goal of having entered the stream.


[3409]
[f. 233a] DMIGS PA NGA LA DMIGS NAS RNAM PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA’I ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I RI BO ‘PHAGS PA’I YE SHES KYI RDO RJE MA BABS PAS,

And so let’s consider that mountain of the view of destruction which takes, as its object of focus, the “me” and maintains an aspect of it which holds it to exist through some nature of its own.  Here is what will happen, if we don’t manage to bring the diamond weapon of wisdom down upon it.


[3410]
NYIN RE ZHING NYON MONGS PA’I BRAG RDO ‘PHEL BA, ‘KHOR BA THOG MA MED NAS ‘BYUNG BA, DPANGS KHAMS GSUM DU MTHO BA, PHYOGS KYI NGOS MA LUS PA KHYAB PA, MA RIG PA’I GSER GYI SA GZHI LAS ‘THON PA,

With every day then the boulders of everything related to the negative emotions will increase.  The heights of the three realms—which have occurred here within the cycle of pain from time with no beginning—will grow ever taller, and spread in every direction.  They will tower up from the planet’s golden base, which itself represents misunderstanding.


[3411]
BDAG MED PA MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I YE SHES KYI RDO RJE YIS BCOM PA STE BSHIG PA NA, BCOM PA’I BDAG TU LTA BA GANG DANG LHAN CIG TU ‘JIG PAR ‘GYUR BA,

Suppose though that we are able to destroy it—to smash it—with the diamond weapon of the wisdom which realizes, directly, that no self exists.  In this case, the view that holds to the self that was destroyed will be destroyed along with it.


[3412]
DE MA THAG TU BSHAD PA’I RTZA BA’I ‘JIG TSOGS LA LTA BA’I RI LHUN STUG PO LA GNAS PA’I RTZE MO MTHO BAR GYUR PA NYI SHU NI, SNGAR BSHAD PA’I PHUNG PO LNGA PO RE RE LA BZHI BZHIR BSHAD PA ‘DI DAG GO

Just after that, we see referenced the twenty high peaks that are found on the massive central mountain of the fundamental view of the collection of destruction.  These consist of the five parts to the person which, as we mentioned before, are each considered in four different ways.


[3413]
,’DIR ‘GREL PA’I ‘GYUR LAS, RTZE MO CHES MTHO BA GANG DAG DANG LHAN CIG ‘JIG PAR ‘GYUR BA DE DAG NI RTZE MO YIN PAR SHES PAR BYA’O, ZHES ‘BYUNG YANG RTZA BA’I ‘GYUR LTAR, RTZA BA’I ‘JIG LTA DANG LHAN CIG CES ‘BYUNG BA LTAR BYA’O,,

In the translation of the autocommentary at this point we read, “You should understand that what are destroyed with the extremely high peaks are what are referred to as ‘peaks’ here.”  This should be read as we see it in the translation of the root text, where it says “along with the foundation form of the view of destruction.”


[3414]
DE YANG LHAN SKYES KYI ‘JIG LTA NGAR ‘DZIN SNGAR BSHAD PA’I NYI SHU PO GANG YANG MIN PAS, ‘JIG TSOGS LTA RI LHUN STUG LA GNAS PA, ZHES RTZE MO NYI SHU’I ‘JIG LTA RTZA BA’I ‘JIG LTA LA GNAS PAR GSUNGS SO,,

That is, grasping to a “me” as the innate form of the view of destruction is not represented by any of the twenty types described before.  As such, when we see the reference to what is “found on the massive central mountain of the view of the collection of destruction” here, the point being made is that the view of destruction in the form of the twenty peaks is resting on the view of destruction itself.
 

[3415]
GANG DANG LHAN CIG TU NYI SHU RGYUN ZHUGS KYIS SPANGS PA’I RTZA BA’I ‘JIG LTA YANG KUN BRTAGS YIN LA, DE YANG DE RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR ‘DZIN PA TZAM LA MI BYED KYI, DE’I ‘DZIN STANGS ‘THAD LDAN DU GRUB MTHA’ NGAN PA LA BRTEN NAS ‘DZIN PA’I SA BON RGYUN ZHUGS KYIS SPANGS PA’O,,

The fundamental form of the view of destruction when we speak of how one who enters the stream eliminates its twenty concomitant forms, moreover, is a learned form.  And it moreover does not refer only to holding that things could exist by definition; rather, the stream enterer eliminates as well the seeds for that stance here—itself brought about by relying upon mistaken schools of thought—that how this view considers things must be correct.



Others on the substantial person

[3416]
BZHI PA LA GNYIS, PHYOGS SNGA MA [f. 233b] BRJOD PA DANG, LUGS DE DGAG PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

Here is that fourth point, where we deny a substantial form of the person that would be neither itself nor something other than itself.  This comes in two parts: describing the position taken by the other party; and then disproving that position.


[3417]
DA NI ‘PHAGS PA MANG POS BKUR BA DAG GIS BRTAGS PA’I GANG ZAG RDZAS SU YOD PAR SMRA BA BSAL BA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

The Arya now turns to an explanation meant to clarify the position made up by the Widely Respected group, of a person who exists substantially.


	[3418]
[VI.146]
Icchantyeke pudgalaṃ dravya santaṃ
tattvānyatvānitya nityādyavācyam,
Ṣaḍ vijñāna jñeyatā ceṣyate’sya
so’haṃkārasyāśrayo hīṣyate ca.

,KHA CIG DE NYID GZHAN NYID RTAG MI RTAG,
,LA SOGS BRJOD MED GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD ‘DOD,
,RNAM SHES DRUG GI SHES BYAR DE ‘DOD CING,
,DE NI NGAR ‘DZIN GZHIR YANG ‘DOD PA YIN,

		Some people say
		It cannot be described
		As precisely those,

		Or something
		Perfectly different;

		Or as unchanging
		Or changing

		Or anything
		Of the like.

		They assert
		That the person
		Exists substantially,

		And they further assert
		That this is something
		Which is perceived
		By the six types
		Of consciousness;

		And they believe
That the same is
		The basis for the
		Tendency to hold
		To a “me.”


[3419]
RANG GI SDE PA MANG POS BKUR BA PA KHA CIG NI, PHUNG PO MA GTOGS DE ‘DZIN MA GRUB PHYIR, ZHES PA’I RIGS PAS GANG ZAG PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA MIN LA, PHUNG PO’I RANG BZHIN CAN YANG MIN TE, YIN NA BDAG DE SKYE ‘JIG DANG LDAN PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here then is the idea of some people who belong to the Widely Respected group.  They would reference the verse that includes, “Because you could never establish the capacity to hold to some that didn’t involve the parts,” and say that there is no person who is essentially separate from the parts to the person.  They would say as well that this is not something which possesses the nature of these parts; since if it were, then the self would be something which exhibited started & stopping.


[3420]
DE’I PHYIR BDAG GAM GANG ZAG NI PHUNG PO LAS DE NYID DANG GZHAN NYID DU BRJOD DU MED DO, ,DE BZHIN DU GANG ZAG NI RTAG PA DANG MI RTAG PA LA SOGS PA NYID DU YANG BRJOD DU MED DO,,

As such, they would say, the self or person cannot be described, relative to the parts to the person, as being precisely those parts themselves, or something perfectly different.  Just so, the person would be something that could never be described as either unchanging or changing, or anything exactly of the like.


[3421]
GANG ZAG DE RDZAS SU YOD PAR YANG ‘DOD DE, LAS GNYIS KYI BYED PA PO DANG, DE GNYIS KYI ‘BRAS BU BDE SDUG GI ZA BA PO NYID DU BRJOD PA’I PHYIR DANG, ‘KHOR BAR BCINGS PA DANG MYANG ‘DAS KYI SKABS SU THAR BA PO’AM GROL BA PO YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

They would also assert that the person is something that exists substantially.  This is because, first of all, it has been described as being precisely the one who commits the two types of karma; as well as the consumer of the results of these two—whether they be pleasure or pain.  It is also the one who is shackled to the circle of pain; and the one who achieves freedom—or, we can say, the one who achieves liberation—at the point of nirvana.


[3422]
BDAG DE RNAM SHES DRUG GI SHES BYAR YANG ‘DOD CING, BDAG DE NI NGAR ‘DZIN PA’I GZHI STE DMIGS PAR YANG ‘DOD PA YIN NO,,

They further assert that this self is something which is perceived by the six types of consciousness; and they believe that the same self is the basis—or the object of focus—for the tendency to hold to a “me.”



Disproving the substantial person

[3423]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second part here: disproving the position just described.


[3424]
GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD DU SMRA BA ‘DI YANG MI RIGS PA NYID DU BSHAD PA,

Now this assertion that the person exists in a substantial way is a perfectly mistaken explanation.


	[3425]
[VI.147]
Naivāvācyaṃ vastusat saṃpratītaṃ
yac cittasyāvācyatāṃ naiṣi rūpāt |
Ātmā kaścid vastusiddho yadi syān
nāvācyaḥ syāc cittavat siddharūpaḥ.

,GANG PHYIR GZUGS LAS SEMS BRJOD MED MI RTOGS,
,DNGOS YOD BRJOD MED RTOGS PA MA YIN NYID,
,GAL TE BDAG ‘GA’ DNGOS POR GRUB GYUR NA,
,SEMS LTAR GRUB DNGOS BRJOD DU MED MI ‘GYUR,

		For what reason?
		We don’t understand
		How the mind’s
		
		Relationship to form
		Cannot be described.

		This same idea
		Can never be described
		As things that exist
		As entitites.

		Suppose that
		There were some
		Possible cases
		Of the self

		That existed
		As entities.

		Entities that existed
		In a way similar
		To the mind

		Would have to be
		Indescribable.


[3426]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR NA GZUGS LAS SEMS DE NYID DANG GZHAN GANG DU YANG BRJOD DU MED PAR MI RTOGS PA STE MI ‘DOD PA LTAR, 

For what reason is this true?  We don’t understand how—which is to say, we don’t agree—that the mind’s relationship to form cannot be described either as it being precisely that form, or something other than that form.


[3427]
DNGOS PO STE RDZAS SU YOD PA RNAMS LA DE NYID DANG GZHAN NYID DU BRJOD DU MED PAR RTOGS PA MA YIN PA NYID DE, ‘DI LTAR GAL TE BDAG ‘GA’ ZHIG DNGOS POR TE RDZAS SU GRUB PAR GYUR NA, SEMS LTAR DU GRUB PA’I DNGOS PO SGO GNYIS GANG DU BRJOD DU MED PAR MI ‘GYUR RO,,

And let’s also consider this same idea that the mind can never be described either as the very same as, or as perfectly distinct from, things that exist as entities—which is to say, as substantial.  Because suppose that there were some possible cases of the self that existed as entities; which here means, in a substantial way.  In that scenario, entities that existed in a way similar to the mind would have to be indescribable, in either of the two senses.


[3428]
DE’I PHYIR TSIGS SU BCAD PA SNGA MAS BRJOD DU MED PA LA RDZAS SU [f. 234a] YOD PA MI SRID PAR BSTAN NAS, GANG ZAG BTAGS YOD DU BSTAN PA’I PHYIR BSHAD PA,

As such, the previous verse is indicating that it would be impossible for something that was indescribable to exist in a substantial way.  And then now we come to an explanation meant to show how the person exists as something labeled.



	[3429]
[VI.148]
Yaḥ skandhebhyo’vācyatāṃ yāta ātmā
sattvaṃ siddhaṃ svātmanā tasya mā gāḥ,
Vastu tvenāsiddha rūpo ghaṭas te
rūpādibhyo’vācyatāṃ yena yātaḥ.

,GANG PHYIR KHYOD BUM DNGOS POR MA GRUB PA’I,
,NGO BO GZUGS SOGS LAS BRJOD MED ‘GYUR BAS,
,BDAG GANG PHUNG PO LAS BRJOD MED ‘GYUR TE,
,RANG GIS YOD PAR GRUB PAR RTOGS MI BYA,

	What is the reason?
	The relationship
	Of your water pitcher—

	Which has an
	Essential nature
	Where it cannot exist
	As an entity—

	To form and the rest
	Is not something
	Which can be described.

	As such, that self
	Is something whose
	Relationship to

	The parts
	To the person
	Cannot be described.

	You cannot understand
	That it itself exists.


[3430]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR KHYOD KYI LTAR NA BUM PA RANG RKYA THUB PA’I DNGOS POR MA GRUB PA’I NGO BO DE RANG GI YAN LAG GI GZUGS SOGS LAS DE NYID DE GCIG DANG NGO BO THA DAD DU BRJOD DU MED PAR ‘GYUR BAR ‘DOD PAS,

And what is the reason why we can say that?  According to you, the relationship of a water pitcher—which has an essential nature where it cannot exist as an entity which stands of its own accord—to its parts of form and the rest is not something which can be described as being just that (the very same) or essentially different. 


[3431]
DE BZHIN DU BDAG GANG YIN PA DE YANG PHUNG PO LAS DE NYID DANG NGO BO THA DAD PA’I GZHAN NYID DU BRJOD DU MED PA’I BTAGS YOD DU ‘GYUR BA 

As such then we can say the same with that thing which is the self; that is, it is something imputed whose relationship to the parts of the person cannot be described as either being the very same as them, or being different in the sense of essentially separate from them.


[3432]
DE’I PHYIR GANG ZAG RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS YOD PAR GRUB PAR RTOGS PA STE GZUNG BAR MI BYA’O,,

As such, you cannot “understand”—which is to say, hold—that the person exists in & of itself: through some nature of its own.


[3433]
DE LTAR TSIGS SU BCAD PA GNYIS KYIS RDZAS SU YOD PA DGAG PA DANG, BTAGS YOD DU SGRUB PA NYE BAR BSTAN NAS, DA NI DE NYID DANG GZHAN GNYIS DNGOS PO’I RTEN NYID DU BRJOD NAS, RTEN DE MA YIN PA NYID KYIS BDAG RDZAS SU YOD PA ‘GOG PAR RTZOM PA,

As such then we have two verses which are indicating here that things cannot exist in any substantial manner; but can be established as existing by imputation.  Now then we will move on to undertaking our denial that the self could exist in a substantial way, as it does not in any way provide a basis, described as the very basis of things of things either as those things themselves, or as something other than them.


	[3434]
[VI.149]
Vijñānaṃ te svātmato’nanyad iṣṭaṃ
rūpādibhyo bhinna rūpaṃ mataṃ ca,
Vastunyete dve gatī nāma dṛṣṭe
nāstyātmāto vastu dharmair viyogāt.

,KHYOD KYI RNAM SHES RANG BDAG LAS GZHAN NI,
,MI ‘DOD GZUGS SOGS LAS GZHAN DNGOS ‘DOD CING,
,DNGOS LA RNAM PA DE GNYIS MTHONG ‘GYUR BA,
,DE PHYIR BDAG MED DNGOS CHOS DANG BRAL PHYIR,

		You would be
		Asserting that
		Your consciousness

		Was not something
		Different from
		Your self;

		And asserting
The position
That it was
No different entity

Than form
And the rest.

With entities
We see that things
Are two types;

For this reason,
The self cannot exist,

For it is devoid
Of the quality
Of an entity.


[3435]
GAL TE KHYOD KYI LTAR BDAG RDZAS SU YOD NA NI, KHYOD KYI RNAM SHES NI RANG GI BDAG NYID LAS GZHAN NI MIN PAR ‘DOD PA BZHIN DU, GANG ZAG KYANG NGES PAR RANG GI BDAG NYID LAS GZHAN MIN PAS DE NYID DU BRJOD DGOS SO,,

Suppose then that—as you would have it—the self existed substantially.  In this case, you would be asserting that your consciousness was not something different from your very own self.  Just so, the person too would with certainty be no different from your own perfect self; and you would have to describe it as such.


[3436]
YANG KHYOD KYI RNAM SHES GZUGS SOGS LAS GZHAN PA’I DNGOS POR ‘DOD PA BZHIN DU, GANG ZAG KYANG PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PAR BRJOD DGOS SO,,

So too if you were taking the position that your consciousness was no different entity than form and the rest, you would have to say that the person was something that was essentially different from the parts to the person.


[3437]
DNGOS PO LA GCIG DANG THA DAD KYI RNAM PA DE GNYIS NGES PAR MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR BA DE’I PHYIR BDAG RDZAS SU MED DE, DNGOS PO’I CHOS DE NYID DANG GZHAN GNYIS SU GRUB PA DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR RO,,

And with entities we see that things are fixed at two types: either they are one & the same, or they are separate.  For this reason, the self cannot exist as a substantial entity, for it is devoid of existing either way: as the essence or quality of an entity itself, or as something other than it.



The seven extremes

[3438]
LNGA PA LA BZHI, BDAG MTHA’ BDUN DU MED KYANG [f. 234b] BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA SHING RTA DANG ‘DRA BAR BSTAN PA, SNGAR MA BSHAD PA’I PHYOGS LHAG MA GNYIS RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA, DE LTAR BSHAD PA LA GZHAN GYI RTZOD PA SPANG BA, MING GI THA SNYAD KYI DON GZHAN YANG GRUB PAR BSTAN PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

The fifth section here—explaining, with the use of a metaphor, how it is that we establish that the self is something labelled through dependence—has four parts of its own:

(1) a demonstration that, even though the self is devoid of the seven extremes, it is still similar to a wagon, in being labeled in dependence;

(2) an extended explanation of two additional positions which have not been covered so far;

(3) rejecting arguments by others concerning this way of explaining things; and

(4) a demonstration how there is another interpretation of the meaning of terms used as names.

Here then is the first of these.


	[3439]
[VI.150]
Nāhaṃkārasyāśrayo vastu tasmān
nānyaḥ skandhebhyo’pi na skandharūpaḥ,
Skandādhāro naiva naivaiṣa tadvān
skandhāṃs tūpādāya yātyeṣa siddhim.

,DE PHYIR NGAR ‘DZIN RTEN NI DNGOS PO MIN,
,PHUNG LAS GZHAN MIN PHUNG PO’I NGO BO MIN,
,PHUNG PO RTEN MIN ‘DI NI DE LDAN MIN,
,’DI NI PHUNG PO RNAMS BRTEN ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR,

	For that reason,
	The basis for
	Holding to some
	“Me” is not
	A substantial thing.

	It is not
	Something other
	Than the parts
	To the person.

	Neither is it
	The essence
	Of the parts
	To the person.

	Neither is it
	The basis;

	Neither is this
	Possessed of those.

	This is something
	That exists through
	Dependence upon
	The parts of the person.


[3440]
GANG GI PHYIR SNGAR BSHAD PA DE LTAR RNAM PAR DPYAD PA NA GANG ZAG RDZAS SU YOD PA MI ‘THAD PA DE’I PHYIR NGAR ‘DZIN PA’I RTEN TE DMIGS PA NI, DNGOS PO STE RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MIN TE,

Now if one does the examination as we have previously described it, we see that it is incorrect to say that the person exists substantially.  For that reason, (1) the basis—which is to say, the object of focus—for holding to some “me” is not something which is a substantial thing, which is to say, something that could exist through any nature of its own.


[3441]
RNAM PAR DPYAD PA NA BDAG NI PHUNG PO LAS GZHAN TE NGO BO THA DAD PA MIN LA, PHUNG PO’I NGO BO TSOGS PA DANG YA GYAL GANG YANG BDAG MIN PA DANG,

If we really investigate the matter, we see (2) that the self is not something other than the parts to the person; which is to say, something essentially different from them.  But (3) neither is the “essence” of the parts to the person—which is say, the collection of these parts, or (4) any one component of that collection—the self either.


[3442]
BDAG PHUNG PO RNAMS KYI RTEN DANG, BDAG ‘DI LA PHUNG PO RTEN DU YOD PA YANG MIN ZHING, BDAG ‘DI NI PHUNG PO DE RNAMS DANG LDAN PA’ANG NGO BO NYID KYIS YOD PA MIN NO,,

But (5) neither is the self the basis for the parts to the person; (6) nor do those parts use this self as something that they rely upon.  (7) Neither is it the case that we can say that this self is possessed of those parts to the person—at least in a way that exists in & of itself.


[3443]
DE’I PHYIR RANG GI SDE PA GANG DAG BDAG BTAGS PAR YOD CES PA’AM, BDAG DON DAM PAR MA DMIGS PAR ‘DOD PAS KYANG RUNG STE JI SKAD SMRAS PA’I RNAM PAS BDAG KHAS BLANG BAR MI BYA’O ZHES BSHAD PA NI, BDAG ‘DI NI PHUNG PO RNAMS LA BRTEN NAS GRUB PAR ‘GYUR BA’O,,

As such, it is appropriate for any of our own groups to assert either that the self is something that exists as labeled; or to say that it is not something which exists in an ultimate manner.  That is, when we say that we cannot accept a self that exists in any of the different aspects described above, what we are saying is that this “self” is something that exists through dependence upon the parts of the person.


[3444]
JI LTAR ‘DI LA BRTEN NAS ‘DI ‘BYUNG ZHES BYA BA ‘DI TZAM ZHIG KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA’I RNAM PAR BZHAG PA MA CHAD PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR KHAS LEN PA NA, RGYU MED SOGS BZHI LAS SKYE BA MI ‘DOD PA DE BZHIN DU,

And so suppose that we simply state our case as follows: “This has happened, depending on that other thing.”  With this, we avoid discounting the description of a reality which is deceptive.  And when this is our position, we avoid accepting the idea that things could arise through any of the four options of having no cause at all, and so on.


[3445]
BDAG GI SKABS ‘DIR YANG PHUNG PO LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PAR ‘DOD PA NA, JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I SKYON DANG LDAN PA’I PHYOGS SNGA BSAL NAS, PHUNG PO RNAMS LA BRTEN NAS GDAGS PA ZHES BYA BA ‘DI TZAM ZHIG ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD RNAM PAR GNAS PAR BYA BA’I [f. 235a] PHYIR KHAS BLANG BAR BYA STE, BDAG TU THA SNYAD BTAGS PA BSNYON MI NUS PAR MTHONG BA’I PHYIR RO,,

If in the present context then we accept the idea that the self is something ascribed on the basis of the parts to the person, we are able to banish those positions of other parties, with all their problems.  All we simply need to agree to is that “it is labeled on the basis of the parts to the person,” and then we can keep all the normal expressions of the world.  That is, by this time we have seen that no one can succeed in speaking against the idea that the self is just something labeled in terms.


	[3446]
[VI.151]
Svāṅgebhya iṣṭo na ratho yathānyo
na cāpyananyo na ca nāma tadvān,
Nāṅgeṣu nāṅgānyapi tatra nāpi
saṃghāta mātraṃ na ca sanniveśaḥ.

,SHING RTA RANG YAN LAG LAS GZHAN ‘DOD MIN,
,GZHAN MIN MA YIN DE LDAN YANG MIN ZHING,
,YAN LAG LA MIN YAN LAG DAG DER MIN,
,’DUS PA TZAM MIN DBYIBS MIN JI BZHIN NO,

		We are not saying
		That a wagon
		Is other than
		Its component parts.

		Neither are we
		Saying that
		It could be
		The other;

		Neither that
		It is possessed
		Of those,

		Or upon its
		Component parts,

		Or that the
		Component parts
		Are there;

		Neither that
		It is the 
		Simple collection,
		Or the outline.

		All this applies.


[3447]
BDAG BTAGS PA TZAM DU GRUB PAR BYA BA’I DON DU JI SKAD BSHAD PA’I DON NYID GSAL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, PHYI ROL GYI DPE STON CING BSHAD PA,

The next section here is presented in order to make even more clear the point we have just made—with an eye towards establishing that the self is only something which exists as labeled.  Towards that end, we present and then explain a metaphor from the normal, outside world.


[3448]
SHING RTA RANG GI YAN LAG LAS DON GZHAN DU ‘DOD PA MIN LA, GZHAN MIN TE GCIG TU YANG GRUB PA MA YIN PA DANG, PHUNG PO DE DANG LDAN PA DANG, YAN LAG LA PHAR BRTEN PA DANG, YAN LAG DAG BDAG DER BRTEN PA RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MIN PA DANG, YAN LAG ‘DUS PA TZAM DANG YAN LAG GI DBYIBS MIN PA JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU, BDAG DANG PHUNG PO GNYIS KYANG DE BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

That is, (1) we are not saying that a wagon is something other than its component parts.  But (2) neither are we saying that it could be the other: that it could exist as one and the same as these parts.  And neither are we saying (3) that the self is possessed of those parts to the person; or (4) that it depends out upon its component parts; or (5) that the component parts depend there upon the self—when we are talking about each of these possibilities existing through some nature of its own.  Neither are we saying (6) that the wagon is the simple collection of its component parts, or (7) that it consists of the outline of the parts put together.  Which is to say, one should understand that all this applies as well to the pair of the self and the parts to the person.



Denying the collection
is the wagon

[3449]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, DNGOS KYI DON, RIGS PA DE GZHAN LA KHA SPO BA’O,,

Which brings us to our second part from before: an extended explanation of two additional positions which have not been covered so far.  This we cover in two sections: the actual point, and then applying this logic to other cases.


[3450]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, TSOGS PA SHING RTAR ‘DOD PA DGAG, DBYIBS TZAM SHING RTAR ‘DOD PA DGAG PA’O,  ,DANG PO NI,

The first section itself includes two points: denying the position that the collection constitutes the wagon; and then denying the position that the outline itself could be the wagon.  Here is the first of these.


[3451]
PHYOGS SNGA MA LNGA NI SNGAR BSTAN ZIN PAS ‘DIR TSOGS PA’I PHYOGS DANG, DBYIBS KYI PHYOGS GNYIS SHING RTA YIN PA ‘GOG PA NI BSGRUB PAR BYA DGOS PAS DE DAG STON PA BRTZAM PAR BYA STE,

We have finished then presenting the first five of the positions indicated; as such, the time has come for us to establish how we deny first the idea that collection could be the wagon; and then secondly the idea that the outline could be the wagon.  Here is how we start with that.


	[3452]
[VI.152]
Saṃhāta mātraṃ hi ratho yadi syāt
kūṭasthiteṣveva bhaved rathatvam,
Saṃsthāna mātraṃ ca ratho na yuktaḥ
santyaṅgināṅgāni vinā na yasmād.

,GAL TE TSOGS TZAM SHING RTAR ‘GYUR NA NI,
,SIL BUR GNAS LA SHING RTA NYID YOD ‘GYUR,
,GANG PHYIR YAN LAG CAN MED YAN LAG DAG,
,MED PAS DBYIBS TZAM SHING RTAR RIGS PA’ANG MIN,

		Suppose it were the case
		That the simple collection
		Were the wagon.

		In that case then,
		When piled together,
		That too would have to be
		A perfect wagon.

Why is that the case?
If the whole which incorporates
The various component parts
Is absent, then the 
Component parts themselves
Are also absent.

It would not be logical,
Either, to say that
The simple outline of
The component parts
Was the wagon.


[3453]
GAL TE SHING RTA’I YAN LAG TSOGS TZAM SHING RTAR ‘GYUR NA NI, SHING RTA BSHIG PA’I YAN LAG GSIL BUR GNAS PA TSOGS PA LA YANG SHING RTA NYID YOD PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

Suppose it were the case that the simple collection of the component parts of the wagon were the wagon.  In that case, then if we were to take the wagon apart and pile together all its separate component parts, then that too would have to be a perfect wagon.


[3454]
YAN LAG GI TSOGS PA RANG GI CHA CAN YIN PA ‘GOG PA ‘DI SNGAR BSHAD ZIN KYANG ‘DIR BKOD PA NI, SNGAR BSTAN PA LAS SKYON GZHAN BSTAN PA’I PHYIR YIN NO,,

Now we have already finished, earlier on, disproving the idea that collection of component parts constitutes their whole.  The reason we return to this discussion at this juncture is to point out still other problems with the concept than those we covered earlier.


[3455]
SKYON GZHAN YANG YOD DE, RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR YAN LAG CAN MED NA, YAN LAG DAG KYANG MED PA DE’I PHYIR YAN LAG [f. 235b] RNAMS MED PAR ‘GYUR TE, SHING RTA LA YAN LAG CAN MED PAR RANG GI SDE PA DE DAG GIS KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And so we can say that there are additional issues here.  And why is that the case?  If the whole which incorporates the various component parts is absent, then the component parts themselves are also absent—these parts then would no longer exist.  And that’s because these particular members of our own school would accept the idea that there is no whole of the composite parts, with a wagon.


[3456]
DE DAG GIS KYANG YAN LAG TSOGS PA CHA SHAS CAN DANG, YAN LAG RNAMS CHA SHAS SU ‘DOD CING, DE BZHIN DU YAN LAG DANG YAN LAG CAN DU’ANG ‘DOD PAS, YAN LAG CAN MED PAR KHAS MA BLANGS SO SNYAM NA,

Now suppose that you were to think to yourself as follows—

But the fact is that they do believe that the collection of the component parts is the whole of the parts; and that the component parts here are the constitutent parts of the whole.  So too, they accept the idea of component parts and the whole of the component parts.  As such, it is not true that they believe that there is no whole composed of component parts.


[3457]
SKYON MED DE RANG GI LUGS NI PHUNG PO’I YA GYAL DANG TSOGS PA GNYIS KA NYE BAR BLANG BYA YIN PAS, DE NYE BAR LEN PA POR MI ‘DOD PA BZHIN DU,

And yet there is no such problem.  Even in our own system, we believe that both the component pieces of the parts to the person, and the collection of these pieces, is something that we take on; and that therefore these cannot constitute the one that does the taking on.


[3458]
SHING RTA’I YAN LAG RE RE BA DANG TSOGS PA GNYIS KA YAN LAG TU ‘JOG GI ,YAN LAG CAN DU MI ‘JOG LA, SDE PA DE DAG GIS KYANG TSOGS PA MIN PA’I YAN LAG CAN MI ‘DOD PA’I PHYIR DANG, DE YANG ‘GOG PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Just so, both the individual component parts to the wagon and the collection of these parts can all be accepted as components; but cannot be accepted as what possesses the components.  And even those groups as well would refuse to agree to any whole of the component parts which was not a collection of those parts.  They would, further, deny such a thing.


[3459]
‘ANG GI SGRA NI DNGOS SU MA BRJOD PA’I TSOGS PA BSDU BA’I DON TE, SDOD TSUL NI YAN LAG GI DBYIBS TZAM YANG SHING RTAR RIGS PA MIN LA, TSOGS PA TZAM PO YANG MI RIGS SO ZHES SHES PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DU’O,,

The phrase “either” in the root text here is meant to include the collection, even though that is not directly mentioned.  The way this would be present is that it would not be logical, either, to say that the simple outline of the component parts was the wagon.  Neither would the simple collection itself be logical.  This is what we are meant to understand from the use of the phrase.



Denying that the outline
is the wagon

[3460]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: denying the position that the outline itself could be the wagon.


	[3461]
[VI.153]
Saṃsthānam aṅgeṣu yathā purābhūt
pratyekaśas te rathatāṃ gateṣu,
Tathaiva cen nāsti ratho’dhunāpi
viśliṣṭa bhūteṣu yathaiva teṣu.

,KHYOD DBYIBS YAN LAG RE RE SNGAR YOD GYUR,
,JI BZHIN SHING RTAR GTOGS LA’ANG DE BZHIN NO,
,BYE BAR GYUR PA DE DAG LA JI LTAR,
,DE {%DA} LTAR YANG NI SHING RTA YOD MA YIN,

		Your outline
		And each separate
		Component part
		As they existed prior,

		And after they
		Have been incorporated
		Into the wagon,

		Would be as well
		Just the same way.

		It would be there
		In those separated;

		Just so, the wagon
Would no longer
Be something that
Was there now.


[3462]
GZHAN YANG GAL TE KHYOD SHING RTA’I DBYIBS TZAM ZHIG SHING RTAR ‘DOD NA, DBYIBS DE YAN LAG RE RE BA DAG GI YIN NAM, TSOGS PA’I YIN PAR RTOG GRANG,

Moreover, let’s say that you agree to the idea that the outline of the wagon alone is the wagon.  And so we ask you: Is it that you think that outline is something that belongs to each of the component parts, individually?  Or does it belong to the collection of the parts?


[3463]
DANG PO LTAR NA SNGAR MA BSGRIGS PA’I DBYIBS KYI KHYAD PAR MA BTANG BA DAG GI’AM, SNGAR GYI DBYIBS KYI KHYAD PAR BTANG BA DAG GI DBYIBS YIN, DE LA GAL TE DANG PO LTAR ‘DOD PA’ANG DE MI RIGS SO,,

If you agree to the first option, then we ask you another question.  Is it that the outline belongs to these component parts as their shape was characterized prior to the point at which the wagon was assembled, or after they had already relinquished that shape?  We assert further that—if you assert that the former is the case—your position is mistaken.


[3464]
CI’I PHYIR ZHE NA, KHYOD KYI LTAR NA SHING RTA’I ‘PHANG LO LA SOGS PA’I YAN LAG RE RE LA SNGAR MA BSGRIGS PA’I DUS SU DBYIBS JI LTAR YOD PAR GYUR PA BZHIN DU, PHYIS BSGRIGS TE SHING RTAR RTOGS {%GTOGS} PA STE GRUB PA’I DUS SU’ANG SNGA [f. 236a] MA DE BZHIN DU YOD PA YIN NA,

And why is that?  According to you, we should first consider the shape of each separate component part of the wagon—the wheels and all the rest—as they existed prior to the point that they were assembled into the wagon.  And then their shape after they have been incorporated into the wagon—that is, after the wagon has been completed—should as well be something that exists in just the same way as it was before.


[3465]
MA BSGRIGS PA’I BYE BAR GYUR PA’I YAN LAG DE DAG LA JI LTAR SHING RTA YOD PA MIN PA BZHIN DU, DA LTAR YAN LAG RNAMS BSGRIGS PA’I TSE YANG NI SHING RTA YOD PA MA YIN PAR ‘GYUR TE,

If that were indeed the case, then there wouldn’t be any reason why the wagon would not be there in those separated parts, when they were still to be assembled.  And just so, by the same token, the wagon would no longer be something that was there now that the component parts have been put together.


[3466]
YAN LAG SO SO BA’I DBYIBS TZAM LA KHYOD SHING RTAR ‘JOG PA’I PHYIR DANG, SNGA PHYI’I YAN LAG SO SO BA’I DBYIBS LA KHYAD PAR MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s because you have posited no more than the shape of each of the separate, component parts as being the wagon—and there’s no difference in the shape of each of these parts, before or after.


	[3467]
[VI.154]
Saṃsthāna bhedo yadi cādhunāsti
cakrādi kasyeha rathatvakāle,
Gṛhyeta nāmaiṣa na caitad asti
saṃsthāna mātraṃ na ratho’sti tasmāt.

,DA LTA GAL TE SHING RTA NYID DUS ‘DIR,
,’PHANG LO SOGS LA DBYIBS THA DAD YOD NA,
,’DI GZUNG ‘GYUR NA DE YANG YOD MIN TE,
,DE PHYIR DBYIBS TZAM SHING RTAR YOD MA YIN,

		Suppose we refer
		To that point
		In time now
		Of the wagon itself;

		There would be
Separate shapes
Of the wheels & the rest;

And suppose that
These were held.

This though
Could never be,
And for this reason
It is not the case

That the simple shape
Could exist as
The wagon itself.	


[3468]
CI STE PHYOGS GNYIS PA STE DBYIBS KYI KHYAD PAR SNGA MA DANG MI ‘DRA BA GZHAN ZHIG PHYIS ‘BYUNG BA DE SHING RTAR ‘GYUR NA,

And suppose then that you swing to the second position, asserting that an alternate shape differing from the original one has materialized later on, and become the wagon.


[3469]
GAL TE DA LTA SHING RTA NYID DU GRUB PA’I DUS ‘DIR ‘PHANG LO DANG LA SOGS PAS SROG SHING DANG, GZER BU LA SOGS PA SHING RTA’I YAN LAG RNAMS KYI DBYIBS KYI KHYAD PAR SO SOR LHAM PA STE GRU BZHI DANG, RING PO DANG ZLUM PO LA SOGS PA’I DBYIBS SNGAR MA BSGRIGS PA’I DUS DANG, MI MTHUN PA’I THA DAD PA YOD NA,

Suppose then we refer to that point in time now when the wagon itself is already completed, and consider the particular of the shape of the wheels & “the rest”—which would include things like the axle, or the pins that hold the wagon together, or other things of the like.  There would be, say, things that were rectangular or squarish, or long, or rounded, or any other kind of shape that the components might have had before they were assembled together.  These shapes would be separate, inconsistent with each other.


[3470]
YAN LAG SO SO’I DBYIBS MI MTHUN PA ‘DI MIG GI SHES PAS GZUNG DU YOD PAR ‘GYUR NA, DE YANG YOD PA MIN TE, DE’I PHYIR YAN LAG SO SO’I DBYIBS TZAM SHING RTAR YOD PA MA YIN NO,,

And suppose that each of these separate, inconsistent shapes then were to serve as what were held by visual awareness, and so on.  This though could never be; and for this reason it is not the case that the simple shape of each of the individual, component parts could exist as the wagon itself.


[3471]
CI STE ‘PHANG LO LA SOGS PA’I YAN LAG BSGRIGS PA’I TSOGS PA RNAMS KYI DBYIBS KHYAD PAR BA SHING RTAR ‘JOG GO SNYAM NA,

Suppose now that you think to yourself:

It is possible though that we establish the wagon as the collection of the wheels and other components, once they are assembled together.


[3472]
DE YANG MI RIGS SO ZHES BSHAD PA, GAL TE TSOGS PA ZHES BYA BA DNGOS PO STE RDZAS SU YOD PA CUNG ZAD CIG YOD NA NI, DE LA BRTEN PA CAN GYI DBYIBS SU GDAGS PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And what we’re explaining here is that this approach is incorrect.  That is,

Suppose that what you are referring to as the “collection” existed in the least bit in a material way—which is to say, substantially.  In that case, we would be labelling the outline that relied upon it using it as the basis.


[3473]
YAN LAG TSOGS PA ZHES BYA BA RDZAS SU YOD PA CUNG ZAD KYANG MED DO,,

In this case, there would not be the slightest existence of anything we referred to as “the collection of the component parts” which existed in a substantial manner.


	[3474]
[VI.155]
Na cāṅga vṛndasya sa saṃniveśo
vṛndaṃ na kiṃcit tava yena nāma,
Na nāma kiṃcit khalu yat kathaṃ tat
saṃsthānam āśritya bhaviṣyatīha.

,GANG PHYIR KHYOD KYI TSOGS PA CANG MED PAS,

,GANG ZHIG CI YANG MA YIN DE BRTEN NAS,
,’DIR NI DBYIBS SU LTA ZHIG JI LTAR ‘GYUR,

		And why would that
		Be the case?

		According to you,
		There would be
		No collection at all.
		
		As such, the outline
		Is not something of
The collection of
		The component parts.

		How then could it
		Ever be the case
		That here something that
		Wasn’t anything at all

		Could be the outline
		Which provided
		The basis?		


[3475]
RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR KHYOD KYI LTAR NA TSOGS PA CANG MED PA STE CUNG ZAD KYANG RDZAS YOD DU MED PAS, DBYIBS [f. 236b] DE YAN LAG TSOGS PA GDAGS GZHIR BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS ‘DOGS PA MA YIN TE,

And why, for what reason, would that be the case?  According to you, there would be no collection at all; which is to say, not the slightest thing that existed in a substantial way.  As such, the outline is not something which is ascribed on the basis of using the collection of the component parts as the basis of what we give the label.


[3476]
‘DI ‘DRA BA’I BTAGS YOD RNAMS NI RDZAS YOD RTEN DU BYAS PA KHO NAR KHYOD KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, YAN LAG TSOGS PA YANG BTAGS YOD DU KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And that’s because what you say is that these kinds of labeled things can only have a basis which exists substantially.  And you also say that the collection of the component parts is as well something that exists through labels.


[3477]
DE’I PHYIR GANG ZHIG CI YANG MA YIN PA STE CUNG ZAD KYANG RDZAS SU YOD PA MA YIN PA DE GDAGS GZHIR BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS, SHING RTA’I SKABS ‘DIR NI SHING RTAR ‘JOG PA’I DBYIBS SU LTA ZHIG JI LTAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR RO,,

How then could it ever be the case that—here at the point of the wagon—there could ever be something that we said was the outline which were established as being the wagon, when you are talking about something that wasn’t anything at all; which is to say, which did not have the slightest existence as something substantial, and which provided the basis for the labeling of the wagon?


[3478]
‘DIR PHA ROL POS BTAGS YOD KYI DNGOS PO RNAMS RANG RKYA THUB PA’I RDZAS YOD RE GDAGS GZHIR YOD PA LA BRTEN NAS ‘DOGS PAR KHAS LEN ZHING, TSOGS PA DANG DBYIBS GNYIS KA YANG BTAGS YOD DU ‘DOD PAS, 

Here what the other side is accepting is that entities which exist in a labeled way are given their labels based upon the presence of something serving as the basis of the label which also exists in substantially, in a self-standing way.  They would also accept that both the collection of the component parts, and the outline, were both things that existed through the labeling process.


[3479]
TSOGS PA DBYIBS KYI GDAGS GZHIR ‘DOD NA ‘GAL BA TZAM LAS MA MDZAD KYANG, SKYES BU’I KHA DOG SKYES BUR ‘JOG TU MI RUNG BA BZHIN DU, SHING RTA LA YANG DE’I KHA DOG DANG DBYIBS GANG YANG SHING RTAR GZHAG TU MI RUNG STE, DE GNYIS NI SHING RTA’I NYE BAR BLANG BYA YIN PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA LA GO BAR BYA’O,,

Taking the position that the collection of the parts is the basis that we label the outline is not in itself to commit a contradiction; but still it would be incorrect to say that the colors of a person were the person themselves.  Similarly, it is inappropriate to say—in the case of a wagon—that the colors & shapes of the wagon are what we establish as the wagon.  And that’s because these two are what the wagon subsumes.  This last is something that one must come to understand.



Applying the same logic

[3480]
GNYIS PA NI,

This brings us to our second part from before, which is applying this same logic to other cases.


[3481]
CI STE TSOGS PA MI BDEN PA BTAGS YOD YIN DU ZIN KYANG, DE LA BRTEN NAS MI BDEN PA STE BTAGS YOD KYI DBYIBS SU ‘GYUR RO ZHES ‘DOD NA,

Suppose then that one were to take the following position:

Let’s say then that, to start with, we agree that the collection of the component parts is something unreal: something simply labeled what it is.  We say though that there would be a kind of unreal thing that would depend upon it: an outline that was itself labeled.


	[3482]
[VI.156]
Yatheṣṭam etat tava tadvad eva

	Is that in this case
	There is another idea
	Which holds [f. 212a],

	The unreal aspect
	Of a result,

	Depended upon
Causes which are
Themselves unreal.

Understand that
All of them
Do their growing.


[3483]
KHYOD KYIS TSOGS PA BTAGS YOD LA BRTEN NAS DBYIBS BTAGS YOD ‘JOG PA ‘DI NI JI LTAR ‘DOD PA DE LTAR DU, MA RIG PA DANG SA BON LTA BU’I MI BDEN PA YI RGYU LA BRTEN PAR BYAS NAS, ‘DU BYED DANG MYU GU LTA BU ‘BRAS BU’I RNAM PA MI BDEN PA’I RANG BZHIN NAM NGO BO CAN RNAMS SKYE BAR SHES PAR BYA LA,

And so what you are proposing is that there is an outline which is labeled, and which itself depends upon a collection of parts which is labeled.  In this case there is another idea which holds, which is that—in the very same way—we are to understand that things like fresh karma and sprouts possess a nature or essence of the unreal aspect of a result, all because they have depended upon causes such as misunderstanding and seeds which are themselves unreal.


[3484]
DE BZHIN DU DE LAS GZHAN PA RGYU DANG ‘BRAS [f. 237a] BU’I NGO BO MI BDEN PA’I RANG BZHIN CAN THAMS CAD KYANG NI SKYE BAR SHES PAR BYA STE,

And we are to understand that—in the very same manner—all causes and results other than these, which possess a nature of being unreal in their essence, do their growing.


	[3485]
[VI.157]
Etena rūpādiṣu kumbha buddhis
tathāsthiteṣvityapi naiva yuktam,
Rūpādayaś cāpi na santyajātās
teṣāṃ na saṃsthānam ato’pi yuktam.

,’DIS NI GZUGS SOGS DE LTAR GNAS RNAMS LA,

	But what’s the point?
	Visible form and the rest
	Are staying in that way;

	And they say we can
	Conceive of this
	As the vase—

	This as well can
	Only be incorrect.

	There exists no arisal;
	As such, neither form
	Nor the rest exist.

	For the same reason,
	It would be incorrect
	To say that these
	Could be the shape.


[3486]
‘BAD RTZOL BRGYA PHRAG BYAS KYANG GANG GI SHA BZA’ BAR MI NUS PA, DNGOS PO GRIB MA’I RI DVAGS LTA BU BRDZUN PA LA BDEN PAR MNGON PAR ZHEN PA DON MED PA ‘DIS NI CI ZHIG BYA

Now you can try as hard as you want to, in a thousand different ways, to make a meal of fake deer: that is, referring to the shadow of a deer.  But what’s the point of this meaningless exercise, of grasping to something false as being real?


[3487]
DE LA RANG GI SDE PA MANG POS BUM PA’I GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I RDUL BRGYAD DE LTAR ‘DAB ‘BYOR DU GNAS PA’I TSOGS PA RNAMS BUM PA YIN PAS, DE LA BUM PA’I BLOR ‘GYUR RO ZHES SMRA BA DE YANG SHING RTA’I DPE ‘DIS BSAL BAS NA DE NI RIGS PA MA YIN PA NYID DO,,

On this point, many in our own schools start by pointing out that a vase consists of a collection of the eight different particles—the visible form and the rest of the vase—that are staying in that configuration, meaning glued together in that way.  And then, they would say, we can conceive of this collection as the vase itself.  This opinion as well though can only be incorrect, since it is disproven by the example of the wagon.


[3488]
GZHAN YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR SNGAR BSHAD ZIN PAS GZUGS SOGS KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PA MIN NO,,

Moreover, we have already finished explaining, earlier, how there exists no arisal of a thing through some nature of its own; as such, neither form nor the rest are things that could exist through some nature of their own.


[3489]
DE YI PHYIR YANG RDZAS SU YOD PA’I NYE BAR LEN PA CAN DU ‘DOD PA BUM PA LA SOGS PA MI RIGS PAS, BUM PA LA SOGS PA DE DAG GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I DBYIBS KYI KHYAD PAR DU MI RIGS SO,,

For the same reason, we would have to say that it is illogical to assert that vases or the like could be things that take in their parts and exist in a substantial manner.  As such, it would be incorrect to say that these entities such as a vase or the like could be considered the feature of shape possessed by their form and the like.



Rejecting arguments
against the explanation

[3490]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third point from before, which is rejecting arguments by others concerning this way of explaining things.


[3491]
‘DIR SMRAS PA GAL TE ‘O NA SHING RTA ‘DI’I BTAGS DON, SNGAR BSHAD PA’I TSUL GYIS RNAM PA BDUN DU BTZAL BA NA, YOD PA MA YIN PA DE’I TSE SHING RTA MED PAR ‘GYUR BAS, SHING RTAS ‘JIG RTEN NA THA SNYAD ‘DOGS PA DE RGYUN CHAD PAR ‘GYUR NA,

Here then is what people say:

Well now, suppose we do look for the thing that we label with the name “wagon,” in the seven different ways laid out before.  When we thus find that this labeled object doesn’t exist, then the wagon itself cannot exist.  And that means then that the very act in the world of using the name “wagon” to refer to something is obviated.


[3492]
DE MI ‘THAD DE, SHING RTA ‘ON CIG NYOS SHIG ,’CHOS SHIG CES BYA BA LA SOGS PA BYA DGOS PAR MTHONG BA YANG YIN NO, ,DE’I PHYIR ‘JIG RTEN LA GRAGS PA’I PHYIR NA SHING RTA LA SOGS PA NI YOD DO ZHE NA,

This though cannot be correct, for we do see that there are necessarily acts reflected in expressions such as “You should bring the wagon,” or “You should fix the wagon,” and so forth.  As such—simply because they are things that are known here in the world—we would have to say that wagons and the like certainly do exist.


[3493]
NYES PA ‘DI NI RANG CAG GNYIS KYI NANG NAS KHYOD KHO NA LA ‘JUG PAR ‘GYUR BAS, NGED KYIS KHYED LA DGOD PAR BYA BA YIN NO,,

The fact though is that the problem you have raised is something that only applies—from between the two of us here—to you!  As such, I will have to turn this around on you.


[3494]
JI LTAR YIN SNYAM NA, KHYOD [f. 237b] KYIS SHING RTA’I BTAGS DON RNAM PAR DPYAD PA STE BTZAL NAS, SHING RTA ‘JOG PAR BYED CING BTAGS DON MA BTZAL BAR ‘GRUB PA’I THABS GZHAN KHAS MA BLANGS PA’I PHYIR DANG, 

And how would that work?  Let’s say that you are examining—or seeking—that thing which we label “wagon.”  The fact is that you have failed to express your support for any method of establishing the wagon other than looking at how we say something is a wagon, and looking for what it is that we’ve called “wagon.”


[3495]
BTAGS DON RNAM PA BDUN DU BTZAL BA NA, SHING RTA ‘ON CIG CES BYA BA SOGS KYI ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD RNAMS KHYOD LA JI LTAR ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR RO,,

Moreover, when we look—in seven different ways—for what it is that we label “the wagon,” we don’t see how it is that this can be established according to you, as the terms are applied in the way of the world at large, with expressions such as “bring the wagon” and the like.  In fact, it could not be established.


[3496]
RTZOD PA DE LA BSTAN BCOS MDZAD PAS NI LAN DE LTAR ‘DEBS LA, DA LTA’I BOD KYI THAL ‘GYUR BAR ‘DOD PA RNAMS NI, RNAM PA BDUN DU BTZAL BAS MA RNYED NA SHING RTA ‘JOG MI NUS SO ZHES RTZOD PA DE NYID DBU MA PA’I LUGS SU SMRA STE,

This then is how the author of our autocommentary replies to this argument.  But certain people living nowadays here in Tibet—who consider themselves followers of the Consequence group within the Middle Way school—would argue that when we seek the wagon in those seven classic ways and fail to find it, then no wagon at all can be established.  They would go further and say that this is the classic position of the Middle Way school itself.


[3497]
DES NI RNAM PAR DAG PA’I LUGS NGAN RTOG GI BTZOG CHUS ‘BAD NAS SLOD PAR BYED PA YIN NO,,

But when they say this kind of thing, what they are actually doing is taking a very pure system of thought and exerting very conscious efforts to pollute it, with the most filthy water of their own mistaken ideas.


	[3498]
[VI.158]
Na tattvato naiva ca lokataś ca
sa saptadhā yadyapi yāti siddhim,
Svāṅgānyupādāya vinā vicāraṃ
prajñapyate lokata eva caiṣaḥ.

	Looking at that
In and of itself,
	Or even in the way
	That the world does,

	Admittedly this doesn’t
	End up something
	That could be established.
	
	But leaving off
	This close examination,
	Confining ourselves
	To the world,

	Here the labeling
	Has been done
	In reliance upon

[3499]
KHO BO CAG LA NI SNGAR BSHAD PA’I RTZOD PA’I NYES PA DE MED DE, SHING RTA DE NI DE NYID DU STE DON DAM PA’AM, ‘JIG RTEN GYI KUN RDZOB TU BTAGS DON RNAM PA BDUN GYIS BTZAL BA NA SHING RTA ‘GRUB PAR ‘GYUR BA MIN MOD KYI,

Now the fact is that the problems raised in these previous arguments don’t apply to us ourselves at all.  That is, suppose we look—in those seven different ways—for that wagon that we have given the name in and of itself; which is to say, in an ultimate sense.  Or even, in the way that the world does, in a deceptive sense.  Admittedly this doesn’t end up something that could be established as a wagon.


[3500]
DE LTA NA’ANG SHING RTA ‘DI NI BTAGS DON ‘TSOL BA’I RNAM PAR DPYAD PA MED PAR ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD NYID LAS, SNGON PO DANG TSOR BA LA SOGS PA LTAR ‘DIR NI RANG GI YAN LAG ‘PHANG LO SOGS LA BRTEN NAS ‘DOGS PA YIN PA

But now even though all that is the case, suppose that we leave off this close examination where we are seeking out what it is that we have used to label this thing a wagon.  Confining ourselves then to the verbiage of the world at large, here we can say that the labeling has been done in reliance upon the component parts of the wagon: the wheels, and so on.  And this is just the same as how we would applies labels such as “blue,” or “a feeling,” or anything else of the like.


[3501]
DE’I PHYIR SA MYUG SOGS LA, RTEN ‘BREL RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM KHAS BLANGS PA LTAR, SHING RTA YANG RANG GI YAN LAG LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PAR KHAS BLANGS PA’I PHYIR, KHO BO CAG GI PHYOGS LA SHING RTA ‘ON CIG CES PA SOGS KYI ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD MI RUNG BAR MI ‘GYUR LA,

As such, when we’re talking about things like seeds & sprouts, the view that we have accepted is this kind of dependent interconnection, this pure sort of causality.  Just so, what we say is that wagons as well are things that are labeled, in dependence upon their component parts.  Thus it is not the case that, according to our position, there is any possibility that the parlance of the world—“Bring that wagon” and so forth—could ever be somehow inappropriate.


[3502]
PHA ROL POS KYANG ‘DI KHAS BLANG BAR ‘OS PA YIN NO ZHES GSUNGS PAS SHING RTA’I BTAGS DON BTZAL [f. 238a] NAS MI ‘JOG PA DBU MA PA’I LUGS LA, ‘JIG RTEN GYI THA SNYAD KHAS LEN PA DANG, PHA ROL POS KYANG DE KHAS BLANG DGOS ZHES BSTAN PAR BYA’I,

And what we are saying is that it would be appropriate for the other side here to accept this way of thinking as well.  As such, when we run into those who say they are Middle Way and also say that when they go looking for what it is we’ve labeled the wagon we can never find it, what we try to clarify for them is that we feel we have to accept the verbiage of the everyday world; and that they should accept it as well.


[3503]
PHAR LA ‘PHANGS PA’I SKYON TSUR BZLOG PA’I TSE LAN MA THEBS PA NA KHAS BLANG MED CES SMRA BAR MI BYA’O,,

It is not though the case that when problems with their position that we have pointed out are implied in it are cast back upon us, you should simply sit there without offering any reply, declaring that “We are beyond taking any position.”



Another interpretation
of names

[3504]
BZHI PA NI,

And with this we arrive at our fourth point from above: a demonstration of how there is another interpretation of the meaning of terms used as names.


[3505]
DBU MA PA’I PHYOGS ‘DIR ‘JIG RTEN LA GRAGS PA’I SGO NAS SHING RTAS THA SNYAD ‘DOGS PA CHES GSAL BAR GRUB PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU MA ZAD KYI, SHING RTA’I MING GI KHYAD PAR GZHAN DAG KYANG BTAGS DON ‘TSOL BA’I TSUL GYIS RNAM PAR DPYAD PA MED PAR ‘JIG RTEN LA GRAGS PA’I SGO NAS KHAS BLANG PAR BYA’O,,

Here in the standpoint of the Middle Way, it is exceedingly clear that this object has been labeled a “wagon” in keeping with the way that things are spoken of in the everyday world.  Not only that, but we can say that we accept other details of the naming of the wagon in just the way that these are commonly spoken of in the everyday world, without reference to any close examination utilizing a search for what it was that received the label.


	[3506]
[VI.159]
Aṅgī sa evāvayavī sa kartā
rathaḥ sa eveti jane niruktiḥ,
Siddho’pyupādātṛtayā janānāṃ
mā saṃvṛtiṃ nāśaya loka siddhām.

,DE NYID YAN LAG CAN DE CHA SHAS CAN,
,SHING RTA DE NYID BYED PO ZHES ‘GROR BSNYAD,
,SKYE BO RNAMS LA LEN PO NYID DU ‘GRUB,

		The thing itself
		Is a composite;
		This same thing
		Is a whole.

		This same wagon
		We can call
		“An agent.”

		Living beings
		Are designated
		In the same way.

		People are thus
		Established as
		Nothing other than
		The ones that do
		This incorporating.

		The deceptive

[3507]
