[3663]
GZHAN YANG JI LTAR TE DPER NA KHYOD KYIS GZUGS BRNYAN MTHONG BA LA YANG BRTEN NAS, NYI MA’I DKYIL ‘KHOR DANG BYAD BZHIN LA YOD PA’I KHYAD PAR RNAMS NYI MA GZAS BZUNG BA LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYI TSE, MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR LA,

And so moreover let’s consider the following example.  You can see a reflection of something, and based on that you can observe certain features that are present in the disk of the sun, and in the form being reflected.  That is, when there is an eclipse of that sun or something else of the like, you can watch it.


[3664]
NYI MA DANG BYAD BZHIN DANG DE DAG GI GZUGS BRNYAN GNYIS RNAM PAR PHRAD PA DANG MA PHRAD PAR SKYE ZHES BTAGS DON ‘TSOL BA’I TSUL GYIS DPYAD PA NA SKYE BA MI RIGS MOD KYI, ‘ON KYANG NYI MA DANG BYAD BZHIN LA BRTEN NAS THA SNYAD KYI DBANG GIS BZHAG PA TZAM GYIS GZUGS BRNYAN ZHIG ‘BYUNG BAR ‘GYUR ZHING,

And now suppose we undertake an examination in that same way where we search out what it was that got the label: we are looking to see whether the sun, and what it is which is reflected, either do make actual contact with their two reflections, or not.  As a result we admittedly find that the starting here is not right; but it is true that—based on the sun and the original image which was reflected—we can say that something, a reflection, did occur, even if we are only speaking about something established nominally.


[3665]
DES KYANG ‘DOD PA’I DON NGES PA DANG GZUGS BRNYAN MI BDEN BZHIN DU’ANG, RANG GI BYAD BZHIN MDZES PAR BSGRUB PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, GZUGS BRNYAN DE LA NI NUS PA YOD PA

Now the ascertainment of the object that we seek—and the reflection—may not be the real things; but still they help us to establish the beauty of the original object being reflected.  As such, we can say that it—the reflection—does possess some force.


[3666]
JI LTA BA DE BZHIN DU, ‘DIR YANG GDONG PA DANG ‘DRA BA’I SHES RAB KYI DRI MA MA RIG PA SBYANG BAR BYA BA LA, NUS PA MTHONG BAR ‘GYUR BA’I GTAN TSIGS RTEN ‘BREL DANG GCIG DU BRAL SOGS LAS BSGRUB BYA RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PA RTOGS PAR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Here, in the same way as with that other case, we seek to clean the impurity of misunderstanding away from wisdom, which is similar to a person’s face.  And we should understand that we come to a realization that things do not exist through any nature of their own: which is the thesis that we are undertaking to establish with classical proofs such as that based on interdependence, and the lack of one or many.  For these are reasonings that we can see have the force to remove that impurity marring the face.


[3667]
DE YANG RANG BZHIN GYIS YOD PAR SGRUB PA’I ‘THAD PA DANG BRAL BA’I GTAN TSIGS SO,,

These can also be referred to as types of reasoning which are “devoid of any correctness,” in the sense of it being correct to establish things as existing through some nature of their own.


[3668]
KYANG GI SGRAS [f. 247a] NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I ‘THAD PA DANG BRAL BA’I SUN ‘BYIN GYIS KYANG SUN DBYUNG BYA SUN ‘BYIN NUS PA’I SHES PAR BYA’O,,

When the root text says “too” here, we should understand it as referring to the force that an attack possesses to successfully attack what it attacks, in the absence of any correctness to the idea that things could exist through any nature of their own.


[3669]
GANG GI PHYIR MING TZAM PA’I BTAGS YOD DU SMRA BA RNAMS LA, BTAGS DON ‘TSOL BA’I GNYIS SU SMRA BA MI RIGS PA’I PHYIR, GNYIS LA BRTEN NAS SUN ‘BYIN PA DANG LAN SMRA BAS DBU MA PA LA RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU GLAGS MI RNYED DE,

The rationale here is that it would be illogical for those who assert that things exist in name only—only labeled—to say that they had gone on a search for the thing that got the label, and found it in either two of the places.  Which is to say, there’s no way you can come out on top against those of the Middle Way school if you use an attack or give a response that depends on either one of those two options.


[3670]
BRGYA BA LAS,

,KLAN KA BRJOD PAR NUS MA YIN,

The Four Hundred Verses puts it this way—

	There are some
	Who have no position
	At all,

	Saying that things exist,

	Or both exist and don’t.

	These are not people
	That you can sustain
	An argument with
	For very long!


[3671]

Wisdom says as well:

When you examine things
With emptiness,

You find that those
Who try to give an answer
Have given none at all;

And it’s the same
With attempting a proof.


[3672]
SUN ‘BYIN BYED DANG SUN DBYUNG BYA LA PHRAD MA PHRAD KYI DPYAD PA BSTAN PA ‘DIS NI, SKYED PAR BYED PA’I RGYU LA YANG ‘BRAS BU DANG PHRAD MA PHRAD KYI DPYAD PA BYAS NAS ‘GOG PAR SHES PAR BYA’O,,

This section—where we present an examination of whether what does the attacking and what is attacked ever make contact with each other or not—should be understood as a  refutation as well which employs examining whether or not the cause that acts to trigger something ever makes contact with its result.


[3673]
‘DIR LEGS LDAN GYIS DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS ‘DIR SKYED BYED KYI RGYU’I SKABS SU BAB KYI, GSAL BYED KYI RGYU LA NI MA YIN LA, PHRAD PA DANG MA PHRAD PA’I DPYAD PA YANG GSAL BYED KYI RGYU LA YIN GYI SKYED BYED KYI RGYU LA NI MIN PAS, KHO BO CAG GI TSIG RNAMS LA LTAG GCOD KYI GNAS MED PA NYID DO,

At this juncture, Master Bhavaviveka would make the following reply.  He would say that all this relates to the section in the classical commentary on the middle way where we discuss causes that act to trigger something; but—

…it is not a reference to the section where we talk about causes that act to clarify an idea.  And the examination of whether contact is made or not is something that relates to causes which clarify an idea, and not to causes which trigger something.  As such, our words are not something which would allow any opportunity at all for a final determination.


[3674]
ZHES SKYED BYED KYI RGYU LA GSAL BYED DAM SHES BYED KYI RGYU GTAN TSIGS SOGS LA PHRAD MA PHRAD KYI DPYAD PA BYED PA’I DPYAD PA BYAR MED DO ZHES SMRA BA NI LAN MA YIN TE,

Which is to say, this is not a reply in which we are saying that “There is nothing here which is examined by what is doing the examination, so far as the question of contact or no contact with reasoning which clarifies something, or informs of something, relating to a cause which acts to trigger some other thing.”


[3675]
GZHAN GYI GLAGS DANG BCAS PA STE SKYON BRJOD [f. 247b] DANG BCAS PA’I LAN BRJOD NA, PHA ROL PO MI BZOD LA SKYED PAR BYED PA LA BDEN PA KHAS BLANGS NA SKYON ‘JUG PA LTAR, GSAL BYED KYI RGYU LA’ANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHAS BLANGS NA SKYON YOD PA’I PHYIR RO,,

And so suppose we were to give a reply with an “opening”; which is to say, where the other person could point out some logical fault.  We know that certain problems would arise with accepting the idea that something which acted to trigger something else was real; just so, there would be problems with agreeing that a cause which acted to clarify some idea could exist through some nature of its own.


[3676]
GZHAN YANG LEGS LDAN ‘DIS DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS SU RANG BZHIN MED PAR DAM BCAS PA’I DON SGRUB PA’I PHYIR DU BKOD BA’I SGRUB BYED LA, GZHAN GYIS SUN ‘BYIN PA BKOD PA RNAMS KYI SKYON SPONG LA LTAG GCOD KYI LAN SMRA BAR BYED PAS,

Moreover, we can consider certain proofs that this same Master Bhavaviveka puts forth to establish the assertions, made in the classical commentary on the middle way, that things have no nature of their own.  Here he does undertake to give definitive responses which serve to deny the problems that are raised by others in their attacks on this position.


[3677]
‘DI NI GZHAN GYIS SUN DBYUNG BAR BYA BA KHO NA YIN PAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHAS BLANGS NA, SKYED BYED DANG GSAL BYED KYI RGYU GNYIS KA LA PHRAD MA PHRAD KYI SKYON MTSUNGS KYANG, DE KHAS MI LEN PA’I PHYIR SKYON MED DO ZHES PA KHO BO CAG GIS BTAB PA’I LAN KHO NA CHES MDZES SO,,

And so suppose we say that if something is only an idea that others seek to attack, we would assert that it existed through some nature of its own.  The problems that arise with contact being made or not being made are equivalent, whether we’re talking about causes that act to trigger something, or those which act to clarify something.  Nonetheless, what we can do is to respond, “Well, since we accept no such thing, then we have no problem.”  For us to do no more than make this kind of reply is perfectly elegant.



Why our position
is not equivalent

[3678]
GNYIS PA NI,

And so suppose then it were the case that this entity or essential nature of what we refer to as a logical statement meant to help others comprehend what we are trying to prove—along with the essential nature of what we are trying to prove, that exact thing which we hope will be directly understood—could exist in a way where they existed through some nature of their own.

But the fact is further that the very fact of something existing through some nature of its own is something that could never exist; as such, we should understand that for those of you who are on the completely correct side of things to point out problems with those who are already on the completely incorrect side of things is just some kind of exhausting or hopeless expenditure of effort for all of us.

DPER NA RAB RIB CAN GYIS DMIGS PA’I SKRA SHAD LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYI GCIG NYID DANG, MANG PO NYID DANG, ZLUM PO NYID DANG, NAG PO LA SOGS PA’I PHYOGS SUN [f. 248a] ‘BYIN PAS,

Suppose, for example, that we worked very hard to attack the idea—held by individuals who have cataracts on their eyes—that the strands of hair that they were seeing were either just one alone, or some great number, or somehow rounded, or black, or anything else of the like.

The fact is that this would do nothing to dissuade the people with the cataracts.  Neither is it the case that it would dissuade the individuals here in this case, if you set forward an attack in which you undertook an examination of cause & effect which in fact had no nature of its own, to check it in both the approaches for searching out what is given the label.

DE NYID KYI PHYIR GANG DAG MIG DANG KHAB LONG LA SOGS PAS MA PHRAD PAR RANG GI BYA BA BYED PAR RNAM PAR BZHAG PA’I DPE DE DAG KYANG BKAG PAR RIG PAR BYA STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR KHAS LEN NA DE DAG LA YANG PHRAD MA PHRAD KYI THAL BA MTSUNGS PA’I PHYIR RO,,

For this reason, let’s look at these examples where we use things like the eye or a magnet to describe how something can be established as performing its function even in the absence of contact.  It would be logical then to deny these examples, since if we accept that a thing can exist through some nature of its own, the consequences of saying that it either made contact or did not make contact would be the same.


[3686]
GANG ZHIG KHYOD RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID KYI LAM DRANG PO BTANG NAS, RTOG GE NGAN PA’I LAM SHIN TU ‘KHYOG PA, RANG GI RNAM PAR RTOG PA’I BZO NGAN PAS SBYAR BA, YANG DAG PA’I LAM ‘GEGS PAR BYED PA LA SPRO BA, TE BOR TE SHIN TU TSOGS {%TSEGS} CHE BA ‘DIS KHYOD LA CI ZHIG BYA,

And so here you are, abandoning the straight path of the idea that things have no nature of their own.  And instead you turn to a very crooked path of poor logic—one which is nothing but a defective creation of your own imagining.  You delight in something that serves to create an obstacle for the true path, and discard this way.  In fact, you go to great pains in this entire endeavor of yours.  But what good will it ever do you?



Beyond any denial

[3687]
GSUM PA NI,

This brings us to our third point from above: a demonstration of how—so long as we are able to establish that things have no nature of their own—the other party will be unable to prove any denial of our position.


	[3688]
[VI.177]

		They are extremely
		Simple ways that have
		The capacity to help people

		Come to the realization
		That all existing entities
		Are those things:
		That do not exist.

Moreover, things like an illusion and a dream are nothing less than examples that can be accepted in the system of the person we are debating with.  They are extremely simple ways that have the capacity to help these people on the other side—people of the normal world—come to the realization that all existing entitites are, as those of the middle way describe it, “those things,” meaning things that do not exist with any nature of their own.

It is not the case though that, in the same way, those other than the opponent here—meaning those who follow the middle way—would be enabled with this ease to comprehend that entities did exist through some nature of their own. What this is saying is that—with something like the concept of dependence, used as a rationale for proving that nothing exists in reality—there is no way that we can conclude, with an accurate perception, that the quality of not existing in reality applies to the subject under consideration, unless we have first confirmed—with reference to a concordant example—that if something is dependent it cannot exist in reality.

As such, why is it that here any of you would expend such devoted efforts—why would you try so hard—to cause meaningless trouble for these people of the world?  People around us in this world are already wrapped deep in the cocoon of their own disastrous ways of thinking—a cocoon woven with the silken threads of their own negative emotions.

And now on top of that, you are smothering them ever more firmly in a massive, additional net of widespreading strands of bad logic.  What on earth are you doing?


[3695]

This argument where you grasp onto things as being real is something that now you really have to give up.  Things are all fake, just like a reflection in a mirror.  How then are you going to prove somehow that they exist through some nature of their own; that they possess some particular or more general characteristics of their own, which could be detected either through our direct senses, or through some kind of deduction?

Here we are saying that there is one—and only one—form of direct, accurate perception towards each and every knowable object in existence.  And that is the wisdom of an Omniscient Being.

And so we have been through sections here where we explained how things like the growing of a sprout occur in a dependent relationship; we gave as well a description of how things are labeled in dependence, as for example in the case of labeling a person depending upon the parts to the person.


[3700]
BYA BA’I SKABS SU, DNGOS POR SMRA BA’I PHYOGS LA SUN ‘BYIN GANG BSHAD PA DE NYID KYI LHAG MA RGYUS ‘BRAS BU PHRAD NAS SAM, MA PHRAD PAR SKYED CES SUN ‘BYIN PA

During these presentations, we covered a number of points that were additional to our attack upon the positions of the Functionalists.  We presented for example an attack upon the idea that a cause could produce a result either through making contact with it, or in an absence of such contact.  


[3701]
GONG DU BSTAN PA YANG NI SHES PAR BYAS NAS, RGYUS ‘BRAS BU PHRAD NAS SAM LA SOGS PAS MA PHRAD PAR SKYED CES BRTAGS TE BKAG PA’I PHYOGS KYI LAN BRJOD PA’I CHED DU,

And then utilizing what we had learned in those earlier presentations, we examined responses that were given by the other side as they examined this question of whether a cause acts to trigger a result through making contact with it, or “anything of the like”—here referring to not making contact with it.  With that, we sought to give a response to express the position that we denied these possibilities.


[3702]
PHA ROL POS SUN ‘BYIN LA PHRAD [f. 249a] MA PHRAD KYI BRTAG PA GANG GIS SMRAS PA DE LA RTZOD PA’I SKABS ‘DIR, DE’I BRTAG PA RANG LA MI MTSUNGS PA’I LAN GYI SUN ‘BYIN PA GTANG BAR BYA STE, SNGAR BSTAN PA DE NI MTSON PA TZAM DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

Which has brought us here to this point where we are debating with positions expressed by the other side wherein they undertook an examination of whether, in a logical attack, contact is made or not.  And then we engaged in our own attack, where we responded that this particular examination did not apply equally to ourselves.  You should understand that all of these points up to here are meant only to offer a representative sample of the issues and their resolution.


[3703]
BSTAN BCOS RTZA SHE LAS NI DGAG GZHAG BYAS PA’I DGOS PA, BDEN ‘DZIN GYI RNAM RTOG LDOG PA NYID BRJOD PAR ‘DOD PA YIN LA,

Now the points of denying others’ positions and establishing then our own, as they are found in the classical commentary entitled Wisdom, are all intended to accomplish one thing: to stop the wrong idea where we hold things to exist in some real way.


[3704]
DE YANG KHO BO CAG GIS SO SO SKYE BO RNAMS NI RTOG PAS BCINGS, ZHES SOGS KYI SKABS SU BSTAN ZIN PA’I PHYIR, BSTAN BCOS LA SUN CI PHYIN DU RGOL BA GA LA YOD DE, SUN CI PHYIN DU RGOL BA NI RANG GI PHYOGS BZHAG NA SKYON BYUNG GIS DOGS NAS, GZHAN GYI PHYOGS SUN CI PHYIN BYED PA YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Now we for our part have already presented the necessary point in the root text earlier on, where it says “Common beings are enslaved by notions.”  As such, we don’t see how one could ever have any further argument attacking the ideas of the classical commentary; that is, any argument in attack would result from setting forth our own position, and then questions coming up about whether there were any problems with it.  This is the only kind of argument against others that would be made at this point. 


[3705]
‘DIR BDAG GIS GZHAN GYI PHYOGS BSAL BA YANG DON DAM PAR MED DE, DON DAM PAR DNGOS PO GANG YANG MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

When we ourselves here disprove the position of the other side, it is not as though it exists in any ultimate way.  That’s because—from an ultimate point of view—there doesn’t even exist any entity at all.


[3706]
DE’I PHYIR SUN CI PHYIN DU RGOL BA GA LA YOD, GANG GIS NA RANG GI PHYOGS GZHAG TU MED CING GZHAN GYI PHYOGS BZLOG PA DON DAM PAR ‘DOD PA’I MTSAN NYID BYAS PA ‘DI, SUN CI PHYIN DU RGOL BA PA’I YANG DAG PA’I MTSAN NYID DU ‘GYUR BA,

How then could there ever be an opponent that we overcame?  Suppose that there were no position of our own that we could ever put forward, but that at the same time we posited some definitive statement that could put a stop to the other side’s position.  This would in itself require a definitive opponent—one that existed really, in order for us to overcome.


[3707]
DBU MA PA SUS RANG GI PHYOGS THA SNYAD DU MA BZHAG CING, GZHAN GYI PHYOGS BZLOG PA DON DAM DU ‘DOD PA GNYIS KA MED PAS, DBU MA PA LA SUN CI PHYIN DU RGOL BA YANG YOD PA MIN PAS, RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU MI RIGS SO,,

But neither of these things exists: there is no adherent of the middle way that would not want to put forth their own position only in a nominal manner; or who would want to disprove the other side’s position in some ultimate manner.  As such, there does not even exist a debater who could undertake to overthrow those of the middle way; and for this reason the entire exercise would be futile.


[3708]
DE SKAD DE DE LTAR SNGAR BSHAD PA’I SUN ‘BYIN PA’I LHAG MA NI, DE MA THAG TU BSHAD PA’I PHYOGS ‘DI NYID KYIS RTOGS PAR BYA’O,,

The remainder of the attack already described in these words, in this way, can be understood from “this very position”—meaning the one that will be presented directly below.


[3709]
DE LA DE NYID DE LAS ‘BYUNG MIN ZHES BYA BA ‘DI NAS [f. 249b] BRTZAMS TE, RNAM DPYOD PA NI MYUR DU GROL BAR ‘GYUR, ZHES BYA BA’I BAR ‘DIS NI CHOS KYI BDAG MED PA GSAL BAR BYAS SO,,

And so we have this major portion of the root text beginning from “This cannot occur through that” [verse VI.8a] on up to “When we are able to analyze things, we find ourselves liberated, with speed” [verse VI.119].  All of this has been a clear explanation of how general things lack any self-nature.


[3710]
NYON MONGS SKYON RNAMS MA LUS ‘JIG TSOGS LA, ,LTA LAS BYUNG BAR ZHES BYA BA LA SOGS PA NAS ‘DI YAN CHAD KYIS NI GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED PA GSAL BAR BYAS SO,,

And then we get a clear explanation of how the person lacks any self-nature starting from lines such as those that say, “Each & every one of the troubles of the negative emotions comes from the view of destruction” [verse VI.120].



Divisions of emptiness in brief

[3711]
GSUM PA LA GNYIS, STONG PA NYID KYI DBYE BA MDOR BSTAN PA, PHYE BA SO SO’I DON RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

This brings us to our third very general section from above—an explanation of the divisions of emptiness we have thus confirmed.  We proceed in two steps here: a brief presentation of the divisions of emptiness, and then a more detailed explanation of what each division involves.  Here is the first.


	[3712]
[VI.179]
Nairātmyam etad dvividhaṃ niruktaṃ
dharmātma bhedena jagad vimukteḥ,
Tad eva bhitvā bahuśo’pi bhūyas
tathā vineyebhya uvāca śāstā.

,BDAG MED ‘DI NI ‘GRO BA RNAMS DGROL PHYIR,
,CHOS DANG GANG ZAG DBYE BA RNAM GNYIS GSUNGS,
,DE LTAR STON PAS SLAR YANG ‘DI NYID NI,
,GDUL BYA RNAMS LA PHYE STE RNAM MANG GSUNGS,

	In order to free beings,
He stated that
	There are no objects

	Which possess
	Some self-nature;

	And that this
	Has two divisions:
	
	That to the person,
	And that to things.

	Having taught as such,
He went on to
Lay out all the
Different divisions

Of this very thing,
For different disciples.


[VI.180]
Śūnyatāḥ ṣoḍaśākhyāya saprapañcāḥ samāsataḥ,
Catasraḥ punar ākhyātā mahāyāne ca tā matāḥ

,SPROS DANG BCAS PAR STONG PA NYID,
,BCU DRUG BSHAD NAS MDOR BSDUS TE,
,SLAR YANG BZHIR BSHAD DE DAG NI,
,THEG CHEN DU YANG BZHED PA YIN,

	He utilized
	Great detail,

	First explaining
	Sixteen divisions
	Of emptiness,

	And then he
	Went over the same
	In a briefer way,
	With four types.

	And he acknowledged
	As well that
These constituted
The greater way.


[3713]
STONG PA NYID KYI RAB TU DBYE BA BRJOD PAR ‘DOD NAS BSHAD PA,

Desirous of expressing the divisions to emptiness, our author undertakes the following explanation.


[3714]
CHOS RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PA’I BDAG MED ‘DI NI, ,BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED PA DANG, CHOS KYI BDAG MED PA’I DBYE BA RNAM PA GNYIS SU GSUNGS SO,,

Let’s consider then this fact that there are no objects in the entire universe which possess some self-nature: which exist through any nature of their own.  The Conqueror has stated that it has two great divisions: the lack of a self-nature to the person, and the lack of a self-nature to things.


[3715]
DE GNYIS SU ‘BYED TSUL DE YANG GZHI GANG ZAG DANG CHOS KYI STENG DU MED RGYU’I BDAG MI ‘DRA BA GNYIS KYI SGO NAS PHYE BA MIN TE, MED RGYU’I BDAG NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YIN PAS SO,,

It is not the case that the way in which we make this division into two is based upon two different types of a self which does not exist, starting off from the division of things into the person and things.  That’s because the self that is not there is one which exists through its own nature.


[3716]
DE’I PHYIR GZHI CHOS CAN PHUNG SOGS KYI CHOS DANG GANG ZAG GI DBYE BAS PHYE BA’O,,

As such, the division is made according to a basis of the division consisting of objects which possess a certain quality: things in the sense of the parts to the person and such, and then the person.


[3717]
DGOS PA CI’I PHYIR DE GNYIS BSTAN ZHE NA, GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED NI NYAN RANG GI ‘GRO BA RNAMS ‘KHOR BA LAS RNAM PAR GROL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR BSTAN LA, BYANG SEMS KYI ‘GRO BA RNAMS THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA THOB PAS RNAM PAR GROL BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR BDAG MED GNYIS KA BSTAN NO,,

“What is the purpose,” one may ask, “of presenting these two types?”  The lack of a self-nature to the person was taught in order to free beings who were listeners and self-made buddhas from the cycle of suffering.  And both kinds of the lack of a self-nature were taught in order to free those beings who are bodhisattvas—which is what happens when they attain the state of omniscience.


[3718]
SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR NYAN RANG LA YANG RTEN ‘BREL RKYEN NYID ‘DI PA TZAM GYI DE KHO NA NYID MTHONG BA YOD MOD KYANG, DE DAG LA SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR GYI CHOS KYI BDAG MED PA RNAM GRANGS DANG, DUS KYI SGO NAS YONGS SU RDZOGS PAR SGOM PA MED PA STE, ‘ON KYANG KHAMS GSUM GYI NYON MONGS KYI SA BON [f. 250a] SPONG BA’I THABS TZAM ZHIG NI YOD DO,,

As we explained earlier on, it is possible for listeners and self-made buddhas also to see suchness relating to this fact of causality: of dependence.  But as we also explained earlier, these groups are incapable of meditating upon the lack of a self-nature to things in the entirety of the different expressions it takes, and relative to different times.  We can say though that these practitioners do have in their possession just that method which allows them to eliminate the seeds for negative emotions relating to all three realms of the universe.


[3719]
DE DAG LA GANG ZAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA’I GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED PA MA LUS PAR SGOM PA NI YOD PAR RNAM PAR GZHAG GO

We do make a presentation which shows that these individuals do possess a practice where they meditate upon all the forms of the lack of a self-nature to the person—of a person who could exist through some nature of their own.


[3720]
,GANG ZAG BDEN GRUB ‘GOG PA’I RIGS PA’I RNAM GRANGS MTHA’ YAS PA’I SHES RAB MI SKYED KYANG, NYON MONGS KYI SA BON GYI GNYEN PO RDZOGS PAR SGOM PA YOD LA, SHES BYA’I SGRIB PA’I GNYEN PO RDZOGS PAR SGOM PA NI MED DO,,

It is not the case that these individuals are able to give rise to that wisdom where we used literally countless forms of reasoning to block the idea that the person could exist in some real way.  Nonetheless, they do possess a practice where they are able to meditate, in full, upon the antidotes for the seeds of the negative emotions.  At the same time, they do not possess a practice where they can meditate, in a complete way, upon the the antidotes to the obstacles to omniscience.


[3721]
DE LTAR BDAG MED PA GNYIS PO ‘DI NYID NI BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS SLAR YANG GDUL BAR BYA BA RNAMS LA DE DAG GI BSAM PA SNA TSOGS PA’I NGOR RNAM PA MANG PO’I SPROS PA DANG BCAS PAR PHYE STE GSUNGS SO,,

As such, the Conqueror went on to lay out all the different divisions of this very thing—the two different types of a lack of any self-nature—utilizing great detail, for the benefit of different disciples, according to their various states of mind.


[3722]
JI LTAR ZHE NA, RGYAL BA’I YUM LAS STONG PA NYID BCU DRUG GI DBYE BA BSHAD NAS, SLAR YANG MDOR BSDUS TE BZHIR BZHAG CING DE DAG NI THEG CHEN DU YANG BZHED PA STE BSHAD PA YIN NO,,

And how did he do so?  In his Mother of the Victors, he first explained the concept of emptiness in its sixteen different divisions.  And then he went over the same material in a briefer way, making a division into four types.  And he acknowledged as well that these constituted the greater way.


[3723]
DE LTAR NA BSDUS PA’I DBYE BA GNYIS DANG, ‘BRING PO’I DBYE BA BZHI DANG, RGYAS PA’I DBYE BA BCU DRUG TU GSUNGS SO,,

As such we can say that he gave this teaching utilizing a more succinct division into two; and then an intermediate division into four; and finally an extensive division into sixteen.


[3724]
JI SKAD DU, RAB ‘BYOR GZHAN YANG BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’I THEG PA CHEN PO ‘DI LTA STE, NANG STONG PA NYID DANG, PHYI STONG PA NYID DANG, PHYI NANG STONG PA NYID DANG, STONG PA NYID STONG PA NYID DANG, CHEN PO STONG PA NYID DANG, DON DAM PA STONG PA NYID DANG, ‘DUS BYAS STONG PA NYID DANG, ‘DUS MA BYAS STONG PA NYID DANG, MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PA STONG PA NYID DANG, THOG MA DANG THA MA MED PA STONG PA NYID DANG, DOR BA MED PA STONG PA NYID DANG, RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID DANG, CHOS THAMS CAD STONG PA NYID DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID STONG PA NYID DANG, MI [f. 250b] DMIGS PA STONG PA NYID DANG, DNGOS PO MED PA’I NGO BO NYID STONG PA NYID DO, ZHES STONG NYID BCU DRUG BSTAN NAS,

And how did he do so?  The Conqueror taught the sixteen types of emptiness, as follows—

The way of the bodhisattva can moreover be described, o Subhuti, in this way:

(1) emptiness on the inside;

(2) emptiness on the outside;

(3) emptiness on the outside and the inside;

(4) emptiness emptiness;

(5) great emptiness;

(6) ultimate emptiness;

(7) the emptiness of produced things;

(8) the emptiness of things that exist but were not produced;

(9) the emptiness beyond all extremes;

(10) the emptiness of no beginning or end;

(11) the emptiness that can never be given up;

(12) the emptiness of any nature;

(13) the emptiness of all things;

(14) the emptiness of its own quality;

(15) the emptiness of not seeing anything; and

(16) the emptiness of true nature, beyond all things.


[3725]
RAB ‘BYOR GZHAN YANG DNGOS PO NI DNGOS POS STONG NGO, ,DNGOS PO MED PA NI DNGOS PO MED PAS STONG NGO, ,RANG BZHIN NI RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG NGO, ,GZHAN GYI DNGOS PO NI GZHAN GYI DNGOS POS STONG NGO, ZHES SLAR YANG STONG PA NYID BZHI BSTAN NO,,

And then the Conqueror went on to teach four different kinds of emptiness—

O Subhuti, there is also the fact that things are empty of being things.  And the lack of things is also empty of the lack of things.  The nature of things is empty of being the nature of things.  And other things are empty of being other things.


[3726]
STONG PA NYID ‘DI RNAMS NI THEG PA CHEN PO ZHES BYA’O,,

And these kinds of emptiness are what we refer to as the “greater way.”


[3727]
STONG PA NYID DAM STONG PA NYID MA YIN PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA NI CUNG ZAD KYANG YOD PA MA YIN TE, STONG PA NYID SO SO BA’I RNAM PA DE LTA BUS ‘DUL BA KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR BSNYAD PAR ZAD DO,,

Neither emptiness itself and everything which is not emptiness exists in the slightest way through some nature of their own.  It is nothing more than the case that we are using all these different types of emptiness as names for what functions in a deceptive manner to tame disciples.


[3728]
DE SKAD DU YANG RTZA BA SHES RAB LAS,
,GAL TE STONG MIN CUNG ZAD YOD,
,STONG PA CUNG ZAD YOD PAR ‘GYUR,
,MI SKONG {%STONG} CUNG ZANG {%ZAD} YOD MIN NA,
,STONG PA’ANG YOD PAR GA LA ‘GYUR,

Wisdom addresses the same idea in the following lines:

If there is the slightest bit
Of anything that is not empty,

Then there can be the slightest
Bit of things that are empty.

And if there were not
The slightest bit of anything
That was not empty,
	
	How could we ever say that
	There was anything empty?


	[3729]
,STONG NGO ZHES KYANG MI BRJOD DE,
,MI STONG ZHES KYANG MI BYA ZHING,
,GNYIS DANG GNYIS MIN MI BYA STE,
,GDAGS PA’I DON DU BRJOD PAR BYA,
ZHES GSUNGS TE,

	Don’t say things are empty;
	But don’t say either
	That they are not.

	Don’t go to two
	Or not being two;

	Describe them as things
	That are labelled.


[3730]
SNGA MA DAG GIS NI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I PHYOGS SU MI BRJOD PA DANG, THA MAS NI GDAGS PA’I DON KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR BRJOD PAR BYA BA’I DON NO,,

The point of the earlier lines is that we cannot speak of a position where we say that things exist through some essential nature of their own; the point of the later lines is to convey that we should speak of things as existing deceptively—as things that are labelled.



The sixteen, beginning with
emptiness on the inside

[3731]
GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, STONG NYID BCU DRUG TU PHYE BA RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA DANG, STONG NYID BZHIR PHYE BA RGYAS PAR BSHAD PA’O,,

Which brings us to our second part from above—a more detailed explanation of what each division involves.  This we will cover in two topics: a detailed explanation of the division of emptiness into sixteen types, and a detailed explanation of the division of emptiness into four types.


[3732]
DANG PO LA BZHI, NANG STONG PA NYID LA SOGS PA BZHI BSHAD PA DANG, CHEN PO STONG PA NYID LA SOGS PA BZHI BSHAD PA DANG, MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PA STONG PA NYID LA SOGS PA BZHI BSHAD PA DANG, CHOS THAMS CAD STONG PA NYID LA SOGS PA BZHI BSHAD [f. 251a] PA’O,,

The first of these has four sections of its own: an explanation of the four starting with emptiness on the inside; an explanation of the four starting with great emptiness; an explanation of the four starting with emptiness beyond all extremes; and an explanation of the four starting with the emptiness of all things.


[3733]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, NANG STONG PA NYID BSHAD PA DANG, STONG NYID LHAG MA GSUM BSHAD PA’O,,

The first one here has, in turn, two divisions: an explanation of emptiness on the inside; and an explanation of the remaining three types of emptiness here.



1) Emptiness on the inside

[3734]
DANG PO LA GNYIS, DNGOS KYI DON DANG, ZHAR LA RANG BZHIN KHAS LEN TSUL BSTAN PA’O, ,DANG PO NI,

And, finally, the first of these has two parts: the actual point, and then an incidental presentation on how we accept a nature to things.  Here is the first of these.


	[3735]
[VI.181]
Cakṣur vai cakṣuṣā śūnyam asyaiṣā prakṛtir yataḥ,
Evaṃ śrotraṃ mano jihvā ghrāṇaṃ kāyaś ca kathyate.

,GANG PHYIR DE YI RANG BZHIN DE,
,YIN PHYIR MIG NI MIG GIS STONG,
,DE BZHIN RNA BA SNA DANG LCE,
,LUS [213b] DANG YID KYIS BSNYAD PAR BYA,

	Why is it?  Because
	The nature of this
	Is that the eye
	Is empty of the eye.

	In the same way
	We also refer
	To the ear, the nose,
	The tongue, the body,
	And the thought [f. 213b].


[VI.182]
Akūṭa sthāvināśitvam upādāyāsvabhāvatā,
Yā ṣaṇṇāṃ cakṣur ādīnāṃ sā matā’dhyātma śūnyatā.

,THER ZUG GNAS PA MA YIN DANG,
,’JIG PA MA YIN NYID KYI PHYIR,
,MIG LA SOGS PA DRUG PA {%PO} YI,
,RANG BZHIN MED NYID GANG YIN PA,
,DE NI NANG STONG NYID DU ‘DOD,

		They are not things
		Which remain
		In a solid manner;

		Nor do they stop
		In this way.

		The eye and the
		Rest of the six
		
		Do not exist
		Through any nature;

		What we accept
		As being emptiness
		On the inside
		Is this fact.


[3736]
NANG GI CHOS MIG LA SOGS PA DRUG PO, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI NANG STONG PA NYID DU ‘DOD DO,,

What we accept as being emptiness on the inside is the fact that the inner entities of the eye and the rest of the six do not exist in way where they are present through any nature of their own.


[3737]
DE YANG MIG NI MIG RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG STE, MIG DE’I RANG BZHIN NI RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA DE YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Which is to say, the eye is empty: it is not an eye that exists through any essential nature of its own.  And that’s because the nature of this eye is that it is empty of existing through any essential nature of its own.


[3738]
MIG LA BSHAD PA DE BZHIN DU RNA BA DANG SNA DANG LCE DANG LUS DANG YID KYANG BSNYAD PAR BYA’O,,

In the same way that we have explained it for the eye, we also refer to the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the thought.


[3739]
DE LTAR STONG PA’I RGYU MTSAN GANG GI PHYIR NA MIG SOGS DE RNAMS NI DON DAM PAR THER ZUG TU GNAS PA MA YIN PA DANG, ‘JIG PA MIN PA NYID KYI PHYIR RO,,

For what reason—why is it—that these things are empty?  The answer is for the very reason that they are not things which remain in a solid or ultimate manner; nor do they stop in this way.


[3740]
‘DIR PA TSAB KYIS THER ZUG TU GNAS PA MIN PA NI RANG BZHIN MI ‘DOR BA LA BYA’O, ,DE YANG DUS CUNG ZHIG GNAS NAS LDOG PAR YANG ‘GYUR BAS ‘JIG PA MA YIN PA NYID KYI PHYIR RO, ZHES GSUNGS SO, ,’DI SKAD BSTAN PAR ‘GYUR TE DNGOS PO GANG ZHIG RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PA DE NYID NI, GOR MA CHAG PAR THER ZUG PA MA YIN PA DANG MI LDOG PA ZHIG TU ‘GYUR DGOS SO, ZHES BSGYUR BA NI

Here the translation of the autocommentary by Patsab reads:

What’s being said here is that “Not being something that remains in a solid way refers to being something which never releases its nature.  Which is to say, they tend to stay for the briefest amount of time, and then come to a stop; as such, they are quite certainly not things that are destroyed.”  What this means is that if something were a functioning thing and did indeed come with its own nature, then beyond a shadow of a doubt it would be something which was not solid, and which never came to a stop.


[3741]
‘GYUR ‘PHYUGS PA YIN TE, DE LTA YIN NA BSGRUB BYA’I CHOS LOG PA LA RTAGS KYIS KHYAB DGOS PAR ‘GYUR BA’I PHYIR RO,,

This is in fact an error in the translation, since if this were the case then what was given as the reason would have to subsume the opposite of the quality to be proven.


[3742]
DES NA NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS, DNGOS PO GANG ZHIG RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS YOD PA DE NI THER ZUG TU GNAS PA’AM, NYAMS PAR ‘GYUR BA ZHIG TU ‘GYUR RO ZHES BSGYUR BA LTAR LEGS PAS, SNGA MA NI DGAG SGRA ‘DON [f. 251b] LUGS ‘PHYUGS PAR GSAL LO,,

As such, we can say that the translation by Naktso is correct here, where it says “When something is, first of all, a functioning entity, and also exists through some essential nature of its own, then it would have to be something that remained in a solid way—or as something that never declined.”  It is clear that the previous version we’ve listed has made an error in the way it brings out the negative particle.


[3743]
‘GREL BSHAD LAS, THER ZUG GNAS PA NYID DANG NI, ,MI ‘JIG MA YIN NYID KYI PHYIR, ZHES BTON NAS MIG SOGS LA RANG BZHIN YOD NA, RANG BZHIN LA RNAM ‘GYUR DANG ‘JIG PA MED PAS, DE RNAMS LA RNAM ‘GYUR DANG ‘JIG PA MED PAR ‘GYUR BA LAS, DE YANG YOD PA MA YIN PA’I PHYIR DE RNAMS RANG BZHIN MED PA’O, ZHES ‘CHAD PA YANG RIGS PA MA YIN TE,

Now The Explanation draws our attention to “If it had an existence as something solid, and if it did not exist as something that stopped,” saying that if the eye and so on had some nature of their own, then since a real nature would never change its aspects, nor ever undergo stopping, then these could never display aspects, or come to a stop.  And then it would be illogical to continue on and say, “Since this is not the case, then these have no nature of their own.”


[3744]
DE LTA YIN NA ‘JIG PA MED PAR ‘GYUR BA LAS ‘JIG PA YOD PA’I PHYIR, ZHES BYA DGOS NA DE NI MDO LAS, ‘JIG PA MA YIN PA NYID KYI PHYIR RO ZHES GSUNGS PA DANG ‘GAL LO,,

That is, if things were this way, then one would have to declare, “If that were the case, then they would have to become things with no stopping, whereas they do have stopping.”  And then that would contradict sutra when it says, “for the very reason that they are not something with stopping.”


[3745]
THER ZUG TU GNAS PA MIN PA NYID NI, ZHES PA YANG NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS, THER ZUG NI NYAMS PA MED PA’I NGO BO NYID LA BRJOD LA, ZHES BSGYUR BA LTAR BYA’O,,

As for this expression “the very fact of remaining in a solid way,” the translation should be done as we see it in Naktso’s version, where it says, “the expression ‘solid’ refers to an essential nature of never declining.”


[3746]
DE LTAR THER ZUG TU GNAS PA’I RTAG PA BKAG PA NA, MIG SOGS DE YANG RANG DUS SU CUNG ZAD GNAS NAS, DE’I ‘OG TU LDOG PA’I ‘JIG PAR BDEN NAM SNYAM PA ‘GOG PA LA ‘JIG PA MA YIN PA NYID KYI PHYIR, ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

And so once we have in this way blocked the idea that things could remain in some solid way, then we come to the question of “Is it real when the eye and so on remain for some small amount of time in their own space in time, and then after that reverse, and come to a stop?”  And to block this idea then it says ““for the very reason that they are not something with stopping.”


[3747]
DON BSDU NA RTAG MI RTAG GANG DU YANG MI BDEN PA’I PHYIR ZHES PA’I DON TO,,

And what this last is saying is that “In sum, then, these things are unreal, whether you are talking about their being unchanging, or changing.”


[3748]
NYI KHRI SNANG BA LAS ‘DI LAS TSUL GZHAN DU YANG GSUNGS SO,,

You can see this same point being made in the Illumination of the Twenty Thousand, from another approach.


[3749]
CHOS RNAMS KYI RANG BZHIN DE YANG RTZA BA SHES RAB LAS,
,RANG BZHIN RGYU DANG RKYEN DAG LAS,
,’BYUNG BAR RIGS PA MA YIN NO,
,RGYU DANG RKYEN LAS BYUNG BA NI,
,RANG BZHIN BYAS PA CAN DU ‘GYUR,

The question of a nature to things is, moreover, treated in Wisdom as follows:

It would be illogical
To say that a nature
Derived from causes & conditions.

Anything that has come
Through causes & conditions
Has a nature that was created.


	[3750]
,RANG BZHIN BYAS PA YIN NO ZHES,
,JI LTA BUR NA RUNG BAR ‘GYUR,
,RANG BZHIN DANG NI BCOS MIN DANG,
,GZHAN LA LTOS PA [f. 252a] MED PA YIN,
ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR RO,,

And how could it ever be right
To speak of a created nature?

Natures can never be artificial,
And can never rely on another.



How we do accept a nature

[3751]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: an incidental presentation on how we accept a nature to things.


[3752]
YANG CI GANG ZHIG SLOB DPON GYIS BSTAN BCOS LAS RGYU RKYEN LAS MA SKYES PA’I RANG BZHIN ZHES PA’I KHYAD PAR DU MDZAD PA DE LTA BU’I RANG BZHIN SLOB DPON GYIS ZHAL GYIS BZHES PA YOD DAM ZHE NA,

And what of the following lines?

One may pose the following question—

The Master, in his classical commentary, specifies a certain type of nature, referring to “a nature which has not been born of causes & conditions.”  Does this imply that he does accept such a nature?


[3753]
GANG GI DBANG DU MDZAD NAS BCOM LDAN ‘DAS KYIS, DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA RNAMS BYUNG YANG RUNG MA BYUNG YANG RUNG, CHOS RNAMS KYI CHOS NYID ‘DI NI GNAS PA NYID DO, ZHES GSUNGS PA’I CHOS NYID CES BYA BA NI YOD DO,,

The Conqueror himself did make a certain type of reference, saying that “Whether Those Gone Thus ever make an appearance or not, the very essence of entities can only remain.”  The “very essence” mentioned here is something that does exist.


[3754]
CHOS NYID CES BYA BA ‘DI YANG CI ZHIG YIN, MIG LA SOGS PA ‘DI DAG GI RANG BZHIN NO,,

And what is this thing we call “the very essence”?  It is the nature of these things: the eye and so on.


[3755]
DE DAG GI RANG BZHIN GANG ZHIG CE NA, MIG SOGS ‘DI DAG GI BCOS MA MA YIN PA DANG, SKYED BYED GZHAN LA LTOS PA MED PA STE, MA RIG PA’I RAB RIB DANG BRAL BA’I SHES PAS RTOGS PAR BYA BA’I NGO BO ZHES GSUNGS SO,,

And what is their nature?  It is the fact that these things—the eye and so forth—are in no way artificial; and that they are not things which rely upon other things to trigger them.  It is that essential nature which is perceived by those who are free of the cataracts of misunderstanding.


[3756]
‘DI DAG GIS NI SLOB DPON ‘DIS DON DAM BDEN PA DANG CHOS NYID YOD PAR MI BZHED CES PA DANG, MA RIG PA’I BSLAD PA LOG NA SHES PA YE MED PAR SMRA BA RNAMS LEGS PAR BKAG PA YIN NO,,

These lines serve as a perfect denial of those who say that this Master does not accept an ultimate reality; or a real way of things—as well as those who claim that, if we can put a stop to the influence of misunderstanding, then we have no remaining awareness at all.


[3757]
JI STE CHOS NYID DE YOD DAM, DE MED CES SU SMRA, GAL TE DE MED NA NI BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’ RNAMS CI’I DON DU PHA ROL TU PHYIN PA’I LAM SGOM PAR ‘GYUR TE MI ‘GYUR TE,

And so do we say that this essential nature to things exists, or does not?  If it didn’t exist, then for what purpose would the bodhisattvas practice the path of the perfections?  There would be no point at all.


[3758]
DON DAM PA’I BDEN PA MED NA NI DE RTOGS PA MTHAR THUG PAR ‘GRO BA MED LA, DE MED NA LAM SGOM PA DON MED PAR ‘GYUR TE, GANG GI PHYIR CHOS NYID RTOGS PA DANG DE MTHAR THUG PAR ‘GRO BAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, BYANG SEMS RNAMS DKA’ BA BRGYA PHRAG RTZOM PA YIN NO,,

If there were no reality that were ultimate, then there would be no such thing to serve as the ultimate object of realization.  And if that were so, then the whole practice of the path would be meaningless; after all, the very reason that bodhisattvas undertake their thousands of hardships is precisely for the purpose of perceiving the real nature of things, and to reach the final end of that undertaking.


[3759]
‘DIS NI CHOS NYID CES PA’I [f. 252b] DON DAM BDEN PA BLO GANG GI YANG YUL MA YIN PAR ‘DOD BZHIN DU, LAM LA DKA’ BA DU MA RTZOM PA NI, DBANG PO SHIN TU RTUL BAR STON PA YIN NO,,

Which is to say that—even as these people make the claim that ultimate reality can never be the object of any state of mind that exists—at the same time they undertake many hardships for the sake of the path.  It must be that they are demonstrating just how very dull their mental powers really are!


[3760]
DE LTAR YIN PA YANG DKON MCHOG SPRIN LAS, RIGS KYI BU DON DAM PA NI SKYE BA MED PA DANG, ‘GAG PA MED PA DANG, ‘JIG PA MED PA DANG, ‘ONG BA MED PA DANG, ‘GRO BA MED PA DANG, YI GE RNAMS KYIS BRJOD PAR BYA BA MA YIN PA DANG, YI GE RNAMS KYIS RAB TU BSNYAD DU MED CING, SPROS PAS RTOGS PA MA YIN PA STE, RIGS KYI BU DON DAM PA NI BRJOD DU MED CING, ZHI BA ‘PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS SO SO RANG GIS RIG PAR BYA BA’O,,

The facts here are expressed with perfect clarity in the Cloud of Jewels:

O child of noble family, the ultimate is something that has no starting, and has no stopping, and cannot be destroyed.

It has no coming, and it has no going.

It is not something that can be expressed in words; no words can ever be given to it.

It is not something that could ever be realized through a state of mind that is still imagining things.

O child of noble family, the ultimate is something that could never be described: peace is something that is seen by realized beings themselves, one by one.


[3761]
RIGS KYI BU DON DAM PA NI DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA RNAMS BYUNG YANG RUNG MA BYUNG YANG RUNG STE, GANG GI DON DU BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’ RNAMS SKRA DANG KHA SPU BREGS NAS GOS NGUR SMRIG BGOS TE, YANG DAG PAR DAD PAS KHYIM NAS KHYIM MED PAR RAB TU BYUNG ZHING,

O child of noble family, the ultimate is there whether Those Gone Thus ever appear in the universe, or not.  It is the reason why bodhisattvas cut off their hair and shave off their beards, and don the golden robe.  It is why, out of perfect faith, they leave behind the home life, leaving the house to go where they have no house.


[3762]
RAB TU BYUNG NAS KYANG CHOS NYID DE THOB PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR, SKRA ‘AM GOS LA ME SHOR BA LTAR BRTZON ‘GRUS RTZOM ZHING GNAS PA RNAM PAR ‘JIG PA MED PA’O,,

For the reason that they leave the home is to attain this real nature of things.  They make efforts with the same urgency they would show if their hair or clothes were to catch on fire; this is how they live, and they have no fear of anything.


[3763]
RIGS KYI BU GAL TE DON DAM PA YOD PAR MA GYUR NA NI, TSANGS PAR SPYOD PA DON MED PAR ‘GYUR ZHING, DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA RNAMS BYUNG BA DON MED PAR ‘GYUR RO,,

And if, o child of noble family, there were no ultimate, then the life of purity that these individuals follow would be meaningless; and there would be no point at all to Those Gone Thus appearing in the world.


[3764]
GANG GI PHYIR DON DAM PA DE YOD PA DE’I PHYIR BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA’ RNAMS LA DON DAM PA LA MKHAS PA ZHES BYA’O, ZHES SHIN TU GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

But because the ultimate does exist, then we can say things like “the bodhisattvas are masters of the ultimate.”


[3765]
BRJOD DU MED PA DANG, SPROS PAS RTOGS PAR BYA BA MIN PA NI, RNAM PAR MI RTOG PA’I YE SHES KYIS DON DAM PA GZIGS PA BZHIN DU, SGRA RTOG GIS YUL DU BYED MI NUS [f. 253a] PA’I DON YIN GYI, SPYIR RTOGS MI NUS PA MIN NO,,

When we say here that things are indescribable, or that they are not something which can ever be perceived by a mind still imagining things, what we mean is that they are things which cannot serve as an object for thinking which is still verbal—not in the same way as they can be perceived by the wisdom beyond all thought, which sees the ultimate.  We are not though claiming that, in general, these things cannot be perceived at all.


[3766]
DON DAM BDEN PA YOD PA MIN PA LA GNOD PA BSTAN ZHING, DE’I LDOG PA ‘PHANGS PA BSTAN PA NA’ANG YOD PAR GSUNGS SHING SNGAR YANG YOD PAR BSTAN PAS, MED PA DANG YOD PA MIN PA LA KHYAD PAR ‘BYED PA NI BLO GROS SHIN TU DMAN PAR STON PA TZAM MO,,

Arguments are presented against the idea that ultimate reality is not something that could exist; and there are as well presentations which demonstrate that the opposite of this idea is necessarily implied.  And it has, already, been described earlier how this reality does exist.  As such, when you try to draw some distinction here between not existing and not being something which does exist, all you are doing is demonstrating just how very inferior your thinking processes are.


[3767]
PA TSAB KYI ‘GYUR GYI DPE MANG PO LAS, BYUNG YANG RUNG MA BYUNG YANG RUNG STE, GANG GI DON DU ZHES ‘BYUNG YANG, NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS, MA BYUNG YANG RUNG DON DAM PA NI NYAMS PA MED PA YIN PAS ZHES ‘BYUNG BA NI, SNGAR ‘GREL PAR MDO DRANGS PA LAS, MA BYUNG YANG RUNG CHOS RNAMS KYI CHOS NYID ‘DI NI GNAS PA NYID DO, ZHES ‘BYUNG BA DANG MTHUN PAS LEGS PA YIN NO,,

Many of the manuscripts of Patsab’s translation read: “For whatever the reason, whether it is the case that it has occurred, or has not occurred.”  Naktso’s translation reads, “For the reason that the ultimate never declines, even if it were something that never came about.”  This latter version accords with what we see in the autocommentary, where it quotes the sutra: “Even if it were something that never came about, the real nature of things is quite certainly something that stays.”  As such, we can say that this version is preferred.


[3768]
‘DIR SMRAS PA, KYE MA MA {%LA? both carvings say MA MA} LA GANG ZHIG DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA CUNG ZAD KYANG MI ‘DOD CING, GLO BUR DU BCOS MA MA YIN PA DANG, GZHAN LA LTOS PA MED PA’I RANG BZHIN YANG ‘DOD PA KHYOD NI, PHAN TSUN ‘GAL BA’I DON BRJOD PA ZHIG GO ZHE NA,

And so we can say it this way.  Suppose you burst out with something like—

Oh my gosh!  You are people who can accept not even the slightest version of something existing through any nature of its own; and yet at the same time you have no problem with agreeing that there is some nature to things which is not something that was ever created in some occurrence of the moment—a nature which has never relied upon anything else.  And so you are expressing two ideas which simply contradict each other!


[3769]
‘DI NI KHYOD KYIS DBU MA’I BSTAN BCOS KYI DGONGS PA MA RIG PA ZHIG STE, ‘DI’I DGONGS PA NI GAL TE MIG LA SOGS PA RNAMS KYI RANG GI NGO BO RTEN CING ‘BREL PAR ‘BYUNG BA BYIS PA’I SKYE BOS GZUNG BAR BYA BA GANG YIN PA ‘DI NYID MIG LA SOGS PA DE RNAMS KYI RANG BZHIN YIN LUGS YIN NA NI, RANG BZHIN DE PHYIN CI LOG GI BLOS KYANG MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA’I PHYIR, TSANGS PAR SPYOD PA DON MED PAR ‘GYUR NA,

But with this, the fact is that you are showing how you fail to understand the true intent of the classical commentary on the middle way.  What this is actually trying to say is that—suppose the essential nature of the eye and so on is that they occur through a process of dependence.  And suppose that people who are still infants hold to this idea.  If this by itself were the ultimate nature or way of being for the eye and so forth, then it would be the case that even a mistaken state of mind could perceive this nature directly.  And then living the entire life of purity would be pointless.


[3770]
GANG GI PHYIR MIG SOGS RTEN ‘BREL YIN PA ‘DI RANG BZHIN YIN LUGS MA YIN PA [f. 253b] DE’I PHYIR, DE BLTA BA’I DON DU TSANGS PAR SPYOD PA DON DANG BCAS PAR ‘GYUR RO, ZHES GSUNGS TE,

And what’s being said here is that the fact that the eye and so forth are dependent is not the ultimate nature of things; which is why it is a meaningful exercise to follow the life of purity in order to be able to see that nature.


[3771]
RANG BZHIN BKAG PA NI MIG SOGS GSHIS LUGS YIN PA BKAG PA YIN LA, RANG BZHIN KHAS BLANGS PA NI BKAG PA DE MIG SOGS KYI CHOS NYID CES PA’I RANG BZHIN DU ‘DOD PA YIN PAS, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA BKAG PA DANG, DNGOS PO’I CHOS NYID KYI RANG BZHIN KHAS LEN PA LA ‘GAL BA CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PA’I PHYIR RO,,

When we say that we are denying a nature, we are talking about denying a primordial way of being for the eye and so on.  When we say that we accept a nature, we are agreeing to the idea that the denial just mentioned is the nature of the eye and the rest: what we call the true nature of these things.  As such, there is not the slightest contradiction between denying that things could exist through some nature of their own, and agreeing to a nature in that sense of a true nature to things.


[3772]
DE ‘DRA BA’I CHOS NYID DE YANG BDAG GIS KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA STE THA SNYAD TZAM DU GRUB PA LA LTOS NAS, BCOS MA MIN PA DANG GZHAN LA MI LTOS PAR BRJOD DO,,

This kind of a true nature to things is “what I am talking about when I speak of deceptive” reality; things that rely on existing only nominally—and it is something which is not artificial, or which does not depend upon something else.
 

[3773]
GANG ZHIG BYIS PA’I SKYE BO RANG DGA’ BAS BLTA PAR BYA BA MA YIN PA’I CHOS NYID DE NI RANG BZHIN DU RIGS LA, DE KUN RDZOB TU YOD PAR KHAS BLANGS PA DE TZAM GYIS DON DAM PAR DE DNGOS PO DANG DNGOS PO MED PAR RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YANG MA YIN TE, DE NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA ZHI BA NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR,

A kind of true nature to things that would not be something which could be viewed by just everyday infants would be fitting as this nature.  And by the simple act of agreeing that this could exist in a deceptive way we can say that it is not something that could exist through some nature of its own—as an entity or a non-entity, in some ultimate way.  This is what we refer to as a perfect state of peace, or the end of existing through some nature of its own.


[3774]
RANG BZHIN CHOS NYID ‘DI NI SLOB DPON ‘PHAGS PAS ZHAL GYIS BZHES PA ‘BA’ ZHIG TU MA ZAD KYI, PHA ROL PO GZHAN YANG DON ‘DI KHAS LEN DU GZHUG PAR NUS PAS, RANG BZHIN ‘DI NI BRTZAD PA’I MTHAR RANG GZHAN GNYIS KA LA GRUB PA NYID DU YANG RNAM PAR BZHAG GO ,ZHES GSUNGS PA ‘DI KHYAD PAR DU NGES PAR BYA DGOS SO,,

Not only is this nature in the form of a true nature to things something that is accepted by our master, the Realized One; it is also possible for others of different positions to be guided into accepting this point.  As such, we can say that “When you come to the end of this examination of a nature to things, you are establishing something quite perfectly for both yourself and for others.”  We have to come to a special appreciation of this feature.


[3775]
GANG DAG ME LA SOGS PA’I RANG BZHIN YIN LUGS TSA BA LA SOGS PAR SMRA BA DE DAG GI LTAR ‘DOD NA NI, RNAM PA THAMS CAD DU DE MI RUNG STE, TSA BA SOGS NI BRTEN NAS SKYES PA NYID KYIS BCOS MA YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG, RGYU RKYEN LA BRTEN NAS [f. 254a] SKYES PA’I YOD PA YIN PA’I PHYIR,

Now there are some who profess that the nature of fire and so on—the way of being for these things—is hotness, or the like.  But it would be totally incorrect for us to agree with their position.  This is because the very fact of arising through some dependence upon hotness is to be artificial; and because this is an existence of having arisen through dependence upon causes & conditions.


[3776]
MIG SOGS DE BCOS MA NYID DU MED PA DANG, RGYU RKYEN GZHAN LA LTOS PA MED PA NYID DO, ZHES BRJOD PA YANG MI RIGS TE, DE LA ZHES BYA BA ‘DIS MCHOG TU ‘DZIN PA’I DNGOS PO MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, KUN RDZOB TU RNAM PA DE LTA BU’I DON BSTAN PA’I PHYIR TE, ZHES PA TSAB KYI ‘GYUR LAS ‘BYUNG LA,

“And yet it would be incorrect to say” that the eye and so forth were devoid of any artificiality; or that “they did not rely on something outside of themselves,” referring to causes & conditions.  “This is because, when we say ‘on that,’ what we are saying is that there is no entity which is considered preeminent; and deceptively speaking we are indicating that sort of object.”  This is the treatment that we see in Patsab’s translation.


[3777]
NAG TSO’I ‘GYUR LAS, DE LA ‘DI LTAR MCHOG TU ‘DZIN PA NYID MED PA’I PHYIR DANG, KUN RDZOB TU DON JI LTA BA BZHIN DU BSGRUBS PA’I PHYIR RO,, ZHES ‘BYUNG NGO,,

Naktso’s translation has: “…because there is absolutely no considering something preeminent in that way, with it; and in a deceptive sense, it exists in the way it should.”


[3778]
DE LA ‘DI LTAR ZHES ‘BYUNG BA LEGS LA, LHAG MA’I DON NI BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA’I ZHEN YUL GYI DNGOS PO MED PA DANG, KUN RDZOB TU BCOS MA DANG GZHAN LA LTOS PA’I RNAM PA DE LTA BU’I DON BSTAN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Here the presence of the phrase “in that way” is well done.  As for the import of the remainder, what’s being indicated is that there exists no entity which corresponds to what the tendency to hold things as real thinks it sees—along with the point that there is an aspect of being, in a deceptive way, artificial; and of relying upon something other.


[3779]
DE LTAR SLOB DPON ‘PHAGS PAS RANG BZHIN ZHAL GYIS BZHES PAR BSTAN PA ‘DIS, CHOS DBYINGS BSTOD PA LAS,
,STONG PA NYID NI STON PA’I MDO,
,RGYAL BAS JI SNYED GSUNGS PA KUN,
,DE DAG KUN GYIS NYON MONGS LDOG
,KHAMS ‘DI NYAMS PAR BYED MA YIN,

Once we understand through this presentation that the master, The Arya, accepts the idea of a nature to things, we can also go on to understand the following lines from A Praise of the Realm of Reality—

All of the various sutras
Ever spoken by the Victors
That presented the idea
Of emptiness

Were meant to stop
The negative emotions;
But they do nothing to diminish
This basic nature to things.


[3780]
ZHES STONG NYID STON PA’I MDO SDES BDEN ‘DZIN GYI NYON MONGS PA’I DMIGS GTAD ‘JIG PA YIN GYI, DE’I DMIGS GTAD BKAG PA’I STONG PA DE BZHIN GSHEGS PA’I KHAMS NYAMS PA STE MED PAR STON PA MIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA YANG SHES PAR BYA’O,,

What this is saying is that the group of sutras that presents the idea of emptiness functions to destroy the point of view of our tendency to see things as real, a view involved with the negative emotions.  These lines were not though meant to say that the emptiness where we block what our mind thinks it saw somehow diminishes or obviates the basic nature of Those Gone Thus.


[3781]
DE LA MIG SOGS RNAMS MIG SOGS KYIS STONG PAR GSUNGS PAS NI, MIG SOGS RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NYID GSAL BAR MDZAD PA YIN GYI, MIG NANG GI BYED PA’I BDAG [f. 254b] DANG BRAL BA’I STONG PA’O ZHES NYAN THOS SDE PA ‘DOD PA DANG,

And so what does it mean, when we say that “the eye and the rest are empty of the eye and the rest”?  This is merely a clarification of the fact that the eye and so on are empty of existing through any nature of their own; but it is not, first of all, as the listener groups would have it, when they refer to an emptiness in the form of the eye being devoid of some inner self-nature.


[3782]
SEMS TZAM PAS MIG GZUNG ‘DZIN RDZAS THA DAD PA TZAM GYIS STONG NGO ZHES MIG SOGS RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS MI STONG PA’I GCIG LA GCIG MED PA’I STONG PA NYID DU ‘DOD PA LTAR NI MA YIN NO,,

Nor is it as the Mind Only school would have it, when they speak of an emptiness which is no more than the fact that the object and subject aspects of the eye are void of being essentially separate—an emptiness where the eye and so forth were not empty of existing through any essential nature of their own, but rather empty—each one—of being the other.



Three more kinds of emptiness

[3783]
GNYIS PA NI,

With this we have reached our second point from above: an explanation of the remaining three types of emptiness here.



2) Emptiness on the outside


	[3784]
[VI.183]
Rūpaṃ rūpeṇa vai śūnyam asyaiṣā prakṛtir yataḥ,
Evaṃ śabdā rasā gandhā dharmāḥ spraṣṭavyam eva ca

,GANG PHYIR DE YI RANG BZHIN DE,
,YIN PHYIR GZUGS NI GZUGS KYIS STONG,
,SGRA DANG DRI RO REG BYA DANG,
,CHOS RNAMS NYID KYANG DE BZHIN NO,

	Form is empty
	Of existing through form,	

	Due to the fact
	That the very nature
	Of it is that.


[VI.184a]
Rūpāder niḥsvabhāvatvaṃ bahirdhāśūnyatā matā,
Ubhayor asvabhāvatvaṃ bahirdhādhyātma śūnyatā.

,GZUGS SOGS RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID,
,PHYI ROL STONG PA NYID DU ‘DOD,

		The fact of
The lack of a nature
		To form and the rest
		Is what we say is
		“Emptiness on the outside.”


[3785]
RGYUD KYIS MA BSDUS PA’I GZUGS LA SOGS PA’I YUL DRUG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA’I RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID NI, PHYI ROL GYI STONG PA NYID DU ‘DOD DO,,

Consider next then the fact of the lack of a nature to things like physical form and the rest which are not taken in by a person’s mind stream; we are talking about the six objects, and the fact that they are empty of existing through any nature of their own.  This then is what we say is “emptiness on the outside.”


[3786]
PHYI’I GZUGS NI GZUGS KYI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NI, GANG GI PHYIR GZUGS DE’I RANG BZHIN NI DE YIN PA’I PHYIR RO,,

Outer form then is empty of existing through some essential nature of being form; and that in turn is due to the fact that the very nature of form—of it—is that.


[3787]
SGRA DANG DRI DANG RO DANG REG BYA DANG CHOS RNAMS NYID KYANG STONG TSUL DE BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

And one should understand—in the very same manner—the way in which sound, smell, taste, tangibles, and things in general are empty.


[3788]
‘DI DANG LHAG MA RNAMS LA MDOR THER ZUG TU GNAS PA MIN PA DANG, ‘JIG PA MIN PA’I PHYIR ZHES GSUNGS PA NI SNGAR NANG STONG PA NYID KYI SKABS SU BSHAD PA BZHIN DU SHES PAR BYA’O,,

When these and the remaining ones are described, in sutra, as “not remaining in any solid way,” or as “never stopping,” you should understand the references in the same way as we explained it earlier, in the section about emptiness on the inside.



3) Emptiness on the outside and the inside

	[3789]
[VI.184b]
,GNYIS CHAR RANG BZHIN MED NYID NI,
,PHYI NANG STONG PA NYID YIN NO,

		It is both;
		And the fact
		That it does not exist

		Through any
		Essential nature

		Constitutes emptiness
		On the outside
		And the inside.


[3790]
SHES RGYUD KYIS BSDUS PA’I DBANG RTEN KHOG PA LTA BU NI SHES RGYUD KYIS BSDUS SHING, DBANG POS MA BSDUS PAS NA PHYI NANG GNYIS CHAR YIN LA,

Now something like the general bodily container, subsumed by our flow of awareness, is an example of something which is both subsumed by mental awareness but is not subsumed by the sense powers.  As such, it is considered both outside and inside.


[3791]
DE RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA’I RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID NI, PHYI NANG GI STONG PA NYID DE LHAG MA SNGAR BZHIN NO,,

The lack of a nature to this container—the fact that it does not exist through any essential nature of its own—constitutes emptiness on the outside and the inside.  And the rest follows as before.



4) Emptiness emptiness


	[3792]
[VI.185]
Dharmāṇāṃ niḥsvabhāvatvaṃ śūnyatetyucyate budhaiḥ,
Sā cāpi śūnyatā śūnyā śūnyatārūpato matā.

,CHOS RNAMS RANG BZHIN MED PA NYID,
,MKHAS PAS STONG PA NYID CES BSNYAD,
,STONG NYID DE YANG STONG NYID KYI,
,NGO BOS STONG PAR ‘DOD PA YIN,

		The fact that entities
		Are without any nature
		Of their own is what
		
		Masters refer to
		As emptiness.

		We assert that
		The fact that
		They are empty

		Is in turn also empty
		Of some essential nature
		Of emptiness itself.		


[3793]
PHYI NANG GI CHOS RNAMS SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR RANG BZHIN KYIS GRUB PA MED PA NYID NI, DE KHO NA LA MKHAS PAS RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID CES BSNYAD DO,,

Now the fact that both outside and inside entities, as previously explained, are without any existence that has come about through any nature of their own is what those who are masters of suchness refer to as the emptiness of any self-nature.


[3794]
PHYI NANG GI CHOS KYI RANG BZHIN STONG PA NYID DE YANG STONG NYID KYI NGO BOS GRUB PA’AM BDEN PAS STONG PAR ‘DOD PA YIN NO,,

That is, we assert that the very fact that outer and inner entities are empty of any nature of their own is in turn also empty of any reality, or existence through some essential nature of emptiness itself.


	[3795]
[VI.186]
Śūnyatā śūnyatākhyā yā śūnyatāśūnyatā matā,
Śūnyatā bhava buddhīnām uktā grāha nivṛttaye.

,STONG NYID CES BYA’I STONG NYID GANG,
,STONG NYID STONG NYID DU ‘DOD DE,
,STONG NYID DNGOS PO’I BLO CAN GYI,
,’DZIN PA BZLOG PHYIR GSUNGS PA YIN,

		We say that
		The emptiness of
		The thing which
		We refer to itself
		As emptiness is
		“Emptiness emptiness.”

		These statements
		Were made in order
		To block the tendency

		Of those whose minds
		Were grasping,
		Holding that emptiness
		Was a real thing.


[3796]
DE LTAR NA STONG GZHI STONG NYID CES BYA BA’I STONG NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI, STONG PA NYID STONG PA NYID DU ‘DOD PA STE,

And so let us consider that emptiness of the thing which we refer to itself as emptiness, now in the sense of being the thing which is empty.  This is what, we say, is “emptiness emptiness.”


[3797]
[f. 255a] STONG PA NYID BDEN PAS STONG PAR GSUNGS PA NI STONG NYID DAM CHOS NYID LA DNGOS PO STE BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA’I BLO CAN GYI BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA BZLOG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR RGYAL BA’I YUM LAS GSUNGS PA YIN NO,,

These statements that emptiness itself is empty of any true existence were made in the Mother Sutras themselves, in order to block the tendency to hold things as being real, in the thoughts of those whose minds were already grasping to the idea that things could be real: who were holding that emptiness or ultimate reality itself was a real thing.


[3798]
DE LTAR YIN PAR YANG ‘JIG RTEN LAS ‘DAS PAR BSTOD PA LAS,
,KUN RTOG THAMS CAD BSAL BA’I PHYIR,
,STONG NYID BDUD RTZI STON MDZAD NA,
,GANG ZHIG DE LA ZHEN GYUR PA,
,DE NYID KHYOD KYIS SHIN TU SMAD,
CES GSAL BAR GSUNGS SO,,

The fact that this is the case is clearly expressed in A Praise of the One Who Went Beyond the World:

You undertook to teach
The nectar of emptiness
To banish all the mistaken
Perceptions that people have.

One thing though
You disparaged completely:
Those attracted
To seeing it wrong.


[3799]
‘DI DAG GIS NI KHA CIG DON DAM PAR BDEN PA ZHES PA BDEN DNGOS RNAM PAR BCAD TZAM LA BYAS NAS DE BDEN GRUB TU SMRA BA DANG, GZHAN DAG DGAG BYA BCAD TZAM MIN PA’I SNGO SER LTAR SGRUB PAR RANG DBANG BA CHOS NYID DU BYAS NAS DE BDEN PAR ‘DOD PA GNYIS KA YANG RGYAL BAS SHIN TU SMAD PAR GSUNGS SO,,

What these lines are referring to is some people who take the expression “ultimate reality” as referring to the simple exclusion of entities that are real, and then say that that exists in truth.  And there are others who point to things like the colors blue or yellow—positive entities which are not the simple exclusion of the thing that emptiness denies—and say that, in their independent form, these are the real nature of things; thus asserting, in effect, that these things are real.  And what the lines are saying is that both these parties would be disparaged completely by the Victorious Buddhas.



The four starting with great emptiness

[3800]
GNYIS PA NI,

Which brings us to our second point from above: an explanation of the four types of emptiness starting with great emptiness.



5) Great emptiness

	[3801]
[VI.187]
Sattva bhājana lokasya niḥśeṣa vyāpakatvataḥ,
Apramāṇopamānena paryantābhāvato diśām.

,SEMS CAN SNOD KYI ‘JIG RTEN NI,
,MA LUS KHYAB BYED NYID PHYIR DANG,
,TSAD MED DPE YIS MU MTHA’ NI,
,MED PHYIR PHYOGS RNAMS CHEN PO NYID,

		Because the vessel of 
The world, or the
Living beings contained,

Extends in expanse
Over no less than
The entirety,

Our example of
The infinity has
No final edge;

And thus is massive
In the extent
Of the directions.


[3802]
SHAR LA SOGS PA’I PHYOGS LAS LOGS SHIG TU SNOD BCUD GNYIS MED PAS, SEMS CAN DANG SNOD KYI ‘JIG RTEN NI MI {%MA} LUS PA LA KHYAB PAR BYED PA NYID YIN PA’I PHYIR DANG,

Now neither of the two of the vessel of the world, or the living beings contained in it, are to be found in some location separate from the expanse of the different directions of east and the rest.  And that’s because the directions are something which extends in its expanse over no less than the entirety of this world composed of both living beings and the physical earth.  


[3803]
BYAMS SOGS TSAD MED BZHI SGOM PA NA PHYOGS KYIS KHYAB PA’I SEMS CAN KUN LA SGOM PAS, DMIGS PA’I SGO NAS TSAD MED PAR BZHAG PA’I PHYIR, 

And when we practice the four infinite meditations of love and the rest, we are meditating upon all the living beings subsumed by all the directions.  From the point of view of the objects we are focusing upon, then, we describe the meditation as “infinite.”


[3804]
PHYOGS TSAD MED PA’I DPE YIS TE TSAD MED PA BZHIN DU, DE LTAR SGOM PA LA YANG MU MTHA’ NI MED PA STE TSAD MED PAR BZHAG PA’I PHYIR PHYOGS BCU NI CHEN PO NYID DO,,

The infinity we’re talking about is similar to our example here of the infinity of the directions; that is, the meditation has no final edge either—it is defined as infinite—and thus it is massive in its extent, of the ten directions.


	[3805]
[VI.188]
Mahattvaṃ digbhir evāsāṃ daśānām api śūnyatā,
Yā mahāśūnyatā soktā mahāgrāha nivṛttaye

,’DI DAG BCU CHAR PHYOGS RNAMS KYIS,
,STONG PA NYID NI GANG YIN DE,
,CHEN PO STONG PA NYID YIN DE  {%TE?},
,CHEN POR ‘DZIN PA BZLOG PHYIR GSUNGS,

	The fact that
	All ten directions
	Are empty is
	“Great emptiness.”

	It was taught
	In order to stop
	The holding that
	They are vast.


[3806]
SHAR LA SOGS PA ‘DI DAG BCU CHAR PHYOGS RNAMS KYI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NYID NI GANG YIN PA DE NI CHEN PO STONG PA NYID YIN TE, PHYOGS RNAMS CHEN POR RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB [f. 255b] PAR ‘DZIN PA BZLOG PA’I PHYIR DU GSUNGS TE, PHYOGS LA PHYIN CI LOG TU ‘DZIN PA NI MU STEGS BYE BRAG PAS PHYOGS RNAMS RTAG PA’I RDZAS NYID DU ‘DZIN PA LTA BU’O,,

The fact that all ten directions of east and the rest are empty of existing through any essential nature of their own is “great emptiness.”  And it was taught in order to stop people from holding that the directions are vast in a way that exists through some nature of its own.  An example of taking the directions in a mistaken way would be where the River school called the Detailers holds that a direction represents some perfectly unchanging substance. 



6) Ultimate emptiness


	[3807]
[VI.189]
Paramārtho hi nirvāṇaṃ param etat prayojanam,
Tasya yā śūnyatā tena sā paramārtha śūnyatā.

,DE NI DGOS PA MCHOG YIN PAS,
,DON DAM MYA NGAN ‘DAS PA YIN,
,DE NI DE YIS STONG NYID GANG,
,DE NI DON DAM STONG NYID DE,

	This is of ultimate significance,
Here, nirvana; because
This is the highest purpose.

The fact that this
Is empty of its own—

This is ultimate emptiness.
	

[VI.190]
Nirvāṇe bhava buddhīnāṃ bhava grāha nivṛttaye,
Deśitā paramārthajñaiḥ śūnyatā pāramārthikā.

,MYANG ‘DAS DNGOS PO’I BLO CAN GYI,
,’DZIN PA BZLOG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR,
,DON DAM MKHYEN PAS DON DAM PA,
,STONG PA NYID NI BSTAN PAR MDZAD,

	The goal here
	Is to help put a stop
	To the tendency

		That people have
		In their mind
		To hold this nirvana
		As actual.

		This is why
		The one who knows
		The ultimate

		Undertook to teach
		This ultimate emptiness.


[3808]
DON DAM ZHES PA’I DON GYI SGRA NI ‘DI LA DON YOD DE ZHES PA LTA BU DGOS PA LA BYED PA DANG, DON LNGA ZHES PA LTA BU SHES BYA YUL LA BYED PA GNYIS LAS, ‘DIR NI MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA CHOS KYI SKU YIN TE, MYANG ‘DAS DE NI THOB PAR BYA BA’I DGOS PA MCHOG YIN PAS SO,,

When we call something “ultimate” or “of ultimate significance,” the word “significance” refers to purpose; as when we say “there is definitely a purpose to this.”  The same word can be used to refer to something that we perceive—an object—as when we speak of the five objects of the senses.  Of these two connotations, here we are speaking about nirvana, or the body of all things.  And that’s because attaining this particular nirvana is the highest purpose of all.


[3809]
CHOS SKU DE NI DE YI RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI, DON DAM PA STONG PA NYID DE,

And so consider the emptiness represented by the fact that this body of all things is empty of existing through any essential nature of its own.  This is what we refer to as “ultimate emptiness.”


[3810]
DE YANG MYA NGAN LAS ‘DAS PA CHOS SKU DE LA DNGOS PO STE BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA’I BLO CAN GYI BDEN PAR ‘DZIN PA BZLOG PAR BYA BA’I PHYIR DON DAM MKHYEN PA SANGS RGYAS KYIS DON DAM PA STONG PA NYID NI BSTAN PAR MDZAD DO,,

And our goal here is to help put a stop to the tendency that people have in their mind to hold this as being real: where they hold that this nirvana, this body of all things, is “actual”—meaning here “real.”  And this is why the Buddha, the one who knows the ultimate, undertook to teach this ultimate emptiness.



7) The emptiness of produced things


	[3811]
[VI.191]
Dhātu trayaṃ niruktaṃ vai saṃskṛtaṃ pratyayodayāt,
Tasya yā śūnyatā tena soktā saṃskṛta śūnyatā.

,RKYEN LAS BYUNG PHYIR KHAMS GSUM PO,
,’DUS BYAS YIN PAR NGES PAR BSNYAD,
,DE NI DE YIS STONG NYID GANG,
,DE NI ‘DUS BYAS STONG NYID GSUNGS,

	The three realms
	Are referred to
	As produced things,

	Since they come
	From conditions.

	That these are
	Completely empty
	Of any was taught

	As the emptiness
	Of produced things.


[3812]
RGYU RKYEN LAS BYUNG BA STE SKYES PA’I PHYIR KHAMS GSUM PO NI ‘DUS BYAS YIN PAR NGES PAR BSNYAD DO,,

The three realms of the universe are referred to as produced things, since they have arisen through a process of coming from causes & conditions.


[3813]
KHAMS GSUM PO DE NI DE YI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI, ‘DUS BYAS STONG PA NYID DU GSUNGS SO,,

And so then the emptiness of produced things was taught; which refers to the fact that these three realms are completely empty of any existing through some nature of their own.



8) The emptiness of things that exist
but were not produced


	[3814]
[VI.192]
Asaṃskṛtaṃ na yasyaitā utpāda sthitya nityatāḥ,
Tena yā śūnyatā tasya soktā’saṃskṛta śūnyatā.

,GANG LA SKYE GNAS MI RTAG NYID,
,DE DAG MED PA ‘DUS MA BYAS,
,DE NI DE YIS STONG NYID GANG,
,DE NI ‘DUS MA BYAS STONG NYID,

		Any entity
		Which is devoid
		Of any arising
		Or changing—

		And also devoid
		Of staying—

		Is what we refer to
		As “an existing entity
		Which has not
		Been produced.”

		The fact that
		This type is empty
		Of its own is

		“The emptiness of
		Things that exist
		But were not produced.”


[3815]
CHOS GANG LA SKYE BA DANG MI RTAG PA STE ‘GAG PA’AM ‘JIG PA DANG, GNAS PA LAS GZHAN DU ‘GYUR BA DE DAG MED PA NI ‘DUS MA BYAS SO,,

Now any existing entity which is devoid of any arising or quality of changing—which is to say, and stopping or being destroyed—and which is also devoid of any staying, and then turning into something else, all these qualities, is what we refer to as “an existing entity which has not been produced.”


[3816]
DE NI DE YI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS STONG PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI ‘DUS MA BYAS STONG PA NYID DU GSUNGS SO,,

And the fact that this type of entity is empty of any existence through some nature of its own was taught as “the emptiness of things that exist but were not produced.”



The four starting with
emptiness beyond all extremes

[3817]
GSUM PA NI,

Which brings us to our third point: An explanation of the four starting with emptiness beyond all extremes.



9) The emptiness beyond all extremes


[3818]
MTHA’ NI RTAG PA DANG CHAD PA GANG DU BZUNG NA LOG PA’I G-YANG DU LTUNG BA YIN GYI, ‘DUS MA BYAS RTAG PA DANG DGRA BCOM PA LA LAS DBANG GI SKYE ‘CHI BRGYUD PA CHAD PAR ‘DZIN PA LTA BU NI MA YIN PAS, 

When we say “extremes” here, what we’re talking about is the edge of a cliff that you fall off of, when you make the mistake of holding that things could either last forever, or simply discontinue.  This is not the same thing we are talking about when we say that existing entities which are unchanging are, in fact, unchanging; or when people hold to the idea that enemy destroyers experience a discontinuation of the flow of birth and death necessitated by karma.


[3819]
GANG DU BZUNG [f. 256a] NA MI MTHUN PHYOGS KYI G-YANG DU LTUNG BA’I RTAG CHAD DANG, RTAG CHAD TZAM GYI KHYAD PAR PHYED PAR BYA’O,,

What we are talking about here is that idea about things lasting forever, or simply discontinuing, which—when you hold to it—serves to throw you off the cliff of the mistaken side of things.  We also need to be able to draw a distinction between this and some normal kind of lasting forever, or stopping altogether.


	[3820]
[VI.193]
Anto na vidyate yasya tad atyantaṃ nirucyate,
Tasya tenaiva śūnyatvaṃ kathyate’tyanta śūnyatā.

,GANG LA MTHA’ NI YOD MIN PA,
,DE NI MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PAR BRJOD,
,DE DE KHO NAS STONG PA NYID,
,MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PA STONG NYID BSNYAD,

	A situation where
	There is no case of
	An extreme

	Was described as
	“Going beyond
All extremes.”

What is the
Emptiness of this,
Simply that,

Is where we use
The expression
“Emptiness beyond
All extremes.”


[3821]
GZHI GANG LA MTHAR ‘DZIN DU LTUNG BA’I RTAG CHAD KYI MTHA’ NI YOD PA MIN PA DE NI, ‘DIR MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PAR BRJOD DO,,

Here next let’s consider a situation where there is no case of falling into holding to an extreme: an extreme of either lasting forever or simply discontinuing.  This then was described as “going beyond all extremes.”


[3822]
MTHA’ BRAL DE NI MTHA’ BRAL DE’I RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHO NAS STONG PA NYID DE NI, MTHA’ LAS ‘DAS PA STONG PA NYID DU BSNYAD DO,,

And what we call “free of extremes” refers to the emptiness of this freedom from extremes; the fact that it cannot be “simply that”—referring to existing through some nature of its own.  We then use the expression here of “emptiness beyond all extremes.”


[3823]
‘DI NI TING ‘DZIN RGYAL PO LAS, YOD MED DANG GTZANG MI GTZANG GI MTHA’ GNYIS SPANGS NAS, DBUS LA’ANG GNAS PAR MI BYED DO, ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR MTHA’ SPANGS PA’I DBUS BDEN NAM SNYAM PA’I BDEN ‘DZIN BZLOG PA’I PHYIR DU GSUNGS PA STE,

All this recalls for example the King of Concentration, where it says that we should give up pairs of extremes such as existing or not existing; or else being clean or not being clean; but that neither should we then stay somewhere in the middle between these extremes.  This was spoken to help us stop our habit of wondering whether or not the view in the middle might exist in truth, once we have eliminated the two extremes in each case.


[3824]
DPER NA SEMS TZAM PAS RANG GI LUGS KYI RTAG CHAD SOGS KYI MTHA’ DANG BRAL BA’I DBUS SEMS BDEN GRUB TU ‘DOD PA LTA BU’O,,

This is similar for example to the case with the Mind Only school, where they hold as a middle view that the mind must exist in truth, once they have eliminated the two extremes of the mind either lasting forever or simply discontinuing.



10) The emptiness of no beginning or end


	[3825]
[VI.194]
Ādir avaram anto’graṃ tad abhāvena kathyate,
Saṃsāro’navarāgro hi gatyāgati viyogataḥ.

,THOG MA DANG PO THA MA MTHA’,
,DE DAG MED PAS ‘KHOR BA NI,
,THOG MA THA MA MED PAR BRJOD,
,’GRO ‘ONG BRAL PHYIR RMI [214a] LAM LTA’I,

	The cycle of suffering
	Was described as having
	
	No first beginning
	And no final end.

	This is because it has
	No beginning limit,
	Nor an ending limit.

	Coming and going
	Are devoid;
	As such, our existence
	Is similar to a dream [f. 214a].


[VI.195]
Svapnābhasya bhavasyāsya yā tenaiva viyuktatā,
Śūnyatānavarāgreti saiṣā śāstre nirucyate.

,SRID ‘DI DE YIS DBEN NYID GANG,
,DE NI THOG MA DANG THA MA,
,MED PA STONG PA NYID DO ZHES,
,BSTAN BCOS LAS NI NGES PAR BSNYAD,

	The fact that
	This is devoid
	
	Was referred to in
	The classical commentaries

	With the description,
	“Emptiness where there
	Is no beginning,
	And no end.”


[3826]
‘DI YAN CHAD DU MA BYUNG LA ‘DI NAS BYUNG ZHES PA’I THOG MA STE DANG PO DANG, ‘DI PHYIN CHAD DU MI ‘BYUNG ZHES PA’I THA MA’I MTHA’ DE DAG MED PAS ‘KHOR BA NI THOG MA DANG, THA MA MED PAR BRJOD DO,,

The cycle of suffering was described as having no first beginning, and as having no final end.  This is because it has no beginning limit in the sense of us being able to say, “Up to here, it didn’t happen; and then from this point on, it did.”  Nor does it have an ending limit, in the sense of us being able to say, “From this point on, it stopped occurring.”


[3827]
‘GRO ‘ONG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG BRAL BA’I PHYIR RMI LAM LTA BU’I SRID PA ‘DI, SRID PA DE YI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAS DBEN PA NYID GANG YIN PA DE NI, THOG MA DANG THA MA MED PA’I STONG PA NYID DO ZHES BSTAN BCOS CHEN PO RGYAL BA’I YUM LAS NI NGES PAR BSNYAD DO,,

Coming and going are devoid of existing through any nature of their own; as such, our existence is similar to a dream.  And the fact that this existence is perfectly devoid of existing through any nature of its own was referred to in the “great classical commentaries”—here referring to the sutras of the Mother of the Victors—with the description, “emptiness where there is no beginning, and no end.”
